I found the first hour incredibly boring and uninteresting. It gets a lot better after the prologue. The turn based "combat" is probably the biggest point of contention in the whole game; you can never be certain which moves will work on each enemy and I found it a little unsatisfying just using each "attack" one by one. However, the little box mini-game mechanic was a breathe of fresh air. It was varied and often challenging. A+ there.
The writing... Some of it is good, but some of it is absolutely cringe-inducing. "Meme language", I guess you could call it, is used a great deal. "Doggo" and "hOI!!!!!! i'm tEMMIE!!" are some examples. Pop-up text occurs too often and intrudes on your experience. Also, two characters have the nervous, frigid crush trope applied. The first character is rather dim-witted and it comes off funny. But the second character, Dr Alphys comes off as a basement-dwelling degenerate and half of her lines consist of ellipses and stuttering. And this pops up CONSTANTLY towards the end of the game. ♥♥♥♥ me, I was ready to smash my head into my keyboard. But like I said, some writing is good. Sans, Papyrus and Mettaton are highlights.
Decent story. Fantastic music, best part of the game.

Pretty awesome game overall. Think Farcry as far as the base/area control and build up goes. You enter an area, get a "base" of sorts, and then you take over said area via missions and DESTRUCTION in order to upgrade Max and his car and the base. It's pretty much ALL free-roam all the time, which is great. They definitely nailed the fights; wether on foot or rolling around in your V8 thunder rod, the fights always feel epic and dangerous and deadly. Very cool.
I WILL note a couple of downsodes I've noticed though: There are some rather frustrating glitches/ bugs here and there (car being spawned in mid-air and falling to destruction, random freezes, that sort of thing) and on first playing the controls feel a little clunky and awkward, both on keyboard AND controller. I elected to stick with keyboard and just switch some buttons around and it's much improved.
Long story short, it's really fun, it looks pretty darn good, definitely EPIC, feels like a little more time on polish/optimization would have been good.
Really cant go wrong for $10, well worth it, not much more to say, if you like the look of it buy it, its ♥♥♥♥in $10 why not?

Love this game!  Big fan of the first two films and the 4th wasn't bad either. The game brings out the action of the movies. You're Max and everyone is relying on you weather you want them to or not. Ya gotta fight for everything and the rewards are small just to get you by. The landscap is vast and in ruin. Open world, ya can drive anywhere. There is a big emphasis on driving. Car chases. Sometimes you are the pursuer, sometime the pursuee. You can slow down the car chases by aiming the harpoon attached to the car while ya rotate the camera and soak in all that action. Graphics are great. They got the dust down. Feels like it is in your teeth. Nothing cooler than being on a clifftop looking through binoculars at enemy vehicles driving down the road as you watch them. There are sand storms that will kill ya making you panic to find shelter. Fighting mechanics are good-great and it really feels like you are crackin some skulls when 12 of them attack you at once. Want to take out the shotgun between punches? Go ahead and send that dude flying. Pick up a bat and really make em hurt. The game is fair. No where did I feel like I was being cheated or something was out of place.. Bosses are beatable and fair. It is a long game to get through everything. The only gripe I have is Max cannot kneel. He always stands. There are tons of photo moments of Max staring out into the wastland, they shoulda let him kneel. I recommend this game. 9/10

Boss Monster is a great game. I love playing it in person with my friends, and I was soooo happy when I realized that it was on steam. Even happier when I bought the game, along with all the expantions, for only 8$. That being said I think I got the bang for my buck. Within the first day I got the game I accumulated more than 5 hours. I dont know where that time went. Be warned though. Do NOT get this game unless you are getting it with friends. The game is no fun when you are playing just against AI. There is a worldwide mode, but I am not sure if it doesn't work, or not enough people play it. There are also a lot of bugs with the rooms and spells. Some of them say they will do something, but the effects don't work. Also, the abilities for some rooms take too long and can waste your entire turn. The game is just out of early access too, so hopefully bugs will soon be fixed. Personally, I would recommend buying the actually card game, because you don't have to worry about any bugs, and you can play at a pace you want to play at. I will recommend this game, but only to people who will have friends to play with, and are willing to deal with a few bugs.

Overall the game is pretty awesome, but it could use some polish.
PROS:
Nice variety of skills and perks available.
Great variety of factions and areas of control.
Good selection of ships.
Can capture enemy ships.
Like the blueprints idea.
Like the compare weapons and ships.
CONS:
Traveling over 10 units takes a couple minutes.
There are four equipment slots to use and only about four that I found were actually useful, ie. shield recharge, strengthen attack, scavenger bots, hull repairs.  Even then, I rarely ever use them.
Crew members do not have special abilities, but rather only bonuses.  A single slot for a special crew member.  Assuming only one special member exists in the game and is almost impossible to gain because the blueprint takes 20.
Blueprints are super difficult to find, but very rewarding IF you ever complete them before becoming near god strength already.  I completed one for a nice fighter hangar jet, but the rest remain far out of reach while I am practically invincible with all the best enhancements and warship.
The only truly useful weapons in the game are rail guns and maybe missiles.  I say maybe missiles because they are only really useful if the shields are already down and rail guns can usually take care of it anyway.  Lasers are useless.  Plasma is too slow to be useful except for mining.
Level 70 bounties are easy kills for a level 50 that has a good battleship with maximum upgrades.  I think I may have beaten one with the next class down at a lower level too because you can stay behind them and they cannot fire back.
Travelling outside the known universe area leads to infinite enemies and loss of whereabouts on the map.  Travelling too close to the sun does the same thing except enemies will start to randomly die from heat damage.
Cannot see what is on a captured ship until it is transferred to the garage and crew is transferred as well.  Crew losses will occur if the captured ship has less.
There are three kinds of heavy weapons, but I failed to see any real difference in shockwave damage.
Exploding ships nearby do no damage.
Has lag and slowdowns most of the time.
SUGGESTIONS:
Make traveling without gates a little faster when in full engine mode.
Make some artifacts that last indefinitely / bonuses or useables that fit in equipment slots.
Change the decimal enhancement descriptions, eg. 0.5, with percentage values, eg. 50%.
Please fix weapon range.  Bonuses are not being counted.
Add a barrier on the edge of the map to prevent getting lost in the void.
Give a warning for pending heat damage when getting close to stars.
Show radiation areas on the map.
Show map sections that are partially visible on the edges of the map.
Allow transfer of weapons and cargo from ships in the garage without transferring crew.
Make plasma weapons hurt shields more, but damage hull less.
Make lasers damage both shields and hull with shield punchthrough for damaging systems.
Make railguns work best on hull, and less on shields.
Do a similar rock paper scissors with heavy weapons.
Fix the pathfinding.
Improve AI for wanted bounties.
It's Okay.

GREAT STORY! It does well in dealing with topics such as PTSD and how war affects the soldiers. It does pretty well in showing that war might not always be a good vs. bad affair - there may also be a gray area within actions are made that while necessary are also detestable.
Cover system is great BUT there are times when I thought I was in a perfect spot to hide behind cover but the game doesn't recognize it and forces you to stand in open fire like an idiot trying to find the sweet spot by mashing spacebar to let you hide behind cover. The AI may also make stupid decisions such as rushing into the middle of a gunfight and getting incapacitated, but I didn't find this as bothersome as the cover system.
Still a great game despite its faults - as the narrative is worthy of being translated into film.

Figured I'd give this a thumbs up while I'm taking a break. The release sucked, but that doesn't reflect the quality of the game in this case, which is amazing.
It's literally Banjo-Kazooie reskined with a much larger world and set of sub worlds. You even have the option of expanding your subworlds for more junk to do and things to see. The game worlds themselves are beautiful, I didn't however expect this to be more taxing on my pc at max than Skyrim on ultra with 50+ mods and a shader. You have been warned.
I like the addition of tonics, which adds to your overall gameplay (make certain moves cost less, hold your breath for longer, etc.). The way you unlock your move sets and the amount of them is awesome too.
Nothing is aggravating, and the platforming is fluid. Everything I try to do, I do. That may sound simple, but you don't take it for granted when you've played shoddy platformers with buggy and/or unresponsive controls. As everyone else has said who's jumped into this game, if you liked Banjo-Kazooie, you'll love this

I'll start with the biggest strength: There is no better series/game for a free flowing lightsaber/force power action game, past or present. Battlefront and Force Unleashed were the closest in the Star Wars universe and others have tried in other universes with similar concepts but none of them touch the feel of this game in my opinion. I have played them all extensively and I still come back to this one when I really want to swing a saber and throw some fools off a ledge with Grip or Lightning. The movement and Force Powers all feel just right and the varied move sets based on saber stances/styles are endlessly adaptable to make for a unique fight every time - or you can find one trick you love and use it till your fingers grow arthritic.
That brings me to the second strongest aspects: It was one of the first games to successfully implement environment running once you level up a bit (aka Jedi parkour). You can hop around, wall run, and just generally be a badass both in and out of fights. The missions are all in unique locations that capture the feel of the universe and provide unique experiences. The graphics and physics have held up well all things considered - at the time they were incredible. That isn't to say there aren't flaws, but nothing game breaking that I have found and generally lots of fun.
The biggest weakness: The story line is a bit predictable but I honestly don't care one tiny bit. The general idea and delivery is good enough for me. If you are expecting something that will cause you to do some serious soul searching, this is probably not going to be the place to find it, but there are two endings for a bit of variety.
Overall I would strongly recommend this game because it delivers on what it tries to deliver on - great gameplay in a fast paced lightsaber/force using environment with a million different ways to approach any fight.
When does one not enjoy the simple pleasure gained from cutting stormtroopers, sith, and even jedi into pieces?

I really wanted to like this game.  It evolves many of the best ideas from EVE Online and favorite old space strategy games, but they're not fully developed or well executed here.
PROS:  Graphics are very nice and performance was good.
CONS:  The storyline campaign is so cartoonish, hackneyed, and poorly acted that it became increasingly annoying for me.  The economy felt like an afterthought - has anyone actually progressed in this game through mining, trading, or anything other than boarding and capturing gunships?  Even that is buffoonishly implemented because your ship's stats and your pilot's skills have very limited impact on boarding success compared to the simple math of winning by carrying a superior number of the essentially unlimited, no-cost "trooopers."
This game is may be a good choice, though, for pre-teens as an introduction to the genre.

Firstly, understand that although my review will say I've only logged 9 hours on this game, it's more like 20 because I played a lot in offline mode.
This game is beautiful, both visually and with the music. But other than some eye candy and a few atmospheric soundtracks it doesn't feel like it has anything else going for it. Saving up for better ships is a slow grind, and combat becomes repetitive quickly. Once you get the better ships all you really accomplish is the ability to throw some more bullets/lasers at people at some different angles, but gameplay never fundamentally changes. Stronger enemies are just like the easier ones only they have more health and higher damage output, but you fight them all fundamentally the same way. The enemy AI is terrible; they have a self-preservation instinct akin to plastic ducks in a carnival shooting gallery. Killing enemies ranges from extremely easy to just downright tedious, but never feels challenging.
The universe is clutterred with interesting stuff (real space doesn't have objects this close to each other) so there's no shortage of places to explore, but there's no real incentive to explore anything. One region might just be another solar system but with a blue nebula instead of a red one and the asteroids are made of some different resource.
I'll give this game an alright/10. It's fun when you first pick it up, but playing for long periods will make the game stale quickly. I'm at a point where I want to play this game, but I just can't stomach flying around in space shooting at the same pirate ships to travel to some samey looking region- not for more than maybe 5 minutes at a time. I feel like there's nothing to do in this big universe the game presents.
Hopefully the mod community will be able to salvage the game so I can feel like I got my money's worth.

Fans of the Boss Monster card game will no doubt find themselves attracted to a video game port, especially for such a bargain price. However, Boss Monster the video game is hardly a substitute for the real thing. Marred by a clunky UI that has quite a large learning curve to master and quite a few instances of cards not even doing what they are supposed to, it's safe to say that you will get what you pay for on this one.
In addition, the several expansions that have been released for the card game are completely missing from this game, as is any opportunity to make use of the customizable rules detailed in those expansions. Allowing for the "Infinite Lives" game mode or deeper mechanics like item cards or multi-treasure seeking heroes would go a long way towards making the game feel like what Boss Monster the card game has become in 2016, but sadly none of that appears to be even on its way.
Check back in on this one every now and then to see if the creators have decided to fix up some of the bugs or add in some of the newer content from the game if you really have an interest in this side of Boss Monster, but if not, skip this game, and go play with the amazing card version instead.

I saw this game out in EA after I first tried tabletop version 5 months ago and patiently waited for it to leave the workshop before buying it. Last week, it came out and I bought the game and all DLCs on sale for the price of a Subway meal. My fears of massive bugginess from what other reviews stated were for nought; I run a Windows 7 Dell Laptop and, after many games (2, 3 and 4 player) I have yet to experience ANY major bugs. The game runs VERY smoothly for me, espcially with the moving parts of timer bars, all the card rules, AI, randomization, etc.
The game is great if you want to waste some time and love the premise of the game. It's equal parts luck and strategy. I haven't tried Multiplayer partly due to that no one is on it, but hopefully that will change in time. Human opponents would be way more fun than AI. The card base, even with 3 DLCs is a bit limited, but the RL game is coming out with new material even now - patience is a virtue just as much as when this game spent a heinously long time in EA.
TL,DR:
What I'd like to see in it: more unlockable features through winning X number of games; a full rulebook (outside of the Tutorial); more card options (likely in future); more warm bodies in Multiplayer mode!
What I do see in it: smooth, bug-free gameplay; tounge-in-cheek humor; well-crafted soundtrack; a faithful and user-friendly adaptation of the tabletop version

Like others have said, this is an incredible story that only gets better as you move through it. The characters grow and you're right there with them. The city itself is also ridiculously beautiful. You even get caught in dust storms at times, which is pretty cool.

It's really unfortunate that the game didn't do so well financially and the developers said they wouldn't make another like it for a while. The Line is a real gem. With very standard gameplay, this game excells in a compelling and conflicting story.
Spec Ops: The Line is a game for a certain taste.
SO:TL is a modern military third-person-shooter. It runs smoothly on my rig, and graphically, the game looks decent to stunning in some areas. The gameplay consists of very linear traversion of diverse environments in a war-ridden, half-destroyed dubai of luxurious architecture and skyscrapers. Often times, the leveldesign relies on simple cover-to-cover movement which unfortunately, especially on higher difficulties, feels more like camp-until-clear engagements, while adding in the componentof vertical gameplay and turret-sections. To be honest, it feels a lot like a cardboard-cutout of MM-shooters like CoD or Battlefields campaign gameplaywise.
But if you feel like turning away from the game already from that, think again as the story of the game throws you in a sea of confusion and inner conflict. As the story progresses and the protagonists role becomes more and more influential, the game gebins to psych the player out of his skin, creating a surreal experience at times. The game comes in rough not to glorify the violence and gore on your account, and will make you feel guilty for everything you do like no game i've ever played before.
Although I considered quitting halfway through due to the bland gameplay, the ending was absolutely worth all struggle. The story told in this game is a reason to grab it anytime. I would recommend it anytime.

When you expand a world it gives you long shots of the areas and zooms the camera through the path, and it just takes too much time. There's not enough "show" and too much "tell" for my tastes, and I'd rather just jump to exploring the place instead of being taken on a tour first.
There's also a narrative weirdness, like where Capital B starts talking on the intercom in the game as if his relationship with the main characters had already been established, but they've never interacted before. Of course, the audience has been introduced to him, but not the main characters, so it just seems weird for him to do that. There's also other little things, like when you first collect butterflies, a butterfly character pops up and describes themselves as delicious. Oxygen Not Included is fun, silly + quirky - all the things I've come to expect from the devs at Klei, but for those who enjoy getting a little technical, this is where the game really shines.
Every new asteriod is the chance to design
...only to realize it gets you just so far before it all, like the many that came before it, goes to sh**!! Then it's back to the drawing board and a fresh new rock to call home and record cycles to be break.
This gets addictive pretty quick, most buildings can be fine tuned till perfection and there are several overlays and reports giving you plenty of information to sink your teeth into.
ONIs game mechanics are simple enough to get you started, but as your understanding progresses you can get fairly inventive with your problem solving. Before you know it you'll find yourself designing your own complex setups, I'm even seeing people design 'hydrogen bubblers' as a means to clean polluted gas into liquid oxygen. o.O
ONI is shaping up to be an addictive and challening management sim and I'm sure that as development continues (new content is being rolled out every 6 wks atm), Klei will keep us on our toes and further add to the depth of this game.
If you enjoy a challenge and nutting things out this is the game for you!

Looks like a simple spacecolony game where you keep your dupes happy and try to survive.
Mainly you have to manage food, gas, temperature, stress and recently added health.
You don't control any of the dupes directly, but assign different tasks to them and can assign priorities, but if they aren't happy they may defy your orders.
A few pros and cons
Pros:
+ Good price (for Early Access).
+ Lots of content and continuously adding more.
+ They have plan and roadmap for future update.
+ Regular updates (4 to 6 weeks) bug & balancing patch in between.
+ Very active Developers & Community
+ Can be played casually, hardcore or tryhard mode.
+ Visually pleasing, love the cartoony feel to it
+ Addictive
Cons:
- Too addivtive??!
- Currently no "point" to the game (but Developers will address this further down), that said still loads of fun.
- May get frustrated when your dupes die off as you get attached to them :P
Definitely recommend this game.
Get it now before the price goes up (once early access is over)

It's a good game, but not as good as people make it out to be.
The story is funny, and overall well-paced. The game does have a relativly diverse morality system that rewards each choice diffrently. All though the story is interesting with fourth wall breaks and funny characters. However I found most of the charcters really shallow, and lacking of any meaningful charcter development. There are some execptions here and there but overall it's pretty cliche. You have the goof, nerd, cool kid, Strong silent type, Diva, Emo, Mother and Evil villian. They lack barley any depth beyond there sterotypes, some however do have more complex motivations and won't spoil who or what they are. However the humor almost always lands, with negligable flops every so often.
And the soundtrack is amazing, I recomend buying it or listing to it on spotify. It carries a basic melody through the entire score. With every song adding new elemnts, and there there is a large portion of the soundtrack that drops the melody completly.
Gameplay is simple and fun. Traversing the world is easy and seemless, offering funny side NPC's shops and secrets. There are also a good amount of puzzles  in the world none of which are very hard. Most puzzles can be solved in less then 5 mins and keeps the flow of the story running well. However backtracking in Undertale is a pain, with no fast travel or even the lack of a sprint key the game adds about an 1 1/2 of just walking. There are very few time you actually will need to go back to past parts of the world though, but when you do it sticks out like a sore thumb.
Battling is by far the most fun part of the game. It's turn based like a retro-rpg but with a twist. On your turn you can of course attack, which bring up a timed event. The closer to the middle of the bar the more damage you do to the enemy. You can you use an item, Talk to the enemy and try to resolve the situation peacfully. And finally Flee and mercy. Whne the enemy attacks the game turns into a bullet hell lite. Each enemy offreing diffrent attacks and powers, and mastering the system can let you go through the turn with out taking any damage.
I finished undertale in about 20 hours the first time I played it, this is because i was terrible with the bullet hell parts. On my second playthrough I beat it in around 5 hrs. So I wouldn't ecpect much more or less playtime out of undertale. (My Hrs played is so high because i left my PC for weekend.)
Overall is Undertale a masterpeice no, Is it bad no way. Undertale is a good game with it's own unique charm. 7.5/10 is a good place to put it. Maybe a bit higher not by too much. There are some bigger problems that I didn't really mention here and that is why I'm leaving it at 7.5. Once you play and you really should play it you wll know what I mean.

It took nearly 20 hours to finally come to a conclusion on this game.
Despite all efforts made to make the combat complex - energy management, 4 different active abilities (with a kinda silly feeling levelups with them),  and up to 4 consumable items (of a selection of around a dozen) useful for combat - it just isn't all that fun. I believe the biggest culprit is turrets. While it is possible to partially blindside a less maneuverable ship than yours in 1v1, ultimately maneuvering and dodging in combat is best done by spinning around in circles. When you're spinning around in circles, you can't effectively target and attack targets manually, and so you rely on fire-at-will auto targetting to do that job for you. This is boring.
The economy is workable, but not that interesting - different stations have a set low-mid-high value for all of the commodities. Buy and sell appropriately.
The storyline is workable. The Gemini universe is interesting, and is worth reading about if you're into that sort of thing. The storyline does an almost adequate job of immersing you in that universe. The voice acting/writing is awwwwwwful.
The good: All around, this is a workable game that will scratch your spacefaring itch, though will likely not leave you satisfied. The graphics are beautiful, each region of space is very well stylized in the coloring, asteroids, and various anomalies. Plenty of the starbases and ships have pretty unique detailed models. Music and sound are good, although the short soundtrack for the music is a mild disappointment there.

Starpoint Gemini 2 is a bit shallow and a bit pricey for what it offers, but it is still enjoyable. Overall the story was okay enough to keep me going, and the combat was fun enough to make my stay in Gemini enjoyable. If you are itching for a space sim that is pretty easy to get into and doesn't require a large time commitment to win (around 24 in-game hours for me), this will scratch that itch pretty well. Otherwise, you may want to think carefully on buying this game unless it's on sale.
However, the developers appear to be actively working on improvements to the game as time goes on. Some concerns raised in this article may be addressed as time goes on. Keep an eye on the updates page if you're interested in this product!
----------
Visuals are nice, music is nice, starship aesthetics are good too, and the combat is solid. The universe feels big, and provides a pretty immersive experience of traveling through space. Said universe is also populated by various starships as well, usually around space stations and various other miscellaneous space structures. There are many different factions that like to use certain types of ships and lay claim to different areas of space, and you can easily see heated space battles taking place at faction borders. The HUD takes a little getting used to, but is pretty nice once you learn it.
The game itself is a bit grindy as it uses RPG levelling mechanics to determine what ship you can pilot, but I personally didn't mind it that much since the combat was pretty fun.
The story is okay. The Voice Acting for the story dialogue ranges from terrible to okay.
Side-story missions boil down to "repair structure there for $$$ and XP" or "kill enemies here for $$$ and XP" or "ferry person over there for $$$ and XP" with little fanfare. After you finish the main story, all you can do are the missions described earlier.
During the main story, certain factions and places will be purportedly destroyed or crippled, but what this actually means is that you will just pretend that the story happened while in practice the universe remains largely intact and unchanged.
Certain mechanics are a bit shallow (i.e. hiring crew = looking up which dude/gal has which bonuses, click hire button). Also, while you *can* be a merchant or asteroid miner in this game, it seems to be much eaiser just to capture enemy ships and tow them back to a planet/station where you can sell them.
Character progression is RPG-like, yet character skills/perks can pretty much be ignored. Your character's power is MUCH more dependent on what type of ship you are piloting and how well it is outfitted. The RPG mechanics are more akin to a gating system, where your level determines the type of ship you can pilot.
For me, the entire game was a bit grindy. This was how it went down: capture/sell ships until I can afford the next weight class of ship, do missions (sometimes main storyline) so I can meet the level requirement of said ship. Repeat until I have achieved highest class of ship.
------

The "Escape Velocity" series of games (plot-heavy 2D shooter space-sim) implemented this rather well; there were multiple plotlines for each main faction AND there were also a lot of side plotlines too.
Examples of side-plots: testing prototype weapons for a starship arms company, or ferrying vacationing CEOs to a jungle planet for big game hunting, or helping a rockstar go on tour throughout the galaxy only to discover that he's a robot! Or picking up a random stranger and ferrying him to a planet only to discover that he's a leader of a small sect of colonists who are trying to resist pirate incursions, and he implores you to help them with their plight since the Powers That Be in the universe are far too busy (or corrupt) to deal with the pirates.
I didn't just do these missions for cash, but to see the story unfolded; to see how these characters reacted to these sometimes tragic events in their lives, and how they would deal with it.
I think it's good to have a big Main Storyline as the main attraction, but there's plenty of room in Gemini for smaller guys with fascinating struggles and dramas in their own lives that an aspiring starship captain can be a part of.
You don't need to have dialogue trees for every one. But it'd be nice to be able to beg for mercy from a pirate and buy him off with credits, or just say hi to random ships and planets. In this vein, they'd also have a message for when you greet them, with each faction having a different way of talking to you. Perhaps even with a random pool of different types of responses from each faction that vary in tone depending on your standing with them? This is a bit small, but I think it would help with game immersion.

Though it might seem like a huge hassle to write up descriptions for every space station/planet/starship, you can build an EXTREMELY immersive narrative with these and make the game feel alive. Again, the "Escape Velocity" game series (mostly Escape Velocity Override and Escape Velocity Nova) used flavor texts/descriptions to great effect.
Why is this station in the middle of nowhere and surrounded by hostile space? Are they revolutionaries or sympathizers with another faction, or are they just badasses? Why is this Frigate cheaper than this other one? Oh, the company that manufactures this one wanted to push out a model to get an edge over their hated rival company who was taking their sweet time with their own model. Hey, this Corvette saved an entire company from the brink of bankruptcy! This Carrier design looks like a UFO because of a revolutionary new frame that allows for rapid fighter launching while providing overlapping fields of fire from all of its turret batteries? Cool. This Dreadnought looks like a eldritch abomination because their designers desperately welded a lot of spare parts together and accidentally created a ship that could challenge all previous starship design conventions? Neat!
Planets and some space stations presently have short descriptions with a little flavor text. But it doesn't help that these blurbs are only accessible via starmap. When a player is on the starmap, their first instinct is not to click "info" and read; they want to get somewhere quick. I think it would have been better if you saw the write-up in an unobtrusive static text box on the bottom of the screen. This provides incentive for an exploration-oriented player to land/dock on every planet/station that they find so they can see the little blurb there. These descriptions can really flesh out the factions and gives you an idea of why they exist and how they conduct themselves (i.e. how they treat citizens, local planetary economic problems, policy problems, military actions, natural disasters, etc.).
Overall, more flavor text would be nice so that the universe that the player travels in would feel more alive.
Also, it would be nice to have an in-game chart of which ranks correspond to player level.

Starpoint Gemini 2 is a great space rpg.
usually a statement like that needs clarification, so here we go.
this game is basically if you took the most complicated parts out of games like x, opened up the game world like evochron mercenary and throw in a control system not unlike eve online. what im getting at is that its not as complicated to play as the aforementioned games but leaves the best parts of each and marries them into a system thats fresh and familiar.
one of the things that irritated me about the x series and evochron for that matter is that missions had to be acquired at a station. my question has always been, why? no long range communications in either universe? in SPG2 that is a thing of the past, when you enter an area, you will be notified when missions are available and you can accept missions directly from the starmap
which brings me to the next point. the starmap is one contigious area, like in evochron, there are no load screeens and while the actual area is smaller than evochron, its a lot more detailed visually. so yes its probably not 100% true to life because there are very few areas that just look like a black void in space, but the visuals are well done and give you more to look at than just black with white dots everywhere.
controls are reminicent of eve online though i havent played it in years, it reminds me of that. not necessarily a terrible thing, but if you are looking to find yourself in the cockpit of the ship, these ships dont feature cockpits. if anything even the smallest class available would have a bridge. so in comparison to the ships in X or EM, youre piloting a capital ship right off the bat. in fact to give some comparison, the M5 through M3 classes of ships in X are basically bought as commodities to place in the hangar of carriers. you wont be flying anything that small and if you were, youd have reason to be very very afraid. it would seem that the gemini system doesnt build much of anything in small scale :)
As of this writing there are a few technical issues that arent game breaking but considering the devlopment team is very active and even communicates with the players regularly i feel that this game will evolve into something even better. if you like rpgs and space games, this will be right up your alley. Graphics are good, action is nice, the gameplay smooth and mostly bug free.  In many ways this game does things exactly right.  So why the thumbs down?
Because it does one thing wrong and that one thing is enough to drag the rest down with it: It tries to use MMO logic in a single player game.  Which is to say that the grind is the whole of the content.  Do this mission to get credits to get a bigger ship with bigger guns so that you can do a mission with a bigger enemy to get more credits to get an even bigger ship etc etc ad hoc infinitum.  Once you hit max level and get the best ship there really isn't anything left to do except mindlessly blow things up at random.  It gets old really, really quick.
Yes there is a story option but the missions in that story are hardly any different than the randomly generated ones from freeroam.  They just add voiceovers to some rather poorly written dialog.
Still, the price is cheap and they game is entirely without it's virtues.  It just doesn't have anything to really hold a person's attention for very long.

As a fan of the Boss Monster Tabletop Game, I was looking forward to this digital version for some time. This version however suffers greatly in the UI design. It feels like the original designers, while able to make a great tabletop game, didn't know enough about the process and or hired the wrong Devs for the job. I cannot imagine any Devs worth their salt, making the counter intuitive design choices I see being made here.
Unless a player has previously mastered the tabletop version and all of its timing, memorized each of its cards including the expansion cards, and has experience playing a wide variety of other card games with strenuous timing systems, there is a good chance that a new player will be utterly lost here. I see even veterans of the Boss Monster tabletop game struggle to get their cards effects to work with this UI.
This UI provides no sense of timing, nor targeting of any kind. This game also provides no explanation of events, obvious or otherwise. Players simply watch as things happen with no explanation as to why. Such as when one of the opponent's triggers a card effect causing you to discard. There is no hint of this, you simply watch a card leap out of your hand for no obvious reason. You aren't even sure of which player caused it.
Some actions require you to drag and drop a card over a specific spot while others require you to click on to zoom in on a card, then click in a green box then "I guess" double click that green box, to make something happen. I honestly cannot tell how to make some cards work, even after playing numerous games over several hours.
Even an experienced player needs to see, or at least be told, what they are doing & why. Instead of just watching a card be discarded or their spell vanish as it was being played.
Instead the UI just provides a generic cue such as "choose 3 cards" or "choose 1 card". Not explaining that you are drawing or discarding those cards or something else entirely. This also happens with choose a player, choose a hero, choose a room, choose a spell. All blind cues with a short timer.
The multiplayer turn timer is also very short. This short multiplayer timer has no way to change or disable it in settings.
This game is not only unpolished in the most obvious way, but it also suffers from rampant bugs. Such as from the "counter spell" card which doesn't light up for use against all opponent spells as they are cast, but only the ones they specifically told it to. They have obviously missed a few here.
If not for this dreadful UI, Boss Monster should have, would have, & could have been a hit here on steam and on PC. Sadly, as it is here upon release, it will likely never be what it might have been. Honestly, I really enjoy Boss Monster the game, and as much as I would like to recommend this title here, I just can't.

I've always wanted to try the actual card/board game, but never got any chance. Now I've tried the electronic version, it's pretty okay. You set up line of rooms with attack power, treasures, and special effects. At each turns adventurers will come, and different adventurers will be attracted to different treasures, and they'll activate the room's effects one by one.
The only significant downside from this electronic version right now is the very obstinate UI and lack of proper tutorial/rulebook/tooltips/whatever that actually teach you the mechanics of the game. There's tutorial, but it's very limited. I learned the game from trial and error myself, but that's totally not how you're supposed to sell a game, don't you think?
Still fun game, and pretty cheap, so you could buy this in a discount to check if you'd like to buy the actual game for your group.

Intro: Boss Monster is a game that rekindled my interest in both card and board games. The video game however, is a big, cheap, disappointment.
Full Video Review With Insight On How The Game Actually Plays:
Below is entirely focused on the port:
Gameplay:
Boss Monster PC is ported from Ipad and it shows. Menus aren't designed for a mouse and keyboard, windowed mode barely works with their being a pseudo borderless that alt-tabs the game without minimizing but requires you alt-tab to get back in which makes it frustrating when you are on a timer. Windowed mode shrinks into a tiny box that you can't make bigger because the game features no resolution options. Controls are at times incredibly sloppy. Some buttons are incredibly close to the corner of the screen which will cause you to "alt-tab" out of the game at times when you click off-screen. Multiplayer is a joke with no one playing and even if you find one person you are given a timed window to get other players, you can't wait long, you can't get AI. Basically, every random game you play online will be 1v1. On the technical side, Bad AI and bugs aren't common but they do happen. Sometimes cards won't work and AI will do stupid things. The porting issue rears its ugly head as it screws with your controls. It can be very easy to make a mistake and you have very few moments in the game where you can correct those mistakes. The game also sells DLC because of course it does. Now I would be fine with this but with the multiplayer as dead as it is, it just hurts the game even more because you will be using these expansions against AI. Now the biggest nut-kicker is that Tools of a Hero-Kind is a pay-for expansion just like in the original card game. The original game had some early-on balancing issues where one player could be completely screwed by hero output and bad RNG. Tools of Hero-Kind helped fix it, they didn't decide to add this or any of the other DLC to make it feel like a complete experience.
Visuals:
Boy oh boy does this hurt me the most. Animations are incredibly static. While the cards are animated decently, almost everything else is lifeless. When heroes move between rooms in your dungeons it is just the same as how you move them between rooms in the actual card game. Heroes pop out of their cards only to slide across each room without move any body parts, boss have no idle animations at all. They just stand their in an incredibly disappointing manner. While there are actual backgrounds that are what you expect, there are no animations or anything interesting happening in them. Static, boring, uninspired, environments. The only thing they got right is the UI, it's incredibly-well layed out with a decent tutorial to back it up. Except they manage to screw that up and not include a counter or a deck or any indication of how many heroes are left in each deck. I thought the whole point of a video game adaption was to bring a card game to life. It certainly isn't going used for playing with others online because as I mentioned before, online is dead.
Sound:
Sound is the closest thing I can consider good about the game but they still don't cross mediocre. There is one music track in this game, it's good but there's just one. Why not have some dynamic music where when it's your turn but you are low on health but about to win the game with no spell cards to protect you from a player attack that could absolutely wreck you. Where's that tension I would get when playing with friends? That music would have at least accounted for the slow pacing in the adventure phase. Otherwise audio is decent with sound effects being nice to the ears but they do re-use a lot of them.
Conclusion:
I am disappointed. This is an incredibly low-effort adapation and port of a great game. If you have friends and you really want to play Boss Monster without meeting at someone's house, this isn't a horrible way to do it. For everyone else, just save up for a copy of the base game. You will get more enjoyment and more value out of it. Until they can fix all these issues most would steer clear of this port.

I didn't exactly have high hopes for this game. I was just expecting a solid shooter with a decent plot. However, that is not even what is offered. What is offered is a lame shooter that takes no brains to play and 5 hours to beat.
The game prides itself on delivering an "emotional" military narrative, but all it really does is force story down your throat. I did not feel anything for any characters in this game. The main characters were boring, and the main villain (Actually, I still have no idea who the main villain was, because there are a few notable anti-heroes) is just a cliche "dude" with nothing interesting about him at all. You fight a few different factions of enemies, and after the entire game, I still do not know who the actual "bad guys" are. Apparently, there were a few chances for me to make a choice that would affect the story. Unfortunately, the game does a terrible job of letting you clearly see what your options are, so most of the time I didn't even know I could make a choice. I would end up doing something that the game considered horrible, and then it would attempt to make me feel bad about it. You are forced into bad actions throughout the game, and then spat on for doing so. I got bored of the plot within the first half of the game, and only pushed on because I thought maybe it would redeem itself at some point. The ending was definetly interesting, but all it did was open up even more questions about the plot, and I still have no idea what actually happened during my entire playthrough. In an effort to keep spoilers to a minimum, it can be said that I made it to the end to find out that my actions meant nothing, because the entire plot meant nothing. What a waste.
As for the actual mechanics, it's a mediocre shooter in the boring urban desert environment of Dubai. You move from room to room shooting enemies, with an occasional cutscene. Every once in a while you can shoot a window, and sand buries your enemies (Wow, so innovative), and there are also a few lame turret segments. There are not that many guns to choose from, ammo is plentiful so you don't have to worry about conserving it, and there are the basic variations of enemy units (Melee, assault, heavy, elite) just like every other military shooter known to man. You can attempt to sneak through parts of the game and kill enemies, but it's not even worth trying. I think that the encounters are scripted, so that everything always ends up in a firefight.
Overall, this game is probably not worth your time. It did not offer me anything that I couldn't find in any other shooter. Avoid it.

Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.
Eat.

This game tried to cash in on the nostalgia of everyone who grew up playing Banjo-Kazooie, but it only manages to be a pale soulless immitation that just makes you want to go play the original instead of wasting your time here.
The game is overwhelmingly generic, with none of the characters being particularly remarkable. The dialogue is awkward and stilted and tries too hard to be funny. Banjo-Kazooie often made cringy jokes, but it also managed to be genuinely clever at times. Yooka-Laylee didn't manage to be funny even once in what I played.
The game is painful to control, essentially requiring a controller as keyboard and mouse support is terrible. All the in-game prompts use an N64 controller layout (nostalgia!) at the expense of making the game frustrating to figure out how to play. There is NO in-game explanation of what the buttons map to on a keyboard. Enjoy randomly pressing every key on your keyboard trying to figure it out, because they're not intuitive! There's also no way to rebind them.
The game is also a big fan of wasting your time. Dialogue is miserably slow, and there's no way to speed it up by holding down "A" like in Banjo-Kazooie. You can either sit and watch the minutes of your life quickly drift away as you watch the text slowly print on the screen, or you can skip it entirely. There are also painfully drawn out quiz sequences frequently throughout the entire game (think Grunty's quiz shows from the Banjo-Kazooie games). If you thought Grunty's were slow and tedious... these are 10x longer and all over the damn place.
Literally the only positive thing I can say about this game is that the music is pretty good. This game manages to be a "spiritual successor" to Banjo-Kazooie in form only. Just go replay the originals.

Why don't people review games anymore?
I keep reading about performance issues. If you cant get this game to work, try to find the problem and solve it before you hit the thumbs down button. If you try everything, wait for a patch or two, and still the game dosnt work. Then go ahead by all means hit it then.
I am using a Geforce GTX 970m (laptop version) to run this game, and it works perfectly. No issues whatsoever. Graphics are great, no screen tearing, its runs perfectly fine on a high setting.
The replayability is also very high, considering that I keep wanting to replay a level over and over to see every conversation, every possible way to kill your target, every object you can pick up, every weapon you can use, etc. It feels like I am playing a different game every time I start the Paris level. Seriously, if a new location is unlocked every month, I will be playing Hitman for countless hours.
You can level up and unlock new equipment and starting points/costumes, giving the player goals and incentives to keep on playing (kind of similar to Blood Money).  You have the ability to go after different targets than the ones in the mission (as used by Absolution). TONS of content. Also the realistic (and sometimes humorous) dialogs for the thousands of character models they can fit on the screen makes the experience feel real.
One gripe, I was frustrated with the controls during my first 20 minutes of playing, but thanks to key binding, and a tutorial I could run a few times, I got used to it.
I really had to dig deep to think of just one complaint, simply because I cannot think of anything I do not like. I am a huge Hitman fan (turning 30 next month and I have owned every single game) so trust me when I say, this plays proper homage to the series.
If you dont like something that can be fixed, please wait for a patch or check your computer before you leave a review. Seriously, hitting that thumbs down button really hurts the developers of games. It literally causes people not to buy when they could be missing out on something great. When the developers dont recieve profit, it harms further releases. There are other ways to report technical issues than screwing them over on steam.

I AM IN LOVE WITH THIS GAME!
That's not an overstatement. I've played so much since buying it a few days ago that I'm even starting to have extremely vivid dreams about it.
I have to admit that I almost didn't buy it at first because of all the recent negative reviews. I obviously didn't get to see the Germ update when it first released but apparently it increased the difficulty of the game about a hundred fold. The developers have since gotten the balance right and I've had zero problems getting into the game and managing the germy aspect. It's a nice little boost to complexity and actually makes for a really interesting gameplay mechanic. If germ management still isn't your cup of tea, there is also an option to turn on "immunity mode" when you start a new game and that essentially removes that aspect of the game and you don't even have to worry about it.
On to my actual review now.
The game is definitely difficult. You've got to really pay attention and think about what you're doing and the consequences of your actions. I've started about half a dozen different games now and lost all but one of them to one thing or another. There are just so many things to learn and keep track of that it can be a little overwhelming at first.
Your first few playthroughs are a learning experience. The game doesn't pull its punches just because you're new. I didn't realize that large bodies of water will erode thin walls due to pressure. Pro tip: don't put your dirty water next to your drinking fountain.
If you can laugh at your mistakes and learn from them, vowing to do better next time, you'll eventually be able to begin exploring the rest of the asteroid you're supposedly stranded on. The different minerals and ores that make up the rock surrounding you all have different properties. Some conduct heat better than others. Some have higher resitances. Some just look prettier and make your Duplicants happier when they're around things made out of it.
That level of complexity extends to everything in the game. Every piece of industry you build has some sort of byproduct that you're going to have to deal with. Converting H2O into breathable Oxygen still leaves behind all that Hydrogen and you've either got to pump it away or use it for something because your Duplicants can't breathe it.
But slowly you'll get the hang of things. You'll start to internalize the nuances of the game and you'll begin to feel more confident in your abilities. You'll reach 100+ cycles without losing anyone and laugh at the stupid mistakes you made in the beginning.
For now, the game is purely a sandbox experience so you make your own goals. There is no real end game or really much of a late game either. However the randomized nature of the maps makes it highly replayable and The developers have promised more of a late game experience as time goes on. Already I've been playing the Oil Update Preview branch and have seen a lot of really postive, promising expansions to the tech tree and what things are available to us.
Long story short, I think that if you enjoy the kind of harsh mistress that was Don't Starve then you'll likely be able to get some sort of masochistic enjoyment out of Oxygen Not Included.

Not having driven anything larger than a box truck, I can't say how accurate the simulation is, but I can say it's not realistic, simply because all the trucks feel the same. Upgrading the engine makes it accelerate faster, and there are a few different chassis configurations, but the feel is barely impacted.
If you come at this game expecting a "king of the road" experience, like the blurb claims, you'll be disappointed. Even if you did feel like king of the road, your subjects (the other cars) have no personality or purpose other than to serve as obstacles. The way to think of this game is as a sort of zen-like experience. Once you get on the highway, turn on your favourite radio or podcast, and begin to relax, you'll see why I've spent over 100 hours pretending to drive shipments of toys around fake Europe.

Like many other people that bought this, I was insecure as to how this type of platformer-item collecting game was going to play out in our modern times. Turns out it is very, very fun. If you want a simple answer, this is basically the same thing as Banjo-Kazooie. The exact same thing you could say, only with different loking characters, but that is not a bad thing, if you as me.
If you have never played Banjo-Kazooie (or Super Mario 64, which is the other game that comes to mind that resembles it, I think) this is a game in which you run around a big area collecting items that will help you progress to other areas. All the while you can use those collectibles to purchase new abilities that will help you traverse the different worlds, help other characters and collect even more items. You can also unlock tonics by completing challenges that give you different bonuses (you can probably unlock many other things, I just have not played for long enough to find all the bonuses/unlockables). There are mini-games to be played, witty dialogue to be read, and fun characters to be met.
All in all, If you are not willing to explore areas looking for as many collectibles as you can find so that you can progress, then you will problably dislike and get bored by this game very easily.

It's here! It's finally freaking here! I waited so long for this game to be released and I've been actively interested in this since it's pre-planning and concept stages. As of this review I've only played for about 2 hours so please take it with a grain of salt.
PROS
+Authentic gameplay that matches that of Nintendo 64 3D platformers like Donkey Kong 64 and Banjo Kazzoie.
+Excellent soundtrack, extremely reminescent of the music in the above games (composed by the same people as well!)
+Gorgeous graphics.
+Worlds are huge and players have the ability to unpgrade them as well.
+Wide variety of moves at the player's disposal once they've managed to unlock them.
+Tonics provide an interesting "modifier" for the player which they can experiement with.
+For the most part, dialogue and voice acting work is pretty good.
CONS
-Controls and platforming in general can be frustrating. I noticed I've overshot and undershot a lot of platforms simply because the controls weren't responding too well (that, and I partially suck at these games xD)
-Exploration can be a hassle, specially if you haven't unlocked an ability neccessary to explore a certain area.
-Buying moves instead of learning them naturally.
-Worlds are almost too huge and everything is spaced so far apart you often wander aimlessly trying to remember what things you've done and what areas you've explored.
-The higher the graphics setting, the worse the game runs if you don't have a high-end computer. You can only change the graphics from the main menu and not in-game.
With that being said, I'll have to reccomend this game for players who are craving a nostalgic experience created from Nintendo 64 3D platformers. This game IS Banjo-Threeie in a sense,but with different characters and collectibles.

There's no denying the fact that Banjo-Kazooie borrows from Mario 64 in more ways than one. Both games are extremely cute 3D platformers with a variation of the same story, a near identical control scheme and a strikingly similar theme of levels. Mario collects stars. Banjo and Kazooie collect jiggies. Mario has a butt-stomp. Banjo and Kazooie have a beak-stomp. Banjo doesn't just copy Mario 64 though, it expands upon the game. For example, Banjo's worlds are bigger, more detailed and are filled with interactive characters at every corner. The Banjo-Kazooie team work as exactly that; some objectives require the use of Kazooie's wings or ability to run up hills while others are perfectly suited for Banjo. The result is an addictive balance between the two characters.

I thoroughly enjoyed this game. The lightsaber combat is amazing, i'd even venture to say the best ever seen. First of all you can decide between 3 different lightsabers: Single saber, Dual sabers, and Double bladed saber. I recommend you try all of them and look at guides to see which one fits your playstyle. Second of all, The reason the lightsaber combat is so good is because its very accurate to how a Jedi would fight. You see, Jedi look slightly into the future when they fight , thats why they are so good at fighting. And how could you incorporate this into a players hand (who is probably not precognitive)? Auto-Block. The perfect solution. You block most things, but enemys can get through it by battering your defenses enough, or cleverly useing the environment and Force powers to get around it. Undertale is an indie, short and ugly game...But who cares about those things anyway ??
With this game, it's all about the experience it brings you, through the art direction, the soundtrack, the plot, etc.
It was warmly recommended to me by a friend, who made me listen to the OST (mind=blown) so I bought the game and I played it...What an amazing game !
The plot is simple : You play as a human who falls into the world of monsters, where you will have to make choices to survive and go home...
You will meet weird monsters, joker monsters, friendly monsters and so on, and so on...
I loved ALL the characters of this game ! Sure, some are annoying but they all fit and they all have something unique.
A rare thing in a game : it is funny. Not funny in the way that it's so bad you laugh at it, but actually funny. Many times, I laughed at something a character said, or a situation you find yourself in, and even the most absurd things fit in this weird but yet lovable world of monsters !
The gameplay also has something unique : it's never the same thing. All fights are mini games, all monsters have a different one, and it really brings diversity to it, I never was bored during a fight.
Also, you can choose to kill everyone, or save everyone (extremely hard) and to the very end (the real end) you will have that choice, and it will determine the outcome of your playthrough. That also gives it a high replay value.
The OST is...simply amazing. Almost to good for the game. Almost. There are so many memorable songs (Bonetrousle, Megalovania, Dummy!, etc) that I can't name them all...
The plot, as stated above, may seem simplistic but it really is more complex if you read all the signs, books, etc ; and I actually found a bit of sadness hidden in it that made me reconsider some decisions I've made in the game.
In short :
Pros:
- One of the best indie OST ever
- A good sense of humour
- The gameplay never gets boring
- I can't think of all the pros of the game, so there they are : ALL
Cons :
- Short (but longer would have made it less awesome)
- Ugly (Aww come on, I got to put something right ?...right ?)
- Ok...none the above then...no cons...at all.
One of the best indie experiences I've ever had. Buy it, play it, love it. That is all.

Starpoint Gemini 2 is hours of constant enjoyment. I've been wanting a great space simulator for years and this fills that gap. Space combat ranges from you being overwhelmingly powerful and slaughtering a weaker enemy convoy, to suddenly being completely outmatched as hordes of enemy fleets warp in. You'll go from shifting your power-flow to fully charge your weapons; unleashing torrents of weapon-fire and watching enemy ships violently explode, to frantically diverting power to your shields and engines, cutting power from your weapon-batteries to overcharge your engines and jettison yourself free from the firestorm.
The space combat, environment, and ships are all wonderful and deserve high praise. The only downfall is the narrative in the story mode. My only noted negative is that the plot dialogue is very poorly written: conversations are written with very simplistic wording, adding unnecessary filler dialogue in the middle of a conversation. The characters have no expression and sitting through the dialogue moments are frustrating to even hear the characters speak. All the character interactions are not written as real conversations, monologues occur at inappropriate times. A complete re-writing of the entire game's plot narrative (by someone with writing experience) would make the game perfect.

I wanted to like this game, I really did. I love space sims and up to a point, Starpoint Gemini seemed like a great game. Better starship fighting than the X series, the potential for becoming the admiral of a whole space fleet, exploring the galaxy, or building an elite-like mercantile empire all sound awesome.
unfortunately the reality falls short. at most you can have two allied ships, plus a few fighters. The spaceflight is boring and the bigger ships just don't feel any different than the early freighters and fighters. There's no heft to a giant battlecruiser compared to the very first ship you get, they feel like the same size ship only with a few extra equipment slots on the top tier guy. all in all, the scale of this game is disappointing. Compare it to a game like Freespace, which came out over a decade ago, and it's pretty inexcusable.
The trading is simplistic. i don't want a spreadsheet game like X3 but there's really no joy in going to a planet, buying all the green-hilighted cargo, then cruising around with it in your bays until you find a decent price. This is often poorly implemented in games and unfortunately starpoint gemini 2 is the same.
the game I'd most compare it to is Freelancer, which was a decent to mediocre arcade spacefighter with pretty minimal trade. the story in this game is even worse than freelancer, though. At least Freelancer was funny. The combat is frankly worse, this game would benefit enormously from a little cursor leading your enemies telling you where to shoot if you want to hit them. the ship design is also worse.
the place it really falls down is in the locations, though. There are no people to talk to, at all. and you don't even get missions from planets, tehy just appear on your map while you cruise around. planets are just there to buy stuff and repair your ship. Remember the really goofy "We don't own this station, but we have an arrangement with the people who do" barks that people on stations had in Freelancer? Well compared to this game that was Planescape Torment level dialogue. There are no real factions to have relationships with, just a good/evil slider with each faction having a set affinity for good or evil. pass 79 good guy points? Well the East Nobody Trader Guild now likes you instead of being neutral, because their threshold is 78. it doesn't matter if you've never encountered that trade guild, have blown up their ships in the past, have done missions for their enemies. all that matters is that you're generally decent.
the voice acting is intolerably bad. that's really vanishingly low on my list of priorities, though. Voice acting is expensive and in a game like this doesn't add much. but still, it's really bad.
Positive things:
you can shoot spaceships
you can fly around in a spaceship

Well. After having to reinstall due to the update breaking the game I come to find that the new items are totally useless. They might be useful if almost everything wasn't already automated. Or if the things that weren't automated could be automated with the new items. I love the transportation tubes. Helps reduce risk from many things - BUT it is absolutely impossible to get them without debug menu for the following reasons.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Extremely unstable build. This build has so many issues that if you don't restart every 5 cycles the following WILL happen. Gas and liquid ignoring tiles, heat and pressure going crazy. (sometimes even melting objects) duplicates refusing to eat or sleep. (they just stand there. Even at night)
All of the above start at cycle 30 and get worse until you shut off the game and reopen it. Then they happen every 5 cycles afterward.
2. Floor tube blocks often don't block gas or liquid. This one's a bit random and I can't pinpoint the cause but out of nowhere all the gas or liquid behind the floor blocks of the transport tubes will give out and can only be fixed by closing and opening the game. Earliest happenings at cycle 20.
3. Huge imbalance of games resources. Over the course of 5 games in 5 different seeds. 25 games total the current resource to input balance makes it impossible to get past cycle 30 without ALL of the following near your starting location.  1 TWO water geysers. ONE Hydrogen Geyser, 5 Puffers (for algae distiller.) and Twelve Mealwood seeds. With that combination you can go near indefinitely without problem. However if you are missing even 1 of the water geysers the max you can go is cycle 40. Without the Hydrogen geyser max cycle is 50. Without the puffers (or a huge amount of slime) Max Cycle is 30.
4. Power lines and batteries are bad. We need a battery that can store Way more than 40J. The current ones are useless for current updates. Ones that can store 1kj or 2kj would be way more effective for the current update. Heavy watt wires need to be placeable in tile. Without this we end up needing to create 4-5 power stations for one medium size base. 2 if your very skilled at best. Large bases are currently impossible.
5. Transport tube use way too much power. Needs to be halved at minimum. It shouldn't take two full time hydrogen generators to power one of those things.
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Other bugs that don't break playability of game.
1. Wires damaging for no reason. After cycle 20 circuits randomly start taking damage. Even if it is a straight isolated circuit such as - Power wheel - battery - Light bulb.  With nothing else connected. Most likely caused by the circuits looking at overall wattage instead of local wattage.
2. Can't cancel build from the power or plumbing overview.
3.Random carbon build up. Out of nowhere burst's of carbon in amounts of almost 30kg will appear in random locations in the map. No clue what's causing this one.
4. Duplicants sliding out the side of the tube. Cycle 25+ Restart seems to fix it temporarily.
5. Living ICE. This one's very odd but sometimes when there is ice it will start to consume all available space regardless of temperature or lack of water to freeze. 3 test with it. 1 with a 20 by 20 room. All space was consumed within 5 seconds. 2nd test I opened the wall to my base and it entombed all duplicates that were in the main area within 9 seconds. 3rd test in magma froze all magma and then continuously produced water until it crashed the game. The only way to stop it is to have the debug console and erase all affected area with vacuum. Resting and reloading does not fix this one.

Please be aware, and do believe all the negative facts everyone else is posting because it's all true.
TL:DR: This could be as Good as Blood Money, in a few months! But do Not buy it now, because you will Hate every second of the roughly 40mins-1hour of gameplay included in this release! Bad AI, bad DRM, multiple choice linearized, fake-sandbox missions, with illogical scripted events. Also always online, locked options, and unoptimised in every way. Console controls are fine, but PC controls are badly set up. Mediocre graphics and animations compared to hardware needs.
The whole thing feels like the old blood money engine torn to pieces by someone who never done any coding, and after ruining it with high-res stuff and console code from Absolution, stuff it was never meant to handle, that same person put it back together while being drunk and paying attention to a stripper instead of his work.
Here are some details:
- the GRAPHics look like Blood Money looked on lowest setting, because some important quality settings are locked and cannot be changed unless you have insanely over the top hardware. This is so the game doesn't crash on you as it is not optimised and the engine code is probably a shameful mess. It could be a good looking game, because the art is there, you're just not allowed to see it unless you bought the highest-end GPU possible. Frame rates are pretty bad considering the very low "quality", clearly no optimization was done.
- Where's Agent 47 ? And by this I mean, where's the cloned superhuman we got to play throughout the series? This time 47 is slow, week, and now has eagle vision for no apparent reason! Taking out two man standing right next to each other from behind with a heavy object like a fire extuingisher  takes over 40 seconds of slooooow animations playing! My 87 y.o. grandma can hit two guys over the head with a fryingpan faster and harder than 47!!!
-You have literally zero chance of taking out two peaple at the same time. This leads to the total linearity in every mission. Two guards protecting a doorway? Get the right disguise or get lost!
You are constantly led around the levels this way, making for a boring experience of trying to find out what the designers wanted you to do. There is now a "right" way of doing a mission, and everything else is wrong and leads to instant death by guards. Stray off this designated path, and you are busted. No freedom, no creativity, no thinking about it. You can't take your chances with situations any more. You can't just observe and be smart about it. Do as you are supposed to or die. There is no tension anymore, as you can only find out the "right" way by trying and trying and trying, and thus reloading and reloading and reloading a savegame from 2 minutes ago, because the "right" way is often illogical until you accidently trigger a script making someone move or do something totally unrelated to the situation.
- the gameplay does have an Always Online element to it, and it is bothersome because the game throws you out the instant it looses connection to the server. Which it will! The servers are unstable still, hopefully this will get fixed. Update: servers seem to be a bit more stable, I could get almost an hour of gameplay in without getting disconnected.
- As stated above, SCRIPTED AI actions ruin the fun of watching, waiting and planning. Instead you have to try to trigger these scripts to see which one does what as they are 100% unrelated to your actions or surroundings, and re-run the mission to get your target to where you want him. This makes up the fake "sandbox" part, and thus gives you "one way to do it only, 100% linear" actions to choose from. So, no freedom what so ever.  Remember how the good old Hitman games were like puzzles you could examine, learn, and solve in many fun ways? Now there is no puzzle, just a stupid maze with no logic or thought behind it, you are just being forced down the road you choose.
- generally the AI is erratic, and mostly dumb, so are some of the setups of who will recognize you in a disguise
- the PC Controls are tacked on, keyboard layeout is for at least 3 arms and 17 fingers on each hand. It feels like a console port no one payed any attention to (example .:Push X to get up on a ledge, but push space to climb down? WTF) Also mouse look is lagging, even around 40-60fps, so aiming in a tight situation is ranging from a pain to impossible, depending on how much the framerate stutters at that moment. Push i for inventory? whats this, an rpg from 15 years ago? Mouse wheel is not assigned in any way? Others said that gamepad support is okay-ish, but I found out that if you want to use the kb+mouse instead you really have to disconnect/disable everything else, even HOTAS and Steering Wheels because the game will try to use them as it would use an xbox gamepad! So if you want to play with keyboard and mouse, unplug all your other controllers!
- ANIMations, like stashing someone in a freezer, are a mess, they look incomplete and unrefined, compared to BM or Abs. Animations like these take ages, despite the fact that they are cut in the middle of the action for some reason. Also 47 stands like his elbows are stuck to his waist with superglue, and so he walks in a silly way. All characters have a very basic motion set, which feels rehashed from Blood Money, or older as they are even less realistic.
-PHIsics are about as bad as any non-simulated game would be from 10 years ago, most of it feels fake and unreal, and not even in the cool "blown away 500yards by a headshot" way. Also, remember how in Blood Money, Absolution, and all AssCreed games you could push through the crowds, and they would flow around you and such? Well here the crowds are like ghosts standing in place, with absolutely no regard or reaction to you. Also you will walk through them, literally! They wont move aside enough, you won't get pushed aside, just pass through each other! Come on Devs, you did a way better job years ago, what the heck? I have to give them one good point though, for the cloth simulation of skirts and such, that's better then most of the stuff I've seen!
- AUDIO is one of the finer points of the game, apart from NPC conversations getting cut mid-phrase if you get too close, it's pretty decent so far. Ambience is nice, and positional audio works fine. Music could be better but that's a question of taste, for me it's entirely forgettable, unlike the previous games.
Conclusion:
- But does it feel like Hitman? Yes and No. The scripted bit with the linearized "right ways" ruins the pretty okay-ish Hitman atmosphere entirely! Buy it in a few months when all the other issues are fixed, if that ever happens, and the later levels may turn out to be more fun.
