I love this game! Boss Monster was actually released a couple of years ago as a popular card game, and I was excited to see it available on Steam.  You play as the final boss of a dungeon, and the goal is to build a dungeon, lure heroes to it, then kill the heroes!
The graphics remain true to the 8 bit design of the original cards - I'm happy to see they kept the retro look.  The cards have a lot of references to geek culture (ie I played a counterspell card that featured Harry Potter fighting Voldemort).
Before starting, I had the option of playing the tutorial, which I highly recommend.  Having a tutorial with pictures really helped me to grasp the concepts of the game (rather than a typical word-only instruction manual).
The layout of the game screen is organized and straight forward.  I could see how many room cards & spell cards my opponent and myself have, how many souls and wounds we accrued, and what type of hero we could lure into our dungeon.
My favorite feature in the game was the ability to "pass all", where the game ran on autopilot, allowing me to just watch heroes run through my opponents' dungeon.  I got a bit carried away watching my opponent take hit points that I forgot to build my dungeon though.  So don't do that! :P
All in all, a very fun game.  Stays true to the original card game.  I'm looking forward to playing the expansions that will unlock after I win x-number of games.

It is STILL a great game! Most of the Negative reviews are from the people who reviewed BEFORE the Hotfix after the Outbreak patch.
Managing diseases is not that big of a deal, even slimelung. Now you have auto-desinfecting!
Slimelung: If the immunity of your colonists is going down; you just seal them out of the contaminated areas as slimelung dies in clean oxygen.
Food poisoning: Because the water filtration process is not antiseptic, you MUST have another clean water source for food and use the contaminated filtered water from the WC for food production (sleet wheat and Berries) or Electrolyzers.
You have a point when you say there is more micro management: for example the food poisoned water from the showers/basins will not be enough to produce oxygen for a bigger base and hydroponic farms, so you will need a second water supply.
As for cleaning the base: yes it might be annoying at start, but once you get used to managing germs it will NOT be a problem anymore. Cycle 220 here, 1st try and I've managed to recover from a food poisoning outbreak.
You just need experience to get used to the new mechanics, because this update was a great one. The food balancing is fantastic, now you can actually make good food for your dups!
Great job Klei! and thanks for this great game and that quick hotfix on desinfectation time. I wish people would be so quick to fixing their reviews as Klei was to correct their mistakes!
(although, I do wish the Thermo Aquatuner would not roast my base at 200 degress C as it does now)

I enjoy a good western-style retro shoot-em-ups, and Sky Force Reloaded is right up there. Its origins are from a mobile game, but you'd be crazy to let that put you off. The mobile version was probably the best schmup on the platform (IMO) and had a smart progression system. This PC update goes all out to improve it in pretty much every way; it's slick, smooth, spectacular and feels great. This is a very good thing, because you'll have to replay levels a lot. This is part of the core mechanic, so let's get it out of the way. Progressing to later levels demands that you get a certain number of medals, and you get medals by hitting specific targets for each level: destroy 70% of enemies (medal), destroy 100% of enemies (medal), rescue all people (medal) and survive with no damage (medal). Do all those, and a new difficulty tier opens up for that particular level so you can do it all again, and then a third difficulty tier. Without solid core mechanics it risks getting old, but fortunately it is a blast to play, and variety increases with each new level you unlock. Some might say you haven't really played a level until you unlock Insane, it's an unrecognisable festival of chaos.
Progression is helped further by collecting stars, of which there are a great many on each level. This "currency" enables you to improve various attributes of your ship, health, weapons, magnet to attract stars, super weapons etc. At first you'll fight to survive, but before too long you'll return feeling like a god. Ever-increasing difficulty once you collect all the medals on a level keeps the momentum going. And every few medals you'll unlock another true level and you can start to tackle that.
There's more. A lot more. Collectibles appear that you had no idea existed, new ships unlock, then a tournament becomes available, and every so often new features open up to give you incentive to keep blasting away. It's one of those "I'll just have a quick 5 minute game" that ends up being 30 minutes. Or an hour. Or more.
So yes, I played the hell out of this on my phone, and the PC version is greatly improved and expanded. Highly recommended if you like these kinds of Amiga-like retro-shooters.

The game on itself is nice and addictive.
However there are too many bugs and design errors to be able to recommend it.
A few examples:
1. The mouse, although an option in the choice of controllers does not actually work. Instead of moving like a (slow) mouse cursor, the ship moves even slower than with the keyboard
2. Buggy Bonuses and Cards: Some bonuses claim to undo the first scratch, others are shields that block damage, or slow down enemy bullets. None of those actually work reliably. Bullets are not always slowed down, shields do not activate or activate but are pierced anyway (happens often during bossfights, where shields are most needed)
3. Controls react with small delays, this is deadly when the boss has a insta-kill gun that has less than 1/10s forewarning time
4. Hitbox is slightly larger than the ship, making it often impossible to squeeze through the enemy shots.
5. Enemy shots will sometimes one-shot the ship, other times only scratch it. This is using the same ship, enemies, level and difficulty of course.
6. Upgrades not always working: The description text for the "side cannons" reads that upgrading them also increases the frequency of shot. This does not happen at all.
7. No restart option in the pause menu: Instead I have to quit, navigate back to the level select menu, select ship, bonuses, and commanders and only then can I start the mission again. On itself not bad but when grinding for stars or medals this becomes a chore.
Oh and finally, the tournament is utterly useless unless you have 2 other frieds that also play this game. Since this is not exactly a mainstream AAA game, the chances of this being the case are very low. Public matchmaking would be very much needed.
Edit: And I just found out that the game cannot detect more than one simultaneous button press: When deactivating auto-fire it is not possible to keep firing the primary gun while firing the secondary one too, the primary gun will stop and not start again depite its key being pressed the whole time.

This game is amazing. I hated Absolution and loved the older hitmans such as Silent Assassin and Blood Money. This game definetly pays homage to them, giving you a huge, open level to play in. I've spent around ~4 hours in the game at this point and I've yet to even complete theParis mission because I've just been running around and looking for which ways I prefer to kill my target. I take it down one path and failed it, then I turn around and try something else. Then I explore the mansion with my newfound disguise and check out the level of detail in the scenery. Some people may run in and finish the level in 20 minutes and get bored, but if you're looking to explore and complete all the challenges this level has to offer, you should be in for a good bit of gameplay.
Graphically, the game is beautiful. Some of the rooms have what look like 50+ people in them. Environments are very decorated. You can see people talking on their phones, playing on tablets, taking selfies of themselves, engaging in conversation with each other. You can sneak up behind security guards and overhear them talking about random things that don't have anything to do with the mission, or sometimes it does. Running through the kitchens and makeup areas, you can see the level of detail put into placing objects into the scenery and making the area seem realistic and lived in.
I initially bought the introductory level to get into the beta, played the Paris level, and it was enough to convince me to upgrade to the full experience. I recommend this game to fans and new players alike as it is a great extenstion to the series.

I wanted to like this game. I really did. Blood Money was a classic and the developer promised to bring this game back in line with the classic Blood Money style. So that was enough for me to purchase the Full Experience for 69.99. A rarity for me in this day and age. Most AAA titles don't deserve that amount at launch. So I bought the game and was ready to get a classic Hitman experience.
Boy was I wrong.
I don't blame the developers wholly for this, but it's up to them to take a stand when their publishers demand ridiculous features like always online DRM. Take pride in your product and defend the people who will be playing it.
The game boots you out if connection to the servers drops (which happened frequently at launch) and your progress cannot be carried over to offline mode.
In addition the game is clearly a console port and is poorly optimized. As of this writing, DirectX12 barely works. No support for 144hz and unless you enable Vsync there will be screen tearing everywhere.
The game itself was fine when it was working and/or you weren't getting booted out for losing connection. It offered many different approaches to taking down a target and all that other good stuff that made Blood Money so well loved. Graphics are pretty poor and look like something off a PS3. The menus themselves are messy and poorly optimized for a M+KB experience. I have a controller, but I enjoyed playing Blood Money with M+KB.
That being said, while the core of the game is fine, it is wrapped in hot garbage. Publishers like SE don't deserve 69.99 for this ham fisted crap they push onto PC Gamers. CDProjeckt Red has set a new standard for customer care and LISTENING to the consumer and there is no reason for PC gamers to put up with crap like Hitman with its always online ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t and shoddy optimization for PC's.
Also the business model for this game is atrocious. At launch you get two training missions and one actual mission. The rest you have to wait for. Don't support this garbage.
Thank god for Steam Refund. This further strengthens my resolve to not buy AAA titles at launch.

The best Jedi game ever made. Better than the hack jobs of Force Unleashed and Force Unleased 2 by a wide margin.
The lightsaber combat in this is actually tactical and requires a fair amount of skill to get good at. Later levels in the game even sport some skilled AI that can result in epic battles or instant kills if you're unlucky, un-skilled, or just not careful.
Environments/Levels in this game are varied and dangerous for both you and your opponents as virtually anything in the game environment can be used to kill/maim/injure.
Powers available to you through the Light and Dark side aren't restrictive and you can mix and match all you want until you hit the power cap (choose wisely!). The power creep in this game isn't overwhelmingly in your favor either, with a nice steady progression through the game as you unlock points to invest into powers of your choosing.
Controls require some personal configuration and the management of them does get annoying. Combat controls are easy to grasp and the seamless transition from saber to blaster is nice.
The game is even fully voice acted and has a solid story behind it that is actually pretty good.
Character choices are neat, but nothing fancy. The same goes for lightsaber customization.

Jedi Academy is the currently latest installment in the Jedi Knight series, that previously starred Kyle Katarn yet, but now you instead control a customizable hero/heroine. The game features both lightsaber combat and the use of blasters, and perplexingly enough some kind of illegal bugzapper weapon that disintergrates people. Odd choice for a Jedi, and nobody seems to give a♥♥♥♥♥♥if you use it. Well, guns are in general pretty awful in this game, and you should stick with the lightsaber. It has a nice feeling to it, it's responsive and the lightsaber battles, as much as it seems to just be flinging the saber around until someone dies, feels cinematic and when you cut someone with it, it's satisfying. Especially against multiple bladed combatants. Unfortunately g_saberrealisticcombat and whatever other command it was to make it so that you could dismember with the lightsaber seems gimped at best, completely removed at worst.
It's a shame since that was one of the best parts about Jedi Outcast.
The story is somewhat unfocused and kind of♥♥♥♥♥♥ you mainly just jump from planet to planet and kill stormtroopers, bountyhunter or the occasional wildlife, much to the dismay of the intergalactic PETA. (I'm joking, I sure as hell hope there's no such thing as People for the ethical treatment of Rancors)
A bit later into the game you get to choose whether to have a double bladed, dual, or a single lightsaber. "Why the hell  would I pick a single lightsaber? That seems lame"
Well I agree, dual lighstabers are badass, but on another level i feel that it's a lot more practical with the single one, especially since you can switch between three styles.
Aside from lasers and lightsabers, you get to choose to use force powers, and can throughout the game upgrade them at your leisure. You can choose from the dark side powers as well as lightside, and you can balance them both without getting a penalty for it. Some of the powers are useless and some are broken, such as level three force lightning. It can kill a whole room of stormtroopers pretty much instantly, but it's useless before level 3.
Aside from fighting there are some minor tedious puzzles such as getting prisoners around a rancor, however you can kill it to make the process less annoying.
All in all it's a rather solid game with good lightsaber combat, but I'd suggest picking up Jedi Outcast 2 as well.

When I was 6 years old, my sister's boyfriend (now brother-in-law) would bring his xbox over to our house and play games on my sister's TV. I watched him and occasionally played with him. Knowing now how difficult it is to play games with a 6-year-old (I play with his son occasionally), I am surprised he even let me. But I am thankful he did, because playing with him was how I first gained exposure to some of my favorite games of all time. Halo, Elder Scrolls, Fable, and Jedi Academy. I had a lot of fun playing Academy with my brother-in-law, even despite the fact that I was just getting my♥♥♥♥♥beat over and over again. So when I saw it on sale on steam, I couldn't pass up the opportunity to experience it again.
This game is everything I remember and more. As a 6-year-old, and again as an 8-year-old when I rented it from the video store, I couldn't really grasp the more complicated aspects of the game, and the story and was confusing. This made it all the more mysterious and intriguing for me. That subtle curiosity that left me both amazed and intimidated by the game has not been lost on me, 10 years later. The aesthetic and atmosphere of this game alone are enough to leave me in awe, but it's the gameplay that really hits home. The lightsaber combat is tight and intuitive. and surprisingly intricate once you delve into its more advanced aspects. The gunplay is similar to that of Quake II, which is understandable, seeing as it's built on the same engine. In today's world of COD and Battlefield and Titanfall and Halo and all that, it's quite refreshing to play a game with straight up skill based arena combat. The mobility is fantastic, with elements of "free-running" that blend flawlessly with the combat. Wallrun, force jump, backflip, and cartwheel your way to victory. Force powers can be taken advantage of as well, with abilities like force heal and force speed coming in handy quite often. All in all, the perfectly balanced amalgamation of melee and ranged combat, fast paced mobility, and usful force abilities makes for a great experience on keyboard and mouse.
The multiplayer in Jedi Academy is incredibly addicting. This late in its lifespan, you'd expect a games playerbase to have decayed into a small group of bored kids with cracked clients and a few veteran players on a nostalgia trip. But surprisingly enough, Academy has withstood the test of time, with a solid playerbase of loyal players. The first public server I joined was called the TNA server, which I soon discovered acted as a "home base" of sorts for the long-running TNA Clan. It's a sabers-only server, and players seeking heated battle with competitive yet friendly players, or even just conversation are sure to find a great time on the TNA server. I certainly have. But with capabilities for custom maps, custom gametypes, and even more, the fun doesn't stop at vanilla lightsaber combat. I've come across some fairly interesting things when browsing the server list. A few interesting roleplay servers. a game full of bots that insult eachother with slurs and expletives, even parkour maps. You won't be without something to do when playing Academy multiplayer.
I haven't played much of the single-player campaign yet, but what I have played is enjoyable. The story seems enagaging, the voice acting is great (JENNIFER HALE!), and the missions provide a decent challenge, at least on the higher difficulty levels. I would absolutely recommend checking out the singleplayer, but for me, the multiplayer is really where I have the most fun.
The visuals of the game are great for their time, and they still hold up well enough as not to distract the player or break immersion. Texture quality is decent, lighting effects are good looking, and even the character models are pretty great for a game from 2003. The game really shines when you incorporate a widescreen fix that allows you to play in full 1080p.
So, that's about it for my review of Star Wars Jedi Knight: Jedi Academy. I loved this game when I was 6, and I love it even more now. I'm sure you will too.

I'd like to write a more comprehensive review at a later date, but for now I'd simply like to encourage others to buy this game with a few quick words.
The game's systems are formulaic and familiar, there's little originality in the basic gameplay loop - however, like Shadow of Mordor, the copywork is excellent - the brawling combat systems originating in games like Batman: Arkham Asylum are put to visually impressive and satisfying use.
The cars look and sound wonderful, though they lack the depth of simulation of GTA IV (while surpassing GTA V) or Burnout. They do what they need to.
The plot is surprisingly good - low key, unepic, but richly Mad Max. This is an open world adventure sandbox done right; the plot doesn't tell you to save the world, SAVE IT, SAVE IT NOW, it simply gives structure to your exploration and liberation of the region in the Mad Max way; a man with a car doing a job, grudgingly, to get favours or pay off debts and stay alive - in a horrible yet strangely beautiful place.
The world... My god, I think this is the single most impressive feat of visual world creation in a game to date. The Great White is incredible. Every inch of its miles feels hand-crafted and real. It's beautiful, it's tragic, it's strange, and it looks absolutely amazing. The authenticity, the endless details that speak of its history/hydrology/geology as a desert populated by fortresses that was once a coastal basin deep underwater and a major sea-trading city.
The game... It's very simple. It's repetitive. These games always are, these open world collect-complete-explore third person toys in the model of Assassin's Creed.
Here, the repetition and simplicity feel right, and work so well with the setting.
Just get out there and wander the wastes. Get out of the car from time to time, use the HUD mod to go pure and walk sometimes. See the sights, ask yourself; Who killed the world?

So far loving it, and only almost halfway trough. It runs near perfect(something i cant say bout most games) and although it has Asscreed inspired repetetive goals, the games openworld and dynamics keep it from feeling repetetive or stale.
Its a perfect game to lash out from spending too much time in horrible traffic of everyday life commute. Side swipe the infidels!

Excellent game for a variety of reasons. I like the attention that was put into the details. Everything looks really nice, there are quirky opponents, and most importantly the gameplay is excellent.
There are two campaigns: one for 8-ball and one for 9-ball. Both have challenges each match to help keep the game fresh. Some example challenges are complete a trick shot or have a streak of potted balls. Their are also a variety of opponents with little biographies that you can choose to read or not. It is nice how this game is not too story dependent as I feel that would interrupt the flow. Each campaign takes a while to get through and was fun for me until completion.
Another mode I've spent time on is endurance mode. It is an addicting, time sensitive, mode in which you try to continuosly pot balls while new balls are being added at increasingly fast intervals. I've spent at least an hour just with that mode, chasing a new time record.
The variety of modes is very extensive. There are also one off matches with a variety of rule sets as well as online multiplayer. It is hard to jump right into a match sometimes due to lack of online opponents but there are plenty of small groups on Steam dedicated to tournaments and matchmaking.
Additionally, throughut all the modes, you can choose whether to play with an auto aimer on or off to toggle the difficulty.
The upcoming free update Box of Tricks looks super neat as well. I'm sure it will further increase the replayability of this game.
Overall, for the low price this game is a must buy.

boredom: about 57 of the 60 levels are so easy a 3 year old would get bored, then you have maybe 2 levels that take a few tries optimize the solution. Let's face it: work sucks. For most of us, there's almost always about a million things we'd rather be doing than our current job. When the clock's laughing in your face, you'll find just about any reason you can think of to slack off. Suddenly, twirling your pencil becomes a sport, the Internet becomes your new work television, and Windows Solitaire has you ignoring every responsible thing you know you should be doing instead.
Enter Monomino, an E-rated casual puzzler developed by final year students from Nanyang Polytechnic in Singapore. A delightfully casual game that's both challenging and addictive, Monomino will have you clocking out early for lunch, then clocking in a whole half an hour late. It's a highly addictive game that's anything but dumb and easy.
That's one way to teach your children about safe sex...
Aside from being slightly weird, the game is strangely challenging. You'll get used to restarting the levels trying frantically to figure out what you have to do to get those Monominos home; it's all trial and error. The little guys walk aimlessly in one direction and then turn around. They won't climb higher than one block, they can't jump over gaps, and they can't fly, so you have to use your head and figure out how to lay those polyforms down. Once you place a piece down, it can't be removed, so choose wisely. As the levels progress, you'll be given other tools like bombs and springboards to help you lead the babies home – and when you finally do get them home, it's pretty satisfying to say the least.
The game is not without its flaws. For starters, it is completely devoid of any sort of options menu. That means the background music that's been playing for the past hour cannot be turned off. You'll simply have to turn your speakers off... or take a power drill to your eardrum, whichever seems logical at the time. You also don't get a lot of time to figure out how to lay out your pieces, which means you'll be restarting the levels a lot. Sure, you can trap the little buggers while you figure out a strategy, but other than that, it's all on the fly.
As simple as the game is, you'd think it would get boring after a while, but instead you'll find yourself getting sucked into it, and with 100 levels, you'll be busy for sure. Obviously not a title for the hardcore gamer, Monomino works on a simple system that honestly keeps you heavily entertained. The game is simple enough to play it casually, but challenging enough to have you banging your fist on the desk like "Oh, come on! I can do this!"
Monomino is a great time waster, and an excellent first attempt for Nanyang Polytechnic. It's good to know there's still a place for simple games like this in the gaming world. You can grab it on Steam now for the very affordable sale price of $4.49 – which is good because once your boss finds out that for the last two days all you've been doing is drinking up the company's coffee and playing Monomino, you're probably going to want to save as much money as you can.

Reviewed on i5-4690k, GTX 970, 16GB DDR3 @1920x1080.
This game is amazing. I hated Absolution and loved the older hitmans such as Silent Assassin and Blood Money. This game definetly pays homage to them, giving you a huge, open level to play in. I've spent around ~4 hours in the game at this point and I've yet to even complete theParis mission because I've just been running around and looking for which ways I prefer to kill my target. I take it down one path and failed it, then I turn around and try something else. Then I explore the mansion with my newfound disguise and check out the level of detail in the scenery. Some people may run in and finish the level in 20 minutes and get bored, but if you're looking to explore and complete all the challenges this level has to offer, you should be in for a good bit of gameplay.
Graphically, the game is beautiful. Some of the rooms have what look like 50+ people in them. Environments are very decorated. You can see people talking on their phones, playing on tablets, taking selfies of themselves, engaging in conversation with each other. You can sneak up behind security guards and overhear them talking about random things that don't have anything to do with the mission, or sometimes it does. Running through the kitchens and makeup areas, you can see the level of detail put into placing objects into the scenery and making the area seem realistic and lived in.
I initially bought the introductory level to get into the beta, played the Paris level, and it was enough to convince me to upgrade to the full experience. I recommend this game to fans and new players alike as it is a great extenstion to the series.

I wanted to like this game. I really did. Blood Money was a classic and the developer promised to bring this game back in line with the classic Blood Money style. So that was enough for me to purchase the Full Experience for 69.99. A rarity for me in this day and age. Most AAA titles don't deserve that amount at launch. So I bought the game and was ready to get a classic Hitman experience.
Boy was I wrong.
I don't blame the developers wholly for this, but it's up to them to take a stand when their publishers demand ridiculous features like always online DRM. Take pride in your product and defend the people who will be playing it.
The game boots you out if connection to the servers drops (which happened frequently at launch) and your progress cannot be carried over to offline mode.
In addition the game is clearly a console port and is poorly optimized. As of this writing, DirectX12 barely works. No support for 144hz and unless you enable Vsync there will be screen tearing everywhere.
The game itself was fine when it was working and/or you weren't getting booted out for losing connection. It offered many different approaches to taking down a target and all that other good stuff that made Blood Money so well loved. Graphics are pretty poor and look like something off a PS3. The menus themselves are messy and poorly optimized for a M+KB experience. I have a controller, but I enjoyed playing Blood Money with M+KB.
That being said, while the core of the game is fine, it is wrapped in hot garbage. Publishers like SE don't deserve 69.99 for this ham fisted crap they push onto PC Gamers. CDProjeckt Red has set a new standard for customer care and LISTENING to the consumer and there is no reason for PC gamers to put up with crap like Hitman with its always online ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t and shoddy optimization for PC's.
Also the business model for this game is atrocious. At launch you get two training missions and one actual mission. The rest you have to wait for. Don't support this garbage.
Thank god for Steam Refund. This further strengthens my resolve to not buy AAA titles at launch.

I understand this review is late, but let me just say how impressed I was by this game.
To be honest, the graphics were mediocre. That doesn't change how much I LOVED this game. Many people critique it for simply just it's fanbase, not caring about how GOOD the game actually is. I played this game a very long time ago, but just today did I want to right a review.
#1 - High Replay Value
For a story based RPG, this is significant. Don't be fooled by the many games that claim they "change based on your decisions". While most games just change how your player looks or what items they use, Undertale
rewrites the plot with every choice. Some not as significant as others, but many decide if you even get to fight the final boss. Also, (if you did what I did) to actually beat the game, I had to restart AFTER doing something in a
save file.
#2 - Outstandingly Immersive
After a few minutes in the underground, you will feel as though you are really there. Not only that, but the game actually plays jokes that have a few characters UNDERSTAND that this is, in fact, a game. (The following could be considered a spoiler but I will make it vague) If you kill a main character, restart, and save that character, one of the other main characters will tease you for it. Multiple times the game will crash or restart, intentionally though.
#3 - The HUMOR!!
Just read the description. It is funny enough on it's own. Undertale has some amazingly witty jokes and puns to share with you. Not just through character dialouge, but in other unique ways.
#4 - The Great Moral
The whole point of this game is to be kind to all sorts of beings. It geniously convinces you to befriend the "monsters" instead of slaying them for what they are. A few of the enemies seem hostile at first, but a bit of kindness can go a long way. One example (Minor spoilers) is when a VERY aggressive and hard monster collapses in battle. You could choose to either help them, or leave them to die. Befriending them offers MUCH more gameplay and hilarious dialogue. I feel as though this concept could be applied to the real world. An even greater example is revealed near the end of the game, yet writing it here would be a massive spoiler.
If you would like to know the plot, I am sure there is somewhere online that can help you with that. If you are looking for a brief overview with minor spoilers, here you go:
The game starts with a short video (whatever it is) that shows a young child climbing a mountain, and falling into a pit at the top. They fall and pass out on the floor. The hole caves in and the child is stuck underground. After that video, we gain control of a gender-ambiguous yellow child with a blank expression. During the journey, we meet plenty of monsters choosing to make friends or kill them. Your ultimate goal is to either 1) Kill everything 2) Free all of the monsters and have humans and monsters live in harmony or 3) Make it out of that place by yourself in one piece.
My recommendation: GET THIS GAME!
My rating: 9.5/10

It is a micro management game that is far from finished. It has bugs and issues.  However there are frequent hotfixes and now they have added a countdown timer to push themselves for updates(mentioned in one of their live feeds).
Since the update disinfecting and hand washing has already been improved, and a auto disinfect has been added.
Each game play is different, even if you load an older save it doesn't mean it will go the same way it went the first time.
To address some issues I have seen in the reviews ( I will try not to go too much into gameplay so you can discover that for yourself).
Stress: My dupes don't stay above 50% for long, I could get it down further but that is not needed. Building massage tables and setting the priority to 9 is needed and sometimes even removing them from other jobs is sometimes needed. 50% is the threshold (adjustable) to start using the massage table and de-stressing
Germs: There is no germs in your starting location, rushing straigt into germ riddled area is a sure fired way to loose controll. With proper planning, having enough wash basins next to the toilets and food areas is a must. heating water when you can to prevent germs is also a good start.
When adventuring into the slime biome (loads of germs) consider limiting access to those with strong immune systems. and think how to keep the germs from spreading.
Priority: Do not set everything to 9 the dupes won't knwo what to do first. I hav't had many issues using 8 as my high priority and 9 for things I want done  now. Also you can control which dupes does what, It can help to have the fastes and strongest on delivering only.
Med-cot: Having a med cot require access to a toilet and food adds to the gameplay. Dupes can be highly contagous, and you don't want them travelling around your base to find food and toilet spreadding germs. They also recover in the cot so less time out of it the more chance of recovery.
I think I have addressed the negatives in the other reviews and pointed out the positives (Iwill have to re-read and update if needed). I have already mentioned it but check out their twitch account for the live feeds gives a good understanding of the game, how to use some features and their passion for the game and interacting with its players.
The game is early acess with frequent updates so any complaint about it being unfinished, not likeing it because their play style has to change, or simply not recomend it because it is a micromange game is simply unfair to the game itself.

This game really caught my eye on steam, and how could it not, it’s so very very shiny. Released originally on PSN Cherry Pop ported their billiards game over to the PC and is available for $10 via steam.
What we have here is really a modern pool game. A sparkling beautiful graphics engine combined with an impressive realistic physics engine all to send shiny balls flying around a table. It’s smooth, it’s pretty, it’s gorgeous. (click on some of my high-res screenshots and see for yourself!) Really what else do you need to know? If you like pool games then it’s for you, if you don’t, all the shiny graphics in the world probably won’t change your mind. What you might expect from a pool game is all here, an 8-ball and 9-ball tour to play through with slowly increasing difficulty as well as some other game modes to throw in some variety.
There are also arbitrary points systems that award you points based upon added difficulty of shots (kinda like the way skater games give you points for harder tricks) and as you progress through each tour there are challenges to meet in each match to unlock extra goodies. It’s all your typical completionist fluff we’ve grown to expect from games these days but they do add some extra challenge and drives you to try to be more creative as you play. I also found I enjoyed most of the challenge modes that are unlocked during the tour play although a couple get a little tedious and boring.
Everything in the game is well crafted, the table is high textured, the balls well polished and reflective, and even the backgrounds are rich with detail and eye candy. The art style is beautiful and there’s even interesting little blurbs written about each opponent you play against. But all of this eye candy is just background noise to distract you from pocketing those balls! The game really shines though when it comes to trick-shots. Jump shots, draw backs, kick shots, even riding the rail is all possible with the engine. With full control to put on as much english and angle on your shot as you’d like you can put together some pretty sweet shots. Thanks to the shot guides they are not very difficult to learn and once you start pulling them off with regularity your options with each shot open wide. Best of all, the AI knows and uses them just as well which creates quite a challenge as you progress through the game.
The trick-shots are definitely best seen in video as screenshots cannot do them proper justice. You’ll be hopping over balls and making crazy draw backs in no time making you feel quite the awesome player. The game is, however, not without it’s flaws. A common complaint I have of many games, the music started to get annoying to me but this is not the first game I’ve had to mute the music and play my own. It is also clear that it is a port rather than designed specifically for the PC.
The menus sometimes feel a bit awkward navigating with a mouse and I feel some of the controls are awkward. For example rotating my cue around the cue ball to line up a shot only involves moving mouse left or right, yet my natural inclination is to try to circle the mouse around the cue ball. It made for some very frustrating moments until I realized this. Also I found the video replay system to be- clunky at best. Still even with these small complaints I’d definitely recommend the game if you ever find yourself wanting to shoot some pool.

You can look at the new HITMAN game from two different perspectives. Either you buy the full package and experience episodes as they come out over time, or you buy the intro pack and dip your feet in the experience that is the world of assassination. I for one went for the intro pack and I personally feel it was worth the purchase; despite knowing I have not purchased the full package.
Let me begin by saying that the intro pack is LOADED. Sure, you get 3 levels, 2 of which are training levels. One of the levels is an active real mission that takes you to Paris to assassinate 2 targets during a fashion show. On the surface, it does not sound like much, but IO Interactive gives you enough that replaying each mission (even the training levels) feels refreshing. This is because they introduced a challenge system that pushes you out of the bounderies of what you originally felt safe about in completing your goals. Another is unlocks.
Yes, unlocks that sounds so familiar from so many other games feels just right in HITMAN. In the real world mission, the unlocks gives you more opportunities that opens more doors of exploration and tactics that were either previously more difficult to obtain or just werent there from the get-go.
So perhaps that is not enough to satisfy your thirst or even worth the purchase. I understand that completely. IO then gives you Contracts mode; which is a psuedo-level maker borrowed from Abstraction. Basically you can assign an NPC to be assassinated in the same level and can be shared amongst friends or the public.
Then you have Escalation mode which increases the difficult of the game, by adding time limits or specific challenges that have to be completed.
Finally, there are the timed live events. These events come for a brief time which you have to assassinate a unique target that has not been seen in the game (but yes are still in the same level you've played previously).
If you're afraid the game will hold your hand, don't be. There are options that will make the game even more harder for you if you so choose. If you're a little lost, the game offers only a small hint on how to achieve your goals.
So far I've put in a couple of hours (I've been trying to hit all the challenges) and I have yet to actually complete the Paris mission primarily because I want to beat the level by killing my targets as perfectly as possible.
As for the game itself. It looks stunning! I have the graphics all at ultra settings and it doesn't even lag one bit. The load times are very quick (depending on your system of course, I put all my games on a Western Digital black series hard drive) and the menu system is elegant and simple. I have yet to really find any fault in the game. For the price, I honestly think you're getting more out of this intro pack than you would have from MGS: Ground Zeroes (which I paid 20 dollars for).  I would highly recommend the intro pack just to get a taste for the game. I wasn't too sure myself if I wanted the game, but now I would absolutely look forward in seeing the full release of the game.

Episodic Campaign, basically the two Beta levels (small maps) that you can replay over and over and the released campaign map - Paris, again play over and over (basically the Intro pack content).  Really they should have released at least 3 campaign levels (not including the beta ones) so you had some actual content before the next few are released. Here's a review from a fanboy
.
As a mostly traditional gamer, and despite bad money always drives out the good, I still firmly believe that mobile gaming is the future - under one condition:
If you've been a long-time Nokia user, it's very likely that you've heard of them. For the Symbian era, I-dreams is THE S#!T: that name equals uber fantastic, quality gaming in a confined 176x144 dimension. Even after moving on to Android and iOS, they still provide impressive and fun products like Can Knockdown.
Before everything, there's this wonderful game called Sky Force. It literally took the Symbian community by storm. Suddenly everyone was playing it in their palms; by then you don't have a storefront for mobile apps like Play or App Store, everything was spread almost purely by recommendation from friends or a pirated sis file sent by Bluetooth - had the Symbian platform get a larger user base, it could have been a larger success.
But history does not accept assumptions. Like many other Symbian developers, I-dreams moved on to Android and iOS to continue developing mobile games. Sky Force Reloaded (the 2005 one, not this) is okay; Can Knockdown is fun and beautiful indeed - but I was desperately expecting something bigger, better, and I-Dream-er.
Fortunately enough, we had a bad-a$$ present in 2014.
And I was blown away.
Why do we have to talk about this? Well, simple:
SF 2014  was exactly what I was expecting from I-Dreams.
Beautiful graphics? Check.
Thrilling gameplay? Check.
Bada$$ weaponry? Check.
New elements? Check.
Smells like 2004 spirit?
Check the S#!T out of that.
And yes, this 2017 remake of Sky Force Reloaded 2005 has everything above. However, I'm still concerned about one issue if it's present in this version or not:
The only thing that grinds my gear for the 2014 version is, well,
. You do have access to double your income through a one-time in-app purchase and you of course have the liberty to buy as much credits as you like - it's 2014 after all; however, after all that jazz, the amount of grinding required to have a fair chance getting objectives done is still horrendous. Even some long-time CAVE fans find it irritating in some challenges that's going to shove a boss in your a$$ if you don't level up enough.
When you grind too much just to find your equipment still suck against bullet-spongic enemies, it's frustrating. It's hard not to compare with Jets'N'Guns when it comes to grinding in STG games. Your life gets better with it, and when you grind enough, it's enough - that feels much, much better.
I have yet to progress enough in Reloaded 2017 to encounter this pet peeve once again. It feels OKAY in the first levels, and I wonder how much it will take in later parts of the game.
I sincerely hope my life doesn't get miserable like I did three years ago, because this game is so awesome ATM.
After all, at this price, Sky Force Reloaded (2017) is a well-made port and remake of a 2005 game. It looks nice, plays well, feels fine - while it MAY have some issues of its predecessor, I would still like to shove my cash into I-Dreams' hand from a fanboy's view, and would definitely recommend it to an average audience.

This game is very personal for me.  I bought this game as a part of a collection called the Star Wars Jedi Knight collection, and my God, was this a wise decision.
Years and years ago, back in 2003, this came was released and my Dad quickly bought the game...and one year later, I got my hands on a pirated version of the game (back when my Dad was a huge pirate) and I played the hell out of it.  Star Wars Jedi Knight: Jedi Academy is one of my most played games, and one of the only games that I was willing to finish over and over and over again as a child.  I didn't grow up with an SNES, NES, Atari, Comodore 64, or PS2...I grew up with this damn game.  And as soon as I saw this on sale I had to buy this, because this game was my goddamned childhood.
This is one of my favorite games of all-time for its amazing combat, horrible voice acting and great level design.  As I was playing through this game, as was absolutely astounded by how little it has aged...yeah, the graphics are quite dated, but the gameplay sure as hell isn't.
Swinging your lightsabre around feels so damn good, along with slicing people's arms off and running around with a blaster rifle, and is in my opinion, one of the few Star Wars games that have actually accomplished the feel of wielding a lightsabre, without a damn Kinect to immerse you in the lightsabre.
And as I mentioned before, the level design is top-notch, fitting the overall feel of each world that you go through and sets the overall tone for the world that you have selected.  The Rancor world makes you ♥♥♥♥ing scared, while the acid rain level gets this feeling of doom and dispair.  The gameplay is something that I have really missed with modern FPSs, andit's a damn shame we can't get another Star Wars game like this now that Lucas Arts is now a publishing company now that Disney owns Lucasfilm.
Star Wars Jedi Knight: Jedi Academy is a wonderful nostalgia trip for me, with great level design, satisfying lightsabre combat, great art design and a great final boss...that's why I recommend this game.

Uncloak and Pirate hapless enemies, Haul freight, Mine, Smuggle, command a Battleship with it's own fighters like Galactica, explore space with an independent powerful Cruiser with beams & torpedo loadout- it's all possible.

Random missions in Freeroam mode give you a foothold on things to do, but they are entirely optional. You can switch sides, and support any faction you like.

SPG2 may not have any entirely new concepts or features but it has taken a lot from past games and the end product does all the little things right.  Ultimately this game meets the same fate as Skyrim, a giant world that is unfortunately only about 5 feet deep.  While I have absolutely no regrets throwing out $28 for it, I can't help but feel this game will be so much better in a year thanks to workshop support and a dev team that truly cares about their B - level game.  While the voice acting is pretty bad, It isn't House of the Dead 2 bad so it's playable, other than the voices the sound is pretty good, I could wish for a few more effects and songs but that's just nitpicking.  The one thing I truly don't like about this game is the faction system, if you do assignments in the Trinity sector your reputation goes towards lawful...Which means all lawful factions like you more, the unlwaful (pirates) well, they never liked you anyway.  If I do things in the Trinity sectors I want perks in the Trinity sectors, not halfway across the solar system.
Unlike most titles I am actively looking forward to DLC for this game, which I'm hoping will greatly increase depth.

I've never had such a mixed opinion about a game. This game has some fairly frustrating technical problems in DirectX 12 (basically unplayable). I also think this entire episodic idea for Hitman is quite off putting for most (including me). The AI could be a lot better, they seem to ignore certain suspicious actions and path through certain objects. All that said, I found myself plesantly surprised by the Paris map (only story map currently available). It is by far the biggest sandbox map used in a Hitman game. In this map, the game provides you with an abundance of challenges, assassination methods and detail, lots and lots of detail. Given the number of approaches available on this map, the mission feels extremely different for each approach attempted. This does add a lot of replayability, and feels like a Blood Money mission on a much bigger scale.
I feel this game could have been received much better if they'd released all the content in one go and fixed all associated issues (it feels like a disguised early access game). I can't recommend anyone buy this in its current state, but I do believe this game has the potential to be better than Blood Money once all the content arrives.

You can look at the new HITMAN game from two different perspectives. Either you buy the full package and experience episodes as they come out over time, or you buy the intro pack and dip your feet in the experience that is the world of assassination. I for one went for the intro pack and I personally feel it was worth the purchase; despite knowing I have not purchased the full package.
Let me begin by saying that the intro pack is LOADED. Sure, you get 3 levels, 2 of which are training levels. One of the levels is an active real mission that takes you to Paris to assassinate 2 targets during a fashion show. On the surface, it does not sound like much, but IO Interactive gives you enough that replaying each mission (even the training levels) feels refreshing. This is because they introduced a challenge system that pushes you out of the bounderies of what you originally felt safe about in completing your goals. Another is unlocks.
Yes, unlocks that sounds so familiar from so many other games feels just right in HITMAN. In the real world mission, the unlocks gives you more opportunities that opens more doors of exploration and tactics that were either previously more difficult to obtain or just werent there from the get-go.
So perhaps that is not enough to satisfy your thirst or even worth the purchase. I understand that completely. IO then gives you Contracts mode; which is a psuedo-level maker borrowed from Abstraction. Basically you can assign an NPC to be assassinated in the same level and can be shared amongst friends or the public.
Then you have Escalation mode which increases the difficult of the game, by adding time limits or specific challenges that have to be completed.
Finally, there are the timed live events. These events come for a brief time which you have to assassinate a unique target that has not been seen in the game (but yes are still in the same level you've played previously).
If you're afraid the game will hold your hand, don't be. There are options that will make the game even more harder for you if you so choose. If you're a little lost, the game offers only a small hint on how to achieve your goals.
So far I've put in a couple of hours (I've been trying to hit all the challenges) and I have yet to actually complete the Paris mission primarily because I want to beat the level by killing my targets as perfectly as possible.
As for the game itself. It looks stunning! I have the graphics all at ultra settings and it doesn't even lag one bit. The load times are very quick (depending on your system of course, I put all my games on a Western Digital black series hard drive) and the menu system is elegant and simple. I have yet to really find any fault in the game. For the price, I honestly think you're getting more out of this intro pack than you would have from MGS: Ground Zeroes (which I paid 20 dollars for).  I would highly recommend the intro pack just to get a taste for the game. I wasn't too sure myself if I wanted the game, but now I would absolutely look forward in seeing the full release of the game.

Episodic Campaign, basically the two Beta levels (small maps) that you can replay over and over and the released campaign map - Paris, again play over and over (basically the Intro pack content).  Really they should have released at least 3 campaign levels (not including the beta ones) so you had some actual content before the next few are released.  I've heard some argue that the Paris map is very large and contains a large portion of Paris (i.e. open world), having played this game and been to Paris recently... ; what you really get is one building and it's surrounding gardens with a Paris scenic backdrop, all closed off from access along with most of the garden areas.
If you really want this game, wait for it to go on Christmas sale as the lack of content will lead to a massive reduction in cost by then which the developers deserve for "Releasing" a full cost product listed as an open and large world game; which is more like a tech demo and a dated one at that.  Gameplay is very much like all the other Hitman's before it and nothing significantly new or rewarding awaits.

Premium price for a freemium game.
After playing for a while, I can definitely say this is the best version of this game.
It's in HD and runs at a constant 60 FPS during every mission; sometimes dips during the menus, but they're menus, who cares.
Controller support is good, but it's either M/K or controller, so player one on controller and player two on M/K won't work yet.
There are no in-app purchases at all after buying the game. Unfortunately, that means that there is no double stars. To counter that, all upgrades are automatic and they seem to be a lot cheaper than in the phone version.
To play in the weekend tournament still requires having 3 friends who own this game. So you have to add random people to your friendlist or else you will never play in the weekend tournament.
There are only two modes in this game: the weekend tournament only on weekends, and the 15 levels. There is no boss rush mode, time attack, or anything like that from other typical shooters.
There are 15-minute cards still, just like the phone version, but the timer stops counting down when you exit the game. So you can save them for the next time you play.
All in all, I would recommend this game to most shmup fans, but I would suggest trying the free phone version first before putting money into this one.

The game is very shiny, the game physics feel like they're very good.   It's got 8-ball, 9-ball, Straight pool, 3 Ball, Rotation, Speed pool and they're going to add more.
The AI seems kinda bland, like all the AI opponents are just "I'll take 3 good shots and then screw up on purpose".  The opponents don't talk to you, and heck, you don't even see them walk around the table or anything.  I feel like they could have gone that extra mile to make the opponents in game seem more lively or personable.
There's also options for various kinds of customizations.  You have table decals (which range from the mildly distracting to the highly annoying), and decorative balls (all of which are EXTREMELY SHINY!).  You can even customize your pool cue though you'll barely notice that in game.  Finally you can change your game location from a huge room with a view, to a huge room with a view at night, and then to another room without that great of a view...  Again, I feel like they could have made the locations a bit more interesting instead of looking like you're inside a museum.
There's an upcoming "Trick shot" mode which may be amusing to play around with, and also snooker is promised as DLC (whether that's worth the extra price or not remains to be seen).
The music is a bit too "jazzy" or "technoish" for my tastes but you can turn the volume down.  It would be nice if each location had its own soundtrack (to add more personality to each place) but that could be asking for too much.  It would also be nice if you could tell the game your music folder location and let it play songs from that randomly.
All in all though, this is worth the full price, and if it's on sale, buy it now... I've already gotten my money's worth out of it.

This review is for the whole game with the Oil Upgrade which came out on 10/05/17. Oxygen Not Included is a true diamond in the rough and one of the most enjoyable games I've gotten my hands on, and it just keeps getting better with each new update.
At its heart right now, this game is mostly about digging, building, and managing systems to provide the resources your duplicants need to survive: oxygen, food. Klei has hinted that we might have other objectives in the final game, but for now this is all we have.
You also have to make sure they have areas they can go to relax or they will exhibit destructive behaviors that can range from mildy inconvenient to terrifying. With the recent updates, you also have to protect them from germs which is actually pretty easy when you get the hang of it, but your first few colonies are likely to fail until you figure it out.
One of the great strengths of this game is that there are multiple ways to do everything. As an example, every base needs power. Will you put your people on hamster wheels to provide clean energy? Will you build a hatch farm and use Coal for your power needs? Will you find Natural Gas geysers to provide steady but fixed power output? Will you expend the time and resources needed to refine oil and just run one huge petrol generator? Or a combination of all solutions?
Do you want one huge power grid with countless circuits running out from it via transformers, or do you want to create smaller one-circuit power grids around your base?
Your imagination is really the only limit to all of the possibilities, which gives this game TREMENDOUS replay value. I never get tired of pressing that "Start New Game" button.
The game is also largely about managing the by-products of your machines. When you build a machine to provide a resource you need, such as a Coal Generator to provide power, you'll need to deal with the waste products. In the case of the Coal Generator, it'll be Carbon Dioxide gas that your duplicants can't breathe.
You can filter this gas out of the air in multiple different ways, some of which produce even more byproducts you'll need to deal with.
A fully functional base that can take care of the byproducts of all machines is a beautiful sight, but takes many hours of practice understanding and mastering the different types of solids, gas and liquids in the game.
The developers are very responsive to bugs and often fix them within days, and are currently pushing for major updates every month or so. It's just going to get more complex and more interesting from here on out.

Starpoint Gemini 2 makes for a pretty enjoyable space sim experience, but it is very lacking in depth.  It tries so hard to give you the complexity one desires in a space sim with features like capturing ships using marines, scanning anomalies, and coming across derelicts just waiting to be scavenged, but in the end, these activities are very superficial.  They eventually become very routine and the rewards are often limited to money or experience.  Levelling up your character doesn't grant much satisfaction, except for when a perk point is given.
Not much is required before you'll be rocking around Gemini in the biggest ship the game has to offer, decked out with the biggest guns, with all the best upgrades.  Luckily, this doesn't make you the ultimate end-all-be-all combat god of the universe.  Combat appears to be balanced in such a way that you will always be vulnerable and dealing with this turns out to require very different strategies depending on the size of your ship.
Combat is one of the things this game does very well, and a challenge always awaits you as the game throws squadrons of enemies at you routinely, even the periodic Legendary or Hero ship, which offers an even greater challenge and huge money rewards for the latter.
Otherwise, this game seems like a pretty casual space sim.  You will get plenty of enjoyment out of it, but you won't get invested in it like you'd like, which makes the sub-40 dollar price tag perfect for the experience it offers.

Hitman is a great game for fans of the series but definitely has some cons right now.
PROS:
-Beautiful richly detailed environments (The amount of detail in the Paris level is impressive!)'
-Amount of interactable objects (Objects are strewn everywhere and the amount of objects able to be used in accidents is very nice)
-AI has gotten a facelift and is much much smarter than the previous games. Guards search areas, grow suspicous, and certain guards can immiediately become suspicious of your disguise. I like it a lot.
-Size of the levels are great (The Paris mission is HUGE! 3 stories of rooms to explore and new ways to kill your target can be found)
CONS:
-Poor optimization of the game (as of March 12th, one day after launch many people including myself are still experiencing framerate drops everywhere and a lower than expected framerate despite having powerful computers.)
-Long loading times for the menus (The menus take quite some time to appear. Perhaps maybe 2-3 seconds and it's slightly annoying. Pressing the F1 key for example to bring up the large map can take a couple seconds)
-Always "online" DRM. This is perhaps the biggest con and is something that is dissuading a lot of people from liking this game. You must always be connected to the internet while you play this game or else you will be ejected back to the main menu. When your internet comes back on you may reload a previous online save. It's ridiculous and I hope they remove this immiediately.
-Proximity triggers. Different events in the world have to be triggered before they happen. For example, Novikov in the Paris level descends down the stairs only when Agent 47 walks through the front door. Novikov only walks down the runway when you pass the guards having a conversation about the lights on the 3rd floor etc etc etc. Many people (including myself) would prefer a "universal timer" where NPCs act without any input from Agent 47. So Novikov would go through his entire route without needing any input from Agent 47. This system also has some pros and cons. Proximity triggers are much better for a large map. This way players can take their time exploring and finding the assassination method which works best. Universal triggers are better in a way because they are much more realistic and require faster decisions from the player.
BOTTOMLINE:
Hitman is a great addition to the franchise through it's addition of beautiful sandbox like missions (ala Blood Money) and it's new AI. There are still some terrible glaring cons such as the online DRM and very poor optimization. I don't consider the episodic release to be a con. Don't listen to any review here that complains it only has "one level". The video game is episodic and it's right in the store description. I have faith in IO Interactive and that they'll do the right thing and release patches to better the performance and HOPEFULLY remove the online DRM. These two actions would unleash Hitman's potential to be a great game.

HOW TO PLAY HITMAN
1 - Wait 24 hours after launch, server connectivity issues no longer a problem after 12 year old vloggers make their unboxing, tutorial, walkthrough, let's play, and review videos, then promply return to their medal of duty: hardlines playing and never pick up this game again
2 - Run the Benchmark, if your card can't run it smoothely at max settings, turn the settings to "MEDIUM" <-- important step sometimes people forget how PC gaming works especially if you're coming from a console
3 - Launch the game.
4 - Before starting the tutorial, go to the gameplay settings and turn off all the in-game help and assists. You don't need them, seriously. Figuring stuff out on your own is kind of the point of the game.
5 - Now play the first episode of the best hitman game ever made.
6 - Cross your fingers that future episodes will be at least as good.
There. It's not as hard as these other reviews make it seem.

The game is very shiny, the game physics feel like they're very good.   It's got 8-ball, 9-ball, Straight pool, 3 Ball, Rotation, Speed pool and they're going to add more.
The AI seems kinda bland, like all the AI opponents are just "I'll take 3 good shots and then screw up on purpose".  The opponents don't talk to you, and heck, you don't even see them walk around the table or anything.  I feel like they could have gone that extra mile to make the opponents in game seem more lively or personable.
There's also options for various kinds of customizations.  You have table decals (which range from the mildly distracting to the highly annoying), and decorative balls (all of which are EXTREMELY SHINY!).  You can even customize your pool cue though you'll barely notice that in game.  Finally you can change your game location from a huge room with a view, to a huge room with a view at night, and then to another room without that great of a view...  Again, I feel like they could have made the locations a bit more interesting instead of looking like you're inside a museum.
There's an upcoming "Trick shot" mode which may be amusing to play around with, and also snooker is promised as DLC (whether that's worth the extra price or not remains to be seen).
The music is a bit too "jazzy" or "technoish" for my tastes but you can turn the volume down.  It would be nice if each location had its own soundtrack (to add more personality to each place) but that could be asking for too much.  It would also be nice if you could tell the game your music folder location and let it play songs from that randomly.
All in all though, this is worth the full price, and if it's on sale, buy it now... I've already gotten my money's worth out of it.

Klei's latest game seems set to become a micro-management classic.
ONI builds upon many of the relatively recently established conventions of the 'fortress management' genre, but as always Klei have added their own unique humour and style of systems focused gameplay to this mix.
This is probably the most micro-management focused game of this genre (even compared to the likes of Dwarf Fortress and Rimworld), owing to the ability (and requirement) to control the flow of gas, liquids and their interaction with other elements of the world. At times, the combination of tricky expansion and involved wiring and piping reminded me of both Boulder Dash clones and Tim's Incredible Machine.
It is complex but the implementation is logical and consistent. The game offers a fun strategic puzzle - gradually expand and improve technology whilst paying attention to things like oxygen supply, environmental hazards and more. The more you expand, the greater the resource demands are, so planning expansion is strategic but does not seem overwhelming (as it can in other games).
Some players who have been playing the game previous to the recent update (which added germs/illness to the game) have commented negatively. However, having only played post-germs I did not find managing this aspect too difficult or bothersome. It does not affect the early game too much, and adds a needed layer of strategy and upkeep to the base after ~6 hours or so of gameplay.
I would recommend this game to any micro-management fans (or fans of Don't Starve's system-based gameplay). The game is relaxing, has a great atmosphere and style, presents interesting and evolving gameplay challenges, and the difficulty feels already well balanced.

Millia -The Ending- is a short but sweet visual novel about the lengths one would go to protect the simles of loved ones. Despite the lack of polish overall, I fully enjoyed the story and what it had to offer. It's paced so well that I was able to become emotionally invested in these four characters in such a short amount of time, and every ending wraps up things nicely.
For $5, you can't go wrong with this purchase. It's not the end all of visual novels by any means, but I found it to be really refreshing compared to all the other VNs on Steam right now. I recommend it to those just looking for a casual, fun, and emotional read. Why I asked for a refund for HITMAN:
Prior to my purchase I had read the information about the game and the plan for it to be an episodic release so this was no suprise to me.  However, the reality of only being able to play on just a hand full of levels for at least a month before a new map is released is just not something that feels right for a game like Hitman.  This current release build feels more like a demo that you pay for.  Coupled with the online server issues that prevent you from accessing material or losing your progress are further proof that this game simply is not ready for release yet.  In the future when the game becomes stable to play with its always online function and there is a moderate enough content to play through I will likely look at revisiting this title.  The potential for a good game is here, but it is not included in this premature release.

After many years those "bugs" were transformed in people minds into "techniques", again like in chivalry .. "advanced techniques". 4.) Shame about this game is how people played it during years, how the way of playing this game constantly changed into something disgusting in my opinion. People in years like 2003-2006 or even 2007 relied more on timing and footwork and proper clean killing, nowadays its block festival, those few people who still playing this artifact are just crouching and blockwiggling everything, it looks noobish and disgusting because of thousands ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ sparks everywhere, and mainly because block system in this game is highly random. Well to cut a long story short, it might look like this game has more negatives but I would still recommend it, personally I played it since end of 2004  til end of 2013 and ocassionaly play it once for a while because this game is part of my childhood. Brief summary of game: you command a bunch of people, called duplicants, to build your base.  You assign tasks of varying prority and the duplicants automatically respond. Lots of resources are required to sustain duplicant life, and most of your time will be spent on this.
Game seems interesting, but at this current point in development, I would say the game is worth about 10-15 bucks. The reason I am put off from this game isn't because of an accumulation of small problems, but rather because of the fundamental features/designs of this game. Here are the three big headaches I get when playing this game:
Resources such as water and oxygen get used up rather aggressively as the game goes on, even though these resources are essential for your duplicants AND they arent renewable. This means that you are on a never ending quest to find more water and oxygen (either directly or from other resources which can be converted). A couple hours into every game I start, and I find that I spend most of my time simply transporting oxygen and water across the base.
The problem with the stress system is that duplicants will level up their skills as time progresses, which is directly correlated to their decor requirements, creating the growing problem of needing more and more decor/stress relievers. The problem is that these individuals progress their skills indefinitely, leading to a runaway problem involving a colony full of ungrateful, uncivilized mooks who would sit around contributing to colony collapse just because their hubris demands that they stop, drop, and f*ck all, unless they were treated like royalty.
This last one really seemed like the game questioned my intelligence. If I queue up the task to build some structures, and I also queue up the task to mine some walls, it really busts my nut when I find out that the guy with lvl 9 digging/lvl 1 construction is building all my structures, and the lvl 1 diggin/lvl 9 construction guy is mining the walls. Does the game expects me to be perfectly okay this? NO, go f*ck yourselves. Also sometimes I queue up a task, and it sends some guy from halfway across my base to respond to this task, when there is a perfectly healthy individual sitting 5 feet away. F*ck you again.
All in all, I'm sure this game will get better along the line, and all it's rough edges will be rounded off, because of my faith in Klei, but if you're looking for a good time, go watch porn instead.

The latest update has elevated this to the most satisfying trading simulation I have ever had the pleasure of playing. Not only can you see what various commodities are trading for at the stations you have visited, you also see the distance you currently are from each of those stations. This adds another level of decision making – is the extra distance you might have to travel for a ‘best’ price worth the time it will take to get there, or is a slightly lower price actually the better deal? A small thing, perhaps, but it does make you approach your cargo manifest a bit more critically when deciding on what and when to trade.
The second thing this encourages is exploration. You only see the prices for the stations and planets you have discovered. I find myself compelled to push into unknown territory on that never ending quest for the ultimate trade route. And the commodity information screen itself is wonderfully easy to use. The filters are a tremendous help, eliminating the need to scroll through every item available. Are you a miner? Click on ores. Love to hunt down pirates? Quickly discover who is offering the best price for those contraband items.
As you may have guessed, I’m a merchant at heart, not a fighter. But I’ve found the battles to be well-balanced and a simple click will tell you if that tantalizing enemy ship you have your eye on has the capability to turn you into so much space dust. Not that the knowledge will necessarily stop you, but at least you’ll know what you’re up against. And for those times when you do take on just a bit more than you can chew and yet somehow manage to pull it off by the skin of your shields, well – you know the feeling.
The graphics are gorgeous, the gameplay is addicting, and personalizing your ship is as much fun as creating a new character in most RPGs. At this point the only thing I’m hoping for is that we may eventually see a larger collection of avatar portraits. The new group was a nice addition, but as a female gamer I find the two current offerings lack some of the personality that the male portraits possess. And that something so minor is the only flaw I can find says a lot about how truly innovative and honestly fun this game is.
Now if you’ll excuse me, I have a trade empire to build.

This is an interesting little game, but it still needs some work. The developer is active on the forums and seems intent on polishing it further, so I will recommend that you check it out if you’re interested in a fun take on a streamlined space 4X game. If you are looking instead for a polished game I would say that you look for something else, even though the game’s price tag isn’t exactly going to be much of an obstacle.
In this game, you’ll be able to colonize planets, build fleets, conduct research, engage in (very minor) diplomacy, and so forth. However, each planet will only be able to perform a single task: build a ship, send out a colony, attack, and so forth. Most of the time, you’ll give a few planets some orders and then click ‘Auto’ in the ‘Empire’ menu to have all of your other planets simply generate revenue for you to spend next turn.
I like the graphics, despite the fact that they were obviously made for a much smaller screen (see below). I especially like the character design for the different alien races, with the Dev’Orn – a warrior species where individuals appear to be encased in metal armour – a particular favourite of mine. I feel that with some spit and polish, the game can be improved remarkably.
In short, this is an interesting game with lots of potential. I love 4X games, but I seldom have the time to spend 20 hours in a single campaign. I’d prefer for there to be more games that give you a 4X fix without being so time-consuming. As such, I’m always interested in more streamlined approaches to space conquest games in the mould of the original Master of Orion, and as such Vincero Totus Astrum caught my attention.
Sadly, there are a few negative aspects that I wish to point out in hopes that the developer may be able to address them. This is a mobile port – the game was originally released on iOS – and as such the interface feels a little large and cumbersome on my 21", 1080p screen. For example, I wish that fleets that were stationed at a planet were indicated using an icon. Right now, when you look at the map, you won’t be able to tell which planets have fleets and which don’t unless you select the planet in question and check out the ‘Deploy’ menu or go to the Colony information screen.
Likewise, the game doesn’t tell you at all if an enemy planet has a fleet stationed there. Before combat, you have to select a few options, such as how to deploy your fleet, but when you have no clue as regards the composition of the enemy fleet, how can you make any meaningful decisions? Do they have a small fleet composed entirely of fighters, or a large fleet complete with frigates and capital vessels? There is, as far as I can tell, no way to find out, except perhaps later via espionage. The game is stingy when it comes to doling out useful information.
I’ve also encountered strange bugs (?) when attacking an enemy planet. Sometimes, I appear to have destroyed the enemy fleet, but the planet doesn’t switch to my side. According to the in-game help, a planet should join your empire if all defences in the system have been taken down. Secondly,  whenever the battle results in a draw (with you, as the player, being the attacker), the game treats it as if nothing happened. You can use the same planet to attack again, using the exact same ships to fight the enemy fleet, with apparently none of the casualties of the previous battle having been removed from either fleet.
Finally, the text in the game is marred by typos and grammar mistakes. The in-game help is much appreciated, but the text is a little mangled at times. Likewise, the introductory texts displayed at the start of the game also suffer from mistakes. Here’s a bit from the Dev’Orn: ‘We are prepared to being conquering [sic] the galaxy Sire,’ and so forth. Punctuation seems to be all over the place, and there are also quite a few run-on sentences. That’s a pity, since there’s not a huge amount of text in the game; these errors could be easily corrected. I’d even volunteer for that.
