I have no idea why Hitman has 49% reviews on Steam, most of the reviews don't even review the game!
Let me just say the following:
I'm running a PC which has a motherboard and CPU from 2011, the graphics card is a GTX 960 4GB and I'm able to run the game at a steady 60 FPS on High. I haven't tried Ultra because I don't know what performace I'd get.
I was hyped for Hitman, and I bought the game in advance on Steam mostly because I had the money then for the game. I also bought the "Full Experience", which by the way will get you the entirety of the game because IO/Square decided episodic content was a cool idea. I can't say much about episodic content since really only indie games and/or story driven games get that, and I don't have much experience with them.
After being let down by XCOM 2 as a whole, and being dissapointed in Just Cause 3's performance (and it forcing a GPU upgrade) I was weary to get into Hitman with another pre-order.
At the Hitman Beta, I was not dissapointed. I highly enjoyed it and I think it calmed my fears.
Let me just say, Hitman is probably (going to be) one of the best in the series. The game has gone to large expansive locations, with lots to do and see. Gameplay is taken almost directly from Absolution, but with the maps having been made large as well as the game taking a much less story driven approach, Hitman hits all the right buttons.
I'll be honest, I haven't played Hitman all that much, being busy IRL, but I can tell you this will probably be one of the best AAA titles this year.
On the topic of the DRM: always online hasn't bothered me that much. I fortunately live somewhere where the DSL broadband is pretty decent, although relatively slow and those complaining at the DRM seem almost to be entited ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s... Also BTW, this isn't actually DRM (because Steam is the DRM), it's some sort of online tracking system which is weird.
Just Cause 3 had this similar problem. Optimisation was poor, although it got better and people complained of an "always online DRM" althogh it was actually just the online leaderboards system which was just poorly implemented and just wasted your time when it lost a connection.
Pretty much, it's good in its current state. £10.99 is probably worth it currently, £39.99 will hopefully be worth it once it becomes a full game.

Lemme make this clear. This is going to be a long review and a detailed one at that.
Euro Truck Simulator 2 is possible the best simulator for heavy vehicals out there and maybe even the best simulator for vehicals in general (not including racing simulators of course). Its great graphics, scenery, playability and the fact that you dont need a great PC to play it are just some of the few reasons why this game is so good. Im actually planing on buying a steering wheel for it, for myself at Christmas time. The graphics are really good and as I said dont require a beast PC to run them on. The trucks themselves have so much detail which they should considering that it is based on trucking and truck driving. Another really good point about this game is that it really helps stress. You will lose a lot of stress playing this game. It is really, really good at realiving stress and helping to make your day better. I know that you may not believe me because it is a truck driving game but you wont believe it till you play it. Another fact is that this game is not that expensive. I managed to pick it up for $10 with a bunch of DLC. I bought the Interior Decorator DLC even though all it does is get decorations on the interior of the truck.
TL:DR: It is really good and you should buy it.
For the multiplayer side of things.
Multiplayer is just as good if not better then singleplayer. It brings everything that I just mentioned before hand and also brings your friends into the game. It does have some downfalls however and you should be careful. First off if someone says to join their teamspeak because they want you to join their trucking clan or whatever DONT DO IT (Yes this is a thing and it happened to me a few days ago [from writing this review]). Another problem you may experience but I have only experienced once are griefers. They will purposely crash into your truck and you will be fined and will also be damaged but as I said it is rare. The only other bad thing that I could think of but hasnt happened to me yet is FPS lag. You may experience frame drops but as I said I havent experienced it yet. Even then the game doesnt require a beast PC so you probably wont realize the frame drops.
TL:DR: Same as singleplayer but with friends.

Definitely recommended.
Perhaps plot wise this isn't anything new - saving the world from evil is hardly a new theme - but what makes this interesting that you play as Dracula himself. He could be good or bad and that depends literally on the player. Choices matter! That is really an interesting aspect that I haven't really seen a lot on hidden object games. So the story isn't new in its genre, but everything else makes up for it.
So, the characters. Besides Dracula, they're not particularly multilayered, but it doesn't matter. HOGs are rarely as much about characters as they are about playing a detective. In this case, the relationships between characters are quite interesting and change, depending on your choices. It was quite humorous at points too, especially the quarrels between Van and Igor.
The art is really, really nice. Dark on one areas, light on others, more realistic on some and fantasy like on the rest. It was extremely nice to look at. Though the Queen Of Vampires' hair is a bit ridiculous..
Gameplay is pretty easy, but some of the puzzles are hard. And the thing is, that even if there's a strategy guide, it doesn't always offer help. I think it's a slight minus because you immediately lose a chance to get one achievement. If there's a strategy guide, it should have solutions to ALL puzzles, no exception. But there was quite a lot of puzzles I haven't seen in other games - or can't remember at the moment - and nice power ups to collect that helped you along the game.
I don't know if it's my PC or not, but the cut scenes seem a bit... buggy, I guess it's the word. Voice comes on time, but the rest of it doesn't. It's better than in the physical copy, so I didn't mind.
Since I mentioned the physical copy, I have one. I can't use it anymore but the fact that I bought a version on Steam should tell you something. It was one of the first HOGs I've ever played and I still like it a lot. For the price it has, I don't think it's a bad game at all.

Dracula: Love Kills is a hidden item and puzzle game.  I enjoy these types of games as a welcome break from frenetic action games.  This one is particularly good this time of year (I played it 3 weeks before Halloween).  The story is fun and the voice acting is cheesy/good.  The painted artwork is lovely and the settings add a nice gothic atmosphere.  The  puzzles range from quite easy to very challenging, but you should never get stuck because there is a hint system available and an option to skip puzzles if needed, thereby eliminating frustrations and letting you move on with the story.  The game is a good value for the $10 pricetag.  It has a lot of replayability since you'll often want to retry areas to improve your time or chase achievements.  If you enjoy hidden item games, I would also suggest the Midnight Mysteries series.  Happy Gaming.

For a slightly older game, Dracula: Love Kills has aged remarkably well. It even holds up against many recent cookie-cutter HOPAs. The story is nothing special, but the voice acting is silly enough that you probably "von't" care. It carries its weight where it matters, through great art, varied and challenging puzzles, and clever HOGs. Definitely worth a play (or two if you're going for both endings and 100% achievements).
As stereotypically "vampire" as it gets, with a heavy dose of camp. Dracula ironically teams up with Van Helsing to defeat a megalomaniacal vampire queen (who apparently wants to cover the world in some kind of crimson Zerg creep). The bulk of the game is their quest to collect various items to appease a bunch of dead vampire-slayer knights in order to gain access to a super-mega-ultra-magic-vampire-slayer dagger, because it's the only thing that can kill the queen (no spoilers, you learn all that within the first few minutes of the game). Dracula obtains a few vampy powers along the way (telekinesis, bat form, etc.), and amusingly ends up acting like a frustrated dad when Van Helsing and Igor keep exchanging schoolyard-worthy barbs.
Depending on how you deal with all of the queen's lady minions (kill or spare) during the main game, you'll get one of two endings to the epilogue/bonus chapter. The 'choice matters' thing is a nice touch, because it actually makes a difference. Not a huge one, but you'll get some alternate dialogue between the good and evil paths, and a totally different companion in the epilogue.
The writing is standard fare, with visual novel style click-to-advance dialogue. It's not perfect, and suffers from more than a few errors in grammar, but the slip-ups sort of dissolve under the characters' ridiculously put-on accents. I didn't find the silliness of the characters or accents annoying though. It's more like the over-the-top acting you'd see in a Mel Brooks film. "Young Frankenstein" was very likely an inspiration for Igor, for example. It really helps that the accents, while hammed up and stereotyped, are stereotyped
(which is a weird thought, I know). I would go so far as to say that the voice acting itself is a big part of what makes this game enjoyable. It's self aware, like a decent B-movie that doesn't take itself too seriously, yet has a good production value nonetheless.
The hidden object scenes are
well-constructed in this game. All of them. Even in the epilogue. There aren't any two-step items, animated bits, or other bells and whistles you find in more recent HOGs - just a static list and a cluttered scene. But they're GOOD scenes. If you've played a crap-ton of these things, you know that many HOGs fall short because of bad scale, placement, art, missing object bugs, or things hidden
well (in a bad way). In contrast, here the scenes are nicely composed and feel totally organic. The artist(s) did a great job of making everything seem like "normal" clutter, so it really is a genuine challenge to find things. There are a couple of mild mistranslations, like referring to pliers or tweezers as "pincers", "shovel" referring to a trowel, or a vase being called a jar. But considering that the incorrect words are all objects/tools with the same basic function as the intended words, it's not really bothersome.
Regular gameplay scenes feature an extra quasi-hidden object hunt in the form of vials of blood that help fill your "power meter". There's an achievement for finding all of them.
There's a large variety of puzzles with an overall average to above-average difficulty. There are a few really simple no-brainers, a handful of classic board games like Go or Connect-4, a fair amount of the typical stuff that shows up in nearly every HOPA in existence, and several that were surprisingly challenging in a "this is frustrating but I understand the logic enough not to ragequit" sort of way. There were a handful that I got impatient with and had to look up, the biggest offenders being the stone tile rooster, "capture the snake", and one where you push small tiles around to match a given configuration (mainly because of the tile placement rules). But I'm not really complaining, because I love it when a game like this really makes me think.
Puzzles just start with no info/rules pop-up. There's a "?" button that gives you basic instructions, but a bunch of them don't explain the objective very well. I found the in-game strategy guide ("SG" in the lower left) more descriptive in those cases.
Nicely rendered. No awkward 3D, just hand-drawn art. The cutscenes are a bit iffy because of a needlessly shaky "camera", but in general the static visual novel style character cutouts work well for the title.
I already mentioned how the over-the-top accents add a lot to the game, but the music and SFX are pretty good too. Maybe it's just me, but I like it when developers take the time to make sure little things like button rollovers or item pickups sound satisfying. You hear them so much over the course of the game, so it's important that they aren't grating.
You have all the time in the world for the actual HOGs and puzzles, but your overall time playing the game is actively tracked. You can see your time from both the main menu and the "Honors" tab of your book in game. The timer stops when you exit to the main menu, as opposed to Steam's timer, which continues to run while at the main menu. This is crucial, because if you're going for the "
" achievement, you need to complete the main game in under 5 hours (according to the game's timer, so exit to the menu for potty breaks) during your FIRST playthrough on a profile. It's a bit of a dumb idea, because rushing through a first playthrough is the opposite of what most people do, and what sucks is that if you miss it and go over 5 hours, you need to start an entirely new profile and replay to try again. What I did was quickly move through the dialogue ("next", not "skip") without paying too much attention to it. I finished with no HOG or puzzle skips in under 3.5 hours, so there's wiggle room for reading everything if you're also fast with the minigames. But I figured I'd just read stuff the second time around on Hard  mode.
is worthy of a spot on your "Play Next" list. It has the satisfying combination of good length and presentation, well-constructed HOGs, and nice puzzle variety/difficulty. The tongue-in-cheek (but well-done) goofy accents may not be everyone's cup of tea, but if you go in expecting a bit of ham to go with your cheese, you're gonna have a good time.
One of the better hidden object games I've tried. Yes, the voice acting is a joke, but there's a good amount of hidden object puzzles, and the difficulty level was just right.

This game is apparently a sequel to 'Dracula Origins' published by the same company, but I've not played that game (yet). I still had no trouble following the story; Dracula is woken up by his servant and together with him and Van Helsing they set on a quest to find Mina; the love of Dracula's life who had been kidnapped by the Queen of Vampires.
As you progress in the game you unlock new vampire powers to use in your quest.
The game has many positives; superb voice acting from all characters, a lot of humour in the dialogues, high quality in the looks of both scenes and characters, and the sweet words of 'Location complete' when you have completed a location (duh). The game also shows on the map where there are things to be done, even in the hardest of modes. The different locations across the world are also pretyt interesting and well done.
The game also has at least two possible endings, depending on your choices throughout the game. These choices also comes into the viewpoint of the bonus chapter.
I left the game on a lot while afk, so my game time means nothing; but I was actually surprised to see I got the achievement for finishing within 5 hours.
All puzzles can be skipped or hinted through, but then will not get you the achievement. You cna however spam hint as much as you like outside of the HO scenes.
Negative for the game is probably that the HO scenes can get easy as you, if you click slow enough on hard mode or spamclick on easy, can pretty much click on every item and eventually get the scene complete without looking at the items you need. The scenes are usually so cluttered though, that it's not that easy this way. All scenes are played at least twice, so you get familiar with them.
Another negative, though small, is how easily Van Helsing and Dracula teams up after just been mortal enemies.
The game also pauses on alt+tab, so you may not ditch out of the cutscenes or dialogues that way (there is an achievement for not skipping any of that). It is useful for the 'finish in 5 hours' achievement though.
Small note; the game Dracula's Legacy, another HOG, has nothing to do with this game and is from another company completely. I did have a sad :(

Honestly, I like it. It's a decent game, it has a strong core and does have entertaining values inside of it. It's pretty, runs well on my AMD machine, and keeps you at least somewhat busy. However, there are some very odd issues and difficulties I have with the game, I'll list them below.
Game is too light; When I say this, I mean that the game is not that deep. The statistics for ships is relegated to a few simple stats (such as hull, cargo and crew). I feel that if I'm going to be driving around a big ship, I'd wanna know more about what's going on with it's internal systems. What makes ship A better than ship B? Well look at hull, cargo and troop capacity. That's it. Where's my statistics?
Scaling for ship size; This is actually a big complaint. The ships don't look..big. They don't have imposing statures or good camera angles. They don't refelct how big (or small) they actually are. I have a small gunship and I'll go past ships marked as frigates or destroyer and I can't tell a size difference. That makes no sense to me. Sure, if I get within "I'll melt you with point blank lasers range" I'll notice a very small difference, but otherwise it's hard to tell. Reminds me of Star Trek (the show).
Lots of loot, nothing to do with it; There's a plethora of loot in the game. Computers, drugs, minerals and ores. ALL YOU CAN DO IS SELL THEM. You can't craft, you can't allocate them for energy on the ship, they are just fluff. They don't have any real impact on the game other than that they can be sold (and what's worse, caputring enemy ships is far more benificial). I wish there was an in depth crafting system, something.
Notifications; The game does not notify you when you pick up loot, meaning, that when I loot a ship with the "auto loot" function, it does not tell me what I got! I have to go into my menues and see what was put in. A prime example of how this is bad. I looted a big ship once, got an AMAZING missle system. I didn't know I had it, it never notified me. So I spent 250,000 credits on a missle system (worse by the way) and then, while equping it, realized I had the other one. Bye bye money!
Camera angles; Not dynamic, not good. No cockpit view. Sadface.
No real interaction with the universe; I will have to state, this is one of my biggest issues. Doing freelance quests gives you no satisfaction. When I'm picking up a VIP to transport, no chat initiates. It's a simple grab and go. Even the quest text is shallow. "Pick up A, drop off at B." There's no context as to what I'm doing this for. When I have a mission to go kill some pirate, there's nothing to it. It's just "We of the Such-and-such want Pirate dead". That's it! There's no interaction with the universe around you, it's all text and empty requests. You can't even interact with the ships system officers!! There's never a point where I feel truly a part of a living organism, I feel like the ONLY living organism in the game.
Difficulty; Thus far, it makes no sense. I'll take on a quest to kill a pirate that's my level. Then I'll go to said zone and find that the pirate has two or more friends and he himself is listed as "Impossible" for my skill level. WHY? The game never notified me on what gear I should have when. The ships I'm going up against are a cool 2-10 MILLION credits, where as in my entire game play, dedicating time to making credits, I've made roughtly 800,000 at most, at one time. I read a forum post stating that some people ran into a sinkhole of difficulty, they leveled up too fast and the game scaled their enemies up too high, too quick. My point is, leveling should be more fluid and less wreckless. Don't allow me to level up to level 20 when I can't afford/fight level 20 ranked ships. EXP needs to be reworked, slow down leveling.
Class "System"; It's strait forward and dull. No real custiomization other than "Put point here, see marginal benifits". It's like old school WoW. Funny enough above I listed the games not deep, but it has a +% based level system. That's okay, I get it. But my skills don't feel impact, even against trivial ranked enemies, they still melt through my shield and kill me.
I could go on, there's a lot to complain about with this game. However, give it a shot. If you really like space-sandbox-adventure action, you can't go wrong here. But there's better out there.

This is a unique idle game, and for real, one of the only game that deserves the name "idle game". It is quite confusing when you first start because there are lots of tabs and you are unable to use many but that's not what happens in idle games. You can use a guide or just do it my way; nevermind.

At first I was very skeptical about this - what can a free *idle* game be, other than boring and loaded with microtransactions, after all? The interface is not very polished either.
BUT after having played for a while, things totally make sense. Real money is not required to advance, albeit patience is required, which is fine for an idle game.
The game plays like a very abstract economy build up game. Think of civilisation without a map. You optimize different parameters that in turn increase your rate of progress. The whole challenge is to distribute current resources optimally across a variety of settings in order to progress at maximal speed.
Check out the FAQ and the forums for information on how to play, you need it. But the game is not too hard to learn.
It is a game that I play in work breaks - as an idle game it is not meant for continuos play. For that purpose the concept makes the game fun and a good interruption of work. You constantly get a little feeling of progress.
Thumbs up, check it out!

This was a great game for me, nice car driving gameplay and decent melee combat. The story is mediocre but has its highlights but.
The real kicker for the game however is the setting, THIS IS MAD MAX. Rarely does a game based on a movie do as well as this game.
If you like Mad Max, deserts, post-apocalyptic settings or just crazy driving then this is the open world game for you.

It's Shadows of Mordor with a better story, guns, and fast vehicles. They did a really good job with this one. Details abound, from visible changes to vehicles to little touches on enemy clothing. Yes, combat can get a bit repetitive, but overall it never feels like a grind (except for the damned minefields. Those suck, but thankfully they're not a huge part of the game).
And there's something viscerally satisfying about driving your car off a cliff, powered by nitrous, and hoping you land without blowing up. Or driving over some scavenger at top speed, who would love nothing more than to beat you dead if given the chance.
Melee combat is fun, even if a bit overpowered (especially in late-game, when you're near invincible). The approach to the level-up system is novel, though I won't spoil the storyline there.
All in all, this is a fun game that I wholly recommend to anyone who enjoyed Shadows of Mordor, or the Arkham games.  Especially when it's on sale, like it happens to be as I write this review, it's worth picking up.

I have no idea why Hitman has 49% reviews on Steam, most of the reviews don't even review the game!
Let me just say the following:
I'm running a PC which has a motherboard and CPU from 2011, the graphics card is a GTX 960 4GB and I'm able to run the game at a steady 60 FPS on High. I haven't tried Ultra because I don't know what performace I'd get.
I was hyped for Hitman, and I bought the game in advance on Steam mostly because I had the money then for the game. I also bought the "Full Experience", which by the way will get you the entirety of the game because IO/Square decided episodic content was a cool idea. I can't say much about episodic content since really only indie games and/or story driven games get that, and I don't have much experience with them.
After being let down by XCOM 2 as a whole, and being dissapointed in Just Cause 3's performance (and it forcing a GPU upgrade) I was weary to get into Hitman with another pre-order.
At the Hitman Beta, I was not dissapointed. I highly enjoyed it and I think it calmed my fears.
Let me just say, Hitman is probably (going to be) one of the best in the series. The game has gone to large expansive locations, with lots to do and see. Gameplay is taken almost directly from Absolution, but with the maps having been made large as well as the game taking a much less story driven approach, Hitman hits all the right buttons.
I'll be honest, I haven't played Hitman all that much, being busy IRL, but I can tell you this will probably be one of the best AAA titles this year.
On the topic of the DRM: always online hasn't bothered me that much. I fortunately live somewhere where the DSL broadband is pretty decent, although relatively slow and those complaining at the DRM seem almost to be entited ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s... Also BTW, this isn't actually DRM (because Steam is the DRM), it's some sort of online tracking system which is weird.
Just Cause 3 had this similar problem. Optimisation was poor, although it got better and people complained of an "always online DRM" althogh it was actually just the online leaderboards system which was just poorly implemented and just wasted your time when it lost a connection.
Pretty much, it's good in its current state. £10.99 is probably worth it currently, £39.99 will hopefully be worth it once it becomes a full game.

This game made an excellent overall impression. The format, while still familiar, is a welcome break from the cookie-cutter puzzle/HO products that populate the market. Not only are the HO scenes well crafted (they rely on clever or innocuous placement of objects rather than the common cop-outs of fading or obscuring them), but the progression sequences, while heavy on the collection of item sets for puzzles, also at least tend to make consistent sense, as opposed to all those games in which you might be asked to forgo your crowbar and find the tiny key to that shatterable glass cabinet. Indeed, the general flow of the story is far more linear and logical than the winding, obtuse, quasi-Wonderland adventures into which we are so often flung. The puzzles are mostly in the same vein of those you'd find anywhere, but a sprinkling of fresh ones (a version of the game Connect Four, for example) keeps them interesting. The most unique addition is the inclusion of vampiric powers - fueled, naturally, by imbibing blood - which act as keys to otherwise inaccessible items.
The big problems here are the game's storytelling, attempts at roleplay, and sheer repetition. The interpretation of the supposed source material (the Bram Stoker novel) is downright laughable when it isn't simply cringeworthy. Dracula himself looks like he was scanned from the cover of a bad romance novel, and sounds - I kid you not - like Antonio Banderas; Van Helsing, an unassuming Dutchman in the book, is rendered as an imposing English noble with a fashion sense ironically more akin to what we traditionally associate with the titular vampire; and Igor is just a pathetic character with an even more pathetic voice who quickly becomes the Jar Jar of the game. The game also tries its hand at roleplaying, letting you choose either to "turn" or set loose each of the three or four minions of the villainess, promising that there will be "consequences" to your choice. In practice these consequences are reduced to a different outcome at game's end, which for most of us comes second fiddle to the actual puzzle/HO gameplay for which we're really signing up. The other motivation in these choices is supposed to be securing blood to charge Drac's special powers, but since the use of these powers is always necessary to proceed, the game is forced to give you the required number of (scarcely concealed) bottles of blood, simply plucked from the environment, which renders the only "consequence" the need to take three seconds to find these in each scene. Finally, the game's formula does get quite old after a time - collect tools and sets of puzzle pieces, complete puzzles, repeat until chapter is complete, repeat until game is complete - but, let's be honest, that's kind of just expected.
Despite all this, the truth is that this game is actually a breath of fresh air. Longer than most, far more innovative than most, and sometimes more creative than most, it's the first of the genre in a long time to make me feel like I was playing an entirely new game. That means something in this market, don't you think?

1. Static universe: Dockable stations and space objects like satellites/gas collectors are all fixed and indestructible. Ships simply spawn, get destroyed and spawn again. Player actions do not have any impact on the universe whatsoever which is a shame because all territories (hexes on the starchart) have an owner and player let wars which lead to territories being conquered would make the universe much more dynamic.
2. Factions are uninspired and interchangeable (see 3.). There is no dynamic between for example traders and pirates. Either a faction is good or evil and will attack all other evil or good factions. All factions could be reduced to 3, one good, one evil and one "I hate you no matter what you do" faction.
3. Weak reputation system: Your reputation with a faction is based solely on your alignment (good/evil). All factions are either aligned with good or evil (there are no neutral factions). When having a high(good) reputation all good factions will be friendly and you can not antagonize a single one of them without antagonizing all
4. User Interface: The game lacks shortcuts for basic actions like docking. There is only a "quick action" shortcut which is used for dropping fast travel AND docking. Should you be in range for docking you will dock otherwise drop fast travel and slowly crawl towards the station until you can dock.
5. Missions: The current mission types are extremely basic kill, protect, fly to and transport missions. They get reptetitive fast.
6. Voice acting is bad: Even if you try to get immersed in the campaign storyline, chances are good that the awful voice acting will make it impossible.
Strong points:
1. Seamless universe
2. Fast travel systems are interesting and remain useful throughout the game with unique pros and cons
I recommend to wait a few month for either the devs or modding community to add more content to the game.

A rather compelling sim game which initially looks simple but the deeper you delve in the more there is to it. An easy going open ended style has you try to get grants based on how you wish to run your prison, gaining half up front while the other half comes when you complete the objectives. A bit of a steep learning curve and sometimnes your mistakes are not easily fixed. I restarted a few times once I realize dmy mistakes weren't worth correcting, once you understand the flow of the game and make sure you understand th reqs for the rooms and how some of the slightly more complex items work you will begin to construct your mega prison or clubhouse for felons, either way. The ONLY complaint I have was when the vehicles on the road stalled out when prisoners were in the road and after several days of trying to tget them to move I realized I will just have to start over, I am truthfully not that disappointed to start off and make one even better.

I heard about this game from a friend of mine who backed it before it ever made it onto steam. He had his own prisoner made for him and I requested he be transfered into my game, lots of laughs there. Now onto the actual game. This game takes some of the best parts of city builders (a la tropico just to name one). The tutorial for the game does not explain everything you can/should do to be successful, but it does enough to get the ball rolling. As for the premise of the game- you are given a plot of land (of varying sizes) and sculpt your prison as you see fit. As the architect of the prison you are given a certain weekly profits amount and a certain amount of money from higher ups in order to build and rennovate your facilities. The profits you get are based on your overhead, how many wages you need to pay for against the amount of money you are paid per prisoner you currently have. Expansion becomes key to being a profitable prison, along with an interesting grant system which gives you tasks to complete in order to expand/improve your prison with the finanial backing of the state. For new players there is an "easy mode" in which you have unlimited funding so you can get your bearings on how things work.
The game is very immersive, you'll need to keep a watchful eye for prisoners smuggling in drugs and weapons; riots fights and murders are all possible and depending on the number of prisoners and guards you have, it can become a common occurance. Please give this game a chance if you're into simulation/ building games; your prison will become your baby.

This was a great game for me, nice car driving gameplay and decent melee combat. The story is mediocre but has its highlights but.
The real kicker for the game however is the setting, THIS IS MAD MAX. Rarely does a game based on a movie do as well as this game.
If you like Mad Max, deserts, post-apocalyptic settings or just crazy driving then this is the open world game for you.

It's Shadows of Mordor with a better story, guns, and fast vehicles. They did a really good job with this one. Details abound, from visible changes to vehicles to little touches on enemy clothing. Yes, combat can get a bit repetitive, but overall it never feels like a grind (except for the damned minefields. Those suck, but thankfully they're not a huge part of the game).
And there's something viscerally satisfying about driving your car off a cliff, powered by nitrous, and hoping you land without blowing up. Or driving over some scavenger at top speed, who would love nothing more than to beat you dead if given the chance.
Melee combat is fun, even if a bit overpowered (especially in late-game, when you're near invincible). The approach to the level-up system is novel, though I won't spoil the storyline there.
All in all, this is a fun game that I wholly recommend to anyone who enjoyed Shadows of Mordor, or the Arkham games.  Especially when it's on sale, like it happens to be as I write this review, it's worth picking up.

Don't let the title and the art fool you, this is (shockingly) no shovelware. For fans of Hidden Object Games, this is actually a very competent, polished and enjoyable game of the genre.
Yes, yes, the story is ridiculous and oh wow, that's some pretty horrendous voice acting. Then again I suppose it all ends up being entertainigly bad in B movie way (read: standard HOG fare). However I haven't enjoyed HOG scenes so much in a while. The art of the backdrops is very good, items are well drawn, the compositions are intelligent, and the difficulty was pitch perfect for my personal tastes. The puzzles offer a nice amount of variety, and the occasional bit of novelty. A few of them are based on board games, which was fine by me. And while most puzzles are of medium difficulty, there were a couple that demanded some attention, mostly in a good way. Bonus points for the fact that everything is skippable.
Navigation is easy with the higlighted maps (a really big plus), the music rather forgettable but not bad, and between the extra gameplay and all the puzzles and HOG scenes offered seperately as extras in the end, there's a decent amount of content here for the usual price. It's also technically competent, with all resolutions offered and without any obvious bugs or glitches - and this is unfortunately notable for casual games.
For fans who understand what to expect this is a very easy recommendation.

This is not an easy review to write.. As a veteran, sometimes elitist, critical gamer, I have a lot of reasons to not like this game in it's release condition, and this review is probably going to drag on a while, to TLDR: Yes, it's worth getting, if for no other reason than the potential it has as a modding platform for other game ideas.
So, where to start?... Contrary to the normal rant I been seeing in the review of how special it is, I see it as a rather run of the mill space game, not too undifferent from many others I've played over the past few decades. It's an external space shooter with turrets, which leads many people to compare it to Eve, but it is nothing like Eve.
Though I have yet to finish it, much resembles the game model set by classics like Elite or Privateer in which you fly around in your ship, in a go wild, lots of things to do and keep you busy, bad guys everywhere type setting with a pretty basic storyline that is format enought (so far) that it coulda been adapted to any setting and is not really science fiction in it's core, but they have set the story in space.
It is definitely fictional through and through, as there is almost nothing realistic about anything in the game.. No real physics, a very cluttered space and so much graphics effects crammed into it that it's a wonder you can see through all the fog, debri, warp tunnels, nebula, etc. that are floating around... The game suffers through and through with what the guys at Penny Arcade's Extra Credits would call designing for coolness, not for actual plot value or realistic immersion... It's clearly programed for visual bells and whistles, cramming in things like they had a long list of 'It would be cool if you could have X" type design notes with little thought or reason to how it all fits together or in any way helps the plot... There are junk clouds, asteroid clouds, nebula, Stargates, wormholes, slipstream channels (or green tubes of suckage as many have taken to calling them).. and most of the combat is pretty basic and uninspired... and it's got it's bugs and design issues as well.
All that said, why do I still recommend it? Well, for two reasons.
1.) It's definitely modable and almost from day 1 various 1st gen mods started rolling out, so the game can be loaded with features and has potential far beyond the state it's in now.
2.) The devs seem extremely involved, are active in the community, take bug reports and comlaints seriously and are still very much in the polishing and debugging state of the game with a very fast iteration speed on fixes.
Putting all this together, it's an okay game that was designed more for visual coolness than anything serious, but it has potential far beyond what it currently is, and will probably get much better before the Devs are done polishing it.

If this had been a stand alone game, I would be all for it, but frankly I'm very disappointed because I just finished Dracula Origin; which I absolutely love and this was supposed to be the second one, the continuation, and yet it is nothing like Dracula Origin, on the contrary; it rather feels like a giant step downwards in comparrisment instead... :(
As a stand alone game of sorts, I suppose that I recommend it if you want something to pass the time with. But personally as a Dracula Origin lover that was hoping for an actual sequel to it JUST like it claims to be, I was disappointed, and for such ones as me, I do not recommend it...

For those who played Dracula: Origin - this game is quite different, more of the cookie-cutter HO/puzzle/adventure kind, albeit with special abilities and two different endings based on your decisions, which makes it distinctive in this genre. It also has 2D painted art instead of the previous episode's 3D.
Pros:
+ Beautiful graphics, especially some HO scenes and the character art
+ The UI is very modern
+ Atmospheric  and catchy music
+ The puzzles of the first half of the game are quite easy
+ It's nice to see all the items I need to find in a HOS right from the beginning
+ Interesting to see the locations of the previous game (Dracula: Origin)
Cons:
- The character accents sound horribly fake and exaggerated, especially Dracula's and the women's
- They seem to have reused a lot of the music and sound effects from Sherlock Holmes and the Hound of the Baskervilles
- The UI is a bit
helpful in Difficult mode, it shouldn't sparkle interactable items at all
- The late-game puzzles are too difficult, had to skip almost all of them on the first playthrough
- The item names in the HOS are often imprecise and the game sometimes doesn't accept potential matches because the creators thought of a different but similar item in the scene
- the same "collect pieces of shields/coats of arms" story progression as in the Sherlock Holmes game, they could have come up with something a bit more original
- also, many puzzles repeat from the Sherlock Holmes game
Suggestion:
~ I like the option for setting difficulty, but it would be nice to add advanced difficulty options for those who want to customise it. Eg. I like easy puzzles, but also don't like when every interactable items shine and sparkle.

I heard about this game from a friend of mine who backed it before it ever made it onto steam. He had his own prisoner made for him and I requested he be transfered into my game, lots of laughs there. Now onto the actual game. This game takes some of the best parts of city builders (a la tropico just to name one). The tutorial for the game does not explain everything you can/should do to be successful, but it does enough to get the ball rolling. As for the premise of the game- you are given a plot of land (of varying sizes) and sculpt your prison as you see fit. As the architect of the prison you are given a certain weekly profits amount and a certain amount of money from higher ups in order to build and rennovate your facilities. The profits you get are based on your overhead, how many wages you need to pay for against the amount of money you are paid per prisoner you currently have. Expansion becomes key to being a profitable prison, along with an interesting grant system which gives you tasks to complete in order to expand/improve your prison with the finanial backing of the state. For new players there is an "easy mode" in which you have unlimited funding so you can get your bearings on how things work.
The game is very immersive, you'll need to keep a watchful eye for prisoners smuggling in drugs and weapons; riots fights and murders are all possible and depending on the number of prisoners and guards you have, it can become a common occurance. Please give this game a chance if you're into simulation/ building games; your prison will become your baby.

Rogue Legacy is a skill based platformer, which means if you make any mistake then it is your fault for doing that and you need to git gud.
It also a risk vs reward type of game - there are situations which are sometime best to avoid unless you are very confident in your skills.
The castle rooms are randomly generated so each run will be different and gold is the resource you must collect to progress and on each area of the castle there is a guardian you must defeat in order to unlock the final boss (you can lock the castle layout to try to do a boss or complete the challenge again but it will lower your gold gain by by 30% for that run).
Gold is an important resource in this game, after each run you get to spend the gold you earned from the previous run in order to upgrade your home castle (improve states, unlock more classes and NPCs, etc…), you also can buy equipment and runes (abilities that can be switched on each piece of equipment to gain new ability to suit your playstyle).
Gold is not saved from run to run, any gold that you didnt spend is taken away before re-entering the castle - so think well on what you are going to spend it on.
The gameplay is really fun, the control are very responsive, it looks very good and there is some great humor.
When you play, you will always have the itch to do one more run because you know you can do better.
This is one of my most favorite rogue lite games and I highly recommend this game to anyone.

As a whole this game is an incredible feat, let alone for something made over a decade ago and is certainly worth the minimal fee of $10. In addition to this game I'd like to recommend a few other classic Star Wars titles including: Knights of the Old Republic, KotOR: the Sith Lords, Battlefront 2, and the rest of the Dark Forces series if you are into older games. This is a better Ubigame™ than the ones Ubisoft makes. The game clearly takes inspiration from Ubisoft it just does it better. It has all the open world tropes such as "towers", camps and more marked collectibles on the map than any sane person could endure completing.
The world is gorgeous and the game runs extremely well. It's truly a joy to witness. The sound design is top notch as well.
Driving is fun and the mechanics are solid. There's a fair amount of variety to the driving physics through the numerous vehicle upgrades and configurations available.
Ground combat with Max is also quite fun and only gets better and more satisfying the more skills you unlock. It's mechanically very similar to the combat in the Batman games.
Clearing camps in this game is great fun. The various camps are really varied, well designed and they stand out as the best "camp" content in any open world game. They're great mini levels to explore and they all feel like lived in parts of the world.
Overall Mad Max is a great open world package with some solid activities that don't grow old too fast. Do as much side content as you can stomach while it's fun, but do complete the main story as it's very good and hits the Mad Max atmosphere dead center.

Great game that runs great on PC.
The driving is good & works fine with keyboard & mouse. You can customize your car in looks, and ability. Make something suited for speed, or make a tank. You have a buddy who can aim & shoot missiles, grappling hooks, and repair your car for you, giving you many more options when it comes to car combat than usual.
You can customize Max as well, mostly in terms of linear upgrades & abilities, but these all add new cosmetic changes to Max along with being able to customize his beard & hair.
The world has a great size, with lots of little things to do in it. Side quests, upgrades for you, your car, and civilian settlements, along with finding water & fuel to stay alive and stay driving. In terms of graphics, it all looks very nice. Heatwaves over the horizon, & explosions that look great.
The on foot gameplay is good too. You can fist fight enemies very similar in style to the Batman Arkham games, & you can pick up weapons to do special moves and do more damage. You block, parry, and eventually get into 'fury mode' I think it's called, which lets you break through enemy blocking & do more damage along with special finisher moves. If you have the ammo, you can always just shoot your way out of a melee combat situation since you have your trusty shotgun at all times, along with some other gadgets.
This game is pretty well done, & is a great representation of the Mad Max universe in game form. It's not perfect, & there are plenty of silly, weird, and unrealistic things in this game, but Mad Max was never known to be without all that. I definitely recommend.

We all get to sit at home and play CoD or Grand Theft Auto and have fun with the shooting, and that doesn't have to be a bad thing.  But when we forget what it's actually like, the impossible decisions that some people have to make.   Such as saving civilians, or a fellow operative, it makes the game more lasting.  I got done with Spec Ops and realized that whether something was the right decisions was alot of times depending on who was looking at it.  It almost bears the question, what are three men that you know's lives worth compared to others you've never met?

Spec Ops: The Line has the best story of any game I've ever played, and I'm not saying that lightly. It sucks you in with a growing sense of confusion, then as soon as you think you have it figured out, that its just like any other game, and the hype was ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, it hits you with more mystery than ever. Although the story takes place entirely in post sandstorm-ravaged Dubai, the various levels are totally different in feel and atmosphere, and run the entire spectrum from long range sniping on windy rooftops, to sand filled buildings, down to dark and wet cramped tunnels. The ending is heartwrenching, and will make you feel horrible about yourself.
The gameplay is exciting and fast paced, and requires a steady, measured level of aggression that puts you much closer to the enemies than most other shooters. Cover is vital to survival, and the controls, being designed around that concept, feel very fluid once you get used to them. This game gives you everything you could want in a military shooter: stunning setting, increasingly difficult enemies with a great AI, convincing characters, stunning setting, variety in weapons, a loading screen that starts off with helpful hints but eventually mocks you, stunning setting, absolutely amazing music, an amazing epilogue level, stunning setting, a very "fairy-tale-esque" structure that makes you into a shining hero....
Did I mention the setting is stunning? There are moments when you simply have to take a moment from shooting, just to admire the scenery. Or, if not admire, at least... observe. Some of the locations are gruesome on their own, and with context become downright horrifying. But the majority of the game imbues a sense of ruin and desolation in a place that was, until recently, almost unreal in its luxery and beauty.
The game paints a picture of humanity's darkest side, and will make you question the moral implications of the very existance of military shooter games such as this one. Its rated M and they damn well mean it. Everything about this game is brutal, and may have given me mild PTSD. By the time you finish the game, you will have most certainly crossed The Line.

First off: I like this game quite a bit. It is neither too expensive, nor bad looking or somehow broken or buggy.
This is a first impressions, not a 100% review, because the game is huge.
The good stuff:
- Fly around in space in your own "capital" ship. I put that in quotes, because your first ship is a small semi-freighter whatever, but packs quite a punch. Apparently you can go all the way up to cruisers, destroyers, carriers and stuff.
- Simple, yet efficient trading system (X3 would have done good to use that). You can see all available goods for trade as well as best buy and sell prices on the star map and can automaticall plot a course to the desired station.
- Space looks good. Graphics are really not all that bad.
- Combat is interesting in a sense that it's a mix between flying and shooting yourself and also using several skills to enhance damage, survivability etc. I'd just have hoped to have more interesting skills to use. You can also use items and fire your heavy guns like missiles etc. The coolest part, however, is to just have your turrets fire automatically while you concentrate on evading. This is not advised 100% of the time, but it's neat. Turrets will also have fire arcs to take into account. You can easily see the status of your shields and hull and can high tail it out of a fight with max engine power. You can also distribute power between engines, shields and weapons, so that is all very solid if basic (whoever played Freespace 2 for example knows what I mean). I would have liked to redistribute power from my forward shields to my rearward shields for example or have some sort of pause mode where I could issue my gunners or fighters to target a certain area of a ship. Either I just have not found a way to pause the game (because I see comments that it was supposed to be a thing) or it isn't there. I also don't know if you can target different subsystems on a ship. So far I have found an option to target "ship systems", but not individual ones. It would have been great to target a ship's engines or weapons individually to disable it, but I guess that would be a task better suited to fighters than capital ships. There are apparently also boarding torpedoes so you can take over enemy ships. The weapon types encompass all you really need, from railguns, to beams, plasma weapons, rockets and torpedoes. I'd just look forward to getting a bigger ship, but the only bigger thing I see costs a million credits and money is hard to come by if you don't invest a lot of time into trade or something like that. The cruiser even costs 15 million! Long way to go.
- The map is huge and full of different factions and pirates.
The not so good stuff:
- You can apparently only have control over 1 ship (and some mercs) but not command your own fleet (maybe in an expansion or so I've heard), which is kind of disappointing, but ok.
- Automated freighters. I don't see a possibility to have those either. You can own different ships, yes, but there seems to be no way to assign a freighter to go trading on his own in order to generate money while you do something more interesting, because seriously...trading is great and all but it IS extremely boring to have to fly the routes yourself every time...that is a ♥♥♥♥ing slow way of making money...but I think you can have stations or something like that at least...
- The flight distance. Crossing from one point of the map to the other could potentially take a looooong time. There are fast travel routes, but those cost money...lots of money as far as I can see...that kinda sucks. There are also worm holes at least.
- The campaign is...ugh...so utterly boring thus far? Go here, collect a core here, help this dude we totally don't even know or get to know...destroy a ship, bam 30 secs, go back...and all the while suffering through the TERRIBLE dialogue...I'm sorry, but this is definitely the weakest part of the game. Especially the main character just does not have an enticing voice to listen to in a game. Some spoken dialogue is even missing lol.
- Scale. The fighting is a bit weird sometimes, because you don't even see a lot of the enemies you are shooting. At least not in the earlier stages of the game. Keeping track of multiple enemies in a fight is painful, because your automated gunners will not necessarily target your target, but whatever they damn well please. Also, the fighting is kind of weird some times. I've encountered an enemy that was apparently "impossible" for me to take on according to the game. I was level 1. I killed it. By staying on its tail and out of the reach of its main guns...really? ;) That was kind of anticlimactic...
- Weapons and ships. I can currently buy some different ships and lots of different weapons systems and stuff, but it all seems worse than what I have, so either the game is not good at giving me information or there is no purpose in me buying new stuff. For example, I can buy a gunship for about 250k. That gunship has less hps than my starting ship, cannot carry missiles and has less power available, so why would I buy that? Also most weapons systems seem to deal less damage than what I have installed. That is weird.
- Contraband. I once picked up illegal drugs from a destroyed ship. I was told I was entering an area where these drugs are illegal. I sold them. Nothing happened. Why can I sell this stuff at a station in a system where the drug is supposedly illegal? I don't get it.
So, take everything with a grain of salt, but I'd say the game is definitely worth the asking price. If I had to rate it I would give it a solid 80+ I'd say. It does what it says it would do. It controls nicely, looks good and thus far I have not encountered any real bugs. There is always room for improvements and I hope an expansion or dlc will come out.

There are a million seek and find or hidden object games. They're in every store that has computer software. Somewhere in the far reaches of the software isle, all priced at 9.99. Steam has plenty, Big Fish has hundreds. They're everywhere. My wife and I have played a good chunk of them. This one stands out as better then your average.
Note: This review is for those familiar with hidden object games
The puzzles are basically what you'd expect, with a few nice surprises. There are too many tile puzzles in my opinion, but not enough to spoil the process.
Visually stimulating for a hidden object game, with nice backdrops.
The story/voice acting is pretty bad, as you could have guessed anyway.
The objects aren't blurry or difficult to find. Resolution is solid.
While mostly what you'd expect from a more "modern" hidden object, this one is polished. It's not clunky in navigation, the puzzles work great, and its very vivid. There's enough here to say this is one of the most polished I've played in quite some time.
Bottom Line: If you want a crisp hidden object game, mostly containing what you would expect with puzzles/story, but doing it very well, this should fit the bill. You'll enjoy it.

This title is very similar to (my opinion better) Sherlock Holmes and the Hound of the Baskervilles by the same developer. Comparing the two however, this title seems lacking. Unfortunately, this game also contains a lot of hidden object "puzzles", even more so than the aforementioned title. Getting through them ends up a chore and annoying when you cannot find an item that more often than not is very hard to see even if you know what you are looking at. The puzzles are similar and they are of adequate difficulty and variety. Whether to a somewhat different pallete,the graphics seem a bit worse, with environments being dull rather than bleak and the models for the few characters appearing being uninteresting.
All those could be looked over by someone with some spare time in his hands who is just looking for a quick adventure game to play. However, add on top of that the ridiculous scenario, annoying "comic relief" Igor and mediocre at best voice acting, are dooming this game. For all the flaws of the previous installment, Dracula: Origin, it was at least a story that you could take seriously and follow on. The story of Dracula: Love Kills seems as if thought up a few days before release, it is completely unimaginative and uninteresting. Replayability is not good either, doing a second run for achievements seemed for like a chore and I was able to breeze through it in about 2 hours on easy mode, realising most of the game time is spend in hidden object "puzzles".
For adventure and Dracula fans, avoid. This title is simply not worth it, even as part of a bundle as I got it, I wish something of better quality had taken its place.

I got this game as a gift from one of my friends. The graphics did not disgust me - really, when you hear so many things about Undertale, you just become curious. The gameplay is not so complicated, but we have to pay attention. Every little action can change something drastically. Every. No excuse, no exception. Even buying something or forgetting of talking with somebody has consequences. So do not miss anything.
Moreover, during our play we choose one of three main routes to complete the game. There they go: Pacifist, Neutral and Genocide. Each route explains Undertale's world and different parts of its plot. Various combinations with them create really twisted plot.
Like in many pixel games, we use Z and X buttons to confirm or cancel something, C button opens our bag. We can equip found items, we can call our funny friends by using cellphone, we even have a special deposit box to keep more important items.
The music is pretty good. Many themes repeat themselves hidden in other songs. That fits pretty well, it is perfect background for the main story.
The characters are very well done. We may love them or either hate them - depends on our route. Each character has their own personality, their own little world. No wonder it is very easy to see them more seriously.
There are a lot of references to RPG as the whole genre. Undertale makes fun of almost everything. To add, people who have played EarthBound may feel some familiar vibes. It is no secret that Undertale's interface was heavily inspired by EarthBound. Speaking about interface, that brings much fun. When we fight against a monster, we can use items on them or on ourselves, we can fight, we can also act, run away or... show mercy. Every monster can be defeated with certain ways of acting towards them, without fighting.
Conclusions? Undertale is one big amount of feels and plot maneuvering. Will you save the monsters or will you kill them? Will you spare your friends, but no one else? That depends on you and your actions.

Mad Max is a third person singleplayer action game which takes place in a post-apocalyptic version of Australia - After humanity burnt through it's resources, such as water and oil, chaos enveloped the world and let to the downfall of society, passing the power to warlords who were able to force as many of the remaining resources under their control as possible.
It's needless to say that this is a cruel and merciless society - And the game manages to convey the feeling of this pretty darn good! If this setting genereally intruiges you, you should check out the Mad Max movies which inspired this game - they are purchaseable on the steam page as well!
Now to the game itself: Mad Max is a game which lays a strong focus on racing and car driving, as well as brutal melee combat. Personally I don't like racing games, but somehow this game managed to make the expection... Wether due to many costumization options or due to the general set up - I found the racing/driving to be very enjoyable. The quests were fun and varied enough for up to 30 hours but got repetetive after this point, mostly due to the large focus on the quicktimevent based combat for which I had to use the same pattern over and over again - this was fun for the first few hours and felt really forceful and good, but bored me after a while due to it's simplicity.
The main quest is unique and interesting enough to keep you playing and there are plenty of rememberable characters aside of the main character Max - who is a broken man with almost nothing to live for. All characters are strongly influenced by this harsh and unforgiving universe, which made them more remarkable if you'd ask me.
The graphics of the game were of a good quality and the game preformed really well on my computer, with no crashes and no framedrop throughout my entire playtime... The voiceacting was supherb and the soundtrack underlined the most stressful and important parts of the game well enough!
All in all I would recommend Mad Max to anyone whos taken an interest in racing, hand to hand combat and post apocalyptic games... If you don't like cars or (partly repetetive missions/combat) but the whole setting intruiged you, you should check it out - If you don't enjoy it after playing for an hour you should probably get a refund...

Getting the bad out of the way:
* Always-on DRM is bad and lame and should never happen again, SQUARE ENIX.
* Episodic content I have mixed feelings about. Would have preferred whole game for $60. Spent $60 on the "complete experience" so I'd have the right to complain about that.
* Lots of people are reporting technical difficulty. I am mercifully not one of them. Windows 10, GTX 980, latest drivers.
Confusing things:
* There's supposedly an offline mode. I could not figure out where the hell this offline mode is and how to turn it on. Halp.
Good things:
* The crowds of Absolution, and very little else from Absolution.
* Contract mode.
* Escalations are super fun, I was doubtful at first but well done.
* Only a few enemies can see through disguises. So far, this encourages creativity rather than stifling it.
* I have gotten in zero gunfights.
* Lets you screw up royally the way Blood Money did.
* Gives you MANUAL SAVES (!!!)
* Auto-saves are on a timer. Why? Because there's NO CHOKE POINTS (!!!) and the levels are NOT LINEAR (!!!)
* Instinct is not necessary, and can be disabled, along with the mini map, enemy icons, awareness indicators, opportunities, and tutorial text.
On the whole, it's a pretty worthy successor to Blood Money. Gameplay-wise, they have clearly learned from their mistakes. The business and technical aspects of things seem to be pretty sloppy, and we shouldn't simply forgive that. Square Enix needs to get their house in order - and I do not mean their studios, I mean SQUARE ENIX - and we need to hold them accountable.
But, do I recommend HITMAN? Hell yes I do. We live in a day and age of Steam Refunds, if you buy it and it doesn't work or you can't get the online portion to connect, then return it! Otherwise, get ready for Hitman the way it was always supposed to be - not a cover shooter, but a complex, systems-based murder puzzle game.

Gang Beasts does not have good graphics. Gang Beasts does not have combo sheets, and it feels like the most boring, stupid and unenthralling game you've ever seen. It feels sluggish to play due to a slight input lag, and you'll find yourself wondering how a game this impossible to control is fun.
That is, until you then work out the controls.
Then you'll start noticing little tricks and tactics. You'll work out how to perform a dropkick without doing a backflip and falling on your head, knocking yourself out in the process.
You'll learn how to grab people you actually aim at, rather than latching onto a piece of wall and spending 10 seconds trying to pull away from the wall you're holding onto.
You'll learn how to climb up from a ledge. You'll scale walls and manage to perform comebacks from situations you initially thought to be a certain losing condition.
You MIGHT even learn how to throw a diving headbutt without missing and flinging yourself off the arena.
You'll still feel as though the game is borderling impossible to control, but the fact of the matter is, at that point it'll be
to try and get your character to do what you want, and watch others try and do the same.
To go a little more in-depth, this is how Gang Beasts' control scheme breaks down.
You got two buttons for punching, one for the left hand, one for the right. If you hold one button, you grab onto an enemy, or a piece of environment.
You got a jump button. Holding it down will make your character run.
You got a duck button. Holding it down will make your character fall over forwards, tapping it will cause your character to smack his head violently towards the nearest enemy.
You have a kick button. Tapping it will make your characters adorable little feet nudge towards the nearest enemy, holding it will cause your character to fall over backwards.
And you have a button to lift your arms over your head in triumph.
There are no predetermined animations for most of those actions; punches are really just "tell your character to flap their arm towards the nearest enemy". If you hit the headbutt-on (pardon the pun) your character might, for example, perform it backwards if the nearest enemy is behind you. So, physics does play a large part in how the game is played and how it's fights play out.
Punches, kicks and headbutts can, if they hit the right spot, knock an enemy out, leaving them ragdolled and vulnerable to be thrown out of the ring for a few seconds.
It sounds simple at first and you'll think "Why would I want to lay back down? Sounds useless.", until you realise you might want to jump before pressing the kick-button, which causes your character to lean back mid-air - essentially performing a drop kick. Raising your arms sounds useless for a second until you realise you can grab enemies, and the only winning condition is to throw someone out of the ring - then you put 2 and 2 together and realize you can lift enemies over your head.
When it hits the point of you having a grasp of the controls, you'll learn how to apply them properly, and then the game's ridiculous combat will begin to really shine. Multiplayer is a bit rough, but extremely fun. The game cycles through a variety of arenas, each adding their own little flavor to the already chaotic combat, such as fighting on top of moving trucks, on slippery pieces of ice that shift if more weight is on one side, swaying containers over the oceans with cables you can tear through to cause the containers to plummet down, or a blimp, whichs round shape proves to be the greatest risk of the map; there's also a good ol' wrestling ring where the deathmatch-style melee combat can commence without having to worry about any environmental hazards. Just plain old brawling.
Combat tends to be incredibly hectic, fast-paced, and it rarely outstays it's welcome. The exception being situations where everyone dies, and the last two players duke it out in a lengthy duel, but I rarely had a match that lasted longer than 5 minutes at a time.
Each round in multiplayer gets you paired up with a certain amount of players, 5 - 8 tends to be my experience. It goes on until a single player has won 4 matches. Then there's a bit of confetti, and a new round starts; But honestly, I couldn't care less about who wins.
This game is all about having fun. It's a hilariously dumb premise, it looks amusingly stupid, and the combat is so incredibly uncontrolled and hectic that it can only be described as "chaotically brilliant".
The screenshots displayed on steam are outdated; the graphics and physics system have been reworked and the balancing has been adjusted a lot. The game is far from perfect, of course. It is pretty rough around the edges, and if you want competitive brawling and tactical fights, this game might be the one for you - but if you want that, you might want to look at games whose cast doesn't consist of playdoh-y men making "Huhuhu~"-noises as they beat each other up and fling themselves off of gondolas when missing a dropkick. On a sidenote: It has a character creation, and you can put clothes on your lumpy clayman.
I also have no idea why it's called Gang Beasts, but if you play with your friends, you COULD for example wear similar outfits and PRETEND to be a gang.
I recommend the classic "leather jacket and aviator sunglasses"-look, personally.

Apart from the common elements that appear in every hidden object game (hints, difficulty levels, extras) the game offers a tutorial / strategy guide which is very helpful for players that are new to this type of game. The game also shows when a location is complete, thus making the game experience very enjoyable since you don't waste time any more looking for clues in the locations that you've already visited.
Most of the puzzles have a medium difficulty, some are very easy and intuitive, but there are a few brain teasers that will surely challenge your logic and patience.

The point and click adventure is the same you find on other games like The Walking Dead. You find an object like keys, use them to unlock the doors somewhere to get another items to unlock another places. Progressing further into the game, you'll unlock special powers for the Count Dracula so he can shapeshift as a bat, has telekinesis power and all seeing eye (Sauron? heh...) that help you to access certain areas the obstacles or see invisible stuffs.

I really enjoyed this game - while being primarily Hidden Object with a story, the art and music are lovely. The voice acting did seem a bit overdone, although Van Hellsing's was good. There was a good variety of puzzles, and while most seemed very easy, a couple did actually stump me. I think this was worth my $10.

A little bit of background information: I generally stay away from hidden-object games as I consider them to be monotonous. However, I have enjoyed many "point and click" adventure games in which hidden-object scenes appear every so often.
I would consider Dracula: Love Kills as an adventure game with an abundance of varied puzzles as well as hidden object scenes. It's not a pure hidden-object game. While it started off in an interesting manner, and while it indeed has many challenging puzzles, I cannot recommend the game, because I feel it completely lacks any atmosphere. As a result, getting to the end of the game felt like a monotonous chore.
What do I mean when I say lacking in atmosphere? Well, I found the storyline and character interaction/progression absurd, and most importantly, I felt like the developers just lumped in a bunch of random objects to form hidden object scenes -- random objects which have no place being there, given the time period and locale (Example: objects of Chinese origin within a medieval tomb). It made the entire game feel rather tacky.
Dracula: Love Kills isn't an awful game, and I think the developers did quite well in coming up with some of the original puzzles. However, I think there's many higher quality "casual adventure games" out there (Azada and Nightmare Adventures: The Witch's Prison are two games that I recall having an engaging atmosphere and storyline).

I really enjoy open ended space sim games. This one is a very happy medium between easy to learn and fun to play.
It does not have the vast options and customization as games like EVE or X, but I would trade that for a more fun and easy to play game.
Like:
-Open world with a variety of play styles.
-Good selection of ships and equipment loadouts.
-Looks great, cool ship and station designs. fairly immersive
-Easy to learn controls and interfaces, even decent camera control.
-Combat is fun and sometimes intense.
Really enjoyed:
-Capturing ships.
-Trading (Easy to use "best buy/sell" interface!)
-Exploring, pirate hunting
-Completing full loadouts on a ship feels very accomplishing.
Dislike:
-Map feels small and underwhelming.
-Copy pasted missions (gets old in any game though.)
-Story started out pretty lame (avenge my father! collect stuf!) but i didnt get far into it. voice acting was passable..
-Random impossible difficulty battleships showing up out of nowhere, or even in a mission.
-I feel like some stats are missing, or hard to manage when making a loadout. Such as:
Weapon energy consumption vs regen. And how to buff regen / lower consumption?
Turret arc max angles. Fix: List this on ship stats, or a visual on the loadout page would be awesome.
A better display of your ships stats (the circular display looks very awesome, but is not practical when zoomed out.)
Is there a display for your own crew size? I may have missed it, from my reason above.
Recommended for any type of space sim fan, but definitely leaning towards casual.

design is good, and it has a bit of that not-really-a-language voice acting.
The gameplay is fairly slow, due to waiting for energy generation, but this also means that once things go bad they snowball out of control. Luckily the rounds are short enough (~5min) that bad luck or a mistake isn't overly costly.
The game could be improved by adding keyboard shortcuts for the spells and having more markers to signal which units are where. A counter mechanic would also be a nice addition, for example having a morale boost once a ram reaches the doors.
I would recommend giving it a try if you like micromanaging games as it surpassed my expectations and for $5 there's a lot of content.

This games is awesome, hands down. You pilot a ship, it starts out a bit small but you can get very large ones. The thing that makes this game awesome is that you can just go anywhere and do anything. There is a story mode but it's not really important or vital to follow, I have mostly ignored it so far. Combat is a lot of fun, there is no "strategic pausing" or anything to strategize, and you really have a ton of stuff to micromanage. That said, your mechanical ability to think quickly, pilot your ship, use items/abilities, and position properly have HUGE outcomes on the combat. If you're good, you can do a lot with a little ship, if you're bad you can to little with a big ship.
Combat is definitely an extremely fun aspect in this game but there is also so much more than just fighting other ships. The exploration in this game is really amazing. The landmarks (stations, planets, asteroid field locations etc) are static, everything else, the quests, the enemies, etc are completely random. You can pick a direction, put all power to engines, and fly to your hearts content. I actually spent an hour flying completely off the map. There isn't really anything noticeable out there except for a few enemies and such but it  definitely took me an hour to fly back. So yea, the exploration aspect in this game is huge, think skyrim in space but no drauger.
So yea, awesome space battles, great exploration in a beautiful backdrop, it's really a lot of fun. The icing on the cake is the soundtrack. It's just ambient electronic but man it sets the mood well. I swear, this is the most relaxing game to play. Just mine asteroids, listen to the music, and be wisked away to a whole other solar system.
Anyway, if you like exploring, enjoy space, and like relaxing for hours on end running cargo, hunting pirates, and looking at stars, you'll like this game.
