Make that a cautious recommendation if, and only if, you really liked the original HTA so much you can live with lots of flaws. Playing it in Russian probably won't hurt either. Let's start with the good stuff though:
Some things were actually improved since the original game. You can now consume commodities to repair your truck, which adds some urgently needed tactical depth. So does the new critical hit system in combat. The pacing is faster, the maps feel denser. You get to drive some of the smaller, more vulnerable vehicles, which is nice but ultimately pointless. There's more vanity options for your trucks, which is also nice but ultimately pointless.
I really wanted to like this expansion because I've had so much dieselpunk-ish fun with the original game. Its gritty, stylish and sometimes cheesy presentation had been one of HTA's strongest points. This time around though, strange design decisions and embarrasingly bad English pretty much ruin the look and feel. You already thought the original game's translation was in need of another proofreading pass? You've seen nothing yet:
Get ready to "push signal" if you want to sound the horn, and finish races "at the place 1 from 4" in this whacky theme park version of North America. Now, don't get me wrong, I'm not a native speaker either. I make mistakes. What I don't do is sell those mistakes in a commercial product just because I couldn't be bothered to pay for a proofreader. They did bother to hire native English speakers as voice actors though, and you'll notice them diverging from the gibberish script every so often, because apparently even mediocre voice actors have standards. Needless to say, all of this doesn't exactly add to the style and atmosphere of the game.
Neither does the homicidal maniac wearing an American Football helmet in his star-spangled oversized RC car pulling stunt jumps all over the famous New York desert. Yes, we're talking about the player character here. He also seems to like made-up proverbs involving vehicle parts. Badly translated ones, of course.
I do realize many of these problems don't apply if you get to play this in its original language. In that case, consider yourself lucky and give this game a chance. For everybody else though, the translation flaws are distracting from the experience so much it sometimes borders on the unplayable. For an already mediocre sequel, that's a critical hit. And yeah, I do realize that wasn't exactly witty. Consider it a taste of things to come if you seriously consider buying this.

I've decided to rewrite this since this incredible work deserves more than just a cute 'feels' joke (still, if you intend on playing - prepere your tissues, since the waterworks will flow). I don't believe this review spoils the unique experience, or the tear-jerking plot, so you may read on.
The game's narrative is one of a kind. It's a deconstruction (and I don't mean it as a buzzword) of the RPG mentality - they took the concepts that build a usual RPG game and redid it with a real-life thought process.
First of all, the world itself (which I believe is a certain take on Dante Alighieri's Hell and Purgatory) has it's history, and you can learn all about it if you talk to enough NPC's (the shopkeepers have a 'talk' option for a reason!), read signs and books (which doesn't feel like a chore, they are masterfully written), and notice the subtle hints in the background.
Second of all, the characters have depth, and they feel real. They all have personalities, wills, ambitions, background stories, interests, and characteristics - good and bad. Be it the shop keepers who won't let you sell anything to them due to their will to survive financially or the NPC's who share their thoughts and ideas through little lines of text. But of course, The main characters who have a variety of facial expressions and text movement variations in order to highlight their depth and story.
And all of this is done to deliver the narrative, along with the commentary concerning the decision making process in today's gaming industry and of us as gamers. "No one has to die" is not just a nice slogan, it's a thought process we should not take for granted. Today's shoot-first policy when it comes to random encounters and boss "fights" is depicted as not just questionable, but malicious. But hey, it's always good VS. evil, and you're the protagonist so you have to be the good one, right?
26.5 hours is just my raw playtime, and even that's due to re-doing the whole thing to study more about the world - after than I deleted the game in order to pay respects to it. But that wasn't enough, so be advised, you're in for at least a 100 hours experience, including all the analysis videos on youtube, reading theories all over the web, and enjoying the fanmade comics and videos (just avoid the cringy ones).
You must play this and experience the whole thing. No game will ever be the same after this one.

Prison Architect is a game about building prisons. Although this may seem like the perfect game for a madman in his spare time, Prison Architect really does feel rewarding in its many aspects, such as advancing your security, organising your prion into carefully dictated areas or just holding on tight when your prisoners eventually get tired of that one holding cell you built. Therein comes the problem: Ineptitude is your manual. It took me many, many hours to find out quite suddenly that you can stop the inflow of prisoners, for example. Therefore you will spend lots of your time trying to work out which button does what and what you really need to do-and there's another problem. The game is good, but once you've played it one or two times the activities become monotonous, once you've left the initial stage of confusion. Yes, you can build a bigger prison, and yes you can try to make the best prison you possibly can, but in the end there is no reward for either. Complex systems are definitely not worth the time and logistics is simple.

I have played a lot of early access games. After about 130 hours of gameplay I definately recommend this one! Its far beyond the average early access game's quality. It already feels complete in its current state, I did not encounter a single bug so far, it has already a lot of content and there is even a lot more to come.
You will need a couple of games before you can establish a stable, self maintaining colony, because every time you think you're safe something (thus far) unexpected happens. Maintaining power? Your oxygen gets low. Oxygen is ok? You're running out of food. There's always something new. And that's the main motivation of this game: Solving all of the problems which come up in a sufficient way and then, eventually, improve it.
Every other colony you start is a bit more well planned from the start, but as soon as you keep satisfying your duplicants' basic needs, the struggle continues. You're now growing enough food and producing oxygen by electrolyzers out of water instead of using algae? Cool. But after several hunded cycles of your machinery running and your colony already reaching an average temperature of 48°C, how the get rid of all the excess emitted heat?
The game reproduces the laws of physics in a very good fashion. While not being too strict and complicated, it lets you experiment with temperatures and aggregate states quite intuitively. My latest achievement was to "purify" polluted oxygen by building a machine thats cooling the polluted oxygen below its boiling point (approx. -183°C), thus liquifying it and then slowly raising the temperature again so that it "boils" into pure, clean oxygen. Getting this to work took me about 4 -6 hours of planning and testing and that's about a hunded times more complicated than just building an "air deodorizer", which is an included simple building that does the same thing. But the satisfaction of seeing your idea working is priceless. ;)

I would not recommend this game to anyone but the most hardcore fans of the genre, and that provided the price comes down.
While I do acknowledge some might enjoy the tedium and vaccum, neither I, nor any of my friends did. Core mechanics are grind, fetch&kill 'quests' and exploration. You also pick up things and sell them off at the nearest friendly station, or buy things at one point and sell them to a trader across the map for profit. The game world is huge and fun to explore at first, but given the lack of variety (it is space, after all) it will get boring afer a while. Combat is nothing like a proper space sim - you either get projectile weapons and miss, or directed energy (beam) weapons and hit 100% of the time via automatic turrets. These make the whole combat thing ridiculous - all the fun is outsourced to your onboard computer. The game seems to be balanced with this in mind - you can either turn on the auto tracking and let the computer do the fighting or die.
Fun parts:
-exploration. the playing environment is huge! Volumetric shadows, nebulas, asteroid and debris fields and planets are stunning. It does get old after a while given the game's shortcomings
-visuals as per above. Nothing you haven't seen in X3 already though
-ship designs & variety
The not-so-fun parts:
-tedious, fetch&kill tasks that pass for quests here; gets old in about 10 minutes
-the game is vacuous. think mmo without quests or other players.
-as of now the game is bugged and some options are greyed out. No, despite what the industry standard for indie games seems to have become lately, it is not okay to release an unfinished game with greyed out options and scenarios that 'will be added later on'. That's what early access is for!
-repetitive, unaccomplished space combat
-the 'RPG' portion of the game comes down to several global stat boosts and 4 active skills, which I've not seen to have any serious impact on the game
Not bad for a first time

I have finally beat the Hard Truck Apocalypse: Rise of Clans (aka HTA: RoC and Ex Machina: Meridian 113).
The impression it left me is... mixed. I'll try to keep this review spoiler-free for those who didn't have a chance to finish the game yet.
In general, it retains almost all the pros of the original game (you can find the review here:
, except for exploration. Here's a short version:
* Truck variety and customization. Even more so with the addition of the "light" playable vehicles: the Scout and the Fighter.
* Weapons of all sorts.
* Sountrack and visuals.
Now in my Hard Truck Apocalypse review I also mention the lore. I didn't have a chance to actually experience it due to me rushing towards the end of the main questline. A few reasons for that will be described further in Cons section.
Before we can move on to the Cons, I must address an issue of performance. Since we all use different rigs and different configs, I do not feel like putting it into a Con section.
You may just not experience what I experienced! Overall the performance of the game was great, and it runs smoothly. But then there are areas (mostly in the Jungle regions) where FPS was dropping significantly, and an attempt to change the resolution or tweak the options caused some atrocious glitches that forced me to kill the game and load it anew.
Sometimes after loading a level I've been experiencing the models in the world, as well as parts of my truck, blinking in and out of existence.
Another thing a HTA: RoC player should be weary of: changing the settings is not a healthy decision and may cause all kinds of problems, from FPS drops to crashing. Also the game refused to remember my preferable screen resolution so I had to go and specify it in a config file.
The Cons this time around are plenty, and I will try to communicate what is wrong in my opinion:
* Compared to the first game, there is less regions, and they feel smaller. All that contributes to almost any lack of exploration. The addition of treasure detector did not encourange it either.
* A few additions to the arsenal, as well as the truck roster, compared to the original.
* The balance issues. Compared to the first game, the trucks are easier to kill, but in return, you are also easier to kill! So many times I had to reload my last save just because I encountered a group of bandits that one-shotted me. You can call it a challenge, I call it BS. And, as a result, the boss fights, as few as there are, are infuriating.
* Case in point, another disappointing last boss battle. Albeit interesting idea, still disappointing in performance.
* The addition of consumables. On one hand, it's a post-apoc, so salvageable materials are a must have. On the other, in the late game the Spares consumables become obsolete due to how underwhelming their "healing power" is. It's easier to sell those Spares and repair your truck with the profit money than to repair yourself on the go.
* Something I don't remember mentioning in the Hard Truck Apocalypse review: The English localization. It's horrible. I am Russian myself, so it pains me how the translation just butchers the language. The wording is awful. The translation is very literal, in most cases more than the others. Like this one Plasma gun that is called "One" in English, but "Óдин" (Odin, the Norse one-eyed god) in Russian. It gives me an impression that whoever did the translation, did not particularly care for the end result, to my greatest sadness.
* As the result of the previous point, awkward voice-overs. I like the cuss phrases Vagrant uses in his speech, though.
* Also, random errors during the loading time made me close the game and run it again so many times, it's ridiculous.
Conclusion: This game feels like a "smaller brother" to Hard Truck Apocalypse; the tighter package reveals less exploration, quicker player progression and frustrating balance changes. It's still a good time for the fans of the series (if we ignore the possible performance issues), so if you bought HTA already, why not buy this one too? It has all the same features, and a bit more on the top.

Copied from my preview on
This review is for an "as yet unreleased Early Acess title"
[Disclosure: Game copy purchased with own money]
Prison Architect is a top-down 2-D construction and management simulator specifically a prison management simulator, made by Introversion Software and produced by Mark Morris and designed by Chris Delay. Introversion have previously made games like Uplink, Darwinia, DEFCON, multiwinia, and Darwinia+. Mark & Chris make regular update videos regarding the current build state of the game.
The beginning of Prison Architect is probably one of the grimmest that I have seen, the game begins with an intro, in which you have been contacted to build a Death Row facility, in order to put to death a prisoner that has committed a double murder.
This is essentially the tutorial level, despite the cartoon-esque graphics there is a rather dark undertone. I should point out that the player does not have to accept death row inmates and even if they do, they do not have to build the electric chair facility.
Putting that aside for a moment, once the tutorial is completed the player can then build their own detention centre. You’re given some money and tasked to build whatever you like. The aim of the game is to build an efficient centre with minimal issues from the incarcerated population.
Which as you can imagine is sometimes rather difficult, the game doesn’t exactly have a difficulty level, however the player can choose the type of prisoners (low risk, normal risk, high risk, Death Row) the type of risk and the amount of prisoners within that risk category, as well as the centre and its suitability of facilities for said inmates is what essentially determines the difficulty levels.
When beginning a new game, building a “good” centre is possibly overwhelming, you have two options, you can continue to mess around in the tutorial level or you can use the in game “prison sharing” option whereby other players who have uploaded their prisons for you to download and run yourself. Failing that, the player is generally recommended to stick with the low-risk category prisoner.
Once you feel you have a decent & efficient prison you can then start accepting normal/high risk inmates. But that’s not all there is to it, there are a number of different nuances that the player needs to be aware of, for example the prisoners need to be provided with various different facilities such as a yard, library, chapel, kitchen and cafeteria. In order to provide these you will need various different staff such as kitchen staff, janitors, gardeners, doctors and of course (armed) guards.
The player receives an income based on the number of/level of risk of the inmates and the challenge to balance the income versus the staff wages required to run the centre, build facilities, hire more staff, etc. To assist with this, there is a grant system that will provide the player with a cash boost to build various different facilities which will improve the entire prison complex and its suitability. It also acts as a guide and directs you to build in order to achieve the completion bonus.
The player has to research various different aspects in order to unlock certain features. Which takes time and money that add to the challenge of the game. Some assist with the day-to-day running such as prison labour, which allows you to assign jobs to prisoners. Others help train/improve inmates to work as cooks or in the workshop (for reducing costs/ bonus cash), as well as assist with narcotic/alcohol abuse and general behavioural therapy. The “endgame” has currently three outcomes:
The player creates a reasonably decent centre that they are then able to sell and use that to start a new centre with a larger start-up capital.
The player creates an efficient well run centre, and unlocks the ability for death row inmates.
Player fails to create a decent centre with too many deaths and/or escapes which results in them being fired.
Prison ArchitectAn example of the needs of prisoners, and current need fulfilment
In order for the challenge to be maintained, the prisoners have a needs system that must be fulfilled. The player needs to be aware of contraband entering the prison by various different means, not to mention new influx of prisoners and/or higher risk prisoners “kicking off”.  The player is provided with a number of tools in order to counteract these. The trade-off is in order to continue to make money the prison must accept new inmates which will invariably upset the current balance. You have control over the amount/level of risk prisoners and can also close the prison, which is generally done initially to facilitate the initial building of the centre or if the prison has reached its full capacity.
The game is completely mouse driven, there are a few keys/keyboard shortcuts, the control works really well. The graphics are cartoon-esque and rather cute which is in contrast to the sinister nature surrounding prisons, inmates and of course the death penalty.
The cartoon graphics do make an otherwise difficult topic rather fun. The soundtrack is minimal which suits this kind of environment, the sound assets however are excellent. Everything sounds as far as I know pretty much the way it should sound and if the player gets to the stage of putting a prisoner to death on death row, the sound assets change to suit that very dark subject.
Overall, I bought this some time ago now, and I absolutely love this game. It is one of my all-time favourites. The game is in alpha stage, so some users have reported problems however I have experienced little to none. There is a lot of depth to the game, which is amazing.
The developers have said the game is very nearly complete and I am looking forward to the finished version. If you like management/building games, this game is a must buy if you are not too bothered about the subject matter. Due to the blood/violence/excretion, in an otherwise cartoon-esque game, buyer discretion is advised.

I wish I could give a "half" thumbs up for this. It has so many problems, but I can't stop playing it. If you loved Borderlands 1, you'll be torn on Borderlands 2 because it changes so much and yet nothing at all.
Pros:
-More fleshed out world that feels alive, unlike the desolate, abandoned wasteland of Borderlands 1
-Super varied enemies
-Guns actually look different for each manufacturer
-People actually seem like people
-The new vault hunters are interesting
-LOTS of content even in the vanilla game
Cons:
-Difficulty curve is in such a way that you will CONSTANTLY be fighting an uphill battle, and it only seems to get more difficult as time goes on to the point that the curve becomes a 90 degree angle, then eventually wraps back around and pokes you in the butt. (True Vault Hunter Mode and Ultimate True Vault Hunter mode will see you CONSTANTLY struggling to stay alive when you can be downed by a fart from a mile away grazing you and then you can't get a second wind because the only enemy in sight just ran off into the sunset while tanking everything you hit them with
-Enemies become ridiculous bullet sponges (like, you can have top-tier equipment in all slots and your bullets practically bounce off of them, even when using the correct elemental type)
-your skill doesn't matter later in the game, it's all about being lucky enough that your enemies miss or that there is always a weakling close at hand in case you get downed
-the game becomes a grindy slog after 2 playthroughs, you begin to realize how padded the content is when (if doing all the sidequests) the game takes about 60 hours to complete (40 of which may be you running back from a New-U station)
-plot holes! plot holes everywhere! there is no dramatic tension, just a bunch of WTF stuff happening because the story demanded it.
I would only TRULY recommend this game to masochists, ultimate Borderlands fans, and people who will ALWAYS have friends to play with (you're going to need them later).

Great game. You can get the game of the year edition which includes almost all the DLC minius one major DLC (the second lvl cap and OP lvls DLC) and some not very important DLCs (Head hunter packs and cosmetics) for litterally cheaper than dirt on a steam sale. Top soil costs about 10 bucks for the cheap stuff, the game of the year edition of this great game can be less than that on a steam sale, like 5-20 dollars. The game play is great and once you master your skills and when or how to use them the game play will feel so rewarding when you mow down extremely difficult enemies with skill and pure awesomeness. The story is incredible from such a cartoony looking game but the voice acting and humor make it work. The story, and I won't spoil this, gets especially good towards the end. This game doesn't look deep at all from the surface but play it listen to the dailog in the background and feel the characters. From my experience of this game an the experiences of people I know who have played the series, I say this is probably the best game of the borderlands series and is a must have. The Villian; Handsome Jack is just beautifully thought out and developed and comparable to great villians like Vas from Farcy 3 in terms of being crazy and making it work as well as overall awesomeness. It's a game I think people MUST OWN on PC. This is one of the few triple A titles here on PC that's super well optimized, has a huge player base that's still active and friendly, and a huge amounts of replayability. Now I know things get very grindy and difficult in the last play through and in OP levels but bear with it, get a feel for what works best for your character in the phase of late game, and I assure you will further extend the enjoyment of your game. Take a look at me, I got like what? 500+ hours maybe 600 at the time of editing this review and I will tell you that 90-95% of this was from learning, and enjoying using just one single character: mah boi Zer0. Of course I hit maxed lvl with both lvl caps a while ago and I could have moved on to many more characters but that's simply how much I enjoy the game from just one character. This game has up to 6 but as I mention before you have to buy them as DLC or better choice, get the GOTY edition on a sale and buy the second lvl cap separate. So worth it. But don't take my word on it, look at the steam statistics, this game is almost always in the top 40 or 50 games played all the time, and check the reviews: overwhelmingly possitive. How many triple A titles on PC can do that. This game is a must have for anyone who likes RPGs, FPS, and loot. A must own PC game. BUT I must say play with friends cuz the game isn't as fun in the begin if you play alone, at least not until the story ramps up and you start craving to play it all the time whether alone or not.
It's only good if you are the type of person that likes to have fun. If you do not like to experience happiness or pleasure, then this game is not for you.

This review is for an "as yet unreleased Early Acess title"
[Disclosure: Game copy purchased with own money]
Prison Architect is a top-down 2-D construction and management simulator specifically a prison management simulator, made by Introversion Software and produced by Mark Morris and designed by Chris Delay. Introversion have previously made games like Uplink, Darwinia, DEFCON, multiwinia, and Darwinia+. Mark & Chris make regular update videos regarding the current build state of the game.
The beginning of Prison Architect is probably one of the grimmest that I have seen, the game begins with an intro, in which you have been contacted to build a Death Row facility, in order to put to death a prisoner that has committed a double murder.
This is essentially the tutorial level, despite the cartoon-esque graphics there is a rather dark undertone. I should point out that the player does not have to accept death row inmates and even if they do, they do not have to build the electric chair facility.
Putting that aside for a moment, once the tutorial is completed the player can then build their own detention centre. You’re given some money and tasked to build whatever you like. The aim of the game is to build an efficient centre with minimal issues from the incarcerated population.
Which as you can imagine is sometimes rather difficult, the game doesn’t exactly have a difficulty level, however the player can choose the type of prisoners (low risk, normal risk, high risk, Death Row) the type of risk and the amount of prisoners within that risk category, as well as the centre and its suitability of facilities for said inmates is what essentially determines the difficulty levels.
When beginning a new game, building a “good” centre is possibly overwhelming, you have two options, you can continue to mess around in the tutorial level or you can use the in game “prison sharing” option whereby other players who have uploaded their prisons for you to download and run yourself. Failing that, the player is generally recommended to stick with the low-risk category prisoner.
Once you feel you have a decent & efficient prison you can then start accepting normal/high risk inmates. But that’s not all there is to it, there are a number of different nuances that the player needs to be aware of, for example the prisoners need to be provided with various different facilities such as a yard, library, chapel, kitchen and cafeteria. In order to provide these you will need various different staff such as kitchen staff, janitors, gardeners, doctors and of course (armed) guards.
The player receives an income based on the number of/level of risk of the inmates and the challenge to balance the income versus the staff wages required to run the centre, build facilities, hire more staff, etc. To assist with this, there is a grant system that will provide the player with a cash boost to build various different facilities which will improve the entire prison complex and its suitability. It also acts as a guide and directs you to build in order to achieve the completion bonus.
The player has to research various different aspects in order to unlock certain features. Which takes time and money that add to the challenge of the game. Some assist with the day-to-day running such as prison labour, which allows you to assign jobs to prisoners. Others help train/improve inmates to work as cooks or in the workshop (for reducing costs/ bonus cash), as well as assist with narcotic/alcohol abuse and general behavioural therapy. The “endgame” has currently three outcomes:
The player creates a reasonably decent centre that they are then able to sell and use that to start a new centre with a larger start-up capital.
The player creates an efficient well run centre, and unlocks the ability for death row inmates.
Player fails to create a decent centre with too many deaths and/or escapes which results in them being fired.
Prison ArchitectAn example of the needs of prisoners, and current need fulfilment
In order for the challenge to be maintained, the prisoners have a needs system that must be fulfilled. The player needs to be aware of contraband entering the prison by various different means, not to mention new influx of prisoners and/or higher risk prisoners “kicking off”.  The player is provided with a number of tools in order to counteract these. The trade-off is in order to continue to make money the prison must accept new inmates which will invariably upset the current balance. You have control over the amount/level of risk prisoners and can also close the prison, which is generally done initially to facilitate the initial building of the centre or if the prison has reached its full capacity.
The game is completely mouse driven, there are a few keys/keyboard shortcuts, the control works really well. The graphics are cartoon-esque and rather cute which is in contrast to the sinister nature surrounding prisons, inmates and of course the death penalty.
The cartoon graphics do make an otherwise difficult topic rather fun. The soundtrack is minimal which suits this kind of environment, the sound assets however are excellent. Everything sounds as far as I know pretty much the way it should sound and if the player gets to the stage of putting a prisoner to death on death row, the sound assets change to suit that very dark subject.
Overall, I bought this some time ago now, and I absolutely love this game. It is one of my all-time favourites. The game is in alpha stage, so some users have reported problems however I have experienced little to none. There is a lot of depth to the game, which is amazing.
The developers have said the game is very nearly complete and I am looking forward to the finished version. If you like management/building games, this game is a must buy if you are not too bothered about the subject matter. Due to the blood/violence/excretion, in an otherwise cartoon-esque game, buyer discretion is advised.

I've decided to rewrite this since this incredible work deserves more than just a cute 'feels' joke (still, if you intend on playing - prepere your tissues, since the waterworks will flow). I don't believe this review spoils the unique experience, or the tear-jerking plot, so you may read on.
The game's narrative is one of a kind. It's a deconstruction (and I don't mean it as a buzzword) of the RPG mentality - they took the concepts that build a usual RPG game and redid it with a real-life thought process.
First of all, the world itself (which I believe is a certain take on Dante Alighieri's Hell and Purgatory) has it's history, and you can learn all about it if you talk to enough NPC's (the shopkeepers have a 'talk' option for a reason!), read signs and books (which doesn't feel like a chore, they are masterfully written), and notice the subtle hints in the background.
Second of all, the characters have depth, and they feel real. They all have personalities, wills, ambitions, background stories, interests, and characteristics - good and bad. Be it the shop keepers who won't let you sell anything to them due to their will to survive financially or the NPC's who share their thoughts and ideas through little lines of text. But of course, The main characters who have a variety of facial expressions and text movement variations in order to highlight their depth and story.
And all of this is done to deliver the narrative, along with the commentary concerning the decision making process in today's gaming industry and of us as gamers. "No one has to die" is not just a nice slogan, it's a thought process we should not take for granted. Today's shoot-first policy when it comes to random encounters and boss "fights" is depicted as not just questionable, but malicious. But hey, it's always good VS. evil, and you're the protagonist so you have to be the good one, right?
26.5 hours is just my raw playtime, and even that's due to re-doing the whole thing to study more about the world - after than I deleted the game in order to pay respects to it. But that wasn't enough, so be advised, you're in for at least a 100 hours experience, including all the analysis videos on youtube, reading theories all over the web, and enjoying the fanmade comics and videos (just avoid the cringy ones).
You must play this and experience the whole thing. No game will ever be the same after this one.

Spec Ops: The Line begins like any other shooter game. It ends like no other.
WARNING: There is a mandatory part of the game that should have a gigantic epilepsy warning in it (In middle of chapter 11). Just a word of caution!
The TL;DR short summary (scroll down further for long review):
Pros:
+Incredible single player story. It is thought-provoking and very refreshing. This is what you're playing this game for. Did I mention the story is amazing?
+The decisions you make, aside from being very morally ambigious and "there is no good choice", are actually pretty creative in that the game does not tell you WHAT you can choose. It plays both on the minds of the characters as well as YOU, as a player.
+Decent gameplay. Standard 3rd person shooter with cover system.
+Using sand as a gimmick mechanic adds a little originality to the title. There is also a little bit of tactical squad use (ordering your squadmates to do things) that is limited, but works very effectively and keeps the game from being too boring.
+Great music, very fitting for the game. A few well-known bands are in there, such as Hendrix, but the original score is not too shabby either.
+Co-op challenge modes are available, but...
Cons:
-Fairly generic gameplay (It's good, just not great or bad. To be honest you can't really innovate modern warfare without getting all ridiculous though).
-Co-op is available but only in the form of challenge modes, not in the campaign. Multiplayer is also available but not worth it. You're playing this for the story!
-Single player campaign is fairly short, although I found it to be the perfect length. Any longer and it would have been too dragged out.
Although I played this fairly late (a couple years late, since this came out in 2012), it still remains a testament to story telling in video games, let alone one that is so focused on the things most people seemed to be entertained by - Ridiculous amounts of violence involving weapons and warfare. One only needs to look at the recent sales of the biggest hits to notice the impact shooters have in the games industry.
Spec Ops: The Line is a terribly dull title and has a "seen that before" cover art. But don't judge a game by its cover, as it contains some truly entertaining and thought-provoking storytelling that is sadly rare in the shooting genre these days.
Taking place in Dubai, the worst sandstorms in history hit the region, stranding many civilians. The "Damned 33rd" infantry battalion of the United States Army is sent in on relief duty, led by a famous Colonel named John Konrad. However, it appears he and his unit deserted; they disobeyed orders to abandon the city, and the sandstorms effectively create a 'wall' that prevents surveillance and communications, essentially making Dubai a 'no man's land' where no one knows what's going on. You play as Captain Martin Walker, who is sent alongside two fellow soldiers as Delta Force operators for reconaissance. The mission is simple: Confirm the statues of Konrad and any other survivors, then radio for extraction.
As officially stated by the game's advertisement/captions, the story is very rich and takes plenty of influence from the novel "Heart of Darkness", as well as the movie "Apocalypse Now". Without spoiling this game any further, I can say it lives up to the hype. Your progression throughout the game will have you feeling disgusted, but not in the same in way a bad game would. As you delve deeper, you will see things you rarely see in video games - Among the list includes horrific imagery, morality, questionable actions, tough decisions and more....
It starts off innocently enough, almost like every other shooter out there. America coming in to save the day, foreigners shooting at you, nothing you haven't seen before. Next thing you know, the line gets very blurry and there are no "good" or "bad" guys, no "good" or "bad" decisions. By the time you enter the credits, you're left looking at war in a different way, and thinking about the actions and consequences of people.
In addition, the little touches are pretty awesome. Be sure to take breaks frequently and see how the main menu has changed throughout your progression of the campaign. Take in the environmental storytelling (additional "stories" you observe by looking at things not necessarily important to the main plot). Pick up glowing objects ("Intel") to reveal additional story threads. And DEFINITELY pay attention to the loading screens - they are plenty of them and they...well, let's just say if you're too good at the game, it's worth purposely dying multiple times to see them.
Also among my favourites from this game are the creative decision-making you'll have to make. The decisions you make, aside from being very morally ambigious and "there is no good choice", are actually pretty creative in that the game does not tell you WHAT you can choose. In fact, it doesn't make it obvious at all - there are no buttons or signs pointing in a direction. Without spoiling much, it offers commentary both on the insanity of war and the characters themselves, but also how you as a player may have been trained to think or behave in video games.
As for the gameplay, it's decent. It's a somewhat generic 3rd person shooter with a cover system. You take cover, shoot, reload, all that jazz. What makes the gameplay a tad more unique is their sand and tactical command mechanics. In various locations, sand can be used to your advantage - for example, shooting out windows behind enemies to break the glass and release a wave of sand that will blind or bury your foes. As for tactical commands, you learn how to use your squadmates more effectively by giving them simple orders. In most cases, all you can do is line up the reticle and tell them to target someone, and they'll focus fire him. However, the squad AI is fairly smart (and actually not invulnerable, which is nice) and will use grenades to take out entrenched foes, and sniper rifles for long ranged attacks. Various times the game will also allow you the option of telling them to throw flashbangs to stun foes.
In addition the game does come with co-op and multiplayer features, although these generally are not worth it. Co-op might be fun if people ever want to revisit Spec Ops, but these are limited to challenge modes, and not the campaign. A bit of a downer as I can see co-op gameplay working well in the story, but nevertheless it does make sense to exclude it. As for multiplayer, as you may have seen from other reviews it's pretty much not worth it. There are better games out there for multiplayer shooters, not to mention the population of Spec Ops multi-players is likely non-existent.
To conclude, play this game for the story. You won't regret it, although you'll certainly feel something by the end of the story. I do not recommend playing this so close to Christmas time like I did - it's kind of the opposite of happy feelings.
This is one of the most highly underrated gems in video games. I certainly do hope more games are made in a similar way, to further show that video games can be more than just violent entertainment for the sake of violent entertainment. Indeed, it is a game that I can definitely list as real "art".
Spec Ops: The Line is different, and all the better for it. Few games leave you feeling like you didn't have 'fun', but instead 'experienced' something on an emotional scale...very drastically, at that too.

Max, a lone wolf who just wants to leave this damn filthy piece of land where survival of the fittest applies vigorously. All Max knows is this post-apocaliptic society stucked around Gastown. It's the last bastion of humanity surrounded by hostile land called Big Nothing. Max desires crossing part of Big Nothing called Plains of Silence in order to find what lays behind and start a new life. Forget what was lost. Rumour has it water and green vegetations are plenty there, but no one ever returned to confirm these legends. Still there would be no reason to return to this brutal and violent land led by masochists and maniacs. Max focuses everything just on one purpuse - build a car able to cross Plains of Silence - but what happens on his way its up to you to discover.
Mad Max offers surprisingly large open world full of brutality, violence and day to day surviving. Wait, let me stop here, survival in this world for Max is as difficult as swimming for Michael Phelps. I would expect more elements and threats, but in this desert it's easier to meet a stranger than in my town on Sunday. Even though the Mad Max's world is welldesigned and every location is unique after a while you won't know whats lack of gasoline, water or even ammunition. On the other hand action parts of the game are spectacular and make the game very enjoyable. Beating to death almost every person you meet, destructing cars of other survivors and dismantling Scrotus's (President of Gastown and surrounding lands) camps makes game very entertaining.
When we move to RPG elements, don't expect much. Story is short and plain. I was so curious about Max, or even about the past, how the world turned into this hellish place, but no, sorry, no explanation for you. Eventhough many relics (usually postcards) and monuments (lighthouse etc.) persisted the decline of civilization, you are here only to look around and examine them. It's not bad, but there could be so much more! Max's memories or just tale from anyone who you meet through the game.
After all this game feels amazing despite all negatives.

This game can be summed up as a roguelike and platformer combo, but it's more than that truly. Once your character dies, his decendant takes his place, rinse and repeat - but don't think you lose your progress, oh no no no. You see, Rogue Legacy features a simple upgrade system that is simply based around buying things with the gold you find scattered around the castle and it's locales - classes, abilities, equipment, etc. Sounds fine and dandy, but combined with the fact that your character dies and his decendant loses his gold after giving it to the gatekeeper, offers an interesting challenge of upgrading what you find to be most valuable for your current playthrough and/or what class you choose (yeah there are classes, one is a Hokage even) It's addicting in a way that can't really be described by comparing it to other games, since it's truly one of a kind, despite being unoriginal in it's main gameplay execution (it's really not the first upgrade-y roguelike platformer out there). That to me, is a clear sign of a truly fun and engaging game...
Also your character can get irritable bowel syndrome, yup.

Currently 130 hours into the game AND downloaded it on another account for my phone.  I enjoy the idle genre, as it gives a sense of satisfaction that is hard to get in most other games.  This one however, is much different from other idle games you have played. I'd recommend giving it a shot, but would also recommend that you watch a youube video to preface it (in place of a tutorial).  Or ask a friend that has played it.  Starting can be VERY rough (I had people telling me how to start it, so my start wasn't too bad thankfully)
Pros:
-Very Cool story.  Seriously, the story is addicting and has me coming back to re-read it while I'm idling.
-A lot to do.  You can play this like an idle game, or (after first few rebirths) can actually spend hours of active play.
-The male hero looks kinda like Goku.  Seriously.
-The descriptions and abilities are hilarious.
Cons:
-Annoying menus.  Takes a few hours to learn the menus, and annoying that you have to swap between them so often.
-Wording of some things is confusing.
-Dark Gray everywhere.  No color.  You can change some of the colors, but lack fine control over it.  You cannot make it look good, no matter how long you try (trust me). I don't know if this is how the end product will be, but it should probably get a cool shell to be played in. (although it is reminiscent of the old text/browser based games I grew up with).  Not a huge con for me, but is a big turn off for most people i know.
TL:DR: I would recommend if you like these types of games, I would rate it 7.5/10 with potential to be a 9.5/10 easily.

ONI in its current state is fun to run through once or twice, failing, and then run through again successfully. There is a real challenge there, but you also have some real tools to help you tackle that challenge. But it lacks longevity. You get your food, air, and stress stabilized in about 50 cycles, then you get your heat stabilized in about another 100 cycles. (You'll pause  a lot, but a cycle at full speed is about 3 minutes.) All in all this is about 10-20 hours of entertainment, closer to 20 for most players, if you don't spoil how to play the game for yourself. The game you get for that chunk of time is good. In particular, some of the particular complaints I see in these reviews, for example about getting duplicants to do what you want, really do boil down to "be patient" and "git gud". You're dealing with some weird problems (for example, gases circulate way less than they do IRL) but they have perfectly good weird solutions (for example, making your floor gas permeable).
But after things have settled down in one colony, the game is over except for sandbox tinkering. And while people have put a lot of time into sandbox tinkering (see for example Brothgar's videos on Youtube), this isn't the best sandbox physics environment, because there aren't many problems to solve (mostly condensing oxygen and boiling water) and because the physics you have to work with are strange.
Most importantly, I got this game in March, it's now August, and there has been one update since I started playing (the Agricultural Upgrade). (In fairness, I picked up the game right after the previous update, the Thermal Upgrade.) That update had quite a bit of content, but it was targeting a system that was already adequate, and it left an "easy button" in the game still for food, which means that the content had limited impact. (For instance, I never grew Pincha Peppers at all, because Frost Buns work fine forever.) The next update will target a much more important problem (disease being a slap on the wrist); with any luck this will turn my thumb around on this review.
Edit: now there has been the Outbreak Upgrade. This did one really good thing: it made toxic biomes serious instead of being trivial to dig through and even a source of air with no penalty. Most everything else it did either made the game easier (like the new food system) or more tedious (the actual implementation of the germ mechanic, and the slowed down research). It gave the game another 5-6 hours of fun for me and now I'm really done with it again. I can't reverse my review for this. I will give Klei props for setting a 6 week timetable between updates now, though.

Max, a lone wolf who just wants to leave this damn filthy piece of land where survival of the fittest applies vigorously. All Max knows is this post-apocaliptic society stucked around Gastown. It's the last bastion of humanity surrounded by hostile land called Big Nothing. Max desires crossing part of Big Nothing called Plains of Silence in order to find what lays behind and start a new life. Forget what was lost. Rumour has it water and green vegetations are plenty there, but no one ever returned to confirm these legends. Still there would be no reason to return to this brutal and violent land led by masochists and maniacs. Max focuses everything just on one purpuse - build a car able to cross Plains of Silence - but what happens on his way its up to you to discover.
Mad Max offers surprisingly large open world full of brutality, violence and day to day surviving. Wait, let me stop here, survival in this world for Max is as difficult as swimming for Michael Phelps. I would expect more elements and threats, but in this desert it's easier to meet a stranger than in my town on Sunday. Even though the Mad Max's world is welldesigned and every location is unique after a while you won't know whats lack of gasoline, water or even ammunition. On the other hand action parts of the game are spectacular and make the game very enjoyable. Beating to death almost every person you meet, destructing cars of other survivors and dismantling Scrotus's (President of Gastown and surrounding lands) camps makes game very entertaining.
When we move to RPG elements, don't expect much. Story is short and plain. I was so curious about Max, or even about the past, how the world turned into this hellish place, but no, sorry, no explanation for you. Eventhough many relics (usually postcards) and monuments (lighthouse etc.) persisted the decline of civilization, you are here only to look around and examine them. It's not bad, but there could be so much more! Max's memories or just tale from anyone who you meet through the game.
After all this game feels amazing despite all negatives.

Undertale is an RPG with a twist not often seen in games of this genre, this twist is of course the perma-death mechanic, what this game loves to do is develop these deep and loveable characters with tangeble real personalities, only for you to hold their life in your hands. In Undertale every deision you make is important and will impact how the game ends, see multiple endings.
Every decision from sparing a common "lesser dog" to going on a genocidal rampage dramatically affects the story as it unfolds, as characters in this game are reactive and even sometimes proactive.
If you kill someone that another character is close to they will be legitimatelu mad at you and even will sometimes remember this anger through multiple playthroughs of the game, either givng you a hand time or maybe even their friendship if you make a decision they like.
When I played through Undertale I was a pacifist for the mostpart as upon killing Toriel and actually seeing her die I felt actual guilt, this woman had gave me hospitality only for me to kill her, this mechanic intitially drove me away form Undertale but months later I returned and restarted determined to save everyone, sadly the first time this was not possible, when it got to the final battle someone had to die, the first monemt when I drew my knife was familiar yet, it almost pained me to do this Asgore was nothing but kind to me and here I was waving my knife at him, There was this brief moment where it seemed as if I could save him, give him mercy I was overjoyed only for that joy to be snatched from me immediatly and turned to sorrow as I watched him die begging to see his wife and family one last time. It didn't make it any better that I was then plunged into an eternal darkness with his killer.
At least I knew that I could reset and become a true pacifist now, this ending had you recount the memories you had with all the friends you made and actually escape with all your friends to the overworld. The point i'm trying to make is this game is not played for it's graphics, combat or world but for the emotional impact it leaves on you.
Undertale is a deeply personal experience best played blind and by yourself and for a mere 10 euro (the price of a burger and chips) it's definatly worth it for what you take away from this game.
Just don't dive into the community, a vocal minority ruins the whole experience ;p

I originally saw this game advertised as a game where "you didn't have to kill anyone". That was enough for me to put it on my wishlist, especially with the humor shown in the description. Playing it, I can expand this. It's concept is also a bit of a deconstruction of the RPG genre. It holds a magnifying glass over the killing of monsters in other games, especially the traditional farming of many RPG's. I know it really made me think.
Unfortunately, to deliver on the promise of "you don't have to kill anyone", it's set up to be very one-sided. Why was there a war between humans and monsters? Because the humans attacked out of the blue. Why can a single child kill their way across the underground? Because humans are much more powerful than monsters. A lot of it just seemed kind of contrived to be all sunshine and roses for monsters, which to me, hindered the concept a bit.
Most RPG's have evil monsters, often that have/will/could kill entire villages of humans. As such, it felt kind of like trying to make a commentary on Lord of the Rings by sending someone to Sesame Street. A character slaughtering Uruk-hai would hardly be judged as harshly as someone striking down Big Bird and Elmo (albeit, Elmo isn't trying to steal your soul. I think).
The game
did a similar thing with slightly better execution. There, you also have the ability to kill or spare those you encounter, and which you do influences NPC attitudes towards you, but the enemies you face tend to be presented as either bullies, or guys just doing their job, rather than as innocent victims. [/rant]
This was one of the best parts of the game. The entire story is extremely character focused, with great dynamics and dialogue, and other than the aforementioned tendency to be a little one-sided towards the intended pacifism, it overall was very engaging and interesting.
This is probably the best part of the entire game. The dialogue, as well as the random descriptions of objects, was the number one thing that got me to play the game for myself, and finish it, despite having already seen the entire story elsewhere. Lots of jokes, both good and bad, and really good character development.
The game does a good job with the minimalist style, though given the minimalist style, it's hard to say too much about it...
...Though on that topic, I have to say that the early graphics were one of the things that made me initially stop playing. If they had had an enemy like Snowdrake or Aaron, monsters with more detailed sprites, in the beginning, I would have expected more of the game from the beginning. The early monsters, though, all looked, well, rather crappy, imho. And the main character's sprite... I couldn't stand it. I still won't say I like the main character's sprite, but I guess you can say that I've been desensitized to it, and I'm more forgiving of the early monsters in light of them not being representative of the whole game.
The music is wonderful... but... the game's music structure is poorly designed, so that any number of factors can cause it to not play at all, including your computer's username having non-alphanumeric characters, installing in any directory other than C:\, or other more elusive gremlins. I install almost all my games on my D:\ drive, so this was an issue for me. The lack of any music the first time I played, which I thought was part of its bare-bones design at the time (given the similarly bare-bones controls, interface, and graphics in general), was another of the reasons I initially stopped playing the game.
In almost every fight, you have to engage in some sort of bullet-hell like minigame to dodge attacks from the monsters you're fighting/trying not to fight. Personally, despite my love of top-down shooters, I'm not a fan of outright bullet-hell games. That made this game, well, a bit less appealing. Further, I found the fact that you have to do so as a little heart representing your soul to be rather immersion breaking. The more I played, the more used to it I got, and the less it annoyed me/broke my immersion, but this was the number one reason why I stopped playing it when I first tried.
If you're still undecided on whether or not to play this game... Do it. Despite getting it as a gift, I would say that a $10 price tag is well worth it for this game. If you're having trouble getting into the game at first, I would strongly recommend giving it a chance. Don't let it gather digital dust for months and months like I did.

A well-made space sandbox game, with great combat reminiscent of Star Trek Bridge Commander and a decent story campaign to see you off into the sandbox. It has a good dynamic side-mission generator, spawning mission locations near where you are so you don't spend too much time waiting when travelling from waypoint to waypoint. Though the game is set only in one star system (except for a short detour in the story campaign), the map is huge and is worth exploring just to see where you can get all the ships and weapons (of which there are plenty). There also seems to be a bounty system where you can find outlaws in powerful ships which can earn you lots of cash, though I haven't encountered any during my run through the campaign.
Combat is similar to the old Star Trek Bridge Commander, where you have 4 sheild facings (and so does the enemy), and it becomes a matter of rotating through your sheilds to spread damage evenly, while trying to focus fire on only one of the enemy's shield face to get at his hull.
You also earn experience which you can spend on 4 abilities to help you during combat. I played the engineer class, which focuses on buffs and debuffs and triggering these abilities do make a huge but not completely unbalancing effect on the results of combat. There are also enough choices in the skill progression that you can specialize your abilities, for example focusing one skill on reducing enemy weapon accuracy and another on dropping their shields.
It does have some issues, The camera is a bit floaty and needs some time to get used to, the early grind can be really painful (I actually got too bored of the grind and just cheated the money), and the framerate can drop hard in the large ship battles in the story campaign. It also seems to have the ability to target enemy weapons and subsystems but I didn't see it make any difference during any of the fights. The UI flow also feels a bit rough in general, requiring too many clicks to do things, a rather unintuitive system for mounting weapons (instead of just having a drag and drop system), missing hotkeys (the 'mark target' action REALLY needs a hotkey, and the fighter launch hotkeys don't seem to work) among other things. Hopefully these will be polished as the game is updated.
In the end though, the combat and the large and dynamic world makes it worth playing through the rough spots, and the campaign is interesting enough to lead you into the larger sandbox, which itself is worth exploring. Space sandbox games seem to finally be coming back into form, and this game is one of the good ones.

If you want a game for managing resources and mostly-passive play in maximum of five-minute bursts, this is probably for you. If you want something that's played mostly actively, maybe not. {there are exception strategies, but not *that* many.} It's also rather complex, though less-so than some of the reviews make it sound.
The game has a lot of different elements to micromanage, but none of them are, on their own, immensely complex. This game has only two clicker analogues/minigames as far as I've gotten- the special fights and the baal slayer. I think ultimate beings V2 are going to be a third, but it's not viable for me yet. None of these is incredibly neccessary.
Anything else's gameplay is micromanaging in some manner. Progress bars will fill with you or without you, but you can optimize through micromanaging or reset to restart building with an exponentially increasing starting multiplier. This is a very reset (rebirth in-game, at least for the simplest kind. Challenges are a higher-level kind.) heavy game, by the way. Active players might "rebirth" as often as every 1-2 hours for optimal progress.
I enjoy this game, you might not. Still, one word of advice- either read the built in FAQ guide or look for a user-made guide. This game might be less complex than people are selling it as, but it doesn't start as simple as most idle games.
And don't pay attention to my playtime, I run it in the background. I spend between 1 and 5 minutes on the game per hour on record, usually, and when it's dramatic in either direction, it's usually less, such as 0 minutes per hour. A more relevant unit is when I started- which is less than six months ago but more than 3.
PS. ignore the people who complement the story. It's not horrid, but you'd probably find reading an average web novel to be a better use of your time. Who knows, your opinion may vary.

My score for this game: 7.5/10
Pros:
- Very interactive game, very fun to play with friends and family
- There is no limit for the creativity of what you can build (unless the server restricts).
- With the naked bodies, funny motion movement, and the aggression of low-quality players, the game shows a strong sense of humor, especially during PVP. You will lose yourself a lot and get laugh-tears during some interactions.
Cons:
- NO AGE RESTRICTION IN THIS GAME! And this is my main complaint to this game. You will find ALOT of little kids who will try to chase you with a rock and yell the dumbest and immature things into their budget microphones. If you are above 20, you will have issues losing your temper because some kids will just♥♥♥♥♥♥you off to a brand new limit. There are a lot of immature 6-14 year olds playing this game with poor logic skills who will interfere between you and this game. There is a severe use of foul language coming from those kids. I haven't encountered this type of a problem even in Call of Duty. They and some of their parents think this game is Minecraft, but it's not. If you read the game description you will see VIOLENCE, BLOOD and GORE, NUDITY, and more. I've encountered TODDLERS playing this game, and I am not joking when I say TODDLERS!!
- Bugs and graphics need to be improved and balanced. As a jr. game developer, it is easy for me to tell that the game has an unbalanced rendering system. My gaming computer has a GTX 960 4GB with i7-6700K and 32GB of DDR4, and I temporarily drop down to 20-40 fps when it renders further terrain (medium-high settings). This issue happens to many people I play with. I have tried a lot to try to fix the issue, even reprogrammed the game and overclocked both GPU and CPU, but that didn't do much with this game. I really do not want to spend another $450 for a top-notch graphics card just because of the unbalanced rendering.

This game looks and feels like a generic third person shooter with Gear of War type mechanics like the cover system (Which I will mention later about) and the running. However, the game was tempting you to follow its story of your standard shooter of just killing the badies and terrorists in a war. It seemed normal, but later on you will feel as though that something is not right. But as soon as you know it, it is too late and shows you the TRUE horror of war. Never I felt a game hurt you so much of showing you the true monster and bad guy... YOU. This makes any other shooter to go down in shame with this game showing the PTSD inducing and fears of what war actually does to us. It doesn't make us heroic. It makes us turn into a monster that we weren't supposed to be.
The gameplay isn't bad since it is just like any third person shooter, but the cover system (like mentioned before) is terrible since it is too sticky that you can run into enemy fire and get cheap deaths. The game has many choices, but unlike other games with morals of good and bad. This game has not a single good moral one, it will hurt you no matter the choice you picked.
The multiplayer is not bad, but is forced to put in. It is basically your standard shooter modes and has classes. It is not the game's best, but is okay enough for a few matches.
Overall, if you want a take from a shooter fan (like me), but want to see something new in a darker tone. I highly recommend this game. This game is like Call of Duty's and Battlefield's (and any other shooter's) dark brother that loves to torment people into crying.

Spec Ops: The Line is a third person cover-based shooter. Your mission in Dubai is to save some people, but how far you go to save them,  the further you will go into insanity.
To give my opinion about the experience of playing the game, I have to say it, at first it felt generic to me. ( like the trailers felt generic to me) I didn't really care about anything or anyone. The game felt like a parody of modern shooters, because it was so generic. But after I reached a certain point in the game I finally saw what makes this game so special. And that is letting you feel the pain of making choices in war.
There were some gameplay parts that were exciting but most of the time it wasn't. The only thing this shooter has that other shooter don't, is the use of sand, which hasn't been used that much sadly in the game. You can use your A.I. partners to help you. Sadly, you can only order them to throw flashbangs or target enemies. So you can't really execute big tactical moves with them. But I have to say on the hardcore difficulty I played the game on they sometimes were useful. Except when you have to revive them...  There are stealth missions, that are just 'kill these 3 people and than just go on shooting again.' I had really hoped that they would expand on those parts just for the variety.
The levels are really well styled with a lot of detail. But, in many places, it doesn't look that amazing graphically, I think the reason for that is due it being an unreal 3 game. This also contributes to the game looking often like a generic shooter.
I really liked when the game let you made in-game choices because they felt well thought out. This occasionally stops the game being a 'shoot everything that moves' game, and allows you, for example, to make a choice whether to kill or not to kill someone. But, often you will be shooting everything you see, which struck me as strange. Sadly, these choices have no effort on the game ending. You will always get the same two endings to choose from. Once I completed the singleplayer I reloaded a save to see the other ending I didn't choose. I also reloaded some missions to get 3 collectables, most of the time they are easy to find, because of the invisible walls. The collectables told some other stories. Also helped with the achievements, which are easy to get in the game.
I would really recommend this game to anyone who is interested in war. The game really made you confront with what you done and makes the line between good or bad people invisible. It also made me think about different aspects of war while playing it.
(Co-op &  Multiplayer:
You should get the game for the singleplayer experience.
I haven't played the 2 player co-op, but, from what I have seen, it is just 5 edited levels from the singleplayer. I guess they are just okay, because nobody is talking about it.
From the multiplayer I have played I can say it is what you would expect from the game after having completed the singleplayer. If you are interested in playing it, you can join the spec ops group
, which has just recently been made. It already has many people joined up, though that could be because there aren't many proper online third-person cover-based shooters on steam. ( correct me if I am wrong ) They are also working on some mods. Still, if you search for an online match normally you will find nobody.)
In short: Spec Ops: The line is a third person cover-based shooter which shows that killing people doesn't make you feel like a hero.

An absolutely engrossing experience examining the human psyche through the eyes and minds of "hard boiled" American soldiers.  Spec Ops delivers one of the most enjoyable and thought provoking stories in both military shooters and video games to date.  The gameplay, the graphics, and the soundtrack helpt to carry the game well, but it's the story that will make you want to keep on going
The gameplay is well refined, with the 3rd person shooting mechanics working very well as you would expect from a game within the past few years.  Decent amounts of environmental disasters and interactions help to keep things fresh and enjoyable.  I was able to complete the game in about 7 hours, though to be honest it seemed like much longer, but in a positive way as I enjoyed my time with this game.
The multiplayer seems to be a bust and thats a shame because when there are others to play with it isn't half bad, especially considering the limited 3rd person shooter options for PC gamers.
Overall I would absolutely recommend this game, it deserves a playthrough for anyone who enjoys 3rd person shooters and/or especially to those who like a good, thought provoking story.

First I want to say: whether you will like this game depends mostly on what you expect of videogames.
The big problem with this game is that there is very little skill to this game - or rather, game doesn't actually teach you how to play it. This is not a skill based game, simply put. It's a well-masqueraded grinding game about watching numbers go up.
If you play any OTHER roguelike platformer - Spelunky, House of Dead Ninjas, Robot Named Fight - core concept of the game is that you are faced with insurmountable odds that you can only overcome with extensive practice.
This is not that game.
If you play any OTHER roguelike action RPG - Risk of Rain, Dead Cells, Crypt of the Necrodancer - you probably expect a tough strategical experience where you're expected to slowly construct your character out of items, perks and weapons into a build that has the chance to withstand what the game throws at you.
This is not that game.
If you play roguelikes in general, you probably expect games with huge hidden depth, with complex system which you can learn how to manipulate in optimal ways over many long playthroughs, allowing you to sink hundreds of hours into it due to drastic replayability.
This is not that game either.
What do I mean by that? Well, by accident of chance, that 20something hours you see on my profile - I haven't actually finished the game in that. That's because it was actually split between three different sessions (because of lack of cloud saves) - one on my PC, one on another PC (irrelevant to this story), and one I started recently.
In my first session, I actually gotten quite far, and unlocked quite a share bit of all the upgrades, I killed two bosses (quite easily) and was mopping up the third area. That is when that computer broke, and while I salvaged some data from it, steam saves didn't make it. Then, I took a bit of a break.
And recently, I decided to give it another go. Surely, I will do well, right? Heh, I can probably beat the first boss in the first attempt... and nope.
I bounced off. It's as if I learned nothing. No other game ever worked like that for me, I always learned SOMETHING. I usually was able to go through the first area with no problem. When I restarted Super House of Dead Ninjas from ground up without all the unlocked upgrades (cloud saves glitched out) , I was still able to easily beat the game like that.
But not here. Suddenly, I realized that my idea of getting better at the game - was just an illusion. It's all an illusion. It's just numbers. You're not actually getting good at the game despite all the hours you clock in.
Classes don't matter, items barely matter at all and 90% of the times you will equip the same items (numerically best items) on everybody. Entire game is one giant numbers game, one giant farming sequence.
And here is the worst part. After realizing the above, I decided to try to FORCE myself to get good at the game. I refused to buy numerical upgrades, instead focusing on unlocking new classes, spells and movement abilities. I tried to play to get good at the game and learn enemy behaviours instead to beat it by brute forcing it. And you know what?
I had a terrible time. When you try to play it with skill instead of numbers, game turns into the worst kind of a quarter-eater. It's a platformer where enemy behaviours are taken straight out of a bullet hell shmup, and you're expected to dodge and zig and zag around bullets in midair, with clunky controls and huge hitbox and health refills being scarce.
For comparison - I recently started a low% run of Castlevania: Aria of Sorrow (an 'igavania' game like the ones RL is clearly inspired by) where I don't use any spells, items or weapons except for knife you start the game with. And the game is still loads of fun! It's much harder, obviously, but doing that revealed a new dimension of depth to the game. You can't say that at all about RL. RL is not a good RPG, or a good platformer. It flubs the basics.
This entire game is a grindfest. It pretends it's something more - but not really.
Bosses are actually pathetically easy (I STEAMROLLED the first boss on my first attempt in my first playthrough) - they have a simple patterns, and handful of attacks. The only real challenge is purely numerical, it's an endurance gauntlet - do you have enough attack to kill them before you make too many mistakes? Or at least do you have enough health to afford to make these mistakes? And question of killing them is simply a question of getting enough numbers for your health and damage. In fact, devs have actually patched OUT a certain SKILLFUL way of quick killing one boss by getting them stuck in a certain way that allowed low-level characters to dispatch them easily. To me, that's the ultimate proof that devs themselves want you to grind, not to get good at the game.
Now, if you're okay with that, if you want a game that you can play to simply turn off your brain and grind for a while - sure, that's fine. But if you like roguelikes, or action platformers, or action RPGs - you won't find what you like here.
With that in mind, I give this game a negative score because that's not what I look for in videogames. If I wanted to look at numbers going up, I'd stare at a clock.

The only thing in common between this game and the game you want to compare to is just that the action takes place in "space". How it makes the gameplay fun is different from the one you want to compare to.
If you want to ask "Does it have <this feature> like <the other game you want to compare to>?", don't. Go back and read my previous comment.

You can do some trading, but I don't concentrate on it like I would have in X or Elite Dangerous. In the end, the question is - does it make you feel that you want to play this more? Does it make you want to see what happens next?

I don't often write reviews, but when I do, it's for a product I love. Starpoint Gemini is probably one of the most fun space games I've played. It feels reminiscent of the X series in a much-welcomed third person perspective(Though you have the option of using a mounted cam perspective instead if you prefer), with the noticeable lack of any empire-building elements to speak of; likewise controlling a fleet is very limited by comparison, and as far as I'm aware you have to be pretty far into the game to even start a fleet.
The game, much like X, has a campaign option(Which I haven't played and therefore cannot comment on) and a sandbox mode. In the sandbox mode, you pick a starting ship and get thrown out into the universe with the usual obnoxious tutorial screens, and then it's pretty much straight into the action. Your prime objective for most of if not the entirety of the game will be to make more money, which you have several options for obtaining, such as mining, hunting criminals, trading goods, or pirating goods. It's all quite fun, but the payouts are generally small in comparison to the price of ships and equipment upgrades, meaning you're definitely going to have to spend several hours chauffeuring sales reps and diplomats through hostile territory and mining asteroids by the hundreds to ever afford that ship upgrade, but this is balanced out by the fact that the starting ships are pretty powerful generally speaking, and should last you as long as you'll use them... Though that doesn't mean that the money grind is any less monotonous.
I'm not saying it isn't fun. It's just not as rewarding as it could've been. You grind money for the sake of getting a bigger ship, for the sake of grinding more money more easily, for the sake of getting a bigger ship. Perhaps the campaign provides more variety, but the sandbox is in desperate need of some more money-sinks.
Graphically, the game is a joy to look at, though the fact that I rarely dabble into anything this modern could be skewing my opinion here a little. The art style is reminiscent of a cartoon or an anime, and colours are very vibrant, making literally everything stand out dramatically. The only thing worth complaining about in terms of graphics is the little debris particles that fly past your ship during movement, as they're practically the size of my tiny gunship's cockpit, but thankfully there's already a mod to remove them.
All in all... It's definitely not a bad game. There are better games out there for the price, but I'd still recommend picking this up if you have money to blow, especially if you're a fan of space games. And if it's on sale right now, slap yourself for even giving it a second thought and then buy it. Just a forewarning however, it will definitely annihilate your social life.
