Undertale is an RPG with a twist not often seen in games of this genre, this twist is of course the perma-death mechanic, what this game loves to do is develop these deep and loveable characters with tangeble real personalities, only for you to hold their life in your hands. In Undertale every deision you make is important and will impact how the game ends, see multiple endings.
Every decision from sparing a common "lesser dog" to going on a genocidal rampage dramatically affects the story as it unfolds, as characters in this game are reactive and even sometimes proactive.
If you kill someone that another character is close to they will be legitimatelu mad at you and even will sometimes remember this anger through multiple playthroughs of the game, either givng you a hand time or maybe even their friendship if you make a decision they like.
When I played through Undertale I was a pacifist for the mostpart as upon killing Toriel and actually seeing her die I felt actual guilt, this woman had gave me hospitality only for me to kill her, this mechanic intitially drove me away form Undertale but months later I returned and restarted determined to save everyone, sadly the first time this was not possible, when it got to the final battle someone had to die, the first monemt when I drew my knife was familiar yet, it almost pained me to do this Asgore was nothing but kind to me and here I was waving my knife at him, There was this brief moment where it seemed as if I could save him, give him mercy I was overjoyed only for that joy to be snatched from me immediatly and turned to sorrow as I watched him die begging to see his wife and family one last time. It didn't make it any better that I was then plunged into an eternal darkness with his killer.
At least I knew that I could reset and become a true pacifist now, this ending had you recount the memories you had with all the friends you made and actually escape with all your friends to the overworld. The point i'm trying to make is this game is not played for it's graphics, combat or world but for the emotional impact it leaves on you.
Undertale is a deeply personal experience best played blind and by yourself and for a mere 10 euro (the price of a burger and chips) it's definatly worth it for what you take away from this game.
Just don't dive into the community, a vocal minority ruins the whole experience ;p

I originally saw this game advertised as a game where "you didn't have to kill anyone". That was enough for me to put it on my wishlist, especially with the humor shown in the description. Playing it, I can expand this. It's concept is also a bit of a deconstruction of the RPG genre. It holds a magnifying glass over the killing of monsters in other games, especially the traditional farming of many RPG's. I know it really made me think.
Unfortunately, to deliver on the promise of "you don't have to kill anyone", it's set up to be very one-sided. Why was there a war between humans and monsters? Because the humans attacked out of the blue. Why can a single child kill their way across the underground? Because humans are much more powerful than monsters. A lot of it just seemed kind of contrived to be all sunshine and roses for monsters, which to me, hindered the concept a bit.
Most RPG's have evil monsters, often that have/will/could kill entire villages of humans. As such, it felt kind of like trying to make a commentary on Lord of the Rings by sending someone to Sesame Street. A character slaughtering Uruk-hai would hardly be judged as harshly as someone striking down Big Bird and Elmo (albeit, Elmo isn't trying to steal your soul. I think).
The game
did a similar thing with slightly better execution. There, you also have the ability to kill or spare those you encounter, and which you do influences NPC attitudes towards you, but the enemies you face tend to be presented as either bullies, or guys just doing their job, rather than as innocent victims. [/rant]
This was one of the best parts of the game. The entire story is extremely character focused, with great dynamics and dialogue, and other than the aforementioned tendency to be a little one-sided towards the intended pacifism, it overall was very engaging and interesting.
This is probably the best part of the entire game. The dialogue, as well as the random descriptions of objects, was the number one thing that got me to play the game for myself, and finish it, despite having already seen the entire story elsewhere. Lots of jokes, both good and bad, and really good character development.
The game does a good job with the minimalist style, though given the minimalist style, it's hard to say too much about it...
...Though on that topic, I have to say that the early graphics were one of the things that made me initially stop playing. If they had had an enemy like Snowdrake or Aaron, monsters with more detailed sprites, in the beginning, I would have expected more of the game from the beginning. The early monsters, though, all looked, well, rather crappy, imho. And the main character's sprite... I couldn't stand it. I still won't say I like the main character's sprite, but I guess you can say that I've been desensitized to it, and I'm more forgiving of the early monsters in light of them not being representative of the whole game.
The music is wonderful... but... the game's music structure is poorly designed, so that any number of factors can cause it to not play at all, including your computer's username having non-alphanumeric characters, installing in any directory other than C:\, or other more elusive gremlins. I install almost all my games on my D:\ drive, so this was an issue for me. The lack of any music the first time I played, which I thought was part of its bare-bones design at the time (given the similarly bare-bones controls, interface, and graphics in general), was another of the reasons I initially stopped playing the game.
In almost every fight, you have to engage in some sort of bullet-hell like minigame to dodge attacks from the monsters you're fighting/trying not to fight. Personally, despite my love of top-down shooters, I'm not a fan of outright bullet-hell games. That made this game, well, a bit less appealing. Further, I found the fact that you have to do so as a little heart representing your soul to be rather immersion breaking. The more I played, the more used to it I got, and the less it annoyed me/broke my immersion, but this was the number one reason why I stopped playing it when I first tried.
If you're still undecided on whether or not to play this game... Do it. Despite getting it as a gift, I would say that a $10 price tag is well worth it for this game. If you're having trouble getting into the game at first, I would strongly recommend giving it a chance. Don't let it gather digital dust for months and months like I did.

I played the android version of this game. I bought it to see what it was like on PC.
The good parts of the game would be - having lot of levels, different gods to choose from (about 20) and some form of strategical placement when it comes to using your spells. By that, I mean that you don't just simply spam the spells as much as you want. You have to make the humans like you by casting "good" spells in order to gain worship, which is the resource used to cast other, more offensive spells for destroying their tower. Basically, you have to find a balance between appeasing the humans and♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥them off by destroying their tower.  It's an interesting combination which makes it unique and offers some depth in the otherwise very standard affair of stopping bad guys from getting from one end to the other.
Now for the bad. The game is an android port. It certainly looks like one and plays like one. The menus on 1920x1080 look pixelated and stretched while the models and textures are pretty lackluster. It's not ugly, but it's not pretty either. The game also starts getting pretty hectic later on, where the difficulty wasn't too well thought out and instead of thinking about enemy unit combinations and synergy, they basically throw in as many of the big units as possible to give some semblance of difficulty. After a while, the game also starts to feel like a grind, but what do you expect from a tower defence game?
Problems aside, this game is pretty good for how much it costs, especially with the sale. It's a solid defence game with some nice depth to keep you interested. It's going to feel like a grind at times but if you don't mind it too much, the game is pretty fun.

Gods vs Humans is a quirky tower defence style game that does not reinvent the genre but does add a neat twist.
Here is my video review and keep reading for a more indepth review here.
First off this game has a lot of depth for a $7 dollar game. The idea is simple. You are one of 20 different gods trying to stop the humans from building a tower to destroy you. Through the levels you will play as Egyptian, Greek, Nordic, and Japanese gods each with unique settings, tower and powers. (Nice rhyme i know)
Each god has their specific set of powers as well as commons ones shared. You will use your powers to destroy pillars to bring down a section of the temple until the whole temple collapses. If the humans reach you then boom your dead and they are now gods. By the way you don’t want that to happen.
The difficulty ramps up because following old mythology you get you power from the worship of humans so if you harm them while destroying the tower they become angry with you and severely limits your power. Also there are evil priests that try to convert the humans and supervisors you have to keep happy or else the workers will repair the pillars faster than you can destroy them. There are also protectors on some floors that will counteract certain spells meaning you can use fire on a level or maybe lighting on a different one.
So far I am finding this game to be very challenging and one that I can't stop playing because I want to see what they are going to throw at me next.
As of now I am recommending this game even more so because it is half off so it is definitely worth it.
I will update this review if I find anything that changes my mind or find things that are cool and you should not about. Don’t forget to click yes if you found this review helpful Thanks :)

I’m pretty much on the fence about this.
To be simple, is Mad Max a fun game? Yes. Is it optimized well? Very much so (i7-4790k, MSI GTX 960...plays smooth as butter despite some small glitches here and there). Will you get anything meaningful out of this game? Maybe.
Mad Max is an open world action game. It makes perfect sense that it is open world. I don’t see why it shouldn’t be anything else. With it being open world, you get to drive around in your own customizable  ‘Magnum Opus’. You get to pick the frame in the beginning (five frames in total) and you have to collect scrap (the game’s currency) and finish various missions in order to upgrade the Magnum Opus.
With driving and car combat, the game really shines! It is so much fun to drive around and ram into other cars as they explode in a fiery blast! The driving feels like being on ice for the first couple of hours but the more upgrades you get, the better the driving is. The vehicle weapons are a lot of fun to use especially when you get the harpoon! The harpoon is your most trusted weapon. You use it not only to tear down gates, scarecrows (monuments dedicated to the big bad of the game) and towers but also to rip off car armor and flinging people anywhere you choose! At one point during the game, you’ll be able to upgrade the harpoon to this rocket launching-ish dubbed the ‘Thunderpoon’, which adds much more mayhem and excitement to the vehicle combat.
On-foot combat, on the other hand, is where the game starts to falter. It uses a very Arkham-influenced freeflow combat system but it feels very unbalanced and immature-ish in a way. Most of the time you are spamming the punch button and the parry button to get a good combo meter. It does work but as the game progresses, the enemies get harder (which is fine) and there are three times as many (which is not fine). Further along, you are spamming the parry and dodge buttons hoping that you get away from the 5-10 ‘war boys’ encircling all around you so that you can plan around who you need to hit first to build a decent combo and go into ‘fury mode’, which is where Max gets stronger and faster. Now, dealing with this in one or two fights is fine but you’re dealing with this constantly! Massive amounts of enemies tend to surround you and the tactics you normally try don’t work and they can overwhelm you quickly. It doesn’t help when you have to have split-second reflexes in order to Parry three people at once (which doesn’t work).
Now, let’s talk about ‘The Wasteland’. The big open world you get to drive around in. It is filled with four strongholds, each with eight projects for you to put together so that you can replenish your health, gas, water canteen, ammo, etc., and each stronghold has several regions that are filled with stuff to do. Regular camps, Stank Gum camps, Top Dog camps, scavenging locations and death run races as well as various sniper towers, scarecrow monuments and minefields for you to take care of. Seems daunting? It is. What’s worse is that all of the camps, yes all 22 of them, usually repeat themselves with the same objectives and the same war boys to fight. It’s worse in the Top Dog camps, which gives you a boss once you reach the end of the camp. He’s a big lug who you have to dodge his charges then go in for the kill, rinse and repeat. Unfortunately, that is the same thing FOR ALL TOP DOGS! This game goes on a rinse-and-repeat cycle for most of the game and in order to get all of the upgrades, and I mean ALL of the upgrades, you have to finish all of these repeating tasks and make sure that each stronghold’s vicinity reaches to 0 and so on and so forth.
The rinse-and-repeat objectives is what brings the game down. The Wasteland itself is beautiful in all of its demolished, rusted post-apocalyptic glory. Each of the regions have their own unique feel, which is a joy to drive through and collecting the historical relics add more weight to the world but not enough. The story itself is interesting but doesn’t feel meaningful or gratifying enough. I understand that Max is a loner and doesn’t trust anyone and has fears of letting people in since everything was taken from him before. You would think that he might rise up from that but at the end, it’s just rinse-and-repeat once more.
That’s the overall problem I have with this game. Nothing really feels meaningful and anything that does have any significance in story or world development is pushed to the wayside. It’s a fun game overall. Vehicle combat is satisfying, the world is beautiful but don’t expect much else.

Lost man ride through wasteland - is best way to describe MAD MAX game. It is open world game where you ride your customazible car in desert, fighting crazy survivers like yourself. Not quite sure that lead to the world state which is represtented in the game, but now everyone is fighting for food, water, fuel and their lifes. You as Max will fight for it too (at least in the begining). But lets break up the game to several key aspects and evaluate them.
Main hero - Mad Max. Brutal, less talking more punching guy. Honestly hard to relate and care for him.
Storyline - Max just wanted to drive far far away but bad guys have taken his car so he needs to build new one (game intro). Players have no impact on storyline, no choices to make. The only choice player have is to do side quest and other things or not. There is like 10 side characters, not well written so ending up not carrying to much that happens to them.
Gameplay - you customize max and his car by unlocking different upgrades, drive while destroying other inhabitants of this game (cars) or punching psychopats on foot. Upgrades for MAX are linear, while customazing car have some depth (for example installing armor on car will make it tougher but heavier and slower). Driving is simple but somehow enjoyable. Combat on foot is batman and assassins creed like, so nothing complecated or new. So I will say it is acceptable.
Graphics and performance - I think it is one of the strongest parts of the game, cause my old gtx560 along with i3-2100 gave me good looking picture on high settings 1080p. So if you have 5-6 year old mid rage PC you can play this without seeing huge, ugly pixels.
But, there is 2 bad things about this game. First - it is boring to 100% complete. Where is a lot of side things to do, but most of them are not enjoyable after few repeats. I wanted to do 100% run, but after fully completing 1/4 of the map I was totally borred, so stopped focusing on that. But still completed all side quests because sometimes they offer something different from main game loop. Second sin of this game - bosses. 90 percent of bosses have same model and move sets. The only thing is differnet is the painting of boss model and setting. Like sometimes there is some addition guys trying to punch along with the boss or some pipes with flames will burn you and/or boss from the side.
To sum up I would say this game is OK. Not great, not bad, but OK. Story tries to teach you something, but bad writting ruins it. Driving and punching saves the game, but not for long. Using Mad Max universe makes game enjoyable. At the moment steam wants you to pay 40$ for the game, would rather wait for discount to get a great deal.

I'm really in the market for a good Twisted Metal PC clone, and looking at the gameplay trailers and screenshots of this, I decided to throw down $2.50 and try it out. There weren't that many negative reviews of it either.
This game is really close to the one I'm looking for, but it's just so painfully slow. I'm hungering for the breakneck speeds, quick turns, constant boosting.
This game does do a bunch of things right, though.
I enjoy the weapons system, where holding down the fire button uses the weapon's alternate fire. The satisfying jump mechanic is also sweet, but the biggest problem is that both the jump and the boost use the same energy meter that runs out after 2 seconds.
There's also a leveling up system for no goddamn reason, other than "multiplayer games just have them". I want to have fun with my vroom-vroom-shooty-deathmatch, not grind in multiplayer lobbies with the My First Buggy.
The maps I played were sweet, and the tutorial taught me the basics pretty quickly so I could just hop into a lobby and go.
The HUD is a bit...cluttered. It's all centered around your target reticle, but it's homogenized so that it's hard to see at an untrained-eye's glance what is your health bar and what the hell "aggressor" means. The getup looks sweet when you target someone with the basic machine gun, though.
If this game just turned up the speed by about ~600% and gave the player a very generous reservoir of energy to jump and boost with, this would be a steal at $5.

This game is my own personal hidden gem. If you like any type of sim games such as Rollercoaster tycoon, simcity, or even cities skylines, then I don't see why this game wouldn't appeal to you. It makes running a prison fun and querky.
The art style of this game is very cartoony and lends to a light hearted atmosphere, even with death, drug abuse, prison beatings, and the fact you can even treat your prisoners extremely harshly.
The game is also extremely accessible to the average joe. The controls are simple, and the rules behind the sim itself are easy to comprehend. Once you get your prison up and running, you will then notice the genius in the depth the game has, the satisfying progression the game has created.
Put gaurds on patrol, give the prisoners TV's in their cells, seperate the Maximum security prisoners from the normal ones, put prisoners in solitary, add armed gaurds, add a pyschologist to help your prisoners, makes your prisoners do labor to make you money, put in metal detectors to slow contraband, add K9 units to your prison, expand your prison to have 200 inmates, add cameras to your prison, tap the phone lines, build automated doors, add visitation. The game is chock full of content, and gets updated every month.
The game even has very healthy mod support via steam workshop. Most notably a Star Wars overhaul mod, making your prisoners aliens, your gaurds stormtroopers, and replacing the textures with Star Wars inspired textures. Lets not forget the Fallout Vault overhaul either. Personally though, Im currently using a winter themed mod for my current run.
With the game coming out at the end of this year, don't be afraid to purchase this early access game. its worth every penny.

Thousands of backers and fans who were eager for this game to come out; several years of development to get it just so; and even early-access availability, supposedly to alpha and beta-test the game before its official release.  Yet still, the game is awful.
I have only played a few hours of it, but I've managed to compile a small list of incredibly important things that you should know before deciding to purchase this game, in the order of importance:
1.  Making in-game currency is slow, almost tedious about 90% of the time.  Granted, you can choose a number of ways in which to generate the income dependent on how you would like to play the game (mining, trading, bounty-hunting, completing freelance missions, etc), but ultimately the amount of money that you generate over time is a very slow crawl and makes purchasing better ships, weapon systems, and other important ship equipment almost not even worth the grind.
2.  Because of the fact that you have to grind in order to make any money, you level up faster than you can improve on your equipment.  Upon checking the official forums, I discovered that this is apparently a known issue that they haven't had the chance to fix yet, so it might be patched up at a later time.  As a result of your leveling which outpaces your ship class and ship's equipment, you will continue to face increasing numbers, frequencies, and difficulties of enemies that you will have more and more trouble dealing with until you can finally purchase better equipment.  Of course, this basically means that you're almost always behind the curve no matter what as there is no way to slow down your leveling and everything gives you experience.
3.  The statistics which indicate to you how difficult a challenge something is in the game are arbitrary.  For instance, the game will tell you the general threat level of red-outlined ships which are about to attack you, which should be an indication of whether you should stand your ground or turn and flee.  This ranges from "Trivial" to "Impossible."  I have been able to easily beat "Impossible" targets with ♥♥♥♥♥♥ ships and almost be totally destroyed by a "Trivial" ship in my brand new cruiser.  This same arbitrary system can be found in the instance of determining whether or not an enemy ship can be boarded and taken over by your troopers.  Generally, the lower the number of troopers on the enemy ship, the easier it'll be to overwhelm them.  This stops being the case after a few levels and, even with the maxed-out perk which increases your troopers' effectiveness by 15%, the smaller number of enemy troopers will steam-roll yours every time.
Anyway, that's my two-cents.  On the plus side, the game is pretty and I liked where the setting was headed, but ultimately this is just a ♥♥♥♥♥ier version of EvE Online and not necessarily worth the price.

tl;dr: If you ever wanted a game that plays like Star Trek Online, but is actually good, buy this game.
You have all the basics of an open world space game - trading, piracy, bounty hunting, mining, scavening etc, but here you don't fly small fighters, but mostly capital ships. The smallest craft are gunships that already dwarf a fighter, and from there you have the entire scale up to massive freighters, dreadnoughts and carriers.
You can outfit your ship with a variety of light weapons (e.g. rail guns, plasma cannons, beam lasers) and heavy weapons (e.g. torpedoes, missiles, ion cannons), plus you can install upgrades to both the weapons and the various components of the ship.
Ships handle basically the same as in Star Trek Online, however you can choose between setting your turrets to fire-at-will or manual crosshair aiming. You have the four shield quadrants, weapons have distinct firing arcs, and thus some ships are better suited for frontal assault, others can deliver heavy broadside attacks. The game also features power distribution - at any time you can freely adjust your power between engines, shields and weapons, and I must say the UI for that is very slick, with a handy snap-on center point for a balanced distribution.
Speaking of ships, there is not just a variety in stats and turret placement, but a great variety in visual styles. From Battlestar Galactica-style bulky ships (my favourite is the Bishop class battleship) to organic-looking cruisers, there should be something for everyone's taste.
Space itself is not realistic. The game takes place within a star system with a binary star, and both the sizes of objects and all distances are massively scaled down. That's the one thing I am missing, that feeling of vast emptiness in space. Though the  Gemini System is large, seamless and sprawling, you come across a space station, mining platform, planet, asteroid field, nebula etc. every few steps. It's a busy place, maybe a bit too busy.
The skill system is rather simple, but does its job. There are 3 classes, each with 4 unique special abilities, and every level you get 1 skill point to upgrade one aspect of one ability. All abilities have multiple effects, and therefore can be developed into different directions. Every 5 levels you get a perk point which can be used on passive bonuses like increased turn speed, better trading prices, higher mining yield or more damage with a weapon category.
The graphics are very nice. The ships are gorgeously detailed, you can zoom in and see things like individual windows, weapon turrets are fully animated and you can even adjust your ship's color and metal glossiness (from dull to polished), you can even choose from a variety of decal and even give it name which is printed onto the hull.
But it's not just the ships. For example, SG2 features some of the most beautifully looking asteroid fields; the asteroids even cast shadows on the surrounding dust!
The sounds are well done, too, the UI sounds very Star-Trek-y and the engines, weapons very Star-Wars-y (i.e. the best of both worlds). But the highlight is the music. I've had the game during Early Access but only towards the actual release was most of the music added, and all I can say is that I was mightily surprised by how epic it is.
Finally, a few positive words about the community. The atmosphere is generally helpful and friendly, and the devs are very active on the Steam forums and are really listening and interacting with the players. The game is also Steamworks modding enabled, and you can already find stuff like the obligatory Star Trek ship packs.

The game, when it works, feels exactly how I remember Blood Money feeling. (key words: "when it works" - details below) With the notable point that I tried playing Blood Money recently and despite loving it at the time I feel that it hasn't aged as well as nostalga would have most people believe. Now, I'm one of those folks who appreciated Absolution for what it was. It wasn't a traditional Hitman game, not by a long shot, but buried in that linear mess were some good ideas that I truly missed when trying to go back and play older versions. This feels like an attempt to combine the best of both, and I think it works. I'm having fun anyway. I'm not even overly upset at the changeover to episodic releases. I am understandably concerned, since most companies promise a full game released in chunks but give up after the 2nd or 3rd one they release, but if IO and SquareEnix keep their word and release the entire game? Honestly my budget can handle $10-15 every now and then a lot easier than it can handle $60 once.
But, that's only when it works. As of the time I'm writing this, the game is plagued with technical problems. Failing to start and taking a couple attempts, running fine even in really crowded areas then suddenly deciding to just slow to an unplayable crawl, and even if you attempt to fight through the ridiculous drop in performance you'll find bodies almost impossible to drag because even the physics calculations are dying along with the rest of the game. I fortunately haven't experienced the connection issues and being unceremoniously kicked out of the game that other people are reporting, but that's a bit crap too. There should be a much more graceful failure state than just forcing you to give up on your current playthrough.
So, would I recommend it? Yes, but with a very significant caveat. Unless you're a diehard fan of the series and are willing to endure technical problems based on the hope of it being fixed in the near future and enjoying what you can in the meantime, I'd hold off on it. I've been playing since the first one came out, and I've been itching for a return to form after the interactive movie that was Absolution. I've gotta get my fix, and broken Hitman with the hope of it being fixed is a helluva lot better than no Hitman.

As a series long fan, I'm having a blast with HITMAN from the beta till now. It has a whole new approach to the way missions are set up. Levels are reminiscent of Blood Money in terms of scale and options -- heck, you can now poison ALL the drinks and drop ALL the chandeliers -- but the overarching setup is aimed more towards completionism.
Like in Absolution, you have an overview of opportunities and discoveries that await you in the level, and you're challenged to find them all and succeed in using them all. I really like this, although it feels a bit too guided. A huge part of this can be fixed by setting 'Opportunities' in the gameplay settings to 'Minimal', which changes the game from a hand-holding fest to a mix of trial and error and paying attention to conversations, which again I love.
Seeing how many ways you 'completed' feels a tad arcady, but having to pay attention all the time feels like you're an actual hitman who's quick on his feet.
Yes, the performance is way below what I expected, there are a couple of big bugs and some PC settings are off, but I really like what the game is in its core and I hope the current issues will be addressed. I'm going to kill Viktor Novikov again, bye.
TL;DR: Mixes Blood Moneys expansive levels and options with a great sense of completionism, that may be too guiding but this can be addressed. It has some technical flaws but these don't stop me from really enjoying this game.

EDIT: this review is not updated for Outbreak since I did not find anything in content and/or other reviews to motivate me to give it another try. Judging by other reviews, mine is still accurate, if not more so with all the new sources of stress.
I'd say I've now given this game a good try and I cannot recommend it in its current state.
Any attempt to play it will go in one of two directions: either you get everything right in first 15 days and will have absolutely nothing to do past that, or you will encounter a slight difficulty and watch everything spiral out of control as you have no tools to control any of your resources.
1) Gas management. Let me just start by saying that managing air supply for the whole colony in one place is not an option. At best you will have to dedicate the entire lowest floor to CO2 removal because gases have miniscule horisontal mobility and you can't do anything about it because the only things that can move gases are the Gas Pump and the gravity, with first being exceptionally unwieldy (in particular it cannot suck air through pipes as you would except a real ventilation system to do). Pressure distribution is painfully slow, leading to one part of the room having no oxygen while the other is at maximum concentration which in turn jams the piping system. On top of that, improper gas distribution is a guaranteed doom to your colony because duplicants will spend most of their time running to oxygen to breathe, decreasing their productivity tenfold.
That's right. A game about a clone space colony has no spacesuits. You have to hold your breath.
Also, there's Chlorine. Staying at the exact height as Oxygen, this gas is only there to make your life miserable. There's no use for it, few ways to contain it, and the only permanent solution involves... cooling it to condensation and mopping it up. And you have to subject yourself to this if you want to get hand sanitizer.
2) Food. While not as much of a pain point as literally anything else, you will most definitely need to explicitly forbid your cook from taking on any other jobs as soon as you can, so that they don't ignore it to go mining. Additionally, unless everyone is full, food is first-come-first-served, meaning that your starving colonist can die watching other people stuff themselves with thousands of kilocalories right in front of him.
Other minor issues include duplicants eating food immediately instead of waiting to cook it, complete lack of food-stocking option (you always have to start and stop production yourself, which is all but guaranteed to end with you either overproducing food that will rot away or starving everyone to death while you deal with something equally lethal) and the fact that after he's done, cook will simply throw it on the ground for you to manually pick up, instead of walking 2 meters to the fridge. Who needs AI when you can simply dump all micro-management on the player.
3) Stress. Oh boy, that's a good one. Ten days in an undecorated environment will lead a medium-level duplicant at maximum stress. The rate is further increased by the following couple of factors: recently standing in water (short), recently diving (short), contacting polluted water (short), low oxygen quality or concentration (while inside) and death of a comrade (several days). While there aren't many of those, each of them adds at least 10% per day, making stress buildup insanely fast.
As for stress effects, there are four possible ones overall, but a single duplicate will only have one: vomiting, destruction, crying and binge-eating. Each and every one of those has insane game-ending potential.
As for reducing stress, your options are 1) spend more than a half of your space on decor and 2) reduce it by miniscule amounts with massage tables. A galaxy of opportunities, isn't it.
4) Duplicants. Remember, the colonists are the enemy here. Incapable of processing anything else than maximum priority tasks, getting lost on their way to the toilet and♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥on the floor, getting themselves stuck EVERYWHERE, walking past their dying teammates instead of bringing them to the assigned medical cot, and only being capable of switching between "it's dark, time to ignore 2 incapacitated friends and a giant chlorine leak" and "RED ALERT, FORGET ABOUT BREATHING", they will mess your efforts up. Don't even try.
8/10 for the idea, 3/10 at most for execution.

If you're looking for a game whose plot makes Camus and Kafka seem positively *uplifiting*, well, here you go.  It's both well-written and utterly depressing.  This is *not* a generic feel-good heroic rah-rah shooter.  In a way, it could even be termed "survival horror" in the purest form... the horrors that emerge from within the human mind and form, rather than mere zombies or mutants.
Mechanically, it's fairly prosaic -- third-person, cover-based, regenerating health, a variety of modern weapons, a couple of companions generally.   The checkpoint system is somewhat obnoxious but checkpoints are fairly common, and if you repeatedly fail the game will start providing you with extra ammunition and even suggest lowering the difficulty (which you can do at the cost of restarting your current checkpoint).
It is not a terribly long game, so don't be expecting a 40-hour run.
There are some technical quirks like encrypted INI files (google around for decryption / encryption utilities) with settings that the menus don't let you change otherwise (notably, depth of field, radial blur... and mouse acceleration!).  It's a minor inconvenience since tools do exist, but just be aware.
The recommendation cannot be generic, as this game is *definitely* not for everyone.

To this day Jedi Academy is the Jedi-knight-simulator to me alongside Jedi Outcast. It's not like the power-fantasy that the Force Unleashed provides, because it comes from a time when Jedi were more like those in the old trilogy than the prequels. The Force is a powerful... force in this game however, giving you a vast arsenal of both light and dark side powers. You won't be punting ewoks for a thousand yards; the most powerful thing you can do is force-push a missile back at the firer (which is as badass as it sounds). Complementing the Force is an arsenal of guns and your personal lightsaber (single-blade only at the start, with staff and dual being unlocked later). The combat is very fun and often light-saber fights are ended in one or two swings for either side, making them rather intense on higher difficulties.
Story-wise you aren't Kyle Katarn, which is a damn shame. You're Jaden, either a man with a feminine name or a woman with a somewhat manly name. Your character is a bit of a blank slate and a dolt, not really a personality to speak of. It's disappointing considering Jedi Outcast has a fairly fun story with a good protagonist. However, the story knows to shut the ♥♥♥♥ up and let the gameplay take over, and besides Rosh being as a git, it's not offensively dull or annoying. It's a classic Star Wars story that shoves Luke Skywalker and Chewbacca in while not really finding its own identity.
However, the missions are varied and the general gameplay is such a blast that I find the meh story to be nothing but a nickpick. The mods are godly here, and should be definitely investigated. There's a simple ini mod that allows your lightsaber to cut anyone apart. I'm talking cut them in half, decapitate them, delimb them, force post their lower half into a rancor's mouth kind of cutting. It makes the game probably the best Star Wars game for lightsabers and the death animations actually work well with the mod. Force-throwing your lightsaber and having it decapitate a stormtrooper on it's way back coupled with him falling limply to the ground like that dude in 300 is ♥♥♥♥ing euphoric to me. I still haven't found a better lightsaber simulator.
It should be noted that the game has an active vanilla and modded multiplayer community. This mode is horrifically unbalanced in vanilla though. If there's a server with maximum force-powers enable and pits, don't play it. I'll be the unarmed guy force-choking you into pits like a deranged garbageman- abusing the game's targetting to prevent you from doing anything to stop me. Lightsaber free-for-all servers are usually just a gathering of people using power-stance with the force-jump attack or other attacks with wide, extremely damaging hit boxes. There are dual servers that exist alongside free-for-alls, and those are legit fun. Guns are obviously usually useless. The particle-disruptor though is every jedi-killers wet-dream, allowing you to instant kill anyone whose back is turned to you. I'm banned from a few servers because of it.
For $10.00 ($20.00 total for Outcast and Academy) I say the Jedi series is a must-have for Star-Wars fans. For anyone else, it's a extremely fun game with varied combat, and is a few hours of fun with a somewhat nonlinear campaign and an active multiplayer community.

Lost man ride through wasteland - is best way to describe MAD MAX game. It is open world game where you ride your customazible car in desert, fighting crazy survivers like yourself. Not quite sure that lead to the world state which is represtented in the game, but now everyone is fighting for food, water, fuel and their lifes. You as Max will fight for it too (at least in the begining). But lets break up the game to several key aspects and evaluate them.
Main hero - Mad Max. Brutal, less talking more punching guy. Honestly hard to relate and care for him.
Storyline - Max just wanted to drive far far away but bad guys have taken his car so he needs to build new one (game intro). Players have no impact on storyline, no choices to make. The only choice player have is to do side quest and other things or not. There is like 10 side characters, not well written so ending up not carrying to much that happens to them.
Gameplay - you customize max and his car by unlocking different upgrades, drive while destroying other inhabitants of this game (cars) or punching psychopats on foot. Upgrades for MAX are linear, while customazing car have some depth (for example installing armor on car will make it tougher but heavier and slower). Driving is simple but somehow enjoyable. Combat on foot is batman and assassins creed like, so nothing complecated or new. So I will say it is acceptable.
Graphics and performance - I think it is one of the strongest parts of the game, cause my old gtx560 along with i3-2100 gave me good looking picture on high settings 1080p. So if you have 5-6 year old mid rage PC you can play this without seeing huge, ugly pixels.
But, there is 2 bad things about this game. First - it is boring to 100% complete. Where is a lot of side things to do, but most of them are not enjoyable after few repeats. I wanted to do 100% run, but after fully completing 1/4 of the map I was totally borred, so stopped focusing on that. But still completed all side quests because sometimes they offer something different from main game loop. Second sin of this game - bosses. 90 percent of bosses have same model and move sets. The only thing is differnet is the painting of boss model and setting. Like sometimes there is some addition guys trying to punch along with the boss or some pipes with flames will burn you and/or boss from the side.
To sum up I would say this game is OK. Not great, not bad, but OK. Story tries to teach you something, but bad writting ruins it. Driving and punching saves the game, but not for long. Using Mad Max universe makes game enjoyable. At the moment steam wants you to pay 40$ for the game, would rather wait for discount to get a great deal.

As a sandbox game, which many other people seem to enjoy, it has lots of possibilities. But, the campaign is very terrible and lackluster, and there's no good tutorial. The help system consists of screenshots and highlighted areas with captions and doesn't really teach you anything - it didn't even kick in until after I had managed to shoot a friendly planet a few times while trying to dock with it and launched again.
Graphically, the ship models and stations look cool, but you don't really get to see details until you're practically nose to nose with them. The external holographic info boards outside stations make no sense to me. The angled third person chase cam makes it very hard to make your ship fly straight unless you're locked in to a waypoint. You also won't see anything happening on your ventral side because of the angles.
The combat AI is terrible - as soon as your enemies get near you, they slow to a crawl, and so if you match speed with them, you're both crawling along. They'll do all sorts of flips to try to evade you while maintaining distance, which makes them ineffective at shooting you, while you chew away at their shields and hull for what seems like forever. Oh, and there's no projected flight marker on the hud either, so forget trying to use your primary weapons at range.
The campaign doesn't do anything to teach you game mechanics either. It just consists of a few 'go here' waypoints, some dialogue, and kill/defend targets. Some of these waypoints are really far away, and take tens of minutes of doing nothing to get to. There are jump gates, but they're ridiculously expensive and you can't afford them doing the campaign alone. There's a few 'freelance' jobs along the way which are generally more kill targets, but they pay out very little. I also accidentally looted a contraband item, and couldn't figure out how to dump it. Oh, and there's no saving the game during campaign mode, you're at the mercy of their sporadic checkpoints, some of which occur before those long journeys doing nothing.

My initial reaction to the game was "Wow, this looks like a massive sandbox space sim! Just look at how big the area map is and how many factions there are. I'll be playing the game for tens of hours!"
Well, after a while I started to realize the game had lots of problems with being a LOT more shallow than what it promises at first. Setting aside the optimization issues and how easily the game can be prone to crashing, It boasts and impressive ~50 factions with a reputation system that ended up being nothing more than a glorified Good / Evil alignment system. If you do missions given out by the good factions you get +rep and they will be friendly to you an the evil ones will be hostile. Vice versa you do missions given to you by the bad guys and your rep shifts to their side making them friendly to you. Unfortunately that is as deep as the faction system goes. Factions don't change opinions as they are completely static.
The static factions leads me to the next problem. The whole world is static. There is absolutely NO sim element in this game to speak of. The game has NO economy, NO dynamic factions, NO dynamic world events. When we speak of sandbox you think of open worlds with things to do in them, but all it is here is the same map as the campaign, just without the campaign missions. Since the game lacks an economy and dynamic factions it makes trading all but a dull and soulless experience. Also, since the world isn't dynamic, there is no real territory control for the factions either. I mean they have their own territories, but they are completely set in stone. You cannot capture territories for the differenct factions. This leaves you with the same Assassination, Taxi, Cargo ferry and Repair missions to grind over and over and over again.
How is the combat then if the other aspects are non-existant and hollow? Well, the combat is rather decent, but what kills it for me is how the game is level scaled. Each time you level up so do your enemies. After certain points their ships get upgraded. If you do like me and other people may have done and only grinded missions for money and XP you'll quickly find yourself in a situation where you don't have enough money to upgrade your ship but you are starting to be too weak to do missions and half the time you simply have to turn around and go away since the RNG pitted you against enemies that simply outclass you. This can be avoided if you salvage derelict ships for parts or capture them and sell them, but then it means that the level scaling system is balanced if you play in a certain way which is horrible, horrible balance in a game that claims to be a sandbox. Simply put if you aren't maximizing your money gains per level then you'll find yourself running into some issues.
It just isn't a good game in the end of the day, and it certainly is no sim either, which is what I was lead to believe. There are no simulations happening behind the scenes, everything is static. The game is hardly an open world sandbox either. It seems to be a loose term that gets thrown around a lot these days. It's a sandbox world if all you had was the big open box without any of the sand in it to be shaped and sculpted by your hands. The game COULD be good, because the flying around, the skill system, the ships, the combat etc. feel good and are fun, but the content within the world is non-existant, unless you want to count repeating Kill X (Assassination and Rescue missions but both work the same. In rescue missions it means that you have to save an NPC ship, but so far they have served as reliable allies that help me take down the enemy ship faster rather than someone who needs help), Fetch Y (there is fetching and delivering cargo and serving as a taxi for VIP, but it works the same mechanically for either mission type so it's only different by name) and Repair Z (there's also Scanning anomalies as missions, but mechanically it works the exact same way as repairing so there is no real difference here either) missions as robustful content.

As a series long fan, I'm having a blast with HITMAN from the beta till now. It has a whole new approach to the way missions are set up. Levels are reminiscent of Blood Money in terms of scale and options -- heck, you can now poison ALL the drinks and drop ALL the chandeliers -- but the overarching setup is aimed more towards completionism.
Like in Absolution, you have an overview of opportunities and discoveries that await you in the level, and you're challenged to find them all and succeed in using them all. I really like this, although it feels a bit too guided. A huge part of this can be fixed by setting 'Opportunities' in the gameplay settings to 'Minimal', which changes the game from a hand-holding fest to a mix of trial and error and paying attention to conversations, which again I love.
Seeing how many ways you 'completed' feels a tad arcady, but having to pay attention all the time feels like you're an actual hitman who's quick on his feet.
Yes, the performance is way below what I expected, there are a couple of big bugs and some PC settings are off, but I really like what the game is in its core and I hope the current issues will be addressed. I'm going to kill Viktor Novikov again, bye.
TL;DR: Mixes Blood Moneys expansive levels and options with a great sense of completionism, that may be too guiding but this can be addressed. It has some technical flaws but these don't stop me from really enjoying this game.

Where so many idlers focus on the fancy art and click effects that you get bored of after the first twenty minutes, ITRTG is all about questing for the next increment.  The game is ugly; there's no denying that, but the underlying mechanics are polished and there's actually a dozen different things to split your non-time on.  For the first couple of weeks of game play, I'd think I was done unlocking new goals only to discover yet another additional mechanic to level up.  Then I looked closer at the Challenges and realized there's a load of reasons to reset from zero for even MORE permanent bonuses.  I've been poking at this thing for most of a year and I haven't even built a galaxy yet.
If you're looking for a time-eating incremental idler, this is a good one.  There are tons of different goals to work towards at your own pace and an honestly interesting back story told through an optional side menu.
Very intricate game, plenty of ways to optimize powering up the way you like it. More advanced than other 'clickers' though it may not look like much. ;)

Tutorial exists, but is incomplete. There are a lot of information that I see that I still have no clue what to do with it. For instance, if you purchase another dealership, you can choose if you put a lot of trust in them or not. What does it do? No clue.
How well other companies are doing don't seem to have an impact on you. It only affects their worth, which is the price to buy them out, and earn a VERY small amount of cash per day.
Customers' pathfinding in the dealership is bad. They'll often run around in circles all over your store before going to a salesman.
Car pricing is unbalanced. You can't leave the sales price to the default. If you do, you will rarely sell any cars, and will often have people complain on the price. Lower it just one step lower (which is 50$), and then suddenly no one complains, and you sell everything. This works no matter the cars' value. Honestly, if you buy a 100k car, 50$ shouldn't makethat much of a difference on your opinion.
Basically, the groundworks is there, but the game really feels like an early alpha game. But seeing as the last update was over 2 years ago, I doubt it's gona be fixed. Even at 5$, it's not worth it.

- Awful Square Enix servers (That you MUST stay connected to in order to play the game normally e.g. unlocked entry points etc).
- Bad optimisation: My GTX 970 can't run this at a fluent 60 fps and DX12 causes the game to stutter and occassionally crash.
I had to tinker with the settings to make it run at a stable 45 -60 fps on my GTX 970.
The instinct lowers my fps when I use it (Must be a tradeoff).

However - The biggest issue is the rubbish online mode.
The servers are unreliable and choppy and when you aren't online.

I really want this game to work as the developers intended - the base game is fun and has loads of potential but SE need to get their act together and fix their servers and optimise the game before Agent 47 gets to Sapienza.

Ok, now that those are out of the way, lets see what it's all about.
The story seems interesting enough, altought it's pretty quickly played through the first steps, it did leave me wanting to know more. I play this with kb and mouse, but the game also seems to recognise controllers too, as it did notice mine right away. The game play was solid, nothing really new there either, but it worked out like it's supposed to do. I'm a bit bad at rating graphics, but for me it really looked nice. Some random npc:s in crowded spaces lack detail, but it's barely noticeable if you don't stare them too much, it's impolite anyways!
The bad (the stuff that most negative reviewers scream about) is the basically always online stuff. If you wanna have a rank from the main storyline missions, or if you wanna play contracts, or any other live stuff, you have to be online. If you are in the middle of a contract and the servers go down, it's mission over, start again after they get back online. I bet that will get people riled up every time a server goes down, it will force you to start over, or you can wait to get the connection back, waiting for servers is not something a pc gamers patience is capable of.
The second bad thing is the shortness of the first part of the game. It's not actually short for a episodic game, but it feels short for those who are not used to it. There's also an annoying DX12 bug (at least for me and few others) that seems to crash the first prologue mission if the dx12 is on, so i recommend using DX11 at least on the first mission, other than that the game seems to be working nicely for me at least.
The Good (that most reviewers seems to completely under rate!) is that this game really is more old school Hitman than the Absolution. You have to sneak, try to find opportunities and ways to move around without being noticed. It's done well. Some may disagree with the way game handles "random events" as they are made so that they seem random, but in reality they trigger when player is near. There are real randomities too, but few of those key thing do wait for player to be around. I think it's a good way for this type of game, but i do realise it pisses some people off too. The game still has a good replayability value as you can do almost everything in so many different ways and after that you can just do your own contracts and see others fail miserably in them!

First off, as a disclaimer: I did back this game on IndieGoGo, even though the campaign was ultimately unsuccessful.
I love car shooting games. I've grown up on classic 90s games like Mario Kart 64, for the N64, and Twisted Metal, for PS1. With that in mind, "Diesel Guns" is arguably the best modern spiritual successor to these types of retro games thus far.
The gameplay is very fun. I love the combat system, everything from the powerups, each of which are fun and cool, to the controls, which are very well implemented. I had no trouble quickly learning the controls.
The AI bots seen ingame, when you set up your own matches, are pretty decent, although they do seem to have the attention span of an ADHD child, often losing interest in who they are attacking, or even will remain passive when they themselves are under attack.
Before I list the good and bad aspects of this game, I do have to report a rather HUGE problem/bug with this game:
The player cannot create their own username, instead it just uses the full name of the computer the player is using, which is compromising information that puts all players at risk, if the wrong person sees that info and decides to hack that PC. THIS NEEDS TO BE FIXED ASAP, PLEASE!
That said, here are the good and bad aspects to this game:
-Fantastic visual style, walking the fine line between realism and cartoony
-Great map design
-Well-animated vehicle models and combat animations
-Easy-to-learn controls
-Great sound effects
-Matches are too long by default. Given the fast-paced combat style, the match length should be considerably-shortened, say to something like 4-5 minutes max
-Few playable maps and playable modes
-Only partial controller support, not full controller support
-Poorly-designed main menu. No game title or game art on the main menu
-No in-game soundtrack
This game is good, but could have benefited more from a longer development period, prior to launching on Steam. It has the feeling of being rushed.

So far... not a polished game.  In fact... it feels very beta.  Then again... in the age of prerelease mania, I'm not surprised.  This is, unlike some games, actually playable.  It's just rough.  Really, really rough.
Like sand in your lube kinda rough.
Considering my machine is a fairly beefy gaming rig, lag makes the controls sloppy, and that makes combat hit or miss (pun only partially intended).  Nothing says table flip like freezing up, only to come back to your ship exploding while you try and get the wild overswings under control.
Is it fun, though?  Well... it's starting to be, when controls don't make you want to ragequit.  Turning settings down doesn't seem to help, which isn't really surprising considering the only way to CHANGE the video settings seems to be to turn off V-synch.  Couldn't get full screen mode otherwise.  Also, devs?  If you're reading this... there's a few simple fixes you should prioritize.  Like every time I restart, having to  reset all the video and sound settings.  Just little things that you should get under control that make me wonder how long before the big things will get fixed.
And honestly, there's a lot more to fix beyond that. Yes, the engine lag is major, yes the fact that video settings don't actually seem to work is major.  But the one scenario the game shipped with is missing voice acting (I swear I saw them say fully voice acted.  Well... it's not.  Or else something went sideways, because my emo little crybab... er... 'hero'... was getting his tearstained hands on the third powercore... and the old man just... stopped talking.  After several seconds... the main character responded... to the popup text.  No voice.  But... whatever.  More than that... there's some serious balance issues.  The fact that if you take some side missions to try and actually GET to the suggested level for the main quest?  Targeting the next waypoint to continue the story... will take you into hostile territory.  By which I mean, your computer will blithely warn you that hostiles are detected... and then you'll explode.  Because they're that powerful... and you're not.
So yeah... lots to fix... on the small, medium, and large fronts.
If they called this a beta?  It'd be telling you how awesome this game was going to be.  Since they claim it's out of beta, though... sorry... but thumbs down.
Also... Devs, if you're still reading this?  Before you release another scenario... give us some real tutorial missions.  Let us grapple some ships, let us marine combat, let us know why we can't tow a deralict back to base and rebuild it.  These are things we just don't have time to experiment with when every mother lovin' two bit space cowboy with a laser and a grudge is shooting holes in our hulls.

Our soldiers who DON'T behave as portrayed in this game.  In reality, our troops [yes, I am ex-military] behave well in the middle of carnage caused by the countries which do not.
Yager is obviously too cowardly to portray the real merciless killers of the region. Before I begin this review, I want to make it clear that
While the game is marketed as a "colony management sim", Oxygen Not Included (or ONI for short) has a punishing difficulty curve and pretty limited micromanagement, despite what a fan of the genre might expect. A more accurate description might be: "A space-colony resource management game" or something similar. It should also be noted that for whatever reason, Klei has decided to refer to all of their major content patches as "Upgrades", which infers to the reader that they might be paid DLC, when in fact every update is free. This leads to review bombing, and in combination with a downvote/upvote bot army, has done some considerable damage to the store page.
tl;dr: The store page does not accurately describe the game
I personally enjoy ONI greatly. The semi-complex systems such as gases, thermodynamics and germs, in addition to managing crucial resources like power, water, and food create a challenging management sim without incentivising micromanagement. Some have complained that germs add an uncessary level of this micromanagement, mainly in the form of the disinfect command, although several adjestments have been made since that update in order to balance disinfecting.
The oil update is an attempt to add greater depth to the endgame, and give players more options for powering their base. The first goal has certainly been achieved, as new the new materials like plastic and naphthalene provide some interesting options for base design. Power production still doesn't have much choice with regards to what a player can reasonably use, though. Petrol produces too much waste heat to be efficient, meaning natural gas and coal will be a player's only real choices if they want to automate things. This problem also exists in food production to a certain extent. There isn't much incentive for players to upgrade from meal lice (a plant obtainable at the start of the game), and this problem has existed through two content patches.
ONI is interesting, fun, and most importantly, challenging. There are a few obvious issues with regards to game balance (most of which are skewed in the player's favor, though) that can make a few aspects of the game uninteresting, but I expect with complete faith that these will be fixed in future patches. Klei is a company that likes to take their sweet time developing a game through the beta stages, but has also consistently shown that they are capable of finishing their games on-schedule and fully implemented, which is why I reccomend it.

I'm not one to trust Early Access. But Rimworld has somewhat warmed me up to the idea. Oxygen not Included (ONI) is no Rimworld and consider me cooled back down on Early Access.
In its current state ONI is barely more than a proof of concept. No story, no goal, no direction, just a handful of objects and an extremely limited tech tree. While the art style is really good, there is no substance to support it. In just a few hours one can construct a pretty much self-sustaining colony and then there is nothing else. The more complicated liquid/gas mechanics don't come into play until later on, but by then there is little motivation to actually to do anything with them (other than setting them up for the sake of setting them up) as they are more hassle to set up than they are worth. From the 12 hours on record,  several hours were spent on setting up a single gas mining/separation production line, only for it to fail and fail again. By the end it just refused to work out of the blue with no discernable indication of what is wrong.
The art style is charming and the concept is intriguing, but don't let yourself suckered in: There is barely any gameplay here. Only can point to Rimworld: While graphically nothing special to look at, it provides a much more engaging and deep survival simulation, proving that developing a good game in this genre is harder than it looks. Throwing a bunch of survival meters and a couple of solutions to them into the game barely provides a foundation.
Also, I think that engagement is paramount in Early Access: Keep the people who upfronted the money interested with frequent and clear updates in an easily accessible format. I haven't heard about the game since purchase and there were no significant updates. And I'm sorry but I have no interest in watching developer vlogs. The game needs a clear roadmap on its page with goals and delivery dates.
I want to like this game as it is right up my alley and I do find the art style charming. But the experience is barebones at best at the moment. Which would be excusable as an Early Access title if I had any confidence that content will be delivered. The only thing that stuck with me from the updates was the developer hyping a completely different game.
In conclusion: Is it a bad game? No. Will it get better: Probably. Should you buy it now: No, unless you really want to support the developer. If you are looking for a colony building experience, it is better to hold off on this one for a while. But its do worth to check back in a year or so.

It's probably fair to say that the single-player aspect of this game isn't as solid storywise as its predecessors (and I do recommend checking out the early incarnations of the Jedi Knight series) but the reason for playing this game is in the action and friends.
LIGHTSABERS: You are able to choose between Single, Dual or Staff, which is a first for the series (only Single is available when you start the SP storyline. The others will become available later.)
FORCE POWERS: You are able to pick and choose which ever powers are offered from both polarities of the Force. In SP you can pick any power at any time but MP is more restrictive -- forcing you to choose one side or the other.
GUNS: Well, maybe not as exciting as the first two, but the some of the guns offered here are the sort of things that only the SW Universe offers and you'll be hard pressed to find similar items in other games.
But what really takes the cake on this game is if you are able to play online with a great group of friends. You will spend countless hours with them. There is a community that has stood by this game throughout the years it has been around and I suspect they will be around for even longer. Much of the community functions in an RPG aspect where people will form their own groups and incorporate SW lore into their gatherings while other aspects of the community will focus on the skill of brandishing the lightsaber or Force. Even further, there are countless mods offered to further enhance gameplay and your experience.
So yes! Buy and play this game. If you want to play this game however, you should do yourself the favor and play the previous games of the series so you are familiar with the storyline, lore and whatnot. It will make the experience much more rewarding once you arrive at this title.

Ok, my first try at a longer review so please be gentle :)
First of all i'd like to clear some things about the game:
1. No it's not Online Only, but yes, the Offline stuff is basically just story/training. So we better hope servers keep up.
2. It's Episodic, wich means there is not much to play storywise right now.
3. It's basically a sandbox. If you like to murder people in every way possible, this is where to do it.
Ok, now that those are out of the way, lets see what it's all about.
The story seems interesting enough, altought it's pretty quickly played through the first steps, it did leave me wanting to know more. I play this with kb and mouse, but the game also seems to recognise controllers too, as it did notice mine right away. The game play was solid, nothing really new there either, but it worked out like it's supposed to do. I'm a bit bad at rating graphics, but for me it really looked nice. Some random npc:s in crowded spaces lack detail, but it's barely noticeable if you don't stare them too much, it's impolite anyways!
The bad (the stuff that most negative reviewers scream about) is the basically always online stuff. If you wanna have a rank from the main storyline missions, or if you wanna play contracts, or any other live stuff, you have to be online. If you are in the middle of a contract and the servers go down, it's mission over, start again after they get back online. I bet that will get people riled up every time a server goes down, it will force you to start over, or you can wait to get the connection back, waiting for servers is not something a pc gamers patience is capable of.
The second bad thing is the shortness of the first part of the game. It's not actually short for a episodic game, but it feels short for those who are not used to it. There's also an annoying DX12 bug (at least for me and few others) that seems to crash the first prologue mission if the dx12 is on, so i recommend using DX11 at least on the first mission, other than that the game seems to be working nicely for me at least.
The Good (that most reviewers seems to completely under rate!) is that this game really is more old school Hitman than the Absolution. You have to sneak, try to find opportunities and ways to move around without being noticed. It's done well. Some may disagree with the way game handles "random events" as they are made so that they seem random, but in reality they trigger when player is near. There are real randomities too, but few of those key thing do wait for player to be around. I think it's a good way for this type of game, but i do realise it pisses some people off too. The game still has a good replayability value as you can do almost everything in so many different ways and after that you can just do your own contracts and see others fail miserably in them!

The port is crap. It's incredibly bad... And the "Always Online" system is ridiculous. It wouldn't be as annoying if the servers actually worked fine, but they go down randomly and BAM, game sends you straight to the main menu without even saving.
But damn, the gameplay is actually pretty great. Very close to classic Hitman games, lots of gameplay options to increase the challenge as well as options to help newcomers play the game easily (sometime too easily actually...).
The level design for the Paris fashion show level is pretty impressive as well. The sheer size of it is incredible, and so is the attention to detail. Shame that it's only one level so far (plus the tutorials, but come on...).
So bottom line is, Eidos made some really stupid decisions (episodic release, always online, cheap port) but the game itself is actually impressive... Kinda polarizing really, but I think it's a good enough absolution after the last game for the game to receive a recommendation.

I had decided to go for the $15 intro pack to see if this installment in the series would be worth it. After having played through the training and Paris missions I'm definitely liking what I'm seeing so far. This game takes the best of Absolution and Blood Money and mixes them together to create the near pefect Hitman experience.
This plays much like past games where guns blazing isn't the way the game is meant to be played. Missions can be completed in a variety of creative ways and there isn't any one specific way to take out a target so there are different unique ways to carry out the mission. The Paris map was relatively big and offered numerous ways to play through the mission without completely holding my hand. The story itself seems interesting so far and it will be nice to learn about Agent 47s start as an agent for the ICA.
Something that many will find annoying are the online only options that seem to be hit or miss right now. When I first started the game it wouldn't connect me online so I could only go through the story. After having complete the Paris mission I tried reconnecting and it seemed to of worked. Navigating the menu is somewhat sluggish but can be overlooked. There is some glitching when dragging bodies as they get clipped through a wall and can't be moved. This can be relatively annoying but I've only experienced it in the training mission.
Overall I'd recommend this game to fans of the series, if you are on the fence about purchase then definitely go for the intro pack and see for yourself.

Let me make my opinion clear. This may not be a fun game, but you owe it to yourself to play it.

Spec Ops is a timely re-imagining Apocalypse Now and Heart of Darkness, one for the modern generation witnessing strife in the Middle East. This is a brutal critique of patriotism, masculine honor, and the "civilized" man which hits with an unparalleled, crushing emotional weight.
This title proves the relevance of video games to artistic statement. Do not miss this milestone.
Do you feel like a hero now?

The vehicle car shooter I've been waiting for. This is as close as I have come to the old memories of Twisted Metal 2 and Vigilante 8, which were hands down my favorite games in their time. I'm hoping this game will pick up in the next months as more content is added and the car shooter genre is refined once again.
Cars - 4 to choose from for now, but each is different and feels like it. Cars are well detailed, especially for such a early release. One thing I would add to each car is somewhat of a back story about the driver. This would let you feel more in touch with the car/driver you chose. Characters with different personalities, and that reflects on the cars they drive and what special weapon/abilities the car has etc. This would tie in perhaps with a story mode, similar to what the old car shooter classic games had. Create some badas*es that makes you want to play them!
Weapons  - The feel is a lot like Vigilante 8, especially the mortar and cannon. Good feel to the guns, nice graphics on the guns too. I was surprised by the detail on the weapons. Can't wait to see the special weapon for each car. I'm hoping it kind of ties in with what the car is, or with the character possibly. This will really set cars apart from each other.
Maps - All maps are open space right now. Good for a quick death match, nice detail, they aren't too different from each other, cookie-cutter like as it's a similar space size wise just different setting. I'm hoping for an addition of cities, suburban areas, special parts of cities such as air ports etc. (Paris level in Twisted Metal 2 is a good example of what I have in mind)
One of the maps in the game has special features that you can interact with to unlock a monster worm to attack. Nice touch, would like to see more interactions with the map and easter eggs.
Some of the things I hope to see in the future would be boss cars, car unlockables, secret areas on map, and I do hope that the game ends up with a little more than just 8 cars to choose from, as that's the plan for now.
Worth the 2.99, I almost didn't get the game because of the low price! I was thinking this will be a low budget feeling game that runs terrible. I was WRONG. It is worth it and I have my fingers crossed as this game develops. PLEASE don't abandon the project, bring back the car shooter genre!!!

Ok. This game is the worst of the two Hard Truck Apocalypse games. Granted, for $1.50 (on sale) you get what you pay for.
Pros:
Trucks with guns
Truck models are nice
More customizable colors for trucks and the ability to add decals (when available).
Like the previous HT:A, you have easy to use driving/aiming using keyboard and mouse
Perks system: This is kind of a WTF. You have them, but I didn't see any way that they helped or hindered. It was never obvious.
Cons:
Voice acting: ABSOLUTELY HORRIBLE! Weird language, lack of inflection, etc.
Story: Disjointed. Nonsensical. Your character is the most naive, trusting, moronic human being in the freaking planet. You are looking for some place called "Edmonton" for no other reason than it is there. Along the way you join forces with the obviously badguy "Sam" (who looks like Uncle sam). You also meet someone named "One-Eyed" who sounds like they are your friend, but (spoiler alert) you end up killing her because she won't give you a box of old filmstrips and she decides to attack you because you bothered to ask. So you kill her. But you seem to think that Sam is an OK guy despite threatening to kill you and wanting to find an ultimate weapon. Also, bad guys are super tough for no reason and they are ALL OVER THE PLACE. You can't even leave a town without getting blown up (seriously, it happened multiple times).
Money: In the first HT:A you could actually make money trading. It made sense. Not in this one. It's cheaper to go out and kill bad guys and sell their stuff.
Side quests: Like the first HT:A, they are essentially "go here, kill this", "guard this slow guy" (p.s. if you let the cargo truck die, you get a LOT more money fromt heir death drop), or "go here, deliver this package." After a while, I stopped doing those as there was no point.
Video issues: There were options to improve the graphics, but the game would refuse to load after I upped them from "medium" (the default). Had to go and reverify the game files before it would load with the default graphics.
If you can look past the bad voice acting, horrible story, and just random goofiness, it's an ok game. It is fun driving around blowing things up and running over pedestrians (which apparently is ok, but bumping into another vehicle will♥♥♥♥♥♥them off).

is a mobile port but it plays pretty well on PC. It's Tower Offense rather than defense as you operate and command a convoy to destroy towers and generally have to get to a specific point to complete your objective. Other objectives are more in recovery of data though for you as the player it boils down to just arriving somewhere still intact.
The game does a good job of introducing mechanics as well as the types of units available and what uses they might have. There aren't THAT many but enough to create some pretty decent strategies as well as make some fairly frantic experiences in real time. Tanks, Shield units, APC's and missile launchers. You're in charge of their order and the path they take through the city.
The main mechanic you'll be dealing with is planning a path (that can be changed at any point) and placing power ups down to aid your convoy in completing the mission. Power ups are dropped from air support and can include things like damage boosts, repair kits, smoke screens and decoys among other things. All are placed with a specific diameter and duration and for the most part are useful in dealing with a specific type of tower. There are also situations where you must travel inside and air support is not available or timers are placed for example to keep a bridge down. Admittedly, these timed sequences are not the most relaxing stages as there is no active pause and this can lead to some sporadically frantic gameplay to keep your convoy alive.
You can also at any time change the order of the convoy. This is especially useful with shielded units to keep the front man from taking excessive damage.
