Pros: The first five to ten hours really are great. There is A LOT to do, so if you can score this on a discount, you will at very minimum get in some awesome driving battles, beat up some bad guys, and explore a bit.  If you like driving around and collecting loot, this is a gold mine. The car audio is top notch. Your car sounds FIERCE.

Cons: Once you've played for five hours, don't expect any more surprises.
There are only five quest types in the whole game:
1) Go kill that boss
2) Go kill all those dudes
3) Go blow up that car with your car
4) Go blow up that place's gas cans
5) Go look for landmines
The first time you do those things, it's cool!  After the 20th time... not so much!
Considering that driving and fighting are all that's left, it saddens me to say that neither of them are that great. They don't work quite right. Fighting is Batman style, but it ignores A LOT of button presses.

Ammo is scarce, so this really isn't a TPS. Do not expect to use your gun more than once or twice an hour.

This game had the potential to be a lot of fun, but unfortunately, it is dragged down by some poor design choices.
The Succession system seems like a really cool idea, and it probably would have been... if 90% of the traits weren't useless or flat out detrimental. Choosing a successor is about "Which of these choices has slightly less trashy traits," instead of comparing the pros and cons of game changing character traits.
The game's default controls are poorly mapped, and don't feel intuitive. Rogue Legacy would have been a lot more fun with precision mouse attacks combined with keyboard movement. Instead there's a cumbersome mix of arrow keys and WASD.
The game's spells are essentially useless for the first 5-10 hours. You don't have enough mana to cast them more than two or three times. Even when you do cast them, the controls make them clunky to aim. Again, the spells would have benefited a lot from aimed mouse attacks.
tl;dr Rogue Legacy is a grindy slog to stack upgrades, and it's innovative ideas are poorly implemented.

I think this game could be a really fun game to play.  In the state it is in, its a bit frustrating.  Has its fun points as well, just feel there is a lot to yet be done.
Probably the biggest thing that bugs me, is the prices of the cars.  Obviously this is probably the biggest part fo the game!  To make this, not even so much like real life, but just better in general, what you sell a car for needs to be fixed.  The customer is never aware of what the dealer bought the car for, new or used, but it almost seems like in this, they do.  You can buy two of the same used car,  say one for $8,500.00, and the other you paid $7,700.00 for.  So now for the two cars, you dont have a listing that shows any difference in mileage, wear, or anything like that, so you should be able to set them both at say $10,000.00, making $1,500.00 on one and $2,300.00 on the other.  That is not how it works in this game however.  You will end up selling the $8,500.00 one for $8,600.00, and the other you will be able to sell for $8,200.00.  This makes it very hard to get anywhere in the game.  I understand you wont make thousands on every car you sell, but you should be able to sell a two cars for the same price reguardless of what you bought them for at auction or brand new!
Another part fo the game is the CSR....It is increadibly easy to loose point by point, but then it is incredibly hard to gain!  Sometimes it seems as if the game is playing against you.  Example: You have two of one brand new car, been on the lot for several turns/Days, you dont change the price, you dont nothing, all the sudden, the two you have get sold, and then everyone and their mother walking in your door is looking for that car.  And guess what, almost every person that is there looking for it, costs you CSR.  Since you can hardly make any money selling cars, it is very hard to upgrade your lot to be able to hold more cars that you cant afford to buy!
I think they need to add that cars are damaged in some way, there are different mileages on them, all the things that make a used car a used car.  It would be nice to if they added a stat to the used cars on either the average bought/sold for price, or highest bought/sold and lowest bought/sold.  Helping you better know what to buy and what to pass on at auctions, as well as what to try to sell them for.
Outside of the salesman, the techs, maybe ther service manager, what is the point of the other employees?  They seem like they do absolutly nothing.  you see no negotiating of prices(another thing that would make this game better), they dont set any prices... nothing.  What is the point of wasting money on them daily, if it seems there is absolutly no point to them?
There are other things as well that i think would make this game great, but these are the keys in my opinion.  In the current state it is in, i cant recommend this game.  If they every make any of these kinds of changes, i would absolutly change that opinion.

There are ultra realistic space sims,  there are slow paced datasheet space sims,  and on and on and on you can go down the laundry list of space games.   What Starpoint Gemini 2 seeks to accomplish is finding a healthy balance of it's predecessors without leaning too far in any particular direction.   Make no mistake,  SG2 will take you hours to accomplish anything substantial,  but it won't take you hours to start doing something fun.
Want to be a trader?  You can do that.   Want to mine for rare materials?  You can do that.  Want to be a pirate?  You'll eventually be able to do that.  Want to be the force of good bringing bad guys to justice while getting paid for your bounty kills?  You can do that to.
My 7 hours have been mostly spent divided between the three classes that you can choose from in the freeform game.  There is the Leader,  Gunner and Engineer.   Each class provides a fairly substantial difference on terms of feel however the common objective between most of these skills is all the same...   kill your enemy.   I was a bit disappointed to see that many of these skills are not overly helpful for more mundane tasks like mining,  trading,  or exploration.  Seeing as how the game puts heavy emphasis on providing you options - this particular part said to me "We're only truly designing this game with combat in mind".   While the other things to do are definitely not afterthoughts,  they're not quite as fleshed out and as robust as I would have liked.
There is a story mode but unfortunately the voice acting is horrible.  Normally I can manage some bad voice acting but found this to be a bit too much.  This turned out to be alright in the end as the sandbox aspects of this game are fun and easy to get into.  The tutorial or lack there of was at least filled with a pop-up tips menu which got me rolling quickly enough.  I had to spend some time rummaging through the keybind menu but after that I was off and racing.
This game still feels very young with a lot of possiblities.  My 7 hours is definitely not enough time to even have a completely firm grasp of what the late game or even middle game will be like but I have a hunch it's going to just be more of the same but with higher stakes involved.  Instead of combat with 3-6 ships,  it'll be more along the lines of 10-20 ships if the trailers and other various videos are telling a truthful tale.   Scaling of this nature is not altogether a bad thing if you're having fun with everything you're doing at the start of the game.  Essentially,  it's not going to mix up the formula a whole lot as you get deeper into the game.  Sure you'll be able to use more skills due to having higher energy and more points to place down extra turrets and systems...  but most of those tools could be used at the start of the game as well,  just within limitations.
If I could pick one thing I wish this game had, it would be co-op support.  Sharing a universe with 2-16 friends could serve for some amazing lan or house hold family fun.  Luckily the mod community seems to be getting behind this game so at the very least the variety of things to do will be getting mixed up a lot.
If you're still on the fence of this game I'd say just keep checking back.  Look at what the devs and the mod community are up to.  There is already a decent amount to do here and it's just done well.   If I had to give it a 1-10 rating I'd say we have ourselves an 8.2 with the clear opportunity to become a 9-9.5 if they continue to add features.   If you're someone who enjoys smelling the flowers and doing assorted tasks with some grinding mechancis involved due to large credit costs to purchase anything substantial,  then this game is the game for you!

Great base-builder/colony sim, lots of buildable items, endless explorable space. Great way to waste a few hours. Would recommend just on art and gameplay style, particularly if you're a science nerd.
That being said, it's definitely not worth $25.
The first few colonies you build will probably crash and burn, usually because your dupes will be crying, barfing, and sh*!ting themselves (pro tip: sweep nonstop, build a trillion paintings, and set high priority on massage tables). Then you finally get the swing of things, and are able to build a few coal gennies so your dupes aren't running the manuals 25/8. By the time you run out of coal (unless you're a dork like me and you feed all your sandstone to hatches so you can use their coal poops), you've probably found a geyser and can power your base off of that. Then....
Well, then nothing.
There's no real goal other than to make a reasonably self-sustaining base, which ultimately isn't that hard. Moreover, the further out you try to explore, the less hospitable the environment becomes - freezing cold, burning hot, polluted oxygen, chlorine, you name it - so exploring quickly becomes more of a struggle than it's worth.
Additionally, there's a lot of buildable items that you learn pretty quickly aren't really worth the effort. For example, building a green house to grow your own food, i.e. meal lice, etc. First, the food you make from the stuff you grow will be barely any better than the dirt and water you've been feeding your dupes since the beginning. Secondly, farming is a b*!ch and a half. Some plants need polluted water, some need clean? Some need hot, some need cold? Plus, there's a set number of harvests, so you have to pay real close attention to each plant and uproot it before it finishes its last harvest or you lose the seed? That doesn't even make sense.
Essentially, there's quite a long list of items that I've built once and then never again cuz they weren't worth the time and resources (textile factory, farm tiles, fan, cook station, etc). But if a lot of the items aren't really necessary to successfully building a base, if building a self-sustaining base isn't really that difficult, and if long-distance exploring isn't really an option, then there really needs to be an additional goal here. Cuz for me, it's usually GG when I find a natural gas geyser.
Again, really fun game, and if you're a science nerd like me, you could waste a lot of hours just messing around with the mechanics - making liquid oxygen by super cooling hydrogen (cuz they nerfed the piping, so you can't just run your dirty oxy thru a buttload of thermoregs any more - LAME), creating a layered jello effect out of carbon dioxide, oxygen, and hydrogen (and tinting the whole thing neon green with chlorine, heheh), trapping like six hatches on one tile (difficult, but pretty funny when it works). But still, there's not really an endgame. At least not one that would validate that price tag.
Still would recommend tho, cuz Klei is good about improving their games, and again, it's a good time waster.

Max & the Magic Marker is a children's game. The game play, platforming, and mechanics are simple and easy enough for a child to master in not very much time. The mechanic of drawing objects is implemented in a much better fashion in comparison to Crayon Physics Deluxe, for example, but that is still far from a compliment. The music is good, and fitting of the game world, but it does repeat quite often. The overall level design is bland, repetitive, and uninspired. The checkpoints are available throughout each level, and they are put to use for the benefit of the player, and not because of difficulty. Because of the game's overall limitation, it is better suited for short play times, as it does get boring very fast. Soon after progressing to the second world, the game has severe crashing to desktop problems with no errors. It simply quits the game and puts you back into the desktop. So when I first played this game it was nice for a casual play now I am going to redo this review after playing it with the new updates.
About:
It is a heavy management game to the very core. If you are bad at Micromanagement stop here and just don't bother getting this game. Otherwise for people who enjoy puzzles, strategy and heavy resource management this is a great game. It is like Rimworld in the way that the characters have some of the same traits (task enablement, leveling, and prioritizing certain task). There is not a whole lot of 'crafting items', It's more of building stations, machines and furniture to enable your minions to do their task. The art style is like Don't starve with a cartoony twist. It also has the 2D mine your base/exploration style. One thing I want to note is The law of conservation of energy applies here, in otherwords there is no infinite supply of resources.
With the Disease update:
It made it considerably harder but not something that makes it unenjoyable (You may disable this feature FYI). I would say it makes it challenging if you choose to do some sort of hardcore mode but it feels more of you just need to be more cautious in what you want your minions to do.
With the Oil update:
What oil? I built a pretty large base and have not struck oil yet so I'll let you know later. But with this update new recipes had been added but it's annoying when you don't have the oil for the plastics but this doesn't stop progression. It just makes you sad you can't explore the feature yet. :(
Goods:
-The ability to make the game as challenging/easy as you want
-They are adding alot of content to the game and starting to flesh out some motivation for exploring our unfortunate astroid.
-The ability to move gases, control temperatures and transfer fluids around and seperate them.
-It's fun to explore, the animation style is hilarious
-Lots of controllable factors such as Minions, Map seed and how you want to build your base.
Inbetweens
-It's difficult. -The learning curve can be as fast or slow as you want it to be. You could start off with easy settings to get into the game, but it becomes difficult because what you do in the early game will definitely affect you later in the game. It requires future planning and for you to learn so many things so that your base doesn't overwhelm you.
-It's complicated and easy to get overwhelmed. -To last as long as possible in the astroid it requires alot of manipulating and micromanaging energy, gasses, temperatures and liquids. It's easy to get overwhelmed because you have things in the game that can control what goes where but you also need to build up to it without crossing your wires. It's also easy to build too big of a base.
Bads:
-No end game and not enough motivation to really 'move'. Base building is fine but... once you actually build a sustainable/managable base there's not that much to do yet. You could explore a bit but there isn't much reward for going pass the middle stage and into the exploration stage. As much as I love it this is really a bummer but the game is in EA so I hope for something to fill the gap here...
Conclusion:
It's a fun game, I personally love management and strategy games. This one required alot of trial and effort at the game to get a decent map with an easy colony (All vomiters). It is a little hard maybe like a 6/10 hard on standard mode. I would recommend this for people really into micromanagment and engineering, but not as much to those who love to go fast because this requires some patience and slower movements.
Why I recommend it?
Because it is a fun survival strategy game that deserves a chance here. At most it can offer several hours of fun and fustration. Also because I love the devs games and they match my games of interest.

There are those who say this game is bad because it "accused them of cheating" I can't speak for these reviews because this hasn't happened to me. There are those who say this game is bad because progression is slow, and what I can say to that is "Have you ever played an incremental game?".
This game is not a clicking simulator like many other incremental games end up being, with this game setting up an autoclicker will benefit you very little. Progression certainly FEELS slower than some other incremental games, but that's only because it doesn't have fancy graphics or sound effects; if you're actively playing this game it will feel slower because of the simplicity of the game.
Let's compare this to other incrementals on Steam:
-Clicker Heroes is a pretty solid game, but it fails to do anything special at all after prestiging a few times.
-Crusaders of the Lost Idols is an EXCELLENT game...assuming you've got the time to mess around with it nearly 24/7, otherwise progression in it is MUCH slower than this game, not to mention the content just loops with increased stats every 50-100 levels.
-Time Clickers if taken at face-value appears to be an in-depth experience, after logging a few hours however you see that it leads nowhere.
-Crush Crush is a fairly solid game but ends up slowing down to a slow, painful, MULTIPLE DAYS LONG grind after unlocking the first 7 or so girls.
-AdVenture Capitalist is certainly not for everyone, I personally hated it but love most incrementals.
-Every other incremental on Steam is a massive joke.
All I can say negative about this game thus far is that the micro-transactions are ludicrously expensive, however they offer such insignificant advantages that you'd have to spend $100 just to save a days worth of grinding. An example of these in-game purchases is a "Godly Liquid", this will increase your production by 100% effectively cutting the amount of time needed to complete certain tasks in half, the catch? It costs $1 and only lasts for 90 minutes.
Tl;dr - just download the damn game, it's like a 100mb download.

Gang Beasts is a bit love/hate for me. I really enjoy playing it with friends and it has had me in tears laughing at some of the onscreen antics. The physics are a lot more clever than they look - it seems that every time I play it my character pulls off a dodgy move I've never seen before and it's hilarious.
With recent updates, they have focussed on tweaking the physics to be a bit more consistent and less down to pot luck, which is much appreciated. Also, adding 'throwing' when you drop a person was a genius move! The game is as pretty as it needs to be and actually the new 'on demand' server setup seems to be working a lot better than the old system - I can actually find a game now.
Now the bad... This is a game that gets a lot of the very difficult things so right and some of the simplest things completely wrong. The game is now on its 3rd iteration of menus and they are still barely usable. How on earth is it SO DIFFICULT to make a coherent menu system for a game? C'mon guys, it's been like this for over a year. The game is still riddled with bugs at certain points that will make the servers start the next level while still showing the scores while you play behind them, then suddenly decide it's going to skip this level and move everyone to another. This type of thing should be really simple to fix compared to some of the other things (e.g. perfectly synchronised ragdoll physics over the network) that it does so well. With a bit of a polish (and no, I don't mean slightly tweaking the menus that are there, I mean COMPLETELY BINNING THEM AND STARTING AGAIN), this game would feel far more complete. Another thing is that the available levels in online keeps changing - some of my favourite levels (Subway) seem to have gone missing. Whilst 'new' (read: singleplayer) levels have appeared in multiplayer, some of the classics have disappeared for no apparent reason - they seemed to be working?! Maybe now would be a great time to add some new levels too?
I'm recommending this game because of all the amazing laughs I've had playing it. Everyone here should try and look past the ABYSMAL menus / polish and enjoy the ragdoll fighting at its finest!

Apparently if you play offline then you will have an offline save. Challenges are also disabled in offline mode, so you wont be able to level 47 up to buy/unlock new weapons or tech to reply the levels in new ways (so much for replayability)
I wish I hadn't bought this via GMG just so I could refund it because I don't support this level of locked in online only bull, at least in a single player game.
Also what's going to happen when the servers shut down in 5 years time, there is a challenge in the game to eliminate 5 exclusive targets.
Exclusive targets are IO's (only online) small offering to keep you enticed because there isn't a lot to do and we don't know yet how big or how many levels there will be. We also don't know if the unlock benefits from completing them will be unlockable any other way it would be scummy if you can't.
(They have said no micro transactions but I bet the costumes/weapons from these exclusive targets will be up for a price)
I would hold off buying this at least till IO or Square Enix change their narrative or change the game regarding the online only elements.
Heres hoping the mod scene can turn this around and stop this, I payed for a single player experience not a tacky online mess but I doubt it because of Denuvo and server checks.

War isn't all  about action, destroying everything and killing the enemy. This game wants to prove that.

What is Spec Ops: The Line in a nutshell? Imagine 'The Last of Us" but set in a military shooter context... and perhaps not quite as brilliant. The characters are not all that deep nor easy to get attached to. Perhaps however, this is a saving grace as the emotions and journey that Captain Walker (the protagonist) and his two squad mates; Lugo and Adams endure brings out some very real themes of remorse and dread.
It's somewhat ironic really; the makers of Spec Ops: The line have given us some very mixed signals where the game entices you to play quite aggressively to overcome all your foes and yet has a strange way of making you feel evil no matter what choice you make. There are not a great deal of choices to make in this game but the few you do make will haunt you every time the game yanks you out of the action for a cinematic to tell you the next chunk or bite of story.
This for me is where this game is weakest. The game play has you playing through what for the most part is a very solid third person shooter and then slaps you in the face with realities and horrors contrary to the fantasy and glory of shooter campaigns like Wolfenstein (the recent one), COD and Battlefield.
While it can be argued that it is, as many shooters, a shooting gallery leading you to play through to the next cinematic, it is indeed unique as it will challenge you and strive to make you feel something real. About 5 hours in I thought; "Yeah it's nice to have a story in my mindless shooter, but I probably won't remember this one." Having completed it now (3 hours of game play later) I can certainly say the ending gave context to the game which now has burned its story firmly in my memory.
Now enough on the touchy feelie♥♥♥♥♥♥ Let's talk about the game-play:
The controls overall or are quite straight forward but the cover mechanics leave a lot to be desired. While it is nice to have a game which allows you to break free of cover easily, sometimes this can work out badly for you when needing to lock into cover elsewhere when getting flanked from multiple directions. It is useful though when a grenade lands close by and you need to move to another cover point -which happens A LOT! This is probably because too many contextual actions are assigned to the A button (playing on an Xbox-One controller).
The guns feel great and each feels unique and appropriate for various engagements as well as play styles. You will quickly find your favorites and gravitate towards them. Personally I liked the M417 Semiautomatic Rifle and the Scar-H with under-slug grenade launcher but the pistols are great too. The game does give you some ♥♥♥♥ time with grenade launchers and turrets but not even close to enough time with the RPG or the AA-12 which are incredibly powerful but only available for the♥♥♥♥♥♥end of the game.
The AI is not overly punishing in that they won't rush you constantly. They will put you down very quickly if you keep your head out for a few shots too many. Also they love to throw grenades. Most of the time I died because they would flush me out with a 'nade and there'd be nowhere safe for me to run. You quickly learn to target the lobbers first. I played this game on the highest available difficulty of the three available before first play-through. I suspect the additional difficulty which unlocks at the end is meaninglessly hard like the 'Veteran' difficulty in COD campaigns. The hardest initial challenge level is a sweet spot. There were sections which I had to replay up to 8 times before I'd make the checkpoint. Thankfully this was due to needing to learn the best tactic and angle of attack as well as strategically allocated my resources -specifically grenades. Of which there are frags, stickies and flash-bang. While the friendly AI are not completely useless sometimes they rush ahead of you which can help you take ground in 'push through' segments but can often lead to them both becoming incapacitated and put pressure on you to get to them before they bleed out. But they shoot, can target long range and flash-bang enemies for you at various times and thankfully don't need much input to be of use to the player overall .
Having been released mid-year in 2012 the graphics won't blow you away but they're certainly not outdated enough to be a distraction or break the immersion. I played it with a Razer 7.1 True surround headset and loved having the volume up. The sound is not incredible but it is great although sometimes squad mate chatter can be hard to decipher from enemy chatter as most of your bullet fodder will be American Soldiers. The sound track isn't one you'll never forget, but it does the job to set the mood for all the chaos.
I won't comment on the multiplayer as I never tried it but from what I hear it's just more of the same in online shooters with nothing new being brought to the table.
The only technical difficulty I had (and this can be a serious deal breaker if you're not 'cluey' enough to 'google' fixes for things) was that there was no sound during cinematics. Thankfully I found a downloadable fix courtesy of the steam community. Aside from that, there were no glitches or grievances with terrible game or level design although I did crash to the desktop once. But no ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t fake difficulty -it's all genuinely challenging and rewards bold decisive maneuvers but punishes the weak willed.
Overall I have to say that this game certainly had its hooks in me even if it was constantly trying to make me feel like a warmongering ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ for all the blood shed it forces you into. This is not one of those games you MUST play but it is one which I would recommend if you're after an 8 hour linear shooter and don't mind having how you feel about military shooters challenged with some thoughtful story telling and complex emotions -even if the game is a little too self-aware with some unnecessary and presumptuous comments in loading screens after dying.
If I had to score it I'd say 8.8 out of 10.
A PTSD-addled Call of Duty, Spec Ops: The Line is incredibly bleak, but that's the point; war is hell, and Spec Ops is all too eager to prove that.

First let me start out by saying this game is still in development so this review is bound to change when the game is completed but for now this is going to be my opinion on it. Prison Architect has its good side and its bad side as well i will be starting off by listing the cons first and then the pros afterwards.


1.   You will get some extremely trouble some prisoners while you are playing this game. They will kill many of your staff and or prisoners in the process of them throwing their little eveing fits while in solitary for killing 5 of your guards as punishment. There really needs to be a drop down box to change their role from supermax to death row that way their reign of destruction is put to an end.
2. The punishment system is very limited in what you can do to inmates when they commit a new felony or offense. The only two options you have is solitary or locking them down in their cells for how ever long you deem fit.
3.  The U.I is organized but can be troublesome if you dont know where to look for certain features.
4.  The $30.00 price tag is asking a bit much for the content that is provided in game as of right now. Even with mod content the game lacks some crucial items and objects ( no diversity all your prison rooms will look the same in one way or another.)
5.  There is no quick build option for construction of your prison. Even with a worker force of 100 plus buildings can take a few minutes to get up an running.
6.  After building your prison there isnt really much more to do with it other than watch your little ant farm work like clock work.

Side Note. (There is a really annoying glitch where your workers and other members of your staff get stuck and will not perform their tasks at hand.  Only way i know to fix this glitch is by saving and quitting out and reloading the prison.)
1.  Building a working and well functioning prison gives you a sense of accomplishment. Makes you feel like you acheived something great.
2.  Inside Prison Architects  core game there is mini game type stuff that you can do to keep busy (Busy work).
Such as tidying wires up so they are not a huge mess  laying down pipes and electrical cables connection for your cameras to your monitors. etc...
3. There is a C.I System within the game which allows you to get prisoners in distress to pretty much spy on other prisoners and rat them out. They will tell you where drugs, weapons, high probabilty assassination targets are that need to be protected. This adds  a new layer of fun gameplay to your expirence.
4. You start off with a good amount of land in the start of your game. Which you can later upgrade into a bigger plot of land if you have enough cash to buy additonal plots to expand your prison.
5. Challenging but solid game play. This game offers a decent amount of depth in the menus for the behind the scenes type of stuff. Such as scheduling classes for your inmates so they stay educated, work shops for prison labor, fully flexible scheduling for all prisoners, grants to earn you money by completeting tasks. ETC..
6. Prison Architect has unique graphics, they are very cartoony and 2D but it does not take away from the actual gameplay of the game it self. It is still grim and gruesome even with cartoon graphics.
Now for the final rating of the game... Even though the game is fun and challenging it does get kind of boring after you built your prison and can expand no more.  So i recommend starting a new prison after you are done with one and it will keep you occupied for the time being.
Prison Architect is still in alpha and is pretty sturdy but due to the lack of content and the asking price of 30$ as is.. im going to have to give the game a final rating of a 7.5/10 Above Average wait until its on sale though.

This game is a great time killer. Its a great casual game as well, something you don't have to worry about spending a lot of time in but still be able to have fun.
Pros:
-It's a neat game, fun, and one of a kind.
-It's easy to play, not hard to understand and the mechanics are straight forward.
-Cost: This game is just the right cost, worth the money.
-It's not system intensive at all or space consuming.
Cons:
-It lacks a sort of feeling, I can't quite place my finger on it but there's a hole in the game. It almost seems like it's lacking content.
-It feels a bit like something you'd have on a tablet rather than a PC, although I enjoy the aspects this game brings it seems like it would be more suited to tablet format in its current state.
Undecided Opinions:
-For as small as this game is, it certainly has a lot of variety of vehicles, that said I can't help but think there could have been more. I didn't list this as a pro or a con because for the price its honestly a lot more than you'd expect.
Things I Wish were in the game:
-The ability to see your cars in your lot. Its something stupid I know but that sense of achievement of being able to see the cars drive off your lot as they're sold would be amazing.
-The ability to set the price of the optional packages. IRL dealerships charge different prices for packages, it would be nice to see that as an option in the game.
-Older Defunt Car Manufacturers/Older cars in general for the used cars and trade ins, I'd personally like to see oldsmobile or pontiac (Names changed accoridingly of course), among other things throw in older models of cars that are in the game, cars you can only get through trade ins or the auction.
-The ability to see the condition of cars for trade ins, and the ability to see a bit of their condition from the auction.
-Milage on used cars affecting price, or just adding milage in general.
-The ability to have "Press Cars" or "Test Drive Cars" Where you can buy a car and designate it for test drives.
Things I wish weren't in the game:
-The dude in the white suit. That dude is just. . . He ruins CSR no matter what.
-Everyone suddenly wanting the car you just sold out of.
While this game lacks a few features that it could have, or perhaps should have had, its definitially worth the money.
Would I reccomend it?
Yes, absolutely, if you love casual tycoon games this is the game for you. If you have a computer that isn't up to par and you're looking for a new game to play, this is also for you, This is more of a "Lets play for an hour" type of game, after a while it gets a bit repetative and boring but thats to be expected. Has it been boring for me? No, I absolutely love it thus far and will continue to.
TL:DR
Lacks some features, but it's worth the $4.99 it for a casual tycoon game that you'll get fun out of.

This game is many things, but the one word that comes to mind is:
Struggle. I'm even struggling just to recommend this game.
It's a mix of Tomb Raider (2013), Rocksteady Batman, and Burnout. I liked all of those games for different reasons, and this is an interresting mashup.
For one, it has the traversing style of Lara Croft, where most platforming is managed with button prompts, but no quick-time events.
The combat is basically the same as Batman, EXCEPT that you can't interrupt punches you are already throwing to block. You have to pick between "Doing damage" or "Countering and well-timed punches" which isn't a bad thing, but it does force you to play just a tiny bit more strategically.
Vehicle battles are satisfying, but early-game they are tedious and not worth getting into.
The best thing about this game is its atmosphere, and how photogenic just about every frame is.
The worst thing about this game is the repetitive camp objectives (blow up x number of oil containers, kill x number of enemies, and blow up the oil extractor (one of these per camp)).
Here are my personal feelings about the game:
It was made with a lot of heart, but busting through the open world filled with samey-camps/objectives scattered randomly across the wasteland feels repetitive. The characters/voices are fantastic yet the story is average. Max feels a bit too philosophical when he comments on "relics" of the past, though it is only a morsel of the complete game. I beat up lots of baddies and got beat lots of times during the gastown race.
The home camps are very useful, but you only actually need one (fully upgraded) that you go back to after a mission to resupply... Though the offline crew was a nice perk to have after coming back from not playing for hours (you get "scrap metal"($$$) for letting time go by). The Buzzard portions of the game are hands-down the biggest breaths of fresh air and are by-far the most interresting.
Why should you play this game?
If you want to be Mad Max struggling to get by in a desert wasteland slowly building yourself, your camps, and your car to beat up hoards of enemies, destroy their structures, and become the people's legend, then try this out. Know that it is a grindy game but its atmosphere is consistently enticing.
Overall?

Starpoint Gemini 2 is a complete turn-around from the quality of the first game. It's prettier, it's satisfyingly complex and most of all, it's a lot of fun. It's blend of RPG elements, freeroaming gameplay and atmosphere is great, and pretty well refined. While the voice acting isn't anything to write home about, the simple joy of adjusting the loadout for your ships, hiring officers, mercs and troopers, and leveling up can be downright intoxicating.
A couple small issues nag at me, however. At the time of this review, the ability to adjust shadow quality or post-processing in the video options menu is still locked. There are some balancing issues that make themselves painfully apparent within the first hour or so of gameplay, namely the rate at which you accrue money. Tackling big number bounties might seem like a great idea, but they're prohibitively difficult (as of level 7, all the available bounties were way way out of my level range) and grinding freelance missions can sometimes feel monotonous. Additionally, the lack of communications chatter between ships can make space feel somewhat sterile. When rescuing a ship from pirates, it would be great to hear a panicked captain's voice pleading for assistance, or thanking me for the help. These are minor gripes about what amounts to an overall great experience.
Granted, I haven't played through a ton of the story campaign content, and my time with the game might be small compared to others, but having seen such a triumphant turn-around from the first entry, I felt compelled to gush a little bit, and congratulate the developers. Well done, guys!
I tend to not be one to jump on the early access titles very often, but it was honestly really cool watching the development of this game, seeing community input being utilized, and watching something grow from nothing. I can say truthfully that I don't regret purchasing this game during early access in the least.

I really really wanted to like this game. It had great visuals, a great premise, nice customisation options, modding, an interesting sounding campaign. I played it while it was in beta and kept on anticipating them adding more and more...but then they released 1.0 and said it was feature complete.
But that's not the biggest problem, it simply is not fun. It goes through the motions of things that one should do to make a fun space RPG like an account ticking off boxes on a to do list....but I never really felt engaged. It doesn't garner my interest as it is so cut and dry. The combat is a bit boring, and so far I haven't felt particularly threatened or in a situation I couldn't easily escape if it was getting a bit too hot to handle. In combat you also have some passive abilities, but you can press 1,2,3 or 4 to activate...boring abilities, and you have consumable items that can buff you for a short time if things are getting a bit more pressing. This is ever so routine and much the same as any RPG and yet Torchlight as an RPG is charming and is full of 'soul' and 'character'.
Starpoint Gemini 2 on the other hand doesn't have any of that, and the campaign...ugh...I wish they had paid for better actors. I don't know who they are and don't care to look them up, but they convey the story along with about as much enthusiasm as those 5 year olds reading their scripts directly from the pages in the 'Avatar: The last airbender' movie. Is it worth the price of admission? Eh...maybe, if you're a first time gamer and want to spend your money on a pretty looking space RPG for a few hours of 'fun' looking at the pretty visual and the pew pew laser death - then yeah maybe drop some cash on it.
Meanwhile I remember the days of Freelancer past when the storyline was engaging, voice actors conveyed the situation, it was FUN and engaging - you could tell the creators behind it had a passion! In summary Starpoint Gemini 2 will not give you numerous hours of entertainment, but it is pretty to look at for a little while until you can find something else to scratch that space RPG itch. I reward this game 50% for all its technical excellence, but I award it no further points for failing to provide fun and excitement.
If you felt that X: Rebirth was boring, then give this a miss as it has far far less content or ability to provide fun.

Whenever you hear something about Spec Ops: The Line - you only hear about its message. Well, when I played it, I didn't see any messages - nor did I care. I wanted to enjoy the game, and "enjoy the game" I did.
10/10

"War is Hell" is a phrase often understood in fiction portraying armed conflicts. Combat can be a scary, deeply unsettling experience that weighs on the mind, however noble the goals.
Most military shooters aren't about that. Sure, they pay lip service to it, with narratives about intricate government conspiracies and pixelated atrocities (remember "No Russian", anybody?)
but at the core of the experience, the player isn't considered. He and his digital avatar are both rewarded (achievements, game progress, etc.) for shooting down everything in their line of sight. Regardless of how many people you kill, at the end of the day, you're still the good guy.
Without being Spoilertastic, you should play this game because it makes you think about how wrong that notion is.
You're player character's still a one-man army,  and killing is still the only way to progress through the game. But with each life you take, both you and your player character learn to hate and fear your aptitude at violence, looking for some reassurance that your actions were justified, or at least, whether or not you had a choice.
When I put the controller down, I didn't feel like a bad person. It didn't make me hate myself.
But it did make me think: how complicit was I in what transpired in the game? And if I was complicit, is it really okay to play games like this?

Edit:

Oxygen not included is a open world based game where you let your colony survive with little starting reasources, it's target is to more or less, DO MORE with what little reasources you have. For some reasources are minimum and can deplete fast, Algae is one, which is your main reasource for oxygen. Then there's the ever so irritating Unbreathable gases such as. Carbon Dioxide, which is one annoying factor to this game since it takes up space for your gases to function. You need good management for your colony to function well and sustain well with out the Duplicants (Workers) to die of suffocation, disease, stress, etc. You get to make your own colony and make your own oxygen to live. This game also has piping systems which can be a problem for rookies like me that can destroy your colony's groove and such. Overall it's a good game.

text:
The Anomaly series is a highly recommended tower defense series of games where you play the wave of units that go up against the defending towers.
Anomaly Korea is basically Anomaly Warzone Earth Mobile Earth Campaign; that is, there's no human to control like there is in the original Anomaly Warzone Earth.  This one contains 12 new missions, several short "Art of War" scenarios, and, overall, this one is much tougher than the Mobile Earth Campaign.  Play the other Anomaly games before attempting this one.
All-in-all, fun and challenging at the same time.
Nice game'o

Anomaly Korea provides an experience similar to the first Anomaly and Anomaly 2. It's a full package, with HD graphics and the exact same gameplay as the previous ones. It's also fairly lenghty, with 12 missions, ranging from easy to moderately difficult and there are a couple of new towers to keep you occupied as well. It's still a refreshing take on the tower defense genre.
Unlike the other Anomaly games there's no commander to control this time, though. You'll only control the vehicles. It actually works better and keeps you focused on taking the correct route. Things can get pretty hectic after all and it's good to be able to see what's happening without having to worry about your commander all the time.
Korea is another solid entry in the Anomaly franchise. If you liked the previous ones you'll like this one for sure.

Scores per field:
-Story: 8  not very long, tho its good enough to make you finish it.
-Graphics: 9 great graphics and very well optimized. Also the screenshot mode its great.
-Performance: 10 Absolutely no lag spikes, ive got a decent computer but other games sometimes give lag spikes (even csgo). This one does not.
-Controls / Playability: 9 (May be biased, i played with Controller) The controls are smooth, nice response. Of course, the car is harder to drive at the beggining as it's not improved, but as you improve it you can drive it very smoothly.
-Sound 8 No weird noises, the music is adecuate. Missed some unlockable option like "Music casette" for the car where you can put your songs and play them, but its good anyway.
-Duration: 8 Around 12 hours of main history, at least the same hours on secondary misions (probably more), and many, many locations to explore.
If you see it at 75% discount next sale, dont hesitate, its a safe buy.

Dispite several short comings, I'd recommend this game to any long time hitman fan/player. That being said, any non-long time fan/player should probably hold off for a sale or atleast the finished game to avoid the bugs/issues currently infesting  the game. All that being said, lets get started...
The Good
On a high end PC (mine is I7 EVGA 980TI overclocked) the graphic look great in 4K
Level design is beautiful and well thought out to allow for multiple replays without getting too stale
AI has been made to a happy medium between Absolution and Blood Money (which is a major plus for me)
The melee and throwing weapons are streamlined reather well in this game and easy to jump in and use like a pro
Stealth seems to work very well in this game and unless you cause a scripting bug normaly works very smoothly
All game related "help" can be turned off allowing a true "purest mode" experiance (Ex. no instinct or tracking)
NPCs are, at least in the first episode, more populated then previous titles and make planning more challanging in some parts.
The Bad
Scripting... can't stress this enough, the game needs a patch here. There are times when the AI will just bug out and fail to react to anthing afterwards
Frame rate drops, again there are time the game will be running perfactly and then out of nowhere it just grinds to a hault. Not just for high or low end users either and the game apparently does this on all settings.
The game also likes to decide what setting you can and can't chose graphicly if it deems your specs too weak.
Episodic, okay this is more a IMO thing here but still, in it's current release your basicly paying $60 for two tutorials and one mission.
The Ugly
Online only DRM... WTF?! Seriously this is the worst part about this game currently. If for any reason your connection is lost you are kicked out of the game, without a save, and all progress is lost. You can play in offline mode after you are kicked but none of your savegames will work and all of your unlocked gear is gone. Also, should you save your offline play it will erase your online data when you get back online... This is something that must change over the next few episodes or my review will have to switch to a non-recommended one because I honestly feel that this is a deal breaker for me on a single player game...

Most boring space game I've ever played. Truly a disappointment. All the positive reviews seemed like people were paid to say that this game was a good buy. Once again, I spend money on a steam game and am treated to crushing disappointment. There needs to be actual unbiased reviews about the games on steam because it seems to me the only reviews I've seen are misplaced positivity.
First of all, the travel system itself is less than slow, it literally feels like I aged 20 years to get from point A to point B. The "fast travel" is a bunch of stargates set up that cost a butt load of credits to go through. Last I checked, it was free in any other sci-fi universe/game to go through mysterious portals to the unknown/known parts of space.
Further diminishing my experience was the combat system. Slow...agonizingly slow. I'm pretty sure when people want to play a single player sandboxy type of game, they expect a sci-fi fantasy to be a SCI-FI FANTASY. Fightercraft should be able to annihilate eachother in seconds, not minutes, or what seemed to me like hours. That sort of time should be reserved for large ships capable of dealing as much damage as they can take. Not to mention the horrible amount of time it takes in the game to make any credits at all. Oh boy, just finished a mission that almost got me killed-what!? only 17,000 credits? Well at least I'll be able to pay for lunch. (Next tier ships are at least 12 times that amount, not including upgrades and new systems/weapons.)
Story is bad...nough said. Unless you want to argue with the "positive" reviews from the esteemed critics like the Escapist....really? You said the game is good? Well I know for sure Yahtzee wasn't the one who wrote the review because honestly I think he'd agree with me that this game is a stinking pile of elephant dung waiting to be carved into a slightly smaller, yet some how even more smelly, pile of dung. And let's not forget the gems. Everyone likes to have their stinky pile of dung encrusted with the jewels of a king who painted a brilliant picture of even more elephant dung. Oh, but the setting is in space! How exciting! I'm sure I'd love to fly around in a massive piece of space dung as long as it looked pretty!
The graphics are nice...but that is all.
Worse voice acting than Darkstar One.
There isn't a lot of customizability either. Ship classes and sizes range from petty-clunking-piece of space dung to giant piece of space dung, but with glasses so as to let you know it's the father of the bunch. Weapons come in a small amount of flavors. You have the shooty speedy laser lights known as railguns which you can barely see because apparently they shoot faster than light and do next to no damage. Next are the beam weapons which have their own subflavors of electricity, less electricity, and holy s*** there's so much electricity I can't even see what I'm shooting at. Which btw, I can't see an enemy ship unless I'm hugging their balls and by the time I can fire a missle at them, it might as well be shooting a fly with a watermelon, but don't fret because this watermelon will most definitly hit the fly because of guidance systems built into the watermelon itself.
Explosions are also completely rediculous. If I'm fighting a large cruiser and I blow it up, I expect the explosion to fit the variant of the ship and it's systems. Instead, I'm treated to a super nova that kills my speakers (and ears), temporarily blinds me, and...the ship is still intact, allthough now instead of being called "Super Mega Death Killer" It is instead refered to by the game as "Derelict" Not Derelict Ship/Cruiser, just derelict. Oh but there's more! Indeed, if you shoot at the thing you were fighting just a minute ago, you'll spend another 10 minutes widdling away at its health bar until it finally explodes again. This time, you get access to the loot inside the ship and the model has completely vanished with no trace of debris. How boring...
At any rate, I should have expected this from some random gaming group I never heard of nor seen any of their work because they don't offer demos. I'd ask for a refund, but I know how Lord Gaben is about the "No Refund" policy. So there you have it. A complete waste of time and money, though if you do buy the game and no life it enough, I'm sure one year later when you've completely forgotten about your friends and the fact that you even exsist, you'll have gained all the credits, mercenaries, and access to top of the line ships and equipment...which, as far as the leveling system goes for you and the enemy, will blow up in half a second due to the extreme damage output of whatever enemy you're fighting.

I'll make this a quick one since unless you've been living under a rock or dont even play FPS games, you just want to know if this game is any good. So i'll get straight to the point. Yes, it's arguably the best COD game of this current generation. (Obviously not counting the superb classics COD4, Black Ops, & World At War) Unlike some of the stumbles the franchise has made over the last few servings, this game 'gets it right' in ways its successors should pay attention to. I'm going to split up the pros and cons between both the singleplayer and multiplayer so you can make the decision for yourself.
The singleplayer is good. It isnt the most amazing thing ever, and the Treyarch AI hasnt changed much since BLOPS with enemies running straight at you like morons. The story has a few forks in the road to choose from, and the setpieces should keep you entertained for a single sitting. Basically, if you play COD for the story, its at least trying harder to be original than most of the "Modern Day Gritty Warfare End of the World" sort of fare. So i give it credit for that. But just like every SP Campaign, it's much like watching an action movie. You watch it once, and thats about it. Its fun though, dont get me wrong.
+ Varied & Interesting Environments
+ Entertaining Setpieces
+ Multiple choices within the story
+ Graphics are pretty good compared to other CODs
- Like most COD SP campaigns, they're really only entertaining through one sitting
- Terrible & Predictable AI that runs straight at you most the time
- Voice acting sometimes isnt the best
- Story sometimes lacks consistency
- Editing and Scene Transitions are terrible
Alright, now for the multiplayer, what everyone is really interested in anyway. The multiplayer is needless to say the best COD experience that uses the matchmaking system. It offers tons of customization for weapons great maps, and map-packs actually worth the money. The game is optimized good and runs well on most PCs able to handle it (Unlike Ghosts) and it has arguably the largest COD playerbase on steam due to these facts as well as a fantastic shortage of hackers compared to Modern Warfare 3. (Which is sometimes infested with them) Dont get me wrong, they're out there, but no game is truly 100% safe and Black Ops 2 does a great job handling them, however they manage it. Now, if you dont mind having to wait for a match in matchmaking lobbies, i'd say this is easily the best bang for your buck, so lets get to the pros and cons already.
+ Fast frenetic & downright dumb fun (Like Modern Warfare 2)
+ Most maps are memorable and enjoyable (They even brought back Nuketown)
+ Map-Packs actually have good maps
+ Zombies is one of the best damn coop modes i've ever played, especially with friends
+ Tons of modes (Hooray for HC TDM anyone?)
- Uses matchmaking instead of dedicated servers (This♥♥♥♥♥♥seriously needs to stop)
- Weapons can be laughably overpowered
- Killstreaks are laughably overpowered (But i guess they are in every game)
- Not a game for campers, or slower players since most maps are CQB heavy
- No kind of user-generated content (But you obviously knew that already)
If you're fine with some of the best in silly unrealistic and hilariously fun Call of Duty gameplay minus the dedicated servers, THIS is the game you want. If you prefer your games to have said servers, i recommend COD4, WAW, or BO1. Even so, i highly recommend this.

This is the  first "roguelite" game I've played and, despite I'm not being a big fan of real-time platformers, it succeeded in making me interested in this fluid genre.
What sets this one apart from other titles with permadeath and random maps I've played is that you can level up your magic-wielding knight after each run, using the money you collect from chests, monsters and furniture you destroy. It is incredibly hard in the beginning (you'll last less than a minute and will get sick of getting the "Useless" score) but becomes easy down the road _ you don't even need to "git gud" if you level up enough, which may be a downside. But I think that this is less frustrating than starting a run from scratch, like you do in "The Binding of Isaac". There is a sense of progression, which I find essential for replayability.
There's also a nice story, some minigames and other features that break the monotony. One thing I really liked were the rooms with big pictures that tell the story of the developer through their previous games. And the music is very good.
I finished my first game yesterday at level 192 and it took me 219 attempts during 52 hours. Now I have New Game+ ahead, maintaining the previous level/gear/powerups but with tougher enemies, reigniting the challenge.

Rogue Legacy is a roguelike that revolves a round an everexpanding family hence the name. Everytime you die you choose an heir to send into the castle. Each life is spent racking up loot and trying defeat bosses. The Castle changes each time. The rooms are different and are in a different order. After enough lifes you will notice repeating rooms, but this did not bother me given the quality of the rooms. Gold can be spent to boost stats before entering the castle and sending your character to their doom. However, each time you boost a stat the next stat boost (even an unrelated one) is more expensive. This means sometimes you want to throw away your gold even when you can afford a stat boost. This brings up a mechanic of the game. Every time you enter the castle your gold is reset to zero (later a stat boost enables you to keep a portion of your gold). The game gets easier as you progress becaus you get better at the game. This gives a real sense of accomplishment. This is lacking in many modern game, but is the hallmark of Rogue Legacy.
If you are up for a challenge try Rogue Legacy.

Yet we all make our choices. Where Coppola put
into the Vietnam war era, Williams puts it into modern day Dubai. This game is not your average shooter. As with most story-driven games I do not care much for gameplay - which is average, yet solid - or visuals - which are mostly good; there are lots of contrasts here: from bright desert day in Dubai to darker scenes which look far better in my opinion. The voice acting is phenomenal, the sound design is theatrical right along with the soundtrack which makes you feel like you're "playing"
. You will likely feel the urge to complete the story in an uninterrupted playthrough.
What many negative reviewers failed to notice is that the game leaves you the option to quit playing at any time - right to the very end. It's main reasoning is proved by the vast majority of players
quitting despite all the choices they have made and even despite all the points where it's the
alternative to the events unfolding. There is no Kurtz eerily whispering
here, but the early
which is ironically reprised in one of the possible endings mocks us for not stopping earlier just the same.

A strategy reverse tower defense game, you set our your troop's directions on a map based on the mission purpose and the enemies  dotted around it. Once you've worked/planned out your route, you then watch the results of your choice with the option to add boosts, repairs,  and abilities to improve your troop's chance of succeeding their mission.  You have to be careful about where and when you use your boosts and upgrades to increase your success in a mission. You can get extra vehicles and boosts added during the level as well.
It's a simple game limited in what you can do as you follow a predetermined path that you set up at the start. The birds eye angle makes it visually easier to see how your units progress and what's coming up.
The graphics are quite good for this type of game, and the effects are pleasing. Its basicly a war tower offense game and that is what you can see on the graphics. The shooting- the towers- everything looks just really nice. And not to forget... EXPLOSIONS
It's like a reverse tower defense game. Instead of you building the towers, you're the mobs running through the defenses, trying to survive. The different POV here to this type of game is something I like.
You complete missions for cash and bonuses, increased by the score you gained. Completing gives gold and a score, which can be used for upgrading and purchasing/unlocking new vehicles. Your missions are timed as well, making you choose the shortest path with the least resistance, though it seems quite a lot of the time the shortest path is the hardest and riskiest for your units.  It depends as well on the enemies you have to face as some are a lot more lethal than others. I find it gets challenging quite fast which leaves you needing to use your boosts and gold to make it through the missions, which can limit the chance to upgrade. It's also tactical to be able to rearrange the order your vehicles move in, especially when they're taking a lot of damage to save them.
The running dialogue from the characters/units at the start of each mission and during help to give it a more urgent feel to the missions.  You don't really get personal info about them, just their reactions in the war zone, and a brief statement of the mission at hand. Though the story isn't amazingly detailed, there is one there and you do know what you're doing the missions for.
The music for this game is actually really interesting during the selection menus - easily the kind you would expect in a movie.You can hear the influence of Korea in it and a driving rhythm makes the game a lot more atmosphere and tense. However, it doesn't take over the game and distracts the player, so it leaves you room to be able to focus on what is happening, so big plus there.
It's surprisingly engaging for a game where you design the outcome at the start then follow through. These kind of games have the potential to get boring really fast because of the limited interaction /direct control  you have, as in you don't personally drive the vehicles through the map – they follow the path that is set out. As a reverse tower defense game, I actually really like this.There is the option for more game modes so there's more to do after you complete the main missions, which is nice.
Seems quite a short game, only 12 missions. I'm aware it's an expansion, though I still think they could have done a little bit more. Though having said that there is some extra gamemodes as well

I'm the type to really get into micromanagement games. The things you build and how they mess with your rather sensitive ecosystem that you painstakingly setup makes it a continous challenge to not get yourself backed into a corner and have duplicants dying all over. Lots of fun.

By the end of the month my little colony is a bustling suburbia. I've printed out every new colonist available and they scurry around the base completing mundane tasks. Slowly the drip, drip, drip of water builds up beneath the toilets. The showers start leaking and break down, the carbon dioxide and hydrogen is rising. Pollution seeps through every crack. I desperately try to start fixing the leaks - but I forget something very basic. Food. I've over built, I don't have enough electricity, my food system is down to nil and my colonists start starving to death. Before long I'm frantically turning machines off left right and centre to cope with a population plunge but I'm just delaying the inevitable. I try to imagine what these final two colonists are thinking as they sleep in fetid, flooded quarters and try to gasp in a few last breaths of oxygen. It's probably "Athravan, you killed us all." R.I.P
Oxygen Not Included is a management building game that basically forces you to sit on a line between constant disaster and a perfect system, making decisions that could wipe out your entire colony. Not today, not tomorrow, but a month down the line when you realize you messed something up, it's coming back to haunt you. My second playthrough was much more successful, but I still had a lot to learn. It's a game that expects you to make mistakes and to learn from them. In that regards I can see it frustrating some, as you're almost destined to fail as you learn the game.
The actual gameplay appears basic on the surface. You carve out an empty space and put up walls. You build beds, places to eat, you add furniture and some decor. You add a toilet, and some showers. You use your resources around you (various minerals, gases and waters) to build, process and power. You grow creepy plants and turn them into disgusting, maggoty mush bars to eat. You continue exploring and your base gets bigger and more people come. It gets bigger, and bigger and before you know it things are spiralling out of control and then it gets complicated. Exactly where should you put your oxygen machines? What is the most efficient way to get water from point A to B? How do you set up your food farm? Why is this person unhappy and how can you fix it? How did 10 people just die? Did that person just get stuck at the bottom of a crevice because you didn't build a ladder? Are these corpses spreading disease and depressing the hell out of everyone? Why yes. Yes they are.
It follows basic physics. Certain gases rise. Ceilings that are unsupported can fall if you dig around them. Water drops downwards. Thermodynamics dicate the temperatures. It sounds simple, but when it's on a large scale it is really anything but.
The UI is intuitive and easy to use from the get-go, with encouragement on choosing your unlock paths and figuring stuff out yourself. It doesn't hold your hand, so be prepared to engage those brain cells.
Your minions have stress levels and need massages (who doesn't?). They will run around on auto based on what you've set as a priority, so you're not in firm control. Sometimes they make dumb decisions and a few folks died due to their apparent inability to understand the concept of "the food is in the fridge just go get it." AI is often a downfall and I do think it is a weak spot here; although it's rare enough to not affect my overall enjoyment and the game is at the end of the day still in early access. Hypothetically you can get a base to a critical mass level, where your AI can do everything it needs to do as efficiently as possible. Produce enough food, oxygen and power whilst recycling and cleaning water in an endless, self-sustaining loop. Good luck with that though, still a work in progress for me. I suspect it's going to take me a long time to get there and I'll leave a lot of corpses in my wake.

Starpoint Gemini feels like a PC game I played when I was younger. It's relatively rough around the edges and there is nothing groundbreaking about the graphics--but it represents a kind of space exploration game in a very cohesive package. The soundtrack is filled with ambient electronica and is a real highlight for me; scanning pulsars and exploring unknown reaches of space feels extremely gratifying and peaceful at the same time.
The game itself lets you explore space however you choose: you can become a merchant flying cargo through sectors, a bounty hunter going after pirates, an explorer of the universe and scanning anomalies and space oddities etc, etc. It's a game with great potential that doesn't hold you hand from start to finish. If you have any interest in Sci-fi/space exploration games (Freelancer/Star Trek: Bridge Commander/Eve Online) this game does a great job filling that role.

While I could see this being a good game, I came into it really wanting to feel like I was flying a big honking capital ship.  Although the game had some nice mechanics like "fire at will" setting for the turrets, I didn't feel like I was really flying anything big and hefty.  I felt more like I was flying a capital ship back when I used to fly the cargo hauler in freespace.
The sound effects could really use some love.  Most engagements I've been in have involved circling at a distance that made it difficult for the camera to track (I wish I could have zoomed out more).  The choice to use "pulse" style weapons really fit a more starfighter feel than if they had stuck with either beam weapons or even just old fashioned battleship style cannon/flak fire.  Oh, and the English localization isn't too good.  You can skip cutscenes, but I often wished I could just stick the spoken plot elements.  I wanted to read the story, and I normally like voiceovers, but either the writing or the direction was off enough for it to turn me off pretty quickly.
It looks like there's a lot of depth and content to this game, and it will probably fulfill someone's dream, but I'm still off searching for a great capital ship game.

To those who are complaining that it doesn't run as smoothly as Absolution, I believe this is because  this game probably needs a harsher detail drop for lower end machines. I am currently running at 4K @ 50FPS. Modifying the level of detail doesn't seem to change things a lot. Apparently, it changes draw distance, possibly LOD distance.
I can see the improvement in the models, the increase in detail, texture resolutions, etc, but this is a game where gameplay is key, and they could benefit from lower end machines just looking a little more plain. Having said that, I enjoy how the game plays, the challenges add replay value on top of trying to perfect the hit, or just mucking about.
I am loving this game, and highly recommend it IF you have a recent, high-end gaming machine. I would recommend at least a GTX970 (nVidia) or equivalent graphics card, and without a doubt 4 core CPU over 3GHz. There is a lot going on, and being rendered in most views, especially the crowds.

Spec Ops: The Line is a third person shooter like no other. I just finished the game and was it worth the purchase? Yes. Definitely. Spec Ops shows significant strength in its storyline, bearing similarity to how Deus Ex: Human Revolution has you chase a rabbit hole which gets deeper and darker with every step you take. It may seem to be just an ordinary third person shooter at first, but as you continue not all is as it first seems.
The game also throws in some moral quandaries as you progress, forcing you to judge the crime of the other Dubai inhabitants. For the most part you really have to think about your decisions, and that is where Spec Ops: The Line really shines. Some decisions, however, felt that they had a lot of weight but ended up doing little, which was a shame, but understandable. Some aspects of the story do really stand out though, even if you are given no choice by the game. Your squad mates feel like living characters that react and evolve to the unpleasant situation you are thrown into, and Intel pickups gives you a nice background on the people you are gunning into the ground. As the game continues your actions eventually leads to Scarecrow-esque psychedelic trips, giving you time to reflect on the people you have killed though out the game. The game comes to a very satisfying, eye opening end which nicely finishes up the experiences.
The visuals are stunning and the performance is very good. Running on a GTX 770 it pushed into 120 frames per second. the only issue to me is the lack of AA, which I forced though the NVidia control pannel. I also ran this game with flawless widescreen to increase the FOV, which was around 70, to about 100. The use of flawless widescreen may have created bugs with some weapon scopes and highlighted some pop in of off screen characters, but those issues were entirely self-inflicted.
The game had a decent length of about 11ish hours, and most of that time felt well spent. However the combat and third person shooter aspect of the gameplay was not on the same level as the rest of the game. Keep in mind I played on the hardest difficulty available at the time. The combat was very frustrating as a person who plays a lot of shooters and whose accuracy is pretty decent. The game additionally suffers from the old "press space for everything" and many times I wanted to swap cover and instead healed my AI squadmates or ran out into the open into the unforgiving bullets of the enemy. The AI for the most part is good, but has an extremely annoying tendency to go down in the middle of nowhere, usually with a LMG and lots of enemies surrounding him and start to bleed out, forcing you to run clumsily towards him and die. Repeat many times and furiously quit the game. The game also suffers from difficulty spikes, usually at the end of a long fight when a heavy (similar to a PAYDAY 2 bulldozer) strides confidently onto the field and kicks you right back to the start of the fight. Some sections I had to repeat as much as 7 times to pass the arena section, each time dying on that last heavy. I would recommend playing on a lower difficulty as the harsh combat would often make me appreciate the story less as I came -fuming- out of an arduous combat section. The main problem is that this time of combat is 80% of the game, and when 80% of the game is a chore you better hope that the story was worth it. Luckily it is. The game has a bad case of Ludo narrative dissonance, the game clearly wants you to feel the pain of death in war, but has you murder hundreds of faceless soldiers.
The soundtrack was quite nice, very atmospheric, but nothing legendary in my opinion, although the Radio Man has a good selection of rock songs that play thorough out.
War is a horrible thing and this game is an experience you will not forget. I'd recommend this to anyone.

Most of the AAA FPS titles out there put you in the heroes position and decorate you as you travel in the story though blood baths. Thsi game can be equated to the Airport mission in COD MW2, where you are able to skip it for moral purposes. But you live that hell though out here.
The player will lead to understand the true taste of war, blood sheds and the consequences of doing it. You will be enlightned on the effect of your action so you can ponder upon them after the credits have rolled out. So if you want to have a once in a life time experince of real war, this is the stop. But don' expect a glory out of it. You will be treated an equal.

OK, so this is my first review of a game. And I choose this game. Why? Because I've played this game from early alpha, where you can only slap hyperion and barely have any hp left to win. I've seen my clones sitting there in the training tab, Whole 40k clones sitting on the training tab and wondering how much clones to Black-barring the skills. Ok enough for the rant, and here's my review.
You start with nothing. Except your name, gender, body, and your ability to create clone. The clones are what you get for doing nothing at the start of the game. And then you realize there's a training tab there. You clicked it and it shows you what can you do with your clone, let them train for you, the lazy one. Then, after a while, you realize that you can smack gods to create more things. Then after a few hours, you realize you just lost to some god. You get a rebirth, and starting your life again, just like reading from the start of this paragraph again. Only to realize you've lost hundreds of hours in this game.
And you realized, you are happy.
Happy for a reason.
Happy because you can smack more powerful gods.
Very steep learning curve, but it's also the most in-depth idle game i've ever managed.

Its hard to justify 35$ price tags on anything, in a crappy progress bar game. A genre which I enjoy but lets be honest... 35$ goes a long way on steam and would easily net more than I would get out of any of the purchases. Not that I like to pay to win, because I wont even when its cheap. But a inexpensive upgrade that nets some long term gain is typically tempting.
So to that end... the game will get some of my time but not likely my money. So I recommend it, because I want to recommend it on content but I would rather pay up front to play a game that is just balanced well, so I wont support the pay wall.

Wow - 75 hours I ended up playing this game for!!!  I certainly did not expect that after reading all the reviews here.
I'm somebody who really likes the Assasin's Creed style of repetative gameplay in an open world.  After a hard day at work it's fun to just kick back and knock out another 10 or 20 different tasks as you take over different parts of the map and increase your stats.  Just before this game I soloed The Division and both games scratch that same itch for me that these open world games have.
Sure there was a couple clunker tasks that I did once and hated and never did them again, like using the dog to find mines, and all the car races. (And the one race you are forced to do as part of the storyline was almost a rage inducing instant quit moment.  Luckily I finally got it and kept playing until the end - a tip is to downgrade your suspension and armor)
But I really loved the environment they had you explore and work in, very cool!  I also thought the totally bummer ending fit in perfectly with the spirit of the movies, well at least the original ones.
Technically it looked and sounded fantastic.  Never had a crash or problem running under Windows 10.
To help put my review in perspective, I tried to play Shadows of Mordor right before this and did not like it at all.  After 7 hours I gave up on that game because the tasks and fighting were just not interesting to me.  THIS game that seems to always get compared to SOM was so much better to me.

Anomaly Korea is an extra campaign for Anomaly Warzone Earth. Gameplay is the same tower offence style where you buy units and select the route they will use to travel around the map, while destroying or avoiding the alien towers. You don't have the commander unit, but can still deploy powers by clicking where you want to use them.
The campaign is only 3.5 hours long, but there are a few additions that provide a fresh tactical challenge. A new type of tank has a powerful special attack that gains charge from each tower you destroy. A new power increases the firing speed and range of your units. And some maps have special conditions such as zones where your powers are disabled, or time limits to clear an area of the map.
If you enjoyed the original game, you should get some entertainment from Korea, but you might want to wait for a sale.
