Jedi Academy is one of the greatest Star Wars games ever made, and possibly even one of the greatest Science Fiction games as well. It will always be a timeless classic, and although aged, its combat mechanics still hold the title of one of the most original, functional, intense, and absolutely fun engines for combat I've ever had the pleasure to experience. The lightsaber combat is at its best, tactical and precise, and at your worst, clicking furiously as Jaden slashes the saber frantically praying to avoid death, which is to say, still incredibly fun. The experience is concise and highly enjoyable, and the voice acting wonderful. The story is nothing new, but there are terrific moments, and never once does it feel unplayable, if only a bit redundant at times (which is quickly forgotten about once you get slashing and deflecting). The only major flaw with the game is a few puzzles that are unfair and require luck or prior knowledge, so keep a walkthrough open. But I assure you, to any Star Wars fan, to any Science Fiction fan, to any video game fan, there's something in here for you that's worth your time and money. I will always love this game and relish the hours of play and replay it has brought and will bring me, and I invite you to do so as well.

To those who are complaining that it doesn't run as smoothly as Absolution, I believe this is because  this game probably needs a harsher detail drop for lower end machines. I am currently running at 4K @ 50FPS. Modifying the level of detail doesn't seem to change things a lot. Apparently, it changes draw distance, possibly LOD distance.
I can see the improvement in the models, the increase in detail, texture resolutions, etc, but this is a game where gameplay is key, and they could benefit from lower end machines just looking a little more plain. Having said that, I enjoy how the game plays, the challenges add replay value on top of trying to perfect the hit, or just mucking about.
I am loving this game, and highly recommend it IF you have a recent, high-end gaming machine. I would recommend at least a GTX970 (nVidia) or equivalent graphics card, and without a doubt 4 core CPU over 3GHz. There is a lot going on, and being rendered in most views, especially the crowds.

Completing challenges will gain you mastery levels over a mission and every mastery level unlocks things like new weapons, entry points and supply drops within the mission.
Like everyone, I am disappointed by the episodic release schedule. I wish I could play more right now, instead of having to wait another month.
The always online feauture also needs to be looked at because currently if you disconnect while in a mission, you will be forced to go back to the main menu and lose your progress.
Despite this, the game itself is absolutely amazing and I highly recommend it to fans of the series.
Maybe get the intro pack for now as it is cheaper and will give you everything that is available at release.
All in all I rate this game: 9/10

Are You a Terrible Person?: The Game
Alternatively: Common Modern Shooters Are [Insert Negative Adjective Here]: The Game
Since the essence of Spec Ops: The Line is well known by now, I'll lay it out straight. The game is set up brilliantly. You buy this for the story, and you play along as it dips you into insanity with the characters. If, by the end of it, you start questioning why the heck you decided to play something that essentially tells you 'what is wrong with you' (and the game really does start telling you things along those lines), then you're doing it right.
The gameplay itself is average (movement mechanics felt a bit clunky at times). But it's not the gameplay that pulls you along through the game. It's that story and the way the game starts punching you for playing it to the end. In a way, it's less of a shooter than a highly-interactive movie.
Another note, the scenery itself is quite beautiful (it is Dubai, after all), and yet manages to give off an unsettling atmosphere. Even while everything around the characters is becoming ripped apart, the scenery still gives off a good effect. Who knew the desert could be so chilling?
There is no glorified ending. There is no glorification of anything, really. And that's what's so glorifying about this game.
(If, by the end of the story, you are still heavily confused, I also recommend checking out its TV Tropes page, which really cleared stuff up for me.)

This is a great concept for a Tycoon game.  Unfortunately, a great concept is completely squandered on this dreadfully boring and poorly designed game.  By about 30 minutes in, I had already figured out a "sweet spot" for pricing and stock levels.  From then on, it was "set it and forget it", with the only "gameplay" being tediously stocking cars and parts before the start of each day.
Pros:
Graphics are not great, but sufficient for the genre
Cons:
Where to begin?
(1) The economic model behind this game is terrible, especially for used cars.  There is no differentiation for quality of used cars in the game (no mileage or condition differences), yet two cars of the same model  can sell for wildly different prices, seemingly at random.  Since there is no method for price discovery, you are left randomly guessing at what a price should be.  This led me to just ignore used cars all together because they could sit on your lot forever, even if you set the price for thousands less than the "estimated" value.  (You only need to keep one or two on your lot at a time to avoid consumer rating penalties in case someone looking for a used car comes by and sees that you have none.  Even then, I just set the price at the lowest amount possible and they would still sit on the lot for a long time.)  This is SO disappointing since used cars are such a big profit generator at a real dealership.
(2) If you have a car that isn't selling, you cannot set the price lower than what you paid for it.  So if you paid too much (like at an auction), you will be stuck with the car for a very long time.  And since it is impossible to tell whether you paid too much for a car (see 1, above) this is pretty much guaranteed to happen to you at some point.  Why not let us take the loss and move the inventory?  Ever hear of a loss leader?
(3) The trade-in mechanics are pointless.  The sale will happen whether you accept the trade-in or not (which is completely unrealistic).  There is no negotiation of the price; you just accept the arbitrary price offered or not.  And because it is impossible to know whether that price is a "good" price (see 1, above), it is almost always better to just pass on the trade-ins.  Negotiating and dealmaking on trade-ins should be a fun and compelling part of the game, but the way it is implemented makes trade-ins completely pointless.
(4) There is no challenge or "gameplay" in the personnel management portion of the game.  Because of the way that the new-car economics work in this game, the amount of money you make on a sale depends more on the quality of your sales staff, sales manager, and finance manager than on the price you set for the car.  Each employee has a single skill number and a price.  Price has no relation to skill level, and is low enough to not matter.  And all you can do with your employees is hire or fire them.  There is no negotiating of salaries or commissions, no promoting, no training or increasing stats/perks/etc.  So gameplay devolves to, hire the highest "rating" available (no matter the cost) at any given point in the game, and fire the lowest "rating" to make room for someone with a higher rating.  BORING!
(5) The "service" portion of the game seems to be there only to add a little more tedium to an otherwise tedious game.  All you do is hire service employees (the highest "skill" you can find) and make sure they have enough parts each day.   Yes, you much manually restock parts EVERY turn.  There is no way to set a standing order to restock each turn.
(6) Typical features of this type of game are missing, such as advertising budgets, buying on credit, comparing statistics to your competitors, etc.  The game misses many obvious elements, and feels unfinished.  I might be excited about it if it was an Early Access game, but sadly this is supposed to pass for a finished product.
I wanted to like this game, but frankly, it just is not any fun.  It isn't even worth it at the $5 price point.  Do yourself a favor and take a pass.

Flawed, but fun.
The game looks perfect. If you are a fan of the Mad Max films, especially Fury Road, you will love how this game looks. The graphics looked incredible if you've got a decent rig and it really brings the film universe to life. I loved the new characters and seeing all the different vehicles and locations. Makes me anxious for a Fury Road follow-up. However, unlike the films, water and fuel aren't all that important. You think they are and staying hydrated and keeping your car fueled will be a central challenge, but it's not. A few upgrades and health, water, and fuel are not a problem. The only time fuel was a problem was when I'd commandeer an enemy vehicle and try to get it back to a stronghold for my collection. Many enemy vehicles have low fuel and if you want to keep the car, you have to scavenge for gas so it can make it home. Other than that, the fuel and water systems needed to be made more of a challenge.
Building your car is fun and the vehicle combat is right out of Fury Road or Road Warrior. Lots of slamming into cars, harpoons, explosions and scraping and grinding, however you never really get to fight anything as big as the War Rig. It is fun however to fight through the convoys, destroying one car at a time so you can kill the lead car and take its hood ornament. Lots of engines roaring, explosions, flamers and chaos. Love it.
Combat is derivative, but enjoyable. That being said, it's not very challenging. If you've played the Arkham games or Shadow of Mordor, you'll have little trouble punching through waves of screaming War Boys. The only times I've died was falling off cliffs or in some of the challenges. Having your car destroyed just means you have to jump out before it explodes (easy) and wait for Chumbucket to repair it. Hardly much of a penalty. Boss battles are easy and I was seriously let down by the race in Gastown. Lasted less than a minute.
The story is good, but loses it's energy pretty fast. The opening is fantastic and you're compelled to move forward, but when the game world opens up and you're left to grind for upgrades, it loses focus and it can get monotonous. The ending is exciting and impactful though. I really felt for some of the characters and was sad by their deaths.
Overall, I recommend Mad Max. It's a great video game representation of our favorite Guzzoline-soaked post-apocalyptic film series and I'd like to see a sequel with a few tweaks. It's not perfect, but definetly worth a look.

This game can be summed up as a modern day Freelancer, but with capital ships instead of fighters. It shares many similarities with the aforementioned game, as well as some enjoyable improvements, and will probably be the best single player Freelancer-style space sim available for a good while. Like Freelancer, you can play with keyboard and mouse, with a rather familiar flight control style to Freelancer players. But although SG2 offers support for other gaming controllers, it's far from polished right now - it's near-enough unplayable with the popular Saitek X52 HOTAS, given the rediculous deadzone on all axes. However, if anything, the keyboard and mouse feels more natural to use in this game anyway, given you're playing the role as a ship (and later, fleet) commander.
Comparing this game to the failure that was X-Rebirth, SG2 comes out on top. Although more arcady, SG2 is significantly more enjoyable from the getgo.

I got really curious about this game after reading other reviews.
When I started playing I thought at first that it's just another regular shooter and didn't get the fuss, but as I advanced I found out I was partly wrong.
In terms of gameplay, this is mostly just a regular shooter, but in terms of story and atmosphere, I've never seen anything like that!
Unlike many other shooters and war-games in general, this game doesn't try to make war look like 'fun' or anything heroic. For the first time (as far as I know) a video game tries to deliver the true meaning of military conflicts, as much as a video game can.
You get to feel the impact on the people and how devastating it can be, for both the civillians and the soldiers themselves.
If you're looking for simple 'fun' with shooting and killing, this game isn't necessarily good for you, as it explores the darker sides of war and has quite a few moment which could make you feel sadness, anger, and such things.. But not fun.
Unfortunately the gameplay doesn't bring anything new and innovative to the genre, and I even found it boring at times. You get to play with one main character which can, at times, command other two soldiers, so there's a little tactical thinking through it all, but mostly it's just a regular shooter.
The story completely compensates for it, though, and throughout the game you'll have to make a few difficult moral choices.
At first I was a little disappointed when I found out they have no actual effect on the story, but I realized that they're there for the psychological impact, and that's what the game is based on.
So, in short, gameplay is mehh and it does get a little repetitive - but for the sake of story it's worth it
But that's not all of course.
The soundtrack is absolutely amazing, as it's masterfully integrated into the game.
The original soundtack for the game is mostly made up of rockish-style tracks - which is very refreshing for the genre and for video game music in general, and also some licensed soundtrack (couple of tracks from different artists such as Jimi Hendrix and Bjork) which greatly contributes to the game and as I said, the music is involved in the game amazingly.
If you're of the type who pays attention to the music in the background, you're going to enjoy this one!
The graphics didn't get much praise generally, but I liked them. There were vast environments in the game and they were all designed beautifully in my opinion, some looked darker and some were colorful and alive (graphically), and I really enjoyed just wandering around and exploring (at least when you're not being shot at)
Technically the game was almost perfect, it worked without many issues. Happened to me twice in the game that after switching guns I couldn't pick up my former gun.. which was really annoying, and also there were sudden moments where the textures quality got really ugly for some reasons, and after dying or reloading it got fine.
Also, the loading screens were an annoying issue, as it took the game about 10 seconds to reload a checkpoint, which isn't that bad but on tough parts when I died over and over again it got on my nerves.
That's it though, and eventually, these things are fully forgiven, as this game gave me a strong and interesting experience, and left a very good impression on me.
Seems to me like the devs really worked with their heart and soul on this one, and I hope they'd work on more things like that.

The D-Day mission is the best example of this, with a big battalion at your orders like a RTS, random deaths on the beach like Saving Private Ryan and big cannons shooting. Contrary to this, the Marine's mission is the only greatly enjoyable stealth stage. The trains mission, one of the best of the game, doesn't works on Windows 10.

I recommend this game...hesitantly. If you're looking for a simple, short diversion and like tycoon games, you probably will like this.
However, while it is a GREAT idea (especially considering how many crappy 'Tycoon' games there are out there), it under-delivers. I cannot disparage it for its $5 price tag - it's difficult to expect great things from a game that only costs five bucks. And yet, there's so much potential here that, if the devs stick with it and maybe add some more stuff to it, both under and over the hood, this could be a classic Tycoon title.
As it stands now, there's not much to it (again, I don't expect much for five bucks), and can be annoying at times. For example, your CSR will take a hit randomly, it seems. I can understand it dropping if you don't have a car in stock and a customer wants it, but otherwise it seems to just take hits randomly throughout the week, and I can't catch up. My CSR just keeps dropping and dropping from its 70 starting point to in the high 50s now.
Also, it's difficult to get ahead financially. I find myself having some good days with selling but if you have a good day selling, this means you're going to be out of cars, which means you have to buy a lot of them to replace those that sold, so your profit goes >poof< really fast. Margins are relatively thin, and that 'sweet spot' that the game talks about is elusive and seemingly random.
I still recommend this game. It is unique and a nice little diversion. Don't expect a lot from it for your five dollars, and you'll probably enjoy it too. It would be good to see if the devs do more to develop this title.

The idea is good, Hitman is good, David Bateson is good but Square Enix managed to still anger people.
Always online DRM that screws you over by kickin you to the main menu without a save if you lose connection to the Square Enix serves during missions. And this time you don't even have to blame your 3rd World Internet Service Provider for the bad connection. That is my biggest concern with this. Besides the obvious launch bugs that every game has these days the game is great. Or is going to be great once more misions are released. I mean come on those guys even dub the movies.
So all in all Hitman is a good game with a good idea but suffers from the "buggy release of triple A games" syndrome. As well as poor planning from Square Enix with the always online DRM. Graphically the game feels nice, not too over done and not so disregarded it tries to substitute quality gameplay with lens flare bouncing off of 47's lovley bald bonce. The paris level has a good scale of detail and at the same time is a pretty large environment that is clearly a "here you go heres a teaser, if you like it buy moar if you dont, dont waste your money" kind of vibe
The focus on bringing the hitman model back to its route is clear and defined, Absolution clearly gave IO the feedback they required to know that it was a shocking mess of a hitman game in most aspects and that having a high graphical fidlity on 47's tie was not going to draw any of the true hitman playerbase back to another iteration of a hitman game on that model, so they dumped it and kept any parts which were not complaine about.
The controls are all very well crafted by default for both keyboard and (Xbx ONE) controller although the actual settings for controllers in PC port were lacking a few features (no turning/aiming sensitivity option, instead a assisted aim snap and some sort of quick aim sensitivity switch) for me personally that is a bit of a dumb move considering the KB&M has a sensitivity option for aiming. On the controls note i will say the movement is a little janky when only applying slight pressur to the analogue stick but for the most part everything functions nicely and i was able to do what i wanted when i wanted and not flap around happlessly getting spotted at key moments due to any control issues.
The actual gameplay, for me personally, is spot on. You have everything we expected in absolution that was missing. Large levels, multiple routes, opportunities, disguise options and challenges to boot. I have not even gone into complete all available challenges mode yet but I shall do when I get a bit more time to get hands on. For any hitman fans that played from hitman 1 through the series to absolution I feel you will clearly be a lot happier with the design focus of this new iteration and if they do the online thing right this game could be one of those games i will fallback to after growing bored of the next over hyped AAA game that falls into half completed territory because of some glaring bug or other or the fact the game gets boring as games do when they are upsold so much your expectations exceed what can be delivered (something i dont feel was the case with this hitman)
The game while causing a fair stir to gamers interested in this genre was not splashed in my face at every opportunity and where some people have mentioned online connectivity issues (something i see as arbitrary due to me A) being able to play the game fully offline AND make saves AND load them just fine unlike some people posting moan here and B) the game is a single player affair with a tacked on competitive creative mode that while i have not tried seemed to be functioning fine as in the menu i was receiving constant updates about player made missions on the paris level so....)
The sound design is great with a nice scale up of the tension music as you get more and more into an opportunity to take out your targets along one of the various opportunity routes and LOTS of dynamic events to be learned from eaves dropp opportunities and so on. The NPC dialogue outside of any task based information is also pretty well scripted with literally tonnes of situations I found intruiging enough to just chill out and watch in a disguise allowing me un suspected access to do so while being blended in. I felt in many situations I was learning more things just by duping my target to discuss things with me and the ability to ACTUALLY talk to your targets or other key NPCs was just baller
To all those people moaning about frame rates and poor performance, i suggest you check yourself because my system had no such issues, (i do have a beast rig but, im seeing reports of complaint on 970- setups and so on which are not that far off from the 980 in a lot of regards) i literally have no points where the game made me want to sledgehammer my rig due to performance and run with vsync disabled on a GSync monitor at nice smooth rates.
All in all if you like GOOD games with interesting design and gameplay and have not tried the hitman series, then this is for you, if you are a hardcore hitman fan (such as myself) then I also say this is for you. It is a marked improvement on the series as a whole and helps already to wipe the sorry state of sadness left in my heart by absolution while still bringing in that level of graphical fidelity that absolution did bring to the series. The only issue graphically so far for me has been one of the mirrors in a section of the training level doing some odd reflective things and another mirror in a certain section of the paris level that is actually diabolical (considering in the SAME level there is another mirror in a toilet cubicle that is a LIKE FOR LIKE PiP that looks perfect....
its your shout but I would not pay too much attention to the drivel that steam allows people to write on a game. I put it down to them having either toaster rigs, or self builds that are not optimised (of which I am in neither crowd)
Game is great, but developers must do just 3 things to make it perfect: 1) Disable online DRM, 2) Improve performance, 3) Make MORE levels available.

This was one of my absolute favourite games in my early teens, so I'm possibly looking at it with rose tinted goggles, but after playing through it again I was extremely pleased to find that it does, in fact, appear to be as good as I remembered it being. The combat is smooth and exciting - getting a chain of force power attacks punctuated by a final light sabre stab is as entertaining today as it was in 2003. It also now has the benefit of modern keyboards and mice, with the extra buttons allowing for a much more fluid use of force powers, now easily accessible at your fingertips rather than awkwardly occupying the function keys.
The singleplayer is a fantastic smattering of vastly different mission types that will see you infiltrating, platforming, puzzle solving, piloting, rescuing and investigating. Your force powers grow in strength after each mission, and when you finally get a real taste of freedom it doesn't take long before you feel like the ultimate badass. Unlike many modern games, Jedi Academy actually lets you enjoy this feeling for a few missions before finally ramping up the difficult to an incredibly challenging and fun last third.
If you've not played it and want some well-aged action, you could do a lot worse than this. There's also a dedicated and friendly modding community.

Mad Max is a very good game, although it does get a shade repetitive doing all the side actions.
Open world, you can go anywhere and do ... lots ... of things. There's a few gated sections, but nothing problematic. The Wastelands is a very big place.
Graphically, it is very good. Looking off at some plateau in the distance looks superb, and knowing you can drive to it is icing on the cake. The audio is fine and doesn't get in the way.
I don't know when the game is set in regards to the existing Mad Max films but the look and feel (environment, style of vehicles, etc) places it before or after Fury Road. It's rather strange though, Max seems quite young, yet going by the films he saw the fall, yet everything in the game looks as if it has been wrecked for decades. It just doesn't fit.
Also, I thought Mad Max was set in Australia, yet the road markings etc look like the American style, they speak of "asphalt" instead of "tarmac" (although in fairness I don't know how Australians refer to it). Another instance of everything being transplanted into America I guess.
There's some weird mystic named Griffa. He lets you spend tokens to level certain abilities. You'll have maxxed these quite early in the game if you've been doing side things, which is a bit of a shame. I ended up hoarding my tokens while doing stuff and only visiting Griffa once in a blue moon. Which was a shame, as he always had something interesting to say and I probably didn't get to hear all the insights due to the hoarding. Oh well.
I only played story missions where required to unlock a gate, and spend the rest of the time doing all the side stuff - clearing mine fields with the buggy (although in boredom I did clear one by randomly driving around in the Opus until I'd run over all the hidden mines), clearing the camps, hunting down all the scavenging sites, etc. This took so long (my play time is slightly exaggerated by leaving the game running while doing other work, but not by much) that I honestly forgot how the game started and what the story was. That was swiftly corrected when I'd done everything (except exotic challenges and most races) and I knocked off the main missions in quick order. And I do mean quick, it took no time at all to do them and it was game over in about an hour... that WAS quick.
And well... I've only seen (all of) the Mad Max films once. And if you like the original Mad Max then you might enjoy the main missions. I didn't, I like happy endings. Hell, even Max Payne didn't have to put up with this♥♥♥♥♥♥more than once. Mad Max though... well, he doesn't get much of a break now does he.
I've spent a very long time in the Wasteland... but I can't see myself playing this game again (except with the current save file to perhaps do some more races or challenges). Strictly a one-time play through, but worth it.
Pretty good game overall, but i gets boring fast. It's not worth 40 euro.

Flawed, but fun.
The game looks perfect. If you are a fan of the Mad Max films, especially Fury Road, you will love how this game looks. The graphics looked incredible if you've got a decent rig and it really brings the film universe to life. I loved the new characters and seeing all the different vehicles and locations. Makes me anxious for a Fury Road follow-up. However, unlike the films, water and fuel aren't all that important. You think they are and staying hydrated and keeping your car fueled will be a central challenge, but it's not. A few upgrades and health, water, and fuel are not a problem. The only time fuel was a problem was when I'd commandeer an enemy vehicle and try to get it back to a stronghold for my collection. Many enemy vehicles have low fuel and if you want to keep the car, you have to scavenge for gas so it can make it home. Other than that, the fuel and water systems needed to be made more of a challenge.
Building your car is fun and the vehicle combat is right out of Fury Road or Road Warrior. Lots of slamming into cars, harpoons, explosions and scraping and grinding, however you never really get to fight anything as big as the War Rig. It is fun however to fight through the convoys, destroying one car at a time so you can kill the lead car and take its hood ornament. Lots of engines roaring, explosions, flamers and chaos. Love it.
Combat is derivative, but enjoyable. That being said, it's not very challenging. If you've played the Arkham games or Shadow of Mordor, you'll have little trouble punching through waves of screaming War Boys. The only times I've died was falling off cliffs or in some of the challenges. Having your car destroyed just means you have to jump out before it explodes (easy) and wait for Chumbucket to repair it. Hardly much of a penalty. Boss battles are easy and I was seriously let down by the race in Gastown. Lasted less than a minute.
The story is good, but loses it's energy pretty fast. The opening is fantastic and you're compelled to move forward, but when the game world opens up and you're left to grind for upgrades, it loses focus and it can get monotonous. The ending is exciting and impactful though. I really felt for some of the characters and was sad by their deaths.
Overall, I recommend Mad Max. It's a great video game representation of our favorite Guzzoline-soaked post-apocalyptic film series and I'd like to see a sequel with a few tweaks. It's not perfect, but definetly worth a look.

Very good space game, I'm so pleased this genre is making a comeback!
I've not played a huge amount yet, but enough to get the feel for it and I'm really enjoying it so far.
In this game you are flyng a large ship with a crew, not a one-man fighter, so it feels more like Freelancer, ST Bridge Commander, or Independence War, but it has it's own feel. The ship handling reflects this and the control scheme works really well. I tried it with a flight stick, but it's not really that kind of game, the mouse controls just feel right for the pace as you seem to spend more time targeting, selecting systems and activating powers and perks, rather than 'hands-on' flying. There is a strong RPG element in terms of building up your character and ship with equipment, skills and perks to develop. There is a lot going on and I'm sure I barely scratced the surface.
Technically it's excellent, great graphics and effects, and not a massive system hog either. The soundtrack is very nicely ambient and helps to immerse rather then distracting.
There is great community around this game, and the developers are obviously very keen to make improvements so I can see that there is a lot of potential for future enhancements, but the game that is on sale now is a totally complete and functional product
My only criticisms would be that the universe seems a bit impersonal, and the setting poorly explained, being a sequel to a game few have played, and the script a bit weak and generic. The English voice acting is very flat, and it might have been better to stick to text to be honest, but it's farily sparsely used and doesn't spoil the game.
Overall, great game, well worth the price which is very reasonable for the amount of content and the mod support and supplied tools mean that it will have plenty of new content  to come.

TLDR – shortened and simplified version of the other 2 Anomaly games since it was made for mobile devices. It’s more casual too so if you didn’t like the intensity of dodging alien weapons fire with your little commander unit, you might find Anomaly Korea more relaxed. 6.5/10
Don’t worry if you haven’t played Anomaly Warzone Earth or Anomaly 2 since the stories aren’t tied together very tightly. All three stories take place in different parts of the world and while the gameplay is very similar in all the games, there’s only a high level overarching story to them. In fact, since Anomaly Korea is a simplified version, you might want to start with this game first and move on to the other 2 if you enjoy the concept.
Just like in the other Anomaly games, the story of Anomaly Korea follows a military commander (you) trying to survive after an invasion by alien gun towers that sprout up out of the ground all over the world. As the name suggests, this time the action is in Korea (not that it really matters) and your job is to guide convoys of military vehicles out of harm’s way while blasting as many of the towers as you can.
Anomaly Korea is a “reverse tower defense” game where the map is filled with various enemy towers, and it’s your just to survive getting through to the end. You see the action in a top down map overview perspective and can modify the path that your units travel through the city streets (to avoid or seek out confrontation). Just as there are a bunch of different types of towers, you have a bunch of different units that you can pick and choose from to build your small convoy. Build a decent force and upgrade them with money you find on the map to make it through each level. Your biggest advantage is the ability to use special “skills” such as repair and smoke screen to power up or defend your vehicles as they pass through hostile territory. You pick up the skills which are often dropped by destroyed enemy towers. The maps are pretty linear with very little room for creativity, but as I said before the game is pretty casual on the lower difficulties.
Pros:
+Gameplay is very similar to Anomaly Warzone Earth and Anomaly 2, except this time you don’t control a little man running alongside your vehicles, you just guide the vehicles in your convoy and “cast” your skills on map areas.  If you’ve played the previous games you can just dive right into Anomaly Korea and kind of breeze through the tutorial. In other words, the game is a lot simpler.
+The game has easy Steam achievements and it drops trading cards. That’s reason enough to spend 3 hours of your time playing right? Additionally, for its small download size (about 600 mb) the game has decent graphics.
Cons:
-This is a mobile port, and it shows. There are very few (if any) game options and everything is controlled with your mouse. There are no keyboard shortcuts or game graphics options. It’s a shame because keyboard shortcuts would really make some of the fast paced levels easier.
-The game is really short. 3 hours start to finish for the campaign.
Overall, if you liked the other 2 Anomaly games, you can give this one a try. The download is about 600 megabytes and you can chill as your cars themselves drive around blasting aliens under your excellent tactical supervision.

If you like the basic vibe of a tower defense game, get Anomaly Korea. It's a great franchise that reinvents an established formula in a very engaging way. I love the strategy and accuracy of keeping your convoy going, and the visuals are top notch. If I have any complaint it would be that the 12 story missions aren't enough. It's not perfect, but for what it is, it's a fairly accurate portrayal of running a car dealership. Some of the negative reviews on this game complaining about not being able to mark up cars more than a few hundred dollars, or the seemingly random drops in CSR ratings actually made me laugh. Truth is, as someone who has spent several years working in the business, I can tell you that most new cars these days, especially on the lower end of $20k, have markups in the 800-1200 range, and that's MSRP, actual selling prices can at times be under invoice, especially where a sales event is happening, like portrayed in the game. The fact that the game will consistently let you make $500 or more on a new car could be considered unrealistic. Used cars you can make a few on, and that's also fairly accurate.
As to the CSR, while at times customers that don't buy a car will go anywhere and everywhere they can online to denounce your dealership, often it's people who actually BUY cars that drop negative surveys, that doesn't happen in this game. Also, that ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ in the white hat in this game really exists. Everyone who has ever worked at a car dealership has met him.
Conspicuously, the "I need to talk to my wife/husband" objection is missing, but the rest of the most common ones are there.
Overall, if you're into tycoon type games, it's not a bad experience. If you're not a tycoon game kind of person, best to keep walking.
It could do with some added features, like being able to spend money to train your staff, or if you have a really good salesperson or manager who is quitting, being able to try and talk them out of it, if they're worth keeping around would be nice. Game could also do with some negotiation on car deals, though it seems the sales manager handles all that. Also missing is advertising budgeting. Being able to spruce up your establishment to help impress customers and bring up CSR scores would be good as well. Game could also do with some detailed stats, like who your top sales people are.
In the end, for $5, it's a decent tycoon game, especially considering it's the only one I've ever seen that takes on running a car dealership.

Why do people still use umbrellas in Modern Society?"
The question is a deceptively simple one, for reasons upon which I will elaborate. Firstly, people use umbrellas for the purpose of remaining dry, or not wet, specifically when their surrounding area is being rained on, pelted with wetness as it were. But whence this desire for retaining dryness when one’s environment is wet, whence this human urge to ostracize oneself from the natural cycle or rather, "To ostracize nature from one’s own life.” –General Custard. Is the clue not in the question? Is it not the same with modern mans’ wish to spend his life in cities, homo Urbanus, removed from the tumult of the organic world. And yet, what is this world? And what is rain? Rain wets, providing plants and animals with nutriment, filling up their cells with cytoplasm and their veins with blood to transport nutrients, allowing them to stay alive. Rain wets, providing the ground with moisture, moisture which seeps down through the sedimentary layers of soil, and without which no repositories of drinkable water would be present for the urban human to hydrate himself. Urban man is desiccated but relies upon the natural cycle to replenish him. Yet he pretends that this ancient arrangement is beneath him, as when he removes his domicile from the wet ground, as when he removes his body from the rain. The umbrella is the symbol of man shunning nature, of woman shielding herself from the life-giving sky. Rain wets, and it erodes the cracking ground creating landslides, waterfalls, floods. It reforms the terrain, allowing new flora and fauna to make their inroads on the surface of our world. Yet from this, modern man and woman shield themselves. Why? Why to keep their clothes dry, to keep their electronic items secure, for you see rain wets and kills technology, and that is the bane of homo "so-called" sapiens. What sapience is there in erecting the edifice of your life and society on a foundation that is enemy to the water? Who’s anathemize cloud and air and sea and sky, for water is in all those things? And then, what is an umbrella? An umbrella is an illusion, a self-delusion that you can keep the wet out of your life, that though you breathe and eat and walk on things infused with it, you can control the dominion of water over your existence. What could be more intolerably vain than the child wishing to control his parent, except the child believing that he can and is? It, is the delusion of created over creator, of art over artificer, but is that…truly so mad? What is the artist if not the channel for the divine, the whisper of muses in the song of demons, wherein lies the purpose of the artist if not an artistry, whose essence is its' product, the work of art and water is the artist. Animal creation the art and human civilization the crowning jewel, the final stroke of the paintbrush. Why do people use umbrellas in modern society? Because they…are life.

Mad Max is a game where the divine meets the driveshaft. Where fates and furies touch a flywheel.
It's awesome.
First of all, it's gorgeous. The monotony of the sand dunes is mitigated by a surprising amount of variety in the environment. Pools of oil, rock formations, and flocks of birds split things up naturally. But there are also traces of the past civilization: broken bridges, artificial roads, and vehicle wreckage abound.
The lighting and particle systems are also excellent. The sun's rays make for a lot of dramatic imagery against what might have been an otherwise dreary landscape. I think I took more screenshots of Mad Max than any game I've ever played. My random travels generated breathtaking vistas at an astonishing rate.
And the first time you're caught in a storm outside away from any shelter - it's an unforgettable experience. Progress on challenges gets lost if you die, so the storms can present a real threat to you. They disable fast travel too, so there's no easy escape. This is all as it should be. It makes for some tense segments where you will absolutely have to improvise to stay alive.
Dying is otherwise not that big of a deal because most other types of progress generate an auto save. This is also as it should be. The system encourages you to be bold and more reckless than you might be otherwise, and that seems really in tune with the spirit of Mad Max.
And that's another positive in general: Mad Max was ripe for an open world driving game, but I had no idea. A lot of the concepts and themes translate perfectly. The explosions, the fighting, ramming cars together - it's all a ton of fun.
That said, the melee combat is one of my chief complaints about the game. It gets very repetitive very fast. I was hoping there would be a way to acquire more guns like a silenced pistol for stealth or an assault rifle for mowing down large groups. Sadly there's only the shotgun, and its upgrades don't feel that significant. There was a chance for a lot more depth in both the leveling system and the combat progression for the game as a whole, and the developers didn't take advantage of it.
The car combat, on the other hand, is fantastic. I haven't had this much fun blowing up cars since Twisted Metal, and that came out 20 years ago. The amount of customization and improvements you can make is great, with the possible exception of the weapons. Having to choose between rockets and a minigun might've made things more interesting. But it's hard to knock it at all because the Thunderpoon is the best weapon I've used in a game in years. Plus it has the best name ever.
THUNDERPOON!
The open world aspects and the collectibles were pretty standard, though I was impressed by the variety. Most of it didn't feel old, even at the end. There are three notable exceptions.
First, clearing the minefields was tedious, and this is largely because you have to get a different car from a base and it disappears if you fast travel - I wasted a lot of time forgetting that fact.
Second, the day/night system. There are some missions that can only be performed at night. There are also only certain enemy and car types that appear depending on the time of day, and those distinctions are necessary to complete some of the challenges. BUT, there's no way to fast forward time. What's worse, time can get "stuck" and not move at all. You can spend literally forever waiting for the time to change so you can do that one mission and it will never happen. Nothing you do will affect it. It's incredibly frustrating, and I don't understand how it survived the testing phase.
Third, the challenges. There's a single achievement related to getting all of them, and if you didn't know that before you finished mopping up everything, then you really screwed yourself over. There's no new game plus where the challenges carry over. And enemy spawns at the end of the game when it's all been cleared out are basically nonexistent. Just Cause 3 solved this problem with its "Re-Oppress" feature. Having now played a similar game where that doesn't exist makes me appreciate it a lot more. Plus, that one achievement will add 15-20 hours to your time even if you're prepared for it. They should've found another way, or at least eliminated the more troublesome, time-consuming challenges. It's ridiculous.
Finally, let's talk about the story. It's generally presented well. I have a minor gripe that some of the cinematic action sequences would've been even better if they were playable. It felt like I was forced to watch instead of do things too often. What's worse is the story they were telling itself - clearly, secondary to the gameplay. Max is very much removed from all the characters in this part of the world: he doesn't know a single soul when he gets there. And whatever connections he does make throughout the game seem forced and one-sided. He's just not that sympathetic of a character the way they portrayed him here. On top of that, it doesn't feel like Max had a lot of agency to make choices or change anything. The world is more or less the same for his passing, despite everything you do as the player.
The writing is amazing though. It makes Mad Max one of the best examples I can think of to showcase how dialogue and diction can be top notch while the overall story and plot is bland. Every time Chumbucket (there's a main character named Chumbucket!!!) opened his mouth I wanted to write everything down to save for later. Each of the characters has their own distinct personality and vocab. The voice acting on top of the writing is solid. These things came together in micro-moments where the cinematic sequences were shining bright examples of what can be done in the medium.
Mad Max is a great game. Probably the best open world game I've played in recent memory. It's easily better than Watch Dogs and Shadow of Mordor. The comparison starts to get more interesting when looking at Sleeping Dogs, as one game's strengths might be the other's weaknesses. If Mad Max had a combat/upgrade system more similar to Sleeping Dogs and an improved story, then I think it would've been unstoppable, and competing with the likes of Fallout 4 for GOTY 2015 awards. Hopefully they make a sequel and improve those few areas while adding things like a true stealth mode and more time with Dinki Di. I'd buy that game faster than you can say "Thunderpoon."

The game is fun, it's sort of a mix between X3(ship control, selling items) and Darkstar One(upgrading weapons, equipment and such). This game has some potential but right now it is still a bit lacking.
Fun factor: You will have fun fighting and dodging enemy fire. Having troops board enemy ships and take them over. Looting dead ships. Seeing how different ships are and act. The joy of dragging a captured ship to a dock.
Unfun factor: You are very much alone, yes you can hire mercs, up to two, but the only person you can talk to is the ship computer who in fact will only say anything to you do an action (move command, fire at will) or when an enemy teleports right to you. The world is pretty empty, NPC's are just sitting there really, and they tend not to do anything else unless an enemy happens to be around.
The makers have stated they plan to add expansions which will lighten things up, but those things are in the future.  They also stated they have plans to change things up, shields will matter later on for boarding and such. Time will tell.
I have put in 13 hours and so far feel a little worried. I ran most of my time in a Frigate capturing ships to sell. I even in fact captured a battleship by running back and forth between two stations to fill my troops and relaunch new boarding attacks.  It took very little time to level, and as well I fear I may never enjoy all the ships this game has to offer in the long run.
So is it worth it?
Positives: Somewhat fun, feels semi-polished, the devs are hard at work fixing bugs very fast, what seems like a bright future for a game.
Negatives: World is full of things, but they might as well be boxes floating in space. No life really. It seems like the same type of AI as Minecraft. Seems a bit short so far even with Freeroam (world is open, no story).
I feel the game's price is sort of almost right at 25 bucks.

Rogue Legacy takes Castlevania and adds permadeath and a randomized castle... Sorta. Your basic weapon attack is almost always going to be this overarcing swing, so it lacks the limited variety of weapons that SOTN had, and the incredible variety that the DS Castlevania games had. But, as you progress and die, you unlock different "Classes" you can play which offer slight variations on this overhead swing swordplay, all of which are fun twists on the familiar gameplay.
That is the game's main mechanic and draw - it expects you to die - and thematically your children continue your quest into future generations until you make it to the end of the castle. Each child has a genetic quirk that you either benefit from, or more often have to deal with. This range from silly things like turrets syndrome where your character lets out swear words every time they get hit (Censored swears mind you), to game changers like walking on the ceiling. The game forces you into making difficult choices with these quirks by limiting your options to three, some of them having classes that you may play better with but combined with traits that you would rather avoid. It's a great mechanic and definitely a good draw that I would recommend.
The castle too, while random, is well designed. The metroidvania format actually works really well for Rogue-like elements. Each room is designed so it could function well as its little mirocosmic sampling of metroidvania level design, and then these rooms are cobbled together to form the castle each time. Occasionally rooms hold important secrets like a blueprint for a new piece of equipment, so it might be frustrating to come back to the castle looking for such rooms and not having the luck for them to appear. However the game does let you pay to keep the same level format you had on the previous visit, so this frustration is mitigated by great options.
Because Rogue Legacy does its unique features so well, it's a fun game. But by design it's a grind. It may be possible to beat the game on your first playthrough (videos on youtube prove that), it's probably not feasible for a normal player. Dying only makes you stronger, and this Obi-Wan approach to the game's challenge mitigates it immensely. In addition, good level and character design aside, there isn't a lot to see from a story standpoint or even from a boss design standpoint. To really stand out as a timeless classic - to really be pushed from "Good" to "Great" - I think this game needed a little more "Oomph" with its challenges and thematic elements with the castle and enemies itself. And, because the game doesn't really end in any satisfying payoff, you might end up like me and play it twice just to upgrade some more - only to find out that the charms wear off with a sad wimper because there was no bang.
But even with that said, I really liked Rogue Legacy, and I recommend it for someone who is looking for a nice relaxing low consequence game to play.

I say this game is reccomened but only to a true Star Wars fan. For the most part the game is fun but there are moments where I wanted to rage quit.
Firstly, the enemies. Basic gun enemies (strom troopers etc.) quickly become easy to kill and pose no challenge after a few missions. Enemies with lightsabres are another story, they can use every power you can making them pretty much your equal, what isn't equal is when you have to fight multiple at once. At several points in the game, the game expected me to take on 5 enemy jedi at once (so I ran past them), but the most frustrating thing is when you kill them. Every time you kill an enemy jedi with your lightsabre, the game decides to do a full 360 spin of your player. It looks cool at first but it wears off quickly and if you kill one enemy jedi when another one is about to attack you, you have to dodge by mmoving, but since the camera is doing a 360 spin, moving in the right direction is hard to do.
Secondly, the force powers. You get given powers like force push, pull, jump etc. given to you at the start of the game and they level up those skills as you progress through the story. Then there are other force powers that you can choose to level up before each misson (cure, lightning, shield etc.). Each force power has 3 levels, some powers are very overpowered and others are totally useless (just be sure to experiment with every force power). The other problem is that your force is limited by a constantly recharging metre. But this metre charges very slowly and when using some powers, it doesn't charge at all, a lot of my time in the game was hitting an enemy with force lightning, running round until my metre recharged and repeating, I would have prefered the metre recharge quicker to make combat flow better.
There's also a lot of little things like enemies insulting you because you ran away to recharge your force or to avoid combat (and it's made even worse since the enemies can shout at you from a really far distance)
That said, there are still some fun and fair challenges during the middle part of the game and there are cool tricks you can do    like throwing your lightsabre and juming up walls (a lot of these special abilities take a while to master).
People who love Star Wars will like this game more than other people, just be ready for rage (and don't be ashamed to use a walkthrough)

If you like open world games, and you like open world games in space, then Starpoint Gemini is absolutely worth picking up.
There's some reviews out there that are comparing this to Freelancer, and I'll say so far I definitely get that same vibe. Is it "as good" as Freelancer? I'd say it is a little early to tell, but I feel like this is going to be a huge time sink like Freelancer in a good way.
Other reviews say this is Eve "Offline" and I definitely see where that is coming from, and in a good way. Trading so far does take some thought, there's random pirates that you can mostly evade if you want, and there's local defense forces around that will jump in to help (even if you don't want them too). Right from the start you can start doing whatever it is you feel like doing without feeling too "new" for lack of a better term.
I started with the Campaign, and I'd say I'm not overwhelmingly enjoying the story, but it's still early so I can't fairly judge it.
As far as free roaming, which I've spent more time on, I can tell I'll be spending most of my time doing just that. I managed to capture a ship I was planning to buy when a pirate attacked me, and so the mechanic for that is interesting. I've done some repair missions, bounty hunting, salvage work, and some trading. You can mine both gas and asteroids, but I haven't gotten around to that yet. No idea if there is any exploration to be had other than wandering around.
It would appear there will also be a huge variety of ships in the game, as different areas have offered different ships for sale. So far, I've seen perhaps 4 or 5 factions of ships and the faction list is pretty long. Also, these are only the small ships which your skill will correspond to purchase ability. How hard it will be to obtain the bigger ships I cannot say, but given how many credits I have versus what the prices are on them, it does not appear to be a grindfest.
The map feels pretty large, and it takes some time to get around each sector. At first, the map did not look all that large fully zoomed out, until I started panning around. Then I realized there was a LOT more and I've barely scratched the surface. 3 hours in, and doing a fair amount of travelling, and I have only made a small dent in the map BEFORE you pan anywhere!
Combat takes a little getting used to, but I was also learning the controls, and I'm pretty competent now which was why I tried boarding a ship. The boarding mechanic is more or less getting close enough to grapple the target ship, then send boarding parties aboard to kill their defenders. Larger ships have more troops, so don't expect to successfully board a battleship with a gunship. You can also go into a "turret mode" to keep your guns trained on an enemy ship. While you might have some turrets blocked depending on ship design, you might also be able to deliver a nasty broadside!
Speaking of those troops, you can replenish those troops at stations, and you can hire officers for your own ship to automate some things and make it more efficient. You can also hire mercenaries to fly alongside you, each with their own ships. So, as long as you can pay the salaries of the officers and mercs you hire, you can have a good leg up on some encounters. This also means traders and miners can have escorts, while the combat pilots can have some wingmen, and the fleet leaders can lead the way if they so choose.
Trading is pretty straightforward, with each station having commodities in various states of supply and demand, which change from time to time. You can check what's in your cargohold against the last known prices of stations you've visited to gauge if it's worth making the trip. I should also note smuggling is an option, as different sectors have outlawed one thing or another, and you can "sneak" illegal goods if you have the right conditions.
Overall, I am really happy to have picked this up, and I definitely look forward to exploring everything this game has to offer.

To preface this review, I did not play Gang Beasts before the free weekend on 9/23, so my review reflects the game at this time.
Gang Beasts.
Basic Summary:
Silly. Fun. Brutal. Ragdolls. Just once of those games that you enjoy playing with friends, or even by yourself to watch the hilarious physics. The idea is simple enough, there are tons of silly costumes you can change into as well, just to add to the hillarity! The idea is simple enough. Be the last one standing, get the other players out of the arena.
Pros:
+ The game is hilariously fun. It's one of those games that just watching it makes you laugh.
+ Physics are wonky (also listed under cons). It's part of what makes this game so funny!
+ Costumes are vibrant, and memorable.
+ Stages are unique and creative.
Cons:
- The games concept can grow stale over a few playthroughs. Granted, this is an issue with any fighting game, and is more opinionated than others, but due to every character acting the same way, (costumes are nothing more than cosmetics) the gameplay stays the same. Whether this is a Con or not depends on your own opinions, but I list it here so people may make their own decisions.
- Physics are WONKYYY. Sometimes, you can wonder to yourself, what the hell just happened? It can be funny, or very frustrating. Just a part of the game you either love, or hate.
- Servers and lobbies need A LOT of work. Though playable and doable if you are connected to your friends by an outside program, say Discord, Skype, or any other messaging app, they are still very glitchy. Sometimes the games crash. sometimes the stage displays the wrong name, sometimes you can't see you friends in the lobby. These are all bugs, and can minimize the enjoyment of the player.
Take each con with a grain of salt. Many of the bugs are being worked on, and hopefully being fixed. The multiplayer on this game is fairly new, and to have it at all now is a blessing. (It was one of the number one complaints reading reviews in the past, the lack of online multiplayer)
This game was enjoyable, though I personally am going to wait till it goes on a heftier sale. But hey, if you played it an enjoy it much more, grab it! OR if you have more friends locally, grab it as well. Fun game, in my opinion not worth the price currently, unless on sale. Have fun beating each other up kids!

The short version:
The game is surprisingly enjoyable, and I recommend it if you are a fan of skill-based simulation games and economy/business games.
The long version:
This one has been on my radar for a year or two, and my first instinct was to laugh it off as some sort of toy truck for grown-ups.  Still, I kept hearing good things about it between the jokes, so I would occasionally reconsider getting it--only to not get it.  Well, now it's on sale for next to nothing, so I decided to give it a try.  I am very glad that I did.
While you spend virtually all of your time driving trucks, the game does not seem centered around the trucks like you might expect if you--like I once did--think this is just a game for people with a truck fetish.  At the end of the day, it is more about the drive, your business, and whichever job you are on.
I have to say they really nailed the driving.  Though I couldn't tell you what it's like to drive big trucks like these in real life, I can tell you that this feels just like driving with touchier controls and an inferior view.  Of course, none of those negatives are really ETS2's fault; rather, a gamepad and a television are just really poor substitutes for a steering wheel and free vision.  I am sure it would be much, much better with Oculus Rift and driving-specific hardware like a force-feedback steering wheel, gear shifter, etc.  I can say that when I started playing this, I felt like I was re-learning to drive, and after I forced myself to use the same tricks I do daily on the road, I found driving in ETS2 getting easier and more thoughtless.  I can almost always make it from A to B now with 0-2% damage as opposed to 10-30%.
Speaking of that... do not expect to jump right in and be able to do whatever you want.  The driving in this game is a challenge.  It is not arcadey, and it does not hold your hand.  You will have to spend some time adapting to it before you can expect to go anywhere without bankrupting yourself through traffic citations, accidents, and/or damage to your cargo and/or truck.  I recommend NOT buying your own truck until you are comfortable with driving, as your employer will at least cover damage to the very expensive trucks.
Beyond the difficulty, this gives me the same zoned-out feeling I get driving on the open road.  I went through a phase which ended 2 years ago, where I would compulsively drive all over my side of the USA whenever I had the opportunity.  For me, it was like a sort of meditation--very peaceful.  This game, when I am not struggling to maintain control of a heavy load at high speeds through winding, narrow turns in heavy traffic--gives me that same feeling.  The graphics are not the best in the world, but they chose very well where to direct their attention.  The sky, the lighting, and the weather are all fantastic.  The AI of the other drivers is, for the most part, very believable.  The game supports streaming radio with quite a few Europian internet radio stations available to choose from, and that can really compliment the experience.
I have been doing missions in my own truck for several hours now, but I have not yet started hiring other truckers or buying/upgrading real estate.  I also have an old force-feedback xbox 360 steering wheel and pedals, which I have never tried to use with my PC.  If/when I give these things a shot, I will try to remember to come back and update the review.
Until then, push whatever jokes you've heard out of your mind and consider whether you'd like to start a trucking business from the ground up, starting as a trucker in someone else's employ with the ultimate goal of becoming a freight tycoon.  If you would, and you think you would enjoy everything that entails, then please do yourself a favor and give this a shot.

I always found it curious why Jedi Outcast and its sequel, Academy, dropped the Dark Forces moniker. I had figured it was for brevity and clarity, since Jedi Knight III: Jedi Academy - Dark Forces IV, the name I would have chosen since it's a badass mind♥♥♥♥, alas isn't marketable.
But I get it now. It's because the original Jedi Knight: Dark Forces II was very much a Dark Forces game, moreso than a Jedi Knight game. This is due to its pretty awful lightsaber implementation versus its pretty awesome gunplay. The original Dark Forces, just to be clear, had no lightsabers. It didn't need them. For the sequel, everybody wanted to use a lightsaber, so LucasArts tried to deliver. Unfortunately, Kyle Katarn couldn't block any incoming shots effectively, and I guess you could say it's because he was still in training and he sucked at being a Jedi. He was better at being a gunslinging mercenary, and thus the original Jedi Knight game made for a better shooter than a lightsaber sim. Hence, Dark Forces II.
The Raven Software sequels are both lightsaber-centered, and ironically, they're both ♥♥♥♥♥♥ shooters. Gone are the Dark Forces days where the gun fights had weight and speed. Now, instead of strafing around like madmen, stormtroopers are content to pretty much just stand there as you shoot at them, and fire back at such a constant rate that you could tap your foot to the blaster's beat. As you sink your shots back into their armor, they stand still, unflinching, as if they didn't realize they had lasers burning through them. It's all very smoothly animated, like butter, but it's also really boring.
The guns are also wildly ineffective, since as an alternative, you can run through these guys with your lightsaber flashing, cutting each one down with one stroke WHILE managing to block every incoming shot automatically by just having your lightsaber equipped. This game is exceptional at teaching you just how pointless the guns are, which makes it surprising that you still have to choose your weapons at the beginning of each mission.
Once the Dark Jedi start appearing, the game gets good, after a very dull first few missions. I was initially amazed at their ability to cut me down so quickly, and I got frustrated, thinking that the combat was just about swinging the lightsaber wildly and getting lucky. While the sabers don't connect in clear offensive/defensive poses very often, there still is a strategy. For one thing, a few defensive force powers are critical to surviving the tougher Dark Jedi, and once you figure out to map them to keyboard keys, the fighting gets a lot easier. (Of course, the game doesn't teach you this.) For another, circle strafing becomes the best tactic, since most of your attacks get blocked when you swing head-on. The resultant visuals look like a sort of randomized dance, lacking choreography but still well executed. And when you get the kill, the camera goes into a slow-motion 360 twirl around your custom-made character as he/she lands the finishing blows, and that never gets old.
You can loosely compare the Dark Forces games' visual style to the original Star Wars trilogy - grungy, old, rough around the edges, beautiful. Likewise, you can compare the Jedi Knight II sequels to the Prequel Trilogy - flashy, pretty, colorful, smooth.
Since the story, environments, music (the John Williams themes are cut up, out of place, and butchered here), dialogue, etc. are all pretty bad (or at the very least outdated), the game relies on its blend of lightsaber combat and force powers to keep you interested. Those two elements are good enough to merit a playthrough, which is why I recommend the game.
7/10
Graphics note: The max resolution available is pretty awful, but can be modified with a config edit (check the forums) to use your HD monitor's native setting. I got it running at 1440p, which looks remarkably good, but the game loaded with a blank white screen every 20th time or so, forcing a game restart. Annoying but not game-breaking, and worth it for the picture quality :P

Star Wars Jedi Knight Jedi Academy is a great game. Star Wars is great on its own. But I'm here today to talk about the final game in the Jedi Knight Saga. Jedi Academy.
Jedi Academy starts off with you creating your character. There are a few lightsaber colours and hilts to choose from, but nothing much. You can customise your character and change them to one of six races, three being Male and three being Female. After you have created your character, lightsaber and everything, you find yourself on a shuttle. That shuttle gets shot down and you crash. And guess what - the person you just met came out with you. Makes sense, doesn't it?
So, you make your way to the Jedi Temple, and here is where the game really begins. After a training session with Kyle Katarn, your Jedi instructor and protagonist of the prequel, you are given a set of six missions. There are three sets of these missions throughout the game. The first ones are easy, the second ones are harder, and the last one is just too hard. But I don't mind, seeing as I have finished the game 11 or 12 times. ;D
The final level *SPOILER* is you venturing through the catacombs trying to find Tavion (main villain of the game). In the previous level, you can choose whether to go with the Dark Side or stay on the Good Side. If you choose Dark Side, it durastically increases the difficulty of the level. EVERYONE is against you. Not one life form on that level is with you. And then in the boss fight, you fight Tavion and kill her, and then Katarn. (Tavion is trying to revive Ractos (I think it's Ractos)) If you choose the Good Side, then the Jedi are on your side and help you fight the Sith. The final boss is Tavion then Ractos's spirit going inside her...O_O And then you defeat her(him...hehehe) and then blah blah blah you win the game thanks for playing credits.
*SUMMARY*
Jedi Academy in my opinion is the greatest Star Wars game. EVER. I give it a 10/10. It's a game from my childhood, what can I say? So learn the force, craft a saber, go out there and stop Tavion!

Before I explain what this game is, I feel it's important to explain what this game is
.
This game is not Clicker Heroes.
This game is not Adventure Capitalist.
This game is not simple.
This game is not a normal idle game. If you want to be able to make quick and easy progress, turn back now.
What this game is:
It's slow. You will not always feel like you are making progress, and if you aren't paying attention you can easily take a few steps backwards in terms of progression.
It's confusing. Instead of having one main currency and one prestige currency (for instance, Clicker Heroes has gold and Hero Souls), you have four main currencies that double as prestige currencies, based on a number of multipliers that are applied before or after your next rebirth, that may or may not be lower than your current ones. It's not impossible to figure out the way some reviews below are saying, but you won't be able to instantly glance at the game and know exactly what you're doing from the word go.
It's deep. You're given a big hit list of gods to defeat at the start, and in a way the entire list is just the tutorial-as you progress you continually find new mechanics, and just when the game seems like it's slowing down, something new appears that demands your attention. I've put many hours into this game, as you can see, and as of this writing I'm not done with the list yet-which means there's still more in the way of mechanics to unlock.
It's thoughtful. There are a number of systems, all of which tie into each other in different ways that create interesting combinations. Your level of skills is valuable for the special battle system as your skills become active abilities, but leveling them too much will increase your mystic level, which will make the enemies more challenging but not empower you because mystic is irrelevant to battles. Your Shadow Clones can fight in the Battle Tab, but pitting them against an opponent too powerful means they will die-but them dying increases your maximum number of clones on your next rebirth, so maybe you should let them be killed. Monuments increase your stats by quite a lot, but only after you have a lot of creations, so you need to buy them with divinity, which you get from the special battle system, or from the divinity generator. All of these feed into your ultimate goal of making upwards of six different sets of numerals grow to increasingly massive amounts, in order to complete your list of gods at Tyrant Overlord Baal and create a universe. Apparently, only then does the real game begin, but all this complexity occurs before that point. Hell, I've not even unlocked planets yet, which leads to some other ridiculous complication.
This game is not an ordinary clicker game. It's complicated and requires thoughtful decisions, with many sets of numbers that all affect each other in different ways rather than just one or two. If you just want to turn your brain off and watch big numbers become bigger ones, play Clicker Heroes (which, don't get me wrong, is a quality idle game). But, if you're ready to take the next step and see how mind-boggling interacting systems of numbers can be, give this one a shot.
Give it some time. You won't regret it.

I've played all of the COD's, yeah i'm a fanboy, I was there in 2003 for the first title, I mean after the pre-release PC demo level on Dawnville I was hooked and so far the franchise has pleased me till no end.
This review is  less about the game and rather the journey for me to actually finish it with yearly releases of CoD from three different teams at publisher Activision it means that sometimes there's too much to play, both the MP game which for me is immediate and then the SP game which usually happens much later on down the road, usually i'll  get around to it when i'm really bored.
For CoD games I'm always keen to discover where the cinematic storytelling is heading in this franchise and I wonder if you can compare it justly to other games which offer both a SP and MP game experience as one neat little package.
In todays games market you're able to choose where you want to go for your Single Player or Multi Player  goodness, for SP games there are many great choices, Bioshock, FarCry, hell even Battlefield is giving us a great single player adventure.
For gaming franchises you run the risk of tacking on a SP component simply to round out the experience or in say the case of games like Brothers In Arms or Crysis you go in the other director and tack on MP as a happy sideshow.
Only Call of Duty or perhaps argueably Halo offers both a SP and MP game that is 100% fully formed and complete on both sides.
I was glad to finally put the time in and complete Black Ops 2, I'd enjoyed the first in this proposed trilogy and found it a welcomed distraction from the Modern Warfare series. Treyarch having always been played off as the number 2 gaming team within Activision is now presumably their first tier team. Sledgehammer having come on board sometime before the release of Modern Warfare 3 were developing their own COD titlle only to be then shoved in damage control after the departure of the Infintiy Ward leads and their department heads to form Respawn Entertainment over at EA for TitanFall.
I was suprised at the rallied efforts of RavenSoft, Neversoft and other Activision houses that came together with the gutted Infinity Ward team and the new Sledgehammer team to finish production on COD MW3. All the while Treyarch was busy polishing off their latest effort and with this release moves into pole position with COD: Black Op's 2.
Generally MW3 was lacking in most areas. The MP was okay, till the hacks ruined it. The story telling in the firsthalf of the game was okay until you're closer to the final take down and it was there i just lost respect for it.
I finished it, then unistalled and moved on.
At the same time of completing the MW3 single player game I was anticipating COD:BO2.
Treyarch COD: BO2 is an amazing package.What a SP game they've delivered here, themeactically it builds on the first game, the flashbacks told through the eyes of the hurt and damaged survivors of smaller wars, black op incursions, the walking wounded in the wake of Empire building.
The storytelling here is worth it. The cinematic thrills and spills usher you along rails, but you're essentially hyped for it, the gritted bared teeth says back the screen - Gimmie Some More.
I liked the dangling of a possible future infront of us, the drone strikes seem so much closer to home and we need is more privateer armies to show up in our videogames and then...the lines between game and now blur.
The future vision here is accessible and the ride on rails experience is a thrill ride of it's own. I love the cinematic experience, fighting through each level, the high points and the low, having achieved a balance in the storytelling makes the journey worth the while.
Ok so I won't say it's a plausible or believeable journey in COD BO2, not even in the slighest.
But I dare you to show me a film or TV show that gives as much action as this.
Even when we're not in the thick of it, here's a story unwinding thats every bit as deep as your favourite action caper.
The difference is how we're brought along for the ride, your contribution, your buy-in of the characters around you allows you to achieve more than just shoot the bad guys and feel great. Because when we get to the end we take a moment to catch our breath and know that this adventure really is something special for action fans everywhere.
COD:Black Ops 2 Single Player is a great cinematic action game that feels great to play and overall satisfying. Get it.
