As a Call of Duty Fan, I find it sad to say that I cannot recommend this game. It is actually an ok game, and it can be very fun, but it has some flaws that even after over a year, havn't been fixed.
Campaign: Probably the High Point of this game. It has an awesome story and the guns are cool. It plays very fluently and the choice system is great. It definitely has high replayability. If you are looking for an FPS to play the campaign, I could recommend it. There is one major issue on the final level, though. Even on hardware that vastly surpasses the recommended settings, your frames can go from being a smooth 60 to 30 or even 20, which really hurts the flow of the game.
Multiplayer: Before I go on with this, the multiplayer is actually pretty fun, but it does have flaws. While most COD games have little to no lag within the game's multiplayer (unless you choose a player from long distance), Black Ops 2 has lag issues from any distance. You can play with 70 ping and still have issues with lag that seem to almost always make you die. And then there is the lack of servers. HOW CAN YOU HAVE A PC GAME WITH NO MULTIPLAYER SERVERS? Could it be because this is just a port of the console game? Most likely, but it also means the developers chose not to. Games like Battlefield 3 (which is 1 year older than this) even has servers ON THE CONSOLE VERSION! Black Ops 2 doesn't have an excuse to not include servers, besides Activision wanting to save money.
Zombies: If you are thinking about buying Black Ops 2 for Zombie Mode, don't press that button unless you want to buy all the DLC, too. The stock zombie maps are boring and not fun. Transit is a good concept, but poorly done. All in all, you shouldn't buy it for zombies unless you are willing to pay an extra $65 on DLC.
Graphics: While graphics don't make a game good, they are still worthy to talk about. The graphics are pretty bad by 2012 standards. Treyarch neglects to change game engines, and the visuals pay for it. If the game was released in 2007 or 2008 (around the time when the engine was new), these would be great graphics for the time, but no. The game was released in 2012 using a 5 (now 7) year old game engine.
So the game has a lot of low points and one very high point. I can't tell you to buy this, especially at $60 ($125 if you want to get the zombies maps). It is not worth that price at all. Once the price goes down or it is on sale for around $20 ($30 even), then I would say go for it, but at full price, it isn't worth your time.

All in all I'm definitely enjoying the new Hitman.
Let's break it down quickly, shall we? Ok.
- The gameplay is smooth - there is the variety of methods, the controls feel very good (albeit after a quick rebinding) and the overall experience is spiced up with challenges that really make you want to replay the levels (not that you havy other ways to prolong the playtime - but I'll touch upon that later)
- The presentation is very slick - the animation can be a bit rough at times but the style and the art-direction is a huge step forward compared to Absolution and is very reminiscent of Silent Assassin and Contracts.
Also, I think the game has a strong Daniel Craig-era James Bond vibe which is kinda cool.
- The usability - tenouttaten. I've already mentioned the controls (each type of action has its own button, and a lot more than MGS5), but the UI and the tutorials and everything is designed so that you won't be distracted from actually playing the game.
- Always Online policy can be very frustrating at times.
If you start the game online and save it, you won't be able to load it in the offline mode. I had to replay one of the tutorial missions because of the lost server connection.
Honestly, I don't really see how this enriches my single player experience. I'd understand if the custom contracts or some other shenanigans were exclusively online, but the campaign should not be one of them.
- It's short. Yes, it has a great replay value, but 2 out of 3 levels are pretty small tutorials and while Paris is awesome, we've seen quite a bit of it in the previews. It would be great to have something new and unexpected in this Intro Pack.
- What's with the settings? The game looks good but some of the settings like Texture Quality are greyed out - I'll be looking for the possible solution.
As a fan of Silent Assassin, Contracts, Splinter Cell 3 and 5 and Dishonored - I'd recommend this game.
TL;DR It's short but sweet - looking forward to the next episode or the full package.

Starpoint Gemini 2 recently left Early Access, and it is now one of the few games of that honour to actually turn out well. If I was to compare it to anything, I'd say it's like Freelancer or an offline EVE, though not quite as complex as the latter. Complete sandbox freedom. Go wherever you want and be whatever you want, whether that be a trader, pirate, mercenary, miner, fighter, explorer etc.
Though it is a space sim, it also plays a lot like an open world RPG. You pick from three different classes - COMMANDER: has a focus on buffing friendly units, GUNNER: all about maximising firepower and ENGINEER:  boosting your own power systems and hacking/debuffing the enemy - and go around doing freelance missions, mining, fighting or exploring, and it all gives you XP (and sometimes money) to level up your character. Levelling gives you the ability to spend points on improving your class skills, which can be used in battle, and attaining perks, which provide buffs to a number of things like increasing troop strength for boarding ships or improving trade prices.
Besides the sandbox 'Freeroam' mode where you are able to freely explore, there is also a recently added Campaign mode. This provides you with story missions, but you lose the ability to pick your class, character portrait or choose from one of the three starter ships (it forces you into a Taurus ship, arguably the best of the three anyway). The story isn't great, and it's a little buggy, but you can still freely explore and do whatever you want while doing it. The story missions are not particularly interesting (go from point A to B, kill target, deliver package, meet NPC etc), but they give you something else to do. If you're feeling aimless and not sure what to do next, the campaign missions can be a good way to provide yourself with a sort of goal or objective. Each mission will advance in level and difficulty, and you will often find yourself needing to gain XP and a more powerful ship in order to advance. I found that It added to the feeling of progression, albeit in a not very interesting way. It's completely optional, but I personally had no interest in it.
There are nearly a hundred ships to acquire by either buying them or grappling and boarding an enemy ship, killing the crew and towing it back to a nearby station to either sell ( for a very high price ;] ) or place in your garage for use, and they are all customisable. You can equip them with a variety of different weapons like railguns, plasma cannons, beam weapons and heavy weapons. You can enhance your systems by purchasing upgrades for things like your propulsion engines or shield generators. You can even give them a new paint job and add decals, though the colours don't stand out too well and the decals are just a short list of basic emblems. You do have the ability to add your own custom ones, but I didn't mess around with that feature. They're nice cosmetic touches, but nothing to rave about. The boarding is also fully automated and you don't actually get to see anything happening. It's nothing more than watching troop numbers rise and fall and choosing whether or not to send reinforcements. Quite unexciting to say the least, but stealing ships this way will be your main source of income, and managing to capture an expensive ship still gave me a lovely feeling of satisfaction despite the lack of a more involved system.
Your ship is freely controlled, you can fly it yourself wherever you wish with the WASD keys and your mouse. You also must manage your power output. Do you divert all power to engines to give yourself a speed boost, to shields to make them hold out longer, to weapons so they fire for longer or do you try to balance between them all? It's very situational and you will find yourself having to tweak it back and forth very often when travelling and in combat. It's a system I quite enjoy as it keeps you occupied and helps with keeping the combat and travel feeling busy.
Speaking of combat, it's very fun, though not too complex. You can aim and fire your weapons yourself or have it done for you with autofire (though it can be inaccurate at times) and positioning is key. You and your enemy have four directional shields, one for each side, and each decreases under fire accordingly, meaning you should focus fire on one side if you wish to do optimal damage. If any of you have played Star Trek Online, the shielding is pretty similar to what that game has. You also have a choice of four skills, which differ depending on your choice of class. Each provides some sort of combat buff and can be levelled to add more effects. On top of that, there are then a multitude of items you can purchase and use whenever you wish, such as temporary speed boosters, repair drones or T-Drives (these allow you to instantaneously jump great distances) and a variety of other things. If used right, they can really save you when in a tight spot.
One issue with the combat however, is balance. I often found myself easily destroying ships marked as 'impossible' targets to beat due to having bought a reasonably expensive weapon or by managing to acquire a powerful ship. This can really mess with the early game and make it far too easy. It does begin to even out the further you level due to enemy scaling, but as long as you continue upgrading, it never gets difficult enough. This is tricky to do however and really only becomes a problem once you're comfortable and good at the game, which takes time.
Overall, and despite some flaws, I believe this to be a good game with a lot of love and care put into it by the devs. It is just oozing with content and interesting, well polished mechanics. If the developer's words are anything to go by, a huge list of future content is still planned for Starpoint Gemini 2 and all of it will, supposedly, be completely free of charge. Hopefully a game to keep your eye on.
I highly recommend this to anyone who is a fan of space sims, sandbox titles and even people who are awaiting Elite: Dangerous or Star Citizen. It's not overly complex and it does lean a little more on the arcadey side of things, but despite that, it's still a deep enough experience to sink some enjoyable hours into.

From a gameplay standpoint, this game is average. But from a narrative standpoint, this game is amazing.
Modern Military Shooters of recent years, while fun, depict war in a very cinematic and "fantasy-like" way. They depict it as a collection of set pieces and high-octane action moments that again, while fun, don't do justice depicting the reality of war and the effect it has on the soldiers fighting in it.
Spec Ops: The Line throws that away to deliver a thought-provoking and, to be honest, cripplingly depressing story about the effects war and conflict have on the common soldier. You slowly see your cast of characters delve deeper and deeper into madness as the horrors of armed conflict takes it's toll on their psyches. The game beautifully achieves  this in perfectly subtle ways that need to be played in order to get the full effect.
I'll be honest with you, I did not have fun playing this game. It's not a game that gives a feeling of happiness or exhilaration or even accomplishment. When it was all over, I spent a good 30 minutes completely still. I needed a day to collect my emotions. No game has had this much of an emotional impact on me and I highly, highly reccomend it.

This game was really held together by its story and works on some interesting concepts, the less you know about the game going into it the better. Overall I felt that the quality of the narrative improved gradually as you play though the first few hours are too much like any other FPS, and were pretty mundane although they are used critically to build up to the ending. The combat was nothing special and got boring pretty quickly to me, it's varied and there are some interesting mechanics but it was nothing all too impressive.
This is the kind of game that's mediocre while you play through it but leaves a nostalgia when you finish it. I think it still sets itself apart from most AAA FPS to be worth the play through.

Because you don't level up or improve your equipment until you die, any good run is followed by a desire to play again and use whatever you've just unlocked.  It also makes death a lot less frustrating than would otherwise be the case, a good trait for any roguelike to have.
The actual gameplay works well too.  Exploration is rewarding when every room is a puzzle of sorts, and there are enough different rooms that you can be finding new ones or learning new approaches for some time.  The controls are quite responsive, and there's enough humour to know that the game doesn't take itself too seriously.  Finally, despite mostly having an excuse plot, there is a nice little twist along the way.
does have some issues.  The most annoying is that it can take some time to go from dying to starting again, even when you're practicing on one of the bosses and don't want to do anything other than start it again.  This is made worse by a number of little bad design decisions: the way your character always pauses after leaving the manor or entering the castle breaks up the flow, for example, making the delay to restarting feel longer than it is.  Similarly, we don't need the boss introductions every time, nor the do we need to go through the final boss's dialogue.
These irritations certainly made the gameplay experience more frustrating than it needed to be.  Yet, they didn't stop me playing and enjoying
.  Definitely recommended unless you hate roguelikes.

This game is alright. It's challenging but in a way that feels more disappointing than fun. A big part of what I mean by this is that player health drains very quickly and it's not easy to avoid damage. So, naturally this results in a lot of death, not unlike other games in the genre. This difference is that in this game it feels more because of the game design itself than because of the player's skill. Since most characters lack an ability to block incoming damage, most of the time the only way to avoid taking a hit is to jump or run away from incoming projectiles but the problem here is that characters are a bit slow. Not only that but most of the time there's not a lot of room to jump out of the way because of how much space characters take up. It certainly doesn't help when you've got spikes hanging from the ceiling which renders jumping from attacks useless because you'll just take damage anyway. This wouldn't be so much of a problem if there were more opportunities to heal your character but there are very few healing items, and the ones there are don't heal very much.
On a different topic, I liked the idea of random character traits and this family lineage thing but in practice it doesn't seem to effect gameplay very much. Since you die so quickly you don't really get to see how these unique character traits effect gameplay in the long run. Every character ends up playing the same way and dying the same way with only slight variations.
Overall, it's alright but I just couldn't get into it.

Well, I finally got Anomaly Korea, so lets see how good this is. (I have played this game a LOT more than 13 minutes)
Anomaly Korea is a top-view reverse tower defense game, when you are in control of a task force whose goal is either destroy all towers or get to a certain point on the map. The game starts off after the events of the original Anomaly. You play as a commander fighting a war against a race of sentient alien machines (that is literally what they are called). They have now targeted korea, and you are the only thing in the way of the machines at the moment. So, lets get to the review.
Pros:
- Good graphics, great visual effects.
- A variety of vehicles at your disposal. From mechs to tanks to mobile shield generators.
- You can change the formation of your convoy. (protip: keep your most powerful unit at the front to soak up damage)
- There are special tactics you can use in the battle. You can use anything from healing to smokescreen.
- Campaign is really good. Got me hooked in the first 10 minutes.
- (I think this is the best part) you can change the course of your units mid-battle, which allows you to make split decisions when something new shows up.
- Runs smoothly even on weak computers with decent graphics.
Cons:
- The game gets a little repetetive later on.
- You have to play the first game in order to understand what actually happened beforehand. (for instance: where did these machines come from? What is their goal other than destroy everything?)
- No multiplayer. :(
Overall, this game is a great game to get if you are into reverse tower defense games. It mixes strategic path making and fast reaction skills to make an excellent strategy game. It's graphics are pretty good for being a port from a mobile game. There are actually uses and purposes for having certain units in your convoy.
I give this game a 7/10 (Definitely worth a look). This game is awesome if you are a fan of strategy and tower defense. If you are new to the franchise, I highly recommend this game to start off with. The storyline is gripping, and it actually feels like you are fighting a war against giant robots.

After putting over one hundred and eighty hours into the game, I decided to scrap my previous review and rewrite it from scratch. I am going to reuse parts of it since those are still true.
Now, when I first noticed the game, I recognized it's type. Idle type games are the sort that you don't need to pay too much attention too. In fact, it usually has an offline mode of sorts that keeps track of your progress. So when you boot the game up, say two days after, then you might find yourself having progressed a lot.
That having been said however, idle type games are also notorious for being hard to finish. Not because of the difficulty, but because the numbers get ridicilously high and because progress seems to slow down by a LOT after a certain point.
Now, one question you must ask yourself, is this pay to win? Because aside from being hard to finish, there are several titles out there that you just can''t finish without having to pay for it. Well, the answer to that question is mixed. Sure, you can keep playing the game without having to pay. But paying real money gets you god power, which lets you boost your character permenantly. Still, you can earn god power for free on your own so if you are patient you technically can get as far as you want. BUT I want to remind you that progress slows down by a LOT and that means you need to spent a lot of time on it. Logging in regularly to direct your character.
Graphic wise, you shouldn't expect anything. In fact, this is mostly numbers and text. Nothing else.
Story wise... Well, there is a story of sorts, but right now it's halted at the defeat of a certain god and you can get to that god within a week. Definetly.
This particular game awards you for exiting the game completely, if you stay offline for a day or so, I actually don't know the exact number, then your stats increase by a whole three hundred percent for three hours.
My conclussion is much the same as my previous review. This game is excellent if you got some time to waste or if you are bored and you don't feel like booting up a more complicated game.
Would I want to pay for it? No. If you are patient, like REALLY patient then you can get to the end. Coughing up real money seems like a waste. I think that the only time that you would need to pay money is a) if you want to support the dev and b) want to get some handy advantages while you're at it.
So overall, I would recommend the game but I still wouldn't pay for it.

The problem with the first is that it gets boring fast and needs constant updates and tweaking to keep kids happy. Plus it doesnt encourage players from diverse mindsets ie buildrs, loners, hunters etc. Its just geta gun and attack attack attack.
The problem with the second is that a balanced survival game upsets the first group. When the prey can fight back and not be offline raided easily then its not so fun.
The latest updates have seen twig building so that raiders can bypass hours and hours of buidling walls with twig structures.

"Mad Max" flirts with great, and dances with brilliant, but doesn't end up marrying either of them.
The main mission path is really well done as a piece of storytelling, especially as it twists the knife in both Max and the player. (You'll know what I mean.)
But...there are all these other, potentially fascinating characters that barely get any exploration at all.
The world is both large AND quite detailed as an environment. The effort put in by Avalanche on that front is obvious and impressive.
But...when it comes down to it, what there is to actually do in the world is very "samey." Sure there are variations on the themes, but those variations are pretty minor. On top of that, all progression pretty much amounts to the same thing (getting scrap to pay for upgrades), and you can get essentially Maxed out (see what I did there?) relatively early. At that point, your actions seem pretty academic and rote, even though there's still lots of territory potentially unexplored.
I personally felt that the vehicular combat was extremely solid, and maybe even stellar at points. If you were going to make a road-warrior sort of game, "Max" would be an excellent template to follow. The controls make plenty of sense after a bit of explanation and practice, and the overall balance is just about right to get challenge without frustration.
But...vehicle combat ends up being rather less central than you might expect. Instead, a lot of what you have to do to advance the game is focused on dismounted, hand-to-hand fighting. The mechanics there actually aren't bad, but the way the encounters are structured makes man-to-man fights boring and repetitive.
The Magnum Opus is a very cool piece of customizable hardware, and it's great fun to experience its upgrades as bits and pieces are added.
But...for some reason, the Opus never seems as durable as Chumbucket's dune buggy. Sure, the buggy isn't good at vehicle offense, but it can roll over almost any terrain and take a HUGE pounding. Your super-rad, armored assault car goes off a small ledge, and a very sizable chunk of structural integrity gets chewed up. The buggy, on the other hand, seems like it could fall from 30,000 feet and not register any damage. It's a little bizarre.
Speaking more generally, I think that one main measure of an open-world game is how well it hides the fact that it's all built on repetition. It's not that something like "Far Cry" doesn't have a similar amount of cut-and-paste as "Mad Max." It's just that the "Far Cries" and the "Fallouts" manage to get enough of both uniquely crafted material and fun, snappy gameplay "loops" into the mix that the repeated elements become washed out. With "Mad Max," the feeling that you're continually leaving and arriving at the same party just isn't countered very well.
Was I unhappy that I spend my money on this game? Not at all. It was worth it. I put a bunch of time into the experience. Avalanche did quite well, but it seems like all the effort got put into the environment when they might have spread out the resources a bit more evenly. It's a touch unfortunate - the game could have been an instant classic if it were smaller but more interesting - but I'm not really "Mad" about it. (See what I did there?)

Im a little baffled by all the negative reviews of this game honestly. Star Chronicles: Delta Quadrant is a great timekiller for extremely cheap (i paid $0.99 for it).  Its a turn-based sci-fi rogue-like/lite with very little story. Combat is simple but fun, all ships have both a shield and a hull rating. You have to destroy the shields first to get to the hull. Theres a decent variety of weapons to use to do so, some work better against shields, some better against the hull, some good for both(some wont even work against the other rating, for instance the ion turret will only damage shields not the hull). You gain levels with xp earned through battles and by salvaging unwanted loot (you can also use unwanted loot to heal your shields or hull, the better the loot the more it heals). You can only level up from the main menu however, which means you must clear the stage you gained the experience level on and then exit back to the main menu to upgrade your skills (the game automatically saves when you clear a stage). You gain one skill point per experience level attained which can be spent on a variety of permanent upgrades to your ship (while the game does have permadeath, the upgrades are persistent so youll become stronger and stronger for future runs). All in all its a fun little time killer for under a buck, what more can you ask for at that price?

TL;DR - Funnily enough, Back to basics gaming is keeping it simple by sticking to their name - BASIC.
easy achievements, easy trading cards, 2-3 hours of enjoyment
Recommended if only for the achievement hunters looking for more perfect games, or traders.
Pros:
- A reasonable price for something so short and simpleminded
- Stat assignment is basic and (too) easy to understand
- Easy achievements and trading cards
- 2-5 hours of enjoyment for the price
- Unity based game, and an Indie developer
Cons:
- Lacking content and story
- Lack of fullfillment after killing enemies with higher stats and getting "Weak" loot
- Most, if not all the weapons / items are useless, once you get a decent item, you use that for the rest of the game (also known as, lack of items and/or inspiration)
- You get what you pay for, a simple-minded game that is easy to complete.
To explain the lack of content and game balance:
Content-wise, there is only 20 "levels" to play, after you complete those 20 levels it puts you back to level 1, rinse and repeat until you die...after a while it gets boring, fast.
Now to explain game balance,
You can easily boost engines to 300 on first level (Weapon: 60, Engine 240, Shield 0) without being attacked (staying in the spot you spawned at) and with that you get +9-11 moves, attack a couple of enemies get a basic engine can put it up to 15-17 moves per turn...this part is where game balance is broken, you can skip everything and just continue to the next level then the next until you reach the last level, skipping all enemies and missions so easily is rather broken - I ended up doing it this way to get the last achievement (complete the game) as my threat level was too high for my current level and equipment.
It would have been better for the developer to "Gate" the warp-gates behind a "until you complete xxx you cannot continue" instead of having it on the map allowing you to skip all the content.
Art: Plain and can get boring fast
Sound: N/A (I had game muted as I had music in the background, so cannot say anything about this)
AI: could've been better....
Once you get all the trading cards and achievements, there is no sense on playing the game any further and uninstall it, like I have.

Recommended for easily 100+ hours of engrossing and entertaining survival challenge!! (Further ups & downs below)
This game is incredibly fun while you figure out the basics of survival. It took me about 6 colonies to build a nearly sustainable base (a 100% self-sufficient colony is impossible with current resource limitations). The early to mid game involves a ton of fun digging and building. After your colony is fully settled though, the late game becomes less fun. For me at least, farming is a real hassle that I derive little enjoyment out of. The late game consists of careful farming, tweaking your plumbing and power systems to perfection, and intentionally stressing out dupes who will cry or vomit for that extra water supply. Hopefully there's more content underway that will liven up the late game.
OXYGEN NOT INCLUDED VS DON'T STARVE??
The main difference between Oxygen and Don't Starve is the need to micromanage units. Patience and planning are key. Learn to set priorities so that dupes work on important tasks first and don't starve themselves to death. Also know that there is significantly less exploration in Oxygen than Don't Starve. The world is smaller, and it is difficult to travel far from base. Oxygen is definitely a base building game. If you prefer a nomadic playstyle in Don't Starve, this game might not be for you. Overall though, Oxygen brings the same excitement of a survival game that Don't Starve does.

I truly love this game.
If you're looking for high-action, really detailed battling with tonnes of options then it's probably not for you.
But if you're looking for a really charming, beautiful game with real autonomy in what you want to do next, that's easy to play for a short time and go back to at any point, this is the one. As a parent, I can't play games much, or for long, and this fits into a window of time, is hugely relaxing and fun, and not ever so demanding.
There are other AI ships on your side if you want to work with them, or you can go off and have your own adventures.
If the worst happens and you do get sunk by pirates, you simply regenerate at a local port, or nearby the fight, fully repaired and without having lost anything.
So you can't really 'lose', there's no pressure or time-limits, just miles of beautifully designed sea and shoreline to explore or fight over. It's perfect for unwinding.
There are actual places in your world to visit and trade in and fight pirates in,  but all of that is scalable each time you play - continue from where you left off, but you can scale combat speed or likelihood of pirates up or down.
You can also opt to go off to explore a separate place, which you can choose as trading challenges or hostile pirate zones to retake. There, the stakes are higher and the battles tougher, and they offer far more options to upgrade, and there is far more valuable debris floating around to discover and take on board.
But you can still exit that at any time if you want to, so again there's no pressure. A brilliant game for relaxation and gentle fun.

So this game has a been of a bit of an addiction for me the last several days since release. There's a lot more to it then one would think.
First off this isn't a CLICKER game. Not like Clicker Heroes, Time Clickers, etc. There are some parts where you click a lot of but it's mainly focused around idling and waiting for stuff. I know, strange that a game with the word IDLING in the title has a lot to do with IDLING, isn't it? Of course you could be an idiot and leave a negative review for just that reason.
Anyway, so here's how it works. You start off as pretty much just a normal guy, stuck on a planet after we humans destroyed our home world....for the 17th time. You end up in a world and universe ruled by powerful gods. Being the last survivor of a war against the god Hyperion, you end up developing your own godlike powers and start to challenge the gods, beginning with Hyperion and progressing up a ladder.
Yes folks this game does indeed have a story, with bits of it being unlocked everytime you defeat one of the gods. Currently the story stops after one of the mid-range gods with nothing remaining for the rest of them, so this might be something that comes in the future hopefully. For now the story that exists is pretty good, as it gives context and reason to your idling.
At its core the game is involved around you training shadow clones, and using these clones to train skills and fight monsters, which in turn raises your own stats. You assign a certain number of clones to each task and wait as your skills get higher. When you're strong enough you challenge a god, and then rinse and repeat until you find you can't beat the next god. At that point you can "rebirth" which starts you over but gives you multipliers on your stats; not much different then a lot of other idle games of this style. But there's a fair bit of depth to it, which i'll leave you to figure out yourself once you start playing.
A solid 'sit around on your♥♥♥♥♥and become more powerful then you can imagine' recommendation.

CONS
-Hard to undertand at first
-Takes a ton of grinding to beat the first boss
-Kind of boring

Star Wars Jedi Knight: Jedi Academy places you into the role of newly accepted Apprentice Jaden Korr, on his way to the Jedi Temple on Yavin IV. You progress in the story plot by doing missions handed down to you from your Jedi Masters. It takes the mechanics from Jedi Outcast and reinforces them into a new journey of experience in the Jedi Order. A truly recommended game for any Star Wars fan!

Even better than its predecessor (Jedi Outcast) and a little less challenging. But more customiazble, you start off by choosing what species you character can be, and your single lightsaber, (Blade colour and hilt) and start off.
Enter Yavin 4 and the Jedi Academy, progressing through your first force trials and chatting to good ol' Luke Skywalker. You then get sent off to your frist set of 5 mission, (only 4 needed to be completed to pass through to the 1st story level but you can complete all 5) At the beginning of each mission, you can choose to level up a force power, both light and dark. It will be upgraded by 1 point, with a max of 3 points all over to get the ability to its full potential. Your character then gets more focused on the storyline, with a 'story mission' where you will go to a strong point of the Disciples of Ragnos. This happens all the way through the game. This game has some epic lightsaber battles later in the game, and also has a wide variety of weapons and force powers. This game and Jedi Outcast both have multiplayer with some great maps and games, such as capture the flag and free for all. Recommended to anybody looking for a cool adventure, and fans of star wars.

tl;dr
You have a lightsaber and you can stab people with it.
Overall, I would proably suggest this game to most poeple.  That being said, it isn't a perfect game, or even great.  It is a good game.  It has weak graphics (even for it's time period), it has a poor story, and the voice acting isn't stellar.  However, it does have character customization, which the previous title did not have.  The weapons in this game are slightly expanded from the last game, and the missions are less linear in nature.
The missions are less linear, but most are still required, and many of them have poor mini-plots or stories.  Some of them are more fun than others; the one with the mega-rancor is arguably more difficult than the noghri mission, despite them being on the same 'level.'
The character creation is nice; if you ever wanted to play as a rodian.  More to the point, it allows purple or green lightsaber blades, which is much more varied than the previous title (in that one, you got blue).  Your name is fixed (for the purposes of the voice acting) and there's very few options when it comes to choosing the light or the dark side: this is done through the force system.
In the force system of the game, you are given eight 'core powers,' which are neither light nor dark.  To make your character light or dark, you choose either light or dark powers for your characters to wield, which in the end doesn't even affect how the game will turn out.  In one of the final missions, there is a choice you must make to show your true allegiance, and this choice is given regardless of light or dark powers.  Choosing different powers mostly just changes your game style, and not by a huge amount.
The choice of weapons is similar to the previous title, with a stormtrooper rifle, a crossbow, and a concussion rifle among others.  You'll probably find yourself using your lightsaber against most enemies, though, because it's really effective.  And awesome.
Multiplayer isn't too bad, but there's nobody to play against. :(
FYI, the default quick-save button is F12, which is kinda annoying if you want to make screenshots.
So, if it isn't fabulous, why am I recommending it?  Because it's like, three bucks now.

In 1942, with Nazis occupying Holland, a thirteen-year-old Jewish girl and her family fled their home in Amsterdam and went into hiding. For the next two years, until their whereabouts were betrayed to the Gestapo, they and another family lived cloistered in the “Secret Annex” of an old office building. Cut off from the outside world, they faced hunger, boredom, the constant cruelties of living in confined quarters, and the ever-present threat of discovery and death. In her diary Anne Frank recorded vivid impressions of her experiences during this period. By turns thoughtful, moving, and amusing, her account offers a fascinating commentary on human courage and frailty and a compelling self-portrait of a sensitive and spirited young woman whose promise was tragically cut short.

This game is fun, for the first while of gameplay; it gets repetitive and boring.
The AI only act as guards against AI enemies; nothing in depth about them. Conquering lands in singleplayer is not worth it. It would be better if conquering land for your faction starts up trade routes, with trade fleets you could pirate or join in; cities can grow naturally by providing a good supply of goods to boost the economy.
Instead, the only purpose of taking extra land would be to get special trade goods required by larger cities to gain gold; even just sinking pirates provides enough income to put trading into a small corner.
"Windward is focused on multiplayer," you might counter.
The multiplayer is only a shadow of its former glory. Newer players would be restricted to the easier provinces. where other new players would either prefer singleplayer or get bored of the game fast, while the dedicated 500+ leveled players skulk around stronger provinces; even then, there aren't that many around.

Overall an enjoyable, good game. A bit simplistic in combat, but still enough to be fun with a large variety of ships and equipment. And the multiplayer is a great bonus. I would say to expect about 12-15 hours before you feel the repetitive coming on, but for the price I'm betting if you already find this interesting at all then you will be more than happy with it.

Game starts. There is no tutorial, no on-screen help, nothing. In minute or so, one figures controls. Then, another ship comes and starts firing on him. Then another. And another. And another. One may manage to kill one or two ships, but they just keep coming.
And that's how game ends.
10/10, would waste 4 minutes of my life again.

- Short -
Trade, travel, fight, upgrade, with extra emphasis on travel, travel.. lots of travel. While this game is presented well, unless you enjoy tedious repetitive tasks with little reward or entertainment, I would sail clear of this one.
- Long -
Since I am a bit confused by all these reviews saying "no wind" let me clarify, there is wind, lots of it; However, instead of being something that could add intrigue and interest in tactics, it's only purpose seems to slow down travel and add another level of tedium to this "game".
My main gripe with this game, is that somehow they have made a game with pirates, cannons, and high-seas combat boring. Battle is setup like a point and click MMO with -very- few differences in combat style. The entire game your combat will be, click target, click attack, move in circles around target to make it harder for them to hit you. That is it, there is no other strategy, which makes this entertaining for 10 minutes before it gets old, fast.
The other main section of this game is trading, which is painfully boring. Pick up item at City A, Deliver to City B for 24% profit. Repeat. Repeat.. Repeat...
Ship upgrades are painfully limited, as I could only suffer to play this game 3 hours, I am unsure if there is more, but from what I saw there is 4 ships to choose from, you then customize each ship with different sails and hulls each with varying stats, with about 10 different slots to customize from ammo to sails to crew.
Pros
Ship customization is a great touch (colors, designs, many different aspects to upgrade)
Cons
Makes piracy and naval combat, seem boring
Game is hollow, no story, no events, no combat variation, no interesting quests.
Map design is strange.. No open seas, just a procedurally generated spider shaped coastal world.
Did I mention boring?
Final
I usually try to give detailed reviews, and I truly wanted to like this game, but as it is, it is hollow, boring, and just not fun to play. There is not much to say about this game because there isn't much of a game.

Tl;dr: This isn’t a mindless timewaster type of game. Time will need to be put into it. Understand what you are getting into before playing.
First off, this game is not a “sim” and you can’t approach it like one. It’s hard. Like Don’t Starve, you will be dying constantly. Your colonies will fail. Many, many times. Yes it can be micromanagey—but according to the developers that issue should be getting better with each major update (if you think it requires micromanaging now, you should have seen it before it was released on steam!!). This game WILL require you to put some time into it, learn the mechanics, and learn how actions affect the game world—and boy do they affect the world. Everything you do will determine how well your colony is going to turn out: the traits of the dupes you accept, the locations of buildings, when you build the buildings, what you build the buildings with, what you allow your dupes to eat, the temperature of your base, what plants you plant and where you plant them, even the spawn locations of the biomes around you. Again, the game is hard. And that’s the point. I have found that with each colony that fails, I have gotten a little better at understanding the game and can survive a little longer a little easier. This isn't a game where you have one group of dudes forever and you happily expand forever. Your dupes will do stupid things, they will die (sometimes you will actually have to intentionally LET them die), you will rage. When I first started playing, I couldn't get past cycle 30 without everything going to heck in a handbasket. But the more you play, the more you learn, and the better you get. Understand that if you get this game, you will NOT be playing something mindless and easy. If you can’t handle delayed gratification, then this won’t be the game for you.

Yep, this is a good game. It's not finished yet, for sure, but the basics are in place to make for a very nice base-builder.
The thing to keep in mind is that this is not Factorio (which I've played, from GOG) neither Rimworld (which I haven't). In OnI the focus is on building systems to generate resources that your dupes need to survive until your colony can reach a critical mass that allows it to go on indefinitely. Not that I've achieved this, mind, but it's obvious that there are some "loops" that you can exploit to create a self-sustaining economy of sorts.
For example, you can build a hydrogen generator that consumes hydrogen and produces energy. You can get hydrogen from Electrolyzers that also generate oxygen and consume energy and water. You can get water from Liquid Pumps that also need energy. The trick is to find the balance between consuming and generating enough energy to keep a generator, a few Electrolyzers and a couple of pumps going just on their own [Edit: oops. You also need a gas pump and a gas filter to separate the hydrogen and the oxygen, and those also consume energy. You can power them pretty comfortably with the Hydrogen Generator however].
Or, a very simple loop is to start with a pump, feed its output to a couple of Lavatories or Showers clean the polluted water they output through a Water Purifier and output it where it will be pumped by the Liquid Pump, starting the loop all over again. It's even possible to connect one purifier to one shower and keep the loop closed and going without input from a pump.
(If those loops remind you more of OOP design patterns, oh my god, no. This is actually fun. But, yeah, otherwise, the idea is to come up with little functional units that you can then replicate as needed, I guess.)
The point of building such loops of course is to keep your dupes alive and for this you need to manage three resources: oxygen, food and their stress. Failing to plan ahead and manage these resources well can send the entire colony in a tailspin and cause your dupes to start dying out pretty quickly.
For example, my latest colony, "Death Trainwreck" (autogenerated names are all optimistic like that) started falling apart when Bubbles, one of my dupes who has the "Binge Eater" stress response trait went crazy for the lack of clean air and proper temperature and started eating all of the available food. Pretty soon she had eaten mroe than 30k calories.  That left very few for the rest of the colony (I suspect that was actually a bug- I think she should have stopped earlier) and then my dupes started dying out because they had nothing to eat. Game over, man.
So, like I say, all this takes a lot of careful planning and careful resource management. Thankfully, you get a very detailed control system where you can assign each dupe to any number of different jobs and can also set a priority level for each job. This way you can even sort of "program" the dupes, by giving a high priority to the jobs that need to be finished first and a lower one to the jobs that depend on the others; say, give a priority of 9 to digging a pit and a priority of 8 to building up the system to fill it with water (or rather, CO2, you generally don't need to move a lot of water around, although it can happen).
The information you get from the game about the dupes' vitals, the energy your buildings generate or consume, the available oxygen, temperature etc etc is not for the faint hearted either. The available food is listed down to the kcal, power is listed in Watts, and so on. This makes it a little harder to eyball the amount of enegy you have, say, or immediately figure out how much you need to heat the colony but there is a certain kind of player that will find this level of detail infinitely satisfying. More importantly, it provides the precision you need to create the kind of system you want- the limit is your own imagination. This is something rarely seen in games and makes OnI a unique experience.
(On the other hand, this level of detail can probably put some people off too).
Of course, this being an Early Access game there's a lot of things missing. For one thing, there are very few options to reduce your dupes' stress. Some decorations, a massage table and that's it basically. There's also probably many more buildings that could be added - for instance, something to farm the (currently, only few) animals in the game. Or, more animals for that matter.
This is not a finished game at this point, but if you like resource management and engine-building, you probably want to give this a try, keeping in mind that its price may be a little bit on the steep side for its current state.
Then again, you're also buying a promise of future content and if Klei is still the same company that made Don't Starve, I think we can expect a lot of that.
I recommend it _IFF_ you don't mind the fact that it's still unfinished.  Otherwise, wait for a year or so.

Usually games based on movies and films are cheap, poorly made and just bad. Mad Max on the other hand, is actually a really good game. Although not perfect, it's probably the best movie-based game I've played since Spiderman first debuted many years ago. Mad Max has amazing visuals and a hefty amount of graphical options, as well as new and refreshing mechanics for vehicle-based gameplay and combat. Foot-combat, reminisent of the Batman games, feels a bit too simple at times, but is still enjoyable. There's a plenty and a variety of fun things to do within the game, including side-quests, customizations and upgrades for Max and your car/truck. There's also a very gritty and realistic sense to the game, especially when random storms come in. Not only do they look really good, but they hurl dangerous amounts of lightning and debris around, both of which you have to either dodge or take shelter from. That, along with the limited food and water supply you have to keep an eye out for to replenish your health and the limited amount of fuel for your vehicle, really gives a survival aspect that I did not expect from a game such as this, yet it's also not as intense to where you're not enjoying the game when you do have to find these necessities.
Again, the game is really good and quite fun, but it is not perfect. My main gripes are that there are certain times where the A.I. could be better. Often I would find myself trying to reason with NPC's, telling them they could have realized or done something a lot sooner than they had. Also, Max himself seems to forget where his enemies are occasionally when in foot-combat, as he will face the opposite way and punch/kick air for a few seconds. There are certain areas were Max can climb or vault on, which are usually marked with yellow paint, but there are also other areas that are much smaller than the things he climbs that are not marked, yet for some reason he still can't climb them. There are also times where I wish there were some sort of options for the HUD, because sometimes I'm left wanting to take away some of the HUD, or at least shoving it all closer to the edges of the screen. This may only be a problem for resolutions above 1080p though. There are a few mission related bugs, for instance, the dog seems to sometimes think mines are buried at locations where you already had defused them. After Death Runs (vehicle-based challanges), the game sometimes gets confused as to whether you lost the Death Run or died, which may become frustrating at times. Some of the larger textures could have been better, such as the night sky and the sludge pits, but all other textures seemed relatively great. Also, corpses tend to disappear too early, the game should at least wait until the player leaves the area.
All in all, Mad Max runs very well, plays very well and is just downright solid and fun, especially for a movie game, and is also a worthy installment to the Mad Max storyline and a great follow-up to Mad Max: Fury Road.

Mad Max, game open world ini cocok banget buat lo semua yang suka dengan game adventure ditambah aksi-aksi fighting moves-nya yang brutal abis. Gaya bertarungnya mirip-mirip Batman combat system, namun di sini lebih bloody and gory. Lo bisa bertarung dengan tangan kosong, senjata atau kendaraan mobil. Mobil pribadi lo (Magnum Opus), shotgun dan juga harpoon bisa diupgrade dan mobil-mobil musuh bisa dijadiin koleksi di garage. Fitur fast travel khas open world game bakal membantu banget kalo lagi males nyetir atau mau kabur dari kejaran musuh. Pemandangan jalan tandus dan gurun ga seburuk yang lo bayangkan, pengaturan cahaya di game ini dan weather effect-nya keren abis. Badai gurun nampak realistis, petir yang menyambar saat badai keliatan jelas dan nyata, begitu juga dengan percikan dan nyala api dari setiap benda yang meledak. Karakter juga audio cukup bagus dan story-nya juga ga kalah seru dengan movie-nya game ini.
Di beberapa bagian game ini bisa bikin lo jenuh, beberapa side quest dan looting scrap bisa agak membosankan kalo terus berulang. Boss battle di sini juga bisa dibilang repetitif, dari mulai tampilan Boss/Top Dog-nya yang cuma beda warna sampai cara bertarungnya yang lo pasti cepet banget hapal setiap pergerakan serangannya. Karena serangan yang lambat dan mudah dihindari, bikin boss battle di game ini kurang menantang. Pergerakan karakter Max juga ada sisi negatif khususnya saat kita lompat, hanya tempat-tempat rendah dan tertentu saja yang bisa dilompati atau dipanjat.
Grafik yang bagus cukup ringan walaupun dengan spec PC yang tidak terlalu powerful. Kisaran waktu tamat game ini 15 jam waktu main dan untuk para completionist atau achievement hunter, dalam waktu 70+ jam semua achievement bisa lo dapetin.

The short version:
The game is surprisingly enjoyable, and I recommend it if you are a fan of skill-based simulation games and economy/business games.
The long version:
This one has been on my radar for a year or two, and my first instinct was to laugh it off as some sort of toy truck for grown-ups.  Still, I kept hearing good things about it between the jokes, so I would occasionally reconsider getting it--only to not get it.  Well, now it's on sale for next to nothing, so I decided to give it a try.  I am very glad that I did.
While you spend virtually all of your time driving trucks, the game does not seem centered around the trucks like you might expect if you--like I once did--think this is just a game for people with a truck fetish.  At the end of the day, it is more about the drive, your business, and whichever job you are on.
I have to say they really nailed the driving.  Though I couldn't tell you what it's like to drive big trucks like these in real life, I can tell you that this feels just like driving with touchier controls and an inferior view.  Of course, none of those negatives are really ETS2's fault; rather, a gamepad and a television are just really poor substitutes for a steering wheel and free vision.  I am sure it would be much, much better with Oculus Rift and driving-specific hardware like a force-feedback steering wheel, gear shifter, etc.  I can say that when I started playing this, I felt like I was re-learning to drive, and after I forced myself to use the same tricks I do daily on the road, I found driving in ETS2 getting easier and more thoughtless.  I can almost always make it from A to B now with 0-2% damage as opposed to 10-30%.
Speaking of that... do not expect to jump right in and be able to do whatever you want.  The driving in this game is a challenge.  It is not arcadey, and it does not hold your hand.  You will have to spend some time adapting to it before you can expect to go anywhere without bankrupting yourself through traffic citations, accidents, and/or damage to your cargo and/or truck.  I recommend NOT buying your own truck until you are comfortable with driving, as your employer will at least cover damage to the very expensive trucks.
Beyond the difficulty, this gives me the same zoned-out feeling I get driving on the open road.  I went through a phase which ended 2 years ago, where I would compulsively drive all over my side of the USA whenever I had the opportunity.  For me, it was like a sort of meditation--very peaceful.  This game, when I am not struggling to maintain control of a heavy load at high speeds through winding, narrow turns in heavy traffic--gives me that same feeling.  The graphics are not the best in the world, but they chose very well where to direct their attention.  The sky, the lighting, and the weather are all fantastic.  The AI of the other drivers is, for the most part, very believable.  The game supports streaming radio with quite a few Europian internet radio stations available to choose from, and that can really compliment the experience.
I have been doing missions in my own truck for several hours now, but I have not yet started hiring other truckers or buying/upgrading real estate.  I also have an old force-feedback xbox 360 steering wheel and pedals, which I have never tried to use with my PC.  If/when I give these things a shot, I will try to remember to come back and update the review.
Until then, push whatever jokes you've heard out of your mind and consider whether you'd like to start a trucking business from the ground up, starting as a trucker in someone else's employ with the ultimate goal of becoming a freight tycoon.  If you would, and you think you would enjoy everything that entails, then please do yourself a favor and give this a shot.

If I were to nit pick, I would say that SG2s UI could use a little tweaking, the ability to zoom out on the map and a tool for selecting your own ships on the map and I'd like to see some of the fleet controls from X3 (for example telling a ships computer to go somewhere, protect something or trade something). I would also like to see space station ownership, and more skills and mods aimed at ship capture. But these are not huge criticisms, just where I think SG could be improved.

Ah, 1994: Games released the previous year (such as Doom and Blake Stone) had proven that the FPS genre could be lucrative. The result was the golden age of FPS, with several solid (and successful) releases as Heretic, Corridor 7, System Shock, Spear of Destiny, Alien Vs Predator, Doom II. There were also about 25 other games released, most of which were less than great. The problem was that many of these games licensed outdated technology; in simply a single year's time one can see the leaps that these engines made (compare Doom I to Doom II, for example).
Rise of the Triad (just barely released in time for Christmas '94) eschewed diagonal walls for some nifty advances of its own. Some things could be expected in the genre, such as stellar gore for the day (what Apogee lovingly called "Ludicrous Gibs" mode), and destructible objects (Duke 3D would make such things famous, but they started here, folks). However, RoTT took the FPS and flipped it on its head, adding some pretty creative touches. For example, jump pads scattered throughout the levels catapult both the player and the enemy high into the air, Super Mario style. These not only make combat more strategic and interesting, but they can also be used to access hidden areas (or otherwise inaccessible areas), leap past enemies, or collect life items (spinning ankhs that appear on the ground, ledges, or can hang in the air). Other oddities include bizarre powerups such as the expected God mode, and the not-so-expected Dog mode.
RoTT also tried hard to improve upon the FPS by tweaking previously existing elements. It was the first game to provide an adjustable violence level (players could kick it all the way up to the aforementioned “ludicrous gibs” or remove the blood and gore altogether). It also was among the first to provide the player with multiple characters to choose from (and, I believe, the first to make some of those choices women). It featured an automap. It also took LAN / network games to an amazing level, providing unique areas and completely customizable games.
The designers were some real geeks too, and this always played to my heart. Adding the ability to carry two guns “Woo” style in a time when most Americans had not even heard of John Woo was pretty killer. Changing the load screen during holidays (for example, having the H.U.N.T. Team wear Christmas hats on December 25) was another whimsical touch. And then, there's the “Shroom” mode!
Yes, Doom II was scary as hell, but RoTT was just plain fun, and easily one of the most influential games of our time. But does it hold up today? Actually, yes. Chunky pixels are certainly prevalent in today's Indie scene, so those shouldn't be an issue. If they are, there are enhanced graphics packs available for free. The MIDI soundtrack by Bobby Prince (if you've played the Doom or Duke Nukem series, you know his work) is rousing and pumps you up for combat, while the handcrafted levels (note I didn't say "procedurally generated!) are clever and full of secret alcoves. As an additional bonus, the Steam version also includes "The HUNT Begins," which was the original stand-alone shareware episode not included in the retail version of the game.
Rise of the Triad is a classic for a reason (several reasons!). Grab a copy, throw on the enhanced graphics packs, don't think too hard, and have a blast.  Recommended.

Rise of the Triad: Dark War is a classic FPS that tends to be overlooked in favor of other classics such as Doom or Duke Nukem 3D. This is a shame, because ROTT is a great first-person shooter.
The game runs through DOSBox, which can have some problems from time to time, but I had a solid experience on mostly "as-is" settings, with a tiny audio hiccup happening once in a while. The game is really tricky to use the Steam overlay on though, so be wary.
Gameplay is as you'd expect, mostly shooting bad guys and occasionally solving a relatively simple puzzle. In terms of difficulty, it's comparable to other shooters of that era, the main game is challenging, but not frustrating. The Extreme Rise of the Triad addon pack is there to challenge you if you feel you've mastered Dark War.
Due to its age, the controls can be a bit tricky to get working in a comfortable way if you're used to the more modern style of FPS controls, but they're not too hard to get used to.
The music (by Lee Jackson and Robert Prince) is fantastic. I would easily rate it the most memorable soundtrack in a first-person shooter of that era.
I had two large problems during my time playing. First one was EROTT's fourth episode. Almost all of E4 is frustratingly difficult and overly gimmicky (in fact one puzzle is pretty much broken). The maps have an excessive amount of trial and error as well as potential softlock situations that can force you to restart the entire map.
The second problem with the game was the final boss.
Overall, this game is worth getting if you want a good old shooter. This game was on my to-play list for a long time and I regret not playing it until recently.

They improved the prestige system. First of all I want to mention that this game has a level cap of 55. Everytime you level up you get a token, which you can spend on a perk/weapon/killstreak/equipment. 55 tokens isn't really enough, and it was done on purpose. Now it kind of gives meaning to actually prestige, so that you will be able to test out everything. There are 10 prestiges in the game, when you reach prestige 10, you receive the rest of the gear. Other then that, the game also has MW3's Prestige Shop and Prestige Unlock Tokens. The Prestige Shop gives you 3 options, you can either erase all your stats and set back to level 1(without prestige), add an additional loadout or keep all your tokens. The Prestige Unlock Tokens give you an ability to choose any gear, and permanently unlock it, you get 1 per prestige. The other good thing is that you no longer have your challenges and weapon attachments/camouflage erased when prestiging.Instead they decided to put it in a separate category. Now there is a weapon prestige, allowing you to completely erase all your weapon unlocks on that specific weapon, once you reached weapon's max level.You are allowed to do that 2 times. They reward you with an ability to put your clan name and emblem on that weapon.
One really annoying thing though, are the outdated graphics. This is an AAA title, so I had to mention that. They don't have a low budget, so there is no excuse for them being that outdated.
Conclusion: I give it a below average score. The game is better then MW3. In fact I have to say, if you judge it by it's singleplayer and coop then you may call it the best out of all COD's, but the core of COD for the past 7 years been the multiplayer, and that's what BO2 is lacking of. So I am not really suggesting you to get it, considering that they don't even give it a decent discount.

I bought Windward because I loved Sid Meier's Pirates! to death, and I was hoping this game would be a modern, indie-flavoured version of that game, with trading and ship's combat and high seas skullduggery. And it is that, in a way. However, the experience is incredibly sparse.
Where Sid Meier's combat had wind, which had a big effect on combat, as well as different tactics in terms of using chain shot, grapeshot or regular cannonballs to target sails, personnel and hull, respectively, Windward's combat is much more straightforward. You sail around the opponent, keeping your broadside pointed at the opponent as much as possible, and then you use one of your many MMO-like abilities to do some extra damage whenever they're off cooldown. There's no boarding, and every ship battle I was in played out exactly the same.
I haven't made it particularly far into the game, so it's possible combat might become more engaging later, but judging from the trailer video, it's just more of the same with more MMO-buttons thrown in.
It also completely lacks the character of Sid Meier's Pirates!. Towns are no longer places of social intrigue with a real feeling of place. Rather, they've been reduced to simple menus. You can see a list of rumours, which tell you where you can carry certain cargo for a profit, or just can pick from a list of quests, which are all variations on either "sail somewhere and maybe push a button" or "sail somewhere and win another identical ship battle". Quests and cargo use the same, limited "cargo slots" on your ship - I started out with 2 - so trying to coordinate quests and trading for efficiency is a fairly limited affair. There's already a million comparisons of this game to Eve, but I'll add another - It's a lot like Eve but with a personal story arc that concerns your character.
Unlike Eve, the space combat is twitchy and fast-paced, and surprisingly deep. There are a million ways you can outfit your ship and plenty of variety in ship types - how you outfit it matters, and the weapons you choose need to suit its strengths and suit how you will be piloting it to be effective.

This is from a post I did on the forum and decided to add it here following a suggestion to do so.
SPG 2 The Good, the Bad, Oh God the Insanity
If you’re on the fence as to whether you should get this or not it will all come down to what you are looking for in a ‘space’ game.
This is not Eve Online so get that out of your head. Seriously, if you want EO you’ll need to go log into EO. There is no online multiplayer, no gate camping players, no griefers and no gankers.
That being said, this game offers something EO and many others, online or not, have simply forgotten or just don’t care about. Interactive Devs.
Yep, you read that correctly. The Devs are extremely active in the forums. I’d hazard a guess and say 99% of all issues, questions, comments etc. are answered near instantly.
They take concerns very seriously and look for ways to address them as quickly as possible, faster even it seems.
While this isn’t to say other Devs aren’t around, personal experience has shown they just don’t answer, are too busy, don’t care and on more than one occasion… are downright obnoxious and rude.
So +1 for Dev support seemingly 24hrs a day every day…
Community… holy crap, where to begin…
There are a lot of helpful people. One or two I have noticed try to step in when the Devs FINALLY get some sleep. This doesn’t mean there aren’t more filling in those roles, only that I can’t read, re-read, and re-re-read each and every post over and over to see who is filling those roles. Though, I will admit, sometimes the forum reading is an exercise in hilarity.
Serious questions for the most part get serious answers. Once in a while they spiral out of control with loose jokes, odd references and such, though more or less after the issue has been handled.
Remember the active Devs from earlier? Yeah… they contribute too.
Don’t be surprised to find one or more of them plowing into your thread to partake of whatever silliness is afoot. Oh yes, my friend, they are characters indeed.
On the whole, the community is developing into a large group of knowledgeable friendly people looking to help out any way they can. Yes, some can be offended easily, but I have yet to see an all-out flame war like everywhere else. In fact, most people just apologize if they upset someone and move on, including myself.
So +1 for a truly friendly and helpful community.
Graphics…
Nothing that will stress your system too terribly. High end or low end, it seems everyone can find a setting that fits the bill and allows them to play. I have seen one or two instances where certain systems (read Laptops) refuse to allow the game to run, but I have yet to see more than those.
Even then, the Devs are still trying to figure out how to get it working on those couple of problem machines. Interesting, since most would just tell you that your system doesn’t have what it takes and to go get something bigger.
All in all, the graphics are very nice indeed. Nothing mottled, disjointed or misaligned. No missing pixels here and there or stand in objects for missing items.
So +1 there for that…
NPC’s…
What do you expect? They are NPC’s. They shoot at you, they kill you and they keep doing it. Unless you kill them first, in which case, they die rather well and don’t whine about it. I seem to remember an account of griefing done by NPC’s, though I believe that was a one-off. Funny though.
They get tougher as you progress through the game. Different levels, different types and different areas. They fight each other if they are opposing factions and will turn on you if you are low enough rep with one, or both. In which case, run.
So I give a +1 for good NPC mechanics.
Missions…
Lots of them. They are everywhere in both aspects of the game. Free play or Story line there are tons. Decent rewards for the time invested as far as I can tell, probably a bit too decent considering some missions you just have to click a button and repair something.
I’ll give a +1 here too.
Storyline…
For as much as I have done, it progresses well. Seems to have substance and a bit of plot for as far as I have gotten.
But…
It is buggy. Missions sometimes fail out. Sometimes you overshoot a zone and they get canceled, dropping you out of the storyline and into free play mode. Other times, you just crash out of the game.
They are working on the bugs as fast as they are made aware of them and that helps out a lot. More often than not, you can just reload from a save point and try to continue.
No points for this one, still needs work.
Mods…
There are more than a few. Something for everyone I suppose. Uber ship, got it. More money, got it. Star Trek themed ships, go those too.
From Star Trek to vastly improve (overpowered) beginning station inventories, there is something to fit most everyone.
The game has a mod community growing faster than the game itself. Even at least one mod I saw that will completely change the game to Mass Effect themed ships and even a new storyline that appears to be in the works.
The Devs seem to support unlimited, no holds barred modding.
So definitely +1 here.
Oh, lest I forget...
Community input...
Look in the game. Look at achievements and improvements. You will see all the signs of active community involvement that has been taken seriously. (mostly)
Yeah, +100 and some Oreos for all you community peoples that report bugs, request content changes and overall general improvements.
All in all, for me, this has been one hell of a ride… and it’s just beginning. The game is only getting better and more is on the way.
If you’re on the fence, get off it. Buy the game and join the fun in the community.
And the insanity? Glad you asked...
There are the elite few who can claim this. They watch you at home while you play. They see you in your boxers. They wear your boxers, like I am right now. The Devs are part of this group, I know one, whom I shall leave nameless, who has watched me in my boxers. Yes, some of us are insane... And that is the fun of it all.
Sincerely,
Virikas
P.S. +1000 to the Devs for allowing us to be insane, taking us seriously when needed and for being on top of everything, everywhere, all at once, every day... always.
Now... which one of you took my boxers, Meep.

This little indie 2d space rogue-like turn-based strategy game is strangely addicting.

Game play is fairly simplistic, but as you progress you keep that progression of your character. Each time you start, you begin with basic equipment, and as you take down enemies you loot their technology, giving your ship an advantage. The AI is pretty simplistic, so don't expect great tactics from the enemies. The more you play the more you undersand how the enemy ships work.
The achievements will take some time to get as you need to become strong enough before you can attain some of them.

Rise of the Triad is a textbook example of a game with good ideas that suffer from bad execution.
The good ideas are abundant, and seem to stem from a desire to create something completely atonal and unfocused (at least thematically) by design. It seems that everything the developers could think of was put in, and they managed to make a lot of the results work. Bizarre powerups! Derpy fat monks! Tons of gore! Absurd rocket launchers! Bounce pads! 5 protagonists, each with different stats! Infinite-ammo bullet weapons that don't do much damage but fire fast and can stun the target, so shooting at more than one enemy becomes an intense game of trying to keep the most dangerous targets stunlocked while also holding the others at bay! Alliteration! Each of these is a good idea by itself, and together they become a whole greater than the sum of its parts, creating an anarchic experience that seems to never run out of new things to show you.
However, the bad design choices bring down the whole experience quite a bit. The levels are huge and sprawling, and while the excellent map helps out quite a bit, it's still easy to get lost. The level design also has the same problem DOOM sometimes has: the moment-to-moment parts are good, like a narrow bridge across a chasm or a series of crushers, but they're more often than not just strung together with no rhyme or reason, padding out the level until it just ends. The difficulty can also just spike out of nowhere; notable examples include the enemy type that gets an LMG
grenades
a ridiculous amount of health, as well as the NME. In addition, the game is about twice as long as it needs to be, with 30 main levels and 7 secret ones; this spreads the game's ideas more than a little thin, and some levels have absolutely nothing remarkable or interesting about them. Finally, some things are just inexcusably unintuitive. Invisible yet vital pressure plates in the floor, hidden pushwalls that are necessary for the player to progress, and arcane button puzzles all didn't make themselves clear and forced me to look up the solutions. God knows how people figured this stuff out when it was released. The absolute worst part of the game is the final boss, which comes in two stages. In the first part, the secret is to NOT shoot him, and he'll die on his own. If you do shoot him, it takes him longer to die. That is atrocious game design on its own, but it gets worse from there. After an admittedly fun chase level, one reaches the second part of the boss. Here, I will relate my experience in full.
I came to the final boss knowing from research that one has to destroy all his eggs in order to get the true ending. I destroyed all the eggs that I found on the way to the final battle (there were about 15), then proceeded onwards. I whittled his health down to almost dead, giddy in the knowledge that I soon would be victorious. Then, I spent the next hour or so shooting at the final head, which didn't seem to be taking damage any more. I decided that there must have been a glitch, so, for the first time, I let myself die and didn't reload a save (like Wolfenstein, this game has a literally pointless lives system, seeing as you can save and reload anywhere). When looking this up, however, I learned that there was another cache of eggs that I needed to destroy in order to truly win that required activating an invisible pressure plate in the floor hidden behind some hazards that I had no reason to go across, going to another room to find a previously hidden key, pick up a powerup impossible to see from where I was, use more invisible pressure plates randomly hidden in a large open area to expose the key's door, using the powerup (which only worked for a certain amount of time and did not respawn) to access an otherwise-inaccessible area, and kill some enemies to get to the second stash, which was twice as large as the previous stashes combined. The game, for the record, made NONE of this clear, not even the fact that I had to destroy the eggs in the first place. Remember, if one doesn't do this, one fails the game. I made another save and did all of this, but came upon the same result: the final boss would not die. I then realized my problem: there must have been some sort of glitch that, upon saving when the boss was on his last head, made him invincible. I made a
save at the cost of another life and, armed with all this information, managed to kill the boss and win the game.
Read that last paragraph again, and this time try to think of the human who thought that any of that was in any way a good idea.
Rise of the Triad has one other problem, too, and this one I don't blame on it. In light of more recent technological advances, namely mouselook and WASD, old-style arrow-keys-and-Ctrl-and-Space-and-Shift just doesn't really compare. It holds up, more or less, but it's merely functional, and just isn't as versatile, responsive, or fun as modern control schemes. I don't blame RotT for this, as there wasn't much it could do in this regard, but it is worth noting.
Rise of the Triad is an interesting case study, if nothing else, in how much abuse a good idea can take before it collapses entirely. Rise of the Triad toes this line in many places, but overall it's a fun enough experience, if a little repetitive and horrible in some aspects. I recommend it (especially if it's on sale), and I look forward to seeing if the remake fixes any of the game's glaring issues. If nothing else, buy this game for Dog Mode. That's worth $7.
EDIT: Also, it has a really great soundtrack. Actually probably the best I've heard in a game yet.
