After 100%-ing this game I have to say, it's honestly a pretty great game, its not the greatest but its pretty under rated and its definitely worth a buy, even if you haven't seen any of the movies.
There are only a few key frustrating things overall in this game. o.o Pros and Cons
Pros
-Alot of gameplay with hours of stuff to do
-Great customization of Max and your ride
-Tons of things to spend in game scrap(upgrade material) on. There was rarely ever a point in the game where I wasn't constantly trying to farm more scrap to continue upgrading
-Huge gorgeous map, deep atmosphere and increidble visuals.
-Great driving mechanics, driving feels pretty great in this game aside from randomly having your back tire
clip and pebble or a desert lizards ♥♥♥♥♥ and spinning you out of control
-The ability to harpoon enemies and drag them around whilst watching them cart wheel across the ground A+ fun time.
-Awesome sand storms that blow in scrap and are pretty intense to drive around in.
-Really cool unique areas, each area of the map looks and feels unique.
-Wide variety of cars to collect and drive including rare cars to find.
-Ability to grow a beard instantly 10/10
-Harpoon
-Harpooning everything
Cons
-The map is HUGE so expect tasks to get pretty repetitive
-Clearing Minefields is really tedious, you have to switch your car to a specific buggy and drive to each and every minefield
, there is fast travel in this game but you can only use it with your main car, if you try and use it while driving a different car
it will automatically revert to the main car upon fast traveling. This makes using any other car than your main nearly useless and also really makes clearing minefields one of the most boring parts of this game. (not required to clear them though, only for completion)
-Combat is a basic copy and paste of the Batman series, but not nearly as polished. Combat at times feels VERY clunky and unresponsive.
Button prompts in combat only work about 75% of the time and stringing together combos and using the prompts usually ends up with the enemy bashing you in the back of the head or kicking your punching your Maxy buttcheeks while you desperately attempt to hammer the A button
-The game handles combat fairly well until too many enemies get on screen, when the game floods the living hell out of the battlefield with enemies its like the game stops thinking whatsoever about combat
Enemies start swinging like angsty teens at a concert and you rarely have time to respond before they hay maker you over and over again 10 billion times
-Maxs' sprinting animation is hard to get used to, it sort of makes him look like there's a fire ant in his asscrack.
-with driving a main aspect of this game they did not include and sort of radio/music or anything whilst driving, so the only sound you hear whlie driving is your mechanic Golem bucket making the same 10 remarks or comeplely obvious hints. So just play your own music and voila.
-One of the most frustrating side missions in the game are by far the Death Races. Most aren't horrible, but many of the cars you are forced to use in these races are awful. With some of the worst handling you could imagine. In the barrel races where the goal is to hit a barrel at each checkpoint to advance, many of the lesser crappy cars you're forced to use actually spin out simply from ramming one of these barrels. The ai in these races is fairly frustrating as well, expect them to not be too concerned whatsoever with winning the race and more concerned with screwing you over as hard as they possibly can in each race.
Bottom line, I think its definitely worth a play through though. :3

It's a little old to boast about now, but Jedi Academy and the Jedi Knight series in general for me were always the bees knees of Star Wars games. Now for those of you looking for a great Star Wars single play experience I highly recommend the old Jedi Knight games, Dark Forces, Jedi Knight: Dark Forces 2, BUT ESPECIALLY Jedi Knight: Jedi Outcast. Dark Forces 1 and 2 are both pretty old games and did what they wanted to do very well, but Jedi Outcast was something truely special when it first showed its beautiful face. Plus the graphics have held up to a point where they wont completely make your eyes bleed. As far as the single player in Jedi Academy however, well at least the gameplay held up. The story on the other hand is pretty meh. Oh well, if you play Academy it's going to be for the multiplayer~!
When it comes to multiplayer, and this here was my bread and butter, I'd recommend both Jedi Outcast and Jedi Academy. God only knows how many hours I truely put into these games back in the day but it must have been a crazy amount because I really knew my snoz. I moved with the speed of a cheetah with a heart full of napalm, and attacked with the strategic & majestic grace of a real patient demon. It was pretty sweet. Too bad there probably aren't any servers left worth a damn in the server list nowadays otherwise i'd likely still be at it. Oh bubble trumps.
Final Verdict: (5 out of 5)

I remember stumbling across the alpha versions of Gang Beasts back in 2014 and quite enjoying it, but I never ended up purchasing it once it reached early access as I felt £15 was a bit steep for what was supposed to be mindless fun with friends. I'm glad I didn't, as the game has been in EA for 3 years and it doesn't feel like anything significant has changed.
The fighting is still pretty fun, but I certainly wouldn't call it £15 RRP fun, especially with as little content as there currently is. You get a local fight mode (Which seems to lack bots that the alpha had?), multiplayer and character customization. In terms of content, that's all you get along with several maps to play on. Online is laggy and often had noticeable input lag as well as characters stretching all over the place due to said lag. Furthermore, it seems to lack a timeout feature, leading to potentially long, drawn out dull battles and spectators staring at the screen waiting for their boring hell to end. Even playing it in what should be a tense 1v1 feels like a bit of a chore as you try to chase down your opponent as he runs away. To add to this, once the final round of a match has taken place, it ends the exact same way all other rounds end but unceremoniously dumps you into main menu again. The menus themselves are also irritating as they have background animation changes to signify you're going into a different selection. My main question to this is: Why? Is this just random flair or does it serve a purpose? It sure feels like its only purpose is to waste time.
The general core gameplay loop is fun but nothing feels like it has any weight behind it. Force of impact seems to have effect on how long it takes to take knock someone out (A big online strategy seems to be waiting on stairs and doing a jump kick at anyone trying to walk up) but due to the lack of any meaningful feedback besides a sound effect means it all feels completely arbitrary. Does it take 5, 10, 15, 20 punches to take someone down? I have no idea whatsoever, because nothing makes me feel like I'm really doing anything to an enemy other than flipping around them and tickling them until they fall over. Due to the nature of the game being so physics based, the attacks look more like interpretive dance rather than an actual punch.
All added together though, it is reasonably fun to play briefly. The destructible environments and the chaos that unfolds due to their design is great and actually entertaining. It's the sort of game you play in short bursts to not wear yourself out, but even then I can't see it lasting longer than a few hours of playtime. While different things take place in each round, such as the elevators breaking in one round and everyone falling to their deathor simply trying to throw each other out of the glass windows in another, it ultimately all feels incredibly repetitive due to how arbitrary everything feels.
In summary, It feels like a great concept that'd be enjoyable with a few friends (As the alpha was), but little time was put into thinking about how to add any form of meaningful content to it or any real polish. Even with 3 years of early access the game only seems to have a few extra levels, character customization and buggy multiplayer added in, While the game is *obviously* still unfinished as it sports the aforementioned early access tag, can the "it's still in early access!" excuse hold weight after 3 years and (according to Steam Spy) apprxomiately 900,000 people have given them their money? For a party game that has so little to it, it should be priced around a fiver at most. Ten quid even on sale? Not a chance.

I really tried liking this game since i have a passion for Plattformers and Metroidvania games. But after spending around 6 hours, beating 2 Bosses and after i unlocked "a fair bit" of the skills, classes and upgrades i still don't enjoy this game.
For my taste it's way too grindy and it doesn't seem like skill will have much of an impact in this game. Sure if you are somewhat skilled you will collect a lot of gold (which is used to level up after you died) but there are locations which are pretty much suicide if you enter them before you unlocked certain upgrades. This will result in grinding and so you play the same location over and over again, to collect more gold to be strong enough to survive in the next location.
The Idea of playing the "child" of a former character sounds fun at first but in my opinion it just doesn't work too well because that mechanic doesn't manage to make each run "special" enough.
It's by no means a bad game and i'm sure a lot of people will have fun with this game but that's not the case with me. The ~6 hours i spent with this game felt repetitive, grindy and i'm not a fan of the controls neither.
Don't get me wrong the controls are responsive, i'd say even TOO responsive which doesn't feel "nice" to me (there is no other way to discribe it sorry). After 6 hours i still take hits i wouldn't take in similar games.
tldr;
To sum it up, there are just too many things i don't like in this game which makes it impossible for me to recommend  it. However i believe that there are a good amount of people out there who would really enjoy this game. So this is a pretty personal review. Anyways, my advice is (if you are really interessted in this game): get it on Sale.

After 100%-ing this game I have to say, it's honestly a pretty great game, its not the greatest but its pretty under rated and its definitely worth a buy, even if you haven't seen any of the movies.
There are only a few key frustrating things overall in this game. o.o Pros and Cons
Pros
-Alot of gameplay with hours of stuff to do
-Great customization of Max and your ride
-Tons of things to spend in game scrap(upgrade material) on. There was rarely ever a point in the game where I wasn't constantly trying to farm more scrap to continue upgrading
-Huge gorgeous map, deep atmosphere and increidble visuals.
-Great driving mechanics, driving feels pretty great in this game aside from randomly having your back tire
clip and pebble or a desert lizards ♥♥♥♥♥ and spinning you out of control
-The ability to harpoon enemies and drag them around whilst watching them cart wheel across the ground A+ fun time.
-Awesome sand storms that blow in scrap and are pretty intense to drive around in.
-Really cool unique areas, each area of the map looks and feels unique.
-Wide variety of cars to collect and drive including rare cars to find.
-Ability to grow a beard instantly 10/10
-Harpoon
-Harpooning everything
Cons
-The map is HUGE so expect tasks to get pretty repetitive
-Clearing Minefields is really tedious, you have to switch your car to a specific buggy and drive to each and every minefield
, there is fast travel in this game but you can only use it with your main car, if you try and use it while driving a different car
it will automatically revert to the main car upon fast traveling. This makes using any other car than your main nearly useless and also really makes clearing minefields one of the most boring parts of this game. (not required to clear them though, only for completion)
-Combat is a basic copy and paste of the Batman series, but not nearly as polished. Combat at times feels VERY clunky and unresponsive.
Button prompts in combat only work about 75% of the time and stringing together combos and using the prompts usually ends up with the enemy bashing you in the back of the head or kicking your punching your Maxy buttcheeks while you desperately attempt to hammer the A button
-The game handles combat fairly well until too many enemies get on screen, when the game floods the living hell out of the battlefield with enemies its like the game stops thinking whatsoever about combat
Enemies start swinging like angsty teens at a concert and you rarely have time to respond before they hay maker you over and over again 10 billion times
-Maxs' sprinting animation is hard to get used to, it sort of makes him look like there's a fire ant in his asscrack.
-with driving a main aspect of this game they did not include and sort of radio/music or anything whilst driving, so the only sound you hear whlie driving is your mechanic Golem bucket making the same 10 remarks or comeplely obvious hints. So just play your own music and voila.
-One of the most frustrating side missions in the game are by far the Death Races. Most aren't horrible, but many of the cars you are forced to use in these races are awful. With some of the worst handling you could imagine. In the barrel races where the goal is to hit a barrel at each checkpoint to advance, many of the lesser crappy cars you're forced to use actually spin out simply from ramming one of these barrels. The ai in these races is fairly frustrating as well, expect them to not be too concerned whatsoever with winning the race and more concerned with screwing you over as hard as they possibly can in each race.
Bottom line, I think its definitely worth a play through though. :3

I remember stumbling across the alpha versions of Gang Beasts back in 2014 and quite enjoying it, but I never ended up purchasing it once it reached early access as I felt £15 was a bit steep for what was supposed to be mindless fun with friends. I'm glad I didn't, as the game has been in EA for 3 years and it doesn't feel like anything significant has changed.
The fighting is still pretty fun, but I certainly wouldn't call it £15 RRP fun, especially with as little content as there currently is. You get a local fight mode (Which seems to lack bots that the alpha had?), multiplayer and character customization. In terms of content, that's all you get along with several maps to play on. Online is laggy and often had noticeable input lag as well as characters stretching all over the place due to said lag. Furthermore, it seems to lack a timeout feature, leading to potentially long, drawn out dull battles and spectators staring at the screen waiting for their boring hell to end. Even playing it in what should be a tense 1v1 feels like a bit of a chore as you try to chase down your opponent as he runs away. To add to this, once the final round of a match has taken place, it ends the exact same way all other rounds end but unceremoniously dumps you into main menu again. The menus themselves are also irritating as they have background animation changes to signify you're going into a different selection. My main question to this is: Why? Is this just random flair or does it serve a purpose? It sure feels like its only purpose is to waste time.
The general core gameplay loop is fun but nothing feels like it has any weight behind it. Force of impact seems to have effect on how long it takes to take knock someone out (A big online strategy seems to be waiting on stairs and doing a jump kick at anyone trying to walk up) but due to the lack of any meaningful feedback besides a sound effect means it all feels completely arbitrary. Does it take 5, 10, 15, 20 punches to take someone down? I have no idea whatsoever, because nothing makes me feel like I'm really doing anything to an enemy other than flipping around them and tickling them until they fall over. Due to the nature of the game being so physics based, the attacks look more like interpretive dance rather than an actual punch.
All added together though, it is reasonably fun to play briefly. The destructible environments and the chaos that unfolds due to their design is great and actually entertaining. It's the sort of game you play in short bursts to not wear yourself out, but even then I can't see it lasting longer than a few hours of playtime. While different things take place in each round, such as the elevators breaking in one round and everyone falling to their deathor simply trying to throw each other out of the glass windows in another, it ultimately all feels incredibly repetitive due to how arbitrary everything feels.
In summary, It feels like a great concept that'd be enjoyable with a few friends (As the alpha was), but little time was put into thinking about how to add any form of meaningful content to it or any real polish. Even with 3 years of early access the game only seems to have a few extra levels, character customization and buggy multiplayer added in, While the game is *obviously* still unfinished as it sports the aforementioned early access tag, can the "it's still in early access!" excuse hold weight after 3 years and (according to Steam Spy) apprxomiately 900,000 people have given them their money? For a party game that has so little to it, it should be priced around a fiver at most. Ten quid even on sale? Not a chance.

First off I'd like to say that I can't recommend this game or not, its still in its development without a storyline yet. It has a lot of potential but also a lot of stuff to work on.
Much of what the others have said is absolutely right. The money/combat balance system is so wonky at the moment. There have been times I fought 2 'impossible' ships and knocked them out almost immediately, and then 3 'trivial' ships have taken me down a little while later. Using manual aiming is a massive handicap because you can only fire from a few turrets at a time and trying to lead a ship is next to impossible at many ranges. I have yet to come across another gun, light or heavy, that is stronger than the ones I started with.
The skills and perks are lackluster at best, you start with all the skills and simply increase the efficiency slightly. Every five levels you get a perk, and again, that just adjusts your efficiency with one thing or another, 8% more money when trading, or 8% more damage with railguns, etc. Very uninspired stuff.
And then the money, over the course of a week I got about a million, which isn't enough for any ship. Then when I get to a particular station I kill a bounty without even realizing the ship was one. After selling at the station, I get another bounty, and another. In the course of an hour I get 17 million and can pretty much afford whatever I want, except I can't fly much at the level I'm at.
All in all it is a game on the cusp of having something really good going for it. There's a lot of potential here and I'll continue to play and explore because I do find it entertaining.

As a long-standing fan of the sci-fi genre, I can say that this is the kind of game I've been looking for. It has everything that any space-fan would enjoy! Anomalies, planets, asteroids, nebulas, and tons more! You can trade, customize your starship, upgrade, and fight against pirates as well as enemy factions. The gameplay is unlike anything I've played before, in a good way, and makes it feel like it's ship-on-ship combat. Fighting in space is dynamic, involved, and intricate so it can be challenging at times but never too difficult. The variety of weapons you can add to your starship also helps to give the game a unique feel in combat. The game has the look and expanse of Eve while remaining a single-player only game.
Finally, it is workshop/mod friendly! Personally, I like to cross-over different franchises into my games so it's really cool to see a Federation Starship flying around space and using weapons from Star Trek as a way to create a personalized and awesome experience.
Definitely would recommend to any sci-fi fan. Better than a lot of AAA titles I've bought. Keep up the good work!

Cons

I've played this game for many hours on Kongregate, and I have to say it's a lovely idle game. A lot of depth compared to incrementals like Cookie Clicker, this game can and will take up a good portion of your time, even if you don't actively play a majority of the time.

This game is quite fun if you like idle games. It has a huge amount of depth to it, and while you don't have to spend any money on it to experience the full depth of the game, it is absolutely worth supporting the developer. Even if you don't normally like idle games, it's something fun to do on the side of anything else you're doing on your computer.
For example, when I was doing schoolwork I would often keep the game open in another tab (I played on the Kong version before this was released) and complete an assignment, and then go change some things around, spend god power, allocate my clones, etc. Then I would go do another assignment, or some reading. It can be a bit intimidating at first, but you'll get the hang of it quickly.

I really want to like this game...
Let me preface this by saying that I avoid multiplayer games in general. I can't say for certain whether the multiplayer is fun or not. However, the game definitely feels geared towards a multiplayer experience, so I'm betting those who like multiplayer would have more fun than I did.
Pros:
The game is beautiful.
Simple and straightforward ship-to-ship combat.
Good trading system.
Controller support with mappable buttons.
Cons:
Single player gets boring fast.
Really grindy. Progress requires a lot of doing the same things over and over and over... and then more.
Controllers don't have enough buttons to handle all of the combat options, and dealing with the menus with the controller is really awkward.
Quests are repetitive and without a lot of variety.
Enemy/Ally AI is crappy.
Pirates are frustrating because they seem to respawn faster than you can kill them (and while you're fighting them, others are busy taking over your towns).
All in all, I love the concept, and for the most part it plays well. It just lacks a lot of the little things that keep your attention longer. It's an unpolished sandbox without any real direction. It could really use a campaign/story mode for single player. I got it cheap, so I don't regret the purchase. If you like multiplayer, it's probably even better.

In truth I both recommend this game and don’t. You see for every good mechanic there is a negative, here are some examples:
-	The game has a lot of side activities to keep you occupied, but these are repetitive with laughable variety.
-	Extensive customisation of your magnum opus, but you can only achieve this be completing many aforementioned repetitive side quests.
-	An okay story, but some missions are locked away until you complete some side quests and only the ending is really that memorable.
-	The game is well optimised with impressive graphics, but the whole game is set in a desert and graphics shouldn’t be a defining feature of a game.
-	The game features survival elements such as water, food, fuel and shotgun bullet, but food and water are only for health, fuel is plentiful and every one of these items can be immediately restocked at any upgraded base.
-	You can enter and collect enemy’s cars for fun and to become disguised, but why use an obsolete car when yours can be upgraded on they fly, equipped with all weapons, be summoned from anywhere and is invincible.

I really enjoyed Mad Max and I definitely see it as one of those games that I will go back to in the future. It can be a bit boring and repetitive at times, but I feel like you will be having way more fun playing this game, rather than feeling boredom. The car combat is very well done, and even though the regular combat got old quick, it was good for it's own right. This game is definitely focused on vehicles, so it's probably something you would expect. There is a story that is just kind of there, but it's really easy to follow and satisfying at some points. The game ran beautifully for me, never going below 60 FPS and never crashing. I was running the game on Ultra.
Overall I had a good time with this game and I would recommend it to almost anyone, especially fans of the open-world genre. It's not as jam packed as GTA V or Witcher 3 (or as good), but it has enough to keep you entertained. I would say it's definitely worth the $40, and I see it goes on sale quite often and for around $20 or so, which is definitely a bargain. Mad Max gets a 7.5/10 in my book.

Having watched the game played extensively online and then purchasing it while it was on sale to play it manually, it is about as unimpressive as it looks.
Save for the poor world building and awkward visual appearance, the production value of the game is quite high between the graphics, randomization, combat and music. The massive weakness of the game is its complete inability to simulate proper difficulty.
Most of the challenges in the game come from it; filling the room with numerous hazards and enemies which it expects the player to counter all at once, putting in pointless hazards in the players way that make no sense other then to make things artificially more tedious, enemies disguised as nondescript objects in the environment, spawning the player into a room with an enemy right near them, having enemy projectiles phase through solid objects including the walls and floor and ceiling, having enemies damage the player just by touching them. The list goes on. The game almost fundamentally relies on trial-and-error, dying until you learn how to counter everything exactly, in order for it to be playable. Why bother playing, why not just purchase and play a game you can have fun with without the need for near double digit hours of experience.
The artificial difficulty is made even worse by the rooms that are simply designed to stop progress entirely. Where the room is simply, spam. The developers just took a room, and flooded it with enemies or environmental hazards, or both. And then just threw that into the randomization system alongside all the normal rooms. So you randomly are expected to be able to fight five different enemies each firing projectiles at you, all at once, or traverse a pit of spikes that has platforms which need a quick time event to be activated, only last two seconds when they are activated, and there are projectiles shooting at you, and there are enemies shooting projectiles at you. And this is just something in the game that you can encounter at any point.
Going beyond that, the only unique aspect of the game is its quirky character handicap system. Which amounts to nothing more, then a handicap. The characters the player chooses from to play after each time they die have random physical health conditions which pointlessly hinder gameplay. Ignoring the immense insult and immaturity that using these real life conditions in a game like they are a joke brings, on a gameplay standard they are exactly as worse.
Characters generated can have conditions which effect the game itself such as: not being able to see game colour,  not being able to read game text, having the world upside down, replacing textures with immersion breaking neon textures, having everything close to the player blurred, having everything far away from the player blurred. Basically, the only unique thing the developers could come up with to give their game is to limit or outright remove fundamental aspects of the game itself. Found a journal entry while playing as a character who cannot read properly, well you just cannot read that journal entry right there then. Want to play as a certain class, but the only character with that class that has spawned is one who cannot see game colour. When then if you want to play as that class you just have to play in black and white. It is absolutely pointless, immature, offensive and downright stupid. Serving no actual purpose but to annoy the player and mock real life illness, and to be an artificial gimmick the developers could tout their game has.
Yes, this is a unique aspect of this game, it is unique because no other developers previously have been this dumb and belligerent as to include something like this in one. Especially one the costs double digit cash.
Additionally, the bosses are terrible. Each boss is literally a common enemy with their sprite size increased; who fights by spawning larger sized and larger amounts of the same projectile the common enemy variant spawns. Fantastic, so exciting. Cannot wait for that at the end of each map type, new content coming to you straight from the assets you have already paid for.
Players who do not mind the trial-and-error pseudo difficult genre of skull-against-wall bashing will find this game quite fun and worth the price.  However if you do not then you might as well go buy any of the other games that cost the exact same amount that are way more fair and enjoyable to play, and have significantly more replayable content as well.

On first glance it looks like a total bro game, but there's actually a surprisingly sophisticated and rewarding story benath it all.

Spec Ops is a cover-based shooting is fairly standard, the headshots are traditional head-exploding fun, and the "team" element is even a bit lackluster, your regenerative health is just the screen turning gradually more bloody, and even the scenery is pretty standard for this day and age; a middle eastern city (Dubai) filled with sand and cityscape.
So why is it positive?
The story. The story of Spec Ops redeems every flaws, or generic gameplay mechanics. Every step in Spec Ops drags you deeper down this dark, horrific look at what war REALLY is to soldiers, what it does to the common man, and leaves you begging for some happy conclusion that can wrap it up with cheer, smiles and some "the end justifies the means" message. You won't ever get that message.
I'd recommend this game to every pro-war fanatic waiting for World War 3 to start, so they can get a glimpse of the brutality and horror that it really is.

This is probably the pinacle of bad ideas in the gaming industry.
I loved Blood Money and enjoyed Absolution but I cannot support a game that releases, episodic or not, as $60 with so little content.
I am very hesitent to buy 'early-access' games on Steam these days as many of the developers have decided to abandon their titles before completion as the game's sales have already peaked.
This HITMAN feels as though a AAA game studio saw the work vs reward of many early-access games and decided they should try it as well.
Basically, you buy the game and must trust that the developer will not only finish it, but finish it in a satisfying manner. What prevents the studio from not finishing this series? What prevents them from phoning in the rest of the episodes?
While I knew of the 'episodes' when I purchased the $60 version I still think the game borders into some grey areas of ethics. The videos shown above show a much more finished product which many, like myself, thought would be a part of the first episode.
75% of the content in the first episode is dull and uninspiring anyway. The fashion show mission called Showstopper is much nicer but still felt unentertaining to me. I swore I heard the words 'open world' somewhere in marketting before this came out and the levels feel very small to me. Maybe the square footage of the Showstopper is larger than some, but it felt clostrophic. I think of a large spanning room where the ceilings are only 4ft high.
Lastly, while I'm sure some enjoy it, I can't help but feel that the completionist mindset of the game is lazy. Many things within the game, all replays of the same missions mind you, are locked unless you complete challenges. These challenges are things like "Kill this person wearing this uniform in this fashion". I feel like they're trying to capture the essense of Blood Money but instead of giving the freedom of Blood Money they force the player. Do this Agent 47. Ok. Now do this.
I'm not sure if I can explain it better than that, but I had no interest in listening to the game.
I just cannot approve of this new direction the franchise is taking. I have no interest in it. I think it's dangerous to customers as well. It feels like a family member asking for money. That they'll pay you back later. In an undefined time frame. With money they're betting on making. From the money they borrowed from you.
No uncle 47- please stop.
EDIT: On a positive note, I received a refund from Steam for this game. I'm pleasantly surprised they refunded me but felt it was worth mentioning. It was not only refunded in full, but the very next day. Thumbs up to Steam.

There's a lot to like about this game, equally it still has room for improvement, but overall I'd recommend it in its current state for the price. If you've ever played EVE, you will immediately see the attraction of an "offline mode" style game, that you can pause when the pizza guy comes or save before doing something stupid.
Things I really like.
* The universe is already pretty big, lots of places to explore but the game has features like wormholes, JumpGate networks and TeleportDrives to get you around faster than full speed ahead into one direction.
* Ships look cool, there is a good variety of designs and varied configurations already, Its obvious there will be more to come.
* Great maneuverability of the ship, it's the type of piloting I really wished EVE had, you can really out maneuver a lot damage if you get good at it allowing you to take out larger ships that claim to be "impossible".
* Shielded sides, you don't fly around in a "bubble" shield like most games, each side of your ship has emitters and if one side is busted you're taking hull damage! That really fits my play style of focused attack. I hope that later one you can divert power to bolster one side or the other depending on where you are taking the most damage.
* You can board other ships with what amounts to raiding parties and fight their crew, if you manage to take them down, you can grapple their ship and tow it (painfully slowly) back to a station and sell it or use it as your own. This will be a good source of income if it didn't take ages to get a ship back to station. I'd suggest adding a towtruck style ship that we can come back with or something and get it there much faster, just let us bookmark the spot and return would be fine.
Areas in need of improvement
* I guess its the pilot's radar, but its way too small to be useful and you can't zoom-in, you can tell if there are enemies in the area the same as if there are friendlies, but it's hard to gauge you're position or distance from them without "looking out your window" by turning your ship or the camera. I'd prefer more thought into that, it needs to be bigger and zoom able and a lot more detailed about what each tiny blimp is. For example, you can drop a ZETH which is basicly an automated sentry fixed in space, but if you fly too far from it you may never find it again and its not cheap. I frequently lose mine if there are NPC friendlys around because it's impossible to tell what anything is.
* Stations need to be able to attack, I love the warnings that tell me any enemy station is nearby, so the first time I heard that I saved the game and flew right at one, but nothing happened, I think they should start firing some lasers if enemy craft turn up.
*Needs more ship system customization and I think this is already on the way based on some of the anomaly scans I've done, cause you need jamming, ECM, shield boosters, etc. The ability to vary your ship should be based on more than just what skills you're pilot has, not to keep bringing up EVE but there's a lot to take for example there.

Visually the game scores 9/10    Just beautiful!
Soundtrack 9/10      Really great soundtrack.
Storyline 6/10     Story was OK, I just didn’t get into it. Just dialogue, no character cut scenes at all.
Voice acting 6/10  Some were hilarious they were so bad.
Gameplay 8/10  Some solid gameplay mechanics, easy to get into but hard to master.
Replay ability 9/10  I got my money’s worth just playing the Beta early access!
General Content 9/10  Some real quality ships, gear, missions, bounties, capture ship gameplay etc…
LGM Dev’s 10/10 Never come across such a great team working so hard with so little.
I just finished the story mode… overall I enjoyed it, I’ve still got a few high bounties to go after and I haven’t explored all of the map. The game as far as the DEV’s are concerned isn’t finished they have a big wish list of features they still hope to implement and honestly I can’t wait.
Starpoint Gemini 2 easily makes it into my top 10 space sim games and if you’e looking for something to fill the void while we wait for Star Citizen, Elite Dangerous etc Just get it already.

**no spoilers here** Overall this is an excellent game, but the ending was really an injustice to the open world and role playing concepts.  I give the game a 9 out of 10, before a 3 point penalty for the ending, making this game a 6 out of 10. On the good side, it brings several concepts into the open gaming world that were either non-existant or were for purely visual purposes.  In this game you impact the frequency of respawn by reducing the enemies control over areas, and are able to have facilities you clear be held by allies.  Bear in mind these "allies" don't do much in terms of returning the favor (you're not going to see allied vehicles driving around out there or get any support when attacking a facility), but its a good incremental step forward in the genre. Additionally the weather affect is much improved in this game where the weather can actually be dangerous and is something the player has to take into account rather than just seeing a visual change of "oh its raining, back to the slaughter". As for the ending, it is very forced and uncharacteristic of both the character of Mad Max who despite surviving in the wastes maintains an honorable character, and leaves no room for the player to have a choice (an anti-role playing move on the developers who apparently wanted to finish the story on their terms. For sake of example, I would say it was the opposite of how Fallout New Vegas ended where the player's choices determined the future).
On the off chance a developer bothers to read this, there is a certain point in the game where the player could (IMO should) have been given a series of choices to choose from to create their own ending. Chances of my buying another Mad Max game is 50/50.... it will depend on the reviews by players, not critics.

It really is that good, but it's definitely NOT for the faint of heart. Forget missiles and drive-bys in Call of Duty; you don't know the real terrors of war until you've played this game.
Unless you've actually been in the military. In that case, kudos to you.
But on a serious note, this game takes run-of-the-mill shooters like Battlefield and Medal of Honor and flips them on their heads. In those games, the more baddies you kill, the cooler you are and less Communism/Terrorism gets spread around. In Spec Ops: The Line, nobody 'wins'. There are no good choices, only bad and worse. Your standard "choose who you're going to save"s are still there, but the game takes it a step further with truly harrowing decisions that feel like they greatly matter. Relatively original colony simulator concept with random generated game world, gas and fluid physics & more. It's still in early development but is actively developed in seems to have a great future ahead. Another great game design by Klei.

Edit: I had originally equated Klei to Darkest Dungeon. Darkest Dungeon is actually made by Red Hook Studios. From what I gather, Klei didn't work on the game, but there is some association with Red Hook. Regardless, my review still stands.
Klei has built up quite a bit of good will with me. Don't Starve, and Darkest Dungeons were two titles that I enjoyed immensely. So when Oxygen Not Inlcuded was first announced, it had my curiosity. Like many others here, I opted to pay full price for the Early Access. Not only that, but I went through the process of going through there forums (before they made it available to pre-purchase through Steam) to sign up for Early Access.
Why have I told you all this and not even mentioned the game? It's to provide you context on my positive favor in the review.
Let's get to the nitty gritty.
As with any Klei game they're not hardware intensive, and they look fantastic. This company has a thing about creating stunning visuals with basic 2D art. The duplicants are bubbly, and cheerful looking, and the "planet/asteroid" is diverse in it's color palette.
The overlays provide a sharp contrast of varied colors, and allow for you to easily view different aspects of your base.
The music is cheerful, and engaging, while the sound effects that your duplicant make are adorable, and interesting.  I've got no real complaints on this field.
Here's the mixed bag. The game at it's core is a management simulation. You've got to manage your Oxygen, Food, and Water to keep your duplicants alive. As you progress with harvesting more resources to maintain the above three items, you'll notice that you're rapidly running low. Resources are finite, which lead you to enter other biomes to get new resources, and these new resources may have negative consequences. Example: early on you build a device that eats algae for oxygen. Once you run out of algae, you can then build a machine that turns slime into algae, but produces polluted water. So you now have algae to make oxygen, but you now need a system to remove the polluted water. This is one example of compounding issues that will continue to grow.  There is a very in depth plumbing, power, happiness, cleanliness, and ventilation system in the game as well.
If you enjoy such management style games, this is a very good one, and very enjoyable. I've been told by friends, the style is akin to Dwarf Fortress (though not as complex and unforgiving.)
If you browse videos on YouTube, you'll see some high end players who have created near perfect self contained systems for their duplicants. Please understand, these people are really skilled at the game; for most players, getting a stable colony will be a challenge.
I know it's Early Access, but as it stands, the following applies. Let's put it simply. There is no tutorial. Casual, or new players to the genre will have a very steep learning curve. You can always ask for help on the forums, or Reddit, but that's extracurricular activities. A game should have a good tutorial to help guide folks into the game.
There is no story. If you're not the type to enjoy creating a self contained colony for it's own sake. There is not much motivation right now to explore, or keep going. Klei has indicated there will be lore style items added to the world, but right now there is no overall history. or back story to engage you with your cute duplicants. There expendable, and the only story they have is one that you give them.
If you enjoy an overarching goal, or direction laid out for you to uncover, or follow; you won't find it here. For some people, this is a big deal.
Nowhere near addicting enough therefore only gets 11/10.

Starpoint Gemini 2 is a sandbox spacegame.
For now it is only about freelancing, while a story line will be added later on.
You can earn your money from various random missions, mining, trading, fighting (loot) and capturing ships.
The game has two huge issues:
- the game mechanics
- the balance
While the balance will most likely be adjusted later on, for now it is just wrong. And i am not talking about the strength balance but about balancing cargo size to item numbers etc. Sell values, ship size to speed and distance etc etc.
Examples:
When mining you need about 5 seconds to fill up your entire cargo hold. So you spent at least 95% of your time flying to the asteroid belt and back to the station to sell stuff, this makes mining insanly boring. The same goes for fighting and selling loot.
After capturing a ship you need to fly it to a station, again, the capture process is a few seconds, the way to the station can be several minutes  depending on where you fought the ship.
Every way of earning money feels like a boring grind.
The game mechanics are a mess as well.
Ships always have the same amount of turret mounts. Larger ships wont have larger weapons. So in the end, no matter how large your ship is, you will still use the exact same weapons you used on your starting ship. Additionally the larger ships are barely any stronger, they only have higher defensive stats.
There is barely any feeling of progression during the game.
All your weapons are turrets and each of them is only facing one side of the ship. So you got front rear and side turrets. Trying to manually fire them will result in only 1/4 of the turrets shooting. On close range projectiles wont hit, thanks to the point of view that makes it impossible to aim. On long range you wont hit anything as well, thanks to the relations between ship size, speed and weapon range. You can only manually aim at mid range.
So after all the full fighting system is "get into range, hit auto fire, wait for everything to be dead".
There is no depth in the fighting system at all. There is no chasing or trying to position yourself etc.
While the map is huge, there is no point to ever explore it, as you get everything in the spawn system. Maybe later on the story line will force you to move around, but "freelancing" means you stay at the spawn station and barely move around.
There is a skill system, that allows you to level and use skills during combat. As a figher you have 4 skills. After activating a skill it grants you a passive bonus to one weapon type for a certain amount of time. Obviously you will only level and use one skill. So the full skill system is only about hitting one button before combat and then wait until auto fire has killed everything.
Once again this system has no depth at all.
Finally:
I know that the game is in early access and not finished, still the game mechanics, meaning the stuff that IS finished, is really bad and not working well. None of the game mechanics has any depth.
After playing games like privateer, freelancer (and basically all other space games of the last 20 years) i cannot recommend buying this game, for now.
However, the devs of SPG2 are interacting a lot with the community.
So i hope that the game will improve a lot during the developement and i will update my review when this happens.

been playing only a few hour but am already finding this game a very enjoyable experience; keep up the great work...

First off I want to say I am really enjoying the game.  Unlike some space games, most things are strait forward, and I don’t feel the need for a spreadsheet full of stats just to progress in the game.  SPG2 does this rather well without feeling like its dumbing anything down.  It really feels like a modern take on Freelancer, which I thought was a fun game as well.
The progression through the different levels is strait forward, but at the same time your profession choice seems to be inconsequential.  I wish you were given the profession choice after your first level up, so you could see what play style you actually preferred before making the permeate commitment.
The camera movement is a bit wonky with no real free look option.  Instead you have a sluggish turret cam that you can manually aim your guns with. Ironically I rarely use to aim since my guns work much better on auto-fire, so I just use it to look around.
The fire arcs for the guns are a neat gameplay mechanic but their representation in 3d space and on the 2d stats are hard to visualize. Often I think I should be hitting an enemy when I turn my camera to find out they are actually below me and outside my firing range since I don’t have a gun down there.
There is a wide variety of ships and weapons in the game, but you are left up to your own exploring to find out what they are and where they are sold. This seems a bit odd to me since the market place has a great mechanic to show you what, and where the best prices for trade commodities are, but none for ships and weapons?
The universe is large and has a good feel to it without feeling like your traveling through light-years of nothingness.  Every once and a while during PTE (Power -To-Engines) an enemy ship will drop out and take a shot at you or you will see an anomaly to scan and many other random events.  This adds a lot of fun and excitement to traveling that many games turn in to pain wrenching boredom just for the sake of realism.
You have plenty of choice as to how you would like to play, pirate, enforcer, trader, miner or just the storyline.  The missions are varied and while there is the occasional grind it is rare and in no way feels necessary for progression.  Also with a large universe there is plenty of places to explore and room for several playthroughs without getting old.
To sum it up I think it’s a great game that has a lot of replay potential.   So if you like the space game genre and would like a fun, non-hardcore game to jump in to, Starpont Gemini 2 is awesome choice.

**no spoilers here** Overall this is an excellent game, but the ending was really an injustice to the open world and role playing concepts.  I give the game a 9 out of 10, before a 3 point penalty for the ending, making this game a 6 out of 10. On the good side, it brings several concepts into the open gaming world that were either non-existant or were for purely visual purposes.  In this game you impact the frequency of respawn by reducing the enemies control over areas, and are able to have facilities you clear be held by allies.  Bear in mind these "allies" don't do much in terms of returning the favor (you're not going to see allied vehicles driving around out there or get any support when attacking a facility), but its a good incremental step forward in the genre. Additionally the weather affect is much improved in this game where the weather can actually be dangerous and is something the player has to take into account rather than just seeing a visual change of "oh its raining, back to the slaughter". As for the ending, it is very forced and uncharacteristic of both the character of Mad Max who despite surviving in the wastes maintains an honorable character, and leaves no room for the player to have a choice (an anti-role playing move on the developers who apparently wanted to finish the story on their terms. For sake of example, I would say it was the opposite of how Fallout New Vegas ended where the player's choices determined the future).
On the off chance a developer bothers to read this, there is a certain point in the game where the player could (IMO should) have been given a series of choices to choose from to create their own ending. Chances of my buying another Mad Max game is 50/50.... it will depend on the reviews by players, not critics.

The best possible way to experience 'Spec Ops: The Line' is to go into it thinking that it's just another run-of-the-mill modern warfare 'Call of Duty' clone.
That's how I first played it, and boy did it blow my mind wide open as it progressed. By the end I knew I would be picking it up again and again. I swear by my love (predominantly) for the 'Metal Gear' series, but as a stand alone title, 'The Line' is by far the most engaging, complex, and well-crafted game I've ever encountered.
I won't give a synopsis of the title's story (astonishing as it is), I'll leave that for you to discover at your leisure, but I will say that 'The Line' is both a visual as well as a psychological marvel. On the highest setting, the graphics are incredible -- the dead ruins of the city of Dubai are brought to life in a breathtaking array of colors and detail. However, from a gameplay standpoint, 'The Line' may lose some people: controls seem copy/pasted out of any generic third-person shooter and can seem slightly unresponsive at times. If you're a fan of simplistic gameplay, you'll be satisfied, but that's not to say the game isn't challenging (especially on FUBAR difficulty). On the subject of sound design, 'The Line' shines again, featuring stellar voice acting from the likes of Nolan North ('The Line' is his best performance, in my opinion), haunting music from popular artists as well as a brilliant original score, and finely tuned sound effects such as gunfire and explosions that will thunder through your speakers/headphones.
I would recommend 'Spec Ops: The Line' to anybody who is ready for a mature story regarding the psychological effects of war on soldiers and what it means to be a "strong man".    10/10

+ skill/progression tree

- keyboard gameplay is suboptimal

There is a story in this game - you and your heirs have to fight a traitor and his minions to avenge the old king and destroy the fountain of youth. But the real massive appeal here is a great progression system where each run counts (as long as you were at least decent in it and collected enough gold) and you can level up your next character/heir. This level up is done through a cool unlockable skill tree. There is a permadeath element for each character and you WILL die a lot. But that is okay, it still is fun to try different traits in characters and along with random dungeon generation it makes each attempt special. You can customize the way you play not only by picking an available class but also by buying armor, weapons and runes to fit your style. **no spoilers here** Overall this is an excellent game, but the ending was really an injustice to the open world and role playing concepts.  I give the game a 9 out of 10, before a 3 point penalty for the ending, making this game a 6 out of 10. On the good side, it brings several concepts into the open gaming world that were either non-existant or were for purely visual purposes.  In this game you impact the frequency of respawn by reducing the enemies control over areas, and are able to have facilities you clear be held by allies.  Bear in mind these "allies" don't do much in terms of returning the favor (you're not going to see allied vehicles driving around out there or get any support when attacking a facility), but its a good incremental step forward in the genre. Additionally the weather affect is much improved in this game where the weather can actually be dangerous and is something the player has to take into account rather than just seeing a visual change of "oh its raining, back to the slaughter". As for the ending, it is very forced and uncharacteristic of both the character of Mad Max who despite surviving in the wastes maintains an honorable character, and leaves no room for the player to have a choice (an anti-role playing move on the developers who apparently wanted to finish the story on their terms. For sake of example, I would say it was the opposite of how Fallout New Vegas ended where the player's choices determined the future).
On the off chance a developer bothers to read this, there is a certain point in the game where the player could (IMO should) have been given a series of choices to choose from to create their own ending. Chances of my buying another Mad Max game is 50/50.... it will depend on the reviews by players, not critics.

Mad Max basically every other open world action adventure game only less guns and more punching and centered mostly around cars.
The story is one of the better types of story telling and world building where they give you a bunch of dots through dialogue or enviormental set pieces or whatever and have you fill the gaps to draw out your own conclusion on what the ♥♥♥♥ is going on not only where you currently are but also how the ♥♥♥♥ did all this come to be in the first place. This is good because it helps players get more involved in the world while giving the players that are playing purely for the action to just dismiss it and get to the fun bits with the barebones alone.
To sum up the story without spoiling it, the world is ♥♥♥♥ed and the people still alive only care about being able to live another day or at least dying of lead to the face than dehydration which sets the tone of how brutal the world has become. You play as Mad Max (obviously), one of the few people that lived long enough to see the world for what it was before turned into sand and dirt, and your only reason for living is just to live. ♥♥♥♥ companionship or entertainment. ♥♥♥♥ fame and glory. ♥♥♥♥ power and control. ♥♥♥♥ pleasure and pain. All you care about is one thing: Survival. And you're so good at it that you're considered a legend to everyone who has ears and a voice. There are no allies in this new world of you. Just people to be tools to increase your chances of survival and for you to be a tool yourself in exchange.
When it comes to the mechanics of the game, it's as sandbox as sandbox can get. Raid camps, help locals, look for items, and all this so you can upgrade your weapons and equipment and getting♥♥♥♥♥♥to make the game somewhat easier. There are a few things here and there that I haven't seen much in other sandbox games like getting rid of a random sniper somewhere on the map or defusing landmines. But these are just as repetative as the other 100% completionist♥♥♥♥♥♥ The only uniqueness of the game I've seen so far in this aspect is the "Survival" part of the game where a lot of things that are usually dropped and found like health pickups and ammo are severely limited. If you're low on health, no regenerating to the closest line on a health bar. You gotta find food which is usually in rare places or drink water which is somewhat easier to find but you can't drink with one hand and throw a punch with the other. You gotta stand there and drink water. And if you go into a fight without filling your canteen, you better make those timed blocks counter because you'll be ♥♥♥♥ed. Or your corpse will be afterwards. This is the postapocalypse, after all.
The combat is somewhat refreshing as it's more about beating people into submission with your bare hands than shooting everything. But it's nothing new. Pretty much a type of Arkham Asylum beat'em up with punching, blocking, rolling, ground or dazed one hit kill animation, yada yada yada with regular, fast, heavy, and buffing type enemies. It's still fun though. Mostly cause it becomes a fluid ballet of blood, teeth, and bone fragments like someone breakdancing in a crowd with very loose and sharp metal bits on their clothes.
As for the graphics, they are well done... For a game with a world mostly made up of dirty and sand. Jedi academy uses the same engine and builds off the story of its predecessor.  However this time around you aren’t playing as Kyle Katarn but as Jaden Korr.  A both gender and species neutral name that allows for character customization.  Something that they took as a integral part of the creating of this game.  You can choose your species, gender, outfit, lightsaber hilt, and blade color.  And given the time period, this was a very new thing for a game like this.
The story starts off great, and fully to what I would expect.  It was nice to be able to choose the missions performed and the order of them.  As well as being able to skip the last one and move the story on to the next plot point.  Of course doing so would effect your characters powers, since you are taking away the chance to level up a Force power.  Its a definite give and take, and I opted to take the short route more often then otherwise.
While the story does start off strong, it quickly weakens, and all but falls to the floor.  The idea that a cult of dark Force users are draining the force energies from different locations across the galaxy.  It has so many holes its just ridiculous, and I haven’t even gotten into the details of it.  But the worst part of the story, is the blatant teenager fantasy.  Its a story that was written for angsty teenagers looking for something to connect to.  It also screams predictability from the first scripted sequence to the last.  You don’t need to be a, well anything, to figure out what’s going to happen next.
There are some locations that felt like they were thrown into the game as a ‘Hey look, where you get to go!”.  And after I played and did a little research I discovered  that’s exactly why they added the location!  Tatooine, Hoth, and even a Rancor and Chewbacca are all there just so they can say they are there.  Taking a thing, and writing a story around it is never a good idea.  And here they have done it four times inside the main story arc.  They only thing that helps this is the way the missions are offered as single objectives that aren’t integral to the plot.
Getting away from the story and focusing on some of the better aspects of the game, like the gameplay.  The lightsaber combat was acceptable at most.  Maybe its just me, but it was also laughable.  There is a move set you can work with, or you can be like me and and just click M1 like a manic and hope for the best.  Button combos have never been my strong point, with only succeeding at them with a handful of games.  And Jedi Knight: Jedi Academy was not one of them.  Sometimes in my rapid clicking I would preform some random move, surprising even myself, before going back to my standard slashing.
I have a problem with games that use lightsabers, because they always weaken them.  A lightsaber doesn’t cut through anything like a hot knife through butter.  But it will do this with most things.  I can forgive a games engine not allowing me to cut the railings off of a scaffolding.  But one swing on a Stormtrooper should be all that’s needed to remove that Trooper as obstacle, one swing.  Unless it is wielding a lightsaber to block the attack or is armored with Cortosis, one hit.
He called it a “laser sword”…  Seriously at one point there was a short scripted sequence where a thug or Stormtrooper or somebody used the phrase ‘laser sword’.  I about turned the game off there.
The AI has its moments of udder fail.  Things like Stormies just standing there and shooting you as you walk right up to them and cut them down.  There are also mission where you are followed by a companion, and often times they show you just how much they love to fall into pits.  I swear Kyle spent more time at the bottom of a shaft than actually helping me.  All the while making comments about how hes ‘got this one’.  It just became a joke, and I had all but forgotten he was a part of the level.
The game ends almost as predictably as it progressed, and just as predicted I didn’t really care.  I was just happy to be done with another game, and ready to move onto something else.  Not as well rounded a game as Jedi Outcast was, but better then the rest of the series.

Spec Ops: The Line is a Third Person Shooter that's focused around story rather than gameplay.
This game has a pretty unique blip on my radar, and for good reasons. Simply, all I can say is the story alone is worth purchasing this game. The basic premise is about three Delta operators: Adams, Lugo, and Walker. They were sent out on a mission to rescue any survivors found in the desolated sand-wasteland of Dubai. You play as Walker, leading your squad to carry it out.
Now this doesn't sound like a complex plot, it sounds incredibly simple, even. But the whole undertone of the story is what it's all about. Without giving away too much, Walker has the good intentions of saving all the civillians he can, and eliminating all evil that walk around them. However, it gets very psychological and personal, as Walker, and you, realize that the choices you thought were justified and well, turns out to be the exact opposite of what they are. It mentally breaks Walker down, trying to lead with his mind intact, trying to figure out good from evil, what he's doing right and wrong. The choices you make, sometimes there's never a good choice, it could be a lesser of two evils, but that's not saying much. War is hell, and sometimes, your best isn't enough. This is what the entire game is focused on: this, and the deeper meaning. It's truly an engrossing story that will leave you wanting more. I promise you won't regret it.
The gameplay is less spectacular, it's your standard cover-and-shoot type. It's pretty textbook if you wanna look at it that way, as there isn't much to do besides... Well, cover and shoot, but there is a good amount of different weapons to use. One thing I do like though is that battles take place in lots of locations, the desolate presentation of Dubai is very immersive and nice to look at, so you can be doing close quarters battle in a broken building, fighting on a large battlefield, or snipe from across buildings. The varying locations do mix up gameplay a little bit, but it's still rather basic. It does work however, and it is still fun, just nothing really pops out.
The game isn't too long, it could take you about 4-5 hours to finish the campaign. However if you wanna play the story again but with different choices, you can probably clock in another 3 if you skip cutscenes.
Multiplayer is there, but this game has a very low population, I doubt you'll find anyone, so I can't give off my impression there.
There is a Co-Op mode where you can play the campaign with a friend, who plays as either Lugo or Adams. That's very fun and it works pretty well. If you got someone to play with and wanna enjoy the story together, that brings up something fun to do as well.
Overall, Spec Ops is an amazing game with a deep, enriching plot that is sure to leave a lasting impression on you, that's what it's all about, even if the gameplay is pretty textbook stuff, and the short length. However, you won't regret buying this, I recommend it.

This is a game which carries a very strong message. While other shooters glorify war through depiction of war heroes and other heroic acts, this is a reminder to all of us about the horrors of war. There are no war heroes in this game, nor heroic acts. All the scenes in this game were probably meant to show the disgusting truth of war, such as (might carry spoilers) abuse of civilian hostages, liberal use of inhumane weapons (White Phosporus mortar), progressive mental deterioration (in the first missions one of the characters took the matter lightly by slipping humor, as the story progresses he starts to feel weary and scarred), and general feelings of distrust, hate, guilt, and anger.
While the story and narrative of the game carries a strong message to the audience, the game fell short on its controls. Controls in this game might feel odd (spacebar for sprinting, what?) which may confuse gamers who are accustomed to WASD for movement and SHIFT for sprint. Multiplayer might also not the game's shining star.
In the end, Spec Ops: The Line is a third person shooter game that excels on dark narrative and storytelling, despite falling short to odd controls and multiplayer. I strongly recommend the singleplayer for its gritty and engaging story.

Spec Ops: The Line gets a little to much praise for my liking, but that doesn't and didn't stop me from realizing how great of a game it is and really enjoying myself as I went through it. There is a bit to much flattery thrown at the game with it being called unique when it really isn't that unique even within the videogame industry. This wasn't the first time civilians are killed in a videogame, or the first time Americans as cast as the enemy and it isn't the first time war crimes are acknowledged. What is unique though is the massive effort put in to give the player a strong sense of ownership over the matter that is complemented by a development philosophy that ensured even the tiniest of details in the background pushed that agenda forward. Spec Ops might be a competently designed shooter at best and I may think that people see it as having more artistic value than I do, but that doesn't stop it from being a great overall game with a strong narrative and commitment to its theme. That alone sets it apart from most games in its genre and the reason that I recommend that you play this it sooner rather than later.
If you want to read a bit more about what I thought of the game, all of which is mostly spoiler free you can have a look over here on my blog:
.

If you think this is just another military shooter like CS:GO or Call of Duty, you couldn't be more wrong. You owe it to yourself to read this review and others like it :)
People who know me, know that on first blush "Spec Ops: The Line" is not my kind of game.  This game sat in my library for a long time collecting dust.  I am not sure what prompted me to load it up and give it a try....but will I be forever grateful that I did.
There are parts of this game that will stick with me for years to come.  To suggest that this is mearly a game would be an injustice; it is a masterpiece.  It is a well-crafted story that took me places I never wanted to go, and will never forget.  Like Oliver Stone's Platoon, it's a powerful story with a strong narrative and superb voice acting that must be experienced to be understood.  To go into any more detail, would be giving away too much.
If you don't own this game; buy it.  If you have this game sitting in your library; play it. And tell everyone you know to do the same.

After only playing the game for 6 hours so far I can give an idication to what the game is like, and whether it is a good buy, but I am not yet able to fully evaluate all of the mechanics and features.
So far out of the 4 colonies which I have attempted, only 1 has managed to survive, this is due to one mechanic. Carbon dioxide. No matter what I seemed to do it would always take over the entirety of my base and suffocate all of the duplicants (a duplicant being one of the characters inside of your base). I have now became aware of the system which gasses use, they all have different densities, which makes it much easier to manage the problem since digging a tunnel downwards causes the carbon dioxide to also go downward since it is more dense than oxygen. This is just one example of the difficulty of the game, since the initial planning of your base requires practice and thought, otherwise it can quickly turn disasterous.
The game progresses through a variety of reaserch tasks, this is sort of like a skill tree in other games where you select an area of research and a duplicant uses either a super computer or a research machine to unlock the new items in that catagory. There are two types of reasech, basic and advanced. The basic research can be done on the research machine whereas the advanced research requires the super computer. Doing reaserch is an essential mechanism to allow the game to progress, since the early items you unlock through basic research and are given recipies for at the start become less useful later on in the game, as the reosurces which they use start to deplete. This means alternative methods ans systems need to be established to make a sustainable colony.  This helps to maintain intrest in the game, as it is not as easy as just establishing a colony and thats it, there are always more items to unlock to replace the obsolete older ones.
Overall with my excperience so far this game is very good and is worthwhile buying, it is in early access so you will have to tolerate bugs and having to start a new save once a update comes out, although this just means the game will continue to get better, which is very promising.

I have not enjoyed an early access game this much since Minecraft went viral when it was in alpha. it took me a few attempts before I really figured out how to approach things, because even in this early state there is a hell of a lot going on, but it was absolutely worth the effort to figure it out.
the more I play this game, the more I love it. it's like Terraria, Don't Starve and The Sims, with the added horror of asphyxiating in the chilling void of space. and of drowning in your own♥♥♥♥♥♥ vomit and stress-induced psychosis.
Klei have once again delivered their trademark stylish pathos-drenched survival crafting, in a new and engaging setting, with a base-building and system engineering twist which appeals hugely to me on a number of levels. I really hope they manage to keep the game working as well as it does now; the odd UX rough-edge aside, it's extremely playable as-is and has remarkable depth, I almost fear that adding too much might end up taking away from it.

I highly recommend this game, though I think currently (June 2017) it's a game that you can wait to play.
If you've played Don't Starve, this has a similar art style and feel to the game, which makes a lot of sense coming from the same developer.
As a sandbox survival basebuilder, it plays pretty well. You have a number of challenges built into the game to overcome as your base expands. The challenges become fairly complicated as the game goes and your population grows. I feel currently that you are kind of forced into only a few solutions to the challenges late game, which partially comes from getting the game balance right, and partially comes from adding content (which they have been doing).
This review may sound a little mixed, but it's not. As I said, I highly recommend this game. The caveat is that if you buy it now, you get the game with the review as I wrote it. Six months from now, I'm pretty sure my review will have changed completely (for the better). So, I don't think there's a need to rush into buying this game (though, if you see it on sale, I'd snap it up, because even now it is worth the $20), but if you buy it now, I don't think you'll regret it.

[Disclaimer: this review is for the content made available in the "Season Premiere" which includes the prologue and Paris fashion show levels]
After sufficiently playing the "Season Premiere" content for Hitman, I feel confident in sharing my opinion about this beautiful mess of a game.  For starters, the bad.  This game runs like a** even on high powered builds.  From my perusal of the forums, it seems like any and all 900 series Nvidia cards aren't running this game well.  Whether this will be patched to improve performance remains to be seen.  I also keep getting this persistent bug where, when starting the Paris level, the game freezes and I have to change a random graphics setting, up or down believe it or not, and the game runs like normal.  I do not know what the deal is with this bug since it hinges on me turning up or down the graphics.  Next, the always online component.  I do not understand why Hitman, an exclusively single player game, relys on an online functionality and if you're unlucky enough to lose your internet connection midway through a level, the game screws you over, sends you back to the main menu without any way to continue your "online" save until your connection is restored.  That is infuriating and unforgivable.  Sure, make the "contracts" mode unavailable when you're online but why completely force you to quit your game?  I hope this is addressed in future patches since, as time has shown, always online never works with games.
If you've stuck with me after that arduous paragraph, you're probably wondering why, after all of that, are you still recommending this game?  Because I love it.  As a long time fan of the series, I was disappointed in the linear structure of Absolution and the lack of freedom that game presented with its "assassination" missions.  Hitman 2016 is, so far, a return to form for the series, combining the great open sandbox structure of Blood Money with the fluid handling of Absolution to form what I expect will be the best Hitman game to date.  That accolade, however, can not be handed out just yet as it will be a half year before the full game is actually available to the public.  While I am not a huge fan of the episodic release plan of the game, there's no denying that the Hitman formula lends itself well to that release schedule, offering vastly different missions that take place all over the world.  This also allows for us players to take a more active role in the development of the game as IO will be able to get feedback while in the process of constructing the rest of the game.  That being said, you are still essentially paying for an as of now, unfished product.
So, if you're a fan of the Hitman series, this is an easy recommend just bear in mind that the game is not well optimized and in need of some decent patches and bugfixes.  If you're new to the series, I'd recommend trying the $15 option and the majority of the content available for that price can be completed under the 2 hour refund limit if you don't find it to your liking.

HITMAN™ as a game is quite refreshing in my eyes. It has improved upon its predecessor, Absolution, and in turn took elements from older games, namely Blood Money to please fans and give a greater gameplay experience.
In turn, you are able to explore your level, choose how you want to kill, how you want to look and how you want to approach your target, or targets. You can choose from a great variety of weapons inside a level, ranging from screwdrivers to lethal syringes, fire axes, various pistols and even rifles and shotguns in some cases.
The only level in the intro pack is the Showstopper level, which is disappointing, but already nice in its own right. The graphics in this game are stunning, of course, and despite people disliking 47's new appearance, I'm content with it as it doesn't necessarily matter.
Do you remember how he looked like in Hitman: Silent Assassin™? It was an abomination. An inflatable balloon, more like.
You can as always disguise yourself, and instead of an action bar to choose your weapons from, it returns to the weapon wheel in a Blood Money style fashion.
The episodic model is overall disappointing if not annoying, but I can safely say that under the circumstances of the company, it's understandable. IO Interactive had lost a lot of money and needed to make some in turn to avoid being closed down or laid off by Square Enix, and the game itself seems very promising as well.
However, not every game is perfect. HITMAN™ suffers from various performance problems, even on my machine, lowering my FPS to >30 in crowds, specifically in the Paris level. I hope IO makes an optimization patch in the near future.
The gameplay can be tedious as well, as sometimes the characters make one cycle onto an area that can be used to kill them, I.E. the showstage in Paris, only to never return or return in perhaps 10-20 minutes.
However, I think the game should still be played assuming you can do so. I suggest you have a good machine, as older machines probably lag like sin.
