Jedi academy uses the same engine and builds off the story of its predecessor.  However this time around you aren’t playing as Kyle Katarn but as Jaden Korr.  A both gender and species neutral name that allows for character customization.  Something that they took as a integral part of the creating of this game.  You can choose your species, gender, outfit, lightsaber hilt, and blade color.  And given the time period, this was a very new thing for a game like this.
The story starts off great, and fully to what I would expect.  It was nice to be able to choose the missions performed and the order of them.  As well as being able to skip the last one and move the story on to the next plot point.  Of course doing so would effect your characters powers, since you are taking away the chance to level up a Force power.  Its a definite give and take, and I opted to take the short route more often then otherwise.
While the story does start off strong, it quickly weakens, and all but falls to the floor.  The idea that a cult of dark Force users are draining the force energies from different locations across the galaxy.  It has so many holes its just ridiculous, and I haven’t even gotten into the details of it.  But the worst part of the story, is the blatant teenager fantasy.  Its a story that was written for angsty teenagers looking for something to connect to.  It also screams predictability from the first scripted sequence to the last.  You don’t need to be a, well anything, to figure out what’s going to happen next.
There are some locations that felt like they were thrown into the game as a ‘Hey look, where you get to go!”.  And after I played and did a little research I discovered  that’s exactly why they added the location!  Tatooine, Hoth, and even a Rancor and Chewbacca are all there just so they can say they are there.  Taking a thing, and writing a story around it is never a good idea.  And here they have done it four times inside the main story arc.  They only thing that helps this is the way the missions are offered as single objectives that aren’t integral to the plot.
Getting away from the story and focusing on some of the better aspects of the game, like the gameplay.  The lightsaber combat was acceptable at most.  Maybe its just me, but it was also laughable.  There is a move set you can work with, or you can be like me and and just click M1 like a manic and hope for the best.  Button combos have never been my strong point, with only succeeding at them with a handful of games.  And Jedi Knight: Jedi Academy was not one of them.  Sometimes in my rapid clicking I would preform some random move, surprising even myself, before going back to my standard slashing.
I have a problem with games that use lightsabers, because they always weaken them.  A lightsaber doesn’t cut through anything like a hot knife through butter.  But it will do this with most things.  I can forgive a games engine not allowing me to cut the railings off of a scaffolding.  But one swing on a Stormtrooper should be all that’s needed to remove that Trooper as obstacle, one swing.  Unless it is wielding a lightsaber to block the attack or is armored with Cortosis, one hit.
He called it a “laser sword”…  Seriously at one point there was a short scripted sequence where a thug or Stormtrooper or somebody used the phrase ‘laser sword’.  I about turned the game off there.
The AI has its moments of udder fail.  Things like Stormies just standing there and shooting you as you walk right up to them and cut them down.  There are also mission where you are followed by a companion, and often times they show you just how much they love to fall into pits.  I swear Kyle spent more time at the bottom of a shaft than actually helping me.  All the while making comments about how hes ‘got this one’.  It just became a joke, and I had all but forgotten he was a part of the level.
The game ends almost as predictably as it progressed, and just as predicted I didn’t really care.  I was just happy to be done with another game, and ready to move onto something else.  Not as well rounded a game as Jedi Outcast was, but better then the rest of the series.

---UPDATE---
This review was posted shortly after posting on the starpoint gemini 2 forum.
I have to say, the devs are absolutely awesome. I posted a post on their forum and within an hour I had a response by both email and on the forum by 2 different devs. I was asked to send them the log and dxdiag report, which i did.
By process of elimination they found that the autosave system had corrupted a save file causing the crash i was getting.
This is the first time I have had such a great fast response for a problem with a game.
10/10 for the devs!
--On to the game--
It's awesome! I have wanted to play space sims for ages since the first homeworld game, but there just wasn't anything on the market that hit exactly what I wanted. Having read a lot of reviews and watched some on youtube i decided to take the plunge on this... and boy am i glad i did, although i've only played an hour or 2 i can see myself being sucked into this world like i was with homeworld.
Graphically it looks beautiful and although i have not played many space games since homeworld i can say its the best iv seen on steam so far.
The audio is great! not to intrusive like many games of this kind, but not lacking so much that it gets boring.
At present the only option is freeroam which is exactly what I was after. Do what you want, when you want! Although when the campaign is added it will be a great bonus!
Mods! its available on the steam workshop! endless possibilities await avid modders! there isnt much on there at  the moment but i can see it blowing up pretty fast!
The ONLY thing i have against this game is the tutorial... or lack of one. being completely new to this type of game it would have been a little helpful for it to have some sort of single mission tutorial or something like that. At present it only offers lots of reading.... and if your like me, reading isnt the way you take things in. DOING is the way i find easiest to learn.
This is only a minor gripe i have to what i have to say is a superb game. one of my favourites this year so far! :D

I don't normally play space related games, nor did I play the first SP Gemini but I decided to give this one a chance based on what I saw and was pleasantly surprised.  Compared to other early access games I wasn't as disappointed as normal, in fact at this point this game could pass as an alpha.
As far as the gameplay this is more of a you against the galaxy type of deal, you fly a spaceship, you may have multiple garaged spaceships that you own but (somewhat like ace combat in a way) but it is 100% open*galaxy*.  Normal gameplay consists of going on randomized missions such as assassinate, ferry cargo/passengers, capture ships, smuggle counterfiet goods etc, you level up/rank up and have a skill tree/rank tree.
You may earn money through missions, trading, mining (asteroids and other such objects), plundering derelict ships, and the best is to find rare high level bounty ships which earn you considerable profits.  You spend your money on new ships, ship systems (weapons) and system upgrades.
Sorry for the long review but I tried to explain what I would have wanted to see before I bought it (well worth the money by the way!)

I haven't written a review in a while.  I have to tell you about this game.  For those of you looking for freelancer 2, well look no further.  What can I say about this game.  I am playing Beta version 0.8004, the release date is right around the corner.  The combat is fun and not too terribly difficult.  The number of ships is high, I think there are 70 purchasable ships available right now.  All ships are upgradeable and can be customized with paint, ship name, custom logos as well.  I've been playing for about 7 hours and have only explored maybe 1% of the universe.  Right now its only a sandbox game, but they will have a story mode on release.  There is no limit to what you can do in just the sandbox mode.  You can mine asteroids for money, you can trade commodities, you can hunt pirates, you can destroy and/or capture ships and tow them to the nearest starbase and either add it to your garage or sell it.  The game also has RPG elements.  You can take freelance missions that are everything from simple taxi runs to assassination missions, sector patrols, capture missions, science missions where you scan anomolies, and I've even done a smuggle mission for big bucks.  Most of all, there is a huge universe to explore.  Its awesome.  Get it.  Do it now!

Where do I begin here? You have obviously heard of this game in one way or another, so I'd expect it to be spoiled for you. Some people have told you that it is the greatest game ever, while others have doubtlessly told you it is nothing more than trendy garbage. In either case, it can be argued that this game isn't relevant anymore, but I'll make a review of this game anyway, just for those who were REALLY late to the party. Either way you look at it, do so with open eyes, because you will find that Undertale is a very good RPG.
I'll start by addressing the most common complaint that this game faces: the graphics suck. As I have said before in my FF7 review, graphics aren't relevent. While they would make anyone but a devout NES fan vomit in the Ruins, the game quicky improves its visual style until it is "delicious" to look at, sort of like Chrono Trigger.
Now I will begin to praise it. The game has an interesting story. While it does eventually boil down to the standard 'save the world' scenario, it is built on the characters. The characters are all great IMO (bar one) and you will come to either love or hate some as I did. The game has an interesting battle system, using several concepts rarely used in RPGs, therefore unfamilliar to the general fanbase of RPGs(such as talking to monsters). The game has a very 'memey' sense of humour, which is give or take, but the game manages to pull it off. Lastly, the branching storyline and multiple endings give it replayability.
Now, I won't finish this by addressing a few faults that I felt you should look out for. The first, and biggest reason why I rate this game lower than others, is the final boss of what people consider the "true" route of the game. How to summarize it? Basically, TobyFox pulled a Necron on us. He comes out of nowhere, and, although being relevant(if you're a lore nut), felt unnecessary to me. His animations were also unsatisfactory IMO, when compared to, say, Asgore for example. Am I nitpicking much? Well, anyway, at least his battle music is awesome, I'll give it that, but it does have the feel of forced emotions when it is heard with this fight. You can also make a somewhat cringeworthy descision after this fight. Lastly, there is some very unexplained transformation from another character into THIS character. How said former character manages to transform into another form with a more powerful source of transformation confuses me. I'm sorry to all those who like THIS character, but I simply hated him, especially his personality. He doesn't compare to his parents.
(To address any concerns, the other two final bosses, especially the middle route's are exellent IMO.)
The only other thing I would complain about would be the music. It is very different in composition, going from 8-bit melodies to disco music and everything inbetween. While it may come off as attempting to be eclectic, it doesn't work, especially when compared to EarthBound, which does. The sad thing about this is that the OST is generally good, with several outstanding tracks(I'm not just talking about Megalovania;D). Essentially, I have the same problem with this OST as I do with Xenoblade Chronicles' OST, it is too disjointed but has several great tracks. I don't lash the game that much for this, though, and you could probably ignore this.
Overall, Undertale is a great RPG and one of the best recent ones. It is a game that can change your character, as I have found by speaking to my friends. While it may have been overhyped, play it and you may see some reasons why it is so cherished.
My Score: 8.8/10(Very Good)
BTW, you were expecting me to tell you to stay away from the fandom, weren't you? Lol. If you get into it, it's your own fault. That is all I'll say.

I didn't know what to expect when I went into this game, I was fairly familiar with Mad Max--watched Fury Road and clips of the originals but never got into it fully. Now that I played this game, and went ahead and watch the original movies, I have to say this game is a fantastic interpretation of Mad Max's Australia!
The combat is very similar to the Batman: Arkham series but the car combat gameplay is like nothing I've played before. The overall story was crafted around the recurring tropes of the Mad Max films: conquer gang territories through car combat and travel long distances with your trusty car to accomplish missions. In this respect, the game pulled it off very well. However, if you're not a fan of Mad Max, you might complain that the missions get repetitive (as having to drive a road trip through the desert for the 20th time to find scrap can certainly become mind numbing). But that's the whole idea of Mad Max! A wasteland badass that goes on epic road trips! I feel like biggest weakness of the game was a necessary piece of the experience.
The plot was very action oriented but in that regard, it triumphed! If you need a story that has plenty of action, this is it! Vengeance! Deception! Fury! And your lowly mechanic Chumbucket, who you come to assume is a secondary character that can be ignored, becomes your stalwart ally and changes the narrative multiple times because of his insistance to be relevant!
All in all, I didn't know what I was going in for, but I was pleasantly surprised. Fantastic action/adventure title that will hold your attention for 30-40 hours and make you think about the cold brutal world of Mad Max.

I really wish there was a neutral rewiew option, my descision to go negative is because this game has some substancial flaws and isn't for everyone.
Quality: This isn't the quality of Uncharted Waters (NES), and nowhere near the quality of Uncharted Waters:New Horizons (SNES). It's closer to Sid Meyers's Pirates (PC), both in graphically and gameplay wise (with a fair amount of content stripped compared to SMP). I havn't played multiplayer, but based on the fact that aoe abilties allow for friendly fire, it seems like it will degrade into a grief fest quickly. Despite the potential issues with multiplayer, the game is CLEARLY designed for people to be playing each faction (although since you can't take another faction's towns, only pirate controlled ones, it seems like it will be a bit of an early land grab).
I don't dislike the game, I was on the edge about it at first, but after an hour or two it was difficult to not do 1 more quest before I quit. Once you put in 20-30 hours and have a maxed ship though, it quickly goes stale. I havn't played around with multiplayer, but based on how the skills work, there appears to be heavy potential for trolls/griefers. Friendly fire is on for heavy damage AoE abilities.
Mechanics: You sail around on a ship, doing quests for towns to to gain money and levels for both yourself and the towns. The game advertised as having options for adventurers, traders and combat types. Realistically, don't expect to be specialized. You'll be doing all three if you want to actually level towns in a sane amount of time. The trade system is weak, combat quickly becomes a joke in anthing other that dedicated combat instances, and 'adventuring' is barely worthy of the name. Despite all that, it is enjoyable for a good 20-30 hours if you enjoy ship based games.
Value: I got this as part of a Humble Bundle package (with two other games worth installing), and have no regrets. Is it worth the $10 standard price? If you like ship based games, yes (although you may want to wishlist it and wait for a sale). If you're not a fan of them or don't know, I'd recommend skipping it.
Pro's:
Sailing Ships (fairly limited genere)
Entertaining for a while
Instances (although only the combat ones have any point to them)
Con's:
Little point once you have a high end ship
Poor scaling (enemies only go up to 3/4 of max level outside of combat instances)
Focus on multiplayer (with a grief friendly system)
AI (tolerable in combat, but terrible at prioritising what to go for)

when i picked this up on steam sale i was expecting to get a short and shallow but enjoyable mindless singleplayer grindy game; and i got just that.
HOWEVER, what i didn't expect was there to be a whole online component attached.  through this i found a great little "mmorpg" lite experience.  connecting to the official server, you can group up for pve raids, contest faction territories in a large pvp board, or just be a pirate and crap on other players you see with cannons and molotov cocktails.
the online play is where the game really opens up.  mindless grind in singleplayer gives way to a surprisingly robust combat system that demands proper ability management and knowledge of item interactions despite their seemingly basic implementations. ex: do i equip acid essence because i expect to meet flyers, or do i want ice for a more rounded look.  do i want to swap out my ranged specialist for a critical one to take advantage of my essence effects?  do i try to flame barrel that player, or do i want to save my cooldown for a water barrel incase i get flame barreled myself?
overall balance is hard to quantify for me as you can vastly diversify your "build" for your ship(s), and have sofar only built a "ranged glass cannon" type of build; but tanky, support-y, and "well rounded" types seem to do just fine from what i can tell?  there's also some soft-hard balancing done between player levels  so you can join in on raids at low skill level and be scaled up to the raid's.  also there's other touches like not allowing flying ships to fly in low level map areas to give some protection to new accounts.
the community on the (as of this review) official Tashdern server is very small but colorful and was very helpful to me when i was a new player.  good peeps here, it's just very small.  haven't witnessed any blatant ganking, racism, or any other sort of social maladies yet.  most people seem respectful, say "gg" or compliment each other.
anyways, the game is a steal at it's full price as it is; a must get on steam sale if you are looking for an interesting little mmo that won't require you to quit your job to grind and compete.

This is probably the oldest game that I still fire up for multiplayer on occasion (and, yeah, people are still playing it a full decade after its release, if you're curious). It might have my favorite capture the flag of any FPS as the combination of lightsabers, conventional weapons, and force powers add layers of strategy to the game that other FPS' lack. Sure, "Team Fortress 2" CTF probably has more depth over all, but I find it less fun to play, personally, as being stuck in one class can get tiring. Jedi Academy CTF flag is like TF2, only every player has all the benefits of every TF2 class, so your role will be determined by the strategy you employ rather than class selection.
On top of this, while the single player is a bit cheesy and no where as good as the previous Jedi Knight games, Jedi Academy is, hands down, the absolute pinnacle of lightsaber combat in a video game. Basically every Star Wars game ever has tried it, but it's distressing how so many have gotten it completely wrong. The last two Jedi Knight games were the only ones to ever nail it: it's fast, fluid, looks awesome, and has just enough complexity to allow for strategic play, but not so much that it becomes an impairment.
Anyhow, this rec is meant as a bit of a requiem given that Disney just shut down Lucas Arts for good. This, sadly, means that we probably aren't going to see another "Jedi Knight" game again. However, the shuttering of Lucas Arts allowed Raven to finally release the source code for Jedi Knight 2 and Jedi Academy, so hopefully modders will be able to do some awesome stuff with these games in the near future.

Jedi Academy is a game I look upon with reverence very frequently. It's the first game I ever clocked more then 300 hours into and was largely the reason I became a PC gamer in the first place.
The singleplayer is unfortunately the weakest part about the game, and is the weakest in the series thus far. Instead of playing as series protagonist Kyle Katarn, you're dopey a student of his. In general it's a fairly weak story with not so great characters. On the flipside though it has great map design, and it has an extremely satisfying Dark Side ending that even features a different final boss.
Where this game shines the most is in it's multiplayer. They expanded the multiplayer of Jedi Outcast to the point of utter perfection. The Quake 3 engine was almost pushed to it's limits with this game. It was elegant, masterful, and truly one of my favorite games of all time. However that was then, this is now. And unfortunately the multiplayer community now is a shadow of it's former self. It's a tragic story that extends to the rest of the series, since it never continued past this game.
I would still recommend this game though as the first one to try out. Since it is the easiest game to get into as a newcomer to the franchise. It lets you jump straight into the lightsaber combat (as opposed to Dark Forces 2 and Jedi Outcast where you don't unlock the lightsaber until a few levels in) and features the most refined lightsaber combat in the entire series.

(Pardon the short play time, I played it off Steam obviously, 200hrs or so, but much more the older games back in the day.)
This game is still good for nostalgia factor especially if you've played the original Exile games back in the day. However, it's definitely far from perfect as a game or even as a niche rpg, ignoring the low-fi presentation. Over time it has evolved into a weird post-retro deformation of itself as it tries to get at any new fan it can by dumbing down the core aspects but I get that all the changes are made with good intent in mind.
I guess the weakest aspect is the rpg itself, it really lacks depths in terms of builds and customization. The game lives and dies by it's indie barebones charm. Be prepared to read room descriptions and be told that things are happening with no indication in the game that anything actually happened. We're in a modern age where people are starting to see that a lot of old games are just out right bad and none suffers more from this than a game like Avernum which gives no quarter to modernization and relentlessly pursues capturing that feeling of playing a bad rpg of filler fights and meaningless text because there is nothing better available to you.
It's a useful game for when your power goes out for example because you can probably still play it without electricity, that's how low budget this thing is. And it is still kind of strange and amazing to see the same old Exile layouts from a new perspective with even some questionable attempts to add new gameplay elements to the combat (Im not super familiar with how much new mechanics there are in this one compared to the first remakes, but I played the other new series they have going and that one is nothing like this and absolutely horrible in my opinion.)
Im not sure what they are going for anymore, honestly. The gameplay is definitely not old school enough to be old school but it laughs at the idea of being up to date on any rpg made in the past 20 years. There is 16-bit era rpgs that probably are more complex than this game's engine. I guess it's just a small niche group of die hard fans that are hellbent on keeping this thing afloat and only the 'dumbing down' aspects that they permit are allowed to be added, no other changes are allowed and Spidweb is completely helpless to do anything about this as it's their only source of income. I have to imagine it's suffering from Kickstarter syndrome as it is at this point entirely crowd/fan funded as there is no viable audience for these games other than very old gamers that... can just play the old games without any of the unneeded 'modern lol' changes.
Nonetheless it is still fun to play through and the original Exile series was sort of a novelty back then. For instance there was a point where it was one of the few easily available games on the Mac and actually one of the best, way back when. Consider now that even back then it, the games were "indie/throwback" and not up to the modern standards of the time.
Yeah, needless to say Avernum remakes are kind of an anomaly on Steam and otherwise by virtue of existing at all, I suppose that itself is commendable more than anything but they also have that feeling of being some kind of weird caricatures of what they once represented in the rpg-fan circles, kind of like the ugly caricatures they use for skills icons that the artist Phil Foglio calls art that they insist on putting in every game. Because they literally cannot find a single artist to make a couple of still pictures for their rpg in modern internet  world of Fiver where a Chinese masterartist will replicate the Mona Lisa for you for 5$, Spidweb software with their small niche fanbase cannot find a single fan with any shred of talent to outsource a couple of still pictures to for their next game.
If you play it on your mobile device (I dont know if thats possible,) it will still be better than a lot of the f2p mobile trash but then again so is Pong, which I would not really recommend to the average end-user any more than this. This is as niche as it gets and the niche is fans of old Spidweb games that hold nostalgia and/or reverence for them.
I think I wrote them upon finishing it to give some feedback and pointed out some bugs. Just like in the days of old, I received a fairly quick, direct email from the dev, but he did seem a bit confused at my inquiry. Not a robot not a forums mod, just the dev answering his own emails! It's like 1998 again! I am old but I guess this dude was my age when he originally made these games, so he could be very confused in this fast paced internet world of technology or suffering from dementia. Again, the fact that these games are even being made at all is commendable! They even play and are on Steam and even have a couple new things here and there! Why, the fanbase must be nerdgasming at every release and they are just doing what they need to do to keep their eternal love.
If you want to experience some throwback old school semi-indie ghetto rpg gameplay with modern up-to-date standards, try out Pillars of Eternity or Divinity Original Sin I + II. They capture perfectly the bitter-sweet feeling of playing old bad games while still looking and sounding great and being polished, delivering a product that is worth money and not just coasting on nostalgia to carry them all the way.
If you are a Spidweb fan and wish to play a Spidweb game, Avernum remake series including Avernum 2: Crystal Souls is for you. These games are bare minimum to a fault as they have always been and no sign of stopping! However I must note that if you are very hardcore into the old games you may hate some of the changes despite them being for the better.
It's a polarizing, hyperniche, barebones rpg with 0 budget and marketing behind it that probably appeals to absolutely no one but people that play these games exclusively, that I personally like to this day, and I like this new remake even with the questionable attempts at modern appeal and overall problems. Though Im not sure if I can recommend it to anyone except someone that is willing to compromise everything to get into it, like a college student researching ancient games of old or something.

Having played the entire Geneforge series more times than I can count, and the Avernum games a few times, I'd consider myself a veteran of the Spiderweb Series games. This review incorporates my background knowledge of both their older & newer games, their mechanics, and overall design choices that have both evolved and devolved over the years.
The short version: Avernum 2 is conceptually a good game, ruined by a laundry list of bad design and mechanic choices that, while aren't necessarily a deal breaker individually, all add up to several frustrating and unbalanced experiences that could have been easily avoided.
The long-winded, mechanics-focused version:
Avernum 2's main story has always been appealing to me; the Vahnatai add a fun dynamic that makes the storyline sit better with me than the previous game. On that note though, I wish they played a more prominent role in the game: they're largely relegated to a small "expansion" map that's roughly 20% the size of the main overworld (which heavily uses assets from the previous game), and beyond a couple of key encounters, they don't really do much overall.
Beyond that though, it could do with a bit more freedom in storyline decision making... and much less with the myriad of instant-kill options.
The early game is... not fun. Navigating your way around is confusing, as you only have a vague map and no access to teleportation until much later on. You can wander from a level of low level spiders to an area infested with giants, just by crossing a single bridge (the older Geneforge games, of the same era as the original Avernum 2, had similar issues, though they were a bit more clear about it). There's also a bad habit of locking helpful spell upgrades behind barriers in early level dungeons, which can be infuriating if you're OCD like myself (or a completionist). You'll also have not enough money for upgrades/weapons for a good part of the game, though conversely you'll have far too much in the later stages (a problem that's ebbed and flowed throughout all the Spiderweb games).
I'm also dedicating an entire section to general mobility: it's awful. Movement in this game is at the best of times awkward, and at worse times can be gamebreaking.
Navigating the overworld can be infuriating, as your movement is restricted to a set number of tiles before the game tells you that you can't move that far (of which there's no tile indicator or anything, simply a largely unhelpful message at the bottom). This is especially annoying in winding caves, or when trying to scroll around the map from one town to another. You'll often get stuck on corners/obstacles, or run into random encounters that halt your progress (ex. hitting wandering merchants that want to sell you useless goods). The former point is further amplified when you're riding around in a boat. Teleporting is also aggravating, as the beacons/portals are often in annoying to reach places (which really adds up when you're hopping from quest area to quest area), and are poorly spread out. For example, the SW corner of the map has 2 that are side by side, but the south and NNE areas are generally devoid of them.
Let's talk combat: in short, it's all over the place. Melee is useful only if you duel wield, and are a high enough level for combat disciplines. Shields are sub-optimal, spears/halberds are inferior, and ranged weapons are all but useless. I tried having a dedicated javelineer in my party, who ultimately switched to melee halfway through the game, as ranged weapons are all but useless (even with extensive training). Disciplines are wholly unbalanced; you will live and die by the ones that grant you multiple attacks, all others are largely useless. For example, why would you use a skill that has a chance to weaken an enemy, but only if the roll lands well, if your hit actually connects, and if they don't resist it themselves, instead of a skill that guarantees you 4 actions in a turn? There's also one that cures binds, but doesn't let you move for the rest of the turn... kinda counterproductive. I'd have liked more options for rogue-like characters, like ones that let you use AoE shots with ranged weapons (which enemy archers already have), do significantly more damage to enemies with their backs turned, or let you move past enemies without incurring action penalties (for assassinating pesky mages). Just something to level the playing field a bit more. What we currently have is "use this ability to potentially roll a single-target debuff that mages can do more reliably with AoE attacks", "use this ability to do slightly more damage for 1 attack", and "use this ability to gain multiple attacks for a turn, or even several turns, which we're trying to avoid parties relying on with previous haste nerfs".
Mages are king in this game. No enemies are immune to the entire suite of elemental attacks, at most they might be resistant/immune to one type (unlike the Geneforge games, which encouraged having a mix of magic and physical damage with magic-immune enemies). Buffs and debuffs can be applied largely without consequence, and to entire squads of enemies. You can also easily spec them into being able to wear heavy armour, so a mage can go full platemail w/ a heavy shield (without any strength investment too), and tank as well as your main melee tank... even better, in fact, as they also get magic resist perks that warriors don't.
The two points that really kill it for me, however, are the "90% rule", and padding run-time with heavy DR. Unlike the Geneforge series, which allowed well-trained characters to reliably hit their attacks (even on evasive enemies), Avernum employs a 90% cap to accuracy. I'm also not convinced it's hard-coded at 90% either, misses happen far too often for me to be convinced that there's only a 10% dodge window. But beyond that, it's an entirely useless mechanic that detracts from the player experience by eliminating the rewards for properly training a high-accuracy character, and only serves to add a constant stream of frustrating experiences throughout the game. It's frustrating the first time it happens, it's infuriating by the time you've gone through 60 hours of it.
The second point of padding run-time with DR has been an issue since Geneforge 5 came out, which went from having an 800HP boss at the end of G1 w/ no resistances, to having common enemies w/ 600HP and 75% resistance to certain elements/attacks. In this game it's worse, because EVERY enemy has DR. I kid you not, I've fought cave bats with 75% omni-DR. It's so disappointing seeing a 400 damage magic attack do 100 damage to every enemy because of DR. Beyond artificially inflating the game's run-time by probably 20 hours, it doesn't add any challenge to the game, only tedium. Encounters should be made challenging/enjoyable with good mechanics, not having face-tank enemies. It's frankly a sickness that I hope the developers can get past with their future games.
In conclusion, I can give Avernum 2 a pass and a weak recommendation, but certainly not the solid one it deserved to have. There's far too many poor experiences and gameplay decisions for me to ignore. I hope the developers can improve themselves in time for Avernum 3, and not fallback on established but poor design choices.

This is what we've all been waiting for, people. A true successor to Blood Money. Thankfully, we can now forget about the absolute abomination to the Hitman name that was Absolution. Sure, it was okay as a stealth game, but it left a lot to be desired as a Hitman game.
At this point, 6.3 hours in, I have yet to even touch Paris. Toss in 5.5 hours for the beta. I've got a few challenges left in the second mission for the Prologue, suit only and such. Will complete those the next time I play. The developers say they've got lots of cool live events to add each week, so combine those with the already existing gameplay and I'm certain I'll be content each month.
The trolls who say they beat Paris in thirty minutes, then wrote their negative review and refunded the game are obviously not representative of the true Hitman fan. For those of us who've been playing these games since the beginning, we all know that with Hitman, you don't simply play a level once. You play them again and again, trying new things, seeing all there is to see. There's no way said trolls even scratched the surface. As far as I'm concerned, they're still hovering over the metaphorical ocean of content this game will have by the time episode seven reaches our hands.
As far as new game modes go: I've completed Escalation mode for Prologue: Mission 2, and it was excellent. Imagine a hit that progresses—or "escalates"—in difficulty. In tier one, you will do basic things like assassinate the officer with a pistol while wearing a soldier's uniform. Tier two will be the same but add an additional objective, like breaking into a safe. And so on, all the way up to tier five. And it was awesome. Had a very tense situation on tier five where timing was essential to the method I'd planned. Wonderful new game mode, sure to test the ability of every would-be assassin.
I've seen lots of people say they're experiencing graphics/performance issues. My game runs fine on DirectX 11. I had texture issues running DirectX 12, so I dialled back to 11—fixed. Then there were some shadows/sunlight issues, but that was fixed by simply keeping my shadow resolution setting on high.
Bugs that were in the beta are fixed as far as I can tell. Fiberwire bug, dragging bodies and having them slingshot back to where they died, sound-related bugs—all fixed.
As far as game mechanics go, it's a mix of what made Blood Money everyone's favourite Hitman game, combined with the few things that Absolution did well. The tighter controls are there. Thankfully, point shooting and a reliance on Instinct are not—the former simply doesn't exist, while the latter can be turned off with no roadblocks to the gameplay. And from the Blood Money genome, we've got that definitive Hitman trope: Here's your sandbox, here's your target, now go play in it however you please.
All in all, a fantastic game thus far, and we can truly say 47 is finally back.
Yes, after ten long years, 47's back.
---
Addendum: 12.7 hours in now. Have played Paris and it is incredible, both in size, scope, opportunities. Just... wow. Brilliant map.

This is a Klei game, so of course it's cartoony and gorgeous.
So far it plays like a Dwarf  Fortress / RimWorld style sim, with the main differentiators being the 2D side-view perspective and the strong focus on fluid mechanics. As the name implies, oxygen is your primary resource constraint, followed closely by food. Gas mechanics mean that you have to pay attention to the placement of your oxygen generators - if you're not careful all of the good air will float to the top of your cave system and your little Duplicants will end up sucking carbon dioxide - or worse. Water pipes and pumps let you slosh liquids around and deal with one of the other innovations - sewage.
In its current form, all of the main systems appear to be in place but there is a lot of tuning to be done before it has the balance and challenge I expect from a colony sim. The stress mechanics don't feel quite right yet - duplicants will put up with horrible conditions for far too long and then snap suddenly. The tech tree feels very coarse and can be completed too quickly. There are no external disasters or raids that I have encountered so far. In general, poorly conceived colonies tend to limp along for a long time instead of going into a downward spiral of Fun. I assume the devs' attention will be turning to this sort of tuning soon as they get the main systems nailed down.
As it stands, there are the bones of an interesting game here. Buy into the Early Access if you want to watch it develop, but don't expect it to hold your attention for a long time except as a sort of digital ant colony.

Such a nice little game...
the gameplay is simple: choose to be part of one of the proposed trading companies (each one has its own pros and cons, such as more attack power or more defence) or customize your own (colours, flag, statistics and motto); then struggle to gain control of all the randomly generated areas into the randomly generated world. There are pirates, there are other trading companies, there is multiplayer too.
Tipically a new "neutral" area is controlled by pirates, and the "game of control" consists of getting to own all the cities. You start alone, but as soon as you conquer a city some allied ships start to spawn. Conquering a city needs time so there is a little strategy involved: will you intercept pirate ships and let your fellow ship conquer a strategic town, will you pack up wit your allies ad gank the enemy, or maybe will you explore alone, far from your town and allies in order to find the enemy city from which all the pirates respawn?
Forts can be built on the shores in order to defend cities or strategic points, and doing this task well ensures victory.
If you die you lose some of ypur resources and respawn in a near city (or at the border of the map if no city is controlled)... a bad move can result in all your team to be wiped, granting enough time to the enemy to reconquer a town or a fort...
There is an experience system too, which allows you to unlock skills to use in combat.
In all the areas where pirates have been wiped out you can trade and accept quests in order to acquire materials like wood to repair your ship and gold to buy upgrades (captains, crews, hull reinforcements, cannon balls, and so on) or to buy a new, more powerful ship. This is a grindy task, but it's so relaxing :)
A very important factor that can influence even combat strategy is the wind: if you travel windward (yeah!) your speed is increased: so it can be very difficult to flee from pirates if the wind blows against you. Very nice mechanic indeed! it compels you to even change trading routes during "peaceful times" if you want your travel to take the shortest time possible. The sails react dynamically to the wind, but I would have liked to see them rolled up when sailing totally against the wind (I'm no expert, but the wind should push the ship backward...)
The music is very nice, but unfortunately there are only a few tracks cycling...
Overall I feel like recommending Windward, it's nice, relaxing and engeging too.

What you get for your buck here is pretty impressive. There is a long game here if you can tolerate the gameplay arc. The graphics are crisp and delightful, the combat though basic is functional and to be honest no more dumbed down than most of the games set in this era: line up a broadside and let rip. There are perks and upgrades to your ship that ca be either bought or looted, and you can buy a better ship as you progress. There are 4 available "classes" you can play with a variation of focus and you get to dominate territory, establish new towns as you go. Its all here  at a bargain basement price.
The problem is its all a little "thin". All fetch quests and trading get tedious, but you realise within minutes its not going to hold your attention for long. Most likeable games, and this is indeed likeable, delude you into believing that you'll never get bored if only for a short time, you settle in get comfortable and let the immersion wash over you until it dawns on you after a while that its like all the others, and has a limited shelf life. This game does not delude you for a second that you're not going to get bored, and whilst the bigger picture of battling it out RTS style with the other factions seems to offer promise, no amount of strategic layer is going to get me to grind long enough for it to grab me. I got it on sale and It cost me a little over half a pint of beer for 5 hours, I can't complain, and if you want to enjoy a few hours or if you need a midless game that just might take off for you this is worth the purchase.
I do not regret buying it.The devs have turned out a professional product that delivers and have priced it fairly, its a solid game for its price point.  Its just the butter is spread too thin for my taste. Think of it as a cheap small game that will keep you occupied for a few hours but has a longer game available if its limited depth does not put you off, and you'll notice some people's game time is considerable. With this caveat I would recommend the game because it deserves credit where credit is due. Would I actively suggest a friend go out and buy it? Probably not but I might well dive in again at some point and would definitely consider any product from these devs, For all its shortcomings I cannot in clear conscience give this a thumbs down.

Spec Ops: The Line is one of the "best" shooters I've ever played.  The quotes are there because, honestly, i didn't have all that much fun with this game.  The shooting works, the enemies pop out like ducks at a shooting gallery, its fun enough and works just fine.  But still, there isn't much fun to be had.  The story takes away the enjoyment of shooting 'Baddies', because they honestly just feel like dudes.  My favourite part of the whole game was a simple conversation between two soldiers, stemming off from a stick of gum.  They talked about the beauty of the landscape, the wind on their faces, and the reality that things were bad, but they could still have something to enjoy in the serene beauty of the sands.  And then your squad mate tells you to kill them, silently.  I wanted to hear more.  I wanted to experience the emotions and sensations these two men were feeling.  I didn't want to kill them.  They were grunts, unimportant to the story, and two shots from a pistol was all it took to kill them.  But still, I didn't want to kill them.  I've never wanted to bypass an enemy for just being likable before.  It showed humanity that isn't shown in war games, ever.  It bothered me, and sickened me that my hand was forced, and I had to kill those men to proceed with the immaculate story.  I won't forget that scene, nor would I want to.  It gives me hope that others may follow suit, and make smarter shooters than just "Shoot the guys who are different than us".  It's groundbreaking, yet so simple, and deserves every ammount of praise it gets, if not moreso than it has since it was released.  Purchase it, and get ready for a hell of a ride.

Jedi Academy is a game I look upon with reverence very frequently. It's the first game I ever clocked more then 300 hours into and was largely the reason I became a PC gamer in the first place.
The singleplayer is unfortunately the weakest part about the game, and is the weakest in the series thus far. Instead of playing as series protagonist Kyle Katarn, you're dopey a student of his. In general it's a fairly weak story with not so great characters. On the flipside though it has great map design, and it has an extremely satisfying Dark Side ending that even features a different final boss.
Where this game shines the most is in it's multiplayer. They expanded the multiplayer of Jedi Outcast to the point of utter perfection. The Quake 3 engine was almost pushed to it's limits with this game. It was elegant, masterful, and truly one of my favorite games of all time. However that was then, this is now. And unfortunately the multiplayer community now is a shadow of it's former self. It's a tragic story that extends to the rest of the series, since it never continued past this game.
I would still recommend this game though as the first one to try out. Since it is the easiest game to get into as a newcomer to the franchise. A great game, but with greater potential.
The game looks beautiful, and runs beautifully - even on my humble PC. Locations, vehicles, characters, story, voice and motion captured acting have all had much attention paid to them and it certainly pays off. I absolutely love this game, and I'm sure that fans of the Mad Max franchise, or similar ones (such as Borderlands) will enjoy it too. The story, lore, and whole feel of the game is moving and thrilling in equal measure.
It may be a tad repetitive, but from the right perspective, most open world games like this are. Fetch quests, races, and things to kill. The missions can be quite similar, but it is how you go about doing them, and what random events happen during, which can greatly change your experiences. Unlike most games like this, it kept me on the edge of my seat, but without making it too difficult. It lets you feel like a badass without making it easy.
But sadly, some of my greatest anger and frustrations in gaming have been at the faults of Mad Max, and a lot of them are relatively simple fixes too.
The basic controller scheme may be strange, but I can see the reasoning behind it - sadly there is NO option to change things though. The control of vehicles is incredibly sloppy (even once fully upgraded; as I expect the wrecks that you first find to be flimsy) making even professional racers like myself struggle to drive anywhere, and that's before you even head onto the sand dunes AND have to turn the camera away from where you're driving to shoot at baddies - so thank goodness that the time slows down when you take aim.
And this sloppiness and delayed steering is because Max is actually turning the wheel realistically (which is hidden from view until you change to the first person driving view - which looks pretty awesome actually). I don't mind this form of steering that much for the thrill it provides when you have to react things, but I can't imagine the nightmare that keyboard users will face, especially if they're not adept drivers.
The button layout is poorly thought out (for the 360 controller at least). The button for firing the rare sniper ammunition is the same as the button for getting Chum to idle the car whilst you're holding the sniper rifle itself; and the button to refuel a car is the same as the one that explodes the jerry can holding said fuel (meaning that you probably blow up your car). And these are just the two shocking conflicts that come to mind.
Most of these issues could be avoided if the
were wider, but for things like those mentioned above, as well as getting into your car or climbing a ladder - you must be EXACTLY in the right place and facing the right direction. And many activation buttons must be held down, despite no conflicting buttons that would give reason for them to be held.
So in short: A fantastic game, but prepare to turn yourself into a "Raggedy Man" as you may tear hair from your head, and clothing from your body.

Avernum 2 is probably the best game from the Avernum series, also known as Exile when it was top-down 2D. While the game can be a little bit plodding at times, the story itself is incredibly rich set in an exotic realm.
That said, this is not a modern RPG game. In fact, it falls more squarely on the classic games such as Baldur's Gate and Icewind Dale. And there is a LOT to do. So much so that even before I purchased this modern remake, I could play the old shareware version of Exile II for hours and still not touch the part of the game you had to pay to access.
The graphics are not top of the line. And that is fine. The interface is lightyears cleaner than the original interface for Avernum 2. This is a very retro game, turn based, and definitely not the same sort of fast paced RPG as a lot of modern ones such as Elder Scrolls or Fallout are. This is for people who deeply enjoyed the original Fallout, Baldur's gate.
My recommendation is this: If you enjoy retro RPGs, or were raised on the classics of the 2D era, this is for you.

Surprisingly fun. It's the first thing that crossed my mind when i decided to bury a few hours into Avernum II.
I got it on Humble Bundle for a very reasonable price and i believe this game is surely worth about 10 bucks.
About the game experience: it has a very old school feel to it. All around. The interface is slightly clumsy, with elements poorly positioned and the whole inventory/character panel has a very serious dependence on your pointing peripheral (mouse or trackpad), unless you're willing to print the hotkey map and stick with it in front of you while playing.
I've tried playing it in the Hard difficulty and i found it to be quite unforgiving, where you ended up dead for the minimal tactical mistake i made. Me, not being a person that enjoys frustration, lowered the diff to Normal, which is much more satisfying if you're just trying to have a good time and you want to enjoy the story.
Yes, the story. Sure, it has a random catastrophical event as its key, which is beyond cliché, but if you get past that, you find a refreshing sense of humor (the spiders!), a well built combat system, an old school atmosphere (which is welcome in this sort of game) and a somewhat clear path of quests which you must complete in order to progress in the game.
The character creation part of the game is limited. You have three races (Lizard, Cat and Human) with none having a practical reason for you to choose it. You have a few options of portraits for each race, which i found sufficiently varied. The classes side is a bit redundant but you have the usual Mage/Swordsman/Rogue trio well represented.
I'd give it a 7.5 out of 10. It is thoroughly enjoyable if you can cope with the clumsy interface and controls and if you're willing to insist on it enough so that you get the hang of it.

I wasted so much time in the middle part of the game trying to find somewhere I could go without getting into combat where half or my entire team was one shot killed in the first round before I even got a chance to respond.  I must have died and reloaded 100 times.  It's cool to have an open world, but some guidance was needed about where I had no chance and where I could expect to make progress.
It was increasingly annoying how late in the game it was before I got high level remove mountain, remove barrier, a decent level in lock picking, flying, and a higher level security clearance, the first two in particular.  Every dungeon and town from the very lowest level of the game on seemed to have at least one barrier, door, rock, or security guard I couldn't get through.  And the journal in this game, the usual for Spiderweb, is useless, so I piled up scraps of paper all over my desk jotting down low level areas I needed to go back to when I was level 30+ and could actually access all the areas.  Most of them were not that important, but there were needed spell level up books in some of these areas.  The game is long enough without having to do so much annoying backtracking.
I guess maybe I'm just bad at this one, but in the end game, I had zero chance against the main villain boss.  I was getting immoblized or ensnared, or terrified, or null effect to block magic so that I could never even get close enough to him to do much damage before the steadily mounting power of this spells was starting to hit each one of characters for like 3000 damage, one shot killing them several times over.  I think I've probably given up at this point and won't be able to finish the game after 80 something hours of play time.
Speaking of which, ensnare and immobilize are WAY too common. Any battle with archers or some other characters, my melee guys were not able to even do anything much of the time.  Charm is also stupid.  It was pretty much instant reload if one of my guys got charmed (even with a mind shield spell in place often), since any one of my characters could immediately kill any other despite taking a dozen hits to do the same to any enemy.  I wanted to be able to use my characters skills in battle, not have members of my team constantly taken out the fight.

The story starts off with you (the vault hunter) nearly dying & being flung from a train crash.  You are awaken by probably the best Navi game character ever invented, CL4P-TP.  He's annoying, gets on your nerves & is just hilarious.  He's become a mascot in his own right.  He wakes you up & leads you to the nearest town that's currently being ransacked by raiders. It's there you learn of the infamous Handsome Jack, the biggest, baddest & best  corporate villain of all time.  Your goal is simple.  Kill Jack.
Gameplay is very simple.  You point, shoot & loot.  That's about it.  There's also a leveling system that gives you passive stat bonuses as well as new abilities but it's really mostly about pointing & shooting things.  The real draw for this game is it's unique cast of characters that you'll encounter throughout the wastelands.  They're funny, crazy & overly dramatic to the point where it's just a good time.  There's also vehicles you can use via Scooter's Catch a'Ride which comes with either a machine gun or rocket launcher attatched to it with infinite ammo.  Headshots also play a big roll in the game as some enemies become stronger when you shoot their head off & then they just run around on a rampage killing everything in their path like headless angry chickens.  It's great.
Sadly, the game gets highly repetitive because shooting & looting is all you do.  Every quest involves killing things or looting something.  Every single one.  It gets even more monotonous in the DLC campaigns where you complete the main quest & then get a side quest that just sends you right back to where you just were.  Why couldn't you just give me the side mission along with the main quest?  What exactly is the point in spanning out game time like that?  It's not fun when the game splits side missions away from the main campaign at all.  It just gets annoying.
The game is good & fun but very repetitive.  It has solid gameplay, fun unique characters, some good story elements, great music & voice acting, etc.  It's just so much of a friggen cash cow though.  There are skins & more DLC that aren't included in the base game or the season pass.  It just leaves a bad taste in your mouth when you think about all the dirty monetization that this game has gone through.  Try not to think about it while you play if you want to have a good time.

Finally we get a real hitman game! This is like blood money all over again, even the two intro missions have tons of ways of doing them and lots of interesting conversations to listen in on, weird mechanics to manipulate in order to get fantastic kills. This is the hitman game we've been wanting ever since blood money! And if the release model miffs you just get the intro pack and check it out, it is more than worth the price as a stand alone mini sandbox.

This is what we've all been waiting for, people. A true successor to Blood Money. Thankfully, we can now forget about the absolute abomination to the Hitman name that was Absolution. Sure, it was okay as a stealth game, but it left a lot to be desired as a Hitman game.
At this point, 6.3 hours in, I have yet to even touch Paris. Toss in 5.5 hours for the beta. I've got a few challenges left in the second mission for the Prologue, suit only and such. Will complete those the next time I play. The developers say they've got lots of cool live events to add each week, so combine those with the already existing gameplay and I'm certain I'll be content each month.
The trolls who say they beat Paris in thirty minutes, then wrote their negative review and refunded the game are obviously not representative of the true Hitman fan. For those of us who've been playing these games since the beginning, we all know that with Hitman, you don't simply play a level once. You play them again and again, trying new things, seeing all there is to see. There's no way said trolls even scratched the surface. As far as I'm concerned, they're still hovering over the metaphorical ocean of content this game will have by the time episode seven reaches our hands.
As far as new game modes go: I've completed Escalation mode for Prologue: Mission 2, and it was excellent. Imagine a hit that progresses—or "escalates"—in difficulty. In tier one, you will do basic things like assassinate the officer with a pistol while wearing a soldier's uniform. Tier two will be the same but add an additional objective, like breaking into a safe. And so on, all the way up to tier five. And it was awesome. Had a very tense situation on tier five where timing was essential to the method I'd planned. Wonderful new game mode, sure to test the ability of every would-be assassin.
I've seen lots of people say they're experiencing graphics/performance issues. My game runs fine on DirectX 11. I had texture issues running DirectX 12, so I dialled back to 11—fixed. Then there were some shadows/sunlight issues, but that was fixed by simply keeping my shadow resolution setting on high.
Bugs that were in the beta are fixed as far as I can tell. Fiberwire bug, dragging bodies and having them slingshot back to where they died, sound-related bugs—all fixed.
As far as game mechanics go, it's a mix of what made Blood Money everyone's favourite Hitman game, combined with the few things that Absolution did well. The tighter controls are there. Thankfully, point shooting and a reliance on Instinct are not—the former simply doesn't exist, while the latter can be turned off with no roadblocks to the gameplay. And from the Blood Money genome, we've got that definitive Hitman trope: Here's your sandbox, here's your target, now go play in it however you please.
All in all, a fantastic game thus far, and we can truly say 47 is finally back.
Yes, after ten long years, 47's back.
---
Addendum: 12.7 hours in now. Have played Paris and it is incredible, both in size, scope, opportunities. Just... wow. Brilliant map.

is really great for as long as it takes to see basically everything, which is unfortunately not very long, and after which point the whole thing falls to pieces. The central gimmick (from which the game gets the 'legacy' part of its title) is that each time you die venturing into the monster-infested Castle Hamson you restart at the beginning of the randomly-generated dungeon as one of your character's children. You get to pick one of three children, whose characteristics include different classes and attributes, most of which have no impact on gameplay (colourblindness makes everything black and white, irritable bowel syndrome makes your character fart every now and again, etc.), whilst others make the game literally unplayable (vertigo turns the entire screen upside down, but keeps the left-right controls the same). Weapons and armour are passed down to your descendants, as are the runes you can unlock through complete little challenges throughout the castle. All of this is towards the ultimate goal of defeating all four bosses (each in a different area of the castle) to unlock the big golden door at the entrance that leads to the final boss.
The game's long-term progression is what really kills it - after each death, you can use the gold you collected to purchase upgrades to your mansion, which impact gameplay by unlocking new classes or increasing maximum health. When you choose to enter the castle again, you have to fork over all the money you have left to the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ at the door, meaning you may as well buy everything you can afford. This is fine, except all the upgrades are more or less the same price, and this static number increases for every upgrade after each one you unlock. What this means in practice is that after a certain point you're actually mandated to collect a certain amount of gold on each run if you want to buy anything at all, otherwise you just have to throw yourself at it again, since money doesn't stick around. For instance, if you upgrade 3 levels worth of maximum health, level 1 of attack damage is going to cost the same price as upgrading maximum health to level 4, putting all the significance of the system in the first couple of upgrades you buy. This quickly turns the game into this horrific grind that strays so far from what it looked like it was setting up to be that it's hard not to be disappointed, because there's a lot to like here. The visuals are nice, and the sound design is pleasant in a soft kind of way that suits the game's light tone, whilst the humour (whilst far from actually funny) is good for a little bit of whimsy.
It's unfortunate, then, that all of this is wasted on a game whose most fundamental aspect is so flawed at it's core. Because of this,
would have made a better platformer than roguelike - the gameplay is so, so appealing that the disparity between it and the long, grindy, RPG-style upgrade trees is almost funny. I guess it's worth mentioning that this is in no way the game's only flaws - a combination of reused enemies for bosses, floaty jumping puzzles and rooms so chock-full of enemies that it's practically impossible to avoid being hit would still have relegated
to being a pretty middling Metroid-vania platformer, but I'd say that's certainly preferable to the decidedly below average slog that the game deforms itself into.
Very promising. Can't wait for more updates.

I've only been playing Oni for a few days now and honestly, I really enjoy it! I like how autonomous the little people are, and how its just about setting them tasks and them getting on with it, that really appeals to me much more than if I had to micro-manage each one, or set each one to a single job. It's a really straightforward kind of game, and the trick is in learning how to play it better not how to play it well, which again, is great if you like being able to play a game and then advance in it. It's all about surviving for longer periods of time than you did before, and overcoming the challenges that arise as both your colony and their new home grow. It's also about managing, which I do like and again, the form of management is much smoother than micro managing, but at the same time it's very much your creation, which is great.
It's definitely challenging, but in a way that's kinda calm and relaxing, so you won't get crazy frustrated like with other games. It's also addictive in that you are continually full of the drive to survive longer, survive better, make more functional bases and learn how to master the plumping, electrical and gas systems. I almost feel like I'm learning! Though I probably still couldn't be a mechanic...
I like the aesthetic of the game a lot as well, it's really cute and generally lovely to look at even when you're looking at garbage or death literally coming for your whole colony you can totally enjoy that kinda thing! The sound effects and the soundtrack are brilliant, calming and warm and full of the rich ambiance you want in this kind of game.
I would recommend it to others, but at the same time exercise caution because right now the main struggle I have with the game is that there's no real end goal. As far as I know, the only goal is survival, and while that is cool, if I was to compare it to don't starve I would say don't starve feels a lot more full and developed because of the optional story mode where there is a clearer end goal.
I think a popular complaint is that it's boring or uninteresting and while I can see where people are coming from, because after the initial set up things can be quite slow and steady, but honestly that's something to enjoy in a different way, once your colony is doing decently, you get to work out how to help them do well! If you're kinda playing it for a calm survival game you'll love it. It's not every day fast paced battle you know? This is a lovely game.

Well.
My mind...wow.
Just. Wow.
I went into this as any other shooter fan did: I expected a good fight, to come out on top, save the day, and maybe hit on some scantily-clad lass with an Australian accent and a nice bum.
But I was bloody well not expecting this.
The game begins with your usual scene of exposition: Dubai has been twitch.tv'd. A huge, unstoppable sandstorm has ripped the city apart, killing thousands, wrecking buildings, and (obviously) dumping sand everywhere. What used to be the shining holiday destination is now a wasteland reminiscent of Fallout. Minus the mutants, of course, since this game's punishing enough already without a Deathclaw trying to perform dental surgery on you. Your former friend, a Colonel Konrad, was sent in with the 'Damned 33rd' to try and rescue civilians, but goes silent.
Weeks later, you hear back from him.
So, since the message isn't all too cheerful, a small Delta Force squad is sent in through the storm wall to find out just what's going on. Average bunch of gaming heroes: You've got Lugo covering you with a sniper rifle, Adams keeping them in cover with a heavy machine gun, and, of course, you're in charge.
Captain Walker.
So, as it goes, once you pass through the storm wall, your first experiences with enemies come from the Insurgents attacking the Damned 33rd's men. Cleverly, almost all weapons in the game have the option of a secondary firing mode. Your starting rifle and pistol can be supressed, preventing enemy detection, the SCAR rifle has the grenade launcher function, the classic AK47 has the option of Burst Fire or Full Auto, and so much more. Being a heavily cover based game, it's important to know the effective range of your weapon, and this is smartly done by developers. With short range weapons (i.e., shotguns), your targeting reticle will change colour to display how much damage your shot will do: If they're out of the way of your shot and will only get spattered with pellets, the reticle turns a light pink. When you're close enough to tear them in half with a shell, your reticle is the good old red you'll come to enjoy the sight of in a tough fight.
So, after you save a Damned 33rd soldier, it becomes apparent that the once respected battalion, and its commander, have gone rogue, no longer under the US army jurisdiction.
Damn.
That means you're an American, and to stop these guys from keeping an iron grip on the city's surviving inhabitants (Who, I might add, have apparently waged war on their oppressors), you'll be fighting Blue on Blue: Friendly Fire.
Of course, once you see the combat, you'll see that there is no chance that they'll even consider stopping to ask what you're here for. Opposing troops sprint out of doorways and vault fences with all manner of commandeered firearms to stop you from getting out of the city and calling in the cavalry. A shot to the head will send time into a brief spin of slow motion, just so you can really appreciate how well you shot him. It's almost a pat on the back: "Nice one, player, you totally kicked him in the face with bullets. Now he isn't going to be able to do oppressive American rogue army things. Good work."
Though...there's a point where that pat on the back becomes a knife to the spine, the game taking almost a dark pleasure in
it every so often. If an enemy goes down, you can 'Execute' them. At the beginning of the game, Captain Walker will punch them in the face and possibly knock them out, maybe shooting them in the head if they're lucky. But as time passes, and you begin to see
what Dubai has been doing behind the sandstorm, these become arguably a bit more...hands on, shall we say.
After all, no finer skull-crusher than the end of your rifle, right?
Continuing on from how it breaks the squad down, the game will occasionally show you signs that Walker is breaking. His originally professional tone upon a kill ("Tango down!") will begin to twist and snap into an audibly darker tone ("Got the ♥♥♥♥er!"). Your squad will notice Walker breaking. They'll start snapping at each other. Arguing for brief instances at first, shrugging it off as just a bit of friendly banter. But further along the line, these arguments become more drawn out, and over more serious things.
And I dare not even mention some of the atrocities the game will force you to commit to carry on. One such choice sees you overlooking the 'interrogation' of a man you've been pursuing for answers. If you open fire on the interrogators and attempt to save his life, his men will kill a set of civilians they...'requisitioned'. Should you just sit and watch, you're going to be watching these psychopaths dragging out his punishment. They open fire by his head, next to the heads of the captured civilians, and kick sand in his face, culminating in the strangling of your contact.
Either way, it's a choice: Your mission's asset, or the lives of the innocent?
However, in spite of its incredible accomplishments in the fields of combat, soundtrack, voice acting, story, gameplay, and level design, there are, as with all things, a few shortcomings.
Firstly, the cover system can be, at the worst times, confusing and unresponsive. Your sprint button and cover button are mapped to the same button, and it's tap to sprint. This eventually means that you'll be pinned down with heavy fire and looking to move forward up the field, and you'll vault your cover, prepare to run...
...and instead, Walker jogs towards a nearby wall and stands there like a gormless tosser as you repeatedly spam the sprint button.
Next, there's the...
elements of the game. Whilst this is not really a shortcoming (on the contrary; they were choices and tasks brutal enough that I briefly paused afterwards to breathe steadily at what I'd just done), it seems that the problem with them is that they were too good. No other game thus far has managed to recreate the horrors of war as well as
. No other game has shown the devolution from hero to monster as well as this, and with physical evidence of Walker's decline showing his uniform beginning to rip and tear, armour becoming visible, bullet wounds, cuts and scars all becoming apparent as you and your squad drag yourselves through extreme gunfights and brutal environments. Not only that, but the good folks at twitch.tv make their appearance known every so often by sandstorming the battlefield, making it impossible to order your squad to do anything and making it damn near impossible to see. And with these storms, the men's eyes become redder, and more glazed, as they see things that nobody should ever deserve to see.
And the difficulty...damn.
Now, I will openly admit that I'm...mediocre, when it comes to shooters. I pick up weapons that look familiar to me, aim for the head, and hope that they're not better than me.
Here?
Everyone was bloody well better than me, and that was on
. I died a good ten times per mission, even more on later levels. On one play through, Walker must have personally met Satan a good two hundred times. So I can thank the developers for making the hardest difficulty (lovingly named 'FUBAR', or '♥♥♥♥ed Up Beyond All Recognition') locked until you've proved that you're good enough to fight through the hard mode.
