I will never forget my first Avernum (Avernum 4). It was a confusing mess where I had too much control over my character development and too much freedom in deciding what I could and couldn't do.  My party at the end of the game was an absolute mess, where one character was absolute garbage, two could hold thier own okay, and one became the star of the whole war by happy accident. It was one of the most epic gaming experiences I have ever had. I will never play it again for that reason.
The new Avernums, Avernum: Escape from the pit, and Avernum 2: Crysatl souls, are not that game. They are remakes of the original Avernums 1 and 2 (which are almost unplayable on modern PCs) dumbed down and made more accessible to the general public. There are pros and cons to this, and I would even argue it is a good thing, but I do feel for those who will never be able to capture that first Avernum experience with these new games, becuase they are, quite simply, not the same.
They are, in fact, more enjoyable, having done away with a lot of the broken rules that made many enemies (especaily wizards) an absolute chore to fight. The new skill trees make party building extremely transparent, preventing the stat flailing at level up that made one of my first characters completely useless. The new overwold map layouts still reward exploration while providing better visibility and more scope to the game in general. Everything done has been an improvement. There is no better time to try Avernum than now. And yet, the game still leaves me dissapointed on so many levels.
I suppose in the end, it's because I'm jaded. In Avernum 4 (and 5 and 6) my characters constantly struggled. Death was frequent. Combat and encounters were unforgiving. The enemy wanted to kill you. You needed to lose. In this version, my end game party killed the final boss like a chump. I had overprepared, and expected a boss more akin to the summon happy bosses of old. My victory felt hollow and underwhelming. I will never have another Avernum 4. I have accepted that. Yet, if you've never played Avernum, if this is your first foray into the series, I could not reccomend it more. Perhaps your first time will end up just as epic as mine was.

First off I'm going to say this game seems to get a lot of unfair reviews, as if it were deceptive in it's advertising or description. If the game looks too 'old' to you, then it is probably best if you skip it, because the visuals are not the only thing that harkens back to games of yesterday.
That being said, it is a very good game if it is the type of game you are looking for. There is many quests, some simple fetch quests to help you build your characters (through reputation and experience), some kill quests that further the plot and they all tie together very well. Simply exploring the map and finding locations is a character building aspect of the game itself.
The environments are well done and varied. There are forts, keeps, towers, ruins, caves and more and they all are depicted in a way that makes sense. These locations contain  armouries, alchemy labs, barracks, kitchens, mess halls, torture chambers and temples amongst others all laid out in a way that feels natural and realistic. Exploring the different interior locations was quite fun, and you can use the building layout to your advantage to a certain extent. Sometimes using choke points or doorways to limit the enemy's ability to fight.
The fights were quite fun, and not typical hack and slash click 'til it's done. Magic plays a big part in the game and properly using defensive and offensive spells becomes very important. There are some battles with several magic users attacking you and they can overwhelm you quite quickly with mass damage spells, curses and charms. I played on 'normal', so there was only a few battles that utterly destroyed me, but it was either due to me overestimating my party's strength or using poor battle strategy.
The plot is engaging and well written, with dialog that doesn't take pages of reading and enough humour to keep it light at times. I wish some of the dialog was more context aware (once you have 'finished' quests for someone, you are just subject to the same dialog over and over, and it kind of breaks immersion a little)
I definitely played it 'wrong' (made some travel choices that probably weren't optimal, or as the designer had intended) but the plot still remained cohesive. It's designed to be played in an almost entirely open fashion, with some elements that keep you out of certain areas until you acheive a certain level of power and noteriety.
There is some bad with the good. The interface is a little unrefined. Shift-clicking to select multiple items from a stack brings up a box that is populated by the total number available. You must then delete that number and type in how many you would like to select. Simple mouse buttons or a slider or even highlighting the number so I can type over it without deleting would have been nice. There are a few things like that here and there that keep the interface from being perfect.
The biggest problem I would say is the graphics. They are certainly dated, however they are more than adequate. I could not play the game at my monitor's native 1680x1050, everything was too small, and it made playing a chore. I found that by dropping the resolution it enlarged the game elements and made playing 100 times more enjoyable.
Don't expect Diablo III or Torchlight. Look at the screenshots, watch some YouTube video. If you ever p[ayed old school RPGs like the SSI series (Pools of Radience, etc), Wizards Crown or Ultima I-V, and enjoyed them, you could definitely enjoy this. Opening secret doors behind the throne room in the castle and getting punished for it is just as fun as it used to be.
Generally if a game doesn't grab my attention in the first few minutes, it isn't going to go well. This felt like a flash game to me...although the set up to the story seemed really good.

is really great for as long as it takes to see basically everything, which is unfortunately not very long, and after which point the whole thing falls to pieces. The central gimmick (from which the game gets the 'legacy' part of its title) is that each time you die venturing into the monster-infested Castle Hamson you restart at the beginning of the randomly-generated dungeon as one of your character's children. You get to pick one of three children, whose characteristics include different classes and attributes, most of which have no impact on gameplay (colourblindness makes everything black and white, irritable bowel syndrome makes your character fart every now and again, etc.), whilst others make the game literally unplayable (vertigo turns the entire screen upside down, but keeps the left-right controls the same). Weapons and armour are passed down to your descendants, as are the runes you can unlock through complete little challenges throughout the castle. All of this is towards the ultimate goal of defeating all four bosses (each in a different area of the castle) to unlock the big golden door at the entrance that leads to the final boss.
The game's long-term progression is what really kills it - after each death, you can use the gold you collected to purchase upgrades to your mansion, which impact gameplay by unlocking new classes or increasing maximum health. When you choose to enter the castle again, you have to fork over all the money you have left to the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ at the door, meaning you may as well buy everything you can afford. This is fine, except all the upgrades are more or less the same price, and this static number increases for every upgrade after each one you unlock. What this means in practice is that after a certain point you're actually mandated to collect a certain amount of gold on each run if you want to buy anything at all, otherwise you just have to throw yourself at it again, since money doesn't stick around. For instance, if you upgrade 3 levels worth of maximum health, level 1 of attack damage is going to cost the same price as upgrading maximum health to level 4, putting all the significance of the system in the first couple of upgrades you buy. This quickly turns the game into this horrific grind that strays so far from what it looked like it was setting up to be that it's hard not to be disappointed, because there's a lot to like here. The visuals are nice, and the sound design is pleasant in a soft kind of way that suits the game's light tone, whilst the humour (whilst far from actually funny) is good for a little bit of whimsy.
It's unfortunate, then, that all of this is wasted on a game whose most fundamental aspect is so flawed at it's core. Because of this,
would have made a better platformer than roguelike - the gameplay is so, so appealing that the disparity between it and the long, grindy, RPG-style upgrade trees is almost funny. I guess it's worth mentioning that this is in no way the game's only flaws - a combination of reused enemies for bosses, floaty jumping puzzles and rooms so chock-full of enemies that it's practically impossible to avoid being hit would still have relegated
to being a pretty middling Metroid-vania platformer, but I'd say that's certainly preferable to the decidedly below average slog that the game deforms itself into.

The short: a fun but sometimes frustrating game.
Long version: I liked Dead Cells and read this was a similar game so I picked it up on sale for $4. It really is very similar to Dead Cells where you start fairly weak and have to navigate various different zones to build up your strength. One thing this game does better IMO is that your strength is not contingent on exploring all areas for power-ups like it is in Dead Cells. With this game you power up through permanent upgrades (paid for by gold) that carry on through death- this essentially means that the game gets easier each time you die with gold in your pockets (though upgrades get exponentially more expensive as you go). The benefit to this is that once you get strong enough you can skip any areas you don't feel like exploring- as opposed to Dead Cells where you need to look for those upgrade scrolls and it can be boring/annoying. As someone who played Dead Cells first, this game is definitely better bang for your buck (at least until Dead Cells is finished).
The only complaint I have with this game is with unresonsive controls at times. This is the type of game that needs to be very responsive but I sometimes felt like it was misreading or not complying with what I wanted to do. Even in it's Early Access state the game offers decent gameplay.
It can be a tough game with a bit of a learning curve and doesn't offer much in terms of tutorial but figuring things out is what some people find enjoyable. Gameplay is the punishing but rewarding type like Don't Starve or Banished but the difference is the later stages where colony issues or challenges can still pop-up later on.
The interface and colonist management are much the same was Rimworld. Assign tasks and set the priority. Each duplicant/colonist also has their own traits and specifice behavior when they get stressed out.
Resources are finite but there are limited ways to recycle certain resources like water-sewage or slime-algae (required for oxygen) cycles. You can also choose to cool, heat, evaporate or melt certain resources and convert it to another form or state.
A few thoughts:
* Interface doesn't seem to have a priority keyboard shortcut for tasks and it can get tedious clicking on that smal number bar and it keeps defaulting to 5 after switching interface tabs. The ore type or building material also often changes and you wind up using a resrouce that you would rather save for later.
*Some minor FPS slowdown on later stages where there can be large amounts of structures and Colonists. i7 and 1070 so there you go.
*Colonists AI sometimes go AWOL and they prioritize certain things over others unless you specifically set it. Lost a bunch of colonists to suffocation when they ignore an order to build the last wiring to connect a much needed oxygen producing machine.
*Be wary of your build order. Colonists will follow that and often get stranded on a single floating ore or another will build over them trapping their friend resulting in death.
It's Early Access, there will be numerous issues and bugs but at it's core the game looks promising. It will NOT hold your hand and you will often lose people or entire colonies.
Also be aware that some people are getting angry over an Alpha stage game and are downvoting positive reviews. Would definitely recommend the game but only if you have the time and patience to learn it as it requires a few playthroughs to understand.
I'm optmistic about the game's future as the developers have a good reputation and have continued to support their older games but will still caution you as it is EARLY ACCESS. You know what you're getting into.

If you happen to be a fan of science fiction and flying around in space, Then this game happens to be for you. There is no out of flight sections of this game or any gun fights that don't end in space. This game is purely a fly around and shoot things kind of game. The game feels like a console adaptation for the most part and there are some frustrating aspects to controlling the main character, like the occasional refusal to take cover or vault over objects. The single player campaign is a harsh, cynical twist on the typical oversimplistic, jingoistic narrative that most military shooter games tend to favour of late. A 3rd person shooter with simple controls. What makes Spec Ops The Line great is it's narrative. Instead of making you a badass killing machine, Spec Ops The Line want's to show you the horrors of war, giving you choices that have no good outcome, and making you do horrible things. It's also worth mentioning how great the characterization is; how Walker is trying to be this "good guy, help the people" kind of person, but, just keeps making bad decisions, or how his two comrades are very sarcastic in the beginning of the story and deteriorate to angry soldiers who are completely serious. In short: Spec Ops: The Line is game you want if you like a good story, and I have to say it's a dam good one, for 29.99 though? No, get it on sale (I got it in a humble bundle). If you're sick of the usually "you're a military badass" campaigns you see in your cods and bfs, and if you like a good story, this is definitley the game to buy.

I have played through the tutorial and Paris levels, and I have to say, right off the bat...what a game. It certainly surpasses Absolution, which some might say isn't a huge feat in itself. I actually enjoyed Absolution as a game, and I think many did, but the problem with it was the shoes that it failed to fill, the shoes of Blood Money. This new Hitman, in my opinion, achieves this spectacularly. Back comes the spawling and detailed level design, back comes the myriad of options in which your enemy can be eliminated, and back comes the good ol' coin.
Not only does the game bring all that made Blood Money the game it was into a triple-A title, but it takes the things that made Absolution better than Blood Money -- the mechanics, and incorporates them right alongside the level design:
- The cover system
- Instinct, redone into a simple tool that allows for a very slight slow-motion effect and the ability to see both individuals and pick out your target from crowd easily.
- The detection warning arrows
-A minor and more personal addition than otherwise, the ability to hide in closets and containers and be one of the bodies out of two allowed per hiding spot
- The minimap
- Throwing knives/other objects
And this new Hitman adds a few new things:
- Multiple ways to unlock doors
- The revamped suspicion system, in which not every single person who shares your disguise can see through it
- New ways of killing people - drowing being the one I have actually put into practice
- Close combat system a perfect blend of Blood Money's and Absolution's, doing away with the long, dull button-pressing sequence required to fight in the latter
I think that this game is very well-done and any misgivings I have about the gameplay and level design are nitpicking and too minor to bother mentioning here. Regarding the problems many seem to have with performance, my game ran perfectly using the default settings for my system, however it was set up. In fact, I did not have to enter the graphics settings once, and the game looks fantastic. For reference, the relevant components of my system are:
- MSI GTX 960 2G Graphics Card
- 8 Gb 2133 MHz RAM
- AMD FX-8350 8-core CPU
The only hiccup I encountered was that my first attempt to log in to Hitman's servers was unsuccessful and I was locked out. After playing through the first tutorial mission in offline mode and trying again, the problem had resolved itself.
From the standpoint of a person who only plays through Hitman games once for the story and experience, this game is not for you, considering the $15 price tag for the Intro Pack and the fact I have 2.5 hours in the game as of this review and am done with all singleplayer story content. However, that's not the way you play Hitman, in my opinion. Each level is meant to be revisted and attempted in ways that challenge the player. In addition, the Elusive Targets feature and Contracts mode will beef up your gameplay.

This game is very fun, reminds me of Blood Money in many ways, it has a nice Prologue that doesn't do a lot of handholding and introduces you to the basic mechanics at a steady pace. Once you are done with that the game moves to the first major destination, Paris; this location is very big and it only has one mission with many challenges to complete.
I found the attention to detail amazing and there's a lot of little things to discover with many ways to kill the targets, the game's opportunity system can get a little bit too handholding at its default setting so I recommend setting it to "Limited"
Other than the Story mode, the game offers 3 other modes:
- Escalation: Which consists in a series of tasks and specific objectives that get harder and crazier as you go on.
- Contracts: Players can tag targets and kill then in creative/fun ways and post it online for others to compete.
- Elusive Targets: You get a limited time and almost no hints to kill a target, this hasn't started yet so I don't know if this node will be any fun, will update once they release the first one.
Performance wise the game did run well on my system, as of right now DirectX 12 seems to be kinda broken, hopefully that gets fixed soon and the game's Offline mode is rather limited, this is something that I hope gets patched because not being able to view and complete challenges offline makes very little sense.
I can only recommend this game to people that like replayability, if you are looking to quickly go through the narrative of the game then I suggest to wait until the game is done or even pick it up at a sale in the future. Overall I think this game is a solid start to the season and I'm looking forward to the next episodes.

- The survival system of hunger and thirst lasts for a reasonable amount of time, so checking on it and eating / drinking only need to be done every now and then and is not a constant thing which needs worrying about. Water is easy to find in ponds and streams, and is easy to carry with you since jerry cans can be found around the map.
- Airdrops mean it is a good way to engage in PvP but to also get good loot, such as high quality metal and weapons. This saves lots of time mining and means the more "rare" items such as assult rifles are easier to aqquire. These are especilally important just after a server restart since if you get the first couple of drops you are basically ahead for the game.
- Optimization, many people are complaining about the optimization of Rust and firstly I (and my friends) have bad no issues with optimization at all and its ran well on a range of different PC's, including my laptop and desktop so unless you have a computer which sturggles to run other games, it should run rust fine. (In my excperience).
- Graphics are very good on rust given it's an early access game, it scaled really well even up to 4K resoultions and runs well while having very good graphics. (Although in windowed mode the maxmimum resolution of the monitor is not available for some reason)
- Base building is also a very interesting aspect of Rust, since you can defend your own base and raid other players bases.  Raiding with a group of friends is very fun since you are able to pool resources and then share whatever loot comes from the raid, this is a good way to prevent yourself from being raided by raiding someone else first so they dont have the resources to raid you anymore. Raiding also means base design has to be well thoguht out, to make it as difficult to raid as possible, but also easy to defend internally if the raiders get inside.
- Mechanics - Such as being able to annotate the map, or use code locks , are very unique to rust and I havent seen them in any other game, items such as those make playing with friends far easier since you can share base codes and mark locations off on the map.
- There are many servers which have varying numbers of players, so you can pick ones with different game modes, such as vanilla or king of the hill, and ones which have higher chances of combat (more players = more PvP), depending on what you want to do.
- Theres not much in terms of variation within maps since the biomes are too distinctive in my opinion, and need to be more gradual, since you can end up going from a field to a desert to a snowy mountian within a couple of minutes. Maybe the biomes should be larger so a whole quater of the map is snowy, then another quater is desert and so on.
- The buildings on the maps, such as the mining outpost and military tunnel are often duplicated, so on the server I am currently on there are several of each kind of building. I think it would be better if more areas were added to make this duplication less common. (But this is early access so should be improved when its launched.)
- Attack Chopper - there is a mechanic where every few days (in game) an attack helicopter will attack you if you are carrying weapons or if you are wearing more than two items of clothing (as ive been told). Now im not sure if the clothing thing is true but if it is being attacked for wearing a cap or jacket is a bit stupid really and should be removed. I just generally find it annoying because it means you need to basically drop what your'e doing and run to your base as quick as possible to avoid getting missiles launched off you. I don't think this (in its current form ) adds anything to the game and should be removed, or made less powerful as a minimum.
Rust has some excellent core features and mechanics which make it a very enjoyable and unique game, and all the complaits which I have are minor in terms of the map. Apart from the helicopter I can't think of much else to fault, even for an early access game since it runs really well and is optimized. (In my expereince)

UPDATE: After lots and lots of play time, I've lost very little enthusiam and this has become my favorite game.
If you find yourself missing Freelancer but wishing it was more robust in just about every measure (barring an in-cockpit view), this game is for you. There is a vast universe, seamlessy connected* so that you can fly between them without having to load at a "waygate" like almost every other space game out there. Sure there are gates and wormholes and all the other staples, but they're not necessary.
The starter ship is gorgeous, and you can customize the look of your ship in small ways. Combat uses a lot of showy glowy beams that seem to trade off well against each other balance wise, short-ranged instabeams, blaster/plasma-beam-ish projectiles, glowy-trails-having missiles and so on. Your turrets don't just magically fire through your ships, so firing arcs are a concern, and multiple turrets with mismatched areas of defense are possible. You can enlist specialists in your crew who cost you extra expense but provide bonuses, in addition to an amazing range of customizations. You can reassign power between guns-engines-shields on the fly.
It's currently an open-world, with promises of guided story plots to come. At the moment you can mine and take run-of-the-mill and short missions, kill this scan that ferry those. You can buy hunting licenses for different groups froim their enemies. The game needs longer more immersive plots, but the dev has already stated there's more to come int hat regard.
There's the controls. There is a wide range of things you can do in this game, giving somewhat detailed commands to your fleet and crew, cloaking, grappling (best to shoot the enemies' guns off first), instructing your crew which guns to shoot off first. It is... daunting... looking at your control customization options. I recommend playthrough with the control defaults at first until you find which controls you will actually use best in your personal play style. You will be using just about every key on your keyboard make no mistake.
That takes me to the tutorials. Just suffer through them they are awful annoying popups but informative.

I made a simple review stating that I loved this game. After reading some negative comments id just like to discuss a few things.
- Everyone is entitlted to their own opinion so this might need to be taken with a grain of salt.
All of the negative reviews are basically stating that the game is hard and all they want is to make a base that can survive forever. They dont like struggling, they dont like losing and they dont like learning. Unless everyone is a genius and in 10 hours figured out thermodynamics, is a certified HVAC technician, and a hydroponic farming wizard, I think the game has plenty of depth and replayability.
My first day of playing was trying over and over and coming up with new ways to build things. Built outhouses too close to the base? Rip. Tried this and that, rip. Rip and then rip. So whats a space colonist to do? I learned. I watched some vids, I studied what the systems do, hell, i ****in taught myself the metric system so I could produce accurate calculations.
That being said, if you only found 10 hours of playtime in this game, nothing the devs do is going to improve it for you. It literally took me 10 hours to just read everything I could build and what it does, how many gallons/second it uses etc. Remember its early access, which means we have the whole game still on the way. Even now, after 60+ hours, I build some REALLY cool stuff. Have a perfect colony, and then guess what, it starts hitting the fan, which forces to me learn and create all over again.
Something I read said "i dont like that resources are limited". Welcome to life man, resources are ****in limited. If they weren't you wouldn't need to do anything in the game to succeed or fail. You wouldn't need to come up with a ventilation, irrigation or power systems, because you'd already have what you need.
Now, I get that sometimes you just want to build and make cool stuff. Me too, me too. I loved DST and I loved making the coolest base possible. This takes that to 1000%. You can do ANYTHING YOU WANT, as long as you have the patience and imagination to come up with it. Maybe eventually they will make a playable mode where you can just sandbox forever, early access.
Also, there is a debug mode where you can actually just free build whatever you want instantly. So, basically all the negative reviews are solved just by having debug mode. A little googling goes a long way.

Assuming you can live long enough and prevent your whole colony going insane, the game is all about gathering algae, until you can buy a machine that can turn water into oxygen and hydrogen. Once you do that, you need to buy a hydrogen based machine to create power. Create a machine to make polluted water into clean water, place a few vents to get rid of polluted oxygen, then you're mostly done as long as you can manage stress.
What to do after that? I dont know, explore? There isn't a clear objective in the game other than getting your colony to thrive.
I recommend this game to people who just love resource management.
I don't recommend this game if you're like me and get bored restarting a game after your whole colony goes crazy and people start breaking massage beds to reduce stress, then if they are fixed one person hogs the bed for 3 cycles of day/night, then people go insane and break everything yet again, but this time EVERYONE is insane and cant fix the massage bed.

Overall, needs more work and a actual goal.

The game is nice. I have 2 remarks – about gameplay and about story.
In short: it actually is quite good (but I agree that there are types of people who would not like it).
Before buying I have read professional review on top review site (forget which one) that gave the gameplay very bad scores. The reviewer claimed that he was shocked how easy his character dies while his comrades are almost invulnerable. After completing the game I was missing several “intel” locations. So I went online, googled (top result) walkthroughs to find out were the missing “intel” was and redo the chapters to collect the “intel”. As walkthrough was on youtube I watched in disbelief how person doing the walkthrough fights “the end game turrets” mostly simply standing and exchanging fire from afar (and not with long range weapon either). That was ridiculous, because turret is supposed to be almost invulnerable from front and turret is supposed to kill you very fast. So I guess only reason why the walkthrough guy was able to win the firefight was because he probably was using lowest difficulty (or/and probably some cheats). I also suspect that professional reviewer I mentioned in beginning was same type of player who loves to run with the shotgun against fortified position and expects to win.
So if you love to slaughter waves of enemies simply by running into them this game is not for you. Me, I personally find that automatic health regeneration makes character incredibly tough. Quite often it is more beneficial to simply absorb fire while you maneuver to better position rather than spending ammunition by shooting back. However you must always make a judgment call which position really is better one and you have to maneuver.
I would also note that level design is good. It has surprising variety of mission types. Waves of enemies are quite manageable and enemies never suffer “never ending” syndrome. Learning curve is very ok with first missions (“chapters”) being easy and demanding very limited tactical knowledge that changes latter. I agree that keyboard controls could be better.
In short: it ok, not as good as some claim.
The story is very good in sense that it forces casual player to think about idea that “enemies” are not bad and do not deserve to die. If this is your first realization that quite often there is truth (right) on both sides, then you would probably go away quite shocked. The most epic moment is also very emotionally done. However to tell the truth this is neither the first time this idea is presented nor this is the best way of presentation. The biggest problem for me was complete lack of choice of action (while in game dialog repeatedly claimed otherwise). I read the interview where developer explained that the bad path was intentionally chosen because in life the good is not rewarded (Here I simplify what he said). While that is technically true. It would be completely untrue in case if in real life you would have option to see the results of your mistaken action and then “reload” and do it differently. If in real life you would have reload button you could easily avoid almost all the bad moral situations presented in game. Actually in real life you can avoid some of them even without “reload” just by applying common sense and prudence. The actions taken by main character was simply childish and idiotic. That broke my “suspense of disbelief” and unlike many other people I felt no real guilt for gameplay actions (but it was emotional nevertheless). However citing the end game “it takes a strong man to deny the reality” – maybe that is the case with me ;-).
That said I must note that “bad ending” actually makes the game into non replayable. Why you would want to repeat the suffering once again?

First and foremost - this game can be found for free online and played in your browser.  Russian Car Driver is a very clunky game that's hard to recommend.  If you're looking for something to roam the Russian countryside in and run over bears or deer then it might be up your alley.  But if you're looking for any sort of legitimate, fun racing experience then this isn't the game for you.
Your car controls more akin to a tank than a car.  The graphics are more reminiscent of the early 2000's/late 90's.  If you play in English then expect a lot of broken English that makes some wording a bit weird.
The game does have some okay music, though.  And I guess you learn a fair amount about the history of the Russian automobile industry.
This game could be worse - but it can also be a lot, lot better.  Even with some polishing it could potentially turn out at least okay - there are definitely some features in there that could work.  But right now I can't recommend people dropping their money on it.

For instance, I have a prisoner who only murders other people. I lock him up, he breaks out and murders someone. I feed him, he kills the guard with the food.

Isn't that more immersion breaking than ignoring the "moral consequences" of putting a 40x murderer on death row?

*Multiplayer Review
The problem with Black Ops 2 is that it attempts to balance itself and stumbles along the way.  Submachine guns rule almost every map. Maps are designed around CQC - giving the edge to SMGs - and often feature long sightlines for Sniper rifles.
While Black Ops 2 is much better balanced than Modern Warfare 2, it’s that balance that makes the technical issues of the game so prominent.  If the game was broken on a gamplay level, it would, I suspect, be much more fun to play.  Instead, most of the weapons are unremarkable, with no real standouts.  The are some more unique entries that lend a level of fun and challenge to the game, like the Executioner, a shotgun pistol, which functions as a close range punch but fails at just about everything else.
Hit detection is some of the worst in the series, and potentially in any shooter I’ve ever played.  Bullets follow character models around corners.  Too often the ebb and flow of gameplay is dictated by the net code. Modern Warfare 2 had fantastic hit detection, even when supposedly at a disadvantage connected to a poor host. Here Killcams show an enemy scoring a kill in mid reload animation. It's perplexing stuff, and often makes it feel as if gunfights are largely predetermined by the net code, rather than the player's own input.
Though the art design is stellar, most maps leave a lot to be desired. The inclusion of Nuke Town is nice, however, the addition of equipment such as shock charges, bouncing betties, and EMP grenades turns it into a bit of mess. It worked much better in the first Black Ops, as the weapons all felt much more balanced and fun to use. But as the key to winning a gunfight in BOII is rate of fire, that balance is blown away by an overabundance of SMGs.
Objective play is near nonexistent due to low player numbers.
Other options such as theater mode and combat training round out the online package and add longevity, but the core gameplay suffers from several marring issues.  The insistence of COD developers to include aggravating mechanics continues to perplex, but these elements, such as the shock charges, can be countered with EMP grenades or perks.
Why view quick exists in these games is a mystery. It adds nothing to the gameplay of an arcade shooter. Requiring the use of a perk such as Toughness to allow the player to maintain basic accuracy in gunfights is silly.
All in all, I’ve had fun with Black Ops 2.  There are fun weapons and perk combinations, and some of the maps are enjoyable.  But the moments of frustration do seem to balance out those moments of exhilaration, and overtime, overwhelm them.  Still, if you enjoy COD and can look past all of its major failings, it’s likely you will enjoy Black Ops 2.

The game is nice. I have 2 remarks – about gameplay and about story.
In short: it actually is quite good (but I agree that there are types of people who would not like it).
Before buying I have read professional review on top review site (forget which one) that gave the gameplay very bad scores. The reviewer claimed that he was shocked how easy his character dies while his comrades are almost invulnerable. After completing the game I was missing several “intel” locations. So I went online, googled (top result) walkthroughs to find out were the missing “intel” was and redo the chapters to collect the “intel”. As walkthrough was on youtube I watched in disbelief how person doing the walkthrough fights “the end game turrets” mostly simply standing and exchanging fire from afar (and not with long range weapon either). That was ridiculous, because turret is supposed to be almost invulnerable from front and turret is supposed to kill you very fast. So I guess only reason why the walkthrough guy was able to win the firefight was because he probably was using lowest difficulty (or/and probably some cheats). I also suspect that professional reviewer I mentioned in beginning was same type of player who loves to run with the shotgun against fortified position and expects to win.
So if you love to slaughter waves of enemies simply by running into them this game is not for you. Me, I personally find that automatic health regeneration makes character incredibly tough. Quite often it is more beneficial to simply absorb fire while you maneuver to better position rather than spending ammunition by shooting back. However you must always make a judgment call which position really is better one and you have to maneuver.
I would also note that level design is good. It has surprising variety of mission types. Waves of enemies are quite manageable and enemies never suffer “never ending” syndrome. Learning curve is very ok with first missions (“chapters”) being easy and demanding very limited tactical knowledge that changes latter. I agree that keyboard controls could be better.
In short: it ok, not as good as some claim.
The story is very good in sense that it forces casual player to think about idea that “enemies” are not bad and do not deserve to die. If this is your first realization that quite often there is truth (right) on both sides, then you would probably go away quite shocked. The most epic moment is also very emotionally done. However to tell the truth this is neither the first time this idea is presented nor this is the best way of presentation. The biggest problem for me was complete lack of choice of action (while in game dialog repeatedly claimed otherwise). I read the interview where developer explained that the bad path was intentionally chosen because in life the good is not rewarded (Here I simplify what he said). While that is technically true. It would be completely untrue in case if in real life you would have option to see the results of your mistaken action and then “reload” and do it differently. If in real life you would have reload button you could easily avoid almost all the bad moral situations presented in game. Actually in real life you can avoid some of them even without “reload” just by applying common sense and prudence. The actions taken by main character was simply childish and idiotic. That broke my “suspense of disbelief” and unlike many other people I felt no real guilt for gameplay actions (but it was emotional nevertheless). However citing the end game “it takes a strong man to deny the reality” – maybe that is the case with me ;-).
That said I must note that “bad ending” actually makes the game into non replayable. Why you would want to repeat the suffering once again?

I have constantly shunned the games that say "We are currently building our Beta version... blah blah blah." As these game companies often move into the vapor ware that we all so hate.  Knowing that; and knowing that I have been seeking a great 4x game, (I just KNEW that one was out there somewhere), I purchased this game in the Beta 0.8 state.
Now one might expect a lot of bugs and CTD from a large scale game like this.  With the small additions coming evey couple weeks I would expect the same.
That all being said: 8/10 in its current form.
I find this game amazing for a number of reasons.  The 4x aspect of this game is in place and you are allowed to pick "free fly" mode and just enjoy.  Fully armed pirates will come try to kill you, and you have to defend ships that ask for help if you are in the region.
The speed of some space sim games have put me off, you know, the three minutes slowly flying to the jump gate or what not.  Well SG2 gives you the ability to max out your engines with the push of one button and cruise wherever you want QUICKLY.
The speed of gaining levels is really great, you feel like you are doing something after you start killing pirates.  Getting an immediate advantage, then leveraging that advantage to kill more raiders and bandits.  You level up quickly because the max level seems to be above 70.  With several hours in I have reached level 15 and have an amazing 2.8M credit ship.  So you can play for a short period and feel great about the results.  But please note, this easy mode still allows for the chance that bandits get fed up and come to kill you.  I have been ambushed 3x and killed them only once... died in a burst of flame the other two times.  Love it, cannot wait for the story line.
Why you need to spend your oney on EVE every months when you can pay for this game only once.

After playing EVE Online (Non-Steam) I've been really looking for a space-sim similar to it but an offline version. X3 (Non-Steam) was the best one I've played so far, and Rebirth I've never touched because it looked pretty disappointing.
Music: The tracks so far are good and fit the game well but there's only 4 tracks I've heard so far but hopefully more will come.
Gameplay: Depending on the class you pick, you'll have a set of skills that you can utilize in combat or other purposes, there's a leveling system as well which you progress by doing missions, mining, exploring new sectors, repairing ships/stations, scanning anomalies and blowing other ships up, with this in mind the game felt like it was a Space Sim/RPG mix to me. Combat is good, I have freedom of movement and aim. It's also cool how you have troopers on your ship and you can get them to board other ships, unfortunately I never succeded.
Graphics: Ship/Station models, anomalies look decent, the background looks excellent, planets look ok but overall the game looks great.
Single Player: So far there's only a Sandbox mode where you can do whatever you want, there's no story mode at the moment but they have said that they are working on it and we'll probably end up seeing it sooner or later.
Summary: Starpoint Gemini 2 has alot of potential and It's pretty good for an early access title, so far I've enjoyed my time with and will continue playing it. One thing I would love to see is the ability to actually fly into the planets and explore the landscapes, not just dock on the planets with a menu and what not.

I have no idea who produces this game, so I am basing this purely on having read previous Steam reviews and purchasing the game to try for myself. I also have never heard of the original Starpoint Gemini, This is based entirely on buying the game, installing it and having a play.
I'm not sure whether this is an RPG pretending to be a fighter sim or a fighter sim pretending to be a space RPG. In any case, it feels very loose as to what you are trying to do.
First impressions:
They tried to do an "epic" video introduction, which looks terrible, a large battleship blows up very smally and very quickly, a male voice-over goes on about some events which we don't know about yet,
The X3 games, You kind of know what you are getting yourself into, they broke that with Rebirth by dumbing it down hugely, with Starpoint Gemini 2, The concept feels a little too loose, Though I suspect being a beta this is because the team are still working on tying up all the loose ends and making it good, sadly in the mean time, I kind of just look at it can go "What shall I do now"
To be perfectly frank, I had played this video game before, In a top down view, feeling the same way.
Google "Flatspace 2" and you will find a space exploration game which is basically the same thing, complete missions, get more stuff, grow wealth; equipment and repeat until you are a bad♥♥♥♥♥that no one can touch.
This game has a lot more graphic work clearly, a huge amount more content written out but effectively, the gameplay is the same, complete mission, do some trading, blow some ships up and repeat.
Maybe I'm too old and cynical now but what is the purpose of this game? What is my end goal? Yes it is a sandbox/freeroam style but what is there to achieve? Better ships? A few wings of fighters to back you up?
Navigation:
I have no idea where I am in the galaxy, Cannot understand the "fog of war" dynamic, surely I should know where each system is on the map and also know the locations of planets? Sure I get that I won't know what is in every system but at least give me a working map to choose where to go.
Combat:
Just feels sluggish and not hugely exciting, There is a classic game called Tachyon the Fringe, you would have a huge amount of excitement in that game from the dog fights, to the inter fleet battles, or perhaps have a think to Freespace 2, weapons fire all over the place as multiple ships engage each other. Or in both games, if it is brought down to a 1v1 battle, there is speed, excitement, skill.
Sadly, Starpoint with the rate of fire of the weapons and slow movement of ships in general, makes it feel just sluggish and poor. I know it is a Beta but I don't see this aspect improving massively for the September launch.
After less than an hour of play, I got bored with the game, the game has no appeal for me to play with it, some of the reviewers here are incredibly excited by the game but I fail to see why, Wasted £19.99 on the game and chances are it will be knocked down to £5 in a sale next year.

If you liked Avernum: Escape from the Pit, you'll like this one. It has the same gameplay, just with a few new spells, and the same ease-of-use improvements over the original Avernum games. The turn-based combat can get a little tedious sometimes, but I love the open world exploration, and I found the development of the story and lore more interesting than in the first game.

This is the third time the same basic game is updated into a new engine, and as of 2015, the current engine looks very... 90's-ish. Not the fancy 90's, either, way behind BG1. Still, the lack of graphical fanciness, voice acting or physics does allow for a really huge gameworld, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s of towns, handcrafted dungeons and combat encounters. The Avernum games (or Avadon, or Nethergate or any of the latest Spiderweb games ported to the new engine) all look cleaner, more functional and less eye-rippingly ugly than (for instance) Wasteland 2.
So far, I've played Avadon 1-2, Avernum: Escape from the Pit and this. This one is probably the best of the lot, insofar as the combat and dungeons both feel... inventive. Not quite as many "yet another dungeon, yet another bunch of ice/fire/giant/brain/plague/tomb/undead/
frenzied/rabid/guardian/ruby/flying/cheese rats" to be found. About half the dungeons have an interesting and memorable gimmick to them, a lot of combat encounters have something interesting and unique going on, and your own powers can combine in ways other than "more damage, better defense".
There's less talking and more dungeon-delving than in the Avadon games (maybe not on an absolute word-count basis), and what there is is mostly functional "go to place, do thing" but it does shine on occasion. "We found this weird orb and broke it. What did it do?" sort of stuff. The Giant Friendly Spiders - designated wacky comic relief mascots that they are - are actually really well written and funny.
There are some bugs and interface issues - the game's creator is apparently very reluctant to listen to feedback, so stuff like "the open loot screen button doesn't also close the loot screen" has been in 4 games now, and I'm not sure if there are fewer problems or if I'm more used to them by now - but nothing exceptionally annoying. (For instance, haven't used up a single consumable item while trying to move them in this game. Just me being more careful, or an interface change?)
Overall, if you're interested in a decent and diverse dungeon-delver than can be run on a toaster, I recommend this game.

Rogue Legacy took me quite by surprise.
It is a fast paced rogue lite platformer.
What does rogue lite mean for this game?
You pick one of three characters, go into the castle and try to assemble as much gold and equipment blueprints as possible.
Don't worry if you die, because you keep the loot from your adventure.
Doing this allows you to upgrade your mansion and acquire a more powerful sword or armor.
Meaning you'll get stronger and will be able to do longer runs, acquire more money, upgrade even more.
Of course this is kind of a grind, but in my first playthrough it never ever got boring or annoying.
The game "map" is divided in 4 areas: castle, wilderness, tower and darkness. Every area gets tougher, has tougher enemies and a tougher boss (although I thought the last area's boss as well as the last final boss were lots easier than the ones before).
Last but not least your hero: this is fun and sometimes annoying part.
Of course you get a new hero after every run as your last one died... obviously.
As you progress you add more available classes, useful and less useful ones.
Your hero can have positive/negative quirks. Some are unplayable, others really hurt my eyes :)
See for yourself, but playing a lesbian colorblind barbarian is something i never had the opportunity before ;)
All in all this is a great game requiring skill and persistence to master and finish.
I would recommend it

I'd like to propose that this game is truly great because of the important questions it raises.. it really tests your mind and your capacity to ponder complex concepts: "How am I still driving if my front wheels are clipping into my car's bonnet?", "Why did that fence I just drove into send me 100ft into the air?", "I wonder how fast I can go if every time I level up I upgrade max speed and engine power?".
These are just a few examples of some of the ways this game will test you, not your driving skills, but your mind...

It has all the Klei charm of seeing cute cartoony people going through slapstick, but I really would like the ability to generate different world sizes and more plants and animals, a lot more. This game would go from Good to Great right there if there was many different kinds of life forms and if it had a greater variety of different meteors to dig around inside of (Rocky, Icy, Lots of Gas, Lots of Liquids etc.), it would get even better.
Face it, the next game they will release, Griftlands, is much more likely to find a dedicated following, but Oxygen is a good starting point for them to break into science fiction, with its unglamorous feel and surprisingly well-thought out liquids, gases and rocks. Like Don't Starve, there are solid mechanics and a bit of dark humor and unlike Don't Starve Together you don't have to deal with the players ruining an otherwise good game because its not multiplayer. Its basic gameplay reminds me of former favorite Craft the World (Former because I took it down to make room for this game.)while being a good deal tricker to deal with in the long run becuase the colonists have the normal human reactions to hunger, cold, wet feet and a lot of other things.
Right now, there is only one serious flaw, namely that there are not a lot of the more dignified sort of ways for your colony to go sour. Adding more lifeforms means there are monsters to threaten, adding cave-ins as a sort of random hazard would be great too. Generally, the physological resiliance of Duplicants is a perk, but I do want there to be some sort of life-or-death situation just to vary up the gameplay. That is the only major issue I've seen so far, and I've spotted no bugs at all.

The physics in this game are absolutely horrendously wrong. The biggest problem is that somehow you don't need oxygen to burn carbon, natural gas, or hydrogen. Maybe if they called the hydrogen generator a "fusion reactor" i'd understand, but the carbon/natural gas makes no sense either. Natural gas generator even produces CO2, but without a source of O. Natural Gas is CH4 or C2H6, no O in there, but somehow the natural gas generator leaks polluted water (H2O) all over the floors and has CO2 exhaust. By definition you need Oxygen to make CO2 and H2O molecules. You can't get CO2/H2O from CH4, there's no O in there! And polluted water? Why is it being spilled onto the floor!? Why doesn' this thing have a proper pipe output if it's going to output things? That brings me to other point, some objects have pipe in/pipe out, while some others just pull from environment or spew directly to environment. Example: pumps have no inputs, you have to put it in the liquid/gas for it to pump. Electroysis Oxygen/Hydrogen generators have input... but no output!! They just spew their Oxygen and Hydrogen directly into their surroundings. If you want to use their output, you have to then combine that with an air pump and an air filter. Why not put some gas outputs on there? Also, since the laws of physics don't make sense, you can create a perpetual motion machine that turns water into oxygen and hydrogen and use the hydrogen to power a generator and end up with free leftover oxygen. What kind of sorcery is this?
Also, the air pressure doesn't equalize fast enough, so you can have a small room with low pressure on one side, and high pressure on the other side, just a few feet away. The water is same way, it's way too viscous. Water flows like honey.
It's a good concept, but there are a lot of things that are just annoyingly wrong about this game.

Admittedly, this game might not be worth the full price if you can't play it online. Where the fun really just begins in multiplayer is where it would end in single-player. The higher level areas are even titled "group-oriented content", which goes to show what the game is ultimately for. A quick note, if you're looking for story-telling and lore, that's not the point here, and there is none, the point is raging sea battles!
That being said, this is a killer little game played accordingly. The player becomes a potentially valuable team member in online situations about LVL 40 (fun starts to really kick in), and can really start to experiment with different ways to play the game around LVL 70. Being able to pick your ship and design your loadout according to which role you want to play on your team is where the real depth of the game lies.
Especially for being a small indie game, it is a very solid release. The core of the game is ship design and combat, and while neither has an enormous amount of depth, they are very solid and offer a lot of very enjoyable play time. everything else is minor support mechanics. Of course, if there was more work put into it, say if it was developed by a larger studio, a fan like myself can only dream of where its areas of lacking may have instead flourished. Windward 2 would be a worthy prospect in this regard, Tasharen Entertainment!
Pros:
- Pirates!
- Hectic and action-packed naval warfare!
- Controls and interface are fluid and light, no heavily complex system of which to keep track
- Relaxing and wonderfully aesthetic sailing and trading.
- On that note, pretty graphics which can also run well on low end computers like lil ol me.
- Decent array of choices for player builds
- Lightning load times, you're in the game and playing in seconds, even online.
- Small but awesome online community
- Plenty of loot!
- Playable for the whole family
Cons:
- Light questing and settlement mechanics leave something to be desired.
- Especially in large online worlds (best way to play in my opinion), the utility of questing/settlements is filtered out even more.
- Other than trying different builds, nothing new after level 70, but if you really enjoy the game, this isn't a problem
- Especially solo, gets grindy (but surprisingly not so bad, normally I can't play grindy games). If something could be done about this, the game would be absolutely spectacular at all levels.
- Exploration doesn't feel that much like actual exploraton
7/10, will be sailing again soon!

HITMAN holds extreme promise and can easily end up being Blood Moneys successor if the games future content holds up and perhaps goes a little beyond what we have so far in the Paris content

- discover stronghold
- lower threat level by destroying Scrotus camps/towers/snipers/convoy routes/minefields
- repeat for 30hrs at least
It wouldn't be so bad if some of the higher level vehicle upgrades weren't tied to how low you can make a threat level in a given territory.  Wiping out all camps/snipers/towers/convoys in the beginning territory only lowers the threat level to 1, and it needs to be 0 to unlock a the final harpoon upgrade.  The only way to get it to zero is by also clearing minefields which is very boring and after a while becomes a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥because they are hard to locate.
Despite this, the game was enjoyable to an extent.  My current game time includes completion of the main story for one run.  At the 24 hr mark I got bored with the same territory discovery/liberation cycle and just powered through the story for the last 4 or 5 hours.  I would reccommend this game if you can get it on sale like I did.  Don't pay full price.

**UPDATE**(9/30/14)
The game is now at full release. I will break the game into categories below and comment my opinion on them.
(+ means positive, * means neutral, - means negative)
Gameplay:
+Fast, exciting and action packed combat
+Plenty of ship customization
+Controls are fairly intuitive and easy to use
+Plenty to explore and collect
+Moddability
*RPG style progression (skilltree and leveling)
*Unrealistic physics makes things easier to play but undesirable to some
*No multiplayer
-Limited to 3 class choice on start of new game, cannot change later
-Unrealistic scale of universe (mainly planets and stars are WAY too small)
-No docking animation for stations
-Occasional crashes
Story:
*Typical story, nothing special
-Bad voice acting/racial steriotypes detract from story
-Some missions "vanish" from map meaning you must load old save to continue story
Graphics/Sound:
+Good quality graphics and visuals
+Good sound effects and music overall
-FPS takes a large hit during a few mission scenes or large battles
-Aforementioned poor voice acting
-Visual bugs with space background images (visible "skyboxes") are occasionally seen
Overall Impression:
This game has been quite a fun experience coming from a fan of RPG style games. The level progression system and skilltree coupled with a highly moddable ship means you have a reason to keep playing and improving. You are able to pilot anything from a tiny gunship to a powerful carrier but do not expect to be a fleet commander. Emphasis on is your ship. The story gives you a reason to play but it is not where the game shines. The most fun to be had is exploring, lucrative bounties and close encounters with tough enemies. Its a shame the game crashes on occassion and the story has some bugs. These things will hopefully be ironed out soon.

Bar none Starpoint Gemini 2 has been the greatest space trading and combat sim experience I've had since I played EV Nova in elementary school, but I can tell it's going to be so much more than that (blasphemy I know). The developers are clearly involved with the community and dedicated to seeing this lore rich galaxy through to the launch without cutting any corners. As is, I already feel as though I've reaped far more than the value of my initial buy into the alpha and though I know there's far more in store I cannot wait to see what they come up with for story/main missions. Showing my bias again here: I hope they stick with the open universe route they've already got going a la EV Nova with various plotlines to follow for near endless replayability. I would also like to see the captains name and profile photo become customizable, but honestly that's the only 'nit' I have to pick. As I've touched on previously there are a few kinks which one would expect of any game in its beta phase that are being tirelessly identified and smoothed out, so don't make the purchase just yet if you'd rather wait for a finished product. However I can't stress enough how cool it's been to be even a small part of an emerging work of art like this. Seriously, these people deserve buckets of money and validation.

Extremely fun game with a lot of good aspects, but pretty savagely destroyed by an exceptionally poorly thought out progression system.  After the first few hours of play, you stop being able to earn upgrades.  I mean, theoretically you could earn them, but every time you spend any gold on upgrades, the cost of every other upgrade increases dramatically.  By the time you start unlocking the higher level upgrades that make you able to handle deeper areas of the castle, you can't earn enough gold to buy them before you die horrifically.
The fact that the game both consistently increases the cost of items and constantly steals almost every piece of gold you ever earn means that eventually, you just hit a wall in progression, and you can effectively never upgrade again, unless you hack your save file to add a few million gold to it.
Despite the fact that I really enjoyed the game up until I hit that wall, I cannot recommend it simply due to the fact that you will invariably have your progress slammed to a screeching halt due to incredibly poorly designed progression system.
All they'd need to do to fix the progression system is either let you keep a good majority of gold without ripping it away from you, or lower the amount that later upgrades cost. The game would be perfect with just a few minor tweaks.

To those unfamiliar with Spiderweb Software games: They are OLD school RPGs.
Heavily influenced by the pen-and-paper days of the role playing games, Avernum 2 delivers a fantastic game for its very niche audience.
With only barebones graphics, next to no voice acting, and no cinematics to speak off, Avernum 2 delivers a fantastic story with interesting forces at work.
If you are someone who enjoys RPGs that stress tactics over grinding, and is more interested in gameplay over graphics, then the most recent remake of the Avernum series will give you countless hours of entertainment.
Avernum 2 has an insane amount of lore to delve through.
Every NPC you can talk to has a story. Even the most common junk vendor has several paragraphs of conversations you can read through if you so choose.
Avernum 2 introduces one of the most unique races in any RPG. Spiderweb does a fantastic job of flushing out the
Vanhaitai, giving them original culture that does not cater to any of the overplayed cliches in gaming.
If you are craving a tactical cRPG, then you will enjoy this game.

I’ve had a mixed bag of feelings when it comes to Spiderweb Software’s games. None of them have been negative, but it’s their approach to character development that usually sets the tone for their games. Avernum 2: Crystal Souls lands on the “correct” side of the formula for me. I haven’t completed the game, but feel I’ve got enough time in the game to give the internet my opinion. (I only wish Steam would update time played when off-line.)
Avernum 2 starts in the depths of Avernum where the top-side dwelling Empire has decided to not let the banished people below the surface live after an assassination attempt on the ruler of the Empire. (Makes sense.) The people of Avernum fought well enough, but even with familiarity of the area the Empire slowly worked down their defenses. You show up with three others hoping for some glory in fighting for your homeland and instead find manual labor. There’s nothing as fancy and digging tunnels for the greater good eh? Also, some mysterious barriers popped up all over the land and nobody seems to know where they came from. (That’s the beginning story in a nutshell. They flesh it out better in the game.)
You are eventually tossed into the fight against the Empire, the fight against some other factions and people groups that also live underground and are also charged with figuring out who in the world created the magical barriers that are now disrupting some access to and from numerous places in the underworld. You set off on your journey to explore the huge world of Avernum. Even though I’ve played other Spiderweb Software’s games, the world size always seems daunting. The kicker is I love to explore everything… you never know when you could stumble onto a secret room with gear that will knock your socks off. You’ve got to touch everything, don’t you? Of course you do!
Going back to character development, it’s done a little different here. In other games like Avadon 2, I feel like your character had more personality and that helped drive the story through your character. In Avernum 2 your character kind of “lacks” personality. It’s not that it’s not there, but it really is given by you, the player. In Avernum 2 the story carries the story (for lack of a better word) and isn’t dependent on a specific protagonist. So this is neat, there’s no real chance of you not liking your character (unless you choose a human with a blue robe and expect it to look different from what it does and then realize that you can’t change it after you find out that it is weird-looking…. but I’m not bitter… much. Also, I’m not sure if the Character Editor allows you to mess with the look, but it taunts me into not touching it so I’m not sure what that feature does.) The reason that you can’t conceivably dislike your character is that you are the one making the choices and making the personality. So if you don’t like your main character, for the most part, it’s all on you and not the developer. It’s also important to note that so far, you seem to be a group of four with the same mind. Individual party members may be called out for their heritage, but you are the mouth of the group. It’s a very interesting method and I kind of like it.
Moving on, Avernum 2 is a tactics game. Some fights you can face-roll through, but some fights will definitely punish you for not setting up your battlefield in your favor ahead of time. There are a few ways of doing it be it summoning creatures or buffing right before a fight. The difficulty of this game is hard for me to measure. If you want a challenge now and then, play on the normal setting. There are fights that just came out of nowhere to me and just wrecked my party something fierce while others were just a “who do I want to kill first” type of difficulty. If you want to enjoy the story, play on casual. That’s what I’m doing and there are still tough fights, but for the most part it allows me to enjoy the story more and get to more of it quickly. With the game being as long as it is, I’d like to experience more of it sooner. (Keep in mind that I like to explore everything.) I don’t even want to think what the Torment difficulty is like.
I’ll hit on the aesthetics just for the fact that some may not fully appreciate the look, but I’ll say it again that I totally dig it. There is an added bonus that I hadn’t really thought of until recently. I’ve been doing a lot of work on my netbook recently and let’s just say it’s not a beefcake of a computer. It is, however, the only thing I’ve got that’s portable and can use while at lunch at work (where most of my playtime has been). I’m not able to play full-blown heavy-graphic games, but with the Spiderweb’s choice of graphics I’m able to play a full-scale RPG with a great story on the go. That’s awesome! I believe they even put the Avadon series on tablets; how great is it to get a great RPG like that for a tablet?
Score: Gewd.
Spiderweb Software has a distinct way they develop games. Love them or leave them, they are great games. If you like RPG’s with a good story-line, then you can’t easily go wrong with any of them. This time, the flavor happens to be Avernum 2: Crystal Souls. I like the story and the writing and since the personality is me, I like the characters as well. The skill-trees are much the same from their other games (which is good) and the music is still well done. Avernum 2 is well worth your money if you are looking for a solid, large RPG and one that you can take on the go and still have it accessible if you don’t own a monster of a laptop.

Last summer my good friend from across the pond Stevie reviewed the title from Spiderweb Software entitled Avadon 2: The Corruption. After reading that review I had to appreciate what the developer was attempting to do, in a sense capturing the heyday of PC role playing games in a generation of gaming that has all but abandoned the old ways. Now I find myself with the similar task of reviewing another sequel, Avernum 2: Crystal Souls. After almost thirty hours of playtime with the title I can echo similar sentiments from Stevie’s review, however what Avernum 2 lacks in presentation and mechanics it certainly makes up for in story and exploration.
The moment the title begins to load, it is apparent that the developer has chosen to capture the look and feel of classic top-down adventures similar to Baldur’s Gate and other entries in the Forgotten Realms series of games. Sadly however the graphics of a game that released in the late nineties looks and animates better than Avernum 2 does. I am unsure if this was an intentional move on the part of the developer or if the budget was just not accommodating to force the developers into having characters and environments as bare and lacking as what is in this entry. It is hard to ignore the barren appearance and because of that I am almost certain that many players would skip spending the $20 to jump into this world.
However once the text begins to populate the screen the story really can hook the player into an experience that can have many twists and turns and smart writing with clever dialogue and interesting characters. I can understand that this can take a leap of faith and many may just not be able to sustain playing through the game on just words and story alone, however after recently becoming more involved in pen and paper RPG’s I was very eager to see what sort of trouble my group of unlikely heroes could get into. The world that is discovered through the multiple paths and hidden areas tells a tale of many nations stretched across dozens of towns and underground lairs, each with a population that may either become friend or foe depending on the choices the player will make. It became very hard at times to follow the core storyline however since picking up so many side quests derailed the progress of what was the current objective.
Sadly the user interface was clunky at times like this, where bringing up a map and the objectives that were currently opened were always on two separate screens. This was unfortunate to continuously open and close several screens just to figure out where I was and where I was meant to go, all while having hardly a clue as to where I was in the world due to the game making the world small as my group traveled in a very unfriendly overworld map. Utilizing the mouse to navigate the map at first was unbearable, and would jump out of control every time I attempted to click on a new area to explore. However after messing with the resolution and taking the game out of the windowed mode, it became easier to control. The point and click mechanics were easy to learn, although I did tend to rely on it too much during gameplay, where learning the keyboard shortcuts would have made gameplay more fluid and progress would have not suffered as much as I tried to click on whichever area I wanted to access. This is a flaw on my part however, not the game itself because I am sure that a veteran of playing this style of game or just being a core PC gamer would have picked up the control scheme very quickly. Apparently I have much to learn when it comes to taking on titles inspired by classic turn based games such as Avernum 2.
With the adventure in Avernum complete for the time being, I look back on the group of exiles that were brave enough to fight back against a cruel empire and I cannot help but think that this can be also be an analogy, albeit a forced analogy of Spiderweb Software. Although they may not have the presentation or timeframe to produce a title in the RPG space similar to other developers such as BioWare or Obsidian Entertainment, this group is still making the games that they have been known for since the mid-nineties, and it is something to appreciate. However we must also acknowledge that other developers will evolve and attempt to change the genre, whereas the developers of Avernum 2: Crystal Souls have struggled with the undertaking of fixing the control scheme and user interface of a title that could have benefitted greatly from smoother gameplay and operating the various menus with ease. As egregious as these problems may be, it is still an experience that I believe many fans should try, even if it may not be as visually alluring as titles such as Pillars of Eternity or Divinity: Original Sin. I for one am pleased to have had the chance to play a throwback to an adventure like Avernum 2: Crystal Souls, problems and all.

I'm an original backer of this game, and I was a little disappointed by the little content the game delivered. I do not, by any means, regret backing this game, as I did it to help the devs make it, not because I was eager to play and thought it was going to be the best indie game ever. But the final product is...well...below expectations.
It has a puzzling story told by diary entries, something that reminds me of Braid storytelling, with a bit pf poetry in it's writing. The art is beautiful and unique, which pleases the eyes of a 2D lover, and the soundtrack is very...unusual. A little to repetitive, but it's somewhat relaxing and different.
The gameplay is solid, but a little bit frustrating. It was a design decision to offer 3 "dungeons" or 3 "trials" where you get your gameplay elements that are used only there and then taken from you. There's a sword in the snake animal god trial, a bow in the spider god one, and a dash in the lion god dungeon. Out of these trials you just walk and approach things to read them. The enemies are dull, executing only predetermined paths, with no reaction to the player. They're there acting more as moving trigger/switches that have to be destroyed before moving forward. They act more as a chore than threat.
The pacing is very very very slow, to the point of almost monotony, which is hindered continuously by stairs that slow down even more the walking speed. This is also related to the poetry-like design of the game, building some drama to the journey, but ending up being just annoying, specially for a re-run.
Anyway, it's a short experience that last roughly 2 hours. There are reports that the game is bugging and not giving a specifc achievement, which will frustrate achievers, and the game unlocks a new mode called 9-lives after you beat it, which gives a little replayability, if you want to suffer with the ultra slow pacing again.
Gather everything and the price tag and you'll end up with a no-no recommendation. The artsy feeling of the game doesn't go well with the little gameplay content, annoying pacing and achievement frustration, making it too expensive for the experience it provides.

The game has a great level of detail, however, the gameplay is lacking. Your Magnum Opus has a constant ride along, the Hunchback so you can get your car torn up to the point of "exploding" but jump out in time for him to fix it. So no penalty messing up your main vehicle.
The secondary story vehicle is the Hunchback's buggy, that has a constant ride along mutt that "sniffs" out minefields and irritatingly barks, wimpers, and howls as you get near them.
There are a lot of locations that require you to go up places, from knee height to waist height. There is no jumping, only rolling, and your character cannot take a step up, and the developers seemed to forget about those glaring collision issues, requiring you to run into those spots for several minutes, rolling and changing angles in hope of going forward.
The combat and map location/discovery is just like in Shadow of Mordor, if you do not have that game, it's repetitive button smashing combat, and holding down an interaction key to use something.
There are tons of cutscenes from putting fuel in the vehicle, eating, drinking, filling your canteen and placing fuel in the back of your vehicle. It adds up to being time consuming.
"Convoy" routes are just circles where vehicles go in a constant circle, nothing else.
You get a sniper rifle, that folds up and tucks away in the back of the Magnum Opus, but you cannot take it with you, or out of the vehicle.
Boos fights include some large asshat with an oversized two handed weapon, a charging mechanic and an oversized health bar, with some environment hazards.
The "sandstorms" bring lightning strikes, massive debris to knock you around, and the Dragon Shout Fus Ro Dah to send you pinwheeling through the air if you're not in your vehicle. Even if you're behind a massive cliff face, be prepared to go flying.
The audio is terrible, going in and out of the map can cause the vehicle's engine sound to muffle. A simple work around is to re-open and close the map. But they couldn't fix that bug.
Places you can go, are typically highlighted with bright colors, what's the point in that?
Don't worry about selecting what body you want to put on your vehicle, as you can unlock the other body styles later.
You can unlock other vehicles, and "store" them at the large player friendly forts, but you can't see them or upgrade them like your main vehicle.
There is an upgrade screen for your vehicle aptly named Garage.... however, it's accessible from everywhere, ruining immersion.
Another immersion breaker is the fast travel system, that works via hot air balloons.
Overall there is fun to be had, but if you'd like this game outside of immersion, pick it up when it's on a steep discount of 66% or more.
