I'm a long time Spiderweb fan and, as such, I'll just start by getting the obvious out of the way: this is a massive game with tons to do that improves on "Escape from the Pit" in many aspects, not the least of which is storyline (which is much more sprawling and epic than EFTP's was).  I enjoyed it immensely and if you at all like Spiderweb games or turn based RPGs in the tradition of Ultima, then you should buy this now.
That said, it is slightly disappointing at times just how little is improved upon from EFTP to A2:CS and how, in other aspects, the game takes a few step backwards.  A2:CS fixes none of the glaring interface issues from EFTP.  While the terrible pathfinding can perhaps be given a pass (as it would most likely require significant rewriting of the engine), other minor problems are less excusable: the right mouse button still cannot be mapped to actions (no scroll wheel either), the buttons that open the inventory still do not also close them, and despite the MASSIVE amount of screen space provided, you can still only map 4 spells/Battle Disciplines to the interface hotkeys.
Combat also remains a slog at times, with tons of trash mob fights that can get incredibly tedious, especially toward the end of the game when leveling slows down and experience starts to mean less.  Many dungeons have large groups of enemies in every room, which often kills the fun of exploration and means lots of back tracking to towns to heal (especially since energy elixirs are a bit rarer than they were in EFTP).
In terms of steps backward, its boss battles are, by and large, pretty forgettable.  Most Avernums, and EFTP was no exception, tend to throw in a few gimmicky or puzzle like boss battles to keep things interesting and make you change strategies from fight to fight.  But A2:CS pretty much sticks to the tried and true, "Dude with tons of hitpoints attacks hard and summons waves of minions as you reduce his health."  It does introduce more area of effect mechanics (such as bosses who cover the floor in fire or ice damage), but it uses them sparingly, and apart from one notable exception, most bosses are susceptible to most types of damage.
That said, I don't mean to give a bad impression of the game from harping on all its negative points without listing its positives (which are myriad).  So I’ll end with a random list of the game’s delights:
-Maxing out Pole Arms and Hardiness on Mages and Priests to create invincible damage dealing tanks with adrenaline rush (i.e. the ability to attack 3 times in one turn).  You aren’t really playing until your Priest can take 5 polearms to the face and live to cast level 3 “Divine Retribution” 4 times in one turn.
-Doomguard fights
-Random 90s sitcom references (“Absolutely Fabulous,” anyone?)
-Doomguard fights on speed (and also on speed in the game)
-Buying 2 levels of gymnastics for everyone endgame just to scratch an OCD itch in your brain
-Leaving a bottle of Almarian wine in an empty room in a Dharmon Inn for your hommies who have gone before

Having played Spiderweb's Exile games since around when they released Blades of Exile, I've been hooked on the games in these series for a very long time.  I wasn't sold on the original incarnation of Avernum, but these newer updated rereleases are really good!  I sunk 50+ hours in Avernum: Escape from the Pit to do everything that was needed to fully complete the game, and I can see Avernum 2: Crystal Souls taking at least that long.
I will admit that I was originally disappointed in the way they reduced the number of party members from 6 to 4 and reduced the statistics and magic system from the original Exile series (there were far more stats to sink Skill Points into, and it cost money to train them, and there were around 9 levels of spells in each discipline with up to around 10-13 spells per level!).  However, once I got into the game, I realized that it actually works pretty well in this format.
As for Crystal Souls, I will say that coins can be hard to come by, even with selling every single thing that has value that you don't need.  Or at least that's how it is for me where I am right now.  Even with that, though, the game is very enjoyable and you get the chance to revisit many of the same places that you did in Escape from the Pit, though there are changes in basically all of them.  It's a much larger game, though, and very much fun.  I highly recommend it to anybody that found Escape from the Pit to be fun.

It was fun for a few hours, but I lost interest fairly quickly.

I have no hesitation in recommending this, as long as you don't expect an epic game with innovative systems.  It's a very solid little game that perhaps makes you think a little, and has graphics and sound to die for,
The Good Stuff:
- The graphic design is magical.  By keeping it crisp and clean, with a unified art-deco style, it gets away with not being especially state-of-the-art.
- The music is equally magical.  Normally I mute sound very quickly, but this game contains a variety of musical themes that are very evocative.  (It's very reminiscent of Zelda games, which meant to be high praise.)
- The game is designed to be played twice.  Once with no penalties for "dying", the second with a limited number of lives but, of course, you've learned some things from your first time through.  This is very clever, and the game is, as noted, quite short, so revisiting it in this way works very well.  (I know it's not a new idea, but it feels qualitatively different to the traditional "extreme" mode that many games unlock upon completition.)  As someone who isn't a twitch gamer, I felt challenged but not overly frustrated and was really happy that I could play the game to the end without artificial limitations - something that other games could learn from, perhaps.
- I haven't played many games that are top-down platformers.  (It sounds like a contradiction in terms, but it's the best I can do.)  This makes for an unusual experience There is definitely a reward in patience: learning the patterns is very possible and the game rarely bounces you into a position where split-second timing is the only way through - I think there may be a couple of cases, but I may have missed the "safe" routes.
The Bad:
- I don't really want to call the story "bad" because it isn't.  But the non-linear way they have chosen to tell it, combined with the weird approach of stamping text onto some of the levels themselves, really does not help.  (And I speak as someone who loves non-linear storytelling.)
- There are some levels where the checkpoints are simply annoying.  I understand why, and I don't really hold it against the design, but it's worth noting.
- The zooming in and out effect is very distracting, and detracts from the appreciation of the style at times.
- There is a distinct lack of clarity in explaining how the different powers work, and where they work.  And there are some choices in the level design that feel as though they are there to frustrate rather than be a challenge (like the double "jumping" sequences.)
Given that these complaints are pretty trivial, it's easy to see that I rate this game.  No, it's not a masterpiece, destined to appear in GotY lists, but it's far better than average.

The game plays out as long stretches of beautiful scenery and music, punctuated by an "Animal God Dungeon", where you gain access to a single ability to use through the dungeon. I fully enjoyed the two hours it took to traverse this very unique game. It's a little artistic, and some may find it pretensious. It suffers from the comparisons that have been made to the zelda series - including from the creators. I found the art, sounds, and light story elements to be engrossing, and the gameplay to be perfectly tuned in challenge given the small amount of game there actually is. I was pushed to near the breaking point a few times (why can't I warp through this laser section!) but never past it; and neither did I feel it was too easy and I was wasting my time. But make no mistake, each "dungeon" has a very linear path with very little exploration to be had.
I've seen complaints about the dungeons giving you abilities and then taking them away. I actually thought it was interesting and focused having each dungeon only allow a single ability, and makes the most out of what you can do with that ability. You only do ONE thing, but the challenge level is very fluid.  They are more skill-based than puzzle-based. There definitely is a lack of variation in gameplay.
The story is a little too light, and told in a disjointed style that makes it unclear what it is even about. It's more of a mood piece. I liked the mood, and if you are into the sort of writing where you have to fill in the blanks yourself to take whatever meaning you can take, you may like it. I found the writing probably the weakest part of the game.
The standout here is the art. It's a very different style, that plays with shapes, lines, layers, and negative space. Nearly every scene has standout elements that are not seen anywhere else in the game. If this doesn't interest you your experience with the game will be diminished. On the other hand, if those artistic merits do interest you, it's probably worth a playthrough for that alone.
Disclaimer: I was a kickstarter backer. I found the game to be... quite different from what I expected.

I usually don't read reviews when Im really interested in a game, boy was I wrong here.
This game offers choices. Lots of them, and one more brutal and morally despicable than the other. It's just that, I didn't get this until more than half way into the game. This game doesn't throw "decision points" around like "press F to ignore the geneva conventions". So, think of your actions. Consider consequences. It's not a really linear game.
And now to the actual review.
You lead a party of three Delta Ops into the City of Dubai that was supposed to be evacuated due to heavy sandstorms almost six months ago. What you search is the remains of the US Evac team including its leader and civillian survivors. What you find is death, despair, war crimes and five hundred million metric tons of sand.
For the graphics and audio, SpecOps keeps on proven grounds. Graphics are as good as UE3 can be. Sound is nice, with a very functional use of background music. The enemy soldiers could have used a few more lines to make their shouts less repetitive.
The scenery is a sad but beautiful apocalypse set in UAE's Dubai, desertified by extreme sand storms. The chapter "The Edge" was visually astonishing, backgrounds in the panoramic shots look a little static but still blend in really nice, The constant change between the hot desert outside and cool building interiors was refreshing and prevented boredom.
A special factor is the high verticality in the game. Dubai is a city of heights, and the game let's you feel that. Basements to rooftops, up and down dunes, a literal pit formed by high sand walls clinging to the many skyscrapers.
The gameplay followed that of a shooter: ambushes, firing from cover, two fairly useful AI teammates you have limited but effective control of. I am an experienced shooter player, some parts still made me to turn down the difficulty to "normal", as I simply died too often, but that's personal I guess. I found no particular glitches that "killed" me, so I guess the game is fair. Beware, ammunition is as scarce as you would expect in a desertified dead city.
For my personal experience, I  really liked it once I understood how the game actually works. It was difficult enough to be challenging, but not unfair. I also liked that the character models change over time to represent the ordeal they are advancing through.
The story begins as casual recon mission and quickly descends into unforgiving survival when the lives of all remaining city inhabitans lie in your hands. Will your choices relief the situation or make it worse? Who is your actual enemy? Are you an Angel of Life or Death? And, depending on your decisions, the game changes to: is it real what you see? Why did you actually come here? What the hell have you done? This game is somewhat "Apocalyse now".
For conclusion, I came to Dubai to help and rescue, and, considering my personal ending, I believe I became f*cking Hitler. I killed those I wanted to protect, starved all I did not kill, melted refugee kids with banned weapons and became a walking war crime. In the end I was happy with my gameplay, but dissapointed in myself.
10/10 should probably rethink real life ethics.

A guard walked into the hallway that i just came from. I could not see him, the door was between us. But he still saw me and shot me through the door. I never saw him but died anyways.
Other then that the rest of the game play was good. They added more complexity to the AI comments and behaviors. One example i liked was if you "accidentally" walked into an off limits area. In past games you would be automatically considered hostile and the guards would start shooting at you. In this Hitman they act like real people, they will tell you that you are not allowed in that area, they will escort you back outside of the area where you came from, then go about their business. They only get hostile if you refuse to comply.
Ive seen alot of review complain about graphics, or settings grayed out, low FPS, etc. I did not experience any of those problems. I could play on high/ultra settings (1920 x 1080), none of the settings where disabled, graphics were smooth, not one complaint. My video card is Nvidia GeForce GTX 780 Ti (12gig).
Alot of people also complain about the constant internet connection. Yes, i also agree that is crap and i had a problem with it. In the middle of playing their server went down, so i got kicked from my level back to the menu. My internet was online it was just the Hitman server that was offline. The game allowed me to switch to offline mode to play. But in offline mode it would not load the game save which was saved in online mode. I just stayed in offline mode, started the mission over from the beginning, and F their online mode.
Now for the really sucky part... If you read the fine print, they say that they are only releasing the game with the Paris content then plan to release more content 6 more times through out the year. The Paris content is literally *ONE* mission on one small map of a house. Yes its a big house, but still one location all the same. Really? I waited two years for this game to come out and paid $60 just to end up with one house and one mission??? I am not counting the two very small tutorial training maps you play first before unlocking the *ONE* mission. If you count those then you have three whole missions for $60. With the release of content 6 more times are those also going to be solo missions? So i have to wait a year just to get one complete game of a whooping 7 missions ?!?!?!?!?!? Oh' boy what a deal, not.
In a nut shell, yes it's a fun game.
Yes, Hitman fans will enjoy how they went back to their roots of being an open world/map with multiple solutions.
Thank you devs for allowing me to skip cut scenes. I hate it when games force you to watch their entire blah blah.
However i feel that the devs took the lazy approach releasing a game with only *ONE* mission. I feel very cheated compared to the past Hitman games.

EDIT: Just so that nobody ends up looking as outrageously stupid as "тнc » smoke", be sure to check the PPS explaining why the gameplay time looks as low as it is, when there was actually a lot more time invested (at least a couple of hours) than what Steam is displaying/recording. xD
Not to be mean, game has some promise and potential, but it just got so boring with only sailing all the time and ship-combat aside from some (sarcasm) rousing menu-simulator going on.
Which is sad, because this is the chain of events that got me to start playing the game.  Ever since playing AC: Black Flag many moons ago, constantly having an itch for pirate adventures.  Today I decided to browse around.  ArcheAge is a waste of time unless one wants to grind and be KoS'ed all the time, but I saw Voyage Century, Uncharted Waters Online, and Pirates of the Burning Sea.  Outside of PotBS, I had tried the other three before, and they were very underwhelming; but for some reason, I never got around, ever, to trying PotBS.  So, I started playing PotBS today, 06/18/17, and I actually rather liked it... in some ways it may be dated, but the game is a blast.
So anywho, what I did come to find in the game (PotBS), was the ship-combat seemed a lot more fun than the ground-combat and running around.  And I recall the ship-combat in AC: Black Flag being loads of fun... so decided to brush the dust off of Windward, which I got in a Humble-Bundle awhile ago, and finally give it a whirl... with a focus on just sailing and ship-battles, how could one go wrong.
Well, that's where it begins to massively unravel.  Game is okay, customization and configuration at the beginning of factions, and color-schemes, etc is really neat... but when the game starts and you play for awhile, it's the classic wide as an ocean, but deep as a puddle dilemma.
It's another of many "pop up menu at the docks" sailing games with a locked isometric-view, where you're constantly staring down at your ship with no means to zoom it in whatsoever, so the view you start with is all you constantly have the entire game (an ability to pan in behind the ship and have more of a graphical 3D view would be awesome!), with nothing but constantly seeing the water and the ship, which might be okay.  But then you just constantly sail, gather, quest (which quests you get at docks and they get put in your cargo-hold like inventory... for some that makes sense, but others not so much), grind, combat, etc.  If this released many moons ago on say the NES, SNES, or even the Gamecube, or even early Playstation 1 or 2, might not have been so bad as a quick time-waster console-game... but this is a PC game, that only released 2 years ago in 2015.
It's almost more of a clicker kind of game... since when you come across pirates or enemies, your ship will auto-fire at it and all you really need to do is circle it and watch the battle commence.  I was trying my hardest not to doze off while playing this, and I honestly wasn't tired when I originally started playing it... and even more bluntly honest, I wanted it to be much more fun than that! -_-
I'm gonna' have to shelf this again... because if all I did in this the entire time is JUST ship sailing constantly and auto-combat and grinding... I might find myself  burned out on other games such as PotBS, etc... which is a shame... was hoping this would be a fun "filler" kind of game when on a cool-down from PotBS and such... oh well, I guess... considering the state of today's gaming-industry, guess I shouldn't be all that shocked.  Even if it were more of a pleasure-cruise exploration, there's so much more that could be done and/or added to make it more fulfilling as such.  Perhaps allow people to get off on land and piers/town and walk around with a top-down old-school pixelated character (think Dragon Warrior or original Ultima and/or Final Fantasy) that can explore around, dig for treasure, fish, etc... perhaps even build/upgrade a house and/or your faction's village.
Another thing that I found bizarre, is even though it allowed me to customize SIX factions, which I tried to make really unique and interesting, even on the largest map (33x33), it would only allow me to place FOUR factions!?  What happened to the other 2 that I customized!? >_<
PS - I also typically rather enjoy when a game comes with native gamepad support, which this does, and perhaps there's a way to reconfigure it, but the default controls are REALLY janky!  The heal skill you press the A button (or X since I'm using a PS3 controller), then press down on the D-pad to apply it... for manual combat/cannons you use B (or Circle on PS3 controller), but no matter what button I seem to push, I can't seem to get it to acknowledge on a target (Circle and X don't seem to do anything) unless I drop the controler and mouse-click (at which point I can see the reticle flicker as if acknowledge, rather than vanish like X and Circle do)... must have missed which button does that.  (Would also be nice if there were more to a docking-process rather than just coming to a stop at the end of a dock and pressing down on the d-pad... maybe more or a process, like furling in sails, dropping anchor, chucking a rope to the dock, and then coming ashore.)
PPS - And even though I played this game for AT LEAST two hours... Steam seems to think it was only played for a single minute!?  *facepalm* (Thinking it may be because I made a desktop icon/shortcut for my Nimi Places container... so this may be old-school enough that unless launched directly from Steam it won't record gameplay time!?  Which actually doesn't happen with ANY other game I have on Steam, and I have a ton!)  Apparently a person needs to have at least 5 minutes "on record" to review, so loaded the game and just let it run long enough for me to post this.  So even though my gameplay time looks low, it's actually quite a bit more than that! >:(
EDIT: After perusing the forums a bit, and perusing around on the webs... seems some devs have "inspiration" (as a developer so eliquently phrased it on the forums) from older shut-down titles/creations to then take said material, roll it around a bit, and rerelease it as their own... sad in a way... to have the ability and opportunity to make something unique and make the most out of the platform/foundation, and instead recycle something that's been done and shut-down numerous times before. :-|
FINAL VERDICT: Game is rubbish/trash... and the overly toxic fanboys defending it rather prove that all too well.  ;)

My only qualm is that the actually fighting system isn't that different from the first Avernum; those who have played the first game may find the second to be a little uninteresting in terms of battle.

Short version: If you never played Exile II or the first Avernum II, play this version.  If you have, I'd skip it.
I really, really, really want to like this game.  I've played every game that Spiderweb has put out since the mid-90s, from the first Exile game.  But this one I really can't recommend.  Short version: this game just feels kind of lazy.
For me the biggest issue is that Spiderweb really doesn't try anything that new with this one.  There are a few additional areas and big fights, but that's really it, which isn't really enough for a third incarnation of the same story; the game is, for the large part, mostly the same as it was in the previous incarnations.  If you've played either Spiderweb's Avadon or Geneforge series (both totes recommended, especially Geneforge), then you known how many choices you face in those games and how intricate the outcomes can be.  Nothing like this has been included in the updated Avernum games, where it is sorely needed.
Nobody plays Spiderweb games for pretty graphics, but there are some things here which I think are just not cool.  Many, many, of the enemy models are also just recolors, some of them used six or seven times, with very few new models introduced from the recent Escape game. If you go and look at the sprite sheets for the original Exile games, which are very lovely pixel art, you can see the huge variety of characters.  A lot of the models are also from older Spiderweb games, some going back 15ish years, and the newer and older models reallly don't go well together  -- it's painfully obvious which are newer and which are older.  Again, it just feels kind of lazy.
There's lots of text I remember reading in Exile II, which says something very good about the writing that I can remember it over 15 years later, but using so much text again just feels kind of cheap.
If you never played Exile II or the first Avernum II, then you may want to go ahead and play this game, but I'd skip it if you've played either.

Just like the first Avernum, Avernum 2 takes a 25-year old story-driven party-based RPG and gives it a modern overhaul. Those who enjoyed the first one will definitely want to keep going through this episode as the formula has even been improved on a little with some UI and design tweaks. (thanks for the weight changes!)
Overall, it's a long and deep RPG experience with full party customization and a gripping storyline and environment. I would imagine this experience would be greatly reduced by someone who hasn't played the first one, since the lore and background represents so much of the game. And as you can obviously tell from the screenshots, don't come here for visual flash -- it's really not the point.

What I think about the game:
Good game. High-end RPG elements and a fun game to try and solo. Lots of secret areas and good reasons to actually get skills like cave lore, and others. I like to compare this to BG2:SOA it feels to me like a successor. It's got a great story and pretty cool how there is a lot of places to explore.
Personal Gripe:
I wish there was more utility when it comes to the mage and maybe even allow for non-cheese solo play. I tend to gravitate to a competitive solo-run because with a party it is really too easy. Blink is an insane spell to have on a mage but, since you can only really cast once a turn unless hasted or potted it's really hard to distance yourself as a mage.
I feel like in these types of games you should be able to solo if you understand the mechanics enough. Then again I am not the dev and TBH they did a fantastic job with the strengths and weaknesses of each class.
Conclusion: If you don't mind reading and near-perfect RPG elements pick this game up. It's literally the best RPG I've purchased in a while.

Avernum 2: Crystal Souls is a modern remake of their earlier game, Exile 2: Chystal Souls.
While I have found it to be an enjoyable game, it is worth noting that in spite of the graphical improvements, there are a few things that were cut back.
1. You now control a smaller party of four adventuriors, where in the past you could field as many as six. That's right, you used to be able to change your party size. You could even take the crazy route and try to solo the game. Not anymore.
2. Food. In the past you needed food in order to survive, needing to either stock up or forage as you go in order to not die of starvation. Now, food is just a weak healing item.
3. Spells have been completely revamped. One noticable absence being persistant area effect attacks. You could, for example, lay a field of ice shards that damages any who enter or remain in the field, creating an artificial barrier as it were. Most of the spell effects seem to be copy pasta from their other games... Fire bolts, buffs and the like.
It isn't a bad game. Far from it. It is just somewhat sad to see it scaled down to fit in a more modern game engine.

I played the original Exile II Crystal Souls when I was a lot younger and fell in love with it. This most recent remake does a wonderful job of bringing the game up to date while staying true to the original. I like the tweaks and changes, the game is much more user friendly, and it's just as addictive. Worth getting if you're a fan of the originals or new to the series and just  really like good indie rpgs.

Short review: Rogue Legacy. A "Rogue"-like game that follows your family's "Legacy" after each death, allowing you to select and heir of your last victim and charge back into the action.
Long Review:
[Possible spoilers, even though this is not exactly a story-driven game.]
Rogue Legacy follows the classic formula of Rogue-Likes; it throws you straight into the deep end, and watches you drown. You begin as a very unskilled player, and a very underpowered character to reflect this. However, the more you play, the better you get. Each death becomes a learning opportunity. To continue the allegory- you learn to swim from drowning a lot. Surviving for long enough will allow you to upgrade your character, and those upgrades carry over to subsequent characters. Essentially, it's a game about your learning curve. Your skills as a player must increase for you to win, but your character's skills do not have to (although it is immensely helpful). You grow stronger along with your character, but at vastly different rates. Once the movement-aiding items are aquired, the curve becomes slightly skewed, due to your sudden influx of power. Eventually, after many, many deaths, you'll defeat the final boss and smile at your attempts.
To aid, harm, amuse, ruin, confuse and humiliate you are Traits. These are some of the most fun (or frustrating) aspects of the game. Whenever you die (which will happen, a lot) you are presented a selection of heirs. Each heir (usually) has 1-3 traits which modify the gameplay experience with that certain character. "PAD" means you have no foot pulse, so floor traps have no effect on that character. "Dwarfism" means that your character is tiny, with a smaller hitbox. "Colour Blindness" makes the screen black and white. "Clumsy" means you destroy all breakable items you touch. These little flavours of intrique spice the game up, like a shooter at a football match.
However, it's not all good. The bosses, although difficult in some areas, are rather generic. Most enemies are simply different-coloured variants of the same sprite. Obviously, this due to budgeting, but I must mention it for the impact it has on the gameplay. The bosses have no phases (except for one) nor "attack patterns" in the conventional sense. Really, they're just harder versions of the same creature, which is reinforced by their re-used sprite. It also lessons the variety of enemy types you can get if you simply have slightly different enemies with slightly different damage and health numbers. Back to the bosses, the majority of them are floating spherical objects. A floating skull. A floating fireball. A floating eye. This lessens the variety between each boss, and makes them just not as entertaining to fight.
For it's developer budget and market pricing, this is definitely a great game for value, and for people who like Rogue-Likes. It's drawbacks are it's relatively small variety in enemies, and lack of additional sprites. But again, this game was made with a small team and low budget.
Worth a buy, but as per usual, try to get it on sale...

Rogue Legacy is a good rogue-lite.  There's heaps of unlockables and seeing all the different "mutations" or "genes" of your successors can be really fun. There's certainly a lot of variety in the first few hours but eventually it sorta becomes a grind and the enemies in new areas tend to be reskins of old. I digress, there's a lot of fun to be had here and it's a very high quality game. Looks good, sound effects and music are serviceable, a decent time-sink all in all. I unfortunately lost my save when I cleared my hard drive and don't really have the motivation to go through the early game unlocks and minutiae of not feeling very strong to begin with. Oh, also make sure you have a controller because keyboard + mouse controls are awful.
I recommend picking it up on sale. $5 is a great price for it imo.

In its current state, I think this game only warrants a purchase if you are a fan of survival games like Don't Starve and sims like Fallout Shelter, but most importantly, you want to support this developer right now.
In my opinion, the game is simply unfinished, and if the developers don't make some serious changes, it will have a serious lack of replay value....
The game is full of interesting mechanics and has randomly generated worlds, which encourages you to play the game like a rogue-lite and experiment with different approaches. However, you will quickly find yourself caught in the similar pattern of relying on certain technologies over others. The real joy comes in refining your approach to these problems and adapting to the world they give you.
HOWEVER
"Stress" is a major prohibitive factor in this game, something the devs placed way too much emphasis on, effectively killing the pacing of this game. Because of this, you will find yourself spamming decor throughout your base to keep duplicants happy, slowing down more pressing (and lets be honest more interesting) tasks, like refining your base and seeking out better pockets of resources.
But by far the biggest issue with this game is the COMPLETE LACK of reward system for long playthroughs. Unlike Don't Starve, this game gives you absolutely nothing if you decide to try for a long playthrough. This confounds me, as it basically loses its replay value with one playthrough. I did everything in my first seven hours... in one try...
Why not give you skill points to spend on buffing up duplicant's skills when printing new duplicants? Why not grant access to more interesting decor items to craft? Why not unlock "special" characters with hyped skill values that you can bring in mid-game? These aren't crazy ideas to implement....
So I have to keep this review as a negative one. I think this game has incredible potential, and it feels like they would be rushing an incomplete product if this is all they have to offer once out of development. They need to offer players something that will make them want to come back for another playthrough, and I think they should rebalance how stress is triggered in this game. Death, combat, starvation - those are stressful things... people shouldn't get immediately stressed out from having to look at ugly pipes, that needs to be rebalanced. Stress should be a mid-game, late-game issue, not something you're fretting over after 3-4 cycles. Terrible balance with that right now.

I want to enjoy this game.  I can honestly see all the potential it has.  But I I have to hesitate in giving it a full thumbs up, but it's also not a full thumbs down.  As this is being written during Early Access, I can forgive any shortcomings.  Like I said, I can see the potential.  But try as I might, I'm just not feeling it.
To start, I've always loved these types of games and felt they never made enough.  A space sim seems to have unlimited potential, but I prefer to avoid things that require subscriptions and groups like MMOs.  Conversely, I recall fond memories of doing just that in Earth and Beyond, lo so many years ago.  But what I loved most about Earth and Beyond is I recall enjoying crafting my ship and making it mine.  I'd say the same for the Lightspeed add-on to Star Wars Galaxies.  Clunky though it was, I thoroughly enjoyed taking those ship parts I blasted out of enemy ships and hoarding them, finally upgrading when I would get the time and adding it to my ship.  I felt like I owned that more.  Though you can certainly buy different ship parts here, there aren't that many right now, and some of the differences aren't readily apparent.  I can't even easily compare the old with the new.
Funny enough, I started drawing comparisons to, of all things, the game FTL.  Though you don't actively fly a single thing, and the game basically consists of just a handful of screens, it does give you the ability to upgrade your ship in a way that makes you feel like you're in control of it.  And while even the upgrades themselves are a simple thing, I never really find myself using the same configuration over and over again because I find random things and random times.  Here, I feel less like I'm thinking on my feet and thinking more about where I'm flying next (fun, yes, but limited).
Similarly, again, Early Access-itis: you get plopped into the game and are told nothing.  Zippo.  Sure, the tutorial is there, but it's not interactive.  It tells you what to do on one screen, then you need to close it out to try it, and  then reactivate the tutorial screen to move on.  Very clunky.  On the plus side, the controls feel pretty good and are easily customized, and yet, for it being space, it feels rather tight.  Granted, it's a game, so not everyone wants to sit there and patiently watch the seconds tick away, but it almost feels too quick.  It is space, after all.  If only to hammer the point home, once I figured out how to get where I was going, it didn't seem like I had to do much once I got there.
I also wonder about the items you get.  They don't seem to have much more purpose than to provide you with money.  And while that's all good, it also seems very limited.  Okay, I've got a cargo hold full of all these different things...that don't have anything special about them other than how much money they fetch you.  Then what?  Wash, rinse, repeat?  I could see where  the full game, story and all, would provide more substance, but I would hope it's substantial, because right now, like I said, I don't feel "at home" in this game.  I don't feel like I have a reason to be out flying, that my ship is no different than any other NPC ship flying around, randomly doing things "just because."
So, like I said to start, I can see the potential: it looks amazing, the controls are customizable and feel natural, and there appears to be a real desire to embrace the mysteries of space.  Unfortunately, things feel like they move real fast, that customization needs to be greatly expanded to get some real tinkering done on ship, and that I'm not just moving from A to B to A again.
That said, I eagerly await more content and gladly support the game.

This, game. I am enjoying it for all the reasons I bought it. Specifically, the play a game with the full freedom to drift aimlessly in space to look at something and say to myself... "I should go there" and be able to go there.  Issues arise in that so far there is no campaign, so there is a no guided leveling structure. Which is nice and freeform, but leaves you with a... "hrmm, now what", feeling similar to the sims or minecraft if you don't have a personal goal.  So far, you start off as  a rather beefy frigate off the bat, and from there are told there are other things you can do with your life beyond be a pirate/merc. Don't listen to that voice, stealing ships via boarding parties is the only way of acquiring money relatively quickly beyond the rare, bounty list job.
Which brings up space combat! This is both so much fun, and so much rage. Fun part! Depending on your choice of weapons, you are able to join random battles in space with next to no reprecursions as the two parties fight for life and you zap your enemy (see red guy), due to some laughably long range and guess shooting. Or you are able to watch in horror as you enter an area of space where everyone has some horrifyingly powerful guns that destroy your shields, hull, and happiness before you can make a pass at escape. Major issue is that you don't know what they are packing in weapons, you can't tell untill they open up on you, and the little info blerp provided is vague, very much so.
The description varies from "trivial" to "Impossible", but you are not informed how they are rated to determine threat level to you. I seem to think it is an unspoken amalgamation of your ships type, and load out mixed with your level. But!  Trivial enemies in twos can wreck your life for reasons you are unsure of (maybe they are small glass cannons that are only GUN). Deadly enemies can just float around you in vain trying to bring their weapons to bare before dying to the explosion of their metal death trap.  Also, each ship has a load out of weapons, that are placed on four compass based directions on your ship, and each has a firing arc that is not discussed much, and even some of the fully decked vessels will always have blind spots in their firing patern.  So you are shooting, zapping, and hitting with all due fun then slightly tilt your ship to the left and stop. The weapons also have a range... which is an ignorable text box since it only matters in "Fire at Will" mode, unless you are being shot at then your AI ignore it just like you do and open up shooting everything like a Ork Freeboota.
Exploration is fun, though potentially deadly since the whole area is teeming with bandits looking for the sweet rolls in your ships captain's quarters. There are about four mains ways of travel. Cruising, which is deadly and fun since for no reason at you can be cruising at a great speed (you think) then are knocked out of your cruise mode by pirates wanting you dead even if they are in no way a threat.  Or there are T-gates! Think stargate and that is exactly it, you anchor at the place and for a modest fee, travel in safety from one end of space to another point in space! T-gates are almost always at a space station/planet you can dock at (if your faction rep says so) and are the safest (relatively) way to go long distances.  Then there are wormholes..... wormholes are kinda like t-gates, if t-gates were a game you pay for up front, wormholes are the f2p that suck you in and slowly rob you with you having no knowledge where you are going. They are free to use, but they will kill your troopers (dudes you have on board to steal ships or keep yours from being stolen) each time and break your ship a little. And when I said sucked in I mean they have a gravity well that pull you into it and spits you out of another one, which is great but that other one has a gravity well too that pulls you into it. If not careful and if there are different pairs of wormholes nearby you can end up alone on your now burning ship on the other side of the map not really wanting to try to return.   Lastly there is an item that lets your teleport your ship in a circular radius of map hexes based on how many you want to use at time. Only to hexes you have already been to, semi safe since you have no clue what is waiting for you, can get expensive (you need a massive amount of the already costly items to even trying moving halfway cross map) but you wont get jumped on route like in cruising so, win?
Lastly for now is the level up process... You can get experience from quests (variable from oh, nice to meh), and pirati- I mean defending your local area from them pirates and invaders. What does it do? lets you level certain skills you have chosen based on a life style of play I do not think impacts game too greatly. Really for most of the area I forget to use the things until I am nearly dying and go Save Me Buttons!  And Perks, perks are like skills but they are not tied to the action skills, they are always active.   Skills and Perks I think would be more impacting if they were not so dang situational, the buttons are very much a maybe use. Perks are very tied to certain aspects of the game, but are not acquired quickly enough to even remember to check for them. Or feel like they even do much when used.  It is a nice, balanced feature, but when you are able to reset your skills and perks the choices are less impacting on your decision time.
I still am very happy I spent the cash on it, and if you like SPESS PIRATEZ, then you can be one in this one.  I do hope they keep this mode active if they come out with a story mode too.

with 1 place being the best. These are awared either on time or points and failing to meet the conditions causes you to fail the mission.
Freeride mode is the where you can follow along with the games story, contacting NPC's with your phone and performing missions for them. The missions you do in Freeride Mode are the same as the missions on the main menu but come about at random times when the NPC's contact you through your phone. There are two story areas for Freeride Mode, Countryside and Offroad and as well as selecting the area, you can select the weather or if you just want to drive without the story.
There are various types of missions in Russian Car Driver, these missions being Drag Racing, Drifting, Parking, Rally and Racing. which are acquired by completing the various challenges in the game.

Before going any further, I'd like to acknowledge the performance and server issues. I'm currently running a GTX 770, and I can say that the performance is alright, my FPS dips in certain places, but jumps back up to around 55-60 FPS. One major gripe for the performance is how certain graphical options are greyed out, depending on your system. I'm not a big fan of this, and would rather it just be removed and let someone select what option they want. Regarding server issues, they are to be expected on day one, but that doesn't make it much better.
The major problem with the servers is that the game is
, meaning if you get disconnected you can and will get locked out of certain options, for example contracts mode, whilst disconnected. Furthermore, challenges and what not are also locked whilst disconnected. This is probably my major problem with the game thus far.
However, gameplay wise the game is fantastic. Whilst playing I didn't personally encounter any bugs, and had fun trying out a couple different ways of assassinating the targets. The animations and sound design also appear quite fluid and nice.
As I am writing this review, I was not able to try out the contracts mode, however if it is anything like the contracts mode in Hitman: Absolution it should be very good.
Lastly, I understand that people are complaining about the episodic nature of the game, however I wouldn't consider that a negative in this review, as you should be well aware of that before going ahead with the purchase.
Overall, once the performance and server issues are fixed, I can recommend a fan of the Hitman franchise to buy the introduction version of this game. I believe with the Paris level and contracts mode; the $15 USD is worth it. However, if you are not a Hitman fan, I suggest reading up on some more reviews and watching some gameplay before going ahead with a purchase. Lastly, I find it very hard to recommend the 'Full experience' version of the game, buying each EP. individually only ends up costing $5 USD extra, and is a much safer bet.
I'll update this review if a performance patch is released, or when EP. 2 is released.
Thanks for reading guys and gals.

Spec Ops: The Line is not a game. No, I refuse to call it a game. Instead, a more fitting way to label this piece of work would be, 'art'. Plain and simple. Just as the 'Fountain' by Marcel Duchamp was a big slap to the face for the art commmunity on 'What is Art?', Spec Ops: The Line does the same for the Gaming Community on, 'What are Modern Military Shooters?' It takes the Badass, Stone-Cold, Heroic and invulnerable killing machine protaganist typical in your everyday Military Shooter and tears it to pieces with its masterful story.
This poigant work will really help making you wonder what it means to be a hero and needs to be played in order to be understood. To be honest, I feel like I ripped off the developers for buying this game when it was on a $6 deal.
The less you know, the better the game.
________________________________________________________________
Story
Dubai was hit with a series of sandstorm that ravaged the city and turned it into a Kid's Sandbox basically. Colonel John Konrad, a decorated Officer in the US army and the 33rd 'Damned' Infantry Regiment volunteered to help the evacuated the city. Nothing was heard from them ever since until 6 Months Later when a Distress Signal by Konrad himself reaches out to the world. This is where you come in. You're Captain Walker, leader of a 3 Man Delta Team Operative sent to investigate Dubai for any survivors. (Cliche, Badass 3 Man Special Forces Protaganist trying to get stuff done and take care of business where others failed.)
This is about as much as you need to know to understand what's going on.
________________________________________________________________
Gameplay
(AI)
Enemy AI seem to be good enough, alway shouting out what their doing and responding to each other in turn. There are 4 types of enemies Regular, Close-Combat, Sniper and Heavy. * = can be armoured, ie more durable
Regular* - The Grunts. SMG/Shotgunners/Assault Rifle all day, everyday. Shotgunners tend to charge at you which can be a danger
Close-Combat - Remember that Banzai Soldier from World at War? This is him except that its 1 hit kill, he dodges and insta-kills you with his knife when he gets close (Yes, no QTE)
Sniper* - He snipes? Also has shiny red laser sight which you can see since its tagging you
Heavy* - Always comes armoured and just like the Bulldozer from Payday 2, his face is his weakspot. There are 2 varieties of the 'Heavy', M249 Saw or AA12. Either way you're boned as they love walking straight up to you... Jerks
Don't worry about your AI though as they are okay-ish enough to get stuff done though they tend to go suicidal when you issue an attack order. They have no problem in getting kills or distracting enemies and will always shout out enemies of interest during a firefight such as, "Shotgunner coming from the right!". Take note that this needs to be heard as battle lines are not subtitled. What can be annoying though is when they take too much damamge, they need to be revived and you have a time limit but you don't have the ability to be revived (On Hard, idk about normal and easy)
(Core)
The meat of the game comes from being a Cover-Based Third Person Shooter reminiscent to that of games like Gears of War. Basically, you sprint form cover to cover (Using a Toggle Key 'Space') and rely on Regenerating Health. The lower your health, the more bloodied your screen becomes in addition to being Black and White (CoD anyone?). There are 15 weapons in total give or take which felt the same with only the diffference being its 'Alternate Function' key which is 'C'. There are also 3 grenade types, Frag, Sticky and Stun which are pretty self-explanatory. You can carry 2 weapons and all 3 grenade types at once. However, you are only limited to 3 grenades per type making the total number of grenades which can be carried to 9(3 Frags/3 Stickies/3 Stuns). Different from other games is how ammo is obtained here. While there is still the basic, 'pick up ammo from dead body so long as same weapon' concept, what Spec Ops has added to spice it up is that in this game is that you can actually Execute wounded enemies to get ammo for your current weapon type. Because you know.. Executions are fun. Be fast though or they'll bleed out to death(GoW anyone)
In a nutshell, it's your run of the mill Third Person Cover based shooter like Gears of War or Future Soldier.. Just like any other games where you're the unstoppable saviour of your country.
(Command)
As Leader, you have control of 2 Squad Mates who use order via the MMB. They are:
Lieutenant Adams
Your Heavy Weapons Specialist carrying the M249 Saw. Order him to attack an enemy so long as their close and he'll do two things. FIrst, he unleashes hell on them with suppressive fire from his weapon. Second, he throws a frag which finds its mark 90% of the time, the 10% due to the enemy running away from it
Sergeant Lugo
Your Sniper. Order him to attack an enemy from long range and he'll kill the guy so long as he has vision. Though it takes some time for him to pull the trigger, its usually a 1-shot kill
As you can see, the command aspect in this game is very weak but simple enough to make life easy.
(Environment)
Alongside your Red Explosive Containers, you also have the sand which can either help or hinder you. Firstly, Sand can act as either an alternative form of Explosive Barrels. Secondly, throwing an explosive into a pile of sand would create a sand cloud which effectively stuns all nearby enemies for a nice amount of time, similar to Stun grenades if I'm not mistaken. Later in the game at set stages, you'll come across Sandstorms which does two things. Making you unable to issue orders and increasing weapon spread. Extremely frustrating, especially on harder difficulties (15+ deaths on Hard)
Nothing revolutionary here really though I'll admit its interesting in theory.
(Misc)
Collectables are available in the game and are called Intels. The number of intels available in each level is shown by pressing Escape. It offers backstory to the world of Dubai and its inhabitants. As of the time this review was written, no Steam Trading Cards are available. Checkpoints in this game seem to be fair enough. 1 checkpoint pre and post engagement.
________________________________________________________________
Music and Sound
I like the music. It's nice... very Vietnam War-esque and is also perfectly timed and well-executed. It's either Gung Ho adrenaline fueled action or music that make you muse over your actions.
Sound also seems to be quite good though the sound of the AA12 doesn't seem to have too much force behind it. Other than that, the sound can of this game can really make firefights here intense, especially on higher difficulties.
________________________________________________________________
Graphics
It looks nice enough if you really care so much about it. It's able to capture the violence and carnage you unleash (Yay carnage and violence cause that's what every military shooter needs right!... right?)
________________________________________________________________
Mutiplayer
There are two types of Multiplayer here.
Co-Op
2 players, 4 levels. A bit of a challenge when communication between the two is lacking. Can be fun for the first few times though I believe that it will lose its charm as fast as you finish it
Competetive
4v4 PvP from what I heard though sadly the cream of this game comes from the SP hence why I never bothered to try it out.
________________________________________________________________
Overall
Story is honestly speaking the saving grace for this game. It's what made it so spectacular as the entire gameplay is bland, rehashed and has been done countless times though it can be argued that the very fact that it copies its gameplay from other Military Games is what makes this so good. This is because of how Spec Ops question our beliefs on said game. Must buy.

I don't know if there is anyone left out there to convince of "Spec Ops: The Line"'s significance in gaming history, but just in case...
This game has done more work towards games being considered an artistic medium than any other game ever made. Period. This game is art. It isn't some floaty pretentious nonsense from the xbox live arcade, the developers of this game wanted it to invoke actual emotion in the player, and that is exactly what it does. Fear, confusion, anger and sadness.
Self-loathing.
I doubt that a game has ever made you really cry before. I mean you're in charge of your own choices, what do you have to be sad about? if you screw up you can start again. We live in a society that consider games escapism. Even a good story well told in a game is often hard to take seriously. Spec Ops is not escapism, it is a massive sucker punch in the stomach. It wont make you cry... it's not that sort of experience, but it will tell you a lot about yourself. It will make you ask questions about why you do some of the things you do. Spec Ops deconstructs what we have made to be "normal" in modern games with such aptitude that I haven't been able to play a military shooter the same way since.
Spec Ops - The Line is a masterpiece.

There are games that can get away with refusing to explain themselves or making use of interesting and alternative art to convey something one could not otherwise do.
This does not appear to be one of them.
The most immediately upsetting factor is the way the game appears to try and disguise the cheapness of its graphics as a stylistic choice. Yet the innumerable rectangular paths, enemies and elements betray the fundamental cheapness of the game. A cheapness that simply cannot be papered over by the otherwise quite interesting art.
Worse still, it simply isn't any fun.
A game of combat must be a test of skill, of mastery. It should challenge the player and demand that they understand how to utilize the mechanics of the game to the fullest.
A game of puzzles must contain meaningfully interesting puzzles, rather than pretend as if defeating enemies moving in set patterns is even remotely interesting.
In the end, I can only ask the developers why they thought anyone would actually wish to play this, and if they don't know, why they tried to push it to sales, rather than learn to make something people would like.

Animal Gods ultimately promises more than it can deliver on; the graphics will draw you in but the gameplay will let you down.
This is not Zelda, it's half action puzzler, half story-focused adventure, but it is master of neither. Each dungeon provides you with a singular mechanic to play with; the Snake dungeon gives you a sword, the Spider dungeon gives you a bow, and the Lion dungeon gives you a 'flame cloak' that will teleport you forward a short distance. Sadly, you can't use these elements together up until the very end.
The enemies are merely boxes; the story suggests they are more, but it doesn't come through in the gameplay. Additionally, the gameplay is quite tedious when trying to overcome the enemy obstacles; you'll find yourself standing slightly away from a box's path to slash at them with the sword, or waiting for the appropriate time to shoot your bow, and you never have to deviate your strategy.
Within the Lion dungeon, you're required to use the cloak to teleport past poison rivers. The cloak will send you a fixed distance away, but there is no indicator of how far you're going to go, and since there's free movement, you'll often just have to eyeball the distance and trial-and-error your way through.
Animal Gods' story is interesting, but lacking; it raises lots of questions about the world, the Animal Gods, and a few characters mentioned within the various diary entries and logbooks, but provides no closure or answers. It feels unfinished and unpolished.
One example of this is a pair of buildings in the overworld with half-hearts on each one. It suggests that you should be able to push them together somehow to complete the heart, but you can't.
The bosses are little more than glorified mazes to walk through, defeating the same enemies as you defeated before them, and progressing to checkpoints. The final boss is no exception, albeit slightly longer. The game clocks in at around 2 hours, which surprised me - the logs gave some backstory and then, all of a sudden, I was at the credits screen with more questions than answers.
Animal Gods is a pretty game, but not a fun one. It's not worth your time or money, even on sale.

*minor spoilers ahead*
As I traversed the toxin flooded snake god dungeon I carefully inched my way forward, decapitating each Husk from one save point to the next, nimbly dancing from one moving platform to the next. As I bash each of their blue shells into finely ground mush I notice their sad looking eyeballs follow me around the room and reflect on my earlier encounters with the creatures in the game. There's a good deal of evidence given throughout the game in the form of dialogue and diaries that they're sapient and intelligent, and at one point were the ancient human villagers who once populated the entire area. After much effort I finally reach the final stretch, a series of fast moving enemy spawns with narrow walkways taking place on the back of the snake god itself.
Looking at how spread apart the enemies are, I suddenly realize that I can run through this entire gauntlet without killing a single enemy. Some parts are tricky, but with proper timing I manage to zip past each obstacle. None of the enemies make any attempt to hunt me down, many of the bigger ones near the end aren't even moving and I have plenty of space to simply walk around them. Why am I supposed to be attacking them again, when they aren't even a threat? Maybe if I continue to avoid them, the game will recognize that I'm trying to show some mercy on these people, I think. Maybe the snake god will comment on my deliberate willingness to make the game more difficult in an attempt to be more than just some single minded killing machine.
But no, nothing happens, the only way you can finish the dungeon is to (once again) kill enough of the Husks near the end to trigger the exit warp.
Why do scenarios like this bother me? Maybe I've been playing too much Undertale lately, or maybe I've just grown into too much of a cynic to blindly accept typical RPG tropes- but a game that requires you to massacre living, sentient creatures as an arbitrary ritual to progress from one hallway to the next is not something that I can consider morally intelligent. I end up feeling like Thistle is really not any better of a person than the supposedly evil unseen antagonist. It would be somewhat acceptable to me if the game made an attempt to present Thistle as anything but a morally pure priestess, but it doesn't, which pretty much tears down the central theme of the game (the ends do not always justify the means).
Anyways, for everything else I like (the laser jumping puzzles are fun and the controls are good) and dislike (the game is way too short and predictable), this experience sticks out to me the most. I don't feel like I can rightly recommend this when it killed any semblance of immersion to me.

TL;DR:
The graphics are behind the curve, and the GUI is a little clunky, but indie RPGs don't get much better than this.
The only slightly longer version:
Spiderweb is a tiny studio that's been making great RPGs for decades, and this one is just as good, if not better, than their previous titles.
The Avernum series, like all Spiderweb games, is focused on tactical combat and exploration. This is a game that rewards you for exploring every nook and cranny in towns, the wilderness and dungeons. There's almost no end to the secret passages to find, locks to pick, chests to loot, and lizardmen to skewer. I'm not kidding. If you aren't checking every dead end, or looking behind every wall, you're likely missing something.
The dungeons are usually filled with a handful of interesting combat encounters, and the turn-based combat is solid. There's plenty of spells, martial abilites, lots of the expected consumables (scrolls, potions, wands), special traits, and skill trees that allow for a classless system while still encouraging you to specializes your party members. Enemies tend to have special abilities that make combat interesting and usually more dangerous, such as poison, damage auras, slowness, elemental immunities, and so on.
If you like classic RPGs, lots of exploration, and tactical combat, and don't need the latest graphics, I suggest picking this up!

Bored of playing low so called "rpg" games like smash-LMB to win Skyrim or ME, where one button does everything? If you don't care about graphics also, Avernum should be perfect for you.  Ideal exploration, tactical combat and party building, with some proper challenge thrown there and there. Who needs more? Screw plot and choices, dungeon crawling in best form here.

Excellent old-school RPG with turn based combat. As the case with other Spiderweb Software games, it's slightly difficult to recommend though. The game delivers in terms of great world to explore, character development and interesting story as well. It is really closer to Baldur's Gate/Icewind Dale type of experience. Coupled with the isometric 2D graphics entire dialogue and quest content is delivered through huge amount of text. Don't get me wrong - story is excellent, but from experience trying to share Avernum series with friends, it really isn't everyone's cup of tea. So, please take my (and others') recommendation with a grain of salt.
The game is natural step forward from the previous remake (Avernum: Escape From The Pit) and while minor upgrades are there, it mostly plays and looks the same. Unfortunately, some of the interface problems are still there, for example the infamous inventory issue is still there (when you press "I", inventory opens, but you can't close it with "I"), but these are truly minor in my opinion.
It's worth to mention that when it comes to system requirements, you can probably play this on your washing machine too, so if you are stuck somewhere with a decade old laptop or something, you can probably play this game without problems.

TLDR version:  If you like tactical fantasy RPGs and don't have to have tip-top graphics, this is an excellent game you should purchase whether you've played Escape from the Pit or not.
Obviously this isn't a full review, but as somebody who's played every one of Jeff Vogel's games, including the prior remake Avernum: Escape from the Pit, I have a pretty good idea what I'm getting into and what you should be getting into.
Vogel's had 2 decades to refine his skills, and while his budget isn't as big as pretty much any other studio out there, he puts a lot of heart and soul into his games.  Especially with Crystal Souls, he's taken the best of fan mods to Escape from the Pit and put his own twist on them, bringing a hugely fun fantasy RPG adventure with very tactical turn based combat.  The difficulty settings make it so that everyone can have the level of challenge they want, even switching mid game if a particular fight gets too hard for you or you decide you've got the hang of it.  He's really tightened up the UI in general since the old days too, making the flow a lot smoother.
The skill trees provide diversity without being confusing, it's easy to see what kind of characters you want and go straight for it.  Magic sometimes feels overpowered, but there's always the enemies that are nearly immune to it, making a balanced party makeup helpful and desirable the whole time through.
The story in the original Crystal Souls game was excellent, and just like the remake of Escape from the Pit, Vogel is keeping the best parts intact while introducing multiple new areas and bosses to the game.  I could go on for a while, but I think I'll just close with the fact that even the games of Vogel's I was sure I didn't like I ended up loving when I tried them, so you really just can't go wrong if you think you're at all interested.

Lots of spoilers are shown, read below at your own risk...
---
Learning curve: Much like titrating phosphoric acid with sodium bicarbonate, slow and long, and even longer in recent updates
The hints shown give you a few information to start with but not until the Amber Hint Sign is shown do you understand some really basic facts about the duplicants ("dupes") like the energy (counted "kcal" in game) required for survival, and more to learn...by trial-and-errors as some are not shown by hints or warnings.
5.5/10
In-game information: Much like what politician says, you must be skeptical to some degree
The term "renewable" is shown for Algae description and yet many will find it must be harvested from terrain squares almost non-stop to keep your lower level oxygen generators such as Terranium and Deoxygenator going (before you find Steam Geyser to use Electrolyzer, but the Geysers are too few and scattered to best utilize them) or your stupid dupes will die of asphyxia.
A few of the minerals and liquids are fantasy but they have very little influence in game (not even Decor[ation]) so it's anecdotal and almost negligible, while information about most of the minerals, metals and liquids are just fine.
In terms of gases, this is the part of in-game information I give critical comments because many of sci-fi creations do their homework more carefully. Unfortunately, chlorine "gas" (Cl2) and carbon dioxide (CO2) can be somehow misleading. In my first instance, I didn't bother dig through a chlorine chamber because I know that gas is caustic in nature. However, this game clearly does not consider it and it's just unbreathable and occupy space when it allows. I once managed to dig through a chamber with hydrogen and chlorine (these two just don't produce hydrogen chloride at 30+ degree Celsius amazed me even more). The dupes feel freezing when going through hydrogen is expectable, and I tried to deal with that (what I "thought" was highly toxic chlorine gas) with coal burners generating carbon dioxide, the "miracle" happened: The coal generator is functional without oxygen and the carbon dioxide goes right down to the bottom and chlorine gas floats between hydrogen and carbon dioxide. I was in such a shock that I just closed the game. And well, some find it "challenging" to manage carbon dioxide, I'd say it only requires a few more moderate researches, a few metal and mineral, ample supply of water, or simply Licks to turn it into crude oil.
So, be warned, do your own research from the Wiki, or from failures.
2.5/10
Music: Rather fine, much better than RimWorld which plays some casual, annoying music even you're struggling in arctic area at spawning. As this is still early access, I expect more music variety.
8/10
Game mechanics other than above: In terms of AI work priority, I've tried Banished, StoneHearth, Life is Feudal: Forest Village, RimWorld and this Oxygen not Included and they're working similarly, i.e. just simulation and not human-like. It is also a difficult part to try prioritize your work but this game works much better than other games and will pay off when you get how it works, including the best time and food to eat.
What's a bit annoying about these games is that the "humans" (whatever they is named) in these games are pretty fragile mentally (said to mimic true human but I think it's just making the game challenging and trying make you Mental Break) and do works worse than invertebrates.
Surprisingly, the liquid pressure on structure and terrain is functional and you must plan well before sculpting chambers or digging for the resources you need, or feel the wrath of flood just like the one shown in trailer.
16/20
Overall: 32/50
Not very bad for an Early Access game, but if you're looking for a more survival-based game, (and want to avoid the Dupes' REEtard-like voices and actions,) find Klei's art style fine, and have not tried the Don't Starve series, try it first.

Pros
-------
- Beautiful graphics
- Unique ship designs and many ships available
- The game has a very good shield design that doesnt link all the shields together instead it seperates shields by left, right, front, and back so if your shields go down on the left side of your ship you can shift your ship so that the enemy attacks other parts that still have a shield up.
- The game world is pretty huge and reminds me alot of the Star Trek films because you run into nebulas, asteroids, chunks of ice, wormholes, anomalies, and all kinds of cool space stuff that make the game fun to explore.
- There is a bounty system so if you want to be a space bounty hunter you can seek out wanted criminals for huge bounty rewards but right now taking enemy ships doesnt work too well.
- The price is pretty reasonable, most new games coming out now ask $60 for new releases but this game cost less than half of that.
Cons
-------
- Ship customization leaves a little bit to be desired at the momment because you can pick the ships name, color, and decal but there arent that many decals available, you cant create your own ships with parts you scavanage from destroyed ships, and there are no hood ornaments or other unique additions to add to your ship to really make it feel like your own.
- You cant view the inside of  your ship, the decks, the crew, or decorate the interior of your ship.
- The current missions in the game are all generic "deliver item from X location to Y location" or "Patrol these waypoints" which are cut and paste from all the other games, nothing really ground breaking.
- Right now in the Early Access you can destroy enemy ships but if they leave a derelict which is like the shell of the ship upon destroying the ship you cant salvage it only destroy it and get the loot that it drops.
- Boarding enemy ships is just a numbers game right now, its about who has the most commandos but there is no gear or weapons that you can add to boarding parties to increase their chances of success.
- Landing on a planet or station will just open up a transaction window but it doesnt have any animations, landing videos, or videos of your character interacting with the local merchants.
- Turrent view seems awkward at times, its hard to shoot from the turrents while trying to drive your ship at the same time, whats the point of manning the guns if you have to pilot the ship at the same time? someone fire those lazy crew members of the player ships.
- Weapons seem underpowered, in some fights you can be fighting enemy ships for 5-10 min before the enemy ship gets destroyed and you will have to wait for cooldown on lasers/plasma weapons to keep shooting.
- Cargo space is very limited, you really have to decide what you wanna carry with you and how much money you want to make from loot. The game isnt very friendly if you want to play as a space trader making profit from trade.
- There are no fleet options in the game yet to command your own fleet of ships.
- Hacking enemy ship systems seems to not be in the game yet, at least there isnt any option to attempt to hack the enemy ships systems but there is gear that you can purchase to add % of chance to defend against hacking attempts on your ship.
- Right now there isnt a story mode in the game yet, only a free roam mode.
- The "Free Roam" mode has a game world that is divided into sectors each controlled by a mining station, space station, planet, or other big structure but none of those structures are capturable at the moment.
Conclusion
------------
Its a very fun game to play with alot of potential for growth and improvement but right now the game isnt in a playable state that I would consider justified to buy it right now. The only reason that people should buy this game right now is if they want to support the developers or if they have hope for the future but with the way the video game industry is right now with games having a million DLC's to get a complete game having hope for the future with developers can often backfire.
The developers are very active in the community page, answer questions, and comment on suggestions that the community makes to improve the game but the development team seems pretty small and progress is slow. It is my hope that the game does well and continues to improve but nobody knows how long it would take for the game to be at a stage where its considered complete and fun to play.

The idea of this game is not necessarily like the title. Yes, the VAZ 2108 'Vladmobile' is Russian, but that's the only car included. It means what it says "Russain Car Driver", that's it - you drive A Russian car. The game howerver, is centered around the 2108. There are little icons placed all around with some short facts or history about it and an accompanying picture. I think the free roam mode was my favorite if I had to have one. The translations could use some work in the story mode, so could the auto transmission in general. For some odd reason, it shifts into neural every time it tries to upshift. It even has this problem in manual mode, which is really weird considering the in-game trans relies on user input. I can only assume that it's because of the clutch. The cars don't deform much graphically, but it is funny to drive around with the front wheels literally in the front. I like that some objects around the world are movable, and there's a way from one map to another. The textures aren't the greatest, but what can you expect from a .99 game? They remind me of gmod in a way, so it doesn't bother me that much. I enjoy the radio, I don't usually listen to Russian rap/hip-hop. It really improves the Russianness of this game. I have yet to unlock the custom paints, but it's nice to be able to change the default collor of the car. As Timrod put it,
I recommend you turn all the car's aids off, and use man mode for ultimate usability. Try to shift around 2-3 on the revs, anything over will stop it. As others have noted, the police will not chase you for more than a few seconds. I'm really disappointed by this, another broken mechanic. It might be fixable through the game's files, but I don't care enough to look into it. As far as I'm concerned, I paid for the music
, and bits of history I could have found with Google if I was really that adamant to learn about it. This game still needs work, but it could turn into something interesting. Include more VAZ cars, their history, fix the transmission, and police chases. Then this would be acceptable to release.
