This game defines the explanation "because it is a video game."
Why can the war crier buff fighters on one side of the fence but not the other? Because the combat areas are rigidly sectioned off. It is a video game.
Why are some hubcaps collectible scrap but other hubcaps just scenic decoration? Because it is a video game.
Why can we use a crowbar to pry open doors and treasure chests but not use it as a melee weapon in combat? Because it is a video game.
Why don't the enemies in the next sectioned-off combat area in the stronghold wait patiently on the other side of the door for you to kick it in, rather than open it themselves to engage the guy who already killed half their base? Because it is a video game.
Why do you use the same gathered metal to upgrade your car and teach yourself fighting techniques? Because it is a video game.
So I understand how all this works in terms of gameplay mechanics, but it is never immersive, because there's one and only one solution to every problem. Tower with a sniper/mortar/scarecrow on it? Break it. Group of enemies? Beat them up. Pod of enemy cars? Don't try to engage them, park next to an impenetrable wall and wait for their drivers to disembark, then beat them up, then slowly, agonizingly back up and smash into their cars over and over again until they blow up, then run around and gather the two to four bits of scrap metal that burst out of them even though one pile of scrap would have achieved the same reward and been far less tedious. You can get an upgrade to auto-collect scrap from destroyed cars, but it won't auto-collect the scrap from downed enemies or structures, and since the entire gameplay loop centers around collecting more scrap, the pacing has to grind to a halt every few minutes so you can wander around gathering all the hidden bits of scrap. And your NPC support character yells at you if you don't.
It's frustrating that the central reward loop is so tedious, because I actually really like the car combat and upgrading mechanics. It's a lot of fun to take on those large melee fights with that Arkham Asylum-style punch-counter combat, and I actually like the way it works in this game much better. Counter windows are a lot less forgiving than in Arkham series, and you can't launch yourself around the arena like Batman, so if you try to throw yourself into a melee and ninja everyone to death in seconds, you'll get pounded into salami. I like that better, though, honestly. Forcing you to take it slow, learn the timing, and figure out attack patterns while also punishing you if you just button-mash actually adds a lot to the combat, and they mix it up nicely with melee weapons, knives, disarming moves, shield enemies, and even some that can dodge your hits, requiring you to learn to deal with different threats in different ways. The car combat is comparitively shallow and repetitive, which I suppose is ironic when you think about it. Nothing about it is particularly broken, but every enemy is defeated by slamming into them then harpoon-gunning their wheels off. Every single time. And speaking as someone who's never been into racing games, I don't know if it's just me, but the enemy all seem to be way better drivers than I am. They're just way too coordinated, so a group of three can maneuver behind me while I'm trying to focus on one and total my car in a few hits. I upgrade my armor, but all that does is weigh me down and make me a slower target. I buy spikes that are said to "make it nearly impossible for people to board you" and then people just board me anyway. Convoy missions require me to disengage five to ten times because taking on a group that outnumbers you seven to one is like trying to take down the Great Wall of China with one sledgehammer. You might have the greatest sledgehammer ever made, but your opponent has a lot more wall than one hammer can really effectively deal with.
Apart from that, the game does look amazing. The PC port is absolutely fantastic, with tons of options and flexibility, and it scales very well. I just upgraded my rig recently with two 960s, and being able to crank the settings to the max is the stuff of dreams. The lighting engine with its dynamic shadows and particle physics as you knock bits and pieces off your enemies is something to behold. For some reason, even though I can get 60 fps out of the game with the settings maxed, the fire in the game always seems to play at 30. I assume this was designed for the consoles, but it looks really jarring up-close when the fire doesn't seem to look like it exists in the same reality as the rest of the environments. The environments themselves are gorgeous and lovingly designed, invigorating what's otherwise pretty basic dungeon design by dressing it up with interesting post-apocalyptic wallpaper. Ocean liners and crashed airplanes that all look like they've been there so long they've practically become part of the landscape.
The character designs are nicely varied, and I like the way Max himself and his NPC hanger-on constantly convey personality, from the way the former holds his hands up in front of his face in dust storms to the way the latter enthusiastically drums on the roof of your car when you boost. The hanger-on, Chumbucket, has VA that's a little grating, but he's entertaining enough. It is kind of a shame that Max is such a♥♥♥♥♥♥to him all the time, because it just makes him unlikeable as he moans and mopes his way around NPCs that all have vibrant personalities and enthusiasm.
Oh yeah, there's a story too, I think. I don't really know. I found Max so unpleasant that I started skipping all the cutscenes about six hours in so I wouldn't have to hear his sourpuss routine any more, but considering every mission in the game boils down to "go to a place and fight all the things" I don't feel I missed a whole lot.
So I guess I can't really hate it. The gameplay is kind of a mixed bag, but it's a fun way to kill some time while listening to a podcast or two and also feeling like your new graphics cards weren't a spectacular waste of money. Then again, I did get it on sale for only $15, and I absolutely wouldn't recommend buying it for a penny higher than that.

This review will cover the 3 main game-modes within CODBO2 - Single Player, Multiplayer, and Zombies.
Single Player: The singly player handles a lot differently than other CoDs in the series, despite having nearly the exact same gameplay and mechanics...(and same old engine). You plan your mission, you decide what weapons and their attachments to take with you, as well as the other equipment. You can make choices that will change your gameplay, which is not only cool but rather interesting to see how the final result of the game pans out. The single player campaign however, did not compete well with other selections in the franchise/series. The single player felt loose a lot of the time and despite being a CoD game, a lot of the action felt very unneccesary. One really cool aspect of the single player campaign is that they mix up the times, one moment you're in the 1960/70's then you're in the future of the 2020's.
Multiplayer: Unlike other CoD multiplayers, BO2's multiplayer feels somewhat unique to that of any other in the franchise. For starters, one of the best features is the high level of customization. No gun is the same! You can customize a huge variety of weapon features, some features new, some the same from early on in the series. This includes;
-Reticles
-Emblems/clan tags
-Camos
-Attachments
-Perks
-Etc
There is a huge deal of customizing to make yourself the soldier of fortune you are. The unlocks may seem really easy after you get used to the flow of the mulitplayer, for example when you start to become better, you'll find that levelling up (depending on your skill and how much time you play) goes by very quick. The prestige and unlock rewards are satisfying and give you a challenege. There is a huge variety of weapons to unlock and use and they all play very nicely. Essentially, the multiplayer is a very good feeling and solid 'gun' game. Not only this, but there's a lot of gamemodes to play, as well as actual leagues and tornemants. The multiplayer has so much replayability and you will find yourself addicted to it when you start getting good! The only bad thing about BO2's multiplayer is that there are a lot of people who exploit or use hacks, as well as a very fowl mouthed community. If you play, it's best to ignore haters and trolls and just play for your benefit of fun and pleasure.
Zombies: The zombies game mode takes everything from WaW and BO1 and refreshes it in this installment of the franchise. We don't see any of the old maps unfortuantly, however there is a more gritty and apocalyptic atmosphere to Zombies. The guns in the map as well as random box are a mixed plethora of old fasion weapons from the Veitnam war era to the new modern weapons of the dawning 20th century. This gives a nice mix of old weapons as well as the cool new ones. The zombies feels and plays fantastically well just like the previous games, however if you don't plan to buy the map packs or DLC, you'll only get to experience one or two maps. The only downside with zombies is errr....not enough zombies!!!
A very good installment into the series, however with the single player being a big dissapointment, the multiplayer and zombies modes make up for it. A good game worth your money and time.

Do you remember the space sim Elite, or perhaps Freelancer, or the X universe games?
If like me you have been looking for a new game to scratch that space sim itch, then look no further than Starpoint Gemini 2.
Though still in Beta, this is already a very polished game with most of the content needed to get a good feel for the finished product in place.
The game allows you to roam freely and explore, with multiple factions and dynamic missions, ( a campaign mode will be added for release ) there is already plenty to keep you occupied for many an hour.
The game also has a great community following, with regular contact from the dev team at LGM who are very willing to engage with the players and to listen to their input.
If like me you have been disappointed by the recent offerings in the space sim genre, then get yourself a copy of this game.

As it stands now, even in Beta, it's a gorgeus game, and you can have great fun with it if you are a fan of the X4 genre or the more arcadish space sims out there. Well worth the money asked for.
But I feel it needs a little push in some directions. It can become much more than it is now, if given enough deep and polish. For instance, weapon stats are confusing, and they have no description. Uniqueness and a little story for each weapon/ship/commodity in the world would make it deeper. The huge starmap needs more deepness too, the different factions are not different enough, more involvement in each of them would make it more fun. You need to love some factions and hate others, to be really immersed in the world. Currently, there are only good guys, and bad guys. You shoot the bad guys, that's it :-). Voiceovers and images of the different factions are a must to achieve this.
Balance is still a little off, but it's to be expected in beta after all. You can destroy large enemy ships (destroyers or battleships) with your starter ship, without much sweating, but overall it's very fun and asks you for fairly involved gameplay, you need to use special powers and equipment to see it through the large battles unscathed.
I know for a fact that the team is constantly updating and expanding the game daily, so I have high hopes for it all to be fullfilled in the end.

If Banished and Rimworld had a baby, this is it.  If you have ever played Don't Starve then you should know that the animation style Klei uses is top notch and hilarious.  The facial expressions and mannerisms still crack me up.  The game runs extremely smooth and has enough variety and challenge to keep you coming back for more.
The great thing about these types of games is that if you like them, you can/will play them over and over just to start a new base or go for a new setup.  There is that urge to gets things 'just right', and upon each play through you tend to pick up on little nuances that help you your next time around.  There are a great many online resources to be looked at, as well as analytical data and player feedback if you are the type of person that like to get in depth or min/max.
The developers (Klei) are active not only in updating the game, and rather frequently at that, but also at making community posts, responding on forums, and keeping the player base up to date with current and future changes.  This is how ALL early access should be, and I commend Klei and the handful of other teams who use the Early Access feature without abusing it and giving it a bad name.  There is no doubt ONI has benefited from mountains of data they have gathered, and this is evidenced by the performance increases, mechanical changes, and bug fixes implemented in patches.  In the 90+ hours of play, I have really only encoutered two or three bugs, all fixed by restarting the game and resuming in a matter of seconds.
OVERALL: This game was easily worth the pricetag (sale or no sale) at it's very first stages of Early Access, and since then it has only been improved on.  For those who say there isn't enough content
Just look at the hundreds of reviews with 100-1000 hours played.  If basebuilding/resource management/sim sounds like your style, you will almost DEFINITELY will enjoy this game.
Happy gaming all!

This could have been a great game but for everything it does right, it does something equally wrong. Every good idea is ruined by a terrible implementation. The AI and the environment exists purely to screw you over. For example, in the vehicle races, each AI car doesn't care that it doesn't win; it purely exists to make sure YOU don't win. You have to get first place and beat the time limit to win, so every AI car will attempt to ram and block you even if it will be thrown off-course along with you.
You will die a lot in this game in ways you cannot prevent. The camera is horrid, often hiding attackers and forcing you to micromanage it in the heat of battle. If you do not, you will see attackers too late and won't be able to counter in time.  Attacks hurt, so failing to counter means a high chance you will die.
The open-world aspect of this game is fustrating as well. Enemy war parties of 3 armoured vehicles often appear out of thin air and relentlessly chase you down until you kill them. You can't even run from them because they home in on you, following you ANYWHERE you go in the open world. Fighting them is an absolute pain because it's three against one, and your vehicle likely cannot take the damage that they dish out. They'll force you out of your vehicle and then proceed to run you over again and again until you die.
Periodlically there will be sandstorms and thunderstorms in the open-world. When those happen you have to immedately drop what you are doing and find a safe place to sit and wait out the storm. Literally you have to sit there and do nothing for 5-10 minutes because venturing in a storm will get you killed. Oh you had a roving war party after you? Well too bad, looks like you have to fight them in the storm because you can't hide from them. Hint: you die.
Now I want to talk about character and vehicle upgrades. To upgrade Max, his vehicle, and his bases you have to scavenge scrap in the open-world. This is done by looting dead enemies or by opening boxes of scrap. However, they only give a pitiful amount of 5-10 scrap. Most upgrades upgrades requires hundreds of scrap. When I finished the game, I wasn't even halfway done upgrading Max and his vehicle. I did the math and found out I needed 20 thousand more scrap to upgrade everything. Yeah, that's not happening.
What could have been an enjoyable experience is marred by terrible and frustrating design choices.

I've logged about 6 hours so far. It's absolutely cut of the same cloth as the freelancer style games. I'm enjoying it, esp. since it scratches an itch I haven't been able to in ages.
It runs fine on my aged machine, without ratcheting down the video options. Haven't had any glitches or crashes. It looks pretty, similar to EVE.

It's nice that each "role" has some special abilities you can use in combat. Combat flows smoothly. It's neat how you can switch back and forth between direct control and letting your crew fire your guns for you if you need to focus on flying.
Oh, yeah: crew. This game isn't single-man fighters like those older games. You CAN stay small, but even then it's a corvette or gunship. But you can also go big, with battleships and carriers. You can hire crew (which grant buffs), and eventually add wingmen to fly a small fleet. I'm looking forward to that.
The trading is what you'd expect, and I'm grateful the game tracks high & low prices for you. Currently [in beta] earnings from hunting outstrip trading, so I hope they tweak the economy by launch. You can also mine asteroids and salvage defeated ships.
The map starts concealed, and reveals as you explore. This often uncovers missions (bounties, supply or taxi runs, science scans, and rescues so far).
Levelling up serves two functions. First you get points to make your special abilities better. Second, for unlocking the better ships. Because it doesn't just give you bigger numbers like a traditional RPG, there isn't a power creep.
Over all I'm pretty happy. This is MUCH more playable than the X games.

This game depressed me.
Not exactly the best thing to hear about a recommended game, but stick with me. At first the game sets itself out to be just another Third Person Shooter about killing insurgents and rescuing the ol' Americans. The gameplay, while fun, is nothing revolutionary. Take cover behind chest high walls, and take turns pelting lead at each other at 900 feet per second until one of you falls over. It is still fast-paced and fun.
To be honest, that's the only thing about spec ops that is fun. Stick with me, it's not that this game is boring. Quite contrary, in fact.
Without wishing to spoil much, at one point in the game, Walker (the main character) unintentionally does a really bad thing. The kind of thing that makes you feel really bad about him and yourself. From that point, you follow the character into an everlasting descent into madness, doing more and more questionable things, things you, the player, may start to disagree with.
Your thinking reflects that of the men in Walker's command, cautious and frightened of him as he tries to rationalise comitting terrible war crimes as just and necessary. Eventually you feel so disconnected from what he is thinking, and the game just gut-punches you at the end, and kicks you while you're down, pulling possibly the largest rug from under your feet.
If anything, this game is very worth the purchase, just for the story alone. It is not fun, or empowering, but damn will it make you feel like a miserable pile of sorrow. And yes, that is a good thing.

Russian Car Driver is a fun car driving game.
For what it is, a cheap game being sold for 99 cents on Steam, it's great (although, I must admit, I bought it on sale for 69c).
If you want to buy a game as good as Grand Theft Auto, then you've come to the wrong place - this is just a cheap game that provides some light entertainment.
Don't take this game too seriously, just have some fun with it.
I read a few of the reviews about the game before I bought it; and, although some people hated it, others gave it a thumbs up.
So I thought that there must be some good in it - why not give it a go?
The graphics are 1990's style, so there is nothing special there.
And the car mechanics are just ok.
However, nonetheless, I actually really enjoyed playing Russian Car Driver.
I had fun driving around the Russian countryside in my indestructible little car.
The occasional bear on the road adds to the Russian ambience of the game.
I've smashed through piles of logs, gone flying through the air (due to deliberately bad driving), and have done lots of cross-country travelling.
Great stuff!
Some reviewers mentioned that the steering wasn't too responsive, so the first thing I did before playing was to maximise the steering ability in the options - so that might have helped give me a positive experience with the game.
You can bash into anything with your car, and it just keeps on going.
After I went through a massive mud puddle, I thought I would try driving into into a river to wash the mud off - but, doh, it turns out that doing so was a bridge too far, and the car had to be rescued (whilst you can't drive for too long in water, I have managed to quickly drive across a river and survive).
Naturally, if you bash into solid objects (such as trees or houses) you will come to a complete stop (but your car can just drive off again).
If you are going fast enough, you can pretty much smash through anything else (e.g. fences, piles of logs, animals).
If you speed past a cop car, they will give chase; but you can pretty much always get away from them really easily (I got caught only once, when I made a mistake and crashed directly into a police vehicle).
You can speed across country. I haven't noticed any difference in the speed you can attain on the roads or in the fields - which, obviously, is unrealistic, but it all adds to the fun of the game.
I've even driven up to the top of the hills/mountains which are the barriers for the edge of the map, just for a bit of amusement.
However, be careful of the big slabs of rock which appear in fields, as I got myself stuck on rock formations twice in the game, so I am assuming it can happen to other players too.
There are missions to be done.
When you complete a mission, you can upgrade aspects of your car, such as speed and steering.
There is also a radio that you can play whilst driving around, although the music is a bit blah - but it does have half a dozen radio stations to choose from.
You need to turn down the other in-game sounds to be able to hear the radio better.
It would be great if you could import your own music into the radio (although you could just play your own music on another programme whilst the game is running, I suppose).
The radio list includes a Russian station, so there's another addition to the Russian ambience.
I had a lot of fun with this - loved it!
There is definitely more than 99 cents worth of fun in this game.
Russian Car Driver is not meant to be on par with the top-grade racing or car driving games on the market, so just enjoy it for what it is - a good bit of fun.

I like this game. I have only played it solo so far, but I imagine the multi player experience would be fun if you are looking for a faster paced experience than solo.  To me the most fun of these kind of games is the map exploration and to a lesser degree, expansion of held territories. The combat with pirates or rival factions is fun, but not really the best aspect of the experience for me.
The maps are procedurally generated and you can set the size of the world from small to huge, so there is a lot of replayability.
Lastly, I like that choosing the faction is less about aesthectis or character flavor and more about play style. For example they have a faction where you get xp bonuses for exploration and discovery, or you could choose another that has xp bonuses for combat. No matter  how you like to play the game, you can still level up doing what you think are the fun parts.
I think the weakest aspect of gameplay is probably the quests. they are all essentially " take cargo here" "take passengers here" or  "go fight this pirate".However, I think if you enjoy sandbox style play you will have fun with this game.

So I see a lot of reviews saying that
“this game is boring all you do are quests and trading”

Well I have to tell you if you are just doing quests and trading, yes you will be bored as heck playing this game like that.

The best way to play this game is to jump into an online server, the official one is the most active despite being in America and I’m getting around 150-200ms ping the game seems to feel mostly fine.

So once you are in a server you wanna level quickly~ to start enjoying this game, sadly the early stages are kinda grindy and boring, You can ask in servers for a combat instance where you will fight against Pirates to retake the land this is how you should be playing the game the PvE is absolutely fun and enjoyable you will wonder where the time goes after playing for an hour or two.
Doing “Instances” with other players will help you gain levels for perks and is also a great way to earn gold to buy new ships, don’t be afraid to ask for help or guidance everyone is friendly and tries to work together to complete the objectives.

“So what next? I’ve grinded to level 50 but there is nothing to do??”
Well if you feel this way, I feel like this game is not for you and you should stop playing right now.

INSTANCES are the foundation of this game in my opinion and doing them are so much fun especially once you can pull your own weight!

Combat is generally the easiest, then Heroic can be slightly more challenging but gives you better loot than Combat, and then we get onto Raids - this is where the game gets the most challenging and fun, everyone has a job to do and if you all do it you will have a good time and get bath in the spoils of killing the Dragon, yes a flipping dragon

tl;dr
Game is awesome, stop trading / questing unless you just wanna chill without a challenge, join a server and have fun completing Instances

This could have been a great game but for everything it does right, it does something equally wrong. Every good idea is ruined by a terrible implementation. The AI and the environment exists purely to screw you over. For example, in the vehicle races, each AI car doesn't care that it doesn't win; it purely exists to make sure YOU don't win. You have to get first place and beat the time limit to win, so every AI car will attempt to ram and block you even if it will be thrown off-course along with you.
You will die a lot in this game in ways you cannot prevent. The camera is horrid, often hiding attackers and forcing you to micromanage it in the heat of battle. If you do not, you will see attackers too late and won't be able to counter in time.  Attacks hurt, so failing to counter means a high chance you will die.
The open-world aspect of this game is fustrating as well. Enemy war parties of 3 armoured vehicles often appear out of thin air and relentlessly chase you down until you kill them. You can't even run from them because they home in on you, following you ANYWHERE you go in the open world. Fighting them is an absolute pain because it's three against one, and your vehicle likely cannot take the damage that they dish out. They'll force you out of your vehicle and then proceed to run you over again and again until you die.
Periodlically there will be sandstorms and thunderstorms in the open-world. When those happen you have to immedately drop what you are doing and find a safe place to sit and wait out the storm. Literally you have to sit there and do nothing for 5-10 minutes because venturing in a storm will get you killed. Oh you had a roving war party after you? Well too bad, looks like you have to fight them in the storm because you can't hide from them. Hint: you die.
Now I want to talk about character and vehicle upgrades. To upgrade Max, his vehicle, and his bases you have to scavenge scrap in the open-world. This is done by looting dead enemies or by opening boxes of scrap. However, they only give a pitiful amount of 5-10 scrap. Most upgrades upgrades requires hundreds of scrap. When I finished the game, I wasn't even halfway done upgrading Max and his vehicle. I did the math and found out I needed 20 thousand more scrap to upgrade everything. Yeah, that's not happening.
What could have been an enjoyable experience is marred by terrible and frustrating design choices.

After 15 hour game play I can say the following :
All the things that other reviewers said about Elite, Privateer etc are correct.   I have played and loved these and have been an Eve player for a long time.  This is a a game in the same genre, but being offline means it has less stress that Eve.  Sometimes you want to reload and redo a big fight, not suffer the massive financial loss of losing a battleship.......
It plays well, draws you into wanting that next ship, and there is a considerable kick from taking down a hero.  Even better was the feeling of success, the first time I managed to reduce a high threat enemy by shooting out their power, grappling the ship, sending in the marines and watching the progress as they swept the decks and captured the ship.  I then had to tow it (slowly so as not to lose the grapple) to a base, fighting of bad guys along the way, before realising the spoils.  This is a really neat bit about the game. the hangers and fighters onboard larger ships is another good idea.
This is a beta, but well down the development line.   The iin game marketing needs a bit if tweeking, and I get occassional flashing screen section, but this goes after docking and relaunching and does not impair the game - this can be sorted.
I thought that this was well worth the money.  I have really enjoyed the game and I keep wanting to come back.

Voice feedback gets a little repetative, UI is clunky, too big and seems aimed at a touch interface, ship control needs a lttle more finesse but overall I like this game, it's like single player Eve Online (not so big and varied) but it has potential. Recommened if you're into Freelancer etc.

The twist is that each enemy (except the final boss) has a way in which they can be defeated without fighting them.  If you don't kill enemies, though, you will not gain EXP, which in turn means your LV will not increase.  I won't spoil things, but I will warn you that EXP and LV
.
I recommend going for a neutral ending first.  That requires killing some, but not all, major characters, or killing all major characters but not every possible random encounter.  It's also possible to get a neutral ending without killing anything, if you fail to satisfy certain conditions.  After you've had some fun exploring the different neutral endings, I suggest going the True Pacificist route.  If you want to do a genocide run, I'd suggest doing it last.

Windward is one of those games where the features are there, but lacks the cohesiveness to be a trully compelling experience.
From the standpoint of a pirate themed game, it ticks all the boxes one would expect and then some. You can trade, you can fight and you can explore, and on top of that there's an RPG layer with skill progression, equipment, quests and even instances. Further on top of that, there's the multiplayability of it, a drop-in-drop-out affair where people are able to join up or compete in maps that are procedurally generated each time. On paper, all those features make for a great game.
The problem however, manifests itself when one starts playing. Trading and questing are promising at first, but developing areas and cities has little to no impact on the world, as areas aren't interconnected and it never goes beyond accumulating resources and money that are ultimately of little to no use once one moves onto the next area or achieves the biggest, baddest ship there is. Ship-to-ship combat is fast and frantic, but of little consequence. There are no boardings, no dueling, no intense one on one chases and maneuvering (in fact I found myself just parking the ship and blasting away), no ammo types, almost no reward and although conquering an area from the hands of pirates is fun the first time, by the fifth the game becomes painfully routine save for select moments when things become sort of intense, but even then it's a matter of continuously blasting ship after ship, inching towards the conquest of the last city and reclaiming the sector for your faction. And once the pirate menace has been erased of that particular area it's gone, meaning the dynamic of the world is a constant all out battle in contested territories, and otherwise absolutely stable in non contested ones, save for the artificial threat of mission spawned pirates.
The heavy compartmentalization of Windward's map is, I believe, it's biggest downfall, alongside it's overly simplistic combat aspect, which dwarves the other, potentially more varied avenues. There's no sense in running lucrative cargo through dangerous waters when you can simply sweep them out of pirates one at a time, no sense in risking it into a dangerous new area, outmanned and outgunned, when you can simply grind your way into better equipment on friendly waters, no sense in developing more than one town one you've gotten your hands on the highest possible ship they offer, no sense in buying low and selling high when once reached a certain money threshold you'll never have to bother with money ever again.
I can't really recommend it to anyone looking for a compelling, enthralling game. Sea Dogs' side activities is an example of why you shouldn't bother with side activities if you can't make them pleasant, but it's naval combat stands head and shoulders above anything else in the genre. Pirates!' ship action might feel overly simplified at times, but it's myriad of activities make for an always engaging game. Windward's unappealing combat, disconnected world, simplistic progression and repetitive nature set the stage for an experience that, alone or in company, will always feel boring, boneless and lacking. I can't complain too much, having grabbed it for super cheap on humble bundle, but compared to any of the 5+ year old, certainly flawed offerings in the genre, it falls squarely on the tail of the pack.

I was initially on the fence with getting this, even on Humble Bundle, as it was the only one of the three I was interested in.
The gameplay looked too arcade-like and the maps looked too restricted.
Once I discovered that you could edit the world and make it less boardgame looking, I was drawn in.
And then I found out that you can set the wind resistance (or rather, how fast ships move when going towards the wind).
I set mine to 0.10 and now I love it.
The only drawback for me right now is the quest-tracker, which gives you a highlighted path towards your destination. Aside from certain quests (namely the settlers one, where it does come in handy), I find the quest-tracker a slight nuisance. I'd much rather have a compass or weather-vane type arrow tucked away somewhere on the screen that's not so noticeable.
There is a way to toggle it off, but it's only temporary as it'll repopulate after combat or leaving a port.
Otherwise, the game is very enjoyable.
The ship, after changing the wind resistance, acts like a real ship. Sometimes it turns too quickly, but that's easy to work around by tapping the direction keys instead of holding them down when steering.
The ship's sails move in the wind and you can easily tell which way the wind is going by the movement of the clouds and a wind-indicator flag that's positioned above the sails (I'm sure there's a name for it).
And the day/night cycles, as well.
Another small quibble is that the wind changes direction too often. Again, being more of an arcade element than a sim element. But once you get used to it, it's not so bad. However, it would be nice to adjust the timer for the direction change. Maybe to twice as long.
It's clearly a sim type game that was made for arcade type players, but is editable to make it somewhat more sim-like for more serious gamers. Although, some arcade elements (wind direction timer and quest-tracking) are baked in and near-impossible to adjust (if at all).
However, the map generator gives limitless possibilities and from what I've seen so far in my own gaming and from reading in the forums, with a good map you could play endlessly. Which is perfect for those who enjoy games for the journey and not solely the end-game destination.
Of course, if end-game is your cup of tea, you could simply make a very simple map and wipe out all the pirates or opposing factions and be done.
Or stop when you reach max level, which I hear is pretty high (another bonus for longterm players).
Another nice thing is that you can choose to play solo or join a server (of which there are many, including the highly populated official server), and your ship and character skills carry over from one to the other.
So if you're the type of player that likes to explore solo until you're ready to intermix with others, you can take all the time you want.
Likewise, if you're the type of player that thrives on social activity and learning with others, you can just jump right in without having to wait.
I, myself, am more solo but do like to be social at times. For me, this is a great option that allows me to keep my progress and still have the freedom to socialize when I want to.
Also, your character/ship can be transplanted to a new world.
So, if you're not entirely happy with the map you generated, you can easily just create another and plop your ship right into it.
The graphics are really good. Although, I haven't seen any weather effects yet in my area.
The music is nice, but I tend to mute it as I mute the music in almost all the games I play to give more of an immersive feel. The lack of bird sounds, though, does become noticeable with the music off. But that's no big deal.
On the bright side, the boat makes creaking noises often and there's nice sound indicators for when you're entering a port.
And the combat sounds are great.
The game has modding/workshop support.
But I've only seen info on adding new sail emblems and ships or editing existing ships. There's probably more options available to edit but I need to look into it further.
Overall, if you're looking for an arcade-type experience, the game plays great right out of the box. And if you're looking for a more sim-like experience, the game can suit your needs with some adjustments.
It's also great for casual players.
I give it 8.5 out of 10.
If the arcade elements were easier to remove, it would get a 9 or possibly even a 10.
Btw... looking through the forum, it appears that the arcade elements that I don't care for were actually requested as features by the testing players, who felt it was too 'difficult' without them. Lol. Figures. :-/
Maybe next time, the test group should include a wider mix of players.
EDIT: If you do get the game, the Camera Mod is a must have.

7/19/2014, First Impressions
I bought Startpoint Gemini 2, in spite of not really caring too much for the first one, but since it was on sale, and since it seemed to be so popular, I thought I would give this development studio another shot.  So far, I am glad I did.  Being an early access game, I expected some features needing polishing, and other features not yet to be fully implemented, which indeed is the case at the time of this initial post.  Having said that, I must say I find the gameplay mechanics very interesting, and the combat compelling.  If you are a fan of the old "X" games (except for X: Rebirth), you'll find some familiar concepts such as trading and boarding.
I also enjoyed how functional the developers made their starmap, making it easy to find missions, side jobs, or other distractions, whilst providing a wealth of information such as reputation and factions of each sector.  My only complaint here, is the lack of a legend.  I hope, in the near future, that will be provided as an on/off toggle.
The combat is fun and flexible.  With the ability to upgrade, enhance, or otherwise customise your ship, each ship type you are capable of flying provides a wealth of possible combat configurations to fit your playstyle, or to try out different tactics.  I found the tactical overlay in combat especially helpful, though I had to manually assign a hotkey for it.  Of course, being an early access game, there are several areas upon which they can improve, such as providing a text-based battle log, or some other method of communicating more detail on what exactly is happening.  For example, when targeting an enemy, you have no consistent view of their shields.  There is some kind of HUD element that pops up when you first target them, but it does not stay up, and there is no clue on how to consistently get the information available.  It would be nice to be able to see, at least, the target's shield status on a consistent basis.  Likewise, critical hits are communicated, but no details are provided, such as what systems were critically hit.
The Skills & Perk system of your officer is pretty cool.  It adds a lot of depth by allowing skills to provide several affects at once, while at the same time keeping the amount of button mashing (or mouse clicking) to a minimum.
I will say one thing in this "first impressions" entry, and that is I was disappointed at not being able to command a fleet whilst directly controlling a ship of my own.  It is my hope that the developers have plans to allow this, as some of the game menus and screens suggest (such as "fleet management"...implying the ability to manage more than one ship in your fleet).

Russian Car Driver is a shovelware game that's not even a GOOD shovelware game. Taking heavily after "skill-based" driving games such as Driver and Gran Turismo, the game puts you in control of a boxy Russian sedan I call the Vladmobile.
The Vladmobile is not governed by any of the laws of physics or common sense, something you'll figure out in the game's required first mode: Parking. Parking mode consists of navigating the Vladmobile through a path made out of traffic cones and stopping it in a glowing "park zone" within a time limit. What you'll soon figure out are two things:
First, parking mode is really glitchy and a lot of the time it's easy to slip out of bounds between the cones (touching a cone automatically fails you) and slip back in at the park zone.
Second, the Vladmobile does not accelerate or brake in a consistent manner. I spent probably ten minutes of the hour I played this game before refunding it figuring out exactly how the physics work. The answer is that they don't. The Vladmobile will not stop simply because you stopped pressing the accelerator or the reverse - you have to figure out that spacebar is the "handbrake" button, which causes the car to come to an absolute dead stop the second you use it. While the handbrake does make parking mode a lot easier, it's not something that comes naturally or is easy to figure out, especially if you're used to driving in games like Grand Theft Auto V that use realistic driving physics.
Once you get past parking mode, you get to the game's second unlockable mode: drifting. Drifting mode is actually impossible with the default settings - you can't drift properly with the "Anti-Lock Brakes" and "ESP Brakes" settings on. With them off, the car goes from controlling like a 18th-century pirate ship to controlling like a stick of butter covered in bacon grease. Drifting mode is extremely easy to clear, since it uses the same course layout for all of the "trials" and the only differences are the time limit and the score you're expected to get. With all of the brake settings off, I was able to do this pretty much effortlessly by building up speed and then hitting left and right alternating until the game broke and gave me thousands of points.
Oh, one thing I should mention about drifting mode: by default, the Vladmobile will not go over 60 miles per hour. To get it to go faster, you have to change the game to manual transmission - which uses controls not listed anywhere in the game itself (A upshifts gears by default, Z downshifts). However, manual transmission is a nightmare because being in the wrong gear for any period of time will cause your engine to explode, automatically failing whatever challenge you're on.
Assuming you figure out parking and drifting mode, you then get to move on to the game's final mode, Drag Racing. Unlike Parking or Drifting, Drag Racing forces you to use manual transmission without any warning whatsoever, so if you have no experience with it you'll be wondering why your engine keeps exploding the second you touch the accelerator. I was completely and utterly unable to finish even the first stage of Drag Racing mode, mostly because of the terrible handling on the Vladmobile and the constant siege of oncoming traffic.
The game is not good for speedrunning, it's not good for streaming, and it's certainly not fun. Don't think that because it cost you $0.69 that it's worth it - even paying that little promotes shovelware on Steam.

This is a well designed naval combat game. The fights are fast paced and often chaotic, and there is a sufficient variety of abilities that tactics can get pretty advanced.
However, positioning is everything in this game. I liked the way that they made the direction of the wind so critical for mobility. If you're clever, you can use it to your advantage while your opponents flounder. If you're careless, you can get wedged into a terrible position while your opponents' cannons reduce your ship to splinters.
The game runs well, and while it's not very complex, it does provide an interesting combat experience.
The ability to create new towns, new guard towers, and new lighthouses is a great facet to the combat as you compete to gain supremacy over a region.
My critique would be that there is very little story in this game, and its questing system is flat. The randomly generated instances have different biomes, but aren't sufficiently unique to warrant exploration for its own sake. In short, it excells at combat, and that's about it. Still, that's enough for it to be a fun game.

I love this game. When I played it for the first time, I was pretty hooked. The whole heir thing going on makes it so that no run feels exactly the same, even when you are using the same items and/or spells. I also love the upgrade system. It made me feel like as I was dying over and over, I was slowly getting stronger and stronger with each passing heir. Another thing I love about the game is how its more reliant on individual skill than luck. Lets use The Binding of Isaac, another roguelike game, as a comparison. While I do love that game as well, TBOI often feels like I need luck more than skill because I have to get really strong items if I want to win. While Rogue Legacy has some luck-based elements (such as the heir system), it has way less, which makes your individual skill much more important. The lack of luck-based elements makes me also feel like it's my fault when I die, and not the fault of the game. Speaking of dying, the game is hard. You will die. Probably a lot. The game provides a really good challenge in a time when more and more developers are focused on making their games easier.
The game isn't perfect though. While the controls are tight, the keyboard controls felt a little bit jarring for me at first. I'm not too used to PC platformers though (I tend to play them on console way more) so maybe that's just a problem with me rather than a problem with the game. After all, you can still change up the controls, so you can change them to suit your style. But if you're like me and you like platformers on console, I highly recommend using a controller for this game. I used a Dualshock 4.
Now lets just go over the pros and the cons.
PROS
- Lots of variety in every run
- Upgrade system makes you feel like you're getting stronger and stronger
- Heir system allows for a variety of fun (and weird) runs
- It's hard
- Skill > Luck
- It's YOUR fault when you die, not the fault of the game
CONS
- Keyboard controls can feel a bit weird (controller recommended)
In short, it's a really good (and hard) game. If you want a challenge, then play it. You might wanna use a controller, though.

I am a little disappointed by this game. Somehow I expected it to be a FPS when I bought it, but it turned out to be a third-person shooter. "Oh well", I thought, "as long as the controls don't suck".... which they do, sadly. Taking cover behind objects is too often a hit or miss and sprinting makes your character uncontrollable. I even bugged and got stuck on staircase after vaulting over a wall. Picking up weapons is a bit iffy sometimes. The voice acting is sub par.
The AI is nothing special, multiple times the enemy slipped from cover and decided it was a good idea to change their magazines, right there, out in the open. Enemies just keep running straight at you and shouting the same voice clip over and over. I haven't seen any flanking or whatever tactical movement, which makes it feel like one big virtual shooting gallery, but I guess that is the type of game the creators were going for.
The gameplay is quite repetitive, since there are only ~5 types of enemies and the shootouts are mostly the same. The shotguns seem useless most of the time and the snipers are very situational.  At some points you are forced to swap weapons because you run out of ammo, which forces you to try out some of the other weapons. Still the standard assault rifle and the AK did the job for me. The sand mechanics feel more like a gimmick than really substantial part of the gameplay, but the idea is nice.
The storyline is ok. The only real problem that I have with it is that game forces emotion on you with melodramatic cutscenes where you can only walk and (mild spoiler)
Apparently, if you need to open a locked door (metal or wood - doesn't matter), you just unload your shotgun at it once or twice and then try the door knob. Works every time!
Oh and then there is the reiterating loading bar.
On the positive side: The graphics and animations are nice. The atmosphere in the game is really strong and the game is incredibly colourful for a post-apocalyptic desert setting.
For me, the awesome atmosphere this game has to offer does not outweigh the iffy controls and repetitive gunfights. You may think otherwise and you can enjoy this game if you play it in a few sessions. I would only recommend it on sale (bought it for 3,39 eu). Spec Ops: The Line will certainly entertain you for a few hours, but there are enough better alternatives.

Opening note: Buy this game on sale,and play it for the story. The story itself lasts for about 6 hours
Pros:
-One of the best stories in a video game, hands down best story in an army based game
-Absolutely gorgeous graphics when set on max settings and vibrant filter. People mock lens flare, but this game pulls it off
-The characters and character models are really nice. Right from the start i liked Lugo and Adams (your two squadmates). And it may be on the max settings, but the character models are so good. For example, Walker has half his face burnt some time down the campaign.While most game have a hideous black patch and make you wish you didnt get burned, at the end of the story all of Adams deformities looked realistic and fitted in
-Like many of them have said, they pulled off sand so goddamn well. the Sandstorm idea is a masterstroke, and the scenery makes you realise the potency of sandstorms, with skyscrapers half covered by dust and hotels submerged in sand
-this maybe a small one, but i really like the detail put into the game. For example, depending on what point you are in the story, the main menu scene changes and its really interesting rather than the standard "here's a bunch of buttons.Press one to actually look at the game."
-The whole game makes you questions the idea of glorifying military shooters. Here's a comparison. In MW2 theres a level where you're the marines traversing through the city after an EMP. Yet all you care about is the area being quiet and optics being down. If that scene was in this game, they would find a way to make it truly depressing with struggling soldiers, teammates dying because their weapons broke, civilians panicking, etc.
Cons
-Cover based shooter. So damn annoying. If youre not standing bhehind a wall peeking every once in  a while, you're dead.
-The mounted turrets are absolutely infuriating. I understand theyre trying to be realistic, but theyre impossible to kill because of killtime+otherenemies+the shield. Yet when you complete the herculean task of killing it, next thing you know some other punk shows up and starts mowing you down
-The lack of ammo is intentional, however it can get very annoying with constant weapon swaps and heavies soaking up magazines of bullets before dying
-The controls are clunky. You dont know how many times i died when i commanded my dude to vault a sandbag wall, but he instead slapped the air and got shot up
Overall,play this game for the story, not for the mechanics or godawful multiplayer. People hail bioshock for an amazing story, but i think this game gives it a great run for its money.

I got this game for 1/3 of a buck at Humble Bundle, so I almost feel bad not recommending it. Did I get 33 1/3 cents worth of enjoyment out of it? Sure. Would I recommend it to others? Not so much.
It's a simple, decent enough little naval commerce and combat themed casual game, the kind of thing that would have felt more at home on a tablet, for what that's worth. Mostly you just sail back and forth from port to port, trading goods, shopping for loot, and circling hostile ships while your broadside guns automatically do all the work. There are shortcut keys and keyboard mapped controls, but you could theoretically play the game entirely one-handed with the mouse.
The world map is randomly generated, and you can spawn instances, but the "radiant" missions are repetitive, predictable, and quickly get boring. It's one of those "mile wide and an inch deep" gameplay experiences that eventually devolves into tedious grinding in order to get anywhere.
It also tends to glitch up a lot, at least for me, with boats getting stuck on collision, maps failing to load, and unexplained, spontaneous crashes to the desktop. The nail in the coffin was when my primary singleplayer savegame somehow got corrupted and refused to load, wasting hours of the aforementioned grinding and all my worldbuilding progress.
Since the devs are so standoffish about cheating thanks to the multiplayer modes, I can't cheese my way back to where I was, so I just quit altogether. The game doesn't really have a story, so I don't feel like I'm missing anything.
With a title like "Windward," I would expect some kind of wind-based sailing mechanics. I was bitterly disappointed.

I love this game. If you're looking for something involved or something deep and meaningful, this isn't what you're looking for. Windward is a fantastic unwinding game. There's really no penalty for dieing, there are no really 'difficult' missions, and I've never been frustrating playing it.
What I have been is entertained. The music is very fitting and while there isn't a huge sound libary, it never grew tiresome. Sailing to the Windward soundtrack is great. Fighting to the Windward soundtrack is great. The graphics work very well for the game - by that I mean they aren't AAA, but they're perfect for the $10 and under.
In conclusion - if you like the idea of a sailing game without a lot of stress or an easy pick-up-and-put-down, Windward is for you.
I've spent 100+ hours sailing around and building a mean pirate ship. I will likely spend 100+ more.

Unfortunately, Mad Max is more filler than thriller.
The scavenger aesthetic looks nice, and the first few hours of gameplay can be enjoyable as long as you stick to the main story - but that isn't what you're supposed to do in an open world game.
Open world games live and die by their filler, but usually they vary it enough to prevent the repetition from becoming too obvious.
Here, the repetitiveness of most of the gameplay becomes extremely obvious fairly quick, making the game feel boring and unsatisfying - especially with the simplistic and shallow mechanics, bland combat and vehicle combat (which was quite fun and
have been the core of the gameplay) becoming almost nonexistent as you progress.
The game feels rushed, disjointed and ultimately unfinished, as if it was a proof of concept prototype padded to full size with quantity of side content above its' quality.
Most of the scrap locations and camps feel repetitive and indistinct from each other - an impression made even stronger by them being constructed from an extremely limited pool of components.
I really tried to like this game, but in the end it failed to keep my attention - I feel no motivation to complete the remaining 25% or so of the "side content" (at this point, a scattering of scrap locations and some of the races) and I don't see any reason to come back to do so in the future.

I got this game recommended to me because I was playing Don't Starve Together, a well-known game by Klei. Since I enjoyed DST that much, I decided to give their new game a try despite reading many negative reviews on the store page. To be honest, I'm not disappointed at all with my purchase.
Oxygen not included is a base building game where you start off with 3 dupes in an underground world. To make your colony survive, you need to produce or harvest all the basic resources like oxygen, water and food through digging and building; building restrooms and managing liquid and gaseous wastes; and producing power while managing heat; expanding the base and your labor force while balancing between the size of your colony and the amount of resource available. Additionnally, the poor dupes are constantly working in harsh conditions, their stress can build up fast and you'd want to keep them happy enough to function.
There are many details to these systems that can also create dilemmas for you. I.e.: Regular wires overloading, but high-voltage ones can't run through tiles and sabotage your decor. I.e.: Tapping clean water from the steam geyser but your water tank and base are going to heat up. Etc, etc.
All in all, the goal of the game is to create and then maintain a functionning (and tricky) balance for your colony by ordering and prioritizing tasks. There are always problems to solve so you'd constantly have things to do.
TLDR: Oxygen not included is a very fun and challenging strategy/management game :D
:
- Rather complex strategy and planning game with many systems to consider (Plumbing, electrical, decor, agricultural, etc)
- Many more features and updates to come
- Cute art
- High playability, a lot of room for creativity
- Addictive and time killing (Or wasting)
:
- Trial and error: though it may be possible that you are very successful at your first playthrough, it's not often the case. Expect yourself to make some mistakes, your first colony/colonies may not survive very long
- Plumbing and circuiting may be tricky (Got me very frustrated at one point)
- I find the background music strange
- Pricey?
- Can't directly control a dupe, can be very frustrating
- Dupes aren't the smartest beings in the universe, they can get stuck somewhere in the dumbest way...
- Choose your dupes carefully, don't blindly look for stats, think about their expectations!
- Keep dupes happy, or things are gonna get really messy...
- If a dupe is just always upset, kill him/her :D
- Find a steam geyser for constant clean water source
- Separate your clean from dirty, whether it's gases or liquids or sometimes even solids (eww to those slimes), and try to keep your base clean
- Think about sustainability, power sources deplete fast so have the manual source ready
- Get those hydrolyzers going!!
- Light gases go up (Hydrogen), oxygen stays on top of polluted oxygen, chlorine and CO2 stay at the bottom. Use this information to your advantage.
- Despite all my farm tiles I still need that microbe musher for food
- Research is quite important for gas/water pumps, decor, combustion, gas permeable tiles, high-voltage wires and HYDROLYZERS
- When assigning digging tasks, always assign ladder building tasks too to prevent dupes getting stuck
- Keep an eye on notifications

This is my early access review - I will change my review for the final product.
If you love the Sci-fi and the adventure of exploring space - particularly Star Trek, Babylon 5, or Star Wars - you will absolutely love this game! It's truly a unique space sim/rpg experience, and this is the first game that has done justice to this genre I believe. The universe is your sandbox, and you're free to do whatever you want - trade, mine asteroids, hunt down criminals, or take part in space battles - take command and boldly go into the beautiful, yet dangerous, reaches of space.
- So far the graphics are excellent; the art style is beatiful; ship designs are unique, yet they will remind you of your favorite Sci'fi. At the moment, I'm flying a ship that reminds me of a Tau Empire or a Homeworld Kadeshi ship - love it. Being able to customize and design your weapon systems, costmetic look of your ship, and having access to a wide range of various kinds of ships, is the best feature of the game for me. Working to get that special ship you always wanted - whether it be a large Carrier class that can launch swarming fighters/bombers; a massive heavily armed Dreadnought armed to the teeth with Missile Launcers and Rail Guns; a swift Gunship or Corevette, decked out in Plasma Cannons; or a stealthy fighter class with cloaking - is all possible for you here.
- Music is atmospheric, and fits the setting perfectly - although, I would like to hear an extended soundtrack in the finished product, or post-launch.
- Combat Missions are fun, and Space combat is the by far the best part of the game. Scientific explorations; Repairing Space stations, Science Vessels/outposts, or even Space prisons, is a nice touch to fill in the world, and make it feel like you're in a living universe. Although, there is need for more variations in these missions; though this is early access, and there is still more content in the works to make the universe feel more alive, and give you more to do as you explore.
The game may be early access, but it's very well made in every way so far - I can only imagine how good the finished product will be. The Developers are the most friendly, and helpful ones I ever came across; they're transparent in their work on the game, and very open in sharing ideas with fans and are open to suggestions and feedback. This is a top notch game in it's genre; and both this game, and it's fantastic devs, deserve your support. Starpoint Gemini 2 has an exciting future, and I'm glad I've taken part in it's journey.

BEWARE! ALWAYS ONLINE DRM!
UPDATE (03/07/2017):
After playing this game for a whole year I can't stress out more how much I've loved it.
Despite the initial issues with connections and the fact that it is basically an always-online DRM, the game is amazing. The best stealth game I've played so far.
----
The first three levels (2 tutorials + first real level) are really well done and so far I "was" having fun.
The game's DRM though prevented me from enjoying the rest of my evening, as apparently the game servers went down and game told me I am unable to load the saved game I made 2 minutes before, because I lost connection to the almighty game server. Stupid me, welcome to 2016 when the game tells you it is late and it's time to stop playing.
Thanks to that hidden feature, at least I have time to write this review. So let's start with three major points:
1. The game is a technical disaster. Two 770GTX GPUs in SLI here - game settings fixed texture quality to Low with no way to change and also fixed maximum resolution to 1080p with options above, greyed out. (found out there is a way to set higher resolution via launch options and it works great, but apparently the devs didn't want to risk someone having a slight dip in FPS)
2. Game divided into episodes. Seriously, this game is supposed to release a new level every month. The game developer/publisher wants me to play one level for a whole 30 days before they decide to give me the next slice of the pie I already paid for. That is of course if it lets you play, which gets me to the next point...
3. ALWAYS F-IN ONLINE DRM! This is absolutely amazing, but apparently if you play with your internet connetion on, the game creates save games that are online-only! The game comes with a parental lock already implemented and it doesn't matter how old you are. When the game servers want to sleep, so should you! Stop complaining and welcome to 2016 world of DRMs. Truly unbelievable.
Honestly I would say to wait for a patch, but the issues I described are design flaws and they won't be fixed. It is a pity as I loved every other previous Hitman game. This one also is very very good, but there is no way to play it... it is either missing levels or missing ability to load save games.
That said I could at least enjoy the rest of the beer I'm drinking, while writing this (instead of playing the game) and I hope someone will hesitate to buy after reading this. Let us all hope this episodic-always-online♥♥♥♥♥♥won't become the new era of video games.

The most important rule of Rust: You MUST have a thick skin to play this game! But it is very fun and very addicting.
The other players online are absolutely burtal and ruthless. I would say 99% of players will kill you on sight for no aparent reason. Even if you're a fresh spawn and have nothing. People will headshot and kill you before you even see it coming and have any chance to fight back. They will steal your loot and materials you've been farming. They will raid your house and destroy all of your work you spent hours on. And you'll be furious. But you'll still keep coming back for more...
It's best to have friends who play as well and team up to build a base together. (don't expect to find any friends in-game)  But i play Solo quite often and manage to build bases that can withstand numerous raid attemps. If you're Solo, find an area to build thats far away from the landmarks and rad towns. That's where all the action is most of the time and being away from that will give you much better odds.
If you've never played before and don't have friends to help you learn the game, watch YouTube videos on it. There's several Rust YouTuber's out there (I like Holdacious). You don't want to dive in with no idea what you're doing. It will seem too difficult and you'll get discouraged. Or at least join a server that's pratcially empty so you can learn how to build and craft your weapons and tools before being dropped into the lion's den of high population official servers...
Overall, its a very solid game that's well worth $20... As long as you can let things roll off your back when you get slaughterd by a group of smack talking 12yr olds that steal all your loot then make fun of you for it.
Recommend For Sure!!!!
P.S.
Trust NOBODY you meet in-game!!!! They will stab you in the back! Believe me. And never use a *Keyed* lock for any of your doors. Always use code locks, as people can steal the key from you and walk right into your house and lock you out. But its impossible to steal your 4 digit code...
Good Luck! You're going to need it...

Rust is an iron oxide, usually red oxide formed by the redox reaction of iron and oxygen in the presence of water or air moisture. Several forms of rust are distinguishable both visually and by spectroscopy, and form under different circumstances. Rust consists of hydrated iron(III) oxides Fe2O3·nH2O and iron(III) oxide-hydroxide (FeO(OH), Fe(OH)3).
Given sufficient time, oxygen, and water, any iron mass will eventually convert entirely to rust and disintegrate. Surface rust is flaky and friable, and it provides no protection to the underlying iron, unlike the formation of patina on copper surfaces. Rusting is the common term for corrosion of iron and its alloys, such as steel. Many other metals undergo similar corrosion, but the resulting oxides are not commonly called rust.
Other forms of rust exist, like the result of reactions between iron and chloride in an environment deprived of oxygen. Rebar used in underwater concrete pillars, which generates green rust, is an example. Although rusting is generally a negative aspect of iron, a particular form of rusting, known as "stable rust," causes the object to have a thin coating of rust over the top, and if kept in low relative humidity, makes the "stable" layer protective to the iron below, but not to the extent of other oxides, such as aluminum.

Spec Ops: The Line (SO:TL) basically isn't a bad game, but I still wouldn't recommend to buy it for the following reasons. While the setting and level design are unique and fresh, the game's mechanics and presentation suffer from some horrible, horrible issues that shouldn't be there in the first place, considering that Ghost Recon: Advanced Warfighter (GR:AW) and Star Wars: Republic Commando (SW:RC) got those things right over half a decade before SO:TL was released.
Seriously, a squad-based tactics shooter, where you cannot control your squad? Where you cannot tell them to stay put, but instead have to watch them run off like headless chickens and get themselves into hopeless situations, causing you to fail the mission? Where you cannot order them to cover you, or advance on your command? Bloody ♥♥♥♥ing hell! The amount of frustration this game causes by squad mates that are about as intelligent as a slice of moldy bread is insane. GR:AW and SW:RC do this whole squad thing about a million times better with explicit orders you can give your whole squad or individual members.
Okay, I get it. You're not Rambo, and guns are lethal. But apparently your squad mates are Rambo, because I cannot imagine any other reason why they are capable of withstanding punishment that would kill you three times over. And when they finally drop, you can get them back on their feet in a few seconds. So while your mates are Rambo McBulletsponge, you seem to be a fragile piece of china that gets smashed when an enemy even looks at you. Also once you drop it's over, because the magic healing syringe apparently only works on NPCs. In SW:RC you can also "revive" fallen squad mates, but they can do the same to you (and are actually quite clever in covering each other to get you back on your feet if you drop).
What's the difference between a FAMAS and a 417? What's the difference between an AK-47 and a M4A1? The weapons feel and play far too similar to warrant the variety, and you generally pick the one that has the most ammo available (either right now, or from what you expect in the next room/section). The only exception are situations that either require a particular weapon (sniper) or where you lose all previous weapons. There are far too many weapons that serve the exact same purpose and have the exact same gun play, making them completely redundant. Also, why the hell would an army battalion use so many different weapons with incompatible upgrades/extensions/calibres? It doesn't make any sense.
Seriously, ♥♥♥♥ heavy troopers. Just ♥♥♥♥ them. Guy with open helmet that exposes face survives several large caliber rounds (or frag grenades) to said exposed face. Are you ♥♥♥♥ing kidding me, SO:TL? For real? If you design enemies to visually have a weak spot (like open helmet), then FFS don't make that visual weak spot invulnerable! GAAAAHHHHHHH. Don't make me think there's a particular tactic to one type of enemy, when they just have twelve times more health than the other mooks! Damnit!
What really ground my gears was the repeated talk of how everyone had a choice, and that there was always an alternative to some course of action, but then the game goes around and forces you into a hamfisted linear rail road plot. No, you can't not use the phosphor grenade mortar. No, you can't not steal the water (and damn everyone left in the city to death by dehydration). No, you can't not destroy the radio tower. And so on, and so forth. Bascially, the only decisions you can make is which of two achievements you get in a particular situation. And that's a lame excuse, both for story and achievments.
If you're interested in the story, a few "Let's Play" videos on YouTube will serve you just fine, and save you hours of frustration.

The game mechanics don't offer anything special and may even lead to frustration from time to time. Storywise, you could hardly find a match in the military shooter genre. The less you know in advance, the better. Keep your questions for after finishing the game, there will be a lot of them.

I had almost no idea of what I was getting into with this game. Getting it as a part of a Humble Bundle, Windward looked like the sort of game I would never purchase for myself. I got the feeling that this game was for a pretty specific demographic that I’m not exactly a part of (long term, methodical strategy/planning in a historical setting).

First thing I noticed is that the game actual seemed to run pretty well with my remarkably low end PC. I enjoyed the art style and how surprising straightforward the gameplay ended up being. Unobtrusive menus and pop-ups were enough to teach me the essentials, but I still would’ve liked a brief and clean tutorial since the game does take a few minutes to wrap your head around.

That being said, the game is really quite simple once you get the hang of things. Float around (rather slowly) clicking on things in the water while moving between cities. Once you have enough gold, buy upgrades. When you're strong enough, move out to other portions of the map and conquest. It’s an addictive experience but one that can only hold you for so long. However, there was multiplayer and being able to interact with real people and not just NPCs really does a lot to breathe new life into games like this.

If it sounds like it might be your kind of game and/or you’ve got some friends that would be willing to go along for the ride, then I would recommend it.

First impressions: I meant to try this game for about 15 minutes before bed and ended up playing over 2 hours.
Windward has a very relaxing and engrossing atmosphere, with gameplay mechanics very much like Sunless Sea, but without the dark theme, deep storytelling, or things going horribly wrong every few minutes.
However, it does allow you far more ability to modify your world (which is randomly generated by seed) by setting down new towns of your faction's colonists and defensive structures for them, and even modifying your environment by blowing up a new passage for your ships to get through!
This game can make even a humble fetch-quest enjoyable simply due to the process of getting there, and then adds in layers of strategic planning where you can be working out a kind of travelling salesman problem in your head in order to maximise the benefits of multiple different conflicting or synergistic goals in the minimum amount of time.
I haven't had a chance to try PVP combat yet, but so long as you can get past its current lack of a tutorial and you don't expect deep physics, I already strongly recommend this game.
It's even running smoothly on a dual-core laptop made in 2008, so you should be able to play this on the move.

If you're into Sid Meier's Pirates! you'll definitely like Windward too. Good combat, nice graphics and a healthy selection of items make for a fun few hours.
The main gameplay elements are trading, ship combat and quests. Quests mainly consist of bringing A to B and protecting X from Y, these are fun for a while, but get dull with time.
My biggest problem with Windward is the fact that the world doesn't really feel alive (in single player), part of the game is expanding your factions territory, but sadly it all feels like a one person job, the other ships in your faction do not autonomously seem to do any quests or seize new territory - they don't seem to do much of anything aside from rushing to the aid of a town being plundered from pirates.
Note that I have barely touched the online multiplayer, my critiques might not be as relevant considering the fact that playing with 99 other people on a fairly confined area could easily give the world life.

About 50 hours into the game, while I was grinding achievements in a hypnosis-like haze the game had induced on me, I slowly realized the kind of man Mad Max is.
Mad Max is the story of a psychologically unstable man who forces his own view of justice and order on a disturbed yet otherwise functioning post-apocalyptic society.
Shortly after being ambushed by the warlord Scrotus the Immortan Jr., "the crazy eyed road warrior" Max, hellbent on revenge, goes completely out of his way: he topples down every single stronghold that probably without option declared allegiance to the tyrant Scrotus, he pillages every single isolated and obscure domicile where starving scavengers survive and get hostile only if anyone trespasses their territory and he creepily collect their private photos and diary entries, reading and cataloging every single one of them for god knows what reason. By the end of his rage induced rampage that he ironically performs in a chillingly and psychotically restrained composure, Max opts to kill a disabled and mentally handicapped man, Chumbucket, whose messianic delusions were ultimately exploited by Max to make him build his war-rig. As Chumbucket continually upgrades his life’s greatest work, appropriately named the Magnum Opus and have creepily ecstatic moments of joy as “his saint” Max drives it, he grows an unhealthy affection for him, most likely as a result of Stockholm Syndrome. The social bond that keeps the narcissistic-codependent duo together is Chumbucket’s ♥♥♥♥♥♥ic joy of having Max drive his car and Max perpetually feeding on Chumbucket’s unhealthy obsession.
Perhaps falling victim to his ever building, self-mutilating, caustic hatred, Max suffers from a psychological breakdown. He becomes the sole prisoner of his rotten psyche and gets trapped in his own subconscious; his personal limbo. At the very end of his saga, every significant person that were unfortunate enough to cross paths with Max inexplicably come back to life in this timeless mental Wasteland, perhaps as a manifestation of his guilt.
And Max spends his days here until eternity, where he was supposed to leave as soon as possible, surrounded by the unforgiving "Big Nothing" - the borders of his own subconscious, driving in his combustible, fire spitting mount restlessly, Chumbucket whispering praise in the wind behind him, with his inner demons only seeping out during fleeting moments as the red in his eyes.

This game has good platforming, combat and art, but the money system is so terrible that I can not recommend it. It's one thing to have everything get more expensive as you purchase items / upgrades, but you lose ALL of your money EVERY single time you start a new run. This means that, unless you have a really good run where you're getting tons of money, you're just wasting your time as nothing you collect (With the exception of rare items) counts towards anything. This game is already hard, so why do you have to make it feel like a chore to play?
To put it in perspective, imagine the leveling of Dark Souls, but instead of leveling at a camp fire, you level up when you die. Now imagine that your souls are taken from you if you don't have enough to level up. That's this game's idea of "Progression". Either you get enough souls to level, or you get literally nothing.
