Amazing Early Access Game!
Here is the summary:
Start with an empty plot of land with $30000 (Or infinite money, if you turned on sandbox)
Choose your first government grants and start building.
Get a perimeter and holding cell, along with required standards (canteen, shower, etc.) up. Bring in prisoners.
Now that you have a basic infrastructure, do WHATEVER YOU WANT with your prison. Make it a resort of happiness, a max security box of death, a balanced prison, etc. you can add a death row block too. A great modding system (thanks to steam as well) lets you add more things to do in your game, as once you have a maxed out prison it gets more boring. Mods help fix the boredom.
If you want to make it even more fun, you can save your game then start a riot. YEAH! Then, reload your save if you want to still have functioning prison. Or, try to rebuild AFTER the giant riot (extra challenge!)
If you go bankrupt, too many people die, or you do have an uncontrollable riot, if you enabled 'failure conditions' you can actually lose the game!
Negatives -
Even now, there are still some bugs left
Even with mods, once you have built everything, it gets a little bit boring.
Overall - 9.5/10
-ALPHA 36 NOTE-
They have added in gangs! If you enable gangs, they add a huge amount of fun and challenge to the game. Once a legendary prisoner joins a gang and becomes leader, all hell breaks loose. The prisoners will start controlling areas. Your guards can still enter those areas, but you cant edit those areas (e.g. placing objects) until you evict the prisoners, which starts a huge fight! AWESOME!
Also, the dev team has added in new rooms and features since my original comments! Buy the game and CHECK THEM OUT!

This game, you guys, is one I've spent countless hours (well like, 133 hours to be exact) playing, and building a ton of prisons for different inmates. I can honestly tell you that you should buy this game, and if you have the money to buy this game right now, and you're reading the reviews to see if you should: BUY IT!
Here's why this game (in my opinion) appeals to a pretty wide variety of people:
-If you are a detail oriented person, you can nitpick at a lot of aspects of this prison, such as doors, scheduling, etc.
-If you are NOT a detail oriented person, there are still a lot of things you do in this game that you do not need to schedule or work at to perfect. Although this game is not quite geared toward people like this, it is still extremely enjoyable without these features. There are also a ton of guides that can help you perfect your prison if this isn't your thing.
So... let's move on to some Pros and Cons of this game...
PROS:
-Extremely Versatile
-Lots of re-play value
-Two major gamemodes (Sandbox and "Survival")
-Many different details
-Amazing mod community
-Still being worked on (more features later!)
-Developers that listen to the community and care about the players *cough*Not Rockstar*cough*
CONS:
-Lots of bugs still around (to be expected with a game still in Early Access)
-Some mods do not work when used at the same time
-Some aspects of managing your prison can be extremely frustrating at times, but eventually work out.
Now, I may be slightly biased on the Pros and Cons, but seriously, this game is certainly at least taking a good look at, if you're still not sure about buying.

Beyond the efforts of survival, the end goals are one's own. See how many cycles you last? Wish to have the best things for your suplicants? or do it again, better this time?
All these reviews with less than 10 hours on record, telling you the game is uninteresting. What puts people off, I assume, is the mid-game. Starting and setting up base is the fun part but is hardly a challenge, which is why most people enjoy it. The mid-game, presently, is where the base needs planning and strict management to survive - where everything starts to fall down a spiral, probably which is where people have a falling out. The difficulty spikes during this mid period, where resources, tasks and dupes need to be managed if you wish to go on further - where it becomes a niche genre - some people love it, some don't. After this difficult and rather annoying period, the game becomes a bit of a sandbox and you can let your creativity flourish, with advanced machineries and systems. Bases evolve to their final form, mostly sustaining themselves and an easier relaxed life for your dupes.

The pricing structure is bizarre and tarnishes the whole experience a bit, but the gameplay is still mostly good. I have to wonder if we'll see discounts on either the first part or the "full experience" before it's finished, which would be bad for the day one buyers.
The first map is tiny but is mostly just a tutorial that the game makes you play at least twice.
The second map is another tiny one that you can finish in minutes without being detected.
The third map is a large building and the surrounding area. It's fun and there are multiple ways to complete the mission.
And... that's all there is.
The first two maps feel very simplistic, almost like a tech demo. The third map really shows how bad the AI is since there's a lot more available for you to do.
The controls feel somewhat poorly thought out but I had no issue with loading times as some have reported. The graphics are not good enough to justify the terrible performance. It's barely playable, but somewhat ugly.
Overall, I don't regret my purchase and that's somehow enough for me to recommend it. But it's a really short experience (under 2 hours) with the promise of 5 more maps to come this year. That's still a really small game. Get it if you really need a new Hitman game in your life and can't wait to see how the game is when it's finished. But this isn't must-have yet.

Hitman is out!!! But you can't actually play it.
Three words, Scaleable Cloud Computing. Although I guess if a company is dumb enough to require online connectivity for single player campaign content, they're probably too dumb to ensure that people can actually get an online connection and play the game. Maybe I'll update this review if the game becomes playable in the future,...or maybe I won't even bother.
No matter how great the content may or may not be. And the little I've played of it is very fun, I can't begin to recommend a game that kicks you out as the least online hiccup.

NOTE: MY OLD-OLD REVIEW IS BELOW, FOR POSTERITY
Hitman 2016 was good when it launched, and with each update that passed, it got better. Put simply, if you're a fan of *any* previous Hitman game, don't hesitate to purchase it.
I'm not going to bore you with an in-depth review as I'm sure there's plenty of them, so I'll cut to the chase: if you loved Blood Money, and liked/tolerated Absolution, this is the game to play. It's brilliant and the unlock/feat/assassination system is well-made.
I predict about 15 hours of content for the one level, not including elusive contracts/user-made contracts. Then there's more levels to come in the next few months.
HOWEVER. The server issues are an absolute nightmare. You are a slave to both their servers being online, as well as Steam's (yes, if Steam servers are down, then you can't play online on Hitman either). It takes (for me) about 60 seconds to go from menu item to menu item.
Provided you can get around this, the game is brilliant. Once they fix these issues, this game will be greater than even Blood Money.
Specs and performance:
Intel i7-4790K @ 4.4GHz
GTX 970 @ stock
Installed to SSD
Windows 7 (DX11)
Set to high settings everywhere except for shadows.
FPS: Anywhere between 45~ in NPC-dense areas to 120FPS in the bathroom.
OLD REVIEW:
> Always-online DRM
> Servers are down
> Can still play game
> No progression, unlocks, equipment, clothing, contracts, leaderboards, feats, opportunities while offline though.

This game is excellent.  I'm only a few hours into it and don't even know the full extent of what it has to offer, but even what I've seen so far is extremely well done.  The system is open.  The ships pilot well from the keyboard or the mouse (haven't tried using a flight stick, yet).  The customization is extensive.  Overall, I'd say it's extremely good as beta releases go.  That's not to say there isn't some room for improvement.  There is.  But, the overall state of the game is very good and shows great promise.
As far as negatives go, I'd have to say the biggest one for me is that there is not enough feedback when your shots impact an enemy vessel, especially on beam weapons.  The beams fire out and follow your targeting cursor, so the actual firing is good and responsive.  But, even at near point blank ranges, there isn't much to let you know that your beams are impacting a solid object.  Even a sound effect would be nice, a sort of deep rumble or a sort of cutting sound as you hit the enemy hull.  Close up, it's not a big deal.  But, at long distances, you aren't sure if you're connecting and wind up squinting at the screen to watch the enemy shield indicator.
As I said, overall, this game is excellent, and it's still in beta.  I suspect there will be a lot more in the way of improvements.  I got this for $16.74 when it went on sale, and I'd say it's well worth that price.  Knowing what I know about it now, I'd likely buy it at full price.  As Early Access or beta games go, this is among the best.  Give it a shot.

Spec Ops: The Line (SO:TL) basically isn't a bad game, but I still wouldn't recommend to buy it for the following reasons. While the setting and level design are unique and fresh, the game's mechanics and presentation suffer from some horrible, horrible issues that shouldn't be there in the first place, considering that Ghost Recon: Advanced Warfighter (GR:AW) and Star Wars: Republic Commando (SW:RC) got those things right over half a decade before SO:TL was released.
Seriously, a squad-based tactics shooter, where you cannot control your squad? Where you cannot tell them to stay put, but instead have to watch them run off like headless chickens and get themselves into hopeless situations, causing you to fail the mission? Where you cannot order them to cover you, or advance on your command? Bloody ♥♥♥♥ing hell! The amount of frustration this game causes by squad mates that are about as intelligent as a slice of moldy bread is insane. GR:AW and SW:RC do this whole squad thing about a million times better with explicit orders you can give your whole squad or individual members.
Okay, I get it. You're not Rambo, and guns are lethal. But apparently your squad mates are Rambo, because I cannot imagine any other reason why they are capable of withstanding punishment that would kill you three times over. And when they finally drop, you can get them back on their feet in a few seconds. So while your mates are Rambo McBulletsponge, you seem to be a fragile piece of china that gets smashed when an enemy even looks at you. Also once you drop it's over, because the magic healing syringe apparently only works on NPCs. In SW:RC you can also "revive" fallen squad mates, but they can do the same to you (and are actually quite clever in covering each other to get you back on your feet if you drop).
What's the difference between a FAMAS and a 417? What's the difference between an AK-47 and a M4A1? The weapons feel and play far too similar to warrant the variety, and you generally pick the one that has the most ammo available (either right now, or from what you expect in the next room/section). The only exception are situations that either require a particular weapon (sniper) or where you lose all previous weapons. There are far too many weapons that serve the exact same purpose and have the exact same gun play, making them completely redundant. Also, why the hell would an army battalion use so many different weapons with incompatible upgrades/extensions/calibres? It doesn't make any sense.
Seriously, ♥♥♥♥ heavy troopers. Just ♥♥♥♥ them. Guy with open helmet that exposes face survives several large caliber rounds (or frag grenades) to said exposed face. Are you ♥♥♥♥ing kidding me, SO:TL? For real? If you design enemies to visually have a weak spot (like open helmet), then FFS don't make that visual weak spot invulnerable! GAAAAHHHHHHH. Don't make me think there's a particular tactic to one type of enemy, when they just have twelve times more health than the other mooks! Damnit!
What really ground my gears was the repeated talk of how everyone had a choice, and that there was always an alternative to some course of action, but then the game goes around and forces you into a hamfisted linear rail road plot. No, you can't not use the phosphor grenade mortar. No, you can't not steal the water (and damn everyone left in the city to death by dehydration). No, you can't not destroy the radio tower. And so on, and so forth. Bascially, the only decisions you can make is which of two achievements you get in a particular situation. And that's a lame excuse, both for story and achievments.
If you're interested in the story, a few "Let's Play" videos on YouTube will serve you just fine, and save you hours of frustration.

The game mechanics don't offer anything special and may even lead to frustration from time to time. Storywise, you could hardly find a match in the military shooter genre. The less you know in advance, the better. Keep your questions for after finishing the game, there will be a lot of them.

About 50 hours into the game, while I was grinding achievements in a hypnosis-like haze the game had induced on me, I slowly realized the kind of man Mad Max is.
Mad Max is the story of a psychologically unstable man who forces his own view of justice and order on a disturbed yet otherwise functioning post-apocalyptic society.
Shortly after being ambushed by the warlord Scrotus the Immortan Jr., "the crazy eyed road warrior" Max, hellbent on revenge, goes completely out of his way: he topples down every single stronghold that probably without option declared allegiance to the tyrant Scrotus, he pillages every single isolated and obscure domicile where starving scavengers survive and get hostile only if anyone trespasses their territory and he creepily collect their private photos and diary entries, reading and cataloging every single one of them for god knows what reason. By the end of his rage induced rampage that he ironically performs in a chillingly and psychotically restrained composure, Max opts to kill a disabled and mentally handicapped man, Chumbucket, whose messianic delusions were ultimately exploited by Max to make him build his war-rig. As Chumbucket continually upgrades his life’s greatest work, appropriately named the Magnum Opus and have creepily ecstatic moments of joy as “his saint” Max drives it, he grows an unhealthy affection for him, most likely as a result of Stockholm Syndrome. The social bond that keeps the narcissistic-codependent duo together is Chumbucket’s ♥♥♥♥♥♥ic joy of having Max drive his car and Max perpetually feeding on Chumbucket’s unhealthy obsession.
Perhaps falling victim to his ever building, self-mutilating, caustic hatred, Max suffers from a psychological breakdown. He becomes the sole prisoner of his rotten psyche and gets trapped in his own subconscious; his personal limbo. At the very end of his saga, every significant person that were unfortunate enough to cross paths with Max inexplicably come back to life in this timeless mental Wasteland, perhaps as a manifestation of his guilt.
And Max spends his days here until eternity, where he was supposed to leave as soon as possible, surrounded by the unforgiving "Big Nothing" - the borders of his own subconscious, driving in his combustible, fire spitting mount restlessly, Chumbucket whispering praise in the wind behind him, with his inner demons only seeping out during fleeting moments as the red in his eyes.

Rogue Legacy is a pseudo-rogue like platformer that rewards players who have the persistence to get better. To describe the game in a few words, it's a lot like 2d Dark Souls. The movement and controls are easy to get into and are praisingly fluid. However, the challenge lies in navigating and surviving the pseudo randomly generated world of Castle Hamson and its surrounding areas--much like Dark Souls. It's simple and easy to learn--but getting around the enemies and obstacles aren't. And this is exactly where the game shines. The drive to get better will further motivate you and everytime you come back with a new hero--no matter how stupid your previous death was--you are always at least slightly better than you were the last time. In fact, this is made obvious whenever you purchase new equipment or upgrades that carry over throughout your line of characters.
With that said, Rogue Legacy isn't for people looking for a cakewalk. At first, you will quite literally die within a few seconds of entering the castle. But if you keep at it, you will eventually find yourself plowing through enemies. The accumulated upgrades are certainly a factor, but what will carry you through will mostly be attributed to your personal skill.
So let's talk specs. This game can run on both my craptops. One of which has a fried battery. This is perfect for when I'm out and about and I find myself with time to kill. The only qualm I have is the fact that it doesn't have the cloud save functionality. This makes it a bit of a hassle for me to transfer my files back and forth between my main PC and my craptops.
As for value for money, for its full price I would not recommend it. I would recommend that you wait for a sale (as I did) and purchase the game for a lot less. I'm not saying that the game isn't worth it--I just think that this is a game that can stay on the shelf until it goes on sale. Its not THE ESSENTIAL game to have in your library, but it is definitely a game I would always rely on when I'm not at home or travelling to keep me entertained. With that said, I am an advocate of smart buying. No matter how much money you have to burn, I still think it is a good idea to prioritize. Having and playing this game would be a lot more satisfying knowing that you bought it for 3 bucks.

tl;dr: Do NOT buy this game in its current state and do NOT support these ridiculous Online-Only, Broken-On-Release, "Don't worry, Day 1 Patch wil fix it"  business practices.
Specs:
i7 4970K @ 4.5GH/z

Have to say I was very excited for this game, and I mean very, having grown up playing Contracts and Blood Money for countless hours on end. And do you know how I was able to do that? The original Publisher and developers didn't force me to be online to play a game that I intended to play Offline, to immerse myself in the world of Hitman and make up my own stories as I carried out my duties as an assassin.
As soon as you load up the game, the first thing you're greeted to is your options menu for the graphics. You'll note that Texture quality HIGH is greyed out, as is 2K Resolution, my native for all of my monitors.
Loading the game up, you're next given a screen advising that "Hitman is designed for Online play, and your save games are not interchangeable between Offline and Online modes". As an Australian that lives out in the bush, where Internet is not always the most stable, this becomes a problem as we're then unable "to play the game it was designed to be" which ultimately detracts from the overall experience. Additionally, should I then desire to play the game Online and get the "full experience", I'd lose all my progress Offline and have to start over.
As of writing this, I've still been unable to play ONLINE as my connection to the Hitman servers has failed over and over, yet here I sit browsing the internet and writing this review for you. Thus, I launched the game Offline. Graphically, the game looks beautiful, and you can really appreciate the amnount of work the developers put into immersing the player into the world, however the game runs like absolute ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. There's been no optimization whatsoever for PC (as should now be expected for most, if not all, AAA titles) and I find myself struggling to hit over 50FPS with at least ONE of my graphics cards. With both my cards in their original and intended SLI configuration, you'll receive jaggies, screen tearing, and no improvement whatsoever to your FPS.
Do not buy this game, wait until the devs fix the game and release it "how it was intended to be played": in a working state.
Thank god for Steam Refunds.

You have installed a new metal detector at the exit of the cafeteria to curb the theft of cutlery, inmates are irate at the unnecessary search this yields and just as their anger hits boiling point all of your guards have decided it’s time to take a break or patrol some far flung region of your prison. If managing the incessant needs of digital prisoners sounds like your idea of a fun evening then Prison Architect may have you covered.
Prison Architect, from developer Introversion Software, is in early access on Steam and is looking to bring a new edge to the management-sim genre. Now, before we start you are going to have to realise something pretty quickly: The first prison you build is going to be a horrible mess. A horrible, bloody, mess. While I thought I got the hang of the basic controls once I had played through the game’s introduction tutorial, I soon came to realise that actually I had only scratched the surface and my first prison mirrored something similar to the film Bronson – a violent, unmanageable mess – rather than the Shawshank Redemption vision I had in my head.
But what sort of Prison Architect will you be? The game leaves that decision entirely on your shoulders once you’re settled with the basics; Prison Architect allows you to feel good about yourself, you will be able to build reform programs through education and enable prisoners to learn vocational skills through a workshop system that improves their morale and ability to reintegrate with society upon release. And, of course, if they step out of line you can chuck them straight into solitary to separate them from the main body of your population and leave them to rot which, in turn, provides a deterrent to the other prisoners who may be thinking of stepping out of line. Each prisoner you take in to your prison provides a revenue stream for you to continue improvements and is, of course, offset by the amount of danger an extra man or overcrowding your prison may cause. This delicate balancing act is how you’ll spend a lot of your game, earning some extra cash to improve but not wanting to throw too many inmates in at once.
There is a simple tech tree which allows you to slowly introduce new ideas, staff members and rooms to your prison. You may desperately need an infirmary in your prison due to a riot that injured inmates and your staff or you have had a sudden intake of high-risk prisoners which means Patrol Dogs and Armed Guards are in order. Whatever type of prison you decide to build and how fast you need to expand is all down to how you set up the game to begin with. For a more challenging trial you can set it so you have a prisoner intake every single day at 8am and this means you’ll be focusing on some rapid expansion and introducing new cell blocks constantly while having the ability to switch off Prisoner Intake means you will be able to sit back and think about your prison design and put something together that makes sense and works far more efficiently and safely for your staff. You may have prisoners in with your main population that are awaiting execution – these are the most dangerous and likely to revolt because they have nothing to lose and need direct intervention by your guards on a regular basis. You can decide on the level of management you want on individuals and ensure they’re kept separate to the low risk, short stay offenders who may not need as much of your staff’s time.
Prisoners will try and escape or smuggle contraband into your prison, they’ll walk around and take every opportunity to skip out on you by utilising any minor flaw in your prison’s design. But, once the day is over and their time is served, your prisoners will be released, reformed and hopefully willing to contribute to society once again. You can drill down and even micromanage every single need of your individual prisoners. You’ll see how long they have left to serve and and whether they’re likely to reoffend once they are released. You can hire a psychiatrist who will help you manage these needs and build the prison’s daily schedule to ensure everyone gets what they need from their day. It is usually the silly things that tend to foil me in Prison Architect – the prison had expanded so rapidly and I had not thoroughly expanded my kitchen to an appropriate level and, therefore, half my prisoners weren’t eating during the one hour of meal time I had allotted which caused the starving to push back against my guards who struggled to control such a large rabid mob.
Prison Architect’s simple two-dimensional art style feels crisp and responsive and allows the game to run on just about every PC or laptop you may have opening up the (Usual resource intensive) management-sim genre to a whole new crowd. The game looks great and brings a slight comedic twist to the violence and dark nature of running a prison full of incarcerated inmates. The interface is simple and so goes a long way into allowing creativity. With a new room or angle in your prison two clicks away creativity is easily embraced.
There is so much promise in Prison Architect, everything it already offers and the constant, major updates that are consistently pushed to Steam it’s hard to imagine how far the final game will go in polishing the base mechanics and adding new systems for the player to develop and maintain a large scale, working prison. With Prison Architect already tied into the Steam Workshop system you can download different mods and spend a lot of time looking at other people’s work to inspire the direction of your prison. The ability to share your ideas and designs means inspiration is only a click away when you get stuck or how to get yourself out of the corner you have built yourself in too.

First off, the title should be, "Oxygen, water, and food not included," because if you don't set things up right, your colony will perish fast. So it's my duty here to be as clear as possible so those who do like to work with piping systems will find a challenging game they simply can't put down.
Oxygen is detrimental in the beginning, but once you establish your hvac system, it's water that becomes the sought after resource. Actually, the full title should be, "Oxygen, water, and food  (and you ain't getting your soul back) not included," because Klei seems to know how make an addict out of you with their combination of procedural generation and deep exploratory play. Even in EA I can't put this damn game down! It's hours and hours that pass by before I know it.
Unlike Don't Starved, there is not much combat in ONI's current state of EA. Here you are dealing with gasses that mingle with each other. For example: You obviously want to control your CO2, because otherwise air becomes unbreathable, right? Yet oxygen, oh life giver, will rot your food. So banking ration boxes in CO2 keeps your food sterile. And since CO2 is heavier than oxygen, placing things right is key.
In its fully destructible environment of assorted biomes--dirt, slime, ice, heat, and magma--the most fun I have is moving large bodies of water that gush and flow so close to the real deal.

I'm loving Starpoint Gemini 2: probably the best space game in year. It's transitioned out of beta nicely, with minimal bugs, and improved optimization. The game has two modes, story and sandbox, and both are quite enjoyable. The control scheme feels a little like Nexus the Jupiter (but not exactly), in the sense that you're the commander of a large ship with various systems (and not just a fighter). Much better than the X series imo.
The game excells at allowing you to create the kind of space captain you want to be, and the kind of ship you want to fly. There are three classes, commander, gunner, and engineer, and each excells at different specializations. Commanders are great pilots, and augment their fleets; while, gunners excell at blowing things up; the engineer can create space anomalies like vortexes that suck enemy ships in, deal radiation damage to crews, or they can hack and shut down ship systems.
The ships are fantastic. Nearly a hundred different ships of varying classes that you can customize and taylor to your play style. You can control frigates and battleships - and command squadrons of fighters (but there are no fighters you can fly). Place different systems, weapons, and then tweak those systems and weapons with different modules. So, for example, you can tweak your teleporter to improve its capacity, or give it a defensive characteristic, and use it to block enemy teleports. (your ships have troops which can defend against and invade and take over other ships which you can later keep or sell.) Do you install a module with better accuracy, damage, or, for a little more money, both?
Finally, there are a variety of things to do. You can be a trader, a smuggler, a pirate (raid and steal ships), or a fleet commander of some sorts. There are anomalies in space that you can simply go out, explore, scan, and document, and gain experience from this. You can ferry VIP or desparately needed supplies between stations. As much variety to the missions as in any space game.
My only real complaints, and by no means are these game breaking, is the lack of documentation (there's very little information available on what different game mechanics do, exactly. Which is frustrating, since they obviously took the time to put different mechanics into the game. For example, some guns do "emp" damages, or "radiation" damage, and no where does it say exactly what it means by this, one is just left to assume that radiation hurts crews and emp drains batteries or shields.
My second complaint is that there's just too much clutter. Don't get me wrong, the game is beautiful, but everywhere you look there's some beautiful nebulae, star, or simply space debry all around you. Your eyes get overwhelmed by the clutter, never are you allowed to enjoy the simplicity of being amongst the stars. You never get the sense that you're exploring unchartered territory, as there are ships and stations everywhere you go.
All in all, excellent game. 8/10.

Borderlands 2 truly is a great game. Why? What makes it differ from the average shooter? Well, the sheer amount of loot is what draws thousands to be addicted to this game. With many mods to be found that either mod your class, your guns, or your grenades, there's usually soomething to be found in every environment.
The classes themselves don't have much room for customization, but this is largely because B2 is mainly a great co-op game, with every character class fulfilling certain needs to complete the mission. Therefore, every character class has a set ability with little customization.
Co-Op:9/10
Singleplayer is still VERY fun however due to the immersive storyline that really draws you in. The voice acting is amazing and this is part of why the game feels so organic. Gearbox really has created a world here, one you won't forget,  even after the journey is over. With memorable characters and unforgettable plot moments, you'll be sad when you beat the game.
Singleplayer:8/10
But beating the game for 100% completion will take you hours. There are SOOOOOOO many side quests, so you won't have to say goodbye to Pandora for a couple hundred hours.
So this really is a good game. The humor is juvenile at best. Suicide Psychos come running at you screaming vulgar taunts, animals are given the titles "Bonerfarts". This humor feels very immature, and while it may get old, I believe that it is an essential part of what makes the Borderlands Saga unique, aside from the Mad-Max-inspired environments and characters.
Overall: 9/10

Trust me, the stories are fun to play. Sandbox mode is just a blank sandbox for you to construct upon. Not much else there. And then, last, but certainly not least, escape mode. This puts you in the shoes of a prisoner and the main objective to to cause enough trouble to upgrade your statistics. With high stats, you will have an easier time escaping. There also little easter eggs to find. Polaroids and Game Bibles are unique little items to come across. Polaroids are simple little photographs you can find in the game, and Game Bibles are pages of the developer's sketches and ideas. Also, there are interesting little achievements to colect, and most are a lot of fun to get. Definitely get this game if you have the spending money. I expect to clock in a lot more hours on this game.

acording to steam, I now have 65 hours on record in this game.
I am currently at new game plus 5, with maxed out stats and everything unlocked. I still regularly play this game.
it's a great game to play if you like roguelikes and platformers. the gameplay varies between numbingly easy to greatly chalenging. it's always fun to play for half an hour with some podcast in the background, to unwind from abusy day. the gameplay is engaging and the controls feel fluid enough that every hit you take feels like it's your fault, and not the game cheating. you are given plenty of tools and abilities to avoid damage, especially in later runs when you get to harder areas, and taking hits becomes more significant.
however, there are some cons to take into consideration.
after a while it becomes very clear that there aren't that many different rooms. this plays a big part in the game becoming repetitive over time. the same goes for minibosses. while I enjoyed fighting them, after a while it becomes so apparent what the easiest strategy is to defeat them that they aren't even a minor threat anymore. and this also goes for the main bosses, the only time I ever had trouble fighting an area boss was the first time I encountered one. after that, I never needed more than two tries to beat a boss. in this context, I almost think the game gives you too many options to make it easier. especially grace runes combined with the architect make it incredibly easy to beat the game in only a few runs, especially at ng + player levels. I also feel like the different classes and traits become kind of meaningless towards the end, when it becomes very clear that some characters and traits are simply best avoided, leading to the player simply never picking them.
a more minor annoyance is the abundant presense of glitches. for a game this old, they really shouldn't be this common. these are mostly visual bugs, like effects persisting, and are usually fixed by leaving and re entering a room, but I've also had my character teleport into a wall and getting stuck, forcing me to restart the game, and other more troubling glitches.
overall, the game is a lot of fun, and I definetely recommend it to fans of the genre. I bought the game on sale, and I'm glad I did, but I'm not sure if I personally would buy it for it's full price of 15 euros.

Now that I've completed all the endings, I reckon I should give a review a try. First of all, the music. BLOODY AMAZING. The soundtrack is full of awesome, emotional and is always on-point. Beautiful. Next, the graphics. Simplistic, but UT pulls it off amazingly. 8-bit has never looked so great (in recent years, at least.). Then there's the gameplay. At first I was a bit sceptical. The bullet-hell fighting mechanics seemed a little odd at first, but it's very enjoyable. In other RPGS, you aren't really given a chance to avoid the foe's attacks, but UT is different. It actually gives a fighting chance. The attacks are very well designed, and help each foe stand out. And the best bit is the fact you don't have to kill anybody. You can befriend every monster and learn more about their lives and personalities. I think that's awesome. And finally, the story. THE STORY. Just moving. It's got a memorable cast with distinct personalities all around, coupled with funny moments, great dialogue, shocking and/or disturbing/scary moments and sad, emotional moments. All of these tie the game up brilliantly. In conclusion: Undertale is amazing. While the fandom is bad, I feel that people can express their creativity in different ways. It all depends on who's viewing the material. Most people see the fandom as 'cringy' or 'toxic'. But others may appreciate it. As for me, I'm not as much on the fandom's side, but I thought it was worth noting. Most people assume Undertale is terrible, but that's because they haven't played it (because of the fandom), but I definitely recommend this game.

IO Interactive is using the latest in file DRM, which is supposedly unhackable. They are using Steam to prevent game sharing. What possible rationale do they have for ALSO including always on server-based DRM?
To top it off, this isn't a complete game. The single player experiance is spread across multiple "episides" which will be released over time. So even if you COULD play it (which you can't), you have two main missions play. They basically shipped a mostly multiplayer-only game and are adding most of the missions over time as DLC. Overall, it's a very, very good game. I've split this review into a few categories, so maybe that'll help you find what matters most.
- Gameplay
Let's be honest here. This game is about space combat, not about mining or scavenging or being a space taxi man. That's where the "meat and potatoes" of this game is. So this is the most important thing for this game to get right. If it fails at this, it fails as a game.
And to its credit... gameplay is superb. Combat is fun, if a bit monotonous once you get a really powerful ship. It only keeps you on the edge of your seat when you're in real danger of losing your ship, such as when facing a really strong enemy while you're flying a much weaker ship, or a large fleet of enemies on your own.
Capturing an enemy ship is very satisfying. Unfortunately, towing ships takes a very long time and can be quite boring, especially if you're being attacked by enemies the whole way there. This game is still in early access, so balancing will still happen, so we'll have to see where it goes. But for now, its an amazing game and I can't wait for more!
There are a few immersion-breaking issues, though, such as the large delay, stutters and pauses when starting up the game, when entering a new area, when receiving new missions, or when auto-saving. However, since this is early access and not full release, we'll have to see what will become of these bugs.
Score: 9/10
- Storyline
None. At least none that I could find. While the game is tremendous fun on its own, with farming resources, capturing enemy ships and destroying enemy outposts, there doesn't seem to be any real purpose to it. At least not until the game is finished.
The story is still being developed, as this is still an unfinished product. But if this turns out to be a game where the war between factions can have the tide of the war turned either way depending on the player's success or failure in certain missions, it could be very cool, especially if areas become owned by different factions thereafter.
Score: Unknown (Not yet finished)
- Controls
The controls are nice and solid, with ships feeling very responsive (small ones) or sluggish (large ones) depending on size. The way a ship accelerates and breaks is also much more believable and immersive than you might believe from early footage. Trying to get a carrier to stop within 100m of a target feels like a feat of piloting at times.
3D space combat has been perfect by this game. I've played many space combat games like Homeworld, Star Trek Online and several others. But this game nails it and then some. At first I didn't understand why all the buttons and controls were needed for. But after enough time playing, I get it. And the position of the keys and what they do really helps give you a great feeling of control in the game.
Score: 10/10
- Graphics and Sound
Let's face it, as time marches forwards nobody wants to see ugly-looking games (unless they like Indie or retro games). And this game has some of the finest looking graphics one could hope for. They look beautiful, and even at 1440p on my GTX 650 Ti Boost 2GB it still performs smoothly (except when there are a lot of ships).
Considering that this is on the low side of a mid-tier graphics card, I'm impressed. With more graphics settings I should be able to increase framerate, and coding optimizations should also help make the game run smoother in the long term.
Sound wasn't much of a focus on this game, but the chatter and computer voice are really nice, and remind me a lot of the voice of the Enterprise-D in Star Trek: The Next Generation. It was a heart-warming surprise, and I can't wait until we get a total conversion mod for Starpoint Gemini 2.
The lack of a large variety of background music did feel a bit annoying and lackluster, but time will fix that. I'd love to have this game include beautiful symphonic and orchestral music, like Star Wars, Star Trek, and other great SciFi series. Music could really help take this game to the next level.
Score: 7/10
- Challenge
The game felt off-balance at several points during my dozens of hours playing so far. Capturing a large ship early on and using it felt almost like cheating on Normal difficulty. I'd like to see more balancing, such as not being able to use more than X amount of turrets on a ship depending on how many ranks below its minimum requirement you are. (So, if you're level 25 and trying to use a level 35 ship, you wouldn't be able to use 2 turrets in each direction.)
The long-term replay-ability right now is hindered because the game hasn't really given players much of an end-game challenge or reward system. Once you have earned 50M credits, and have several Dreadnoughts in your garage, the game just doesn't feel challenging anymore.
I'd like to see something to give the players the ability to hire commanders and bridge officers to command the ships in their garage, to they can join the player in large scale battles. This way it helps the player build his very own Armada to wipe out large (and challenging) enemy structures.
Right now all the fun is at the first 30 levels of the game. Once you reach that, it gets monotonous. But given the early development of this game, I think we can expect great things from it, especially with modding support.
Score: 6/10
- Fun
What can I say? I had a blast (no pun intended)! It was exciting and challenging for a long while, and it's consumed me for the past few days. I've lost sleep planning what my next ship upgrade should be, or where to lurk around under cloak waiting to capture the ship I wanted (but couldn't afford). Few games drag you in and hold your attention like that. All I can say is that I'm beyond impressed!
Score: 9/10
- Conclusion
I guess here's what I've got to say. For a game on Early Access on Steam, this is as much promise as I could dream of. (Unless you count Star Citizen, but that isn't fair.) It's fun, exciting, supports modding... it just isn't finished.
If you're looking to buy a whole package that's neatly wrapped up, ready to go, this game isn't for you. When you play an Early Access game, you're getting a sneak preview, you're beta-testing a game that will (of course) be filled with bugs (and your job is to report them), and your feedback this early on will also help shape where the game goes. You get to be involved in the creation of the game, and if it succeeds you get the satisfaction of knowing you helped a little.
This is a sneak preview. It's a taste of what's to come. And so far, I like what I see. They've got the game where it counts. Now it's just a matter of the final touches like faction warfare, dynamic economy, trade blockade, storyline, and so on. But given how far this game has progressed, that shouldn't take too much longer. I haven't seen many bugs, and for 25$ right now this game is a steal!
I give this game a wholehearted approval, and my recommendation to buy it. I can't wait to see what kind of amazing mods we'll see. Here's hoping the team that did the Star Trek Armada III mod for Sins of a Solar Empire can start working ASAP on Starpoint Gemini 2.

After putting an enjoyable 140 hours into the Binding of Isaac, I decided to give Rogue Legacy a shot in order to fill the rogue-like gap in my gaming life.  Rogue Legacy was fun for the first few hours, but I reached a point in the game where I was not bringing in enough gold to continue upgrading my character.  The "heir" gimmick got old really quickly as well.  Furthermore, there's just something off about the controls and hitboxes in this game.  Even after 8 hours I never really felt comfortable controlling my character.  I'm sure if I put in more hours and meticulously played the game that I could get over the hump, but there's no point in doing that if the game itself is grindy and boring.  The redeeming thing about the Binding of Isaac was that if you had a poor run you could start again completely anew.  In addition, even runs that ended in failure could still be FUN depending on the items you got.  With Rogue Legacy, you could potentially have a number of pointless runs that leave you right where you started.  Also, those runs are not fun at all because the traits, items, and upgrades lose their luster really fast.  For some games, pushing through might be worth it.  For this game, there is no worthwhile pay-off when you consider the countless other games out there.

Solid game overall though! An easy 9/10 in my book.

A great survival simulation base building game that is still in early access. You start off with 3 duplicants in space, having to dig around, collect materials to build a base whilst monitoring your duplicants' needs, oxygen, heat level and more. It can be hard work maintaining everything all at once as well as building a sustainable base which is suitable for accomodating more duplicants when they arrive. You can assign jobs to certain duplicants and you have the ability to research for enhancements. This makes the game more fun, major breakthrough for the colony. It can be challenging as there is currently no tutorials in game but there are lots of YouTube videos of the gameplay which are very helpful. If you like Klei's other games such as Don't Starve/Don't Starve Together, you would definitely like this game! Immerse yourself in space and see what happens :). Rogue Legacy adds an interesting RPG element to the classic roguelike formula, by having the treasure gained in one run pay for stats, upgrades and gear (of the player's choice) that can be used in all subsequent runs.  As the protagonist starts off incredibly weak, it's nearly impossible to beat the game before the player has attempted enough failed runs to make themselves strong enough to actually survive to the end.  Combat is fast and simple, but scales in difficulty as the character gets stronger and before long turns into a dangerous dodgefest.  Each new character is of a random RPG-style class, and has random strange personal traits like nearsightedness, dwarfism, or OCD, which when combined with a randomly-generated castle makes for a genuine and enjoyable roguelike experience every time.

Take into consideration that i am a long term fan of the HITMAN series. But i will give this an honest review, from my personal experience! Sorry for any grammatical problems during this review!
To start of, yes, this game is unsharpened, but not bad. (The internet thing is ridiculous tho)
Personaly, i havn't experienced game breaking bugs, but a few...
For example, a few through the wall melee glitching, but only like 2.

Belive me, after completing 75-80% of the challanges, you'll just be bored and feel done with, right now, Paris.
The contract mode works, no issues.
The internet system is not good, especially since they brand it a "Singleplayer" game.
Getting to the graphic settings, it's not optimized vary good. I personaly use a MSI Radeon R9 390 Gaming - 8GB.
First time i got into the game (helipad) i thought "Holy crap i can max this out with 130 FPS!" Then you get to the boat level, and the frames drop to around 20-40 FPS, jumping alot. With the crowd system, it does give your CPU a good run aswell.
I hope they don't release "episodes" with months in between
The price for the game, is probably not worth it at the moment, tho i got it for free with the graphics card.
Conclusion. At the moment, i would wait to buy the game, after 2-3 more "episodes" added, you'll have a huge amount of things to do, and it will take you around 6 hours to complete 75-80% of the challenges on one map, depending on your speed of course. It can't be ran on anything under a high/ultra setup, atleast i wouldn't recommend it.
It's a ~meeeeh~ game at the moment, lacking, but good. And they realy need to fix the internet things.
Good luck out there, Agents!

Yes, it has it's own problems (like the one with launching Paris episode, which DID exist but was solved within 1 hour after release), it's not perfect, but, in my opinion, it is at least a solid Hitman game, and a good game in general (just turn off all those minimaps, hints, etc.).

Do we have another" Blood Money quality" stuff here? Maybe - it's too early to judge this, but Paris episode reminds me of good BM missions - many angles of approach, interesting environment, well area design.
The only thing I don't like is the episode idea, but it does not change the general impression of playing well designed game.
PS. Yes, it's true, you can finish the main mission quickly. But, on the other hand you were able to do this in all good Hitman games - it's not the time of a single mission, but replayability that defines, at least for me, interesting Hitman scenario.

First problem came when i needed to upgrade my harpoon.
To do this i needed to clear threat from one zone completely. That includes clearing minefields which should be something you do for achievement. To clear minefields you need different vehicle that isnt your usual one.
It's almost defenseless, without good weaponry or ability to fix/upgrade it, so you are banging your head to the wall multiple times with the patrols.
And the patrols, never, stop, coming.
I do understand that to keep wastelands interesting and fun you need enemies.
But these things come just too often. Its like my car has gps tracker or huge kite attached to my car.
And thanks to rubberband a.i, they never stop following you.
So for good time of my playtime i was just eliminating these patrol cars.
When patrols aren't pestering you the storm will. Its nice way to add 5mins to your gametime while you idle in corner waiting it to go away.
But the thing that broke the camelback for me was the mandatory races you had to win in order to continue story.
I'm no good when it comes ticking time or races in games and assumed they too were just something you do for fun/achievements.
So end of a game is mystery for me.
In the end i did still enjoy the game for the 30'ish hours i played it.
Sadly the games good things are too bland, so after time goes on, i will only be able to recall the bad things.
+slowly upgrading your car.
+arkham style fighting.

-repetive camps.

If there were ratings I'd give this three out of five. Maybe even six out of ten? Maybe.
But that isn't enough for me to recommend a game.
Still, Mad Max in video game form. Very awesome. Who didn't dream of being Mad Max?
Does the game live up to the dream? Not entirely.
Driving around the desert is insanely fun... especially after you trick out your car, which is not super difficult to do. It becomes very smooth on handling. Bad guys seem to be able to drive their cars a million times better than they should, but that's good because they are all weak and puny.
Driving controls I don't even mind. I can get the hang of it, and I usually suck at driving in video games.
Convos are an okay challenge, but sorta fun.
Melee on the other hand, is not challenging, except for when it's suddenly super difficult.
The difficulty primarily comes from the ridiculous controls. This isn't smooth free flowing combat like in an Arkham game. This is herky jerky, I swore I pressed Y, how come he isn't parring combat. Oh and there's weapons in the game except it takes far too long to pick them up during a fight for them to be useful.
It takes far to long to do basically anything. You have to hold A and wait to kick open a door, pick up an item, put down that item, collect a shiny, knock down a war crier, pick up a can of gas, climb a ladder, accidentally drop your gas can when you are trying to climb a ladder, There's this slght delay on every action that makes Max seem like he doesn't want to do anything.

Shantae: Half-Genie Hero is the 4th game in the Shantae series and it's a game any Shantae fan, or any platformer fan will enjoy.
***NOTE: I HAVE ONLY PLAYED THE BASE GAME AND NOT DLC***
The series is known for its Metroidvania gameplay, however this game in particular feels more MegaMan-like than its previous titles. After getting a power-up you'll find yourself re-treading old ground and exploring new pathways and passages in search of goodies multiple times, but stages are selected via a menu this time around and it feels a lot less like exploring a world in comparison to the other worlds. Backtracking is common here and some people may find it tedious, but that just comes with the territory of playing a Metroidvania/MegaMan-style game, it's enjoyable to those who play these games and it is definitely fun in this game as well. Even if it lost a bit of its Metroidvania touch, it is still very rewarding and satisfying to play.
The controls are extremely responsive and fluid, the characters are cute and wholesome and the OST is absolutely stellar and is a blast to listen to. The whole game is a bundle of joy and it's impossible not to smile when you play this game.
The story in this game is nothing to write home about, however if you haven't played the previous titles you'll miss out on some of the emotional attachment and love from the recurring cast as their stories have already been explained previously, but it's not enough to detract from the experience. If this is your first Shantae game then you'll be fine. Although, I do wish that the story was more in-depth and involved. Previous titles had a surprising level of ambience and mystery revolving around Shantae and her world and there was far more involvement the Shantae cast had to do with the main storyline. There is a DLC that revolves around her friends, but I haven't played that yet so I can't comment on it.
Regardless, I enjoyed every second of this game and I believe anyone will if they give this a shot. For fans of the previous entries, this game is a must-buy. It's not as good as Pirate's Curse, but it's still great.

The game relies WAY too much on backtracking this time around. The level design doesn't feel intentional, platforms and enemies feel placed at random. The overall artstyle in this game isn't as great as it could be. It's almost there, but it still looks like a cheap flash game at times. In the time I played, I didn't find the dialogue to be as funny or interesting as in Pirate's Curse. Finally, the transformations break the flow of gameplay unlike the upgrades of the previous game.
Overall, Half-Genie Hero is a much worse version of Pirate's Curse, and although I wouldn't say it's a bad game, it certainly isn't a great one either.

TLDR: the game is too short, only buy when 50% off
Is it a bad game? No. Is it an enjoyable game? Certainly. Would I recommend it? I don't know, but steam doesn't have a neutral option, so whenever I'm neural I don't recommend a game since I feel like there are other games which I would rather play and recommend. The fundamental issue is that this game has a lot of back tracking. This is not a problem, I'm a metroidvenia fanboy, but contrary to a metroidvenia, this game has multiple individual levels which are linear. This makes it feel like it has a bit of an identity crises. This doesn't kill the game by itself, but in combination with the lacklustre length when compared to its price, 10 hours to 100% the normal campaign, it feels quite short. Other games, such as momodora, had the same price and length relatively speaking, yet I felt inclined to replay it because it was a lot more fun. The one thing that really definitively killed this game for me is that they released a 10 euro dlc with roughly 3 hours of playtime. It just feels like a ripoff. If you wanted to buy this game, buy shantae pirate curse instead. If you already owned that I would recommend shovel knight or hollow knight.

Despite the massive graphical face-lift, the level design, mechanics, and climax they build to are underwhelming as a follow-up to The Pirate's Curse.  The mermaid factory and its boss grabbed everyone's attention, but following it, things become far slower and more repetitive.  It's not a bad game, but I'm really hoping its assets become a springboard something better later on.  I'd be regretting it if I hadn't grabbed it on sale.
The backtracking in this installment feels excessive.  There are now 8 different forms that each have their own upgrade ability, which sounds great on paper.  But in practice, since none are great against the game's damage sponge enemies and many move slow, all but the monkey form see seldom use beyond getting through their obligatory required spots.  Re-entering the same 6 areas to slowly sift for the one new ability that lets you repeat the process somewhere else.  It becomes soul-crushingly dull when you have to comb the underwater depths as the crab, slowly entering each new body of water to find out there's nothing there, even more slowly jumping your way out, and repeating with the next of 4 neighboring lakes, trying to remember which pool needed which of three upgrades to get past.  I'm thankful they list all the items you haven't grabbed for each level to prevent it from being too confusing, but there are other issues with flow here.
Shantae is one of those side-scrollers that did away with one-hit death pits and spikes, instead just taking some of your health and moving you back.  I think they got carried away with that penalty in Half-Genie Hero, because some of the one-shot lasers and spikes are excessive, moving you all the way back to the entrance of an area.  This can mean walking through long, empty stretches that you depopulated of your enemies to try the one spot again.  While the penalty is technically lenient, the long walk still wrecks whatever sense of flow you had and retrying feels like a chore.   For areas that call for the harpy form, it's mainly difficult because you probably have no experience navigating obstacles with that form, so it's just a very annoying learning process.  Once you beat those spots, you're not going to use that form again, so it's not like you mastered anything.  I feel like these spots miss the point of what makes platforming rewarding.  It's neither snappy, nor makes you feel triumph for overcoming stuff.
Writing-wise, it's... actually kind of weird this would come off as a disappointment, given it's a comedic series that brushes off all sense of consequence.
===================================================
SPOILERS FOR STUFF THE GAME NEVER REALLY CARES ABOUT, I GUESS
===================================================
No matter what Risky does, she gets thwarted, curses Shantae, and goes back to plotting something evil.  She usually takes and destroys something of Shantae or her uncle's in the process, but whatever, it's not permanent.  In Half-Genie Hero, she corrupts an entire world, and to prevent further damage (depending on the ending), Shantae has to blow it all up including her own mother.  Which is a little dark, but nobody really reacts to Risky herself over it.  The last time the series had an especially evil megalomaniac, it ended with satisfyingly pulling no punches, working in the previous installmetns' plot thread, and blwoing him up.  I'm not saying Shantae has to murder Risky in cold blood for my amusement, but it's a little hard to write off what just happened with "Oh, that darn Risky, up to no good with her slavery and genocide!"  After the last game implied there was more to the villain than one-dimensional evil, it's such an awkward regression.
If anything, I just think the game is tackling dramatic subjects it doesn't know what to do with.  Partway through, Shantae gets corrupted herself, but shakes it off thanks to all her friends cheering her on and thanking her for all she's done.  Even if you've played the previous games, it feels unearned and out of nowhere, since the surrounding story doesn't build up to it.  That and the titular heroine's already fought and beaten her own corrupted genie side before, so it's redundant and has no bite.  She still drones about feeling inadequate as only half gnie when she's had her best written and playable adventure as 0% genie, and something something proof she was all hero all along.  You're left with a long, drawn out dialogue sequence that ultimately adds nothing.  If the game is going to force drama and raise stakes, it really should have let its characters develop and try something new.  Otherwise, I think all the side villains work better as antagonists and rivals, since their plots end in far more satisfying punchlines, schadenfreude, and fourth wall breaking that fit the games' tone.
I'm still giving the game a thumbs up because all the work that went into the animation and music shows, and monkey Shantae is adorable.  I can only be so disappointed while doing Dennis Hopper impressions.

Half Genie Hero makes me kind of sad because it goes a step back from Pirate's Curse. It is no longer a metroidvania. Instead, levels are super linear and most understandably require you to backtrack to them once you gain new transformations. The problem with this is the transformations take a lot from the pacing of the game, like in Risky's Revenge or the original. In Pirate's Curse, the items you found were designed to keep the flow of the game going. They could be combined to get to new areas or to gain speed. This made getting those items rewarding.
In Half Genie Hero, you cannot combine transformations very easily, as you could only transform on the ground and not in mid air or underwater, making super-quick transformations or ability combinations an impossibility. And even if you COULD transform in mid air, selecting a transformation takes ages in 1/2 Genie Hero, playing a little animation every time you transform instead of just transforming right away, which negatively impacts the pacing of the game. There's also something else to note: not every transformation has an ability anyway. These abilities need to be found in the game world, and they require a lot of backtracking, which is not very fun here. Not to say that it's HARD, it's just very unrewarding in my opinion.
That being said, I still think there is a lot to like about the base game. The bosses are all pretty fun to fight, the artstyle is great (though i personally prefer Pirate's Curse's artstyle a lot more), and the music is ♥♥♥♥ing banging. Unfortunately, however, the game is very short and can be beaten in just one sitting. Thankfully there IS a hero mode just like in Pirate's Curse, which ramps up the difficulty a bit.
I don't know, man. Overall this game left a slightly sour taste in my mouth. This is one of those instances where a "Mixed" option would be useful, but I know Valve will probably never add it. So I'll give it a positive review just because I like the series.
I recommend getting Shantae: Half-Genie Hero while it's on sale.

XO-Planets heavily reminds me of Risk of Rain, an indie rogue-like platformer that was released two years prior. While I learned Risk of Rain’s control scheme relatively quickly, XO-Planets has more complex controls in my opinion. I found myself dying over and over again at the start, which was very frustrating (I don’t wish to remember how many times I died to spikes!). Patience and determination are required if you want to play this game. After dying more than 30 times, I felt I had gained a relative understanding of the game’s controls and how to progress without dying in the first 2 minutes. This was due in part to my accidental discovery that one of the only ways to get batteries (the game’s equivalent of life points) was to destroy receptacles that spawn small monsters. This is where I wish there was a more detailed tutorial, or even some hints (although games like these rely on player discovery rather than detailed tutorials). The thing that kept me involved in the game were the RPG elements. There are 9 different weapons to collect and weapon enhancements/modifications to apply. Another thing that I enjoyed about XO-Planets was the freedom of choice to blow your way through the levels or simply traverse the platforms by jumping. You have explosives that can be used to destroy enemies and the environment alike. On to the highlights:

If you would like to compare XO-Planets to other games then Risk of Rain would be that. XO-Planets is an side-scrolling rogue-like game combined some rpg elements, platforming and even little tower defence thrown into mix and it works well! Oh. Did i forgot to tell you that this game is hard as hell too (but in a good way).
You can play single play or co-op and first you choose you AI character and you can also buy permanent upgrades to you characters. Levels are procedually generated (with free terrain destruction) and your mission is to reach the bottom where the boss is. In your way there you must fight monsters with your melee and ranged weapons and do some light platforming to avoid traps and you can use your bombs to destroy terrain freely. You get materials from killing enemies which you can use to buy some upgrades (only lasts for that game) and Xolyriums which can be used to permanently upgrade your AI or buy different kind of turrets which can only be placed in pre-arranged fixed positions. Each planet contains one upgrade shop, miniboss and side objective along the way to bottom. You get random drops of different melee and ranged weapons and you also can get enchantments to them.
