"Ugh, another rogue-like/rogue-lite game. Great, as if we needed another!" you may be thinking to yourself. And, yeah - I'd agree with you completely. I'm getting a little bored with the whole "permadeath" concept; it's been done dozens and dozens of times to the point that it's getting a little stale. So hey, why not toss in some pretty rainbow blood splatters, a kickass soundtrack, and some run n' gun fun to add some spice to a stagnating genre?
It feels a little weird trying to place XO-Planets into any one particular genre, actually. Is it a platformer? A nail-bitingly difficult RPG rogue-like/lite? Or perhaps just an "action" game, as a sort of catchall. Well, it's pretty much all 3 of those! See, XO-Planets allows you to choose from a variety of unlockable characters, each with their own starting traits and weapons. It then thrusts you into a randomly-generated alien planet and tells you to just "go!" From there, it takes a bunch of running, gunning, stabbing, and slashing to work your way to the bottom of the planet, where a boss awaits.
Now, it's a little more complicated than that though. First, almost everything is randomly generated of course, from the loot (whether that's one of a few weapons, melee or ranged, or some form of currency to upgrade your character with) to the enemies to even the environment itself, which you can freely destroy using some explosives. On top of that, each planet contains one upgrade shop, a miniboss, a side objective (which could range from simply destroying the terrain to killing a certain number of enemies), and an optional "defend the object" goal. I personally never successfully defended the object (I can't remember its name) because it was both difficult and not necessary at all, so eh, what's the point? There's also towers that you can place occasionally, but they don't seem to be very useful currently.
Of course, there's also the boss of each planet! Now, initially the bosses made me a little sick. See, they're not disgusting or anything, but when you start fighting one the screen goes all crazy and it just gets unnecessarily disorientating. The screen flashes a little too and the lighting gets a bit weird. I mean, I get it - the game is trying to be trippy. Honestly though, I preferred playing with the light flickering and screen shaking
, which thankfully there's an option to turn off. For the bosses themselves though, they weren't anything particularly special. I managed to kill most of them with little difficulty once I'd found some good weaponry (I beat the game using a rapid-fire pistol that had incredible knockback and healed me simultaneously which was awesome). The final boss was pretty interesting, but the rest were just mostly frustrating to try and kill. See, with any weapon besides the base weapon, it seemed to me like the knockback on everything was simply crazy. I'd shoot a boss with my gun, take off a tiny bit of their health, and then they'd fly all the way across the screen. This wasn't just with one gun either - it was pretty much all of them. It got to be annoying after a while and made killing bosses take way longer than it'd have needed to. It's a somewhat minor gripe, but definitely something that could (and very well might) be fixed in a future update. (EDIT: Hey! Look at the cons section for more on this)
Speaking of updates, I think it's particularly noteworthy to mention how great this game's updates are. They come frequently, and not only that, but they also tend to be chock-full of either new additions, key changes, or bug fixes. It's great! For instance, Steam achievements were recently added right before I started playing, and then the game got a huge update adding local co-op while simultaneously improving gun firing (previously you had to stand still while firing a gun, but now you can move while firing). If the developer keeps it up with these fantastic (and frequent!) updates, I think this game may very well turn out to be something very special.
Sure, XO-Planets isn't super innovative. If you've played Risk of Rain, this game is quite similar. Yet, in many ways it still manages to distinguish itself from the competition. The vibrant visuals (for better or for worse), fast-paced, action-packed combat, and overall fun gameplay make this game a blast to play. The frequent and important updates the game has been receiving so far only serve to improve the game in a multitiude of ways, and if the developer keeps it up, this game will turn out to be something special. Even in its current state, XO-Planets is an absolute joy to play, and I'd definitely recommend it.

is best described as a roguelike/roguelite platformer. When I first saw it on Steam it immediately reminded me of a Risk of Rain with the visuals of They Bleed Pixels and Probability 0.
One thing that intrigued me from the start was the story. After an alien invasion Humanity is forced to accept to coexist with the aliens in order to avoid extinction. Soon enough, an evil plan that involved the aliens is found and Humanity decides to bring back the fight to them and this is where you come in. You play as one of various AIs sent to XO-Planets in order to scavenge resources and wipe out the hybrid alien creatures living there.
In terms of visuals, I think that game looks pretty good. It is certainly not the best pixel art I’ve seen but, when in motion, some of the effects look really cool. Some people will find it appealing while others will despite it, it is up to you.
As for the sound, I think the music is probably one of the things I enjoyed most when playing the game. The sound effects however, despite sounding rather simple and nothing to be amazed at, they provide some pretty useful auditory feedback as to what is going on, thus making it really easy for tou to realize when you take a hit or hit an enemy, especially when you’re still learning the game.
Before anything else, you start with only one AI and you’ll unlock more as you play the game. Each one of the characters has its own unique set and the game also gives you a little background on each one of them, which helps giving them some character.
Despite the fact that the game is difficult by nature, one thing that for me makes the game a lot less welcoming to new players is the fact that it has no tutorial, you have to figure out everything for yourself. That said, the gameplay itself is pretty simple to understand once you figure out the controls. Your character has two different weapons besides bombs, a melee weapon (sword, dagger, battle axe, whip) and a ranged weapon (pistol, shotgun, sniper rifle), which you’ll eventually change once you find better ones while playing the game. And, like most platformers, you’ll find yourself jumping a lot of times in order to reach other places, dodge enemies and so on.
Before you’re thrown into a mission, you’ll get a very short briefing by one of your contacts. Once you’re in a XO-Planet, your objective will always be to defeat a certain boss but you’re also given a secondary objective via email, which might be something like “kill X type of enemies” or “collect X”. You might also come across these things that look like terminals which, once you activate them, you’ll have to defend them while it downloads some intel for you. After completing these, you can pick up your reward on one of the vending machines that you can find on each level. Besides killing enemies, completing these side activities is a very good way to earn resources. That said, the game resource system is divided into “components” and “xolyrium”. Components can be used to repair drones that you find scattered throughout the levels, build turrets or buy weapons or upgrades at vending machines. On the other hand, xolyrium is much harder to come across and it is most important because it allows you to upgrade your characters once you die, thus providing a permanent progression system which I really enjoy and keeps me playing.
As for the combat system, it is pretty solid, which combined with a small, yet challenging range of enemy variety keeps things hectic and interesting. When dealing with small groups of the same enemy you can easily get rid of them by just adapting your movement to them, but as soon as the game throws you everything at once, well, good luck with that… you’ll find yourself jumping franticly and using a combination of your abilities and both your melee and ranged weapons to fight off the hordes of aliens.
With that in mind, the game does incentive you to go out of your way to explore the levels, other than just rushing the boss. You’ll find these loot chests that can contain resources, weapons, health, bombs or even AI mods (passive and active abilities for your current playthrough) which help make your life a lot easier. One small feature that I really like about this game is the fact that you can activate a “visor”, which shows you very different kinds of information about your enemies and surroundings (which can be increased by picking up mods) while also changing the look of the level due to some sort of filter, think of it like the terminator visor.

In XO-Planets you play the part of an AI sent to wipe out hybrid life forms on various Exoplanets far in the future when most of humanity has been wiped out. You'll fight your way through various levels killing aliens and bosses whilst collecting loot and upgrading yourself. When you start the game you can choose which character you’d like to play as, though right at the start you’ll just have one. Each char has a different loadout as well as different starting AI enhancements so as you unlock more you’ll have more options to play. You’re dumped right into the game world and you’ll find yourself on a planet with just your gun and a melee weapon. Each planet is inhabited with various nasties who will try their hardest to kill you and your job will be to fight your way through these until you reach the bottom and destroy their boss.
Similar to Vertical Drop Heroes HD you’ll find each level you start at the top and must fight your way down rather than left to right like most games like this. This adds another level of challenge to the gameplay as once you go down it’s not always possible to get back up. But the levels themselves can be fully destroyed allowing you to create your own paths up and down if needs be.
The gameplay seems simple at first glance but the more you play the more you realise you must play a little more carefully than most games like this. The enemies you encounter are not only quick but they are strong, each with their own attack and attack style and they are only interested in your demise. You have two weapons you can use to defend yourself, the first being your gun and the second a melee weapon. Though you start with a specific weapon as each character, you can find new weapons in canisters and some enemy drops as you play through the level so you can find ones that suit your fancy if your default one is not to your liking. Weapons have three stats: Damage, Speed and Knockback and each weapon will differ in these stats. Weapons come in tiers and the higher the tier the better the weapon usually, though higher tier weapons only drop from mini-boss and boss fights and occasionally as ‘Intel’ or secondary mission rewards.
You can also find weapon mods and AI enhancements that’ll increase your stats or give you perks throughout that run. Weapon mods are automatically added to your current weapon and can do things such as increase the attack speed or damage for example. AI enchantments can be found from canisters and monster drops but they can also be bought at a Distro Machine (I’ll explain this a little later on). There are various different types with various different perks and each is different to the last. There are some basic ones that allow you to do things like dash left and right, give you a basic shield when you stand still or jump higher but others get a little more advanced. There are enhancements that allow you to navigate the map better (rocket jumps, wall climbing, floor smashing), enhancements to help you with vision and tracking (treasure trackers, radar, enemy stats) and some that’ll help with combat (fire trail, slowing enemies, rocket fire). These can be bought using ‘units’ that drop on enemy death and can be found in canisters also. AI Enhancements will often be integral to completing the game because the difficulty will increase each level and there are very few ways to get stronger other than them.
The two currencies in game are Units and Xolyrium. As I explained before units are found and can be spent at distro machines, but when you die you lose all your units. There is one Distro Machine on each level and it is here that you’ll be able to buy your AI enhancements as well as refill your batteries and explosives. Since units can’t be carried over from run to run you’ll want to spend as much as possible whenever you can because you never know when you’ll die. Xolyrium is also found in the same places as you find units however it does not disappear when you die. Xolyrium has two main uses, the first being upgrades. Upgrades are can be bought between runs and are permanent. They will carry across no matter which character you are playing so the more you play and collect Xolyrium the easier the game will get in theory. These upgrades are more simple things such as extra life bars and increased explosive damage but you’ll find upgrading these things to be a priority if the game is too difficult. The second thing you can spend Xolyrium on are drones that help you out within the level. These can only be bought in-game and they die at the end of the level but they are very strong and can help you out a lot. You can also use your Xolyrium to upgrade these in the upgrade menu to make them stronger or able to navigate slightly better.
Your main mission is to find and kill the boss of each stage but most levels will have a secondary objective which is optional. These can range from killing a certain amount of a mob type, opening canisters or destroying a certain amount of terrain. Once completed you can turn these into the Distro Machine for a reward which is usually an assortment of Xolyrium, units and weapons, maybe a weapon mod or two if you’re lucky. You can also find an intel node on every level which when activated you must defend until all the data is downloaded. Waves of enemies will spawn in this time making this particular objective very difficult but the rewards are more than worth it if you can survive. Once you’ve completed the game you’ll unlock a new character so you can play again with different tactics.
Each level is randomly generated so no two feel the same and the game has tons of replayability because of this and the randomly generated drops, planets and side mission means the game can be played over and over and never feel boring.
There are only a few issues with the game but the main one can be pretty problematic. Nothing in the game is explained and I mean nothing. It took me a long time to figure out what the basics did and even after 4 hours of playing I figure out something new here and there. The gameplay is so fantastic and there are a ton of awesome features but you really wouldn't know it from the first 20 minutes of playing. A simple tutorial would solve all of these issues and make the game a lot more accessible. My second con is the story. I know this is a personal opinion but I found the story to be thin and barely understandable. This isn't helped by the fact that the only two snippets of story you currently get are at the start and when you finish a game. The story you get at the start is poorly written and the grammar in it stops the sentences from making sense, for example 'The United Earth Alliance caused more harm than good trying to go along with the inevitable. By supporting their own agenda of mass producing AI combative force and alien weaponry, to invade other planets called The Exoplanets.' and 'wiped out of the planet'.  Lastly an option to turn off the flashing when playing would be so helpful. Fighting a boss becomes very chaotic and I found myself feeling sick a few times despite never having experienced this before because of the constant flashing from both the bosses and the background. Also with enemies jumping everywhere, bullets flying, loot spraying around and explosions it all becomes a big flashy mess at times. I really do love the graphics but sometimes they just become too much after an hour of playing continuously.
Dying a million times but only getting minimal upgrades is not what i consider fun at all.

This game is mediocre at worst and great at best. Let me tell you why i think this way:
What do you like in characters or about your best friends? Their ability to express themselves without any shame? The fact that they're able to pull off great jokes with great timing? Or maybe because of their wealth of experience and background story they have?
...or maybe you like them because they're one dimensional.
You see, in undertale, the characters are so paper thin and predictable that you can describe them with one word, or even two, i'f you're lazy enough.
You'd think that it wouldn't be a problem i'f the story made up for this mistake, but even there, you'd be wrong, because the story relies on you caring enough about the characters to get to certain endings, and that's a massive missed opportunity there, because the characters are so flat and placed in such an odd spot that on your first playthourgh, you'd kill them on the spot,and by the second/third try, you'll spare them just to get the endings and still not care about killing them again i'f you wanted to. And i'f you don't want to kill them,that's because the game outright shames you into liking and sparing these characters. (Neutral endings wink wink)
I know that Toby Fox, the creator of this game, intended to do all of this, but that's in no way an excuse, because using the "mate i have a job,and a family f*ck you cheers" trap card is not a good way to make and introduce characters, i'f it wasn't an accident, it is LAZY.
While we're talking about character introduction in a story, let's talk about it.
ALL of the characters either have no background story at all or extremely little, and when it's the second case,most of it always comes from heavy theorizing or datamining (yes, there can be hints about characters in the game's files sometimes), While it's nice to think about how X character got to this point or how Y character got to be X thing, and how mysterious characters can make for the most intresting (and sometimes favourite) characters, it's idiotic and pointless to make the whole cast mysterious without expanding on them at the cost of adding more content.
To be fair, it tried to do that with 4 (5?) characters, but i'f it was intended to expand on characters, it just feels like some filler to unlock endings with characters left as side notes. Leaving more questions while not answering the actual questions that the fans would have wanted.
I am confused as to why pepole are so unhealthily attached to the characters, i'f i was asked about why the characters in this game became so bloody popular, i would have no answer.

Undertale,2015
Ah, yes, the endings of this game.
There are three endings:Genocide,Neutral and the "True" ending (the good "ending").
I'm not gonna spoil you anything about the endings, but unless one of your douchey Tumblr friends spoiled you the whole game by virtue signaling that they finished the game with the true ending (i'll get to that,be patient), you just learned that the game has a "bad" ending.
I'f you intend to play this game, didn't browse youtube around Chirstmas of 2016, and avoid Tumblr like it's cancer, there's a 99% chance that you'll never know about that bad ending,because of multiple things:
-Because UT actively guilts you for your bad actions.
-There are next to zero hints in the game that it exists. Hell, it's so hidden that i think that it's the TRUE "true" ending.
-ALL of the game's characters are so inherently good (Spongebob levels of kind,they're just that sheepy and innofensive) that it'd be hard to figure out that there's a bad ending.
-It's locked behind a grindfest that could take several HOURS for each area.
Undertale has a karma system, where each action you make, every gameplay choice you do determines the type of ending you'll have. But that doesn't matter because the game always chasties you for not daring to spare the mobs of things that would rather gladly try killing that one human child who fell underground (maybe because he had an intense death wish, idfk), than just staying in the alice rabbit hole forever.
This tactic works on the weak-minded and the guillible, but it annoys and/or pisses off the rest, me included, not because of the message itself, but because it's so in your face everytime that i'd go as far as to say that it's so pretentious it can't look at itself anymore.
Anyway, the point is, the game will always try to discourage and distract you from going out of the already made road.
Harsh criticism aside, there are moments where the game gets good or downright incredble.
The gameplay, which consists of a mix between RPG mechanics mixed with a bullet hell type of game, is pretty enjoyable and challenging,especially when you're not used to both of these types of game (like me), the game's pretty nice to look at and OH MY GOD THE MUSIC.
It's by a long shot the best soundtrack i have ever heard in a video game. Seriously, listen to it.
There's also moments where the game truly spooked me or pleasantly surprised me, which is something that hasn't happened to me in a while, but i'm not gonna point out when these moments arrive, because i feel that it would ruin the surprise and strip off the moments that first time players would enjoy the most.
You can feel that there has been efforts to make the game as good as possible, but that the game tripped,fell and failed,and that's a shame.

Undertale is a roleplaying game created by Toby Fox. In the game, players control a human child who has fallen into the Underground, a large, secluded region underneath the surface of the Earth, separated by a barrier.
Now this game I waited to buy, as I never really considered buying it in the first place. I decided to give it a try one day. And boy, I do not have any regrets!
Now Undertale is, I cannot stress this enough, NOT A GAME FOR EVERYONE. It is a story rich game, in an older pixel style format. There are multiple choices, which all depend on the choices you made. There are 3 major endings, one of which is basically an ending that has multiple versions in of itself. Now if you aren't an emotional person, this game may not be for you, but if you are an emotional person who loves story, you may really like this game. I personally love the game, and find all the characters very memorable.
If you had the story spoiled for you before buying, I don't recommend buying the game. It is extremely story based and can be quite boring if you already am aware of what is next.
I really recommend you play through  the game to try to get all 3 major endings, for a full experience.
These are my thoughts on the game. I really enjoyed the game, loved the story and the characters, and now am a fan of the game. Just... don't let the toxic part of its community get to you. Just ignore it.
Thank you for reading this, and have a wonderful day.

A sandcastle is no fun without a tide. Thankfully, ONI has tides aplenty.
Many colony builder/sandbox games fail to learn this lesson - including the granddaddy of the genre, Dwarf Fortress. Oxygen Not Included, by contrast, takes its lessons from its older sibling, Don't Starve. Something is always in danger of breaking down or running out, so you never have a shortage of puzzles to solve. For a genre veteran who's grown tired of participation trophies, ONI is already a breath of fresh air.

So I played the whole game, and to be honest I mostly regret it.
I went in thinking this game had a lot of cool ideas. Its a metroidvania style game that has more distinct levels, as opposed to an open world, which is something different. Plus the transformations seemed like a nice twist on the standard powerups you'd find in metroidvania style games. In practice though, both these just ended up being annoying. The more traditional style platformer levels didn't lend themselves to being fun to explore, and the way in which you explored the world was so methodical that it felt more like a chore. Futhermore, the transformations ended up being rather annoying as they really slowed down game play. Getting to the bottom of a water section as a crab, only to realize that you had to go all the way back to transform because you need the mermaid for this section was not fun in the least.
Furthermore, combat is rather clunky. They're a bunch of broken power ups, and you can sort of just smash you way through the game if you choose. However, if you choose to disable the power ups, the enemies don't really feel designed in a way that rewards tight play.
Overall, it was meh.

Spec Ops: The Line has the typical scenarios that a 3rd person shooter with cover-based mechanics has, so if you enjoy that, then Spec Ops should be a decent addition to your library. It doesn't do anything particularly exciting in this regard, it's okay.
What does stand out in this game is the gripping tale of a small operator squad that find themselves in the middle of a Dubai that was declared a no-man's land. The game will remind you of how cruel war can be, with some particular scenes and levels being not for the faint of heart, reminding us once again that war isn't always a conflict of villains and heroes, just a bunch of unfortunate encounters and events.
With that said, there is something that doesn't feel right about Spec Ops: The Line. The way it tells its story doesn't really match your typical cover-based TPS conventions. As you progress, the disparity becomes even more apparent, as the game seems to have trouble deciding whether it should be entertaining you with a series of explosive, ridiculous fights, or whether it should delve deeper in the psyche of the main character. It tries to do both anyways, and that leaves some to wonder whether things should have been done that way. SPOILER:
For the typical sale price, I'd say it's worth it, if you like emotional war stories and TPS games. Just don't ask questions about the multiplayer, it's dead and sad.

Gang beasts in still currently under development so some parts of the game are subject to change. With that out of the way, Gang Beasts is an extremely fun local multiplayer game that let's you beat the crap out of up to 8 of your friends and throw them off of trucks, Into Subway Trains, Off a building and a lot more. The game is 100% physics based so you must learn to use your characters weight and movement along with not getting knocked out from the hail of fists coming from other players. What makes Gang Beast unique is that there is no set way or rules to play the game, everyone has there own methods and styles they apply to the game in their own way. Some people treat is more like a game of fist a cuffs and just swing for days or others go for a more direct approach trying to toss others out of the map quickly. This is what makes the game so fun, watching you and your friends flail around the map trying to finish one another off but struggling to do simplest tasks because your chubby gummy bear type character handles like he's drunk but that's OK because its extremely hilarious/fun and you enjoin every second of it.If Gang Beasts had online Multiplayer It would be an almost perfect game but sadly you are limited to the amount of friends you can get together. If you are looking for a fun Party/Local Multiplayer game to play with some friends and have a good time, look no further.

While there are some issues, Black Ops 2 proves to be a largely positive experience. Since these could be pros or cons for you, I'll just list off some points.
-Tankier players- You seem to be able to tank more, and it gives the player getting shot at an opportunity to turn around and try and get the kill instead of getting instantly melted by someone laying in wait.
-Weapons- while the weapons are starting to wear on me at the 700-800 hour point, they still feel just varied enough to be enjoyable. Still wish the game didn't have riot shields and C4.
-Perks- The perks are pretty solid, only perk I truly hate is toughness, because the idea of magically controlling hitflinch bothers me...
-Attachments- Largely positive, but I hate stock with a burning passion because they are so poweful and give your assault rifle close range capabilities and helps you strafe around shots. Strong dislike for it. I don't really mind everything else.
-Anticheat- Used to be very good. Now, there are definitely hackers.
-Player count- Not many still play, so keep that in mind when considering purchase. This means that the players left are generally at least decent, if not downright good, and you tend to run into the best very often.
-Engine- Still running same/similar old engine, not much to say here.
-Lag Comp- Helps players with bad internet by nerfing the ones with good net, take it for what you will.
Still recommend.

Whilst it's still in early access it still has enough content to chew on. The newest update/patch has definitely improved a fair few things to do with the general balance and ux of the game. If you're into survival roguelikes ala Risk of Rain then this will probably float your boat!

Anyway, onto the review.
XO-Planets is developed by BohFam, and was released on October 23rd, 2015. XO-Planets is an Early Access, Indie Action Platformer with Rogue-Lite elements in procedural generation levels, as well as frequent updates (the last update at the time of writing this review was on April 28th, 2016 with many new additions not just bug fixes to the game). The story of XO-Planets takes place billions of miles away from the Earth, in a dystopia between warring factions.
XO-Planets gives off a very Risk of Rain esque feeling, in fact, when I first played it the very first thought in my mind was "Risk of Rain" , and that thought is in no way a negative one. XO-Planets has many features that differentiate itself from Risk of Rain. For one, the levels as well as the weapons are procedural generated (which is a big plus in my mind) as well as a ton of upgrade opportunities.
The art style of XO-Planets is very visually pleasing, however, as previously mentioned, those with Epilepsy should stay away. The art style is pixel art, and is all in dark neon colors. The enemies in XO-Planets are VERY unforgiving, and getting cornered is a death sentence. The XO-Planets soundtrack is in the 8-bit format, is very catchy and does not easily bore you. When you play XO-Planets, you can definitely feel the developer's heart and soul which he or she has obviously poured into the development.
The only downsides of the game in my mind are the lack of a tutorial, lack of settings for windowed mode as well as very strange controls, which leave much to be desired. Some people may adapt to the controls easily, but not me. However, those three cons are no reason to turn away from XO-Planets. If you are a fan of rogue-lite, procedural generation, or indie games in general, I would definitely recommend this game.
XO-Planets is a great game that I
recommend for those who enjoy indie games. Every playthrough is different and challenging, with different levels, weapons, and monsters.

What a strange game.
Six and half billion miles from the Earth, I'm digging, slashing, and shooting my way through one of the most nonsensical platformers in recent memory. Though its design tenants are conventional (double jumps, simple controls, focus on accurate movement), the application is anything but.
Enemies are difficult and unforgiving at close range, which would be a great incentive to use the gun, except properly landing shots is itself a challenge. Without a tutorial to explain a few of its nuances, be prepared to stumble through the first few lives working out the timing required to take out lesser enemies before progressing to the boss. This game has the appeal of trial and error, as well as a high difficulty curve who those that want a challenge.
Ultimately, this game is oozing with creativity from the mind of a talented developer. Despite this, it has unfortunately fallen by the wayside, ignored largely for no reason.
Plastered in visuals that range from stunning to vision-ruining, and unfettered by the laws of conventional sound design with sounds both satisfying and irritating, its certainly one of the more interesting games I've played aesthetically speaking. Its worth mentioning here that you should take the epilepsy warning very seriously. If you have any history of reactions to flashing lights, avoid this game at all costs.
It's a strange game, and I recommend it not because its perfect, or even great, but because playing it is a trippy, awkward experience. It's like stumbling through the first kiss; its like dealing with parental disappointment; its like a trip down a road you haven't seen in twenty years. Refreshing, but something's changed. Something important.
Its an experience.
Hell, that's more than I can say for most of the triple-A industry. Good on ya, dev. Looking forward to your future projects.

This is striking me very much as what X:Rebirth was supposed/hyped to be. The game is rendered in a beautiful 3d environment and, while fiddly to get used to (it's a little more clunky than the X series of games), once you're used to it, you won't encounter much in the way of problem. Right now, there's not a whole lot to do other than explore the universe but then, what did you expect? It's a pre-release game!
I decided to support LGM because, quite honestly, I didn't with SPG 1 and, in hindsight, I wish I had because it's a company that hasn't forgotten the golden rule in the gaming industry;
"Listen to what your fans want, then make it for them."
So many authors make the game THEY want and then wonder why the game bombs. In my own experience, Mass Effect 3 was that game but I'm sure most of the readers have at least one recent title they can apply that to. LGM listens, they adapt and incorporate into the game and they're not shy about it, either.
So, if you're after a non-mmo space simulator (Elite springs to mind), this is definately for you. Hell, for less than £20, you're not going to do much better at the moment. Get it while it's hot because it promises to be an amazing experience. Graphically and audiably it's breath taking by anyones standards..

I purchased this game when in Alpha.  It is a pretty game that on the surface seems to offer a lot of depth but after playing it for many hours, it really is just an incomplete sandbox game with very little variety of what you can actually do.  That is understandable since it is still in early access, but I am concerned about the ultimate prognosis for this game given what the developers seem to be focused on and how the date of actual release just keeps moving out in time.
For example, their are posts back to January asking about some form of story or campaign with responses of hopefully next update.  Here we are almost six months later and no released story or campaign progress.  We do however have the ability to rename your ship and prettier asteroids.  Not to say the developers are not adding content slowly as they are quite active on the forums and updates are pretty regular, I am just wary of the progress on the story/campaign aspects of the game and concerned the devs are focusing on the wrong things.  Will someone care if they can rename their ship or mod the game if the story never comes out or is not great when it does?
Most recently the devs said Q1 or Q2 for the full game release, now they are saying September earliest.  Perhaps I am just a skeptic but my advice would be to wait this one out and see what actually comes to fruition and not invest in it at the current state.  If on the other hand you like the sandbox experience, and would be satisfied flying around in space doing a handful of freelance style mission, perhaps this is for you now.  For me that got old after a few sessions of play and I was longing for more content.
I really hope the devs proof me wrong and they are just incubating this very slowly.

.

This game was decent. Good, not great though. I think a lot of the great things about the game are kinda surface-level. The game looks beautiful, the script is funny and the music is fantastic, but once you get past that, you just have a servicable platformer that doesn't seem to want to be anything besides a cute little game with a couple of metroidvania type elements thrown in. The game isn't long. I think I beat it in about 8 hours, and that was a lot of time spent backtracking through levels. Don't expect a Hollow Knight experience when it comes to exploration. Collectibles are few, and made simple by a very small, linear map.
Bosses are pretty standard here. There are some weapons which interact with some of the things bosses do. For example, some of their projectiles can be reflected if you purchase the mirror upgrade. But none of this really matters, since bosses that can be hit by Shantae's hair can easily be face-tanked, thanks to an extremely forgiving health pool, an armor upgrade and an over-abundance of restorative items.
I am just barely recommending it because it's a fun game. But with the caveat that it's not anything besides a basic platformer with cute graphics.

== Mad Max Review ==
RATING: 8.0 / 10 - 35 Hours of Fury Road
Played on Hard difficulty
+ Great melee combat system, similar to the one seen in Batman Arkham series, but improved
+ The Mad Max post-apocalyptic world is wonderfully depicted
+ Great variety and quantity of things to do, places to find, secrets to discover
+ Great quantity of upgrades and vehicles to unlock
+ Very good graphics, particulary regarding environmental effects, explosions, and models
+ The story stays true to the brutal, harsh world of the Wastelands, to the character of Max and the lore
+ Good variety of gameplay situations, from car-to-car combat to platforming sections to hand-to-hand brutal combat
+ Intelligent unlock system that incentives the player to complete side quests and find collectibles and objectives
+ Very few bugs, and only minor
- Late-game gear and upgrades are a bit overpowered compared to what enemies you fight, even at maximum difficulty
- Bosses of Top Camps are all the same copy-pasted model and all have the same attack pattern (!)
- Car to car combat becomes too easy after a certain overpowered weapon is unlocked
- It is impossible to perform Fast Travel on any vehicle that is not the main car
- Final boss fight is truly anticlimatic and dull

I tried Euro Trick Simulator 2 because I enjoyed playing Farm Simulation 2015.  I thought it was interesting that I had a choice to use either the keyboard+mouse for steering or the traditional keyboard-only steering.  I initially opted for keyboard+mouse steering thinking it would be more accurate.  I found that it was very senitive and I didn't care for it.  I went to the traditional keyboard steering model and found it easier for me.
I tried a couple of missions, but became pretty frustrated at the precision needed to back-up and park the truck.  I didn't find any helpful tutorials.  I had been playing Farm Sim 2015 which also requires backing a vehicle with a trailer, but this was much more difficult.  I finally had to give up and use the auto-park feature.
When I went on a longer mission, I found that it was difficult to stay in the lane.  Anytime I hit another vehicle or scraped the wall, I was given a fairly substantial money penalty.  After a couple of times, I found the game just wanted more precision and accuracy than I wanted to give it.
This isn't saying that other people won't enjoy the game or there is a flaw in the gameplay.  I just personally found the game to be more annoying than I thought it would be.
I ended up getting a refund on the game from Steam.  I'm very thankful for that feature.

This procedurally generated game has a big emphasis on death and each time you die, you lose your character forever and start with one of three characters with a random class and trait. It’s clearly inspired by Dark Souls in many ways so if you like that game, chances are you’ll like this one. This game makes death a reward in a way because that’s when you finally get to level up, this makes this game extremely addictive. It should be noted that the game lacks variety, especially in the boss design which seems like the idea between all of them is a giant version of a normal enemy. The first four bosses are just a floating ball that shoots stuff at you. The game feels like it could use some more types of combat or weapon upgrades, since the only weapon is the sword and the shield is never very affective. Every new area doesn’t introduce anything interesting besides a few enemies and a there is a huge overuse of flying enemies that gets worse with each area. Since the games aren’t completely randomly generated and just chosen randomly from a selection of pre-made rooms, you start to notice repetition a few hours into the game. Even though I have a few complaints with this game it is really fun and addictive. There’s not the same kind of issues I see with other indie games which are unpolished. I think the main failings of the game aren’t really the developers fault as much as the game needing more time and funding. But taking the game as it is, I think it’s an extremely fun, satisfying, challenging, and rewarding game.

This isn't a game a plan to beat. It's not so much that I can't, it's more that I don't want to. I enjoy the gameplay too much. I like the humor, the generational tree and genetic traits that affect gameplay like colorblindness, or being huge, or small, or fast, etc. The enemies are fun and varied enough that I don't mind that the harder ones are basically bigger reskins with a slightly larger attack radius or faster attack speed. I like this game so much, because it's a great game to play with some friends to see who can live the longest or kill the most monsters or gather the most gold, etc. in one life.
Over the 30 hours of gameplay I have in this, my friends and I have unlocked most of the upgrades and have gotten enough upgrades so that we only lose 50% of our gold as part of Charon's fee to reenter the castle. (Charon is the entity you give all your gold to to gain entry to the castle. You can spend it on upgrades before entering and you keep all your gold when you die. It's only when you want to reenter the castle that you must give up your earnings.) And we have enough upgrades that regardless of which class we choose, we have a good chance of making it to the first and/or second boss before dying. But our lust for gold and desire to kill the most ensures we most likely will never beat the game. And that's fine for me. I just love clomping around this castle as various offspring and classes and seeing how many enemies I can kill and how much gold I can get.
If you're really good at roguelikes and just want to play this game to beat it, it might not be worth the $15 price tag for you. But if you're like me, and enjoy a game with good gameplay, then you might like this one as much as I do. Keep in mind that it is pretty difficult and you'll likely die a bunch, but eventually, you'll be raking in so much cash each run, your deaths won't matter.

This game gave me mixed feelings, actually. It tries and tries hard - it has everything, good metroidvania/rogue-lite needs to have. But, sadly - everything goes wrong. There are lot of reviews, talking about pros of this game, so - I ll focus on cons:
-
. There are 2 types of rogue-lite/like games. Ones are fun to play. I means - rlly fun. Ever if they include unlockables, they are completely optional and only extends gameplay, but doesnt force you to have em. Sadly, this one belongs to another type - games, where grind goes above lvl of korean mmorpgs. Basically, you are
to run over and over, again and again. There is no way to beat game in 1st run, ever if you are Chuck Norris, coz you unlocks not only new classes, but also stat points, passive skills, gear and such, and there is no way to affect this tree inside dungeon - only after death.
-
. There is not much variety of room design at all - I think, in 2 hours, I've seen every preset of castle's rooms. Its not that bad itself, but here comes another problem.
-
. At 1st - this game's levels arent completely random - there are few presets, you may get for each room, depends on location. Its extremely good thing, coz it should be way easier to balance pre-made rooms. Should be. You will stuck without ability to get loot, coz your hero is way large/doesnt have required skills/etc. You will get lot of cheap deaths, coz of terrible enemy/trap placement (for example - there is small room with spikes on both floor and top. Only way to get to another side is to jump between platforms. But you CANT do that, if you are giant - each jump causes you to hit spikes with your head). But, ever if you will manage to get good character, good gear and good castle design, you still will die a lot, and not coz you did anything wrong. Here comes one of biggest problems of this game.
-
. Most of my deaths was not coz I didnt notice something, but cuz character did something wrong. For example - it takes few seconds for character, to change its focus. So - I got LOT of situations, when there was mob on left from me, when I ran right, I tried to face it and hit, but instead slashed to the right side, while it pounded my butt. My experience is based on playthrough with xbox360 gamepad, so - maybe you will be slightly better with kb+m (is someone rlly play platformers with kb?), but thats it. And ever if you will master, how to deal with controls, you still will get hurt.
-
. Sometimes you clearly think, that "this bullet will hit my head", but it goes tru you, without dealing any damage. Sometimes your legs get cut off by something, that clearly isnt that close to you. Etc etc. Enjoy wasting hours to understand, how hitboxes work here!
Dont read me wrong - there are cool things in this game. Just like bearded lesbian dwarfs, or hostile chickens. But ever if you will enjoy author's sence of humor, ever if you will fall in love with game's concept, ever if you wanna have every exist rogue-lite/like metroidvania - its hard to recommend this game. It tries so hard, but everything goes wrong. Wasted

This game has suprised me with how well it has been created, sculpted and polished.
And its in Early-Access.
My Scorings:
Gameplay - 10/10
Features - 9.5/10
Replay Value - High
Audio - 6/10
Graphics - 7/10
Playability (Since Early Access) - 10/10
Overall I would give it a 9/10, just due to how well it is put together. My only real complaints about this game are the Audio. Sound Effects specifically. I'll get to this in a bit.
Gameplay:
You should get the jist: You're the warden. You're in charge of the prisoners, building the prison, and maintaing it. The game in intricate and well designed. Its got lots of factors to consider, but nothing you can't keep track of. It has a large variety of features and mechanics, and they keep adding new ones. For instance the lawyer, smaller cells, and cell quality. The game has evolved quite well and is quite the product. I quite enjoy it, its rather good.
The game is fun, and you're constantly trying to make a better prison. You learn from trial an error. Its a time-sink. I can't tell you how many times I've come back and realized I've played until 3 AM because I wasn't paying attention to the time.
tl;dr: The Gameplay is awesome and is constantly getting better.
Features:
Really this goes hand and hand with Gameplay. However, I took a .5 off due to the fact I'm irritated by the danger level. Its a rather important feature, but I don't think it gives enough information.
"85 Prisoners have Serious Complaints"
What are the complaints? Is there something I missed? I just can't seem to find an answer as to what specifically the problems I am having are. I would like a tab listing the major problems plainly. In a way, how it is now makes the game harder. However, it can be frustrating that you can't figure out what the issue is when you've got a prison you spent several hours on constantly rioting.
Graphics & Audio:
Graphics aren't some kind of next gen thing. Its 2D blob people and buildings. Its got a nice feel. Its simple. While I like it, I do think it could be a bit better. Having moss and tall grass on my walls is irritating.
Just saying.
As for audio. I've found that the audio effects can be irritating. There isn't enough different ones in my personal opinon. I've had audio playing over itself. In short, the audio needs work at the current time. Some kind of music would be nice as well. Now, credit to the Devs, it has gotten better since I first bought it. So, take this complaint as you will.
Playability:
I've experienced few glitches. Those I have have been humorous and non-gamebreaking. In short, the game is really stable and plays well.
In closing, I highly recommend Prison Architect. Its a fantastic game and I have enjoyed it. I paid full price on it, but I don't regret dropping the money on the game. Its paid back every penny. The care and detail on this game is amazing. I Love it. If its on sale, grab it. You won't regret it. Its a great game. Its complexity and detail in gameplay I haven't found in a long time. Its absolutely awesome!
Cheers!

Boots final battle it could an endgame optional story (which this game doesn't have.)

In some ways, Shantae reminds me of the Kirby series, even though they are quite different in style. It is kind of funny to think about it, but there are similarities here.
Shantae: Half-Genie Hero is a cartoon platformer that has a main world map where you run between a handful of levels, and each level has a few stages inside of them; but you can return to any of the levels or stages throughout the entire game (as you unlock them). The reason you return to them is to find new items to progress in the main story, because the items are usually hidden behind new passages that are inaccessible until Shantae (the main character) unlocks new powers.
I think Shantae's powers made me think of Kirby, even though the mechanic is not the same. Essentially, Shantae either gains new powers in the storyline at certain cutscenes, or finds them in chests hidden through stages. These powers allow Shantae to transform into specific types of creatures to navigate things like windy hallways, swimming underwater, flying in the air, and so on. On the other hand, Kirby is a pretty old platformer series where the main character was able to eat enemies and mimic their bodies to gain their abilities, which could also be used to get around. Different mechanics, but Shantae went along with a similar idea.
In any case, I enjoyed the main storyline of Shantae because the characters you encounter are all very funny in a tongue-in-cheek style. There's definitely some low-bar jokes in here, but I still laughed most of the time.
The visual style is a mix of 2D and 2.5D between the characters/enemies and the level design. The music of the game is quite catchy and I enjoyed listening to the majority of the songs along the journey. I really liked the art overall.
For the gameplay described above, it actually works for this game, even though you backtrack to certain levels many times. There are a few places where I got stuck and a little confused on what to do. I can understand that some people might get bored if they are unable to progress easily, because the backtracking then becomes painful. Thus, I would highly suggest to pull up a guide if you get stuck for a considerable amount of time.
I would say that a big improvement to the game would have been to add more levels overall and to lessen the number of times you had to revisit certain stages. Similarly, some of the transformation powers only get used a couple of times, and some of them are quite annoying. For instance,
Overall, though, I had some fun with the game here and would recommend the main storyline.

Having played periodically from legacy onwards, if one desires a brutal unforgiving survival experience this game is for you. The only purely negatives i can associate with this game is the fact that due to the weekly updates servers can only operate on a life span of normally one week but servers "wiping" on a bi-weekly basis and monthly basis can be found as well but they will of course not have the most up to date version of the game available. If this bothers you extensively i would reccomend waiting a while until this issue becomes less of a problem. Additionally another minor dimensional aspect is that occasions can arise where joining a server too late into the wipe can lead to a less than optimum experience. i.e. one may feel not entirely apart of the party. Or feel that what they are doing constitutes pointlessness as there are others who are much more advanced tech and resource wise. All that being said this game is continuously improving, updates are regular, and there is a real community surrounding this game that like the game, is ever changing. If you enjoy a good multiplayer survival experience i.e. a challenge, Then this game is and has been for a long time a pionering force in that regard.

Literally just stayed up all night playing Spec Ops: The Line and I am absolutely floored by the ending I received. Absolutely floored.
I don't typically like FPS games at all and didn't really get into them until this past spring, and I LOVED Spec Ops! The graphics and attention to detail highlights small details like blood, cuts, bruises and dirt very well, the characters are believeable and could easily be people you know, and have their own personality that challenge your charachter's moral compass after particular decisions and situations are chosen and seen through, were made only enriches the story as you progress further and further. You want to root for them when they are stacked against the odds and taking turns covering each others' backs during huge firefights, going back to save teammates...
You also feel downright disgusting and hollow inside when those odds suddenly require more and more sacrifices to reach the next level, where the results of your actions - once pasted together at the very end - paint a completely different picture of yourself that (at least in my case) you never expected.
"Right" and "Wrong" choices start to blur and turn to gray. Choices and actions you once thought were "good" suddenly becomes something else. Not bad, but not good either. Other times, the results are soul-crushing and agonizing.
If you love RPGs and you're on the fence about Spec Ops, belive me when I say that you will completely forget that this is an FPS in any sense of the word and you will be completely absorbed into Spec Ops' story from beginning to end.
Bought it while it was 75% on a previous Steam sale and it was the best $8-$9 ever spent.

First of all, I have to underline the fact that I'm writing this review after half an hour of playing the game. In those 30 mi minutes I got really fascinated by the way the game flows.
Starting your truck and making the first turn on the main road for the first time is enough to get you hooked. It takes a little bit of time to get a hang of handling the truck and its cargo, but if you choose to manually shift gears it might be a bit of a challenge especially if you're playing on a keyboard like me. Still, when you start to feel the truck and its weight that's when the fun starts. It's easy to get a speeding ticket but if you're a fanatic like me following the rules of the road will be a beautiful experience (I used to play GTA and Mafia following the rules of the road). The only thing that's missing is the radio with various music stations to fulfill the atmosphere but the game offers a special folder where you can put your music which will play in-game. Therefore, listening to GTA San Andreas' K-DST or K-Rose while driving a truck at the country side is as atmospheric as it can be! :)
The graphics are totally 2013 which is really good since the game was released in that year and taking into consideration that the map is huge (half of the Europe) plus the two DLC's with the Scandinavian countries and plus new cities. The sounds are just awesome. When you stick your head out through the window while driving you can hear the engine louder, plus sounds of the road so once again you're getting a fantastic -- realistic -- feeling of you as a trucker dude.
In the conclusion, this game is THE game for every drive simulation fanatic. I just hope In the future developers will include other Slavic speaking countries like Croatia and Serbia, and even Russia.

An excellent game, with varying degrees of intensity. It can be quite relaxed and sandbox-like, or combat-heavy according to the player's whim at the time.
The interface is simple, efficient, smooth and foolproof. The graphics are okay, nicely acceptable. The sound is great, though: you'll hear your ship creak and swoosh the waves. Music is limited, but excellent. The nautical physics work great. The quest system is limited in scope, but endless in numbers. The goals are the player's own: Upgrade their ships, upgrade a town, gaining access to other factions etc. There is but one "true" quest, towards the mid-high levels.
And that brings on the less appealing aspects of the game: Once that quest is done, so is much of the game's appeal: Once you have all ships, all skills and all affiliations, it's pretty much the same over and over again. It is probably a lot more interesting as a multiplayer fighting game at that point.
Another thing: These barrel-like weapons you get at mid games are way too powerful. One in particular pretty much negates all movement as soon as it hits the same ocean you are on, for a good while, making the battles as sluggish as if they happenned on tar, which in returns makes me put an incredible amount of stress on my keyboard out of frustration while uttering "move... move..." under my teeth-clenched breath.
It would be good in a later iteration of the game to have cyclones, rain, dead calm sea areas, ghost ships and the such. But even as it is, it is a great game for all wooden ships lovers. There is definitely something for you in that game, whatever that may be.

If you're looking for a game about exploration or high-seas trading in a setting inspired by the golden age of sail, this isn't it. The game is combat focused and designed as a multiplayer experience, full stop. It's not something you can play by yourself unless you really enjoy the feeling of being the only person on an MMO server. So when the description said "Windward can be played by yourself", it's in the same sense that one could set up a private WoW server and play alone: technically possible, but really what's the point? If you aren't planning on playing multiplayer, then I wouldn't recommend buying this.
You can't get tied up in a conflict between factions in the way you could in say Uncharted Waters (1991) because none of the factions do any kind of building or planning without a player's direct input; the only ones actually fighting and trying to expand are the pirates, but only when a player is in a zone they're trying to expand in and even then it's completely one sided since no one but the player takes direct action against them (there's no adjacent factional forces invading a pirate occupied zone while you're in it for instance) and the NPCs will do nothing but protect the handful of meager settlements they start off with, never establishing new ones or trading between them to build them up.
Outside of new towns and endless shipwreck pieces, there's nothing to discover (for instance there's no tribal villages, ancient ruins, or landmarks for you to find and the cultural designs of the architecture are aligned with the biome of the zone, meaning every town in a temperate biome looks exactly the same) and the rough shape of the game world is revealed when it's first generated. You can't pick a direction and endlessly sail off into the horizon because the game is divided up into small, randomly generated sectors which often times don't even match the previous zone's geography at all.
Trading resources between towns will eventually make them grow, but ultimately is an inefficient way to earn money compared to just fighting combat instances and since as far as I can tell the only thing you lose on death are quests (which even in high risk zones aren't worth the effort to complete, meaning there's no real penalty for death) and there's absolutely no resource management aspects to running the ship the only reason to bother with trading at all is to increase the size of the cities.  You don't have to buy food, or pay your crew, or worry about ship configuration or maintenance costs, and if you manage to get blown up your ship just magically reassembles itself back at port no worse for it.
The AI is so atrocious that trying to capture high level zones more or less requires a friend to play with you because the AI is apparently incapable of playing defensively or prioritizing targets. Meaning they'll completely abandon their one controlled city while it's being shelled by pirates to instead try to take out a guard tower on the other side of the world, rather than say, forming a blockade with the majority of their forces and sending a few more powerful units out to capture new cities. The AI is so bad they've managed to lose tight corridors dotted with guard towers on either side because they refuse to defend, even as the enemy AI takes out each tower one by one.
While the game is beautiful and the combat is tight and punchy (if a bit MMO-styled), it's too simple to really hold you, and for a game set in the age of discovery there's not much out there to find.

This game has suprised me with how well it has been created, sculpted and polished.
And its in Early-Access.
My Scorings:
Gameplay - 10/10
Features - 9.5/10
Replay Value - High
Audio - 6/10
Graphics - 7/10
Playability (Since Early Access) - 10/10
Overall I would give it a 9/10, just due to how well it is put together. My only real complaints about this game are the Audio. Sound Effects specifically. I'll get to this in a bit.
Gameplay:
You should get the jist: You're the warden. You're in charge of the prisoners, building the prison, and maintaing it. The game in intricate and well designed. Its got lots of factors to consider, but nothing you can't keep track of. It has a large variety of features and mechanics, and they keep adding new ones. For instance the lawyer, smaller cells, and cell quality. The game has evolved quite well and is quite the product. I quite enjoy it, its rather good.
The game is fun, and you're constantly trying to make a better prison. You learn from trial an error. Its a time-sink. I can't tell you how many times I've come back and realized I've played until 3 AM because I wasn't paying attention to the time.
tl;dr: The Gameplay is awesome and is constantly getting better.
Features:
Really this goes hand and hand with Gameplay. However, I took a .5 off due to the fact I'm irritated by the danger level. Its a rather important feature, but I don't think it gives enough information.
"85 Prisoners have Serious Complaints"
What are the complaints? Is there something I missed? I just can't seem to find an answer as to what specifically the problems I am having are. I would like a tab listing the major problems plainly. In a way, how it is now makes the game harder. However, it can be frustrating that you can't figure out what the issue is when you've got a prison you spent several hours on constantly rioting.
Graphics & Audio:
Graphics aren't some kind of next gen thing. Its 2D blob people and buildings. Its got a nice feel. Its simple. While I like it, I do think it could be a bit better. Having moss and tall grass on my walls is irritating.
Just saying.
As for audio. I've found that the audio effects can be irritating. There isn't enough different ones in my personal opinon. I've had audio playing over itself. In short, the audio needs work at the current time. Some kind of music would be nice as well. Now, credit to the Devs, it has gotten better since I first bought it. So, take this complaint as you will.
Playability:
I've experienced few glitches. Those I have have been humorous and non-gamebreaking. In short, the game is really stable and plays well.
In closing, I highly recommend Prison Architect. Its a fantastic game and I have enjoyed it. I paid full price on it, but I don't regret dropping the money on the game. Its paid back every penny. The care and detail on this game is amazing. I Love it. If its on sale, grab it. You won't regret it. Its a great game. Its complexity and detail in gameplay I haven't found in a long time. Its absolutely awesome!
Cheers!

Umineko is one of my favorite stories of all time, and I'm so proud to see Witch Hunt finally get all of their hard work published. I started playing with the original patch years ago, back before the PS3 sprites patch was available, and it's definitely the same experience. Thank you so much to Witch Hunt and Ryukishi07 for years of patience and pushing to get the Umineko games an official release for your English speaking fans.
Umineko is a VN in the truest sense -- you don't have any control over the story, you're just watching it all play out. But the storytelling is phenomenal, giving you just enough hints to make your own theories without giving everything away. And the use of sound is absolutely masterful. The sound effects are really great at evoking just the right amount of creepy, and the gore isn't explicit but the sounds that accompany it will still make you cringe. And the music is some of the best video game music out there.
If you're a fan of Higurashi, one of the original bar-setters for the horror VN genre, Umineko definitely keeps up the horror levels and the theme of blurring the lines between reality and illusion, but the romantic undertones really push it over into Favorite VN Of All Time territory for me.
If you're a fan of other horror VN series like Zero Escape and Danganronpa, definitely check out one of if not the greatest precursor in the genre.
Basically, if you're looking for a really fantastic horror mystery visual novel, Umineko is one of the best.

If you like visual novels and/or the mystery genre, then buy this game. I can't say anything beyond that it is utterly fantastic. The mystery is great, the characters are some of the best I have seen in a game (certainly the best I've seen in a visual novel), and a great part of the storytelling itself is wonderfully unique, original and engaging. I don't think it is a thoroughly perfect visual novel, but none of the games I think are 10/10s are.
If there is something specific I can say about this game, it is its use of meta-storytelling. I have played and seen a lot of games that employ this, like Undertale's save and load mechanics, the entirety of pony island, the recently popular Doki Doki Literature Club, and not to mention the sleuth of 4th wall breaking characters, lines and plot threads in a lot of contemporary media. I mention all of this because none of what I have seen of meta-storytelling has, I feel, actually added anything of substance to the story that it is present in, it has merely been an interesting and sometimes clever gimmick which can be fun for the audience (me included). Umineko, a game around 10 years old actually did something with its meta-storytelling. It actually made me reflect on how I as the reader relate to and interact with the mystery genre. This was by no means something only I experienced by chance, the writer of Umineko, Ryukishi07, obviously intended for his game to have this effect on the reader.
Of course, this is just one theme in this long visual novel, however the fact remains that, in my limited experience at least, it is the only game I've played to use meta-narrative in such a meaningful way to evoke thoughts from me that only meta-narrative specifically could with such effectiveness.
I just remembered that The Beginners Guide and
also used their meta-narrative in a meaningful way, but my point still stands, only with less force. Far less force. However in those games the meta-narrative only became meaningful to the story near the end, while in Umineko it is a pervasive theme throughout and integral to the game's very nature. What I'm saying is that Umineko actually managed to change my attitude towards the mystery genre, and any game that can actually change my views and/or attitudes is pretty sweet in my books.
Wow that was a long-winded way to say a simple thing.
TL;DR You like VN's? Like mystery? Get Umineko, grab a pen and some paper, solve the mystery yourself, and never find out whether you were entirely right or not. 10.8/10 not enough seagulls.

Most military games start with shooting at whatever that decade's topical enemy is. Spec Ops is no different; you are greeted by a group of insurgents who yell at you in a language you can't understand and you put them down. You might be able to justify shooting them; they were being aggressive, and you were defending yourself.
But is there a point where you can't justify what you do? What does it take for you to stop and realize what you've done was brash, reckless and wrong?
I cannot recommend Spec Ops for its gameplay; it's a cover-based shooter with somewhat wonky controls and little variety. Story-wise however, it's a military shooter that leaves a strong, lasting impact depending on how you play it. A lot of games have some sort of tragic death of a squadmate to demonstrate "the horrors of war" after mowing down hundreds of faceless enemies - Spec Ops will make players regret pushing forwards at all. The genius of the game is that a fair portion of the regret experienced is self-inflicted, making it sting just a little bit more.
When do you stop being able to justify your own self-defense? Does it take a landscape littered with American soldiers? The charred remains of innocents? Firing into a crowd of confused civilians?
When is violence justified, and where do you draw The Line?

Before I start, this review contains minor spoilers, which, while minor, will significantly reduce the impact this game has on you. I recommend playing the game before reading any reviews or analysis of the game.
This is perhaps one of the most immersive games I've ever played in my lifetime. It's a scathing critique on modern modern militiary shooters, and pulls it off by juxtaposing the surrealist fantasy of FPSs and the real world effects conflict has on people.
First and foremost, I should point out that this game is not fun. This is intentional, and if you play the game you will understand why. The developers didn't want to deliver a power fantasy, they wanted to call you out for wanting to live those fantasies in the first place. Be warned, this game will make you feel like a terrible person. Yet this is exactly why I love this game so much.
After completing The Line, I felt horrible. This was genuinely the first game that made me feel guilty over my actions in the game, despite being forced to do so in the game. It's an experience I will never forget, and even impacts my experience when playing other games.
Perhaps one of the most impressive features The Line pulls off is its choice system. Choices are never given to you in a dialogue box, instead relying on the players to see the options presented to them. By doing this, the developers are essentialy saying "We trust our player base is intelligent enough to make their own decisions", a far cry from most AAA games developed these days.
In conclusion, buy this game.
Gameplay itself is satisfactory, but combined with an AMAZING story it really does make this game worth buying and playing. Definitely recommend.

I don't like basketball, but I used to like  F2:SB quite a bit.  It has all the strange thematic styling of an anime, it's got (I'm pretty sure it's purposefully) hilariously bad hip hop in the background that grows on you, even if you're not generally a fan of the genre, and climbing my way up the rookie ranks,  learning how the game works and learning how to work together with strangers to win was very rewarding for a time.  I've spent a day and a half total playing on steam, and I imagine I'll spend at least a little more, before I get frustrated enough to start playing good games again.
If they wanted me to keep playing, they shouldn't have given away premium characters (which is still going on at the time of writing!  Get yours now!  Or don't!)  A premium character starts with a set of cards that boost their stats, and 40 free stat points(earned at a rate of 2 per level otherwise).  At first it made me feel a little proud at how well I'd done against this characters in the past.  Now it's just♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off.
So I made a character in a position called a score guard, who specializes in making 3-point baskets.  My old character had 181 points, and... did fairly poorly most of the time, sinking less than half of her shots, despite having more points there than any other class.  My current character has 201 points... and perfoms at about the same rate.  If your opponents are close to you, you have a little defense circle that indicates your shots aren't as likely to go in, that veteran players may want to scold me for after reading this.  I am aware of it, of course I make bad shots every now and then, but the vast majority of the ones I take are green.
I stick on the other scoregaurds, scoreguards I can clearly see aren't these special characters, and they sink basket after basket over me.  The miss too, but they usually have a good rebounder that will feed them again, and again, and again, until it finally goes in.   I haven't made a basket in a day and a half, despite my understanding of how the shooting system works, and my adherence to it to minimize my risk of missing.
If I had known sinking all 40 points into my 3 point stat wouldn't make a lick of difference, I would've made a different character, and maybe I would've continued having fun.  As it is, I can't help but feel like the awful stat system in this game makes the build I wanted to try worthless, and I am not enthusiastic about trying another, especially if I have to pay real money for it. (You don't, but free characters won't get all those bonuses I mentioned).
In summery, this game was fun to a point, in the early stages where everyone sucks, there is potential here, but I hate the mechanics behind the game, now that I've seen in explicit detail how poorly they work.

Everything I've read says I should love this game but I don't. I certainly don't regret supporting them as I love this style of game but this one just doesn't do it for me and here's why.
I keep it installed and keeping dropping in to see if anything changes but so far I simply cannot get over some very core elements. From the very start I'm hit with the gigantic brightly colored cartoonish UI that makes it feel more like an arcade game than a space sim / RPG. Then there is the winged atmospheric flight (no strafe) where the vacuum of space fails to allow momentum to be carried (or the ships naturally brake when decelerating?) either makes no sense but regardless without any of the natural roll or feel of atmospheric flight which would at least make it fake but fun the ships feel completely disconnected from the environment and non-intuitive. It's like flying a fighter jet underwater.
There is a lot of work required to figure out where and how to do things in the game and as of now it's a pure sandbox with a limited variety of activities and not even a hint of direction. This is somewhat normal for this genre and I would have no trouble digging in and doing the work but the payoff just isn't there for me or at least it isn't apparent enough for me to put in the time. Maybe a lot can be solved by the community through mods and content but with everything already available and on the horizon for space sims & RPG's, again I'm lost for motivation.
I wouldn't go so far as to condemn the game. They are putting out content regularly and they claim to have a lot of plans although delays for the content that I'd like to see seem to come up every time. If ship movement and flying by turning on X and Y axis only isn't a deal breaker and you're willing to overlook a huge distracting UI you have a chance at loving this game, many do. If you have no need for instruction (beyond simple functions) or direction within the world you really should pick it up. For the rest I would recommend videos.. Watch gameplay videos and if you still feel it's something you'd be willing to play than do it.

Still trying to get the hang of the flight instructions but okay, well lets see if I remember how to remap those abilities BLAM Tutorial - Let's talk a little about map functionality..
