Starpoint Gemini 2 a sequel with lots of improvements, while keeping to the free form of the predecessor.
This game feels as motivating as Freelancer with its extensive Universe to explore, dozens of ships, different ship classes and moddable loadouts.
I did enjoy this game very much, it plays like a cross-over between freelancer (free to explore universe, dozens o ships) and the Star Trek Fleet Command titles (tactical fights, commanding capships).
Whether you want to relax mining and trading, or engage in combat missions and piracy, this game will be worth its money.
Did i mention you can capture enemy ships by boarding combat? You can!
If it flies, it is there for the taking!
As a captain your first and foremost crucial choice will be your class.
You can either be a Commander, featuring buffs for your fleet, empowered strike craft, retaliatory attacks and defensive boosts.
Or you can try to outgun the enemy by becoming a Gunner, who can specialize his offensive power by adding effects like disabling hits to his beam weapons, firing more shells with railguns, adding a higher refire rate to his high damaging plasma canons or boosting his heavy weaponry (schockwave cannons, missiles and torpedos).
Last but not least the Engineer, a very versatile class with a lot of debuffs.
Ever got tired of fast moving corvettes and gunboats dodging your railgun shots?
Just place a Rift-Anomaly and slow them down, then hit 'em hard!
Your second decision might be to specialize in a ship-category, as you can boost the efficiency of your ship by spending perk-points granted every 5 levels.
What will be your choice? A fast and mobile light ship(gunboat/corvette)
A merchantship, to rule the market with your cunning? (transport/freighter/freight-liner)
A medium class mobile Warship? (Frigate/Destroyer/Cruiser)
A vessel of personified dread? (Battleship/Dreadnought/Carrier)
The Choice is yours to make, though it is not final,
for you can reset your spent skill- and perk-points while being docked to a station or planet and try anew.
Currently this game is in Beta Version 0.7, so there are still some issues and lacks:
- ingame descriptions of skills and mechanics lack some love and proper english translation
- the weapons need some diversity, e.g. faster firing weapons need a higher projectile speed to use them against fast moving targets (railguns and plasma weapons)
- boarding combat is currently a numbers game, lacking the predecessors ingame videos and feedback
- the missions currently are restricted to Assassination (search and destroy), delivery, repair of beacons and rescue missions
- they need to put in some ships from the predecessors (prokhorov for example) to add even more diversity to the allready well modeled and animated ships
- ship special abilities are not included yet (like a full frontal arc auto-canon for baeldor frigates or high-energy blasts for dreadnoughts)

Vagrant Hearts Zero is an amateurish, janky, and very easy 3-hour JRPG.
The graphics are never terrible, but they never go beyond decent, and the maps are full of graphical errors where parts of buildings are cut off or you can walk through things that seem like they should be solid. (Or the opposite - you can't walk through flowers, but there's some places where you can walk through barrels and trees.) Similarly, the music, story, and characters all ... exist, but are pretty unremarkable.
For characters, you have the two main characters Jenko and Jullia, siblings with unusual magic powers which both amount to clobbering things with physical attacks, Amanda, a woman who can supposedly sense the location of people with magical powers but can't find the (magical-power-using) pirates that wiped out most of the main characters' home town, Lynch, a somewhat senile immortal with 999 max HP in a game where no one else has more than mid-200s by the end, and two fairly generic spellcasters, the black mage Hellius and the white mage Telma, who don't really get much characterization. None of them are very interesting, and you're forced to keep Jenko and Amanda in your party of four for almost all of the game, which would be more annoying except that Jenko, Amanda, Jullia, and Telma is basically the best party under all conditions.
The majority of the game systems feel half-implemented, what with the game providing multiple elemental skills to half of the cast and then having essentially no enemies with elemental weaknesses or resistances, or the items from the hidden dungeons not actually functioning, or there being shops that sell incredibly expensive and yet useless spell scrolls, or the game providing you with very little money to buy the items you are offered - not that you need them, because the game is incredibly easy. In fact, for most of the game even bosses went down in a scant few hits, and only the last two bosses and some enemies in the final dungeon were at all threatening, and that not seriously: given that almost nothing resists status effects, I paralyzed the final boss on the first turn of the final battle and it never took a single action, and Telma was more than capable of healing any damage my party suffered, given that she could heal the entire party for more than their max HP a dozen or so times before running out of MP.
Also, there's no getting around it: Vagrant Hearts Zero is trying to be a classic-style JRPG while only 3 hours long, with characters gaining their final skills at level 12 at the latest. While a short length can work in some JRPG-styled games, here it just ended up reinforcing my feeling that it was not a finished product.
So, yeah: no. Short and still a waste of time.

Spec Ops: The Line is a towering Skyscraper among average buildings. It doesn't stray far from the typical MMS formula: lots of killing, fun but plain combat, and handholding from the AI. Where it does set its self apart, is the campaign. While not the most finely crafted narritive I have experienced, it does lend its self with a serious attitude that leaves the player pondering on the morality of their choices. As a fan of games where the story is big, evident and emotional, it hit the spot for a few hous (It only took 7 hours to complete the campaign). Although the campaign quite linear, the game often offers you choices in both the story, and in gameplay, but these choices are black and white, very little middle ground is to be had.
It is a beautiful looking game; there are many times when I was on a tall building and I looked out into the horizon, and just stayed, admiring the view. It runs well too, I was able to play it on almost all the max settings, 1080p at 60FPS with only a GTX460m.
I recomend this game to anyone who likes a good story, or is a massive fan of the MMS genre.

From the author of one of my favourite VNs
, 07th Expansion presents its spiritual successor:
, or
. (You don't actually need to read Higu first tho; they're completely different)
First things first, Umineko is a kinetic visual novel with no choices to be made, so let's be real here: it's more of a lot more of an e-book with sound and graphics than it is a "game."
The "question arcs" package featured here is only the first half of the story (episodes 1-4) and focuses on establishing the mysteries, world, and providing hints; it took me about 50~ hours to complete. The story is concluded and "answered" through Umineko Chiru (episodes 5-8), also referred to as the "answer arcs" (recently released on Steam).
Umineko has a great soundtrack, and the crimes and mysteries aren't straightforward even if you know who the culprit is. It's extremely well thought out; there's always hints and foreshadowing that you might not even notice until it's pointed out later. The characters are also very colourful and varied, and I didn't really find myself disliking any by the end.
Umineko admittedly starts off slow; as the start of the first episode focuses on introducing the world, it's honestly kind of bland up until the debut of one of my favourite OST tracks,
. This is also a problem with most question arcs (each episode was originally released seperately), but once you get into the later arcs you're expected to know how things go so these intros become shorter and less necessary. However, once you get past these intros the novel
picks up.
If you have the time, please give Umineko a read if you can as it's definitely worth it!!

Best hitman since Blood Money.  I've played over two hours and am still on the tutorial trying to get all the challenges before I move on to the real game.
You can try a mission over and over taking different approaches to see what works the best.  I was hoping they were going to take this approach like they have on the new mobile version and I haven't been dissapointed.
The save game system is the best ever for hitman, no limits to how many times you can save per mission.  And nothing resets when you load a game like the abonimation Absolution.
I also love the how you can buy just the introduction to see if you want the full game.  There is nothing nefarious about this, in fact, I think it's just the opposite.  It's no different from an episodic approach like a TTG.  And with all the challenges and contracts and such, the replayability even with the Intro version is huge. I got it for $11.50 from GreenManGaming with a 25% off coupon.  I'm sure I'll be buying the full upgrade when the time comes.
It plays pretty smoothly on my 3 year old laptop with an Nvidia 670 MX on 1080P on medium settings.  So I'm not sure what to say to everyone who has had issues with performance.  Also I had to keep pausing the game and switch to my desktop which usually games don't like and I never had a CTD.
TL;DR I've played Hitman since the original and this definitely is the proper successor to Blood Money.
Get. It. Now.

Now for full disclosure I grabbed SG2 a couple of months ago while it was still in Alpha stage and initially I wasn't too impressed. While issues are to be expected when you are playing an Alpha version, on my low-mid system, frame rate and stability issues kept me from playing for more than a couple of hours and I left the game alone for a while until some of these things were worked out.
Boy! What a difference a couple of months makes. I figured since it finally got it's nice new "Beta" tag that I'd fire it up again and I'm really glad that I did, over 12 hours in the last 3 days can attest to how much fun I've been having with it.
The basic premise of the game is your a star ship captain dropped into a dynamic living game world and your free to do pretty much whatever you want in a sandbox environment. (As of this writing the more linear campaign option has not been added yet, but is coming down the pipe shortly) :
Feel like transporting VIPs or cargo from one sector to another, while enjoying the scenery? Check.
Want to make your fortune by mining asteroids and junk yards? Check.
Indescriminately want to blow up (Or at least try) any ship that comes near you? Check.
Pros:
Mind blowing number of ships to choose from (If you have the cash of course!)
Plenty of factions to work with or against.
3 unique classes with choices on which enhancements and perks to put into different skills when you level up.
Galactic news and events that actually happen in the gameworld rather than being just Lore or Fluff.
Excellent ship to ship tactical combat.
Player driven goals, shall I save my money for a new ship or shall i upgrade my weapons and components?
Cons:
UI needs to provide more feedback. (Not being able to see the target summary unless your looking right at it, is a bit of a pain)
Easy for a new player to be a little lost when first starting out, text tutorials are not ideal, but they do the job.
Still a few performance and stability issues at times, which is to be expected with the game still being in BETA stage.
Still some balancing issues with certain weapon types that need to be fleshed out, Beams being the prime example.
Suggestions:
Trading - Someway of knowing where to buy low and sell high would be nice, right now it's a bit of a crapshoot.
Mission markers - How about different markers for each mission type? Would also be nice in the case of a point A to point B mission if the point B marker was a different color on the map screen.
Event markers - After reading galactic news it would be nice to be able to at least select a few of them and have location specific news appear on the galactic map. (Bob spotted in the smith sector, should be able to mark the smith sector on the map so you don't have to go hunting around)
Overall SG2 is shaping up very nicely and I highly recommend it, with a great DEV team who constantly provide feedback to player comments, it's only going to get better and better.

This is one of those games that just looks so damn good, you can't help but just stop and look around at where you are sometimes. Add in it's intuitive UI and control setup, epic combat mechanics, and ease of navigation and you have the makings of what could be one of the best games in the genre.
Even in it's beta form, there is enough sandbox, 4x, space sim fun to make it worth the price of admission. With the new modes and 'scenarios' promised for the full version (hopefully one of which is a story campaign that's epic enough to keep up with the setting and gameplay), this one could turn in to a true gem (No pun. Shut up. Don't judge me).
That said there are a few balancing issues with the missions at the moment. Right now, the randomly generated missions seem to cap their pay at around 5000-10000 credits a piece, and none of them give you more than 100 XP, no matter how far you level up. The only way get enough XP to meet the prequisite for buying a better ship is to kill bad guys. LOTS of them.
This makes buying a frieghter and becoming a miner or a trader pointless. Not that you would ever be able to afford that new ship since the pricetag for anything better than the frigate you start with starts at around 3,000,000. Factor in expenses and costly ship upgrades you have to keep up with and after 10 hours of play, I only had about a third of that. 30+ hours of play before you can even buy your first ship seems like a bit much to me. The missions are way too repetitive to justify that much grind.
Same story with trading and mining. Mining never makes you more than a couple thousand creds a trip, and the amount of XP you get is effectively useless. It's even worse with trading. I haven't noticed any difference in prices of goods from one place to another, which means you can't make money (or XP for that matter) buying low at one place and selling high at another like you can in games like X3.
Add a story mode, balance the missions so the pay and XP increase steadily as your level goes up, make them a bit less repetitive, and make the trading/mining mechanics of the game more lucrative, and this game would be just a tick below perfect.

Gotta say, as these sorts of space sims go, this is one of the better ones I've played in a while. Its got the resourceyness and good mission flow you want, with a list of well designed ships you'll always be drooling over. Mechanically some parts are a little clunky just yet (boarding and such) but, seeing as how its still very much a beta, I'm sure they'll iron out the kinks. All in all a VERY fun game!

Your goal is to enter a castle where you have to defeat 4 bosses plus a final boss. You start out weak and will die quickly after entering the castle. Collecting gold from enemies and objects will let you buy items, perks and abilities like upgrading your health or draining health from enemies when you damage them. Most upgrades are permanent and will be used by all future characters.
When your next character enters the castle he will be a bit stronger than its predecessor and will probably survive longer. Each new character has different traits than your previous one like faster movement or doing more damage, together with the randomized castle layout each playthrough keeps the game fresh. Once a boss has been defeated it is gone for good (meaning you won't encounter it in your next playthrough).
The castle layout is reminiscent to the castlevania series or any other metroidvania. It also plays like the castlevania games as far as attacking is concerned but without inventory management and complex magical abilities. You also don't need to have certain perks or items to unlock parts of the map, everything is unlocked from the get-go. You can't go wrong with this title if you like old school action platformers.

I was worried that this game wouldn't be as good as the other game due to having a different developer. However, I wasn't disappointed. It was a great prequel to the original Life is Strange.
Play as Chloe Price, before she was expelled from Blackwell Academy and before she had her hardcore attitude, as she has a lot of run-ins with dangerous characters. While the story is shorter, it was still a deep, interesting telling of some of Chloe's past, which involved Rachel Amber. It gives context to why Chloe was so desperate to find Rachel in Life is Strange. The player gets to see their friendship (and possibly romantic feelings, if the player chooses) quickly develop, with touching scenes over life problems that teenagers shouldn't have to face. The portrayal of Rachel Amber stays true to what was said about her in Life is Strange, as she does, indeed, project light and darkness.
The game mechanics have been simplified and there's no messy time rewinding like in Life is Strange. This causes the player to think more carefully about their choices as well, as choosing unwisely means not being able to go back without restarting an episode. The soundtrack, for the most part, was excellent as well. I did miss Chloe's original voice actress, as I felt she had a lot more attitude in her voice that matched Chloe's personality better, but the new voice actress wasn't terrible. Also, I didn't come across any glitches or typos, which is always a big plus for me.
I definitely recommend Life is Strange: Before the Storm to LiS fans and newcomers alike, as I believe this game could be played before the original without problem.

You're given choices every chapter and you have to choose - and it has never been more difficult. You affect many people and it doesn't matter that they're "only" in the game. This story makes you thing everything that is happening there is real and you see it through Chloe's eyes - and you FEEL like her. It makes you laugh, it makes you cry... and warms your heart.
I love reading and finishing a book I fell in love with tears my apart. I never thought I could experience it with a game - but it happened.
Twice.
So if you only played LiS and you don't know whether to buy this game or not; do it. You won't regret it.
P.S.: This game doesn't have tissues DLC, you have to bring your own.

Picked this up when it was on sale, and probably wouldn't otherwise. It's an enjoyable romp, but it's not without its flaws.
PROS:
* Non-vehicle combat is pretty fun, even frustrating at times, for the right reasons.
* Vehicle combat is similarly fun and occasionally frustrating. You'll find quick though that both of the above get kind of repetitive, and the difficulty spikes up and down for a lot of areas/missions/whatever.
* There's usually something to do. You can spend time on side quests and exploration for quite a while before needing to progress, plus there's random(ish) events.
* Strongly reminiscent of the Batman games, both in the way it's presented and how the ground combat is... well, basically identical to Batman, let's not kid ourselves there. But that's a good thing!
* Everything's well animated. Everything feels crisp. Overall it's just a pretty game that's well-optimized and has plenty of customization. You will find yourself thinking "that was pretty cool" a lot.
*Admittedly, the level design in the enemy forts is pretty solid. You might spend a while in one looking for everything after you've cleared it out. But that also brings up the first con...
CONS:
* Repetitive... stuff. You might find yourself bored at times just because, yeah, while there's a lot to do, this isn't exactly a scenic environment we're talking about here. In otherwords, the novelty wears off.
* Characters aren't all that interesting. However, they have plenty of spoken dialogue, and the acting itself isn't bad, they're just all kinda one-sided.
* The mine field side quests are annoying, especially because you *have* to bring your pupper, and you *have* to bring a certain vehicle to bring him. The range at which he detects mines just feels off, and it just seems more like a chore than a minigame.
* The level-ups on Max himself... well, they feel like they don't really do much. They're so minor you kinda don't notice them.
NEUTRAL:
* The whole survival element is cool, but never very threatening. Food is just your health, water is pretty easy to come by, and fuel you can keep spare tanks of in your trunk (and they're plentiful).
All in all, pretty fun game, might revisit since I never finished it.

This is a game that involve lots of busywork (running/driving around doing stuff that doesn't directly involve the main story arc, in this case it lets you upgrade your car and Max gear)
However, even though you may be someone that dislike that kind of gameplay you can always just play the main story. It will still involve some busywork in order to get a strong enough car to survive the missions. But that's the only forced busywork that must be done to progress the story. What you sacrifice when rushing trough the game like that however is the ability to have an awesome car at the end of the game. Because getting the best stuff will require busywork, no way around it. But again...it's not required to beat the game if you want to focus on that.
Anyway....if you have no problem with busywork then you'll love this game because doing busywork is awesome in it! You'll always have the next cool thing you want for your car that, at least for me, makes the driving around and destroying stuff very fun and not tiresome at all to be honest!
Probably helps a bit if you enjoy cars if you're going to enjoy this game too, I should mention this. Because the main part of the game is driving around in your awesome car that you constantly upgrade troughout the game...but if you know Mad Max then this shouldn't come as a surprice to be honest. You only go by foot when you need to enter areas the car can't get to, othervise it's the car what you use for everything. Of course there's fighting both on foot and in the car but the focus of the game is the car. Not hand to hand combat.
The main story isn't a deep and involving one either, so don't expect it to be...but hey, it's Mad Max, if you expect crap like that then you clearly doesn't know anything about Mad Max. The story of the game is good enough and I really enjoy it for its simplicity. I don't need Mass Effect stories in every game I play :).
TL;DR
Dislike busywork in open world games? Avoid this title!
Enjoy busywork in open world games? Get this title!
Busywork: Running and driving around doing stuff that doesn't directly involve the main story arc, but instead lets you upgrade your car and Max gear in this case.

One of, if not, the best colony management game I have played. Feels like a mix of Rimworld (with way better graphics) and Fallout Shelter (with way more interesting environments and building layouts). That's not meant as a slight on either of those mentioned games, I've had a bunch of fun with both, but it's high praise for ONI which I have enjoyed immensely more! The 2D side scroll setting of the game is more contained like that of Fallout Shelter, yet the maps/environments themselves seem much larger and are way more resource intensive, like Terraria. Your sims find themselves trapped in an air pocket in the middle of an asteroid, having been flung into it through a mysterious portal. With great fervour they will attempt to follow your guiding hand, leading them through harsh early survival periods into the possibility of a new comical, yet utopic and self sustaining, colony of misfits -or- probably not. Because the high likelihood of abject failure is even more comical in the most disheartening of ways
In terms of the devs previous games, the gothic, Tim Burton, style of Don't Starve didn't really appeal to me so I never got around to trying it, even though I enjoy survival games. I can't compare them, but I know Don't Starve received very high praise and a loyal fan base for the devs at Klei. I tried Inivisible Inc. and it had a lot of great parts but I couldnt get into a turn based game that was rather pushy in it's gameplay. ONI on the otherhand will get plenty of attention. I really love the whimsical steam punk art style. Its slightly muted tones serve it well. Its cartoony but beautifuly realized. The environment, object, creature, and duplicant (sims) animations are also excellent. The duplicants are hilarious and a blast to just sit back and watch while they go about trying to mitigate stress, hunger, injuries, hygiene needs, etc.
Briefly touching on gameplay, it is very involved and interesting. There is however very little to guide you as far as in-game help on your first few tries. You will likely start over many times getting used to the mechanics of the game and having "just one more go" at creating that more efficient colony which will let you explore further out into uncharted territory, resources, and creatures. That is, of course, one of the great things most folks enjoy about good colony management games in procedurally generated worlds. Restarting to learn from your past failures, then building and improving upon your knowledge and succesful strategies is fun to keep trying while adapting to randomly generated maps. This game is great in that regard despite being skimpy on tutorial material. Whether more tutorial elements come later in early access or not, they seem to have found a pretty good sweet spot overall, with gameplay being quite tough but not brutally so.
Lastly, one of the highly unique aspects of this game is how closely you must manage various gases and liquids (most importantly oxygen, of course) via piping and filtration systems as well as other tech upgrades. This sounded rather boring to me when I first looked at getting the game, but it actually makes for a better play experience as it fits the setting of the game so well. It challenges you to think critically and plan ahead while you'll likely be stifling both dismay and giggling fits as duplicants contend with your failed attempts. It gives the cartoony sci-fi vibe a realisitc grounding and lends a lot of weight to your decisions. May even be quite educational as well!
TLDR: If you enjoy colony management games, even though it's early access and oxygen isnt included, breathe easy in deciding to get this one!
Strengths:
- Art style and animations. Beautiful, cartoony, and outstanding!
- Duplicants (sims) are a big strength of the game. Unique, hilarious, and so fun to monitor!
- Resource variety is great. (liquids and gases make it even more interesting)
- Initial gameplay and management mechanics seem pretty tight overall. Very positive for early access.
- Pathfinding has been largely hiccup free.
- Very solid core game from which to build on as early access moves forward.
- The game has run very stable for me.
- Replay value is excellent.
Weaknesses:
- Soundtrack is ok but very ordinary, I feel the game could reach it's greatest of heights with a unique techno score (Paging Alan Walker)
- Aside from briefly enduring bad traits like flatulence, interpersonal interactions between duplicants seem non existent. I'm not expecting Rimworld intensity here, but even more endearing comedic value could be had if this was given some more love. Tripping over each other on occasion, silly greetings in passing, etc.
- Current Tech Tree is useful and decent, but quickly played through once you know what you are doing. Looking forward to seeing a more expanded list and progression curve in future playthroughs.
- Needs a few more exotic and weird creatures rummaging about in the terrain, even if just for fluff or show. The staples that are currently in are great though.
- Duplicant build range limitations are described in early tips, but it'd still be nice to see more apparent visual cues on the affected items or blocks...instead of relying on the hover descriptors
- Deconstruction can get a bit wonky sometimes. Duplicants following a strict start to finish sequence based on users mouse drag direction would largely solve this I think. That instead of the current "all pile on different points, peice meal" operation
- Tutorials/tips are extremely lite atm, which can be good or bad depending on how you like to approach these types of games. With odd looking pockets of different liquids and gases scattered around, fairly close by the start portal, the early game confusion is probably going to be a lot higher than usual for new players. Nothing a good guide or youtube video cant solve, but I tend to like figuring things out myself with what the game provides.
Note: As you can tell, many of the weaknesses are very minor and most will likely be taken care of or improved on greatly as the game moves through early access. They are some faults I find in the current snapshot of the game and at no point did any of them make me regret getting the game or take away from the fun of playing.

Umineko is honestly such a good mystery novel. The nature of the mysteries are so unique. (SPOILERS IF YOU DON'T WANT TO KNOW THE MAIN PLOT) This review is meant for people who have watched or read higurashi.
What is so unique about these mysteries is that sometimes (more times to the later chapters) you see how the event clearly played out, but even when you do, there is still a mystery. The event you see is what happens with magic, but the mystery has to explain the scene with human logic. Battler, the main protaganist, is trying to escape a loop similiar to higurashi's. But there are a few different perameters for it. The most important one is that, unlike higurashi with Rika, Battler 'doesn't remember his memories' from loop to loop. Instead, he is given a connected alternate existence while the events happen. In order to defeat the which, he has to proove that whiches aren't real by going through the mysteries with human logic.
Unlike games like danganronpa where you have a lot of evidence and scheduled time to find it, in umineko, there is barely any evidence. So Battler really has to twist logic and reason into his evidence, while Beetrice narrows down his reasoning with the absolute truth. So unlike murder mysteries, in umineko, Battler's goal isn't really to find the culprit, but to find out how the murder was even possible in the first place.
Umineko has the best story I have ever seen in my life. The characters are very fleshed out, and you can really feel their pain. Umineko has the best romance and one of the only couples that are realistic. I didn't like Higurashi's romance, and I didn't like clannad's romance either. But in Umineko, you can really see the picture and you can really understand it. I've cried so many times for the romance in this.
Umineko also has so many logical twists too. *AHEM CHAPTER 3*. And it is just so logical yet it does such a good job of letting the readers understand. Umineko has easy vocabulary so you don't have to worry about stupid words that you can't even understand. I love Umineko, it presents it's plot in an easy to understand way, but it is also very complex at the same time. It's so much better than reading a book that just had a simple plot but bogus vocabulary that gets in your way of understanding what's happening.
Umineko is one of those stories that you can't judge on first impressions, and it always can find a way to surprise you, but there are no times where it tries to surprise you just for the sake of it. It surprises you while still making sense with the story.
There are no edgy characters too. And the characters that get spotlights are great. It's pretty hard for me to choose a favorite because they are all great. You can't really determain the character on first impressions, some characters are actually very different than how they act on the outside, and you're predictions will problably be wrong most of the time with them.
The one problem I have with this game, is that the first character that gets a spotlight never gets a spotlight again. And that was pretty annoying for me. Most likely that character will probably get a spotlight again in chiru.
10/10 You might hate it if you don't like it, but for those who like it, it is the best thing.

Umineko is not for everyone. For me it is the best story I read in my whole life but for someone the twist at the EP 5 can be really annoying. Umineko is not a pure mystery. It's real genre is much more different and for me much more satisfying. If you can accept it for what it is and try to understand it, it will reward you by giving you a really important life lesson. I still believe that Ryukishi07 is a really good guy who tries to show people something rather than writing a "heartless" mystery. Umineko will not going to give you all answers. But you can still find them all by just thinking about it. If you can't find some pieces, there is a manga which gives every answer and even shows new things. If you want to read a life changing story with some mystery sauce, buy it and play it. The first EP starts a little bit slow but when you finish it you will understand that even those slow scanes were actually very important and not just some fillers to make the story longer. If you going to read it finish it before talking about it. Just because you didn't liked the first 4 episodes doesn't mean that you will not like the latter ones. Just give it a chance and finish it and then rewiew it. Also don't forget to download the PS3 patch for better character sprites and backgrounds and one of the best voice acting in a VN.

Umineko is a sound novel. It's a book with music and atmospheric sound effects and, if you install a patch, voice acting that is frankly incredible. And it never had any questionable content to remove. It's not one of those thirsty games where the patch makes anyone's clothes fall off. It's a beautiful story that takes 60 dang hours to get through. Your interaction with the novel is turning the page and nothing more.
The plot is a love song to mystery novels. The soundtrack is at times haunting, puckish, teasing, triumphant. You feel so much of the plot through the choice of accompaniment.
To say any more would rob you of some of the experience of trying to define what, even, Umineko is. And my personal definition changed multiple times while reading.
When steam opened the anime pandora's box and let all the thirsty demons out into the world, this is the hope that was left over. This is the one anime game on steam worth a dang.

So it starts with a premise of a fairly straight forward family gathering, it seems like it is going to be a murder mystery over dear old grandpa's inheritance. A bit cliche but whatever. Glad I got into this finally. The fame this game has received is not misplaced. The overall premise of the game is you are shown a murder mystery involving people stuck on an island, and it is narrated to you in what appears to be complete fantasy. Don't make the same mistake I did and rush through the game thinking this is a fantasy game though. Everything is solvable without the absurd theories that are presented to you throughout the game. If you want to take part in trying to solve the mysteries given as you read through, I recommend looking through Knox's commandments on detective fiction so that you have a real shot at thinking about the murders. Note that the visual novel does not actually ever give you the explicit answers to many of the murders, instead choosing to give increasingly obvious hints to the answers as you progress through the chapters, and you'll have to go through wikis and forums for the "answer key."
There's a lot here besides just mystery fiction though. This game has some great world building and a ridiculously good soundtrack. The characters all have believable backstories and motivations for their actions, and some of them are so smart and deceptive that you'll be thrown for a loop at least a few times throughout the read. Admittedly, the first chapter was somewhat dull on the first read, since the setting and characters feel very generic. If you keep reading though, you'll be as addicted as me and ruin your life for a few weeks by the ridiculous story that this game has to offer. You don't have to be a mystery fan to enjoy this experience. Umineko spans many different genres.
Definitely install the PS3 version art patch and voice patch as well. The new art is not nearly as good as the PS3 art.

I enjoyed the first arc. I'm a mystery fan, and the story is set up to be a perfect mystery: a cast of interesting, mostly-likable characters with extensive interpersonal drama and interesting reasons to hate each other, all trapped on an island when bodies start dropping. It's set 99 years after the first Sherlock Holmes mystery, and the author has a keen appreciation for mystery tropes. Like a lot of the classic mysteries, there's a tension between natural and supernatural explanations, but clearly the natural will - inevitably, as per the genre - win out.
Nope! No explanations, no natural solution. The second arc happens, instaed, and the genre changes completely. Now it's supernatural horror with a deliberately meta edge. Now the plot consists of the likable characters being tortured forever by a vicious and omnipotent witch, a GM with limitless powers whose goal is 'make the cast suffer before they die', and the possibility of a happy ending is absurd as that of a solution inside the mystery genre.
I like dark stories - up to a point. This point: when all hope is extinguished. When the second arc got into full swing, I stopped caring what happened to anyone. Sure, there's some variation in what could happen - how they're doomed - but they're all doomed. The only question is how, and given villainous omnipotence, I don't care about how.
It's absolutely a "love it or hate it" game. Most people love it. I don't. I really don't. The themes that interested me were a decoy, limited to the first arc; the characters the story is "actually about" are the hero, Battler, who I found to be the least interesting of the original major characters, and the villain, Beatrice, who I can't stand.
In the end, I said the eight deadly words - "I don't care what happens to these people" - and uninstalled the game.

4X space games are my absolute favorite. This game may be great down the road, but has little content at the moment and many attribute that other 4X'ers have. Some of the biggest improvements that could be made, in my opinion, is the targeting and/or tracking system. It works great so long as you are facing the chosen target, but as soon as you are not, all information pertaining the target disappears.
Another gruling task in the game, at current, is boarding. Board is quite easy to accomplish so long as you have shot down the shields or hull of the target and have more troops than the target. The problem lies in after you have captured the ship. Unlike any other 4X out there, you actually have to tow this ship back to a space station even though you have troops onbaord still. The problem is, is that after 4-5,000 KM's, the ship blows up and you loose it all. And with the lack of any content at this point, other than capturing in this game, there's only missions, and if you've done 3, you've done them all.
There is also an inherent lack of challenge, even on hard. Your starting ship can easily best the biggest and strongest of battle cruisers currently roaming space.
In my opinion, I would give this game another couple of updates and revisions before throwing some cash at it. If you want to see an awesome 4X game that is extremely balanced, well thought out, ultra realistic and graphically amazing, check out X3 Terran Conflict or Albion Prelude. There is a bit of a learning curve to the controls, but it has satisfied me with over 300 hours of addicting gameplay. X3, in my opinion, has alot that these devs could assimilate from.

Where to begin?
I have known about the Shantae franchise for a while now. I never got to play the physical copy of the original, but I have played it on my 3DS. Since then I have enjoyed the Shantae games from the original to Pirates Curse.
When I heard that Wayforward announced HGH via Kickstarter, I was hyped and managed to contribute to help make the game a reality a few years ago. Now I am aware Kickstarter has a bad rep. Many products there have been mediocre at best and a disaster at worst. However I am safe to say that despite waiting years for this game, I can announce that this game has not dissapointed me.
First off, the leap from the pixel style to the cartoon-ish look was a great choice in the art direction. I know that some games tend to stick with the classic look like Sonic Mania. But this is a beautiful game. The animation is smooth and appealing to those who can appreciate 2d animation in games.
The soundtrack is on-point. Jake Kaufman has once again done a tremendous job with the music for the game. From the upbeat updated version of Scuttle Town to the catchy electro sound of Riskys Hideout, it definately gave me various earworms. Dance through the Danger by Cristina Vee is a great theme for the game and she did a great job at it.
Now for the gameplay. HGH both feels like a Shantae game but at the same time doesn't. It has all the classic mechanics: upgrading hairwhip from the shop, unlocking dances that give you access to other areas, backtracking to get the items needed to progress. At the same time though, it feels a bit more streamlined than the other 3, they had the focus of exploring dungeons to progress the story. Here it goes for a more simpler approach, having a level select screen (taking a page from Pirate Curse) and getting from point A to B to beat the level. I personally don't take issue with this, but I know some who'd prefer the original style and might find it too easy.
Fortunately, Wayforward included a free update including Hardcore mode, I'm still having trouble getting through it as it makes you more cautious due to bein able to die much sooner so players wanting a challenge will likely enjoy that.
Speaking of additional content, with Pirate Queen Quest being the only one available at the moment with Friends till the End coming up, I really like this style of DLC, actually adding to the game rather than just giving a new weapon or a skin. It's an interesting concept, taking place at certain points in the original game and expanding on it. It takes all of the Shantae levels and flips them around with how each character (Risky only for the time being) gets around the level differently compared to Shantae. Though perhaps a bit too pricy.
Overall, I really enjoyed HGH, Wayforward is a really hard working company, and Matt Bozon should feel proud that not only did his game make it through Kickstarter, but one of the few that didn't backfire and worth the wait as they wanted the game to be the best it could be.

22 hours in, and I have yet to beat a single boss. Am I that bad? Sure, there are times I want to throw something when I die, but even after taking a break, I love coming back and playing "just one more." Something about this game makes it fun to keep coming back, makes it feel like I'm making progress after those hundreds of deaths. That family tree.

Like any Rogue-based kind of game, dying isn't so much a matter of if, but moreso a matter of when.  Thankfully, dying is not nearly as agonizing or painful as it could be.  You keep whatever treasure you had gained up 'til your death, which can be used to purchase either stat upgrades, equipment, or runes.  Progression is pretty slow at first, but over time you do start seeing advancement in all of these areas.
Since you do have to work for and earn progress in the game, it feels rewarding as you become more capable of exploring larger areas of the castle.  This is especially poignant later on as you overcome the hardest parts of the game, because earlier you were dying repeatedly in only the first couple of rooms.  One element that helps this sense of advancement is seeing the myriad of enemies and the different varieties of each one.  Each enemy has 3 levels of difficulty, with visible differences and changes in how they attack.  Each one also has either a mini-boss or boss equivalent as well, and developing in the game to the point where you can defeat all of them is a milestone you end up striving for.
The game is balanced really well as far as a sense of making progress because there are four distinct areas on the map to explore, with each one being clearly different from the other in respect to the color configuration on the map, background setting, music cues, difficulty/damage taken, and which enemies spawn.  Early on you will immediately recognize when you've inadvertantly found one of these new areas, and if you want to live, you will flee from the area as soon as possible.  It's programmed quite well as far as generating random set-ups that feel unique each time, even though there are only so many pre-programmed styles and arrangements of rooms available.  You don't feel like you just played the same map earlier, even if you recognize similar room layouts here and there.
A nice aspect of the game design is the variety of classes and traits available.  The game designers allowed their sense of humor to shine in some traits, while others are very creative and have significant impact on the gameplay/design.  There were times where I liked all of the choices available and also times where I didn't like any of them, but that's just the roll of the dice.  You'll wind up finding which ones you can't stand or love yourself.
Finally, I like the additional boss remix challenges available in the game.  They are quite gruelling, but allow for rapid, unlimited retries.  However, if someone doesn't want to bother, they can still beat the main part of the game, as it takes far less then maxed out stats to vanquish all of the bosses.  I've beaten it twice myself, and I still haven't purchased all of the upgrades yet.  I suppose that would be one complaint I have, since the gold requirements to buy everything is so excessive, though it's thankfully not a necessary aspect to win.  Overall I highly recommend this game, as though it can be disheartening to die, it only winds up giving the player a chance to upgrade and try again stronger than last time.

The game was praised for being a masterpiece of modern shooter due to it's "self aware" story, where it isn't the call of duty's nor battlefield's usual routine of "Grrrrrr X nation has turned againts 'MURICA, TERRORISTS, KILL KILL KILL".
The game is set in Dubai, but it's future Dubai and it's buried unter 500 ******* meters of sand. You are playing as the commander of a special squad, forged out of you and two friends (one is black, cause there's always a black guy [no offense]).
The gameplay consists of running between cover to cover, shooting americans (I'll get to that) and dying quite alot.
The thing is it gets really dull quite fast. Your drones squad mates shoot almost everything for you, can heal each other, can throw infinite stun grenades when the game feels like you don't know how to defend yourself, snipe distant enemies and all that with the click of a button. It's the usual problem where the game treats you like a child. Another aspect is sand, which is laid in strategic locations for you to shoot at and then it drops on enemies and enemies die. Whoo hoo.
Some aspects are quite nice but at the same time make you over-powered, like when you can crouch when you controlling a stationary machine gun, to make you an offensive beast while still hard to get attacked (yeah you lose some accuricy big deal). The graphics are pretty good, to be honest. I liked the little detail where if you step on sands in leaves trails of steps. The scenery is beautiful, everything makes you feed like you're really in the deserted (hu hu pun intended) city of Dubai, and that's a big plus.

Mad Max is a terrible game, adored by fanboys who think they're just like Max every time they log on. I hope you're better than this.
WHY THE STORY SUCKS:
Mad Max is a degraded man who loves eating dogfood and maggots.  And this is what this game is all about. It should be called Dogfood and Maggot Eating Simulator 2015.
This is the goal that drives Max through the wasteland: finding more dogfood and maggots to munch on. He will fly into a rage if anyone tries to stop him, and punch them to death.
There are some other people in the game, but Max treats them like♥♥♥♥♥♥(he's afraid they want his dogfood) and [Spoiler!] they all die.
Some more spoilers:
- There is a MILF and her child locked in a cage. Max don't care! They die.
- There is a crippled man who does all of Max's work. Max mercilessly insults him and his disability, and then he kills him. Becase Max work alone!
- There is a crippled dog. When he's not neglecting him in the back of the truck, Max makes him run through minefields. For true! Then he abandons him. Max don't need no crippled dog!
- There is a character named Griffa, who spends the entire game trying to get Max to realize that he's a complete ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ (no exaggeration). It's unclear whether he succeeds, but the message to gamers couldn't be clearer: look in the mirror, please! (Also, do something about that acne.)
All of this make Max awesome, and model for REAL MAN. Fanboys love so much! If you win playthrough, you become Lord of Your Basement, Real Man just like Max! Eat some dogfood and maggots - delicious, make you strong!
WHY THE GAMEPLAY SUCKS:
Endless grind. It's basically Far Cry 4 crossed with a bad racing smash-em-up game, but less fun than either on their own. You run the EXACT same missions OVER and OVER again, with no variety - but you're in a new area! With a slightly different boss person! So.... Progress! Winning!
Only buy if you are really bored, or love spending hours grinding each little update (5% better tires? Need to unlock missions!). Combat is just button-mashing in the direction of the nearest opponent. Most of the driving challenge comes from steering so loose it's almost impossible to drive straight. Just bad all around.

At first this games gives you quite an easy start even without much tutorial. After a few hours you start to think "that's it ? I'm gonna live forever" just to realize a moment later that one of your critical ressources runs out and your whole base concept gets wrecked. At this point you start to realize how much bigger the game is thank you thought at first... it's a really complex simulation of liquids an gasses, you have to mix and cool and heat them to get a bit of extra water or oxygen that allows you to last a few extra cycles. Since most ressources are limited in this game, you only succeed "forever" if you really really think things out and plan your base accordingly from the first minute. Not to say that this is necessary to have fun with this game, I started over and over again, every time with something new learned from the last play, and it's really rewarding to watch your base being operated by well-fed and well-motivated duplicants.
This game has TONS of potential, and i cannot wait to see what the devs will add in the future.

This game is incredibly addicting. It's concept is in some ways similar to don't starve, except now you are working with managing a colony and have them survive by gathering food, constantly resupplying oxygen so they don't sufficate and die, and maintaining a warm home to stay in where you have to find ways to keep their stress levels low.
Each Duplicate has their own personalities with pros and cons. Pros include Divers Lungs, which a Duplicate can hold their breathe underwater for longer periods of time and also consumes less oxygen in your environment, while that same Duplicates con may be that he is a coward, who refuses to battle monsters, or is a Yokul which means they cannot do research. One of the worst stress reactions from a Duplicate is Binge Eater, they will start over eating if they get too stressed which can be catastrophic for your colony as food is not the easiest thing to come by. Another bad one is Mouth Breather, they take up more oxygen than normal.
For being released for just a few months as an Early Access, the game is already fun in it's current state that I can't help but feel excited for whatever future ideas they add to it. Although there isn't much in the game yet in terms of the research tree and ingame features, but that's expected with an early access. I do not regret my purchase. Although it was $5 off, so... yeah. :P
NOTE: Unlike Don't Starve Together, this is a single player game. As far as I'm aware, the developers have no intention of including multiplayer feature in the future. (as it wouldn't really make sense with the way the game is designed)

I tried Euro Trick Simulator 2 because I enjoyed playing Farm Simulation 2015.  I thought it was interesting that I had a choice to use either the keyboard+mouse for steering or the traditional keyboard-only steering.  I initially opted for keyboard+mouse steering thinking it would be more accurate.  I found that it was very senitive and I didn't care for it.  I went to the traditional keyboard steering model and found it easier for me.
I tried a couple of missions, but became pretty frustrated at the precision needed to back-up and park the truck.  I didn't find any helpful tutorials.  I had been playing Farm Sim 2015 which also requires backing a vehicle with a trailer, but this was much more difficult.  I finally had to give up and use the auto-park feature.
When I went on a longer mission, I found that it was difficult to stay in the lane.  Anytime I hit another vehicle or scraped the wall, I was given a fairly substantial money penalty.  After a couple of times, I found the game just wanted more precision and accuracy than I wanted to give it.
This isn't saying that other people won't enjoy the game or there is a flaw in the gameplay.  I just personally found the game to be more annoying than I thought it would be.
I ended up getting a refund on the game from Steam.  I'm very thankful for that feature.

A great return to form for the Hitman series and while Episode 1 (The Intro Pack) didn't astound me, I see a bright future ahead for this Hitman entry. I absolutely loved it and I can't wait to see what they do with the rest of the season. I might not fully support the whole splitting the game into chunks ordeal but I can faithfully say that while that might suck, the game does not disappoint me. I wasn't a big fan of Absolution, but I absolutely loved Hitman 2: Silent Assassin through Hitman: Blood Money.
-Gameplay: It's better then Absolution, feels like Blood Money to me. They took some of the best things from Absolution and applied them to this game.
-Graphics: They are absolutely fantastic. (even with some of the framerate issues)  Everyone and everything looks absolutely amazing and the people look like... actual people. My jaw hit the floor on a few occasions at how beautiful everything looked, and seeing April's content trailer made my jaw hit the floor even harder. I cannot wait to see the map for April on my computer screen.
-Audio: The world feels alive and responsive, I felt like I was in a real place during the Paris Fashion Show. I don't think the audio ever broke my immersion at any point during my playthrough of Paris.
-Music: It might not be Jesper Kyd, but it's there and what is there didn't sound like absolute crap to me. I liked it, but I would like Jesper Kyd back.
-Story: While there isn't much here, it intrigues me and I actually can't wait to see where it will go throughout the rest of the Season.
-Some framerate problems. It will probably be patched eventually but I noticed some issues during my time playing the game.
-Graphics options were greyed out for me, it again, will probably be patched but it's a current issue with the launch state of the game.
-Always online, I understand why it's like this but I don't support it.
-Poorly added in DirectX 12 support, this is my first game that I own that supports DirectX 12, and the way it's added into this game is♥♥♥♥♥♥ I had to switch over to DirectX 11 because 12 kept crashing the tutorial level for me.
-Slightly too easy for my tastes but as I do replays I will probably tinker with the games numerous options to make it harder for myself.
Do I recommend you buy this game in it's current state?: No, if you aren't a die-hard Hitman fan.
Do I recommend you to buy this game down the line?: Yes, I'm sure by 2017 when the physical version releases a lot of these bugs will be addressed and fixed.
Did I enjoy my time with this game?: Yes, and I'm not done playing through all of it yet. I still have yet to touch Contracts Mode, Escelation Mode, and Elusive Targets (When we get one)
This review will remain updated throughout the course of 2016 as my opinions shift and change with the later levels of HITMAN™ and I will of course edit the review when I finally get around to Elusive Targets, Escalation Mode, and Contracts Mode.
Was I given a key for review by the developers?: No, of course not, I bought this game with my own hard-earned cash and so far I'm getting my moneys worth of enjoyment.

Starpoint Gemini 2 is a game I've been following for a long time, hoping for a game that would dethrone Freelancer from its rightfull place. So far things look good and this might even be the case in the future, but as of now there's still plenty of work to be done. That doesn't mean SG2 wouldn't feel good to play. Does it?
The game features a rather large open area The Gemini Star System. It's filled with stations, shipyards, bases, asteroid fields, junkyards, enemy ships, friendly ships, planets, anomalities, practically everything you would expect from a sandbox-type space game. It feels like there's a lot to do out there but at least for me that's not the case. This is because the game features very few different types of missions for the moment. There are freelance missions which you'll accept over the map view and then start them by docking with the correct facility, ship or planet. These missions usually involve hauling passangers or goods from the dock point to another. There are also scanning, repairing, patrolling and I think I even saw an assassination mission. These might keep you busy for a while but the samey repeating content of each mission type quickly lose their charm.
The game's main emphasis is on space combat which for the most parts feels good. Ships fly in space and trade fire with missiles, beam weapons, plasma and railguns. Fighters fly out from the bigger ships and engage the enemies and boarding parties can devastate the enemy ships from within. You can fire manually or tell the game to target and fire on the target for you. I find this helpful since handling the ship in combat can be a real pain.
You control your ship through two different control mechanics. The default one uses WASD to steer the ship while the mouse is used to target, shoot and activate buttons on the GUI. The second method is using the mouse to steer the ship. The ship turns along your mouse movement much the same way the default steering in Freelancer was handled. I prefer the former method in this game since using the mouse flight feels overly sensitive and I can't seem to make the ship fly straight or stay on target.
In combat you also have to keep your ship from taking damage and face the stronger shield at your enemy while also focusing on distributing fire from your weapons evenly enough so you can have a sustained stream of fire at the target. I'm not sure if this is the intended way to fight but I've found it effective. You can also enter the turret view to move the camera and aim targets around your ship freely, this helps you to shoot targets your ships is not directly facing at.
The combat is fairly entertaining, although like I mentioned above, steering the ship can be difficult and the default camera angle isn't helping much. When you need to fly on target it seems you have to place the target somewhere above your ship, close to the top edge of your screen. This is the actual direction the ship is moving towards to and it might take a while to get used to that. Also because of the odd camera angle I often had to keep the enemy "above" my ship to be able to fire the majority of my weapons at it. This just feels wrong, at least to me.
The GUI is what really bothers me the most. It's overly colourfull, oddly clunky and the sound effects are horrendous. I have a tendency to go for a "minimalist" kind of look when it comes to user interfaces and such. In this game the UI makes me think of children toys, the large plastic kind with full of teeth marks and bright flashy colours. Actually, now that I think of it, the overall design and look of the game is overly shiny and gleamy. The ship designs could also be a tad more imaginative. Even the large battleships just look and feel like one-man fighter crafts even though they are supposed to be much larger than that.
Overall the game has potential to be extremely entertaining. I like it so far even if the things I mentioned above might feel a little harsh. I've got great expectations for this game, although experience has taught me not to, but I can't help it. I'm longing for a good space combat/sim/whatever that has the feel and openness of Freelancer.

You know that one game in a classic franchise that plays nothing like all the others? That's how I feel about Half Genie Hero. Half Genie Hero doesn't stick to the classic formula of traversing through one open world, going through dungeons, and collecting the main mcguffins before the villain can get ahold of them. At first, this really made me skeptical of the game. I bought this game about a month ago, and I did get a lot of enjoyment out of it, for the first couple of playthroughs anyways. It was fun the first time because you don't really know where all the collectibles are, unless you're following a guide of some sort. Then by the time you replay the game, you really start to notice how tedious getting 100% completion is, how the majority of the side plots go absolutely nowhere, and ultimatly how simplistic the gameplay and story is, (providing you're not going after all the achievements of course). I don't think the main campaign is bad pre se, but it does make me miss how the original Shantae, Risky's Revenge, and Pirate's Curse was structured. It was a formula that worked, and with WayForward getting rid of that structure, this just left me wishing there was more to Shantae's campaign. I can only recommend this campaign for those who don't really care about getting all the achievements and beating all the modes because this game really drains you around the third or fourth playthrough.
Pirate Queen's Quest, on the other hand, is structured better and really gives you more of a sense of non-linear progression. I love how this mode automatically lets you choose which level you want to play, and I wish Shantae's campaign would've been structured similar to this. True, you can't get any of the pirate equipment in any order, but being able to choose the levels in any order really adds a depth of strategy similar to how the robot masters are handled in classic Mega Man games. Plus the Dark Magic skill tree is genius as well, letting you develop Risky as you see fit. Of course, part of the reason I like this mode is because you get to play as Risky, and Risky Boots is probably one of the most over-the-top villains in any video game franchise, hence why I love being able to play as her and see things through her perspective.
Friends to the End, oh where to begin...
For starters, let me say what I think Wayforward did right. First and most importantly, they got rid of the hubworlds and world select. This is how I perfer Shantae; an open world with all the different areas connected together that contain plenty of secrets that can be found once you get the right tools and explore everything. Wayforward also made this mode linear, which works out with Bolo's, Sky's and Rottytop's gameplay. Each character has unique abilities at hand as well, which can make for some interesting puzzles. This is extremely noticable in the last world, where you play as each character seperate, with each character having their own set of challenges. Rottytops is extremely broken as well, since using her decapitation powers gives her brief invulnerability, (which is a Godsend for the Nega-Shantae battle). Now for the negative aspects. This mode is difficult for ALL the wrong reasons. All the characters share a health bar, which wouldn't necessarily be a bad thing, EXCEPT Wayforward wants you to do a 3 heart run of the mode. In other words, your limited to 3 hearts, period. No heart holders to be found, no heart squids, just 3 hearts. Albiet Rottytop's can restore your health to full providing you have enough magic, but even then, if you don't have enough magic, then you have to be even more careful. It doesn't matter who you play as; none of these characters are built for combat.  This is especially noticable in boss fights such as the Giga Mermaid. I do like the Level Up system, but the least Wayforward could've done was made it to where all 3 members max health increases once someone levels up. Combine the poorly executed combat and the 3 heart run dibacle, and this mode will hand your butt to you on a silver platter on many occasions, especially when fighting the Giga Mermaid. As long as we're talking about rehashed assets, did Wayforward REALLY need to bring these bosses back? I don't look forward to Cape Crustacean or Hypno Baron's Castle because I can only imagine how much harder these bosses are going to be in this mode. I know people were complaining that both Shantae's and Risky's campaigns were relatively easy for a Shantae game, but this is how you make a game that's hard for all the wrong reasons. I want to praise this mode for the puzzle-platform aspects, but the combat could've used a lot more work.
Overall, I don't think Half Genie Hero is a bad game. The main campaign and Friends to the End could've used a lot more work, as they are easily the most poorly executed parts of this game. And you know, it's sad that the only mode of this game that I really enjoy is Risky's campaign. I can see potential in Friends to the End, but the issues I've mentioned really makes me loath it more than I like it. This was an ambitious attempt Wayforward, but next time, go back to your roots...
Please change back to the more open world next time, though.

I was so sure that putting magical elements in the story would just complicate and mess up the setting, and it did but surprisingly not in a bad way. Infact Umineko's story thrives on these themes.
This is what makes Umineko great! by adding these elements it forces you to keep thinking ("Turn the chessboard around") to understand it further. It never felt repetitive even if the events themselves keeps repeating, and its all thanks to the addition of magic. never have I thought that magic would really add to the mystery side of the story, to help you better understand what I mean I'll give you a minor background
of the story.
It starts of with a annual family conference about the inheritance of the familiy's wealth on an isolated island called rokkenjima, when a typhoon passes through isolating the island. The basic premise of the story is
From there an epic story about mystery and fantasy is set. TL;DR: The game we wanted... but not the game we deserved.
I was looking forward to playing this game. I whole-heartedly loved Life is Strange, so when I heard this was available, I bought it immediately, driven by the strong impact the first game had on me. I loved the immersive, magical, trippy nature of the game, and I really liked Chloe. She was now our main character, so this has to be good, right? Right?
Spoilers & long read!
At first sight, this game is doing okay making you believe you are playing Life is Strange. It's got some pleasant soundtrack, the same familiar interface, and - wait Chloe was making the exact same kind of journal Max was? That's cute, I suppose. Then there is Chloe Price, our dear troubled Chloe, and we got Arcadia Bay, the virtual synonym for Bumble♥♥♥♥. What's that Unity logo at the startup? Oh, nevermind, it's Life is Strange!
I desperately wanted to like this game. The mechanics were the same as in the first one, except for the time travelling aspect of course. Chloe's "superpower" is eh, I guess, arguing? Instead of taking photos, we got tagging and graffiti in this. Armed with our new skills we are allowed to explore the prequels and get to know a little more about Chloe's life and her relationship with the mysterious Rachel Amber.
First, let's talk about what I liked about this game.
I think the music, for the most part, was interesting and fitting. I was also cool with the voice acting. And well... that's about it.
As I played more and more I couldn't shake this feeling that something was off. I often noticed that the movement of the characters, the way they were animated looked odd. Has it always been like that? I was moving around in larger areas that somehow seemed a lot less detailed and a lot less intriguing. It didn't help that the maps were repetitive, and the school, the dorm, Choe's house just didn't have the same level of surprise as seeing it for the first time, and I was really wishing there were more new places.
I do realize that this game was done by a different dev team, on a different engine (Unreal 3 vs. Unity). I have a lot of respect for Dontnod, the developers of the first Life is Strange, who had some practice with Unity, creating Remember Me, and now working on a promising title Vampyr that is using Unreal 4. According to Google, Deck Nine has been working on Playstation games prior to Before the Storm, none of which I know anything about as I don't own a PS. But it seems to me they were rather new to a hard task, and I acknowledge that it must have taken tremendous effort to recreate an existing world on another engine and kick it to life. However, it did feel very different and sometimes oddities like character animation ruined the scene for me.
Some of the things that were done well in the first game were forced in this, often feeling awkward or unnecessary, like some of the weird shots that were just meant to take the characters' odd animation out of focus, or those episodes when you are just sitting around, daydreaming. It works well in some cases, like when Chloe and Rachel are sitting on the train, listening to music, but for the most part, it just feels like overusing an element that doesn't seem to play part in the story whatsoever.
I can't help but compare it to the first game on every level, and to me, the characters felt a lot less developed. Here, nearly everyone seemed flat, with a simplified personality, and the storytelling often fell into putting them on one end of the good-people-do-good, bad-people-do-bad dimension. But one exception that needs to be mentioned is definitely Drew, who shows more than one side to his character throughout the game. But since everyone else lacks any 3D characteristics, I didn't have strong feelings about anyone in the sequel - prequel? What happened to the character development of David? What about Frank? Victoria? They seemed bland and Before the Storm didn't add much depth to their personalities.
And let's talk about the story. Is it just me or is this game completely lacking action? Do you remember the rails scene where Max has to save Chloe from getting hit by the train? Or when she is in a trippy nightmare maze of her past decisions, trying to sneak around evil Mark Jefferson clones? Or when she is trapped in the Dark Room? To me, these were nerve-wrecking moments, which I didn't have much of in the prequel - sequel? Sure, Before the Storm has a few memorable moments too, like Chloe and Rachel sitting on that train, or the Tempest play. Sometimes I wasn't even sure where the story was going. Was it trying to be about Chloe's father? Or Rachel's mother? About the loss of a parent? Chloe and Rachel love-slash-friendship? As much as Rachel is an adorable character, her out-of-the-blue relationship with Chloe was confusing, and I'm guessing it was going more for the love story than the friendship thing, but who knows, really (if it matters)?
Also as a part of the story, Frank sometimes appeared to act as Deux Ex, magically steering the storytelling when it was navigating itself into a corner. I was baffled that we saw Damon waving that knife around twice (!!!), only to be removed from the scene by Frank both times, and letting the scenario resolve itself off screen. The second time it happened, I thought Chloe might still be unconscious, and that chat with Sera might be one of those dream scenes she had with her father. But it turned out to be real, I guess, so Frank just removed Damon from the scene, untied Sera, and left Chloe laying on the floor for some reason... okay? And what the hell was that sudden jealousy fit from Elliot at the Amber house? He totally didn't come across as that type of guy, and it felt more out of character than an actual twist.
At the end of episode three, we are cutting to the scene where Rachel's phone is ringing at a place which looks like the Dark Room from the first game, suggesting that it is the night she died.
My biggest problem with Before the Storm, is that I didn't feel like it added that much to the original setup. I realize that Rachel was keeping her relationship with Frank from Chloe, but we didn't learn anything about it here, not even the slightest hint, unless we interpret Frank's occasional willingness to help them as a sign of affection. Side characters were uninteresting and sometimes disturbingly inconsistent (Elliot, Frank), The whole buildup also led to an awkward conclusion, I think that last scene at the mill was one of the weakest points of the plot. And even after, they make you choose between telling or not telling Rachel the truth, even though none of these have any major consequence, since we are already jumping into the closing cutscene. Rachel's relationship with Nathan Prescott was also very underdescribed.
All in all, I feel like I've been playing a game that looks like Life is Strange, behaves like it, but almost everything that made the first game good, is missing from it. I don't feel like I gained anything, except for maybe destroying Chloe's character, reducing her from a badass to a tryhard. In retrospective, I would have liked it more if certain things about her remained mystey.
I thank Deck Nine for the effort, but I would not recommend playing it. Stick to the first Life is Strange game, and see what Dontnod may come up with in Life is Strange 2, which they are announced to be developing.

The exploration of PTSD in this re-imagining of Heart of Darkness is where it really shines. The gradual loss of sanity - in Walker, in Dubai, and even in the game interface - is palpable and powerful. On its own, Spec Ops' gameplay is plain, but it's also never bad, and the game uses it masterfully and fluidly to further embed the player in Walker's mindset.

If you looked at this game and thought "oh great, another ♥♥♥♥♥♥ CoD clone", you're right; it would be a pretty ♥♥♥♥♥♥ clone - if that's what it was actually aiming for. No, ladies and gentlemen, this game's developers knew full well what you were expecting, so they use it to punch you in the gut. Even if you have a knowledge of this before hand, the punches just don't stop coming.
I wouldn't exactly call this game fun, it didn't leave me feeling empowered and heroic. It ripped my heart out, made me feel guilty and disempowered, smacked me in the face with hard choices and left me feeling very discontent with the choices I had to make. So no, it's not fun in any real meaning of the word, but it's the most engaging game I've played recently. I couldn't close the game or quit because this darn thing had such an iron grip on me. This game actually tackles some pretty deep issues - PTSD, use of white phosphorus - actually I should let you see these for yourself. I don't want to spoil anything accidentally while trying to encourage you to play this game.
While you're playing it (which you should), I do have some suggestions: listen to/read what's being said - they're not just talking to Walker; they're talking to you - even in the loading screen text; particularly as you get closer to the end. I should also mention that, if the controls and combat sequences feel a little dissonant, they're supposed to. I'd elaborate, but spoilers.
I love this game, but I wouldn't play through it again unless I wanted to feel horrible about myself! :p
If that didn't convince you, perhaps the guys at Extra Credits will:
Just don't watch part two until after you've played; it's spoilerific.
"Do you feel like a hero yet?" You must play this game at least one time to the end and then you know why I said this.
PTSD Simulator 10/10

Even in alpha, this game is an extremely exciting experience. I've only been playing for a few short weeks, but I've definitely learned that life isn't easy in the clink. Just when you think you've figured out how to stop showers from flooding your halls, you discover three prisoners in the middle of your undeveloped property in the middle of the night. There are so many options and so many details to think about. Laying water pipes and electrical cabling is only a part of the utilities you need to worry about: determining the best location for remote doors and CCTV cameras is where you'll find most of your time spent. If you love to create a little world and think about everyday things in a different way, then this game is a requirement.
