Umineko no Naku Koro Ni ("When The Seagulls Cry") is the second sound novel by Ryukishi07, after the similarly named Higurashi no Naku Koro Ni ("When The Cicadas Cry"). The two do not share a plot and can be experienced separately, but rarely some characters from Umineko mention minor plot points or concepts from Higurashi. It is inspired by Agatha Christie's And Then There Were None and S. S. Van Dine's The Greene Murder Case, sharing themes such as members of a same family being under threat, and people being stuck on an island with a murderer on the loose.
Unlike most visual novels that get to the West, there is little to no interactivity to Umineko in general and none at all in  Episodes 1 through 4 here, which make up the first half of the complete novel. There is no gameplay, no choice-making, no dating system. Just reading and listening to the soundtrack (which, by the way, is awesome). It is, effectively, no more than a novel with music, background art and character sprites. But what a novel it is.
Umineko's plot starts out kinda normal: you're being asked to solve murders, as in any other piece of detective fiction. But as you keep reading (= Episode 2 and on), stranger things start to come up. If you aren't deterred by these oddities and keep on reasoning instead of going "screw that", Umineko rewards you greatly.
If you are expecting a traditional murder mystery, this is not it. If you are intrigued by having to fight tooth and claw for your clues against unreliable narrators and Jedi truths which are technically true, but ambiguous and potentially misleading, Umineko is for you. While it isn't straightforward by any means, I feel it is never unfair. Its storytelling has hidden rules and it follows them closely, even if it's not immediately apparent: once you do understand the rules, you start regaining ground and fighting on equal footing. It never insults your intelligence by going "if you didn't figure it out yourself here it is".
Don't be misled by the relatively low hour count and achievement count I have for Umineko on Steam. I've already read through all eight Episodes on the original PC version, but I simply had to pick up this one for the updated translation and... Well, general love I have for Umineko. So if what I've mentioned so far has appealed to your curiosity, pick it up and read it! It's worth it.

Mysterious, romantic, magic, fascinating, mindscrewing, absurd, philosophical, deceiving. There are thousands of reasons why Umineko is the most unparalleled masterpiece in the history of visual novels. Umineko No Naku Koro Ni (When the Seagulls Cry) is a eight episode visual novel written by the author of the Higurashi When They Cry series, but the overall game is on a whole new scale when likened to its spiritual predecessor.
It all begins during the time frame of october 4 and 5, on a small, secluded island named Rokkenjima:
The plot begins with a flat slice of life-ish premise that could lead the readers to regard the VN as a simple-minded story: enter the entire Ushiromiya household, one of the wealthiest families in the world which struck it rich thanks to the head of the household, Kinzo, whose means of achieving his vast fortune remains shrouded in mystery. In view of the death of his aged grandparents, Battler Ushiromiya, the missing member of the household who has been living away from his parents for six years, decides to attend the gathering. Subsequently, upon coming together for the presumed last family meeting, each member is introduced, however, the situation takes a turn for the worse when a fierce typhoon preys upon Rokkenjima, the phenomenon marks the death sentence of the whole household, as one by one each member becomes the victim of a bizarre and brutal chain of murders attributed to a mysterious serial killer which later is revealed to be the Golden Witch Beatrice, Kinzo's secret lover and owner of the gold stack of the island. Battler refuses to believe in magic in spite of the given evidence, and concludes that the culprit of the accident is merely the 19th and hidden human on Rokkenjima, until the ultimate proof is shown to his eyes: The Golden Witch in flesh and blood. This insane happening paves the road for a magnum opus in which occult, braintwisters, love, action, tenderness and sympathy intermingle with each other to give life to a true work of art that remains unsurpassed even a decade after its initial release. Pretty much everything in the VN is executed flawlessly, ranging from the ample assortment of nearly one hundred BGMs to the writing, the art, and the multiple narratives throughout the game. The author succeeds in providing an accurate portrayal of the psychological situation of every character in the game, as such, providing remarkable backstories for the entire cast. The writing is one of a kind and absolutely phenomenal, likewise the author manages to strike right into the hearth of the readers, making it one of the most stunning works of the century.
The first half may sound slightly slow-paced, but I can assure the readers are in for one hell of a ride, Umineko No Naku Koro Ni is the ultimate life-changing experience that simply cannot be missed if you're into visual novels or complex, intriguing and thoughtful stories. I have gone through the 100 hours of the game twice, and not once have I been unsatisfied; Umineko is a VN that can easily be replayed over and over at any age. The game is best played with the PS3 sprites patch and the voice acting which makes for a whole new experience;
at the end of the day, I wholeheartedly am willing to replay it once again when Manga Gamer will release the Answer Arcs. Umineko simply cannot be explained with words alone, moreover it's incredibly hard to spoil to someone because of its sophisticated depth, no other VN can be compared to Umineko because no VN is as unique and breathtaking as Ryukishi's.

This game is exactly what it says on the tin. It's got strategy elements reminiscent of Battleship and chess, though, unlike both of those, it is not turn-based (it has "action bars" that you can't see until they're full up). You can adjust the speed of battle, though, and on the slowest setting you should have a decent amount of time to figure out what you want to do. Doing each mission for the first time is pretty exciting as you find out where everything is, but on subsequent playthroughs of the same mission you'll find that the enemy force uses the same machines and start in the same locations each time, and may only make different choices in movement from behind those "Unknown" spaces. This means that when you grind those missions later on for additional crates -- and you will, because you'll probably want to see just how powerful a tank your little sister can build -- you'll be able to breeze through just based on prior knowledge, and it may start to feel like a chore. Fortunately, if you just want to beat the game, grinding is only slightly necessary, depending on how many of your tanks die from enemies you didn't see until they popped up right in front of you.
Of note, the game seems to be structured like an anime, of which the protagonist Shoutaro Daihon'ei is a fan. Each mission plays out like its own episode, complete with an OP, a title card, a story segment, another story segment afterwards and one of several different EDs. You may find the OP and ED sequences annoying, but they're easy enough to skip over.
Also of note, the music they chose for the game isn't terribly fitting at times. I repeatedly found myself wondering what kind of mood they were going for in certain scenes. This is also easy enough to disable, if it bothers you as well.
Ultimately, if you like quirky doujin games and simplistic strategy games, then this one'll do you pretty well.

Pros
- The best looking desert and flame effects ever. The Mad Max punk rock style is spot on.
- A big map (well I guess that's expected with a desert setting).
- Enough stuff to do.
- Confronts pretentious game critics with their irrelevance.

- Storms add to immersion
Cons
- Possibly the most linear open-world game ever (which seems like an oxymoron). The story forces you down a very specific character progression. The game perfects the Ubisoft formula of locking up all the features of the game and then letting the player unlock them one by one by doing busy work and the linear main story. Most new unlocks are better than the previous ones so the upgrade tree itself is quite linear and the truly cosmetic options are few and even those are linear (for example, you can only grow Max's beard and not style it or shave it off).
- Feels too gamy. There are a bunch of rules / peculiar game mechanics the developers want you to follow. So it doesn't feel like a natural living open-world.
- Some story points make little sense. For example, from the beginning, Max wants to get away from the dangerous place he is at and for that purpose he goes through a whole lot of danger to get a V8 engine instead of his V6, which sounds like the logic of an 8 year old boy who is just learning about cars.
- Car turns slowly and the handbrake doesn't really work as you would want, which can get annoying in car combat or races.
- Some of the acting is sub-par.
- When you interact with an item, the game insists that you hold the button down instead of just pressing it.
- NPC citizens you meet are all realistically covered in rags and soot, but then the game introduces your to-be love interest and she is all boobs and pretty face and long hair. I am not for political correctness in games, but this was so out of place and unsubtle that it felt in poor taste.
- Storms are terrible from a gameplay design perspective
Conclusion: The visuals and the fun sandbox combat pull this game through.

My original review (while the game was still in EA) is shown at the bottom. Please note that the sections on performance are not entirely relevant now, since the game runs much better.
REVIEW AFTER RELEASE:
---------------------------------------------------------
The game is a mix between Freelancer and X3. You can command fleets, hire wingmen, level up skills, buy massive battleships, trade, do missions. It's a lot like Darkstar One too, if we are comparing - but a lot better.
The focus here is on large ship battles - and with many ships, rather than smaller dogfigthing. Your starting ship is fairly large ( gunship), and some of the stuff I have seen to buy looks cool. You can climb the ranks and get battleships, dreadnoughts and the like, and command officers and mercs to help you out in battle, either on your own ship or as a wingman. You can even board enemy ships and take control of them, or tractor ships back to stations to sell them.
It looks lovely and has a massive open map to explore, complete with anomalies, slipstreams, wormholes, gates, planets, stations asteroid fields, nebula etc. - all you would come to expect from such a game and more.
The campaign is basic, but enjoyable. The voice-acting is absolutely atrocious though - the accents are all over the place and it is detrimental in an necessary way. You also have the option to free-roam, doing missions as they come along, trading or becoming a pirate. It has a complete reputation and trading system, allowing you to become anything you want.
A lack of multiplayer hits hard, since this game would be infinitely better with it and a real shame it is not included. It also seems to have a fairly repetitive and grindy feel to it - hence the mark of 6/10. If it had multiplayer I think my score would jump to 8/10 instantly though.

One of the better "movie games" available.  Stays faithful to the stylings of the source material while going its own direction with the storytelling.  Crazy raiders driving equally-insane rolling deathtraps, and a heavily customizable Magnum Opus of your own.  The Arkham-esque melee combat is alright, but the driving battles are where this game stands out.  Firey explosions and pulsating engines make for a solid rush.  There's plenty of ruins to explore and raider camps to conquer as well.
And for being set in a barren wasteland, this game is a looker - think Fallout New Vegas with better tech (I also find the game reminiscent of FUEL, but with a lot less trees).  Gorgeous lighting paints long shadows across the sands, and the skybox always manages to stun.  The environment also proves to be quite diverse, ranging from volcanic mountains and red mesas, to a dried up seafloor, all the way to an old airport overrun by sand dunes and the burning refineries of Gastown.  Maintains a steady 60FPS with High settings on my FX-6300 and R9-380.
A must-play for fans of the movies, and strongly recommended for anyone else.

A fast-paced strategy game combined Advance War + Battleship classic game.
Your moe gal army want to literally die for you.
Command them as a faceless protagonist through this a bit heartless story.
My rating : roughly 6/10
Reasons of playing:
- Moe gals (...but of course, the most rightful reason)
- The kind of gameplay you don't see often.
- Actual skippable story with few branches, not just battles.
- Not too high in price. It's worthiness comes from how much you enjoy gameplay and features.
My experience:
- Completed the game 10 times, beaten all stages, too lazy to complete research.
- This game can get pretty grinding over time, but you don't actually need to grind in order to complete the story.
- Breeding cats is hard but rewarding (or game-breaking, up to you).
- Advance war element: Grid battlefield with every actions have their own range and area.
- Battleship element: Shoot into the unknown hoping it will hit, then expect attacks from the unknown hoping it will miss.
What I like:
- Moe gals (let's drop this already...)
- Good battle system and well-thought research line.
- Decent plot and story. Some things are predictable, but still well-written.
- Decent older-styled musics... most anyway. Some could use a bit of improvement, the opening in particular.
- I'm not gonna spoil anymore than this.
Most of the fun is from personal taste as well as gut.
I reccomend this if you have them.
What I don't like:
tl;dr Three things - Evasion, Grinding, and Strange pacing.
- Evasion... While it does give excitement for the game, I don't think they should resort to RNG just to make the game more difficult and challenging, especially when there's nothing to counter this evasion.
It also makes many units you can research in a late game seem like a joke. Also, having evasion means that the possibility of 'not being able to hit anything even after the 3rd set of 10 shots' and 'not being able to evade anything the enemies shoot' exist. (spoken from experience where I got an unexpected crushing defeat even with 6 cats and a few units with Diet Cola boost).
- Grinding... To keep this short: Most income per stage ~5-6m, Most expensive stuff
~100m minus 1. While it's true that you don't even need 1m clear the game and 10m to complete everything else, it just means you can't exactly 'truly complete' the game without passing a hellish test of gut. Also, imagine how long and how hard can you get that 5-6m.
- About pacing... Sometimes it is too slow, like having to check every single grid in a target range. It's a pain for most units with 13 grids (3 in diameter) and some units with ~100 grids for their target range. Remember, you'll be grinding. Sometimes, it is too fast. You can't take too many actions before your opponent gets one. I have no problem with this because it's more fair to the AI.
Something else to say:
- Some stages take longer to beat than one would expect. Some enemies will give you surprises. Some developments raise your desire better than others. Some plot may make a twisted turn. (The characters all kinda twisted already anyway...) Expect these on first playthrough.
- Have trouble breeding cats? Reduce Battle Speed to Minimum, drink cola and feed them radiotoxic.
- By the way, there's no random or custom maps, so things can get old fast.

I think it is a crying shame that the episodic nature of HITMAN has been the focal point when discussing the game, and to see it colouring people's perception in regards to the quality and quantity of what is on offer here is incredibly sad, given how much more there is to talk about.
In terms of atmosphere, ambience, scale and sense of immersion, the opening Paris chapter is a classic slab of Hitman and a true assassination sandbox. It's exactly what fans of the franchise have been asking for after Absolution's more linear, narrative driven approach. We're given an an overwhelmingly large sandbox map, a couple of targets to kill, some useful hints and thent sent on our merry way. The Showstopper is a mission with more ways to approach and complete it than you can shake a stick at. The more you play, the more tools you unlock for use in future replays - Replay value has always been very important for a HITMAN game and this is no different.
I'm also enjoying the compromise that comes with choosing your loadout - You can't have every useful tool at once, which adds replay value but also makes you carefully consider your tools. If you want the coin and the fibre wire, that means you have to forfeit the lockpick - But you still get the option of brute-forcing a door open with a crowbar found in the level. It's a really, really good balance.
That said, my hunger pangs for Hitman aren't wholly satisfied like they would be with a full retail release, and without additional levels to get stuck into after Paris, the achievements, challenges and opportunities do feel more like padding than they otherwise would- But this opening chapter has left me incredibly happy and excited as a hardcore Hitman fan since 2000.
This isn't the main course, this is just the starter - an incredibly tasty one. Consider my appetite whet!

It feels good. Controlling 47 is once again comfortable, precise and empowering. IO had the decency to allow for all the in-game assistances to be deactivated (I did keep the icons indicating which enemies can be suspicious). Overall, there are tons of good ideas, and an undeniable attention to detail. You feel free to explore and tackle the objectives how you see fit. By now most people might already know what big changes have been made since Absolution, like the revamped disguise system and the sandbox-ish open levels, so I won't say anything about this. These latter had been promised, they're here, there's nothing to complain about.
I'll seize the opportunity to briefly mention the story: while we are just given a little glimpse at it, it does seem well-crafted and interesting. The prologue/tutorial takes place at the beginning of 47's career, when he first joined the ICA. The Paris level - and the rest of the game after that - takes place a few years after Hitman Absolution (without direct link to said episode, like a new start, a clean slate, in order for us to better appreciate the experience of playing as 47 when he does what he does best).
Each destination will have its own ambience and each target, his background story. An overarching story ties it all together, and the balance is perfect : it is there, it is interesting, and it manages not to feel too intrusive.
Nevertheless, some design choices do manage to ruin the fun for me : the game requires you to be online. Should you be disconnected from the servers, the game will quit and you won't be allowed to load your saves. A distinction is being made between online and offline saves. This is unacceptable.
The game will slow down for no reason after shooting someone is the head, and so far this unadequate, inelegant "feature" cannot be deactivated. I hope IO patches this.
There are a few bugs here and there. For instance, I had a knocked out character stuck in a wall and I couldn't move him out of sight, it got me spotted and ruined an otherwise perfect run. Alright, probably it was also my fault for forgetting to save my game.
The AI can be exploited, it can be broken, it can feel dumb at times, but really, it still does its job, and overall, the NPCs truly feel alive and convincing. The scripting might need another debugging pass - I saw an (important) character ask for a drink
he had taken it and started drinking on it. I know, I know, it's just a detail, but still, one might expect such things not to happen.
The graphics are pretty. Once again, the Glacier engine delivers. The modeling and the texture works are good, even with the quality set to "medium". Lightning is really beautiful - not groundbreaking, but still - and overall, there is not much to say about it. The design itself appeals a lot to me, with plenty of details that help immersion and make the game feel believable.
I play on Dx11, at 1080p, on the following setup :
Windows 7 x64
GPU : AMD HD7950 3Gb
CPU : Intel Core i7 4970k @ 4GHz
8Gb RAM
And the game runs from a SSD.
I had to put the in-game settings on medium because I had big framerate issues. Sacrificing a few settings - texture quality, detail level, shadow quality, texture filter, AA, etc - didn't render the game much less beautiful. Sadly, it did not improve performance either. Looking at the forums and other reviews, it appears that some people with similar or superior setups are reporting performance issues as well. So, based on that hardware, I should expect a higher performance. Don't get me wrong - it is decent, with 60 fps when the field of view is directed towards the extremity of a level, or when indoors - and it falls to 45 fps when looking at crowds or towards the center of a map. I also notice a slight stuttering when rotating the camera.
I experienced two crashes so far is less than 3 hours of gameplay, once on the very first tutorial mission, another time upon launching the game, as the IO logo was appearing.
The sound design is great. The effects are diverse and a particular attention to detail has been paid in that regard. The voice actor work is, as in previous Hitman games, accomplished with a lot of care.
The music is pleasant to hear and contributes in building a proper Hitman ambience. Niels Bye Nielsen did a great job, even if, I'll admit it, I'll need quite some time to get rid of this sour taste Jesper Kyd's absence is giving me.
This is just the first episode of the "season", so, be warned - it can be finished in just an hour (or less). But that's not how a Hitman game is played. There are tons of contents beyond the completion of the three missions. Achievements, challenges, user-made contracts, elusive targets... Well, that part is the job of Square Enix's PR department, I won't do it. In short, there are a lot of things to do if you like Hitman games. Good enough for this first episode.
Now, I decided not to recommend this game for several reasons : first of all, the use of Denuvo. That's right, they chose to put quite a lot of money into buying a licence for that recent DRM. Yes, that's the one that doesn't want to be called "
". That means money that could have been invested into paying developers to fix above mentioned bugs and performance issues, has instead been redirected to the pockets of the guys who made the StarForce DRM. And if you buy Hitman, you'll get some files coded by these people in your computer. I would rather have nothing to do with that shіt since I bought the game and since it's already protected by Steam's DRM.
Alright, moving on. The episodic format made a lot of people suspicious. Some of said suspicious people decided to trust IO and Square Enix and bought the game. I am among those people.
I do not regret buying it. I'll admit it, I'm having a lot of fun with this Hitman game. However, I cannot help but feeling like "I don't like where this is going".
Being tethered to the servers is not okay. Being plagued with Denuvo is not okay. The bugs and terrible design choices are not okay.

(I've completed this game using the Witch Hunt translation, so everything I say will be coming from that)
Umineko is a visual novel released between 2007 and late 2010 (with these episodes, the Question Arcs, being released in 2007 and 2008). It is a murder mystey/fantasy novel packed with tons of content to keep you on your toes at all times... for the most part.
The story itself is probably one of the best things I've ever read, including all visual novels, regular novels, fiction/non-fiction, etc.. In short, it involves a family going to an island that is only inhabited by the family head and a some other family members. They go there, and they recieve a letter from a mysterious entity calling themselves "Beatrice", saying they must find the gold hidden on the island, or she will be forced to recieve "interest" from them. From then on, strange things happen, and people start questioning their trust for each other, yada yada other murder mystery things.
While the story is amazing, it DOES drag for a bit for the first 4-6 hours, basically the entire first in game day in the first episode. After that though, the story hooks you in and refuses to let go until you've ended up binging the entire episode, and it only leaves you craving more.
One thing I especially love about Umineko is how, even though it has LOTS of them (There are at least 18[!] of them introduced just in the first day of the first episode alone, and there are MANY more introduced later), it uses all its characters efficiently. You're never left feeling some characters are under utilized or under developed. Even though some characters definitely get more development than others (but really, in a cast of so many characters, can you blame them?), even the most under developed character still feels complete.
All in all, Umineko is probably one of the most visual novels, let alone novels, in the past decade. I would 100% recommend it to anyone looking for a good read.

In its opening moments, the reader is introduced to the ailing head of the Ushiromiya family, Kinzo. He is a man in the midst of his final moments. He has lived a long life and in that time has amassed an incredible fortune but he is not without his regrets. Kinzo cries out to the Golden Witch, Beatrice, the witch who lent him the vast Ushiromiya fortune, and proclaims that he will return everything she has given him if he is able to see her once more before he dies. Kinzo’s maddening desire sets into motion a bizarre string of serial murders on the island of Rokkenjima. In the main hall of the Ushiromiya mansion rests a portrait of the Golden Witch, Beatrice, and next to it, an epitaph detailing the location of the key to the Golden Land. The epitaph goes on, detailing a gruesome sacrificial ceremony for resurrecting the witch, and the treasures that will be acquired when the Golden Land is reached. Kinzo’s children believe the one who is able to solve the riddle of the epitaph will inherit not only the witch’s gold but also the headship.
Without giving too much away, the story is gripping and mysterious and will leave you awake at night, thinking about the riddle of the epitaph and the various closed-room murders. Ryukishi07, the author and artist, is a fantastic writer and he breathes life into the story’s characters. An argument could be made for nearly everyone if someone were to say so-and-so was their favorite character in Umineko.
Most people not familiar with Ryukishi07 and his work on Higurashi no Naku Koro Ni and later titles will look at the screenshots on the store and be put off right away. For those people, there’s good news. A team of dedicated fans and programmers, 07th Mod, have taken the time to port the PS3 sprites, backgrounds, and voice work from the PS3 release of the game for use with the Steam release. It’s not quite perfect yet but given a little more time, it will be the definitive way to experience Umineko.
But if you’re a little more open-minded I’d recommend sticking to the original sprites. I love both sets of sprites but I love the original just a little more. Ryukishi07’s facial expressions for his characters are second-to-none and can’t be so easily emulated, despite the improved body proportions of the PS3 sprites.
Lastly, I want to touch on the “new” sprites MangaGamer included in this release of the game. They’re taken from a pachinko game titled Pachi-Slot Umineko no Naku Koro Ni. I’d recommend steering clear of these sprites as they have a low-quality look to them and a few characters in the 4th Episode don’t even have a pachinko equivalent. In these instances, you have the Ryukishi07 sprites onscreen with the pachinko sprites and it looks terribly inconsistent. Characters also lack many of the expressions present in the original and PS3 sprites, making them feel more like cardboard cutouts than characters.
Umineko is (or was at the time of its original Japanese release) considered a sound novel rather than a visual novel due to the minimalistic graphics and the importance of sound in setting atmosphere for scenes. More than the story, more than the riddles, more than the goofy and sometimes horrifying facial expressions, what I love most about Umineko is the music. From its sound effects to the battle themes that play right before a big stand-off, the sound sets the mood for what’s to come.
It’s been nearly two and a half months since I read through the entirety of Umineko. From the time I completed the first Episode, I had every intention of writing a review for this game. I’m the sort of person that loves the idea of visual novels more than actually reading them. Because of this, I’ve amassed quite the collection over the past few years over various platforms. I assumed I’d play Umineko for a few hours at most and then throw it onto my growing pile of incomplete visual novels. That wasn’t the case, as you can see from my total hours played. Every hour was spent engaged in the game in some way, whether it was listening to the music, revisiting favorite scenes, or rereading parts of episodes in an attempt to better understand and attempt to solve mysteries. My final time clocked in at around 90 hours but if you’re just interested in the story alone I’d estimate 70-75 hours for most readers. If you’re a fan of mysteries or just visual novels in general, you owe it to yourself to read through Umineko. It’s as important as any Clannad, Fate/stay night, Muv-Luv, or Steins;Gate. Keep in mind that this is only the first half of the Umineko story. This is the “Question Arc” and the “Answer Arc” will be releasing at a later date.
Even though my time with Umineko may have been brief in the grand scheme of things, it's not a story I'm likely to forget any time soon.

Even though "Before the Storm" wasn't developed by the French studio Dontnod (which did "Life is Strange") anymore but by the American studio Deck Nine (which doesn't really have an impressive portfolio), it's a very well-made successor (well, predecessor story wise). While we're at it, also the voice actor of Chloe was exchanged, but again, this is not as big an issue as it might sound. You might not even notice given that Chloe is quite a bit younger here.
In short, even though the story is not nearly as dark and mysterious as that of the original, the whole mood and emotional depth that made "Life is Strange" so great is still there. Of course, the prequel it's overshadowed by the tragic things we know will happen in the main story which adds a melancholic atmosphere even in the happier moments. Which maybe explains that this game left me somewhat heartbroken again.
It was great to meet Chloe again even though the roles have changed in more than one way. When we played Max and wanted to spare our time with Chloe, she was the one that was fragile and behaved wayward while Max was the calm and reasonable type. Now that we play Chloe and develop a deep friendship with Rachel, Chloe (despite of her still being sad and broken) is the calming influence while Rachel tends to have emotional outbursts. I guess it's not only me who found Chloe to be a much more interesting character than Max. And again, while this whole game is about caring for Rachel, I felt I only did this to help Chloe recover from the losses she endured.
Game play wise, the biggest change is the lack of Max's time rewinding ability. While this was one aspect that made "Life is Strange" very special, "Before the Storm" works surprisingly good without it.
I missed the rewinding mainly for two reasons: firstly, it was the key puzzle element which leads to "Before the Storm" being more or less puzzle free. Secondly, it allowed to check the outcome of different dialog options or actions to let you choose the best one. In "Before the Storm", you'd need to restart from a checkpoint to do the same - which is a bit frustrating in comparison. As some kind of substitute, the developers added a "crosstalk" element which allows you to reach a slightly different outcome by selecting the most appropriate answers under time pressure. Honestly, I never liked the idea of time pressure (specifically in dialogs), especially when mixed with somewhat misleading roundups. In combinations with the lack of retrials, I found this whole game element a little bit annoying. Besides, in the end winning or losing a crosstalk doesn't make much of a difference anyway. I.e. there is no actual story branching resulting from them.
Talking of changes, the optional photos were replaced by graffiti/tags and Max's diary by a collection of (unsent) letters from Chloe to Max. No complaints about that. Ah, and there are no stealth sequences anymore (like the one in the final Episode of LIS).
Technically speaking, there  are issues with tearing at high resolutions if you enable the frame rate limitation. Disabling it diminishes the effect a lot but also causes much higher (and totally unnecessary) GPU load leading to fan noise on high end setups. I can't actually remember if this happened with the 1st part too. After all it was based on the Unreal engine and the prequel is using Unity.
There are also (still) some very lowres textures used here and there and quite a few animations look wooden or awkward. At least the lip sync is better now and IMHO the supporting characters look less cartoonish.
Maybe my memory is playing tricks on me but I also think they screwed up the savegame mechanism of the original. As far as I recall, you could restart a game with a different savegame slot at every checkpoint. Now you can only restart a chapter with a new slot and accessing checkpoint is only available in "collector's mode" after you finished an episode. As a side not, you can only skip dialogs in collector's mode. I mean, you certainly don't want to skip them the 1st time, but when you restart a chapter to check a different outcome, there are probably some things you would like to skip.
Then there's the music which was one of the things that made Life is Strange so special. The good news is that despite of a different development team and a quite different selection of music, the game score is just great. Most of the instrumental tracks (and some songs) were specifically written by the English band Daughter but there's other gorgeous music by bands like Speedy Ortiz, Wolf Alice or Brody Dalle. Actually, "No Below" by Speedy Ortiz doesn't only perfectly fit the story but is just a terrific song by itself (as was Obstacles in LIS). It's just a shame that there's no MP3 soundtrack even in the Deluxe Edition and the "Mixtape Mode" is a somewhat lame excuse for that.
All in all, I guess there's no doubt that everybody who loved "Life is Strange" won't want miss "Before the Storm". Letting aside some technical issues, it's probably the best predecessor you could have hoped for.
For everybody else, it's somewhat hard do describe how unique both games are. I couldn't tell any other game which feels like moving around in a (concept art) picture or which causes the same empathy and emotions.
Above the very good voice acting and cinematic cut scenes, the specific look, very good use of lighting and gorgeous music create an unparalleled atmosphere. Plus it's like the ideal combination of adventure and interactive movie in the best possible sense. The comparison with Telltale games doesn't do the LIS games any justice. The only thing that comes somewhat close to it, IMHO is "Dreamfall Chapters" which is bigger, better in about every technically aspect, has more real adventure elements but isn't nearly as moving.

Life is Stange: Before the Storm is hte the prequel to the original Life is Strange, but playing the prequel before the orignal isn't just possible, I would strongly recommend it if you haven't played the original. If you already played the original and liked it, I am pretty sure you will like this one.
Story:
Definitely the main focus of the game, as such it is quite good, even tho the last episode felt a bit rushed. I never felt bored and always was eager to find out what would happen next. Still, the story of the original definitely had more tension to it.
If you don't absolutely despise stories about friend- and relationships you will surely like it. I also quite like how the game shows a different perspective of already known characters and how it explains the attitude and behaviour of Chloe in the original.
9/10
Characters:
Absolutely incredible. I can't remember when I felt more atached to characters than in this game.  Almost no character is just a flat stereotype, everyone is on some level relatable. Especially the main character Chloe is extremely relatable and sympathetic.
10/10
Voice Acting:
The new voice actor for Chloe does a really good job, if I hadn't known it was a new one, I maybe  wouldn't even have noticed a difference. All the other voice actors all do a pretty good job and are convincing, nothing to really criticise here
9/10
Dialogue and Writing:
The overall writing is really good, dialogues are interesting and engaging. Some dialogues are even pretty funny. The diary Chloe keeps is interesting to read in comparison to the one in the orignal, which I found not that interesting and fun to read.
9.5/10
Animation:
In such a story-driven game with many cutscenes animation is quite important. The animation in this game is definitely a step up in comparison to the original, but it still isn't great. At least it isn't distractingly bad as in the original, where facial animation looked pretty lifeless and robotic and other animation clunky. Now it is on a level where facial animation looks pasable and other animation looks still a bit clunky and robotic, but less than in the original.
6/10

Gameplay:
Well in this category the game is definitely lacking, even in comparison to the orignal, which itself wasn't known for its amazing gameplay. But atleast the orignal had its rewind machanic, which came into use in dialogue and a few puzzles.
This game only has its "Backtalk" mechanic, in which you have to choose the right dialogue answer in set amount of time. The mechanic is definitely fitting for the character and it is fun, but otherwise you only walk around, look at things and talk. I personaly don't mind this absense of any mayor gameplay, as the very good story makes up for it, but a bit more gameplay could have been nice. If the origal already had too shallow gameplay for you, you will probably be also disappointed with this game.
4/10
Graphics and Technical Stuff:
The drawn looking art style is a perfect fit for the game an looks very good. It is a bit more refined than in the original, where some objects looked a bit weird. Through the artstyle the game gets away very reasonably taxing graphics, which still look very good. With my RX 480 I experienced a steady framerate with no real dips. Bug-wise the game is very polished, I experienced only one bug, which wasn't mayor and didn't influenced the esperinece at all. In comparison in the original I had bugs on multiple occasions and had to reload one time.
But know to a real complaint: WHERE IS VSYNC ? The tearing that resulted in a lack there of was really annoying and ugly.
7/10

The game Rougue Legacy is a unique twist on the classic rouglike dungeon exploration rpg. The games unique mechanics, as well as it's overall high and proffesional quality would lead me to recomend Rouge Legacy to anyone without question. The game can be difficult, but in most cases is fair about it.
*Gameplay Mechanics: 9/10
The controls are a little wonky, and take a bit to get used to. My favorite part of Rougue Legacy however, is it's unique twist on the classic rougelike rpg. Once your character dies, you are able to choose a heir (each with their own unique shortcomings) and continue the game with a newly randomized dungeon. The game can be difficult, but it fits with the game and the type of game it is.
*Music: 3.5/5
While the music isn't that memorable, it is still catchy and of good quality.
*Story: -/10
I didn't pay much attention to the games story, as Rougue Legacy seems to focus more on the gameplay aspects. There is a story, however I feel the game would still be enjoyable without it. Becuase of this, I chose not to rate the story.
*Characters: 8/10
Most characters in the game are either merchants or enemies, and are mostly forgettable (besides Charon, whom steals all your money before re-entering the dungeon). The characters whom are player controlled, while all being unique and memorable, will most likely die before you can get attached to them.
*Level Design: 8/10
I like the overall level designs of the areas. Although random, the rooms seem to flow together and are fun to explore. Some areas, however, seemed somewhat unfair, leading to my character's death. These where far and few between however, and don't mess up the overall experience of the game, besides a few frustrating moments.
*Art: 5/5
I really like the art throughout Rougue Legacy. It is of high quality, matches with the game fantastically, and looks amazing as well.
*Total Score:
33.5/40 or an 83.8/100
If you're looking for a game with crisp controls and decent combat, look away.

If you are somebody that enjoys simulation/resource management/survival, then this game is for you. It can be relatively simple, but can get extremely complicated if you want it to. Very fun, and expansive. So much to do, and so many resources to manage. Played it for 5 hours the very first time I loaded it up.

This game reminds me of the Martian. You solve one problem... and you solve the next one... and then the next. And If you solve enough problems...well...
You might not get to go home but you could certainly survive for a very long time.
It seems Klei have done it again with a great survival simulator. The game is a lot of fun and it combines strategy, survival, exploration and creativity while taking inspiration from real science.
Problems arise organically and it's up to you to work out how best to solve them. Sometimes solving a problem leads to other problems. Sometimes everything seems to be fine until 50 cycles later when you start noticing something that you should have started working on 20 cycles ago.
If you're effective and efficient at dealing with these situations, you're colony will get to keep on living and being happy. Get it wrong, and things start to unravel. Keep getting it wrong and things will start to spiral out of control to the point where you know there's only a few more days before everyone dies.
And then you start from scratch and do it all over again.
It's absolutely brilliant!
Very addictive and well made game. Very unique game play, good design, and never the same play. Big thanks for the developers.

AI needs some work.
Frustratingly hard when you try and play the game how you want to play it.
Easy when you play the game the way its meant to be.
Potential bugs/issues:
A balance between playability and optimization needs to be tweaked, if possible. Duplicants will not readily do work outside of your view. You need to move view to tasks to get them prioritized. For example, my base has gotten quite sprawling. I am working on the far east, but my crops are central within my base, and westward. I generally start to run out of food and get food shortages, even though I have dozens upon dozens of crops. If I pause and move to crops, it will generally show them as not ready. When unpausing, they'll update and become harvest ready, and my duplicants will swarm to harvest.
Duplicates carry a max of 1000g of spilled / cried water. Duplicates will prioritize grabbing thin water at 1000g at a time to deliver rather than absorbing 150kg from tank.
If you mop up spilled / cried water while a duplicate is grabbing from that source, the water disapears and can no longer be mopped. However, duplicates will still grab water from the same spot, 1000g at a time. Reloading will fix. Possibly something to do with pore water? Does water move through single-tile thickness?
Priority. Duplicants with deliver tasks will prioritize delivering materials to qued construction tasks rather than other deliver tasks, when priorities are the same. Duplicants will more-or-less totally ignore my coal generators until EVERYTHING else is done. Incredibly infuriating. Power priorities should be tweaked. Duplicants will prioritize fertilizing plants instead of other deliver tasks, however turning priority down on plants (from 9 to 8) leads plants to generally be totally ignored.
More on priority. Had a dupe to dig and build. Had several buildings slated as a "9". For whatever reason they chose to dig sub-9. Another dupe was fixated on building a base-block (8) instead of digging the 9's and building the 9's I've got set-up for him to specifically do. Nothing is in his way; nothing is out of reach. Had to cancel everything else to them to focus on what I really wanted to build. This seems to be a bug arising from setting up lots of qued tasks, and switching their priorities around on the fly.
Frustrations:
Upscaling is not simple.
Food management. Something to auto-stop food making after a certain food limit (set by user) is reached. At the moment juggling priority with cooking stations / deselecting cook profession is all that is available, leading to walking a fine-line between food shortage and rotten food.
Duplicate Stupidity:
If you have slated something to be built on a tile, but there is un-mined material on that tile, the dupe will do nothing but idle if digging is not one of his assigned tasks. A little smarter duplicate would be nice; something that allows him to do another task that is not necesarily on his job list, if it lets him get something done that is on his list, on that same tile.
If a large area is selected to be deconstructed, duplicates will prioritize tiles over the buildings resting on them, leaving themselves / objects stranded. Not really an issue, since the fix is simply going in, blanket deconstruct priority low, manually changing buildings higher. But seems an inconveniance when the base priority could be flipped.
Duplicates acting out from frustration (the sub-100 meltdown) seems to clear their task/job, and drop any carried items. Afterwards they resume their task, however rather than picking up the recently dropped item, they'll go all the way across the map to the original source area.
It seems the material they grab for tasks is someetimes badly selected. Several times I've noticed duplicates running all the way across the map to another dig section to source raw material for building, when available raw material of the correct type is littered all over from recent digs. Might be an issue with having build qued before exposing the new material.
All things considered, its good, and will likely only get better.

I think it is a crying shame that the episodic nature of HITMAN has been the focal point when discussing the game, and to see it colouring people's perception in regards to the quality and quantity of what is on offer here is incredibly sad, given how much more there is to talk about.
In terms of atmosphere, ambience, scale and sense of immersion, the opening Paris chapter is a classic slab of Hitman and a true assassination sandbox. It's exactly what fans of the franchise have been asking for after Absolution's more linear, narrative driven approach. We're given an an overwhelmingly large sandbox map, a couple of targets to kill, some useful hints and thent sent on our merry way. The Showstopper is a mission with more ways to approach and complete it than you can shake a stick at. The more you play, the more tools you unlock for use in future replays - Replay value has always been very important for a HITMAN game and this is no different.
I'm also enjoying the compromise that comes with choosing your loadout - You can't have every useful tool at once, which adds replay value but also makes you carefully consider your tools. If you want the coin and the fibre wire, that means you have to forfeit the lockpick - But you still get the option of brute-forcing a door open with a crowbar found in the level. It's a really, really good balance.
That said, my hunger pangs for Hitman aren't wholly satisfied like they would be with a full retail release, and without additional levels to get stuck into after Paris, the achievements, challenges and opportunities do feel more like padding than they otherwise would- But this opening chapter has left me incredibly happy and excited as a hardcore Hitman fan since 2000.
This isn't the main course, this is just the starter - an incredibly tasty one. Consider my appetite whet!

It feels good. Controlling 47 is once again comfortable, precise and empowering. IO had the decency to allow for all the in-game assistances to be deactivated (I did keep the icons indicating which enemies can be suspicious). Overall, there are tons of good ideas, and an undeniable attention to detail. You feel free to explore and tackle the objectives how you see fit. By now most people might already know what big changes have been made since Absolution, like the revamped disguise system and the sandbox-ish open levels, so I won't say anything about this. These latter had been promised, they're here, there's nothing to complain about.
I'll seize the opportunity to briefly mention the story: while we are just given a little glimpse at it, it does seem well-crafted and interesting. The prologue/tutorial takes place at the beginning of 47's career, when he first joined the ICA. The Paris level - and the rest of the game after that - takes place a few years after Hitman Absolution (without direct link to said episode, like a new start, a clean slate, in order for us to better appreciate the experience of playing as 47 when he does what he does best).
Each destination will have its own ambience and each target, his background story. An overarching story ties it all together, and the balance is perfect : it is there, it is interesting, and it manages not to feel too intrusive.
Nevertheless, some design choices do manage to ruin the fun for me : the game requires you to be online. Should you be disconnected from the servers, the game will quit and you won't be allowed to load your saves. A distinction is being made between online and offline saves. This is unacceptable.
The game will slow down for no reason after shooting someone is the head, and so far this unadequate, inelegant "feature" cannot be deactivated. I hope IO patches this.
There are a few bugs here and there. For instance, I had a knocked out character stuck in a wall and I couldn't move him out of sight, it got me spotted and ruined an otherwise perfect run. Alright, probably it was also my fault for forgetting to save my game.
The AI can be exploited, it can be broken, it can feel dumb at times, but really, it still does its job, and overall, the NPCs truly feel alive and convincing. The scripting might need another debugging pass - I saw an (important) character ask for a drink
he had taken it and started drinking on it. I know, I know, it's just a detail, but still, one might expect such things not to happen.
The graphics are pretty. Once again, the Glacier engine delivers. The modeling and the texture works are good, even with the quality set to "medium". Lightning is really beautiful - not groundbreaking, but still - and overall, there is not much to say about it. The design itself appeals a lot to me, with plenty of details that help immersion and make the game feel believable.
I play on Dx11, at 1080p, on the following setup :
Windows 7 x64
GPU : AMD HD7950 3Gb
CPU : Intel Core i7 4970k @ 4GHz
8Gb RAM
And the game runs from a SSD.
I had to put the in-game settings on medium because I had big framerate issues. Sacrificing a few settings - texture quality, detail level, shadow quality, texture filter, AA, etc - didn't render the game much less beautiful. Sadly, it did not improve performance either. Looking at the forums and other reviews, it appears that some people with similar or superior setups are reporting performance issues as well. So, based on that hardware, I should expect a higher performance. Don't get me wrong - it is decent, with 60 fps when the field of view is directed towards the extremity of a level, or when indoors - and it falls to 45 fps when looking at crowds or towards the center of a map. I also notice a slight stuttering when rotating the camera.
I experienced two crashes so far is less than 3 hours of gameplay, once on the very first tutorial mission, another time upon launching the game, as the IO logo was appearing.
The sound design is great. The effects are diverse and a particular attention to detail has been paid in that regard. The voice actor work is, as in previous Hitman games, accomplished with a lot of care.
The music is pleasant to hear and contributes in building a proper Hitman ambience. Niels Bye Nielsen did a great job, even if, I'll admit it, I'll need quite some time to get rid of this sour taste Jesper Kyd's absence is giving me.
This is just the first episode of the "season", so, be warned - it can be finished in just an hour (or less). But that's not how a Hitman game is played. There are tons of contents beyond the completion of the three missions. Achievements, challenges, user-made contracts, elusive targets... Well, that part is the job of Square Enix's PR department, I won't do it. In short, there are a lot of things to do if you like Hitman games. Good enough for this first episode.
Now, I decided not to recommend this game for several reasons : first of all, the use of Denuvo. That's right, they chose to put quite a lot of money into buying a licence for that recent DRM. Yes, that's the one that doesn't want to be called "
". That means money that could have been invested into paying developers to fix above mentioned bugs and performance issues, has instead been redirected to the pockets of the guys who made the StarForce DRM. And if you buy Hitman, you'll get some files coded by these people in your computer. I would rather have nothing to do with that shіt since I bought the game and since it's already protected by Steam's DRM.
Alright, moving on. The episodic format made a lot of people suspicious. Some of said suspicious people decided to trust IO and Square Enix and bought the game. I am among those people.
I do not regret buying it. I'll admit it, I'm having a lot of fun with this Hitman game. However, I cannot help but feeling like "I don't like where this is going".
Being tethered to the servers is not okay. Being plagued with Denuvo is not okay. The bugs and terrible design choices are not okay.

Grouping them together for ship sides is a good idea, but it would be good to have access to all single individual mounts anyway, also showing where they are on the ship, Star Wolves style (since they avoid fireing THROUGH the ship, which is as unexpected as it is brilliant), for enabling a more tactical loadout.

In general, a good game even at this stage, just needs tweak and a good plot implemented. The latter would make a good game a great game.

RUST
Do I have a lot to say for this game. Lets begin with a summary of what my review is going to include, I will be covering 5 aspects of this game and ratting them on a scale of 0-5. Closer to the end of my review I will include my personal opinion, what made me buy this game, and what I dislike about it and what I want in the game to be added.
GRAPHICS: 4/5
The graphics of this game are quite georgous. From the reflections of the water to most of the textures this game is with no question, one of the best looking games I played. Now, some people will say I am over exadurating, but I'm really not. The look of this game will appeal to most people who have played First Person games before. Using a 1050ti I was able to put this game on the highest settings, and run it at around 60 fps most of the time.
Here are my specs:
I5 6600k 3.5 GHz
MSI GTX 1050 TI
16 Gigabytes Of DDR4
SERVERS - 5/5
This all depends on where you live; but I had no trouble what so ever finding a server. I never experienced any server lag while playing on this game. But do take this with a grain of salt because not all servers are official servers and it will always depend on your Internet connection. There are many different types of servers to choose from, there are free for all servers where you can spawn in with a few weapons and instantly jump into a fight. These can get quite chaotic, but some people will enjoy this madness. There are also servers that split people into 2 teams sending them to fight each other until either team is killed. And there are tons of regular rust servers, you spawn in, gather supplies, build a base, and etc. But to sum it up, for most people there is always something to do.
GAMEPLAY - 2/5
Gun shots everywhere, arrows flying, explosions roaring. This is what you might imagine Rust to be like, and so did I. But most of the time I ended up being killed by someone hitting me to death with a rock, or just being killed with a spier. This might not be the case for everyone, if you have maybe ten friends or more you can build a base in a few hours and there are no worries if you die because you can just run back and pickup some extra loot that you have stored. When your ready to fight or your friends are you would search for a base near you and raid the loot thats left in hope of getting something good. But when you and your friends wake up the next morning and jump on Rust to find that your base has been raided, it's not a pleasant experience. But playing this game alone is painfuly hard, there will always be people who will troll you, trick you, or just try hard in general. And most of the time I spent in this game was looking at the beach, where I spawned.
COMMUNITY - 2/5
Piggybacking off of my last aspect, this one is almost as equally bad. Now, don't get offended for reading this, because it's not you that I'm talking about; it's the people who have given me this experience. One word can sum up the people I have met; TOXIC. I have only been able to properly talk and maybe friend one person while playing this game (hats off to you.) Everyone that I have attempted to befriend, try to talk to or get to know has back stabbed me or trolled me. There are a lot of games that I have started to play and enjoy just because of how friendly people were. But whenever I was in a server and needed help with controls or basics of the game someone would either say KYS or laugh. Only %10 of the time I got a legit response which is quite sad because some of you need to grow up. Maybe if more people tried to be inviting to new players or at least nice I would have enjoyed the game a little more.
DEVELOPMENT - 3.75/5
I would have given a higher score but there is one thing that bothers me the most, Early Access. I can not explain to you enough how long this game has not been officially published. And don't get me started on the amount of glitches this game has, it's mind blowing really. I see a few patches coming out here and there every once in a while which I'm fine with and I support beIause it shows that the developers did not completely run off with my money and still support the game.
So why did I buy this game in the first place? A few reasons actually, I was about to build my PC and move on from my laptop so I wanted something to play when I finished so I picked this up and GTA V. But what really made me want to get the game were the insane youtube videos of people building huge hotels, mansions, and bases. The insane and intensive raids and also the funny moments. It looked fun until I got the game and realised the amount of grinding I needed to do to achieve that. And the toxicty brought me to the last straw making me write this review. So don't think you will be able to achieve all of that, maybe with some help of friends you will be able to do it. But if you do decide on achieving these things, good luck getting sleep. What I would have liked to be added into this game is a single player mode, with more enemies maybe NPCs that would try to go after you and kill you. Maybe something thats a less pain in the♥♥♥♥♥
My final score for this game is 12.75/20 giving it a %63.75 percent.
But the final question, should you buy this game? Do you love being a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥? Are you up to face the grindiest game of them all? Then this game is for you. But on a serious note, if you think you might enjoy this game, pick it up on sale for $10. You might enjoy it more than I did.
Thanks for reading!

Umineko is without a doubt one of the greatest visual novels I have ever played. Although the gameplay is minimal (there are no choices) the story and characters more than make up for it. If you enjoy murder mysteries which constantly keep you guessing and force you to wrack your brain for the answers, you'll want to play Umineko. If you enjoy horror games which send chills up your spine while playing at night, you'll want to play Umineko. If you enjoy fantasy stories about battles between magical beings, you'll want to read Umineko. The story is so intricate and full of depth, you're bound to like it, and you'll keep coming back to it again and again. The only drawback, which you may notice at first, is that the story has kind of a slow beginning -- but if you just give it some time to get started, you will be in for one wild ride.
I first played the game years ago when it first came out, but I'm really happy with the changes made for the Steam re-release. Personally, I liked the old sprites, but the ability to switch to the new sprites is a good alternative. I also really like the fact that you can switch between English and Japanese text instantly.
Lastly but certainly not least, Umineko's soundtrack is pretty amazing. Every song is memorable and properly conveys the mood of each scene. Even the lack of music, replaced by the sounds of wind or rain, does a fantastic job of immersing the reader into the story.
So in summary, if you're into those kinds of stories and visual novel kind of games, Umineko is an extremely worthwhile (and sometimes life-changing) experience, and I would recommend it to anybody who is willing to give it a read.

To be fair, I'll start this review by listing what I percieve this novel's flaws to be. It suffers from a few factors caused by its low initial budget, namely some weak sound effects and low resolution backgrounds. And, this coming from a major fan of the author, there is definitely some hammy writing in places, although some of this may be intentional. The new character sprites are good for the most part, but most of the women are unnaturally well-endowed and several characters' lines are a bit too sharp, but this will eventually be moddable to use the PS3 port's sprites in addition to the original and newest sets. Finally, there are a few moments that suffer from absolutely crippling pacing issues, especially in chapter 4.
And yet, I wholeheartedly recommend this novel/game to anyone who thinks they can stand Ryukishi's occasional weirdness. Why? Because when the game is on and things are moving along, it's one of the most engrossing works of fiction I've ever experienced. Battles of twisted logic and brutal murder, supernatural closed room mysteries, some seriously powerful emotional scenes, and the moments when a random background detail reveals an incredible amount of depth to a character all make Umineko such a great ride at its high moments. Topping this off is the soundtrack, which is absolutely superb. The tracks have a good amount of variety considering how long this novel is, and they are a huge factor in why it's so capable of creating atmospheres of mystery, tension, horror, and whimsy so effectively. While it's certainly not perfect, Umineko is the kind of niche classic that is definitely worth looking into.

War of the Human Tanks is a game I really really really wanted to like. Seriously, it's awesome! However, a few things really killed my interest in continuing this game any further than I did.
First, the game really shines in the story and character development department. It had me completely interested from the get-go. The story centers around a war between two empires using human tanks. They're pretty much just machines that look like humans. They are fully at the command of the leaders to live and die in battle, despite their human appearances. You play as the army unit that's just been released from a 'frozen state' to help take back critical objectives. A bunch of ... oddballs that are completely hilarious!! haha.
The music in this game? AMAZING. You can hear some of it in the trailer above. I really enjoyed what i heard throughout my time with the game. The art works well enough too! More of an anime-ish look to everything.
However, the gameplay is where I really struggles to enjoy this game to the fullest. You run around on hexagonal tile sets, where fog of war really rules the surrounding area. Think of a game of battleship, where you fire into unknown areas and hope to hit something. Everything in this game dies in one hit. It works well enough but your units only move a couple of spaces at a time so it feels really slow. Then on top of that, you have a strict time limit, so if your RNG is bad ... you run out of time and fail the mission. Honestly, it happened more times than I would have liked and I grew frustrated with it before long.
I still recommend playing this game because you might not mind the gameplay as much as i did! It's an excellent little indie game that I got on sale for $3 and still managed to get about 3 hours of game time in.

In my Opinion "Umineko no Naku Koro ni" (or [more or less] translated in english "When The Seagulls Cry") is on par if not better than most of literature I've read over the years, and I've read a lot.
This might sound a bit strange, some might say, isn't this supposed to be a game, some might say. Don't worry little fella' Uineko in deed qualifies as a game. Though not in the traditional sense of a video game. Umineko is a so-called "Sound Novel" by developer "ryukishi07". Their work (In the english realm known as the "When They Cry" series) focuses on mystery/"fantasy" novels with fitting and emotional BGS/BGM. Their games(novels) thereby have overarcing plots, though in a rather unconditonally way that the scenery and main plot more or less stays the same but the course of actions throughout the plot change from game to game.
With this rather unique way of telling a story, the games are definitely not for everyone, though I'd recommend buying the first Chapter of "Higurashi" to get a insight about the writing style. Up to date I think it's a perfect start to the series though it has a tough start.
Same goes for Umineko. A lot of the intriguing plot point and turn of events come from episode 2 ongoing though nothing will be understand if the first chapter isn't played. Even then this series isn't solved in this game. This collection contains the first 4 out of 8 novels in the Umineko-Series (Also shown by the Tag "Question Arc" in the title). Therefore the mystery is shown and tried to explained at some points though this half is the mere start into the mystery rather than giving any real proof to substain any evidence.
But! even if this migt sound to some as a negative point, it definitely isn't. The emotions portrait in the stories of each arc are one of the kind to me. I might have a soft spot for neglection and brutal acts in books and stories but in my opinion Umineko tops it all, sourrounded by a perfect mystery that let's you guess through the whole 60-80 hours one might need to read through the four chapters.
I probably rambled quite a bit without giving any real information if someone might buy this or not. So
If you want a superb story with extremly well-written characters built around a unconventional mystery-story buy Umineko. It seriously is worth it. Though if you search something where you need to act on the game board rather than being forced to think outside of the games bounds than this shouldn't be your first pick.
Ths story is interesting to read but still, it won't help you when you hate reading.

TL;DR version: The game is fantastic, and slightly depressing. Great story, good enough gameplay. And now for the particulars.
Spec Ops: The Line is a big question mark for the military shooter genre, disguised as a 3rd Person Shooter. The major point of the game is the story, the journey of three Delta Force operatives within the doomed city of Dubai. The focus is on the progression and the change of the characters and the world that turns more and more surreal and a mirror of the madness you descend into.
You start the game as you would a lot others, shooting mostly arab-looking opponents, running and gunning into the outskirts of Dubai... but you will certainly not finish the game as you would most others. The twists and turns of who is the actual opponent is a very nice thing, morality gets murky very quickly and some of the intel you find will make you think a lot about your enemy (very nice format to introduce collectibles into a serious game). The only fixed point in the swirling madness you walk into is the main character's certainty that he is doing the right thing. You be the judge if that is the case....
Some of the most striking bits about this game are the visuals and the sound. It isn't the most technically impressive title, even considering its age, but the way the sand-filled city of Dubai is presented to you is simply stunning. A very important thing is that the visuals will evolve together with the story and the characters: in the beginning the world is what you would think it is, bleak desert, with some remnants of civilization hanging around, but as you advance into the Heart of Darkness, the landscape will change accordingly. Inside the crumbling towers you will find the luxury mixing with brutality, surreal scenes painted with lots of colors, contrasting very sharply against the state of mind of the characters.
The visual transformation of your character and your squadmates is equally impressive and important in driving home the messages of the story. You start out as proper looking soldiers coming to the rescue, but by the end of the game you will look like demons murdering dozens upon dozens of soldiers... and then the game will ask you: "How many Americans have you killed today." And you might feel an urge to put down the controller/mouse and walk away from the game at that point... it is one of the possible endings, refusing to finish the game.
The sound and voice acting evolves similarly. In the beginning of the team your small team of Delta operatives behaves and talks like you would expect from elite soldiers. Your opponents and the world around you also sound proper. But there is a very subtle change happening to all these things along the game. Your orders go from the likes of the calm "focus fire on my target" command to bellowing furiously toward you comrade: "I want him dead", and your squadmates will respond in the same way, from professional acknowledgment to a disturbingly savage war-cry.
The genius in all this evolution is that it happens almost unseen, and the atmosphere of the game is so powerful that you won't always notice the changes as they happen. You will just be surprised at some point of the game that... wait.... when did we start shouting obscenities at out enemies and each other? Why the hell did I just execute a wounded US soldier with utmost brutality? Why did I just gun down that civilian?
The "tooltip" messages that pop up on loading screens will also change... at first they will be actual tooltips, but as the madness progresses those messages will turn increasingly more intimidating ("Do you feel like a hero yet?" "If you were a better person, you wouldn't be here."), rubbing the salt even deeper.
That fact that the changes are subtle but powerful is the whole point of the game, as is the fact that it is very good at sucking you into its world and making you miss all these little details when it would still matter.
Gameplay-wise, Spec Ops: The Line is good enough to carry the story. The TPS shooting mechanics are a bit stiff, aiming  isn't as smooth as it could be... but combat is gritty and action-packed enough to be entertaining on most difficulty levels. For the best experience I would recommend Combat Op or Suicide Mission difficulty depending on your skill. These can make the combat challenging enough that the whole "war is brutal" message isn't lost, but not as unforgiving that the combat would blur out the message of the experience. The tactical part of the game is very shallow, you can command you squadmates to attack a target you choose, heal each other, and occasionally to do a specific action (stun, flush). It is very barebones, and the AI isn't particularly bright either, but it is good enough.
"Good enough" is the staple of Spec Ops: The Line's actual gameplay mechanics. It isn't really good, not very memorable in itself, but not bad either.
I do have one major problem with this game however: what the bloody hell are "Kill x amount of people with y gun" kind of achievements doing in this game? Who's genius idea was that load of steaming something? Actually why are there even achievements for this game? That seems to be completely against the spirit of the game...

I'm recommending this mainly for the story. While the initial antagonist is somewhat lucklaster, the main character and other supporting characters I found very relatable and engaging. The concept of human tanks and the story behind them while unfurls as the game progresses.
The gameplay was interesting enough and the ratio of fights vs. cutscenes was more than enough to keep me wanting to reach the next chapter and find out more.
Just to clarify, the story here is not deep and rich - this is no game of Thrones. It's a relatively simple game with a relatively simple premise. But if it is something that you connect with, you may find like me that this was a very satisfying experience. Even an emotional one, as much as I feel embarrassed saying it.
As for the rest of the game:
Cons:
- repeated cutscenes between chapters are somewhat annoying
- Strategy lacks some versatality. Predictable tactics by the AI result in somewhat dissapointing replay value.
Pros:
- Interesting if limited soundtrack
- Cute character designs gave me a desire to cherish my units. Contrasting with the fact that right from the start one of your units is a living bomb creates a tension that I found very enjoyable throughout the game.
All in all, if a story about human tanks, and a game involving simple turn-based, grid-based chibi tank combat appeals to you, buy this game. If it doesn't, try something else ^^. Here's to hoping that someone else has a great experience like me though!

Do you know this feeling when there are two voices in your head arguing over what is the right thing to do and it makes you extremely uncomfortable? It's called cognitive dissonance and Spec Ops: The Line makes you take a nosedive into a sea of that feeling.
It shows war as what it is. Not as the glorified, heroic, romanticized ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t that we get stuffed with from games like Call of Duty and Battlefield, but as horror, pure, unfiltered horror. If you felt like the moral choices in games like Fallout punched you in the gut, what you'll have to do in Spec Ops will leave you feel like the game punched you in the face, wrenched open your jaw, reached down your throat and ripped out your guts.
Spec Ops makes the player feel what the main character is going through, but not simply via making you identify with the character you play. Its gameplay, world design and everything makes you feel uncomfortable, nauseous and morally torn apart. It really is brilliantly crafted.
I'll stop here to avoid possible spoilers or how you perceive the game while playing, but if you feel like dropping the game after playing for an hour because the combat feels generic and/or bad, please, please don't do that and press on, it's well worth it.
There's one last thing I'll say, if you decide to play it: When you hear the line "Because you wanted to be something you're not.", that's aimed at you, not the character you're playing.

It's like those side scrolling motorcycle games, but in 3D and with cars. Forget the single player campaign, it's about multiplayer and its thousands of user built tracks and servers with 50 people on it playing crazy maps.
The game's low user score indicates that it is a divisive niche game: either you like full contact racing or single player (in which case avoid this like the plague) or you want a track editor or a lively multiplayer community (what are you waiting for?). There is one issue: it is essentially a HD remake of the old Trackmania Nations, which was (and still is) free. However, $10 is NOT too much for this game. Many people have played Nations for years it really is that deep if you're into what it offers.
The other issue is that developers Nadeo have lost their marbles and are trying to push their horrible Maniaplanet platform which forces you to download patches for games you don't own and makes it all too obvious that every -mania title is the exact same game with a different car (or robots with guns in the case of Shootmania) and different tileset..
For good or bad, Nadeo are a unique studio, but objectively speaking this is an amazing game. Didn't we all wish we could climb into our slot cars as a child and drive them around wacky tracks with loops and compete against tens of other drivers? Here's a version for grown ups. Enjoy!
