This game was designed to be a carefree entertainment for a few friends. Level up a bit, enter a bland, randomly generated map to fire away at some ships until you get bored of it - fun level equivalent to shooting blanks into the sky for the sake of hearing gunfire.
Pros: The game is simplistic, intuitive, user-friendly and has just about nothing negative, punishing or challenging to it that will stress you out - besides it's repetitive and limited nature. In that sense it's a great way to relax and have some fun.
Cons: The game gets extremely boring and tedious quickly, especially once you reach level 100 and have nothing to spend your talent points on. There is no difference between being lvl100 or 750, it's just a meaningless, slow grind which can be done much faster in solo mode than multiplayer - so you've got most of the regular players sitting in their separate games, grinding by repetitively destroying towers in a small area and such (a lot fun).
Content is unorganized and doesn't scale in quality with the levels. There are several types of instances but their differences and relevance to the game are minimal. Once you get the first dozen levels and can enter all of the instances, they don't change whatsoever from that point onward - so don't expect to find new, creative and challenging content as you gain experience.
Multiplayer starts and ends with having a couple of friends doing an instance together. There is no grand scale player content nor does the game encourage PvP - any regions you conquer on a MP server can easily be retaken without a fight by creating embassies (only one faction is immune to this tactic), which makes fighting over regions a futile endeavor. Not to mention killing enemy players doesn't accomplish anything and even if you do it just because naval combat is somewhat fun, you've always got the flying ships and air crafts which completely remove naval combat and its mechanics out of the picture as well as strategical relevance of the map's landscape.
The trading system comes down to buying single units of cargo (you can carry five at most), so you never get that feeling of grand scale trading.1
There's more to dislike about this game, but the above should be enough to help you form a picture about it. All in all this could've been a great game because the interface is very user-friendly, but the low expectations set by its creator and his lack of knowledge in creating multiplayer content has made it a bland experience, like a Hubba Bubba chewing gum it's good for a brief moment and then all its flavor is gone.

Enjoyable as a "simulation-business-type" game.  Not sure where it fits "morally" considering the "prison culture" we currently live in.  I can't play the game without making the connections to our society and popular culture.  I'm constantly reminded of Shawshank Redemption, and I suppose if I got to the point of building a "death-row" I would start pondering The Green Mile (or some other Stephen King book-to-movie adaption).
Initially my reaction to the game itself, before I played it, was that it was a bit on the morbid and/or macabre-side.  However, after some time playing the game and falling victim to the glee that comes with bringing about "order" and setting down harsh rules to punish those who oppose my will, I can see this game as just as much a commentary on our culture as it is a "gamification" of a necessary, but tragically imperfect component of our society.
As an aside, after I came to this realization, I found it sort of lame that this game is an artsy graphics overhaul and a few "thoughtful" prose (with maybe some "clever" marketing thrown in) short of being lauded as a "masterpiece" rather than what I initially took it for, a "low-brow and vulgar black comedy."
All in all, I enjoyed playing the game, it runs smooth, it's satisfying to build a working machine (and occasionally watching it implode), but I don't see it having much long lasting appeal for me other than as an occasional diversion.  From a more emotional point of view, I'm glad I played it and I felt like it expanded my mind in a way that merely watching a documentary or listening to a news story could not have accomplished by itself.

Basically, Prison Architect is a game about building and managing of your prison, but it becomes more complex than that.
Want more profit? Then you will need more prisoners, but the guards are expensive, and you need a lot of staff to control your prison. In addition, more prisoners also means an increase in the relentless flow of contraband that inmates try to sneak by. If you are not careful to control this, then someone may be stabbed in the back, which undermines your daily bonus.
Reform programs exist to try to control your prisoners, but these cost money and inmates are not guaranteed to pass these courses. However, if they pass, they may be able to work for you and generate additional profits.
It is a vicious circle and finding the perfect balance is not easy. Every prisoner who joined yours jail comes with new challenges. If you fail, then its game over or worse, you could be arrested and sent to your own prison.
I highly recommend this game. It is challenging and fun.

So far there doesn't seem to be much of a story. Spoiler alert: it's literally about a man fixing up his car. The beginning touched on his former family as well as a rivalry with some guy but then that was just sort of it... You run around playing a stereotypically douchey male that can shoot a shotgun one-handed in an effort to appear 'cool'.
I just personally didn't find it very interesting. There wasn't much to do other than driving around doing main missions or the occasional search for scrap metal. One section of the game involved your companion's home being attacked. You're told that you can't take them on so you may as well leave. Not only is it extremely predictable that you'll take the dog in, but your friend urges you to immediately help him, claiming the dog will die very soon without help. The dog doesn't get help for ages, even a few missions later once you've settled into a 'home'. Despite lack of treatment, the dog remains fine even though it is stressed early on that he needs immediate medical care.
I guess one plus is the graphics and the fact that it supports PS4 controllers as well as the usual Xbox and Steam controllers. And his creepy little friend is kind of adorable. But all in all, the negatives far outweigh the positives for me, despite not actually hating the movies. The lack of plot and persistent repitition is enough to drive me away from the game - no pun intended.

As a PC gamer I was a little apprehensive going into this game, after feeling let down by Shadows of Mordor, which was similarly designed mainly with the console player in mind. In particular I was worried about the lack of difficulty levels or any real mod scene that could make the game harder. I like a challenge and I often find that lacking with these kinds of run-here collect-that kill-him kind of open world console games. I'm going to compare Mad Max below to Shadows of Mordor quite a bit, because its a nice way to highlight what this game does well.
The best thing I can say about Mad Max is this: Twenty hours in I definitely want to play this game right through to the end, unlike Shadows of Mordor, which I enjoyed initially, only to find that I just couldn't be bothered to pick up again after finishing the first area.
It does suffer from some similar problems. Repetition of a few basic tasks, looting, killing, looting, killing, again and again and again. A world that is a little too forgiving, allowing you to rarely feel seriously threatened even when vastly outnumbered.
However Mad Max, I think, is at its core a superior game.
Yes, Shadows of Mordor has the Nemesis system, which gives you a dynamic army of orc captains to fight. Meanwhile the bosses of Mad Max are your old static type. The orcs themselves in Shadows of Mordor are also a great enemy to hate, while a lot of the enemies in Mad Max feel bland. Going further, the combat in Shadows of Mordor is fluid and very professionally done, while movement and combat in Mad Max can feel a bit clunky. There is no sneaking, no acrobatics, and you often feel frustrated by your inability to even climb over simple barriers.
However the wasteland is a much more realised and lovingly crafted setting than mordor. From the overall design of the different regions, to the huge variety of gorgeous textures and colors, to the tiny details put into the little camps you raid, you really feel like you are in an actual world that is a pleasure to inhabit. The landscape nicely balances your two modes of play: Open vistas for high speed racing, and more cramped nooks and crannies for exploring on foot. Switching between these two helps alleviate any sense of tedium of always doing the same thing.
Meanwhile the world is also responsive in a way that Shadow of Mordor's is not. Bases can be taken over. Towers and snipers removed. Minefields cleared. And as a result the threat level of the area drops. The strongholds you "upgrade" are also being saved by you from the brink of destruction, slowly coming back from the edge and developing into actual decent little towns.
This sense of progress is perhaps the strongest aspect of the game, beyond the pure fun of racing about the place. Your car gets better. Your equipment gets better. And these upgrades directly relate to your ability to take on harder enemies. Most importantly, the upgrade path seems well balanced, such that you won't quickly become capable of taking out everybody and everything, which is the biggest problem in Shadows of Mordor. As you progress further you find that you have to put a decent amount of work into getting the scrap you need to upgrade just one part of your car.  Basically, Mad Max will reward your OCD tendencies. It's repetetive, but in a good way.
Above all, this is a fun game. It's been made with plenty of love and care, and with a decent budget. It's a little clunky in places. And the design falls down here and there. But it has a fully realized setting, a responsive world, a fairly decent difficulty scaling, a good upgrade path, great racing mechanics, and some fun characters (Chumbucket alone makes this game for me). I'd definitely recommend it to any PC gamer, even if not on sale.

Thank you for the loyalty discount Klei Entertainment, after reading and learning about this game, the discount is what pushed me over the edge to give it a real shot.
To help people better understand what kind of game this is, I like to make these comparisons...
The gameplay stylings of Fallout Shelter and The Sims are involved because of the base building aspects, as well as the Stress mechanic of the game. You have to keep the Dupes happy or their automated selves won't do the work!
The resource management and building mechanics of Factorio are involved because you have to build logical electrical lines and gas lines and liquid lines all around to keep things moving. Things can get damaged and require repair. It's fantastic. Plus, physics are at play. On a side scrolling format, it's important to remember that some gases rise, some sink, some are in between. There's alot of depth to it, it's awesome!
And finally, the crafting and tech tree system of Klei's very own, Don't Starve. Build science labs so you can research better tech and so on and so forth. Build things so you can make better food, store the food, etc...
With those comparisons, I hope you have a better grasp of what this game is. I personally LOVE this game, I've put over 20 hours into it way too fast.
To be frank, survival games have grown stale for me. It always ends up being this futile endeavor of "Well, I'm going to either live forever or die. What's the point?" Morbid right?
But there's something about this that changes it for me. It's not me trying to survive alone against the world, It's a bunch of silly clones that I have to manage and they need my direction in order to survive. And there's something about that separation that refreshes the survival genre for me and if you're feeling the same way as I did about survival, maybe it'll do the same for you?

When I first started Rogue Legacy, I wondered what all of the hype was about. I mean, I had read the reviews and I had seen the positives, and I was dying - a lot. I expect to die in this gaming type, too, but I felt like I had missed something. After hanging on for a few and unlocking my first weapon upgrade, I noticed things getting better. After a few health ups and other upgrades, it got even more fun. Hours later, and I see what people had been talking about.
Here, you die - often. When you do, you get to choose one of three successors. Each has a class, which will decide what type of stats they have. You have the combat heavy, the balanced types, and the magic heavy. At first, I found the combat heavy ones helpful for grinding, but later the others became fun. Almost all of them have something 'off' with them, and some have some really OFF items. Thankfully, not all are illustrated (you will see what I mean when you play). Some issues like ADHD are not bad. Others, like gigantism or nearsightedness or not being able to see in 3D can be a bit more bothersome.
After choosing a successor, you will be given the chance to hire the blacksmith and raise abilities. This includes health, how much armor weight you can carry, and your magic. Now, your blacksmith does not come with weapons; you find the blueprints for those as you explore the castle. As you unlock your weapons, you can add them on and they will start added to your characters - the one thing that matters is weight, which you will have to level up as you add more and more. You also have other abilities you can unlock as you progress, and you end up with more magic-type add-ons to select as well. These are fun, and they do require some grinding to get the funding to push them up. Like most games, this seems impossible at first, but as you move forward, the funding gets easier to get.
Enemies come in all different shapes and sizes, and they approach in different ways. You have ranged, flying, shooting, melee, and on to contend with, as well as bosses. The castle also unlcoks different areas as you move forward, giving you enemies that reflect your combat skills.
A good thing with the castle is that it maps, and you have teleporters in some prime areas. This means that you can tell if a boss area is a boss area, and if you run into an area you cannot handle, simply teleport back to where you want to be. You also have challenges that periodically pop up, and a lot of other stuff to do.
It's pretty fun.

So, you've played Freelancer, Wing Commander or Privateer. Its been years since these games were released and perhaps, for you, just like me, they left behind a massive void. I've leapt at EVERY space sim/rpg that been released in the hopes, that one day, they'll replace what I lost with Freelancer. Sadly they never did. So I saw this on the front page of Steam and thought, heres another disapointment. Well Starpoint Gemini 2...blew me away. This game is THE best space sim I've ever played and its in beta!!
Beta will always be beta, that said, this game is solid. When you read the description and see theres only a dozen planets, don't be fooled. The galaxy is ♥♥♥♥ing huge. Absolutely enormous. Open world to boot. No loading screens. Just you, your ship and the stars. There are some absolutely amazing locations, zipping through asteroids, cruising the nebulas...its awesome.
Theres a diverse choice of ships for you to cruise the stars with. Gunships, Corvettes, Frigates, Destroyers, Cruisers, Battleships, Dreadnaughts, Carriers, Freighters and freightliners. Each ship category has multiple choices and each of those choices allows you to build your ship in the fashion you want. Do you want a ship decked with heavy batteries, rain missiles and torpedos down on people. Do you want a majority of light batterries, decking your ship with railguns, beams or plasma cannons? Perhaps a ship that can deploy a large number of soldiers to board the enemy ship and take it over. Yea, you read that right. You can board an enemy ship, take it over and either destroy, loot it or sell it.
Perhaps the trade life is for you, with a vast hold and fast engines to shoot you away from the pesky gunships. Trade hasn't been completely implemented atm. In Freelancer if you remember, you could see what planets were buying what for what price etc etc. That hasn't been implemented yet so you have to find them yourself. Perhaps your a miner at heart and want to reap the profits from those floating rocks. Go right ahead, blast away. If you want a huge yield you can buy missiles especially dedicated to obtaining larger yields.
You can tailor your ship to fulfil what ever role you require. If you need more energy to fire you weapons, buy system attachments and upgrades to improve their energy reserves and recharge rates. Missing that little gunship too much, you can increase their accuracy or their damage against their shields. You can hack the enermy ship and disable their systems if thats the approach you like. You choose a career role. Each role has various abiliies for use that augment your fleet, turrets, shields, movement and various other cool things. Yea, thats right. You can build your own fleet to travel around the galaxy with you.
Sounds perfect for a bounty hunter right? Your going to need it to tackle the toughest bounties in the galaxy. You track the bounties yourself and take them down. Be warned though, they aren't alone and they're prepared to fight.
Seriously guys, I can't praise this game enough for what its doing. Yea, theres only free roam available atm but you can do WHAT EVER you want. Want to be a pirate, theres a huge array of choices for you and they're everywhere. You want to own your own carrier and deploy fighter wings, YOU ♥♥♥♥ING CAN!!! THIS GAME IS IN BETA and despite that, you can do soo damn much. I've crashed twice and that was in the first 2 hrs, since then, I haven't had a single problem. The galaxy is yours for that taking atm. I highly reccomend this game to all Freelancer, Privateer and Wing Commander fanatics. Even to those who are new to the scene. This game is so diverse and intricate in all its details...but god damn its so easy and simple to understand and master.
This game is in on-going development, if its this good already, I can't wait till its finished!!

Do you know this feeling when there are two voices in your head arguing over what is the right thing to do and it makes you extremely uncomfortable? It's called cognitive dissonance and Spec Ops: The Line makes you take a nosedive into a sea of that feeling.
It shows war as what it is. Not as the glorified, heroic, romanticized ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t that we get stuffed with from games like Call of Duty and Battlefield, but as horror, pure, unfiltered horror. If you felt like the moral choices in games like Fallout punched you in the gut, what you'll have to do in Spec Ops will leave you feel like the game punched you in the face, wrenched open your jaw, reached down your throat and ripped out your guts.
Spec Ops makes the player feel what the main character is going through, but not simply via making you identify with the character you play. Its gameplay, world design and everything makes you feel uncomfortable, nauseous and morally torn apart. It really is brilliantly crafted.
I'll stop here to avoid possible spoilers or how you perceive the game while playing, but if you feel like dropping the game after playing for an hour because the combat feels generic and/or bad, please, please don't do that and press on, it's well worth it.
There's one last thing I'll say, if you decide to play it: When you hear the line "Because you wanted to be something you're not.", that's aimed at you, not the character you're playing.

A fantastic prequel that is easily worth playing. Rather than taking away from the original story of 'Life is Strange', this 3 episode arc builds upon the groundwork laid in that first season to grant players a new perspective on Arcadia Bay and the familiar characters you will encounter (along with some very memorable new ones).
The game mechanics are similar enough to the original game so as to not put off returning players while also being very easy for new players to pick up. I particularly enjoyed the 'backtalk' feature that helped keep scenes very fresh. My only gripe is that some results are unchangeable regardless of what I as a player do. On one level, that is fine but, given the original game's myriad of possible events that were under the player's control, this immutability is a bit of a shame this time.
A fantastic game that I would recommend to any players of the original 'Life is Strange', I would recommend new players purchase the original game first to get the full experience of this prequel.

It's hard to comment on this game without spoilers, but I'm trying my best to avoid them. Also note that I didn't try the multiplayer and I'm only going to comment on the single player campaign.
The game presents a well-crafted story that starts out as a mission to scout the city of Dubai as it suffers from the destruction caused by a gigantic sand storm. Civilians are trapped inside mile high dunes of sands after the military lost contact to a former evacuation squad and they send Martin Walker and two companions to investigate after they received a distress signal. The deeper the squad dives into the city, the more gruesome events get. You witness atrocities done by American soldiers who lost track of their goal as the horrible story of the fallen Dubai unfolds with your discoveries and the game doesn't hesitate to shock you when it wants you to see what terrifying things people can do in a struggle for survival. (if you don't have a thick skin, you might want to plan to take breaks)
If it weren't for the story, the game would be forgettable, and that is the biggest danger if you don't know it yet - those who don't know what to expect will easily lose interest. The shooting itself plays well enough to work - there's cover-based shooting with various real-life weapons, there are melee attacks and finishers, a small selection of squad commands, you can sometimes destroy terrain to take out clusters of foes with sand dunes. There's not much traditional gameplay evolution, except that the selection of weapons grows as some weapons only appear later in the game.
If you ONLY come for the shooting, you will most likely be disappointed or even confused through the first couple of chapters. If you want to give this game a fair chance, keep on playing until the end of Chapter 8 at least. If you get there and still only come for the shooting, but want to give the game a chance nevertheless, start over again and pay close attention to the dialog and try to think about the twists that happen in the beginning of the game, which are admittedly a little hard to follow the first time around.
A word about the length of the game: The play time is rather short (I beat the game in 6 hours on easiest difficulty.. there is a reason you don't want to turn up the difficulty in the late game, which I leave up to you to find out), but if you get into it, it probably won't let you go for a while, especially since many discussions on the internet send you away with spoiler warnings right away. Once you've played through the game and see the revelations, you will want to play it again to see things in a different light. If you find yourself in an obsession about the meaning of the game, a good reading after you finish it is "Killing is Harmless" by Brendan Keogh. It's an affordable eBook that expands on a lot of details that you will easily miss on a casual playthrough. It links a good amount of articles on the internet, some of which include stances by the developers and lead writer. My Steam profile says I've played this game for only 16 hours, but I spent well over 30 hours reading up and watching on YouTube on what others thought about it.
Spec Ops: The Line deserves more attention for the sheer courage the developer showed for demonstrating such a cruelly honest truth through a video game, and I recommend it wholeheartedly to everyone who likes unconventional games. It makes you think about the nature of good and evil and takes a harsh stance on recent topics like Western military interventionism and the cruelty of modern warfare. It made me think for long, and it pulled something off that is impossible to do with a book or a movie. I want more people to play this game, because it deserves to be talked about, but can't be talked about unless you've given it at least one complete playthrough.

Pro - Beautiful graphics and an engaging, meaningful storyline.

Another game in the Shadow of Mordor "pocket" (more FarCry towers and Arkham combat), this is a game just as with SoM I seldom finish and grow bored of well before it's complete, but thoroughly enjoy through the first half of the game and have replayed repeatedly. They're both very good for integrating talented voice acting, enjoyable graphics/effects, and engaging combat mechanics to create an immersive experience despite how repetitive the otherwise scenic environments tend to be.
MM especially does (for me anyway) successfully evoke the sense of existing in a badlands dystopia where you're navigating the desert like a fish in shark-infested waters. Forlorn and varying topography, creepy post-civilization barbarism, and lots of subtle attention to the construction of the background art of each location you encounter- all contribute to an almost horror-genre tension. Unlike the jarringly irrelevant lore items you find in SoM, the "history" items you find in MM are sometimes thought-provoking or mood-provoking, often speaking of contemporary society in the past tense, though hearing Max's pessimism after each photo is a bit needlessly depressing. Then there are the allusions to the "Mad Max" movies like eating Dinky Di dogfood which they've incorporated into the mechanics and experience without any sense of contrivance. In short, it's a fun environment to find myself in and interact with, even with a pregenerated character and a great deal of general repetitiveness.
The key asset and liability of MM is its character/vehicle development system- also similar to SoM. I thoroughly enjoy a game that starts me with diddly and lets me gain skills gradually over time by simply playing the game, exploring, and getting better at the controls as I go. MM's skill acquisition system is very fun, usually giving you something that lends you yet another key advantage or improvement- i.e., rather than giving you stuff you never use or improves nothing. The game requires you to play as a completionist (or use online guides) if you're going to unlock everything- something I enjoy anyway, but in this case causing you to get lots of extra development boosts as a result. Thus ultimately I end up with Max's combat/armor at maximum improvement by 1/3 through the game, and the car by then is sufficiently improved for most everything except late-game story missions. So... by 1/3 through you're no longer making developmental strides at all. You're just completing the otherwise repetitve territory-clearing activities or story missions in order to complete the game: tedium. The main story isn't profound- even lame in some spots- and I genuinely had to struggle to keep going all the way to the end of the first playthrough- almost like... a mundane job. Not to mention that unsurprisingly the ending was absurd, sloppy, and felt like rushed writing.
But, like I said, I enjoy the game thoroughly otherwise and have now taken to perennial replays of that initial 1/3 to 1/2 of the game whenever I know it'll be fun trying to master it all over again. I'll simply never likely finish MM (or SoM) more than the one time I have. Perhaps an odd way of getting one's money's worth, but, oh, well.

(which is really short and you won't do much since it's the tutorial), the "tanks" are also some kind of tiny anime girls that will scream funny things when attacking or dyeing.

The difficulty of the battles is harder as you progress in the game (that's expected), but
, however, this also adds some extra challenge but some people really enjoy that. There are several different units, all of them belonging to 6 different classes: Command, Assault, Barrage/Battery, Shock, Scout and Interceptor with some extra surprices here and there. Let me start by saying I am usually not a fan of simulators.  At all.  I tend to find them lacking in purpose and direction, and can't bring myself to play them more than the opening experience.  That being said, it's almost impossible to describe why ETS2 is so enjoyable.
The premise is simple.  You pick a job, pick up the trailer, drop off the trailer and collect money and XP.  Money goes towards new trucks, equipment, garages and hiring drivers, and XP goes towards unlocking new jobs or increasing rewards (or lowering fuel usage).  There's really not much more to it than that, and yet, ETS2 is strangely engaging.
You can approach ETS2 like a genuine simulator, where you obey traffic rules, take a nice, slow pace for jobs, listen to the soothing 'taps' of your indicator and relax along to the gentle hum of your engine.  It sounds simple, but it's oddly cathartic.  Alternatively, you can haul♥♥♥♥♥ roaring down the highway at breakneck speeds, praying your trailer doesn't tip around the corner as you cut off AI and weave through traffic, racing against fatigue as you listen to jams like "Convoy" and "East Bound and Down" (more on this later).
If you're like me, like I know I am, the most you know about trucks is that they're big.  And slow.  ETS2 lets you jump straight in and drive from A to B simply with WASD, and you can even skip parking the trailer in exchange for an XP loss.  Alternatively, for the full truck simulation experience, you can opt to manually control everything from your gear selection to your retarder to your axle height, use of your exhaust brake, and even manually using your mirrors and on-board GPS system instead of the user-friendly HUD elements (you can even adjust your mirrors to suit your needs).
That being said, there are some limitations to the simulator.  From what I understand, the physics aren't fully 100% accurate, for things such as being able to use any chassis size for any job and not seeing much of a difference in physics (there may be some) during storms.  Speed limits change without warning in some sections (usually just before a speed camera), but these are relatively predictable once you're familiar with an area.  AI behaves in strange ways, particularly around roundabouts, so you'll probably end up with a fine for causing a crash because some driver tried to overtake you on the outside.  That being said, the AI is often predictable and you can avoid these incidents with a bit of practise.
There is no in-game music (outside of menus) and the radio station requires an internet connection, so you'll have to bring along your own jams for the offline experience.  The graphics are starting to show their age, but the sounds are quite authentic.  And of course, there is mod support and .ini tweaking to create the experience you desire.
Overall, this is definitely my favourite simulator, and I now look at trucks and truck drivers from a whole new perspective.

This is exactly what a Hitman game is supposed to be like, and I ♥♥♥♥ing love it. Great gameplay, huge levels and SO many ways to kill your targets, there's a ton of replayability here. And the game also runs very smoothly on my pc. With a GTX970, a I5 4690 @3.5GHz processor and 16GBs of RAM, I get over 60 fps at almost all times with nearly everything maxed out, except when I walk into crowds, but even then, the frame rate never drops below 40 fps.
Now here are the bad things.
Always online DRM: Why, just ♥♥♥♥ing why? The game is 100% single player, the only multiplayer aspect that it has are the leaderboards, so why is it that I have to be connected in order to have access to a playable version of this game? For some people, this might not be an issue, but I don't have access to relayable internet, so I'm ♥♥♥♥ed there. But even when my internet works flawlessly this type of DRM still sucks, because if I'm downloading something on the background or watching a video on a different device, the game just gets SO FREAKING SLOW. And even people with good, relayable internet will have trouble with this, as the game's servers aren't stable at all and will, sometimes, simply not work. I seriously don't understand why bother with DRM like this. The only good thing about it is the fact that people can't cheat on the leaderboards, but that's 500 light years away from being worth all the problems it causes.
Bugs: Half the point of this game are the challenges. Given the fact that you have very little original content, due to the episodic nature of this game, you are left with challenges to complete after completing the mission the first time. But these are VERY buggy, I'd say about a quarter of them won't unlock after you complete them, making you have to redo the whole damn thing and just hoping that this time it will be unlocked. This is completely random, as doing the same exact thing will sometimes grant you the challenge and other times it won't. There are other minor bugs in the game, but the real significant bugs are all challenge related.
Episodic Content: This game is episodic. The game will be released by updates of little original content at a time. In this release, for example, there's about 60-90 minutes of original content, half of which are tutorials. After that it's all replaying the same exact missions in different ways. The major problem with this is that it's going to ruin the story. I can't see how we can get engaged in the game's story, if we're only going to get 5 minutes of cutscenes every month. There's a tiny little bit of story in this first release, but I don't even think about it and completely forget it even exists, just because of how little of it there is.
Overall, I think it's an incredible Hitman game, and I personally love it. But they made so many stupid choices not while developing the game itself, but all the things around it, that I just cannot recommend it. It's too late to fix the whole episodic thing, but if they get rid of the damned always online DRM, then I'll give this game a thumbs up. But for now I say: Get it if you're a Hitman fan and you like the replayability aspects of the old games, who doesn't mind replaying the same level over and over, who knows the always online DRM isn't going to make the game completely unplayable for you at most times and who doesn't mind the episodic content. It's a long list, I know.

I mean, yeah, dying is part of the "fun" and getting to pick someone with IBS, but at the moment you re-enter the same castle (as there is no other location) it can re-roll into a stupidly unforgiving hell mouth and you die within 10 seconds of entering the first room. I am the most patient person I know, and I'm finding random re-rolls of instadoom annoying.
2. Even when you get past the first room, you might get to the second, or third, or even the fourth or maybe even the fifth, until you die, and then the dungeon monsters reset even if you lock the dungeon layout to prevent it re-rolling (at the cost of 40% of all the gold you'll earn in the run). So to advance, you have to repeatedly do the same things, over-and-over, learning the positions of spawned enemies and where you can and can't jump. It reminds me of playing Ghouls & Ghosts on the Megadrive, except with less visual variety and atmosphere. At best, the feeling of progress is, well, slow.
3. You have to give over all the gold you have on you in order to re-enter the castle after dying, which will be often, and as it's the only location you can go to, you're tied into doing this seemingly forever. I genuinely don't understand why this feature was put in.
4. In order to exit the game, you have to go into the options menu, and in amongst things like resolution settings is the quit game option. Why? Just... why?
I get the feeling you need a joypad to get the most out of this game. I don't have  joypad; neither do any of the PC gamers I know, because, you know, it's not a PS4. It's not natural. It'd be like buying a Ferrari and fitting it with a chemical toilet because you like cars and music festivals. Festivals are awesome, nice cars are awesome (although not as much as festivals), but combining the two is just an inexplicable mess (especially around sharp corners).

I can wholeheartedly recommend Prison Architect. While still in Early Access the game is already very enjoyable to play without any bugs or missing features that would hinder anyone from enjoying it.
The game has a very short story segment which mostly serves as a tutorial which quickly guides you through the basic game mechanics before letting you to build your very own prison in a sandbox environment. Besides the tutorial, everything in the game has very helpful tool-tips, which allow you to trouble shoot problems, like dysfunctional cells or canteens.
The many mechanics and available features all come together nicely and create a very enjoyable experience. While the game is very competent when it comes to constructing your prison to accommodate new inmates. It also allows you to do a lot of macro and micro management of your existing prison. For example, you always need to be on top of your inmate's smuggling operations and fight contraband and many other tasks like preventing escapes, managing your prisoner intake, allocating rooms and times for various activities for your prisoners and staff.
The only downside is that you can go through the content relatively quickly and once you have built a prison of 100+ inmates there is not much motivation to keep building because you will not see any new content. We have to hope that the game adds more content or will have scenarious besides the tutorial or other objectives because now you can really build at your own leisure and the game stops giving you a challenge relatively quickly.

Another game in the Shadow of Mordor "pocket" (more FarCry towers and Arkham combat), this is a game just as with SoM I seldom finish and grow bored of well before it's complete, but thoroughly enjoy through the first half of the game and have replayed repeatedly. They're both very good for integrating talented voice acting, enjoyable graphics/effects, and engaging combat mechanics to create an immersive experience despite how repetitive the otherwise scenic environments tend to be.
MM especially does (for me anyway) successfully evoke the sense of existing in a badlands dystopia where you're navigating the desert like a fish in shark-infested waters. Forlorn and varying topography, creepy post-civilization barbarism, and lots of subtle attention to the construction of the background art of each location you encounter- all contribute to an almost horror-genre tension. Unlike the jarringly irrelevant lore items you find in SoM, the "history" items you find in MM are sometimes thought-provoking or mood-provoking, often speaking of contemporary society in the past tense, though hearing Max's pessimism after each photo is a bit needlessly depressing. Then there are the allusions to the "Mad Max" movies like eating Dinky Di dogfood which they've incorporated into the mechanics and experience without any sense of contrivance. In short, it's a fun environment to find myself in and interact with, even with a pregenerated character and a great deal of general repetitiveness.
The key asset and liability of MM is its character/vehicle development system- also similar to SoM. I thoroughly enjoy a game that starts me with diddly and lets me gain skills gradually over time by simply playing the game, exploring, and getting better at the controls as I go. MM's skill acquisition system is very fun, usually giving you something that lends you yet another key advantage or improvement- i.e., rather than giving you stuff you never use or improves nothing. The game requires you to play as a completionist (or use online guides) if you're going to unlock everything- something I enjoy anyway, but in this case causing you to get lots of extra development boosts as a result. Thus ultimately I end up with Max's combat/armor at maximum improvement by 1/3 through the game, and the car by then is sufficiently improved for most everything except late-game story missions. So... by 1/3 through you're no longer making developmental strides at all. You're just completing the otherwise repetitve territory-clearing activities or story missions in order to complete the game: tedium. The main story isn't profound- even lame in some spots- and I genuinely had to struggle to keep going all the way to the end of the first playthrough- almost like... a mundane job. Not to mention that unsurprisingly the ending was absurd, sloppy, and felt like rushed writing.
But, like I said, I enjoy the game thoroughly otherwise and have now taken to perennial replays of that initial 1/3 to 1/2 of the game whenever I know it'll be fun trying to master it all over again. I'll simply never likely finish MM (or SoM) more than the one time I have. Perhaps an odd way of getting one's money's worth, but, oh, well.

So don't try doing a rotation next to a cliff, you might fall 9/10 times... And about fighting... Well, commands doesn't respond very well from my feeling, if you ever have the chance that the camera let you see the signs over the head of the enemies (most of the time, my combo are broken because of an enemy off camera).
Additional review on the lore: the game begins with an exciting in game cinematic... Where Max is driving... So you wait for the game to cue you in and drive the legendary Interceptor. This won't happen... You wait 5 min, then you can play. You start by WALKING (Mad Max, such a great CAR GAME) to see you car dismanteled... So no Interceptor for you... When would it be a bad idea to let the player drive it at least 10 min, during a straight forward and locked level AND THEN you destroy it? Well, just because of this, you start to play and understand you might not enjoy the game as much as expected...

Imagine you go to the movie theatre to watch what you figure will be a bombastic, Michael Bay action movie. Only every 15 minutes or so, the action stops, zooms in on one of the bodies and a voiceover comes on, telling you all about his parents, childhood dreams, and the 2 kids and cancer stricken wife he's left behind. And every time it ends with "and we wouldn't have had to kill this guy if it wasn't for you and your sick entertainment habits. You horrible, ♥♥♥♥ing monster, stop enjoying war."
This game doesn't hold your hand, it doesn't make you feel self-rightous for playing the hero. It just tosses you a gun, throws you into a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ situation, and actually makes you feel for what's going on. You will not find another modern warfare game that dares make you think this hard, or even at all, about what it is you're actually "enjoying" doing.
If you play games just for a bit of fun, move along. But if you think that gaming can tell affecting stories just as well if not better than other mediums, you have to pick this game up.

This is exactly what a Hitman game is supposed to be like, and I ♥♥♥♥ing love it. Great gameplay, huge levels and SO many ways to kill your targets, there's a ton of replayability here. And the game also runs very smoothly on my pc. With a GTX970, a I5 4690 @3.5GHz processor and 16GBs of RAM, I get over 60 fps at almost all times with nearly everything maxed out, except when I walk into crowds, but even then, the frame rate never drops below 40 fps.
Now here are the bad things.
Always online DRM: Why, just ♥♥♥♥ing why? The game is 100% single player, the only multiplayer aspect that it has are the leaderboards, so why is it that I have to be connected in order to have access to a playable version of this game? For some people, this might not be an issue, but I don't have access to relayable internet, so I'm ♥♥♥♥ed there. But even when my internet works flawlessly this type of DRM still sucks, because if I'm downloading something on the background or watching a video on a different device, the game just gets SO FREAKING SLOW. And even people with good, relayable internet will have trouble with this, as the game's servers aren't stable at all and will, sometimes, simply not work. I seriously don't understand why bother with DRM like this. The only good thing about it is the fact that people can't cheat on the leaderboards, but that's 500 light years away from being worth all the problems it causes.
Bugs: Half the point of this game are the challenges. Given the fact that you have very little original content, due to the episodic nature of this game, you are left with challenges to complete after completing the mission the first time. But these are VERY buggy, I'd say about a quarter of them won't unlock after you complete them, making you have to redo the whole damn thing and just hoping that this time it will be unlocked. This is completely random, as doing the same exact thing will sometimes grant you the challenge and other times it won't. There are other minor bugs in the game, but the real significant bugs are all challenge related.
Episodic Content: This game is episodic. The game will be released by updates of little original content at a time. In this release, for example, there's about 60-90 minutes of original content, half of which are tutorials. After that it's all replaying the same exact missions in different ways. The major problem with this is that it's going to ruin the story. I can't see how we can get engaged in the game's story, if we're only going to get 5 minutes of cutscenes every month. There's a tiny little bit of story in this first release, but I don't even think about it and completely forget it even exists, just because of how little of it there is.
Overall, I think it's an incredible Hitman game, and I personally love it. But they made so many stupid choices not while developing the game itself, but all the things around it, that I just cannot recommend it. It's too late to fix the whole episodic thing, but if they get rid of the damned always online DRM, then I'll give this game a thumbs up. But for now I say: Get it if you're a Hitman fan and you like the replayability aspects of the old games, who doesn't mind replaying the same level over and over, who knows the always online DRM isn't going to make the game completely unplayable for you at most times and who doesn't mind the episodic content. It's a long list, I know.

Umineko is a kinetic visual novel (meaning that there are no choices, you only read) or a “sound novel”, like the developers said (more focused on the soundtrack and BGS), brilliantly written, and with a soundtrack so good that it will literally make you lose your time sense and just keep reading. All the characters have an important role in this story; you’ll love some of them, hate others, and even have mixed feelings between wanting to hug and punching them in the face for being so mean or dumb
.
This is, without doubt, one of the best (if not the best) visual novel I’ve ever read. I have a special place in my heart for Higurashi (from the same developers), but Umineko is just… It gets to you. The first episode starts slowly, but I understand that’s necessary in order for the reader to get to know better the characters and how they normally act. But after that, things will change so drastically that you’ll wonder if you’re reading the same story you had been previously reading. Considering that there are four games worth of 50+ hours of reading in total, it’s worth every cent.
This is a must read for mystery fans. And keep your mind open, because lots of surprising things will happen. Choose the better explanation that suits your tastes. After all, it’s the Witch Hunt season. Uncover the truth with your own theories.
10/10.

I'm tempted to gush endlessly (or until the Steam review character limit) about how much I love Umineko, and extrapolate on why its my favorite piece of fiction, or how its changed my life. But this is not the outlet for a review that in depth. Instead I'll just say these opinionated blurbs:
Umineko has in it the scope and depth of a novel who is familiar with literary critical theory.
I first started read Umineko over six years ago. Before and after Umineko I've read and watched hundreds of different stories, but none have stayed with me like this one. I still think fondly about it, and reread various parts to get my creative gears running. As an aspiring author this is the story that has arguably inspired me most of all. For reference some of my other favorite authors are Alexandre Dumas. Stephen King, Joe Hill, Neil Gaiman, George RR Martin, Robert Rankin, and David Gordon. While this story is not like any of those authors stories, in my mind Umineko stands right next to them, or in some cases above them.
It has an anime aesthetic (and unfortunately some tropes early in), but please, if you're like me, and you can't take things as seriously just give this a real shot. It goes well beyond what the medium of anime or Japanese authors (from what I've read) normally delve into.
Umineko will surprise you. It's a surprising story, with many many layers. And it has the replayability and forshadowing of that of a masterwork. Considering it released serially this is doubly impressive.
The soundtrack is awesome. Look it up if you'd like.
Okay so there was a bit of gushing here, and I'm trying to control myself. Basically if you get anything from this random review on the internet, just give Umineko a shot. This is only half the story (Episodes 1-4) but it will still take upwards of 50-100 hours to complete. The last half Umineko breakdown, is going to be released at a later date.

Oh my sweet God, Umineko.
It looks like a game, but reads like a book (Actually, four books in this collection) with a killer soundtrack and some clunky animations. Essentially no direct interaction. Just some text on a screen-- are they supernatural thrillers or detective crime dramas? Still, that's all.
Except... there's something else going on here. Each tale ends abruptly without a satisfying conclusion or an answer to who-dunnit, but you begin to realize that they are layered in an overlapping, snaking way that frames a direct challenge to the reader- YOU are demanded to pull the pieces together and find the answers, if there are any.
There are another four books still not officially translated (Though fan translations exist, and have even gained the author's notice) that layer on a few more hints and a winding guide to various solutions-- but in many cases there are no answers but the ones you find.
I've never read anything like it. I can't recommend enough that you check it out.

This is the story that could change your life, if you have the patience for it.
However, at the moment I simply can't recommend the Steam version as it's clearly inferior to the PS version released many years ago.
While the new sprites are arguably as good as the PS ones, unlike the PS version this version has no voice acting and only the classic backgrounds made up from old filtered photos instead of proper digital art BGs (because of licensing issues).
So if you want the complete original experience - grab this game asap (and don't forget to turn on the classic sprites).
Otherwise, if you prefer voices and a little more visual appeal in your VNs - I suggest waiting a bit more for a PS fan-patch (in the works). Perhaps by that time the rest 4 episodes will be available as well.

Great murder mystery Visual Novel/Sound Novel. By the person who made Higurashi, but this is much more deeper. Do recommend to anyone who wants a good read, something to keep thinking about.
Update: I forgot to mention, the music in this game is great. It's some of the best music I've heard in video games, and I still frequently listen to it. I still know exactly what song plays at what moment, and can still experience the same tension/emotions I experienced first time reading through.
If you've ever watched the anime and found it lackluster, believe me, the source material is much better. These four "Episodes" span the entire anime, but everything is much less rushed. The anime also butchered the story to the point where the mystery was left unsolvable, so there's that.
As for the specifics of this release, a couple of notes:
- The sprites have been reworked, and in my opinion the PS3 sprites are superior.
- No voice acting
- Only the Question arcs for now
However, there is a patch in the works by fans that aims to fix the former two. Per writing of this review however, only the voice acting has been modded in and it hasn't officially been released yet, so expect bugs if you do end up using it (like me).
Translation is an updated version of Witch Hunter's fan translation.
You'll get the Question arc episodes all in one, so that's Episode 1-4 (ending with Alliance of The Golden Witch). But make no mistake. That is still plenty of reading to do. You could count each "episode" as seperate novels if you will, you'll be getting plenty of content for you money's worth.
I really hope that Umineko Chiru (the Answer arc) will be released too at some point. Those would be episode 5-8, explaining the questions posed int he Question arc.

After playing Risky's Revenge and Pirate's Curse, I had to pick up Half-Genie Hero and this is possibly my favourite in the series. The controls are simple but refined, the visuals are gorgeous, the music is catchy as all hell and the game knows what it's aiming for - pure, unadulterated fun!
The overall look is vibrant and crisp, the aesthetics are fantastic as always and the character design manage to be fun and sexy without crossing the line into sexualised. Shantae herself of course mostly wears her genie's outfit (a.k.a a bunch of ribbons with delusions of grandeur) and the mermaid's wear little more than seashells, but you're not going to find any panty shots or gratuitous boob close-ups here.
RR and PC were a little more open-worldy, even metroidvania-esque at times, but while HH has a simpler level structure you're unlikely to ever get lost, with a couple of artifacts available from the get-go that let you duck in an out of levels as needed. The dancing transformations make a return and while they'll never be a seamless as the Pirate's Curse controls they're very well streamlined, especially the dancing.
Story-wise it's an odd mix, being something of a soft reboot. Basically they've kept all the stuff that's useful (Shantae good, Risky bad, Rotty misunderstood and her brothers aren't trying to kill you)  but there's sadly no trace of the surprising depth given to Risky or her relationship with Shantae in Pirate's Curse. Maybe these things will be re-explored in a sequel but for now it's a little more black-and-white.
In any case, great fun, highly recommended and bonus points for bringing in Christina Vee on the vocals.

I got this in a humble bundle (12 bucks) and haven't played much other recent sandbox games, so I can't compare much. I absolutely like this game, but I cant' really flaw the reviewers who disagree on that opinion.
What's certainly clear is that Mad Max is doing everything by the books. It has the combat from Batman-games, a world that resembles fallout (even more than the mad max franchise, if you ask me) and (after the initial 'training levels') a sh**load of stuff to do like ubisoft's games. And perhaps the hookshot from just cause.
Does all of this appeal to you? Then MM is certainly your kind of game. There are so many ways to upgrade both your character and your car that it's almost ridiculous. The game looks good and plays smooth, but it's obviously desert, desert and more desert.
The story is, as mentioned many times, not an important factor. I'm not a Mad Max fan, but even I can see that it doesn't exactly break new ground on that aspect.
What remains is just pure fun and carnage. Explore some beautiful areas, fight everyone you see, loot everything, upgrade everything. The car and the storms are perhaps the only unique things about this game. The latter is pretty "meh" after a couple times. The first is...interesting, at the very least. Car to car combat happens quite often and is fun in and of itself. Can't find fault there. :-)
The only thing I'm wondering is whether it's worth it over (say) GTA V, the witcher 3 or MGS. As said, I don't know as I haven't played 'em. But still...for the amount of fun I'm having with it, it's an easy thumbs up. :-)

This games has tons of potential. It has decent graphics, good game controls, easy to learn and best of all, it's pretty addicting. There are three character classes, different type of ship classes, different kinds of ships within the classes, four different weapon types and tons of missions to do in sandbox mode.  I've been playing as the gunner,  especializing on weapons systems,with the ability to adds different bonuses to the weapon system of choice. My weapon of choice being rail-guns.
It's up to you how you want to play. You have the option of playing as a pirate, enforcer, bounty hunter, miner, trader or a freelancer (combination of all). How effective you are doing each type of job depends on the ship, the combination of skills you select as you increase in experience and buying a license. License determine how much money you will receive depending on what the license is for. For example, a mining license will get you more money when selling ore, a police license will reward you with moneyfor everykill, and so on so forth. The point of it all is to make money, so you can get better ships and better gear, you know, the same old formula that keeps us coming back for more.  Overall I really like this game and if you are a fan of freelancer and games likes these I dont think you will be disappointed. The best part? It's only  going to get better.

First Impressions:
For an early access game this game is already really playable as the sandbox mode works just fine. See this game as EVE offline. You fly your own ship (which you can upgrade or just buy a bigger one) around a HUGE universe that has highway like wormholes and natural wormholes. You can also move around anywhere under your own power so just traveling on highways or through wormholes isn't a must. There are hints of fleets in thwere but haven't been able to start one, although you can already by extra ships and leave them in your garage.
Your Ship:
Upgrades for your ships are plenty and the weapon systems include, lasers, plasma cannons, railguns, missiles, and much more which you can freely add to any supporting hardpoint on your ship (light for guns, heavy for ammo consuming launchers). All upgrades and repairs happen on the station and I've noticed you really need to shop around the stations to get the best stuff.
Your Crew:
Yes, this game has crews as even your starting ship is more then the usual fighters you get in other games. There are 3 shipstations which you can hire crew for. The crew gives you boosts on weapons or ship systems like engines, shields and cloaks depending on their skills. Again every station/planet offers different crews with different skills.
Gameplay:
Random missions are generated all the time wich includes simple "go there and shoot.." missions, scan anomalies and bringing around cargo and passengers. You can visit many many stations (and planets) to upgrade, repair, hire crew, trade and lots more. The universe is very much alive as you encounter friendly and non friendly ships all over the place. Some sectors and stations really don't like you and can form a real challange when fighting in those sectors (enemy reinforcemants and stations blasting you). Fighting is mouse controlled, aim and shoot your light weapons by clicking the right mouse button and fire your heavy ammo consuming weapons with X. Also you can give the command "Fire at will" which will basically unleash all weapons on all in range enemies (this can be very much fun to watch while you just fly around avoiding damage with guns blazing).
Trade is already present in the game but is still in it's first stages so you get very little info on prices except for a news scroller that is viewable on every planet and station.
Development:
Patches are rolling out in a steady pace and the devs are very active on the forums (Post a question, suggestion or comment and you'll likely get a reply within the hour). This just gives you extra confidence to buy this game in early access and help in it's development.
Current Verdict July 18 2014:
Highly recommended early access game that is only getting better with each update.
*My above opinion still hasen't changed, latest update is again full of content. Recommend to pick up on current sale :)
Current Verdict September 16 2014:
Latest patches have added full controller support for fans of those things. Also the game is nearly complete as release is almost here, they've been busy with optimizing the game and adding final features, complete campaign/story mode is not finished yet but devs have indicated it's coming soon! (And in the past they've proven time and time again that they uphold their word!).
So still a big fat recommend from me at this final stage of early access.

Great murder mystery Visual Novel/Sound Novel. By the person who made Higurashi, but this is much more deeper. Do recommend to anyone who wants a good read, something to keep thinking about.
Update: I forgot to mention, the music in this game is great. It's some of the best music I've heard in video games, and I still frequently listen to it. I still know exactly what song plays at what moment, and can still experience the same tension/emotions I experienced first time reading through.
If you've ever watched the anime and found it lackluster, believe me, the source material is much better. These four "Episodes" span the entire anime, but everything is much less rushed. The anime also butchered the story to the point where the mystery was left unsolvable, so there's that.
As for the specifics of this release, a couple of notes:
- The sprites have been reworked, and in my opinion the PS3 sprites are superior.
- No voice acting
- Only the Question arcs for now
However, there is a patch in the works by fans that aims to fix the former two. Per writing of this review however, only the voice acting has been modded in and it hasn't officially been released yet, so expect bugs if you do end up using it (like me).
Translation is an updated version of Witch Hunter's fan translation.
You'll get the Question arc episodes all in one, so that's Episode 1-4 (ending with Alliance of The Golden Witch). But make no mistake. That is still plenty of reading to do. You could count each "episode" as seperate novels if you will, you'll be getting plenty of content for you money's worth.
I really hope that Umineko Chiru (the Answer arc) will be released too at some point. Those would be episode 5-8, explaining the questions posed int he Question arc.

Despite the low playtime, I've read it before, both the question and truth arcs.
Umineko is quite literally some of the best written works out there. I normally only read "the classics" when it comes to literature, such as Don Quixote, Kafka's works, Camus, Tolstoy etc, and I've gotta say, Umineko is without a doubt in my top 3 in the world of written entertaintment. I can't recommend Umineko enough. It's an absolute must read for any fan of meta layers, murder mystery, logical puzzles or the concept of faith and love itself.
I personally dislike the new Steam artwork, but there's a patch in the making that will allow you to switch it to the PS3 artwork. Which, IMO, is the definite way to play. It's either that or the original artwork, which has it charms.
Seriously, go buy it. It's long, it starts slow as hell, but my God, it's absolutely fantastic. Bordering on life changing for me.

Fun fact: I actually finished this game about a month ago over the course of about a week of bingeing, and wasn't planning on reviewing it. I'm somehow still thinking about this f****** game a month later, and desperately want more. TL;DR version, if you already have a good idea of what Umineko is and are familiar with both the genre and the loosely related, not-super-necessary-but-pretty-good-anyway prequel Higurashi, get it, it's great. For everyone else, read on.
First things first, there are two points of immediate interest that need to be covered so that you can understand what you're getting into: Umineko is only a game by the loosest definition (yet is very much a game), and that this release is the first half of the full story, the question arc. Umineko is known by nerds on the internet as a "sound novel", but for everyone else you should think of it like a book. And no, this isn't a choose your own adventure novel, or one with random minigames, for 99% of the game you read, you listen to the amazing music, and you watch static sprites change between expressions on a weird distorted photo background thing. That's it. And then you hope we get the second half.
Still with me? Good. Because despite not being a game you can interact with, Umineko is definitely a game, with a compelling, complex set of rules and developments throughout.
The premise of the game is initially fairly simple. 18 people gather together on an island in the middle of nowhere (as you do), broadly speaking to discuss that matter of who inherits said island and a bunch of money. When the grandfather guy they want the stuff from isn't actually dead yet. Kind of rude, honestly. But a chunk of the 18 people spend the first day on the island arguing about this, whilst the uh, staff of the house (close enough anyway) do their thing and the children/teenagers talk about stuff no one really cares about. I think they mention a riddle of some sort that might be loosely related to the plot, but I'm sure it's not important. Then around dinnertime, they get a letter from a mysterious person who calls themselves Beatrice, who claims that she's the gal who lent grandfather guy money for his island and business ventures, and wants her money back or something. Naturally, the group ignores it, since they want the money for themselves and they have no reason to believe the letter.
The next day, some people are dead.
I won't go into details because that's what playing the game is for, but broadly speaking, the circumstances of the deaths are highly suspect. There are supposed to be only 18 people on the island, and communication with the outside world has been cut off. The murders seem difficult to pull off without a hitch. Some suggest possible theories as to what happened.
"A witch did it", some say.
A while later, more people are dead. This time, it seems impossible for anything other than a witch to have been involved. Some argue against it anyway. And then more people die. And then more. You, the player, begin to run out of suspects as to who could have done all this. Eventually, things come to a head, a witch was CLEARLY involved, there's no other way around it.
Or was there a trick to it?
This is the true mystery of Umineko. Are you playing a traditional murder mystery? Is the culprit one of the 18, who through the use of particularly clever tricks managed to fool the entire cast into believing in magic, killed them in an increasingly ridiculous fashion, and got away with it? Or was it really the result of magic, and you're in fact playing a fantastical tragedy surrounding very untrustworthy characters? The answer may seem obvious before playing, but believe me when I say that Umineko puts up a pretty convincing argument for both.
*Brushes away sweat* wow, that was a long plot introduction. It's important though, it's all the game has. To point to my favourite aspect of Umineko right off the bat, it would have to be the inclusion of one particular plot wrinkle that makes itself known around chapter 2, and that's that everything spoken in red is absolutely, 100% the truth. Normally in a murder mystery you look towards evidence for what exactly happened in a crime, yet in umineko you are often given information that evidence just won't provide. For example, in a traditional mystery, you might hypotheise that it would be possible for a spare key to exist for a door somewhere. In umineko, if a character brings that up they may be contradicted. Umineko is very happy to quickly deny MANY possibilites for how a crime took place, to the point that the question isn't "how did this happen", but rather "how COULD this happen", which I find super interesting. In fact, super interesting could be applied to the mystery as a whole, because holy cow it is mysterious and stuff. (I know, vague, but it's a mystery, what do you want me to say)
The cast is also pretty strong, although I do have my issues with a few aspects surrounding them. The writer of Umineko quite frankly has a pacing problem, and is quite happy to spend several hours at the beginning of each chapter developing characters before moving on to whatever the main event is. Now I have no issue with this in theory, but as with most plots involving murder, the characters are at their most interesting when they're, you know, being involved with murders. And whilst I overall love the writing in Umineko, when murder isn't happening the plot can get very anime, and not in an endearing way. Also, maybe this gets corrected in the second half, but the game quickly establishes Kyrie as best girl, but then rarely gives her the spotlight she deserves.
Also also, YES, I GET IT, INSERT CHARACTER HERE LOVES INSERT CHARACTER HERE, DO THEY HAVE MUCH TO THEIR PERSONALITY ASIDE FROM THIS IN A NORMAL SETTING? NO? OK THEN, CAN WE GET BACK TO THE  MURDERS PLEASE.
*Ahem* moving on, as I mentioned earlier the music is great.  Not all of the tracks are winners, but they keep introducing new tracks at a consistent enough pace, with enough different styles, that you'll probably find something you'll enjoy. Also, I have no idea what the rest of the internet is talking about, I actually rather enjoy the so called "pachinko sprites", aka the new sprites that are part of the advertising. The old sprites are also there, and they're charming enough in their own terrible way that I always switched over briefly whenever a new sprite appeared (which by the way you can do and I greatly appreciate that), but there is nothing wrong with the new sprites. Forgive me internet I have sinned.
I'm a fast reader, and it overall took me about 40+ hours to finish the question arc, so plenty of bang for your buck in that regard. The ending naturally has plenty of sequel hooks for the second half, but it's also not a terrible ending in its own way, so it's not so bad that it makes waiting for the second half a nightmare. (APPARENTLY it's possible to solve most of the mysteries independently of the second half anyway, just stupidly hard to do so. I have not, although I may replay some of the game with a fresh mindset)
So yeah, play it. It's good.
(...And skip the anime adaptation, it covers this half of uminekmo but TERRIBLY. It's really not worth it, even if you want to see some scenes animated. Because chances are it skipped them.)

This is a very difficult game to write a review for. As I'm sure most of you will notice, many people simply write "Just buy it!" and I'm tempted to do the same. FYI: This was my first time playing. I did not play the original Umineko. Several of my friends told me of how life changing it could be and I was tempted to watch the playthrough on YouTube but never did. I'm glad I waited to experience the game for myself.
As you can imagine...writing a review for such a long game can be a bit challenging. If you have played Higurashi, you will definitely like this game. If you enjoy mysteries, fantasy, kinetic VNs...you'll like this game. I can't think of a target audience who would not enjoy Umineko unless perhaps one lacks patience. The thing is, I lack patience. I haven't made it to every ending of CLANNAD, or Tsukihime...after so many hours I usually give up and say I will return to a VN.
I played this through to the end, every day until I was finished. The character development was gripping, really there was never a dull moment. As soon as I thought I had one piece of the puzzle figured out, ten minutes later my grip on reality was ripped to shreds.
My humble recommendation is that ANY VN fan would enjoy this game and that it is absolutely worth its full price.
An added note: For those on the fence, please purchase this game and support 07th Expansion. Also if you want a taste of what this game is slightly like, look for the Higurashi titles (released before Umineko by the same author). All gold in my opinion. I love games that leave me at the end just utterly and thoroughly confused.

Shortly:
4th Shantae game that continues the story further., however Shantae: Half-Genie Hero is quite different from its predecessors.
First recognisable difference is how the game looks. Unlike the pixxelated art style in the previous Shantae games, this time the game has this more cartoonish art style which isn't half bad. The character movements and the world feels more alive.
That leads to the 2nd noticable difference, which is the world itself. In the previous games, you had this semi-open world that you could explore once you obtained powers to do so. There's no such thing in the Half-Genie Hero, but instead the world is diveded into stages/worlds. Each stage/world has several areas lined after each other that you can explore and at the end of each world there's a boss waiting for you. Once you defeat that, the world is cleared and you can move on to next one. Its kinda similar to how the islands worked in the Pirate's Curse, but this time they have this "super mario" feeling in them. It's just not the same as it was in the previous Shantae games, which is kinda disappointing for me. I would have preferred the semi-open world like the Risky's Revenge had.
Unlike in the previous Shantae games, the Half-Genie Hero doesn't have any dungeons either, which is mostly because of how those stages/worlds wokr that I mentioned earlier.
Other than that, the game is pretty much the same old Shantae games that we're used to.
Pros:
+ Improved art style
+ Familiar gameplay mechanics with few additions mixed in
+ Entertaining 2D platformer
+ Bigger variety of different abilities
Cons:
- Semi-open world replaced with stages/worlds
- No dungeons
- Save points way too often, which means that dying is no longer punishing as the game asks you every 2-3 minutes if you want to save your progress  (why couldn't they just implement auto save instead if they didn't want people to feel punished for dying, though personally I hate auto saves if they save your progress like that )
- The Soundtrack isn't as good as it is in the previous titles - The OST is similar but too...modern.. if you could call it that. Didn't enjoy it personally
Do I recommend?
Yes. Shantae: Half-Genie Hero is entertaining 2D platformer and it continues the story where the Pirate's Curse left on. I have to warn you though, the game is not as good as its predecessors are, because of the stage/world system.
Verdict:  6.5 / 10 - Good game  (though not as good as its predecessors are because of the stage system)
